NOTIFICATION. 


No. 3851W.T.—8th June 1954.—The following draft of by-kews, which the 
Governor proposes to make for the Chakdah Municipality, in the district of 
Nadia, in exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the 
Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919 (Bengal Act I of 1919), is published for 
the information of persons likely to be affected thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after 25th July 1954; 
and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto which may be received 
before that date through the District Magistrate, Nadia, shall be duly 


considered: — 


Draft by-laws. 


By-laws relating to hackney-carriages, cycle-rickshaws, rickshaws and palanquins 
under section ‘71(1) of ‘the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919, for the 
Chakdah Municipality in the district of Nadia. 


1. Appoittment and duties of the Registering Officer.—Every hackney- 
cariiage in the Chakdah Municipality shall be annually registered by the Register- 


ing Officer appointed for the purposé by the Commissioners. 


The Registering 


Officer shall keep a register in which he shall enter the class and number assigned 


to every hackney-carriage. 


2. Qualifications of drivers and bearers—-Every person applying for a 
driver’s or bearer’s license shall be required to satisfy the registering officer— 


(a) that he is not Jess than 18 years of age; 


(b) that he knows how to drive and contro! horses, cycle-rickshaws, or rick- 
shaws or palanquins and is in all respects a fit person for such 


employment, 


part T] 


০ 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 


(c)-that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, offices and places 
of interest in and around the town of Chakdah; 


(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and distances 
prepared by the Commissioners; 


(e) that he is familiar with the rules of the road and the signals used for 
regulating road traffic. 


3. Licenses for hackney-carriage drivers and bearers of palanquins, cycle- 
rickshaws and rickshaws will be in different forms prescribed by the Commis- 
sioners. There shall be attached to each license, in such manner as the Com- 
missioners may prescribe, the following, namcly:— 


(a) the thumb mark of the driver or the bearer; 
(ط)‎ a photograph of the driver to be supplied by him; and 


(c) a table of fares and distances to be prepared and printed by the Com- 
missioners and to be fixed in some conspicuous place inside the 
cartiage Or cycle-rickshaw or rickshaw or palanquin approved by 
the Registering Officer. 


4. Every driver of a hackney-carriage or bearer of a palanquin or a cycle- 
rickshaw or a rickshaw shall carry with him and produce, when called upon to 
do so by any police officer or by his hirer or by any Commissioner, his license 
with the table of fares and distances. 


5. No driver of .a hackney-carriage shall be allowed to drive any licensed 
hackney-carriage other than those specified in his license without the permission 
of the Registering Officer, 


Uniforms. 
6. The uniforms of the drivers shall be clean. 
Description of horses, carriages, palanquins, cycle-rickshaws and rickshaws. 


7. No horse shall be used to draw a hackney-carriage unless it has been 
passed by the Registering Officer and no horse shall be passed unless it is— 


(i) thoroughly broken to harness, 
(ii) free from any infectious disease, and 


(iit) (a) not less than 14 cubits high if intended to be used in a pair in a 
first class hackney-carriage; 


(b) not less than 14:2 cubits high if intended to be used singly in a first 
class hackney-carriage; 


(c) not less than 13 cubits high if intended to be used in a pair in a second 
class hackney-carriage; 


(2) not less than 14 cubits high if intended to be used singly in a second 
class hackney-carriage; 


(e) not less than 12 cubits high if intended to be used in a pair in a third 
class hackney-carriage. 


(f) not less than 13-2 cubits high if intended to be used singly in a third 
class hackney-carriage. 


8. The harness shall be of a decent appearance, black m colour, strong 
-and in good repair; rope of iron chain traces may be used, provided they be 
covered with leather. No string fastening will be ‘allowed. 


9. Hackney-carriages shall be of three classes and of patterns fixed by the 
Commissioners and of dimensions and colours prescribed by by-laws Nos. 13 to 
16. 


10. There shall be one class of cycle-rickshaws, of rickshaws and of palan- 
guins of patterns fixed by the Commissioners with the approval of the State 
Government, and of the dimensions and colours prescribed by by-laws Nos. 17 
to 19. 


11, Every licensed hackney-carriage, palanquin, cycle-rickshaw or rickshaw 
shall be distinctly marked on its panels and on the inside with the registcred 
number and the number of the 01855 to which it belongs, the figures to be not 
less than 8 inches in length, the colour of which shall be changed every year. 


12. The lamps of every licensed hackney-carriage, palanquin, cycle- 
rickshaw or rickshaw shall have the registered number painted on them. the 
figures to be not less than one inch in length, the colour of which shall be changed 
every year. :

and be of a pattern fixed by the Commissioners:—— 


Feet. Inches.

Provided that, hackney-carriages registered before the issue of these by-laws 
may, at the discretion of and on such conditions as may be fixed by the Com- 
missioners at a meeting, be exempted from conforming to these dimensions, if 
such conformity is likely to cause hardship to the owners. 


The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run true and 
without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by properly fitted splash-boards. 
The springs and axles shall be in perfect order and all iron work must be strongly 
put together. 


The lining and cushions shall be clean and in good condition and the inside 
of the carriage perfectly clean. 


The hood and apron shall be made of strong leather and shall be so fitted as 
to make the carriage water-tight. 


The body, wheels and shafts of the carriage shall be painted dark green with 
plain yellow or gold lining; the hood and apron shall be painted black. 


The doors shall close well and shall not rattle: 
All iron works shall be painted black. 


Each carriage must have a thoroughly good pair of lamps and each lamp 
shall have a red glass window in the back and shall be so placed that the light 
from window shall be visible from a point ten yards in rear of the centre of the 
vehicle. 


14. Second class hackney-carriage (Phaeton type).—Second class hackney- 
carriage (Phaeton type) shall have the same dimensions as those prescribed for 
first class hackney-carriages, but of lighter make: 


Provided that, hackney-carriages registered before the issue of these by-laws 
may, at the discretion of and on such condition as may be fixed by the Commis- 
sioners at a meeting, be exempted from conforming to these dimensions, if such 
conformity is likely to cause hardship to the owners. 


The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound, so as to run true and 
سم"‎ rattling or shaking, and shall be protected by properly fitted splash- 
boards: 


Provided that the provision about rubber-tyres shall not apply to hackney- 
carriages with iron-tyres registered before the issue of these by-laws, 


The springs and axles shal] be in perfect order and all iron works must be 
strong and put together. 


The lining and cushions shall be clean and in good condition and the inside 
of thé carriage perfectly clean. 


The hood and apron shall be made of strong leather and shall be so fitted 
as to make the carriage water-tight.

17, Cycle-rickshaws.—(a) The body of the cycle-rickshaw shall be sound 
and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. ۱ 


(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound so as to run true and 
without rattling or shaking. 

(c) The springs and 25105 shall be made of good metal, strong and properly 
riverted and free from rust. 

(dq) The hood, apron and cushions shall be made of and covered with good 
cloth, canvas or other materials approved by the Commissioners. 

(e) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicles water-tight. 

(f) The body, wheels and shafts of all rickshaws shall be painted dark blue 
and all iron works shall be painted black. 

(g) Every cycle-rickshaw shall have two good lamps—one facing the front 
and one in the rear. 

(A) Each Jamp shall have a red glass window in the back and shall be so 
placed that the light from the window is visible from a point ten yards in the 
rear of the centre of the vehicle. 


18. Rickshaws.—(a) The body of rickshaw shall be sound and clean and 
all the boards strong and properly sccured. 

(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred or iron-tyred, strong and sound so as 
to run true and without rattling or shaking, and shall be protected by properly 
fitted splash boards:. 


Provided that rickshaw registered before the issue of these by-laws need not 
be rubber-tyred. 

(c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and properly 
riveted and free from rust. 

(d) The iron supports of the back shall be properly curved and securely 
fixed at each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 

(e) The shafts shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and furnished 
at Se fore-ends with a ring-shaped metal support and connected by a collision 
guard. 

(f) The hood, apron and cushions shall be made of and covered with good 
cloth, canvas or other materials approved by the Commissioners. 

(g) The hdod and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
tight. 

(h) The body, wheels and shafts of all rickshaws shall be painted dark blue 
with thin red lining. All iron works shall be painted black. 

(i) Every rickshaw must have a good pair of lamps. Each lamp shall have 
a red glass window in the back and shall be so placed that the light from the 
window is visible from a point ten yards in the rear of the centre of the vehicle.

(b) The doors shall close well, work easily and shall not rattle and shall have

(c) The body and pole shall be painted dark blue with thin red lining.

Identification of horses. 


20. Every horse passed by the Registering Officer shall be branded on both 
fore hoofs in the following manner:— 
(i) The registered number as shown in the register of horses on the off 
fore hoofs. 
(ii) The year of registration on the rear fore hoofs. 


(iii) The owner shall produce the horse before the Registering Officer at 
the end of every three months for inspection. 


21. Licenses for horses will be in different forms according to the class in 
which they are registered.

Passengers and luggage. 


24. No hackney-carriage shall carry more than four adult persons altogether 
in addition to the driver and the attendant. : 


25. ( No cycle-rickshaw or rickshaw shall carry more than two adult 
passengers. 


(ii) No palanquin shall be allowed to carry more than two adult passengers. 


For the purpose of this by-law two children under twelve years of age shall 
be reckoned as one adult. 


26. The driver of every hackney-carriage shall carry, if required, in or upon 
such carriage without any charge over and above the fare a quantity of luggage 
not exceeding two maunds and, if the number of persons other than the driver 
and the attendant carried in the carriage is less than four, a further quantity of 
luggage not exceeding in weight such number of maunds as together with the 
number of such persons shall make four. 


A charge not exceeding two annas may be levied for every ten seers or part 
thereof in excess of the above free allowance. 


27. No luggage shall be carried on any cycle-rickshaw or rickshaw except 
a small box or hand bag not exceeding 24x15x9 inches. 


Inspection of hackney-carriages, palanquins, cycle-rickshaw and rickshaws. 


28. It shall be lawful for any police officer of and above the rank of Sub- 
Inspector and any Commissioner or Health Officer or Sanitary Inspector of the 
municipality, at any time between sun-rise and sun-set to enter any premises on 
which any licensed hackney-carriages, palanquins, cycle-rickshaws or rickshaws 
or the horses or other animals, harness, or other things used therewith are kept 
in order to carry out any provisions of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919, 
or these by-laws, and the owner, occupier or his agent shall afford every facility 
for such officer’s inspection. 


Protection of weak and lame horses. 


29. It shall be lawful for the Registering Officer at any time to cause any 
animal used in a hackney-carriage to be produced before him for the purpose of 
inspection and it shall be compulsory upon the owner to produce any such animal 
within twenty-four hours from the receipt of such notice. 


30. The owner of any animal declared under section 29 to be unfit for use 
in a hackney-carriage shall, if he disposes of it, or removes it from the premises 
in which it is Stabled, give notice of the fact to the Registering Officer within one 
week of such disposal or removal, intimating at the same time the name and 
address of the person to whom he has disposed of it and the place to which it has 
been removed. 


31. Notice of the death of a registered horse shal! also be given to the 
Registering Officer, who, on receipt of such notice, shall cause the entry concerncd 
to be cancelled in the register of horses and the certificate of registration to be 
withdrawn. 

Regulation of use of horses. 


32. No owner shall permit any horse to work continuously in any hackney- 
carriage in excess of the following scale of time:—

NOTIFICATIONS. 


Darjeeling--—No. 5354M.2B-1/54.—17th June 
1954.—The following draft of u set of by-laws 
which has been framed by the Commissioners ot the 

alimpong Municipality, in the district of 
Darjeeling under section 465(3) — of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1982 (Bengal Act XV of 1932), as 
modified in its application to the district of 
Darjeeling, and which the Governor proposes to 
confirm under aection 506 of the said Act, 18 hereby 
Published for the information of persons likely to 
be affected thereby. 


The draft will be taken into consideration on or 
after the 918৮ August 1954 and any objection or 
suggestion with respect thereto which may 09 
received by the undersigned on or before that date 
through the Deputy Commissioner, Darjeeling or 
ee 8ہ‎ ۹ِ Commissioner shall be duly consi- 
dered :— 


Draft by-laws for the licensing of dogs and 
prevention and control of rabies. 


1. (1) «Every owner or keeper or person other- 
wise in charge of a dog ordinarily staying at 
Kalimpong or brought in from outside to stay 
there temporarily but for more Ahan 16 days shall 
get his dog registered in the municipal register 
kept tor the purpose by paying a license fee which 
shall be Re. 1 per year per dog for dogs ordinarily 
staying at Kulimpong, and four annas per quarter 
per dog tor the dogs staying there temporarily but 
for more than 15 مات‎ and take from the Munici- 
pal office a metal token bearing the registered num- 
ber which shall be firmly attuched to the collar 
which shall be put round the neck of the dog ৪০ 
registered and licenced : 


Provided that a dog not more than three months 
old shall not be required to wear a token or to be 
registered but a collar shall be put around its neck 
as soon as it is fit to wear one: 


Provided also that within one month from the 
date on which a dog has become liable for repgis- 
tration the owner or the heeper of a dog or the 
person otherwise in charge thereof shall apply for 
its registration. 


(2) Every application for registration of a dog 
shall contain the following particulars :— 


(i) description (such as sub-species or kind, 
colour, sex, age, pedigree, if any) of the

Short title.

Interpretations. 


2. The several words, terms and expressions to which by the Indian

(vii) The expression ‘‘the commencement of this license’’ shall mean

in writing of the Government in each case and subject to such 
conditions and/or limitations as the Government may impose. 


(ii) Aerial lines in the vicinity of a building or structure shalt be 
erected to comply with the Indian Electricity Rules concerned 
and in no case shall an aerial line be at a less distance than 4 
feet horizontally or 8 feet vertically from any building or 
structure whether permanent or temporary. 

(411) In narrow lanes, passnges or streets where it would not he 
possible to maintain a horizontal clearance of 4 feet between 
acrial lines and buildings or structures underground cables 
shall be provided unless any special method of construction of 
aerial lines have been expressly sanctioned in writing by the 
Government for any such lane, passage or street and such 
sanction shall be obtained by the licensee before beginning 
construction of any such special aerial line. 

(iv) ‘Where any electric supply lines cross or run along the routes 
of a taboot, temple car or similar other religious processions, 
the supply lines shall be laid underground or placed at such 
height as will allow of the free and safe passage of those 
processions. In case of dispute, such routes and heights shall 
be determined by the Deputy Commissioner to whom the 
licensee shall refer before running any such lines. 

(v) Removal of lines.—The lincensee shall remove or replace at his 
own expense any aerial line which runs along or across any 
8৬৮6 if in the opinion of the Government it is considered 
necessary to do so. 


(vi) For the purpose of rule 68(2) of the Hules, the maximum wind 
pressure shall be taken as 20 pounds per square foot.

Nature of supply. 


18. Nature of supply.—The systems and pressures of supply which 
shall be adopted for the supply of electrical energy under this lincense are 
the following :— 


*(i) Three phase alternating current, three-wire supply at a 
pressure of 6000 volts. between phases at a frequency of fifty 
complete cycles per second. 


*(ii) Three phase alternating current three or, four wire supply, at 
pressure of 400 volts. between phases and 230 volts. between 
each phase and neutral at a frequency of fifty complete cycles 
per second. 

*(ii1) Single phase alternating current, two wire supply at a pressure 
of 230 volts. between the phase and the neutral conductor at a 
frequency of fifty complete cycles per second. 


Within three months from the date of grant of this license, the 
licensee shall declare to each individual consumer for the time being 
connected to the licensee’s distributing mains, and_ thereafter to every 
new consumer the pressure at which he undertakes to supply energy. 


The pressure as declared in accordance with the foregoing paragraph 
shall be as measured at Consumer’sa terminals und shall not vary therefrom 
beyond the limits prescribed by the Indian Electricity Rules, 1937, 
throughout, the area of supply. 


Provided that the licensee may from time to time with the previous 
consent in writing of the Government and subject to such limitations and 
conditions as shall be made in writing by the (overnment, adopt any 


other pressures or systems of supply or both for the purpose of this license. 


*The licensee may adopt 6600, 440 and 250 volts. respectively in the 
sub-clause (i), (ii) and (iti) above as declared pressures instead of 6000, 


400 and 230 volts.

(ii) The rates for sale of electrical energy shall be subject to the 
provisions of section 58. ٠ 


Purchase of undertaking. 


15(A). Purchase by the State Government (where the State Electricity 
Board is not formed).—With the concurrence the licensee the Govern- 
ment may purchase the undertaking at any time on the payment of an 
amount to be mutually agreed upon. In the absence of agreement as to 
purchase price the matter shall be settled by arbitration. 


5 Bulk supply. 


16. The licensee will take from the State Flectricity Board, if set up 
by the Government or from the Government such bulk energy as required 
by the licensee at any time such Board or the Government is prepared to 
supply at a rate not more than licensee’s cost of generation. 


The decision of the Government on the operation of this caluse shall 
be final. 


If energy is taken as provided above, the licensee shall, if so required, 
sell to the Electricity Board or to the Government its generating plant 
at its written down value, or if such Board or Government does not wish 
to purchase, the licensee will have full discretion to dispose of such plant. 


Distribution of revenue. 


Ww. (i) When the surplus (excess of revenue over cxpenses) made by 
the licensee is sufficient to compensate for past losses, if any, the surplus 
after payment of income-tax may be utilised in accordance with the 
directions of Government, for the benefit of the ratepayers of the munici- 
pality and the consumers of electricity. 


(ii) Surplus in this case is defined as the excess of the gross revev- 
over the working and maintenance expense of the electrical undertaking 
which include amounts set aside for reserve and sinking funds for loan 
repayment. 


(iii) Working and maintenance expenses include— 


(a) Cost of power (when purchased in bulk from another source) of 
fuel, oil, water and _atores consumed, salaries and wages, 
contribution for pensions, provident fund,  superaunuatioa 
and insurance for officers and servants, cost of repuirs, muinte- 
nonce and renewale of small parts not chargeable to the 
capita] account.

OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT MACISTRATE 
OF NADIA. 


ORDER. 


No. 2492(43)J.—16th June 1954.—Whereas it 
has been brought to my notice that a large scale 
smuggling of 90৮00 yarn and cotton clothes 
from Indian Union to East Pakistan is being 
carried on ¢n the boarder areas of the district of 
Nadia, and whereas other measures to prevent the 
same have proved ineffective, and whereas in my 
opinion it 18 necessary for maintaining supply of 
cotton yern and cotton clothes which are essential 
to the life of the community, to prevent the move- 
ment of the said commodities, viz., cotton yarn 
and cotton clothes, within aedepth of three miles 
along the entire East Pakistan aud Nadia border 
of this district, and whereas the previous order 
No. 1428(43)J., dated 818۲ March 1954, made 
under section 20, sub-section (1) of the West 
Bengal Security Act, 1950, to this effect expires 
on 218٦ June 1954 and a fresh order is considered 
necessary and expedient, I, Shri B. R. Gupta, 
District Magistrate, Nudis, in exercise of the 
powers conferred on me by order No. 6218P/ 
445/50, dated 19th September 1950, issued by the 
Government of West Bengal, Home (Political) 
Department, do by this order under section 20, 
sub-section (1) of the West Bengal Security Act, 
1950, prohibit the movement of cotton yarn and 
cotton olothes within oa depth of three miles 
excepting the movement of the above commodities 
by hona fide dealers, weavers and consumers under 


a permit from the President, union bosrd, local 


7 D. N. BANERJEE, 
Additional District Magistrate, 24-Parganas. 


4 


Inspector or Sub-Inspector of Food and Supplies 
or any éther superior authority along the entire 
East Pakistan-Nadia border. 


This order will remain in force for a period of 
three months, with effect from 22nd June 1954. 


Given under my hand and seal this 16th dav of 
June 1954, | 
B. R. GUPTA, 
District Magistrate, Nadia.

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 
ORDER. 


No. 3048Dis./D/15L-11/54.—19th June 1954.—Whereas under the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department order No. 4705Dis./D/15L-19/53, 
dated the 10th December 1953, the industrial dispute between Messrs. Gulf 
Oil (India), Ltd., P/13, Mission Row Extension, Calcutta-1, and their employees 
represented by Gulf Oil Workers’ Union, 47, Chowringhee Road, Calcutta-16, 
regarding the matters specified in the schedule thereto was referred for adjudica- 
tion to the Sixth Industrial Tribunal ; 


And whereas the said Sixth Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the State 
Government its award on the said industrial dispute ; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Gulf Oil (India), 
Ltd., ۲/13, Mission Row Extension, Calcutta-1, and their employees 
represented by Gulf Oil Workers’ Union, 47, Chowringhee Road, Calcutta-16. 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. 


PRESENT : 


ওলা MOTILAL 2 Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 
ribunal. 


Appearances ৪ 


For the Company: Shri S. کا‎ Mullick (Jr.) of Sandersons & Morgans, 
Solicitors. 


For the employees: Shri Jagannath Pandey, assisted. by B. K. Sarkar, Office 
Secretary, B.P.N.T.U.C. 


Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, by order 
Nos. 2870Dis./D/15L-8/52, dated 28th October 1952 and 4705Dis./D/15L- 
19/53, dated the 10th December 1953, referred, under sections 7 and 10 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Gulf Oil (India), Ltd., P/13, Mission Row’ Extension, Calcutta-1, 
and their employees represented by Gulf Oil Workers’ Union, regarding the 
matters specified in the following schedule to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


SCHEDULE. 
(1) Bonus. 


(2) Whether the Company was justified in terminating the services of Shn 
T. C. Mehta? What relief is he entitled to? 


AWARD. 


At the outset the Company’s lawyer raised the preliminary objections that 
the Union through its the then Secretary Mr. Basu settled the case and filed a 
statement to the effect that the bonus issue has been settled and the issue con- 
cerning Shri Mehta is not at all a part of the cause taken up by the Unica and 


2158 THE OALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 (Parr I 
পাটি 


therefore it has been contended that the Union or the workmen cannot now take 
uP the case of bonus at this stage. The other point taken is that Shri ۸۷۹ 
claims that he is a permanent employee of the Company in its branch at Delhi 
and therefore his discharge at a time when he was working in Calcutta Branch 
on deputation cannot give the Tribunal of West Bengal, any jurisdiction to hear 
the said issue. On the two points my decision are as follows :— 


It appears from the record that on the 13th August 1952, Mr. Basu, the 
then Secretary of the Union, expressed that the bonus issue has been settled and 
that the issue regarding Shri Mehta was not a part of the cause taken up by the 
Union. It also appears that thereafter Shri Sarkar appeared on the scene and 
ousted Shri'Basu and himself appeared as the representative of the said Union 
after taking into confidence the whole body of the workmen concerned. Gov- 
ernment made this reference long after the said settlement of Shri Basu of 
August 1952. The workmen are now represented by Shri Sarkar who challenged 
the said statement of Shri Basu and ousted him. As the said statement has 
not been recorded and as the reference has been made on the basis of the 
challenge made by Shri Sarkar, I hold that the alleged “no dispute” as entered 
by Shri Basu cannot be taken cognizance of by this Tribunal and I hold that 
the dispute as referred by Government is still continuing between the Company 
and its workmen. 


Regarding Mehta it is admitted that Mehta was sent to Calcutta Branch from 
Delhi by the Head Office at Bombay and that the satd Head Office at Bombay 
terminated his services when he was working at Calcutta. The fact is not that 
the Head Office struck off Mehta’s name from Delhi Branch establishment ; on 
the other hand, the Head Office terminated the services of Mehta in the Calcutta 
Branch where the name was being borne on its establishment for the time being. 
When the Company has its Head Office at Bombay and branch office at Calcutta 
and when the termination of service was done by the Head Office in respect of 
an employee working in the Calcutta Branch, the Company is to be held to be 
existing at Calcutta as well, where it has its branch office and where Mr. Mehta 
was working at the time of termination of his service. So this Tribunal has 
jurisdiction to hear this reference regarding discharge of Mehta. 


Issue No. 2.—Whether the Company was justified in terminating the services of 
Shri T. C. Mehta. What relief is he entitled to? 


First I take up the کت‎ of Shri Mehta. He was appointed by Messrs. 
Bird & Co. (also called F.W. Heilgers & Co.) on the 13th December 1948 on 
probation for six months at Delhi Branch. Bird & Co. was the Managing 
Agents of Messrs. Silvertown Lubricants (India), Ltd., under which name the 
Gulf Oil (India), Ltd., was then doing business. From the ist April 1949, 
i.e., before the probationary period of Shri T. C. Mehta expired the Silvertown 
Lubricants (India), Ltd., got rid of the Managing Agency of Bird & Co. At 
that time Shri Mehta had not completed his کی و‎ period and it is not 
his contention that at that time he was confirmed in service. It was clearly 
stated in the letter of appointment (Ext. 1)— 


“You will be on probation for six months after which your appointment to 
our regular staff will be considered.” 


This letter of appointment was given by Bird & Co., not on behalf of any other 
Company. On the other hand, the following lines seem to be very significant, 
ںی‎ 
“We have pleasure in appointing you to our staff in the Silvertown Lubri- 
cants (India), Ltd., section in grade ‘C’”. 


“You will be on probation for six months after which your appointment 
to our regular staff will be considered”. 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 2159 


০৯ صطد‎ ডিপ ও مد جج جھ‎ Reino یلوا‎ পি এ Rts সপ ৯ সস حم‎ — = পি es. 


The Company contends that Bird & Co., i.e., the Managing Agents, had their 
own staff also and Shri Mehta was appointed by Bird & Co. as its own employee, 
it may be, to deal with the matters relating to the said Bird & Co.’s business, so 
far as Silvertown Lubricants, Ltd., was concerned. So it was stated in the 
letter-— 

“To our staff in the Silvertown Lubricants (India), Limited, Section”’. 


It appears from the evidence that the “ihe pean appointed by Bird & Co. on 
behalf of Silvertown Lubricants (India), Ltd., were given option to join or not 
the services on the Ist April 1949, after the Managing Agency of Bird & Co. 
had ceased. There is no clear evidence that Shri Mehta was given any such 
option. No document to show any such option is forthcoming. However when 
there is 20 evidence that Silvertown Lubricants (India),  Ltd., 
appointed Shri Mehta as a probationer and when there is 10 such 
case at all on the side of the Company, the question is whether 
Shri Mehta was appointed by Silvertown Lubricants (India), Ltd., as its own 
employee on the Ist April 1949, as a permanent hand or as a_ temporary 
hand. I find from the evidence that Mehta was transferred from Delhi office 
to Calcutta Office in August 1949, Ext. D5, dated 3rd August 1949, is the 
introduction letter by which the Delhi Office introduced Mehta to the Calcutta 
Manager Mr. Hempson and I find that in this letter it was clearly stated that Shri 
Mehta was being sent to Calcutta Office on deputation from Delhi. It also 
appears from the evidence that after reaching Calcutta Office he was taken in 
as a member of the provisional Provident Fund which had effect from 151. 
August 1949 and contributions from his salary were deducted from month to 
month for some time and that afterwards when the said Provident Fund System 
did not meet with the approval of the Head Office, the matter was dropped and 
his contributions were refunded like those of other employees. It also appears 
that from July 1950, the Company introduced a Provident Fund Scheme and 
since then Shri Mehta was a member thereof and he made contribution regularly 
from his salary, It also appears from the evidence that the Company paid him 
advance for travelling allowance to cover his expense of travelling from Delhi 
to Calcutta. It also appears that when a month later on Shri Mehta’s wife 
came over from Delhi to Calcutta to join Shri Mehta, the Company bore Shri 
Mehta’s wife’s travelling expense also. From these circumstances I am clearly 
convinced that Shri Mehta was neither a probationer nor a temporary hand when 
he was transferred from Delhi to Calcutta (in August 1949) and that on 
the other hand I find that he was a permanent employee in the services of this 
Company and that he was transferred to Calcutta from Delhi on deputation to 
deal with some specific job. He was also paid Calcutta allowance, originally 
at the rate of Rs. 100 per month and later on at the rate of Rs. 150 per month 
in addition to his basic pay at the rate of Rs. 100 per month. He received 
Calcutta allowance at the rate of Rs. 150 per month up to March 1950. There- 
after he was not paid any Calcutta allowance but he was paid house rent at the 
rate of Rs. 20 per month with effect from April 1950. ৮4 Shri Mehta’s 
wife came over to Calcutta some time in November 1949, the fact is that Shri 
Mehta continued to get the Calcutta allowance at the rate of Rs. 150 per month 
up to March 1950. From the circumstances I may reasonably infer that the 
said Calcutta allowance was paid to him as “deputation allowance”. So when 
his family came over to Calcutta, the Company was unwilling to pay him the 
Calcutta allowance any longer after March 1950, and since that time he was 
being paid house rent at the rate of Rs. 20 per month. 


Mehta’s specific job in the Calcutta Office was finished in the latter part of 
1951 and accordingly the Company by letter, Ext. 3, dated the 26th October 
1951, terminated his services with effect from 15 November 1951 and proposed 
to pay him one month’s salary in lieu of notice and two months’ salary in lieu 


2160 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Parr 1 


of earned leave due and he was asked to receive payments of his Provident 
Fund dues. 


Shri Mehta’s contention is that he has been victimised because he was insist- 
ing upon having payment of his Calcutta allowance at the rate of Rs. 150 per 
month in addition to house rent at the rate of Rs. 20 per month and when after 
specific job he was concerned in in Calcutta Office was finished, he applied for 
two months’ leave with effect from 190 November 1951. Taking this advantage 
the Company terminated the services with effect from 156 November 1951. 
This termination of service of a permanent hand having led to the industrial 
dispute between Shri Mehta and the Company, the act of the employer, viz., the 
Company, becomes subject to scrutiny and it is for the employer to justify his 
act as having been inspired by real trade reason and not under the influence 
of a motive of unfair labour practice or any other extreneous consideration 
reflecting on the point of bona fides (Imperial Tobacco Company vs. Their 
workmen, 1952, 2 L.L.J., page 829). In the letter, Ext. 3, the Company 
made out that— 


“As Delhi has no vacancy, and as the task for which Mr. Mehta was 
specifically employed in Calcutta has ended, the Company have no 
other option but reluctantly to terminate his employment”. 


It appears from the newspaper (Ext. 4) (Statesman), issued on 7th March, 
Friday, 1952— 


that applications were invited by this Company for Delhi Office for the 
post of Junior Accountant on a scale of salary, 100—7/8—160 and 
dearness allowance. 


From the evidence I find that Shri Mehta was doing the work of Assistant 
Accountant at Delhi Office when he was transferred from Delhi to Calcutta 
Office and that his job at Calcutta was also one of accountancy. The fact that 
so soon after the termination of the services of Shri Mechta, the Company wanted 
a candidate for similar post in its DeJhi Office clearly indicates that there was 
really no reason to dispense with the services of Shri Mehta in the way as has 
been done by the Company. So my finding is that the Company was not 
justified in terminating the services of Shri T. 3 Mehta. 


Now the question is what relief he is entitled to? In the long written state- 
ment Mr. Mehta did not claim his reinstatement. Later on he prayed for 
reinstatement but it was an alternative prayer. At the trial however he prays 
for his reinstatement in service. The ordinary and normal remedy of such 
unjustifiable termination of services of a permanent hand would be reinstate- 
ment but in the present case there are certain circumstances which cannot be 
overlooked in order to consider whether reinstatement should be ordered or 
not. The claim for compensation as made by Shri Mehta is a long one con- 
sisting of as many as ten/eleven items and the total amount of the claim is to 
the tune of Rs. 27,490. The Company by its letter [Ext. B(3)] admitted the 
following claims only :— 


(1) Extra allowance up to 31st October 1951. 

(2) Salary for two months and a half in lieu of earned leave, with this 
remark that although two months’ leave is under the rules of the 
Company allowed to be accumulated, additional half month’s leave 
as a very special case and an exceptional one too, granted to him. 

(3) Salary for notice period. 

(4) Railway fare to Delhi. 

(5) Provident Fund moneys. 


Shri Mehta’s claim for increment in salary and for compensation for throwing 
him out of permanent employment is not accepted by the Company. Mehta 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTH, JULY 1, 1954 2161 


wagts to say that the words “extra allowance” in Ext. B(3) mean the Calcutta 
allowance but it appears from the perusal of the letters [Exts. A, A(i)], and 
B(4), that extra allowance here means Calcutta house rent allowance 
of Rs. 20 per month. The reasons 88 stated in paragraph 2 
of this letter [Ext. B(4)] are quite satisfactory. It appears that 
the other employees in the Calcutta Office were being paid house 
rent and not Calcutta allowance. So the deputation was over 
Jong ago and when Shri Mehta’s family also came over to Calcutta about a 
month after Shri Mehta’s transfer from Delhi, the Company rightly discontinued 
the Calcutta allowance from April 1950. As regards the claim for increment 
J find there is no evidence that there was any rule for such increment or that 
the Company ever agreed to give him such increment. The certificate purport- 
ing to have given to Shri Mehta by the Calcutta Manager Mr. Hempson, dated 
15 November 1951, cannot be used as an authority to bind the Company and 
compel it to grant Calcutta allowance and increment in pay. In this letter also 
there is no mention of any increment in salary, The sentence runs thus :— 


“All along he was drawing a salary of Rs. 100 with dearness allowance 
amounting to Rs. 100, house rent of Rs. 20 and extra allowance at 
the rate of Rs. 150, all making a total of Rs. 370 per month”. 


Mr. Hempson always looked upon Shri Mehta with favour. It is not correct 
that Shri Mehta was receiving house rent and Calcutta allowance at the same 
time or that he was receiving house rent “all along” or that he was receiving 
Calcutta allowance “all along.” It is a fact that before April 1950, he was not 
paid any house rent and that after March 1950, he was not paid any Calcutta 
allowance. The contention made by the learned lawyer on behalf of the 
Company is that it may be that Shri Mehta himself wrote out this certificate on 
an old letter form of this Company and put it up before Mr. Hempson for his 
signature and the latter simply put signature without verifying the facts stated. 
The other documents produced by Shri Mehta, viz., Ext 5, has evoked serious 
controversy about its genuineness. This letter purports to be a letter written by 
Shri Mehta under date 12th May 1950 to the Calcutta Division Manager and 
it purports to have been endorsed by Mr. Hempson in the following way ; 
“Confirmed, Barry Hempson”. The Company contends that Mehta’s evidence 
that Hempson was in Calcutta on that date and he made this endorsement and 
put down his signature is entirely false, and that on that date Mr. Hempson 
was in Bombay. Mr. Hempson is no longer in the service of this Company. 
He is now in England. It appears from Ext. L., dated the 11th May 1950, 
and Ext. L(i), dated 12th May 1950 and Exts. H, H(i) written by Mr. J. Ball 
from Calcutta to Mr. Barry Hempson and from the abstract of the travelling 
and entertaining expenses of Mr. Hempson for the month of May 1950 and 
from Ext. E that Mr. Hempson left Calcutta on the 10th May 1950 and was 
in Bombay on the 12th May 1950. In these circumstances the Company may 
rightly contend that it has lost all confidence in the honesty of Shri T. C. 
Mehta. So I am of opinion that there should be no order of reinstatement in 
this present case. He is however entitled to get his salary and dearness allow- 
ance for 24 months in lieu of his earned leave and salary and dearness allowance 
for one month in lieu of notice (and his wages and dearness allowance for 
the month of October 1951, if the same are in arrears) and also Provident 
Fund dues and house rent allowance at the rate of Rs. 20 per month up to 
30th November 1951 plus railway fare (inter class) from alcutta to Delhi 
by Express Train and compensation for unemployment at the following rate:— 


He will get basic pay Rs. 100 and dearness allowance Rs. 100 per month 
for a period of 4 months and ٢ direct that these payments shall be 
made i the Company to Shri T. C. Mehta within 10 days from the 
date of publication of the Award. 


2162 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 ]8 83:1 1 


Issue Na. 1.—Bonus. 


Next I take up the issue No. 1, i.e., bonus. In the reference the year ror 
which bonus is claimed is not mentioned. But in the statement filed by the 
workmen (excluding the clerks) bonus is claimed for the years 1951 and 1952, 
and the contention is that although in the said two years, September bonus 
equivalent to one month’s wages for each year has been paid to the workmen, 
no bonus out of profit was paid in respect of the said two 
years. The bonus already paid is claimed by the Company as 
a condition of service and they are now out to demand profit 
sharing bonus for the said two years and they claim for the same at one 
month's wages. The September bonus is called Puja bonus. From the evidence: 
I find that before 1948, the Company did not pay any bonus. It would appear 
from Ext. J, a certified statement filed by the Company that in 1948, the Com- 

any made a profit of over Rs. 1,57,000 and in that year it paid Puja bonus at 
/3rd month’s wages and April bonus at one month’s wages. In 1949, the 
Company made profit of Rs. 58,000 and paid both the bonuses at one month's 
wages on each occasion. Similar payment was made in 1950, also, although 
in that year the Company suffered loss of over 2 lakhs. In 1951 the Company 
made profit of Rs. 63,000 and paid the Puja bonus at one month’s wages and 
in 1952, the Company suffered loss of about Rs. 2,23,000, and still paid Puja 
bonus at one month’s wages. It is a Company, the business of which is to sell 
oil products and not petrol or motor spirit. So it is not a big concern like the 
reputed Oil Companies operating in India. As there has been huge loss in 
the year 1952, the claim for profit sharing bonus for that year is to be rejected. 
The question is whether out of the profit of about Rs. 63,000 in the year 1951, 
the workmen (about 31 in number) should get profit sharing bonus in addition 
to Puja bonus already paid. From the system followed by the Company it may 
be said that Puja bonus at one month’s wages is a implied condition of service 
of these workmen because I find that in the years of loss also such bonus was 
paid ungrudgingly. The Labour Commissioner’s file shows that the dispute or 
demand for bonus was not made before latter part of 1952. So the claim for 
bonus in respect: of the year 1951, is a belated one. Moreover before Sarker 
came on the scene, his predecessor Mr. Basu once settled the matter with the 
Company and gave up the claim for bonus. As the account of the year 1951 
had already been closed long before the demand for profit sharing bonus in 
respect of the said year was made, the said claim is now untenable. The 
closed account of the Company cannot now be re-opened. Therefore my award 
is that the entire claim for bonus for the years 1951 and 1952 is to be rejected. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
M. L. CHAKRAVATTI, Judge.

AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department. by its order No. 2933- 
Dis./D/11L-181/53, dated the 6th August 1953, referred an industrial dispute 
existing between Messrs. Venesta, Ltd., Kamarhati, 24-Parganas, and ٣ 
workmen represented by Venesta Factory Workers’ Union, Sagore Dutt Ghat 


2166 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1964 [1 ১৪০ I 


Road, Kamarhati, 24-Parganas, regarding the matters specified in the schedule 
to the order of reference under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (XIV of 1947), to this Tribunal for its adjudication. 


‘The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 12th August 
1953 and usual notices were issued to the parties for appearance and _ written 
statements. Both parties filed written statements and 18th May 1954 was 
fixed for hearing, on which day the case was heard. The Union in its statement 
stated among others that the relation between the Company and the Union was 
cordial. In 1950, the Company introduced a number of new machines and 
made far reaching alterations in its lines of production, as a result of which the 
workmen found that their workloads have intensified und increased. After lapse 
of sometime, the workmen demanded revision of their existing scales of pay and 
introduction of production bonus. The Company, however, produced incentive 
bonus Scheme for a trial period of 12 months from the date of commencement 
of the scheme. The trial scheme was made operative for certain classes of 
workers from 2nd June 1952 and the Union provisionally accepted it. It was 
understood that the scheme would be applied to almost all employees within 
a reasonable time. There was certain anomalies in this scheme and the Union 
demanded the inclusion of all employees within the scheme. The Company 
proposed certain amendments which the Union could not accept. The percentage 
of bonus earned by the Metal Foil Department and Fittings Department are 
widely divergent. The bonus of the Metal Foil Department was never more than 
12 to 13 per cent. whereas bonus in the Fittings Department was much _ higher. 
Since the number of workers receiving the higher rate of wages is very small, 
the trial scheme has not been of much help to the already starving employees. 
The Union therefore suggested that there should be separate scheme for the 
Fittings and Metal Foil Departments and that bonus for the productive workers 
and maintenance workers and general mazdoors should be the same. In place 
of 1/Sth in the proposed scheme, the Union suggests that the indirect workers 
should get 50 per cent. of the bonus. 


In the Company’s statement, it stated among others that it increased basic rates 
wherever workloads have intensified with the introduction of the new machines 
in recent years. Over and above, and not connected with this increase in basic 
rate, the Company introduced a Scheme of incentive bonus for productive 
workers. This scheme was prepared by a fully qualified expert who later on 
worked out a scheme for non-productive workers. The incentive scheme under 
review is however for the non-productive workers whose work are in most cases 
shared between both Metal Foil and Fittings Departments but rarely in the same 
ratio. It is for this reason that the Company offered the non-productive workers 
an incentive bonus based on the combined effogts of both departments. The 
Company considers that this basis for the non-productive workers’ incentive 
scheme calculation is a more equitable system for the two departments also. 
Unfortunately, the trial period set for the original scheme for productive workers 
coimcided with the well-known recession in the tea trade. This recession com- 
menced from about fourth month of the trial period and_ still persists. ‘The 
Company submitted that the incentive bonus is not a condition of service, etc.:— 


The issues as per schedule to the order of reference are— 


(1) Are amendments which the Company proposed to introduce to the 
incentive bonus scheme introduced in 1952 for the benefit of the 
workers in Metal Foil and the Fittings Departments fair and reason- 
able and if not, whether the amendments should be dropped ? 


(2) Is the incentive bonus scheme which the Company propose to introduce 
for the general mazdoor and the maintenance workers a-fair scheme 
and should the workmen be asked to accept 10? 


Paxt I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 2167 


a লস্ট عحیعصیچجبییپیک‎ 
FINDINGS. 


Issues Nos. 1 and 2.—Both are taken together. The trial scheme of incentive 
bonus was put into operation from June 1952. It was provisionally made for 
the trial period of 12 months from the date of commencement. The Union 
accepted the scheme. The Union says that it understood that the scheme would 
be applied to all categories of workers within a reasonable time. In fact, the 
incentive bonus scheme for the general mazdoors and maintenance workers is 
one which the Company wants to introduce to meet this demand of the Union. 


The working of original scheme during the trial period revealed certain 
anomulies in it and they required alteration. Mr. Wilton, the present Manager 
of the Company, has in his evidence before the Tribunal explained those 
anomalies and the changes which are sought to be introduced to do away with 
them. The incentive scheme in original was prepared by a_ U. K. expert in 
Time and Motions study. His services were requisitioned to frame this scheme 
after local survey. Unfortunately, the expert is not available now. The 
original scheme which was the result of very careful and detailed examination 
and scrutiny of work and time taken for its completion is a document which 
has been produced by Mr. Wilton. There being no dispute regarding the 
original scheme and I am not making any attempt to quote it in this award. 
The basic part of the scheme is given in an extract (Ext. A). Previous to this 
scheme, there was a system of profit earning in the Fittings Department. This 
system had a low basic wage and a high profit earning. One of the main 
purpose of the new scheme was to get rid of this anomaly and also to pay a 
fair incentive to be earned on the increased basic rates. Mr. Wilton explained 
the utility of the scheme by working out examples of the earnings of a particular 
man in 12 weeks before the scheme in a slack period and 12 weeks after the 
scheme. The basis for the scheme is af course the world wide standard which 
puts the incentive scheme at 33 per cent. of the basic wages. The reasons for 
introducing the amendment in the scheme are explained in paragraphs 3 and 4 
of the Company’s letter to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, dated 27th 
February 1953 (Ext. C), and those for introduction of the new schem: or rather 
extension of the scheme to general mazdoors and maintenance workers is out- 
lined in paragraph 2 of that letter. Mr. Wilton has explained what he meant 
by an indirect worker. He said a worker who is not actually concerned with 
the manufacturing process is an indirect worker, eg., import and export 
mazdoors, maintenance workers and general mazdoors who are attached to 
these two departments—Metal Foil and Fittings Departments—come under this 
category. Durwans and the clerical staff are of course excluded from operation 
of this scheme. Mr. Wilton explains the purpose behind lumping of bonus 
earnings together and taking. them into one pool for its distribution among the 
direct workers of the two said departments. He said that the main purpose 
was to equalise the average bonus earnings by all the direct workers. The 
essence of the incentive bonus scheme is to ensure a small amount of money 
as bonus payable to the employees of a particular department which if kept 
separate from other departments, may not earn anything while others may earn 
profit during a slack period. There is slack period in these two departments. 
It may be that the direct workers of the Fittings Department left to themselves 
may earn more profit comparatively higher than that earned by their colleagues 
in the Metal Foil Department and in the Metal Foil Department the direct 
workers would be going without any profit at all during the slack period. This 
incentive bonus scheme was prepared only to remove this apparent anomaly. 
The Union is anxious to see that the benefits of the scheme go to workers of all 

ides in the factory. It is only reasonable that the two departments. Metal 
Foi and Fittings, should share the incentive bonus equally. The entire thing is 
a now in an experimental stage. The scheme is provisionally made for a year 

nly, and there cannot be any reasonable objection to give the scheme after the 


2168 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Parr I 


changes made in it a fresh trial for another year and to see at the end ofa the 
period how it operates, not only in the case of the direct workers, including 
those of the Fittings Department, but in case of all. 


The Union's objection to the introduction of the new scheme for maintenance 
workers and general mazdoors is that in place of 1/Sth of the total earnings 
under the incentive scheme, being set apart for distribution among the indirect 
workers, 50 per cent., i.e., 1/2 of the earnings should be set apart for them. 
Mr. Wilton said that the suggestion was unacceptable for in the first place, it 
would take away all the incentive from the workers who come under the benefits 
of this scheme to become some day as direct workers and at the same time, it 
would place them almost in the same position as the direct workers although they 
are not making any contribution in any way to the manufacturing process. 
Lastly, it is undesirable that the bonus payable to an indirect worker should be 
equal to that payable to direct worker who contributes to the manufacturing 
process. 1/5th would approximately be 14 per cent. of the earnings. Further, 
in setting apart this money for the indirect workers, the Company is not drawing 
from the pool mentioned above but drawing on from its own funds. The Union, 
on the contrary, could not assign any particular reason why the indirect workers 
should be placed almost on a footing of equality with the direct workers under 
the incentive bonus scheme. On a consideration of all these, I find the amend- 
ments to the incentive bonus scheme are fair and reasonable and should be 
introduced. The scheme as amended be put into operation for a period of 12 
months only from the date of the operation of this award. 


The incentive bonus scheme for the general mazdoors and the maintenance 
workers is also a fair scheme and I wceuld ask the workmen to accept it. This 
should be also put into operation for a period of 12 months only from the date 
of the operation of this award. This is my award. 


Taken at my dictation and corrected by me.

his post.

informed the Labour Commissioner about the necessity for drastic reduction of

Opposite Party which they knew were entirely false. Since the section in which 
Rabi Ranjan Chatterji worked was itself abolished and it was only manned by 
one employee, the question of ‘last come first go’ does not arise and the applica- 
tion of Rabi Ranjan Chatterji should be rejected.

AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. 3361Dis./D/9L-3B/53, dated 4th September 1953, referred an industrial 
dispute existing between Messrs. Bloomfield Tea Estate, Darjeeling (Manag- 
ing Agents Messrs. Goenka & Co.) and their workers numbering twenty 
represented by Darjeeling District Chia Kaman Mazdoor Union, Chowk Bazar, 
Darjeeling, regarding the matters specified in the schedule to the order of 
reference under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV 
of 1947), to this Tribunal for its adjudication. 


The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 9th September 


1953 and usual notices were issued to both parties for appearance and written 
statement. 


The parties filed their written statements in due course and the case was 
heard on 4th May 1954, the day fixed for its Riot and the days following. 
The Union’s case, briefly stated, is that Shri Balman Manager and 19 others, all 
permanent workers of the Estate, were dismissed from service without assigning 
any reason whatsoever. They are active members of the Union and Union 
Organisers of the tea gardens. Shri Balman Mangar is one of the leaders and 
the executive committee member of this Union. They incurred the displeasure 
of the Management for their Union activities. Purna Singh Ray, Dalbahadur 
Ray and Gokul Sing Ray were dismissed by the Manager. Purna Sing was 
since reinstated. Regarding the remaining 18 workers including Shri Balman 


2172 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 4 [Part I 


Mangar, the Manager refused work for them from the date of the reopening of 
the garden on the 16th March 1953 without assigning any reason whatsé,ver. 
The garden was closed on 26th November 1952. The Union enclosed copies 
of correspondence between them and the authorities. Regarding the dismissal 
of the workers, it claimed their reinstatement and compensation alleging that the 
dismissal was arbitrary and opposed to principles of natural justice. 


The Bloomfield Tea Estate Company, Limited (hereinafter called the Com- 
pany), in a written statement denied the allegations of the Union and stated 
among others that the workers were dismissed, not arbitrarily but on justfiable 
grounds. They were retrenched for economic reasons. It alleged that— 

(1) Balman Mangar was residing in the garden with family. His employ- 
ment was opposed by some workers of the garden. Accordingly 
a panchayet, was summoned and the Panchayet's letter, dated 7th 
October 1953, will be produced at the time of hearing. 

(2) Kabirdhan Rai—Wife and daughter are working. He has_ been 
dealing in meat at Phulbazar since the garden was closed. 

(3) Dhanbahadur Bhujel—Only wife is working. He is carrying 006 
clothes of the dhobi at the garden. 

(4) Bhudiman Bhujel—He has always been irregular in work, suffers 
from illness and age is 55 years. Only wife is working in the 
garden and his son is in military service.

daughter are working in the garden. He is aged 80 years. 

(6) Shomraj Mangar—Only wife is working. He was a_ daffadar on a

(14) Madan Kumar—His one daughter is working. Wife expired and he

produced at the time of hearing.

working in Risheehat Tea Estate.

(19) Dalbahadur Rai—Retrenched in June 1952. Reported to have 
been working in Risheehat Tea Estate.

FINDINGS, 


One of 20 employees mentioned in the schedule to the order of reference 
named Shri Tekbir (No. 16) is dead. His death is admitted on both sides. 
He is said to have died in September 1953. Any proceeding regarding a dead 
person is a nullity. His case is, therefore, left out of consideration. Of the 
remaining 19 employees, Dhanbahadur Bhujel (No, 3), Budhiman Bhujel (No. 

), Bahadur Bhujel (No. 5), Shomraj Mangar (No. 6) and Manbahadur Kami 
No. 7), in all five—were re-employed after the reference was received. This 
ig admitted on both sides. The question of their re-employment or refusal of 
employment and/or compensation do not arise in this case. None of them 
has been examined. No one is coming forward to press any claim for com- 
pensation. Therefore, their cases are also left out. It is not in the interest of 
the industry to unnccessarily rake up the past and thereby create bitter feelings 
where such feelings had been removed. 


Two out of the remaining employees stand on a different footing. They are 
Dalbahadur Rai (No. 19) and Gokul Singh Rai (No. 20). They were 
retrenched before the garden was closed. They were also refused employment 
when the garden reopened. Admittedly, the garden was closed on 26th 
November 1952 and reopened on 16th March 1953. The cmployment was 
refused in cases of all these employees, when the garden reopened on the 16th 
March 1953. This is the Union’s case in paragraphs 1 and 3 of their written 
statcment. 


The written statement of the Company is a hopeless document, for it is 
impossible to make out what the defence of the Company really is. It is 
included in the written statement, a report of an officer who made an enquiry 
on the spot. It is only in paragraph 3 of it that the Company denies that there 
has been any arbitrary and/or high-handed action in the matter of retrenchment 
of the labourers mentioned in the terms of reference. ‘This apparently conveys 
the idea that all of these employees were retrenched. )ا‎ does not state any- 
where the reasons for such retrenchment. On a reference to the Labour Com- 
missioner’s file and the correspondences that passed between the Union and the 
management, some of which appear as annexure to Union's written statement, 
it appears that only Dalbahadur Rai and Gokul Sing Rai were retrenched before 
the garden was, closed and the other employees were refused employment on the 
day the garden re-opened for their refusing to sign an undertaking in favour of 
the Management. ء‎ learned representative of the Company, who conducted 
the case before the Tribunal, made an endeavour to place some materials 


2174 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 4 (Parr I 


relevant to the enquiry but not all. 1 was not a little surprised to find thattthe 
Management has at last taken up an unhelpful attitude in the matter of defence 
in this case. All that 1 was able to gather from the learned representative for 
the Management that the retrenchment was made for economic reasons and that 
the management did not really refuse employment to any of these employees 
but that the majority of the workers objected to their employment. These 
جو و ا‎ did not sign the undertaking which the majority of the workers did. 
Only two out of them, namely, Lagha Mangar and Dhanbir alias Dhanbahadur 
Mangar joined but they also left on receiving higher wages elsewhere. Others 
stayed out on an inducement from the Union in the hope of getting very hand- 
some compensation for the period of unemployment. Lastly, all worked in the 
neighbouring gardens during the period of their unemployment. The cases of 
the aforesaid employees are to be examined in the light of this defence. I will 
take up the 0950 of retrenchment of Dhal Bahadur Rai and Gokul Sing Rai 
first. lt appears from the materials on record that Purna Sing Rai, Chowkidar, 
was also retrenched along with these two employees. Dhalbahadur was a 
Munsi and Gokul Sing was a chaprasi. All are permanent employees of very 
long standing and residents within the Estate. It further appears that Purna 
Sing was subsequently taken into service. It has naturally been very seriously 
commented from the side of the Union that the plea of retrenchment on econo- 
mic grounds is apparently a false one, for otherwise one out of three would not 
have been taken in by the Company. It has also been urged by the Union 
that the economic grounds suggested now on the side of the management for 
retrenchment are not supported by any reliable evidence in the case. At any 
rate, an economic crisis could not be averted in the way as alleged by the 
Management. Further, in effecting this retrenchment, the well-settled principle 
“Last Come First Go” was not followed. It is clear from Annexure “B”, a 
copy of a letter of the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Darjeeling, dated 16th 
June 1952, to the Manager of this tea estate, which has not been controverted 
or denied in any way from the side of the management, that the management 
prepared “a list for retrenchment of 71 persons recruited between 1947 and 
1949 and that these three persons were not in that list. Admittedly, Dalbahadur 
Rai and Gokul Singh Rai are very old employees of the estate. The manage- 
ment has not made any attempt to explain this very significant fact, namely, why 
লা who are ce junior to these two persons were left out and that thesc 
two old employees with a good record of service, holding position of trust and 
responsibility (one of them has filed a good cerfificate from the Manager) were 
retrenched. This establishes two points in favour of the employees, namely, 
(i) the principle “Last Come First Go” was not followed; and (1) the econo- 
mies sought to be made by this retrenchment is negligible in comparison with 
the alleged heavy losses sustained by the Company. Regarding the question 
of loss sustained by the Company, the entire onus is upon it to show by 
evidence that at the relevant time, the Company was running at an enormous 
loss-and that it decided to economise in all possible matters. 


The evidence on the side of the management consists of sworn testimony 
of O.P.W. 1 C. B. Rai, Head Clerk and Accountant of the estate and a few 
reports of the Directors previous to that of 1950 and two slips signed by the 

resent Manager, who has not deposed in this case to prove that. The present 

anaging Agents Messrs. Goenka & dl se a the garden from the 
last owners Messrs. James Finlay & Co. in 1946, He said that the financial 
condition of the garden is bad. He proved the balance-sheets of 1948, 1949 
and 1950 and the siatement prepared by Mr. Wallace, the present Manager 
(Ext. J). The accounts were not produced before the Tribunal. The state- 
ment (Ext. J), said to be drawn up by Mr. Wallace showing a total loss of 
Rs. 1,51,848-8-Op., in 1952, is mot supported either by the evidence of 
Mr. Wallace or by the accounts of which they are supposed to be an extract.

The accounts of 1951 are also not forthcoming. Ext. K——Directors’ report of 
1930—shows that the future of 1951 is very ‘brigh and the accounts of that 
ear show a profit of Rs. 27,769-2-9p. The accounts of the relevant years 
1951 and 1952 have been withheld, and the only natural presumption, which 
a court of law is entitled to draw is that the same, if produced would be un- 
favourable to the management in this casc. Tea Industry as a whole was 
passing through critical times and the State Government had to intervene 
in the matter to help the اس‎ as far ag possible, to carry on _ its 
work of production as before, This Tribunal can take a judicial notice of this 
fact. But that does not amount to saying that all the tea gardens, including 
the one in dispute, had suffered considerable loss in the relevant year, namcly 
1952. No such presumption can be drawn from them. Two other documents 
purporting to be notice issued by the Company dated 13th November 1952 
and 10th March 1953 (Exts. E and A), closing the garden and reopening it 
were Casually referred to. They are, beside the point, Ext. F which shows that 
the garden was closed sine die wih effect from 26th November 1952, in view 
uf the heavy losses sustained by the Company during the past years and the 
present financial crisis due to slump in the tea market and the uneconomic high 
cost of production, the services of the employees were terminated with immce- 
diate effect. The monthly paid staff was promised a month’s salary in lieu of 
notice. This neither proves the loss which the Company is said to have 
sustained in the past, nor the crisis due so slump in the market, nor it shows that 
the services of the employees were terminated on proper payment. In fact, 
this has no connection with the retrenchment of the two employees now under 
consideration. It appears from Exts. 2 and 3 that these two employees were 
erved with notices on 7th May 1952. They were continuing in service despite 
at Exts. 2 and 3, dated 12th June 1952, is the second notice which threatened 
the employees with stoppage of rations from the next ration date. It is not 
the Company’s case that the services of these two employees were terminated 
by notice (Ext. D) along with others when the garden was closed. Ext. F 
does not refer to this Company. Even if it is assumed for the sake of argu- 
ment, that a similar notice was issued by this Company as well, this only shows 
that a material change in conditions and circumstances has been brought about 
by the food relief and financial encouragement by the Government in the form 
of guarantee to the bankers and the consequential interim sanction of funds by 
the bank. In fact, the financial crisis, alleged by the management, was over 
by this time. This in any event, does not relate to the relevant period, namely, 
May/June 1952, when these two employees were retrenched. P. W. 1 Dal- 
bahadur has deposed in this case. He said he had been in the service of this 
Company for the last 27 or 28 years and was getting wages at the rate of Rs. 58 
per month at the time of retrenchment. He did not work anywhere since the 
retrenchment. He is a resident employee and as such a permanent one. He 
categorically denies that he worked in the Risheehat Tea Estate. He said that 
his employment was opposed by the other workers when the garden reopened. 
He went for the employment of the garden sometime after, when he was refused 
on the ground that he would not get it without signing an undertaking offered 
hy the management. Gokul Sing Rai has not deposed. I will presently dis- 
cuss the case of refusal of work in connection with other workers. In my view, 
the undertaking, pursuant to a resolution contained in°Ext. G, of which Ext. 
G-1 is the English translation, is a document, which an employee is not under 
the Standing Orders obliged to sign, or execute as a condition of getting re- 
employment. The undertaking is not an agreement for it does not bind the 
Company. It contains, among others, clauses which take away an acknowledged 
legal right of an employee to approach the authorities in case of delay in pay- 
ment of wages, and encourages, among other things, espionage in _ service. 
Both are objectionable, and the employees in refusing to sign this document did 
nothing wrong to justify refusal of employment to them. In any view of the

matter, the retrenchment and refusal of employment to these two employees are 
not justified. Both of them, in normal course, are entitled to reinstatement in 
their former or equivalent posts. As to compensation, they being permanent 
employees in the service of this estate, are ات‎ entitled to wages for the 
entire periods of non-employment. But regard being had to the present condi- 
tion of the tea industry and of this Company in particular, it is undesirable that 
they should get the wages for the entire period. Further, both these employees 
had worked temporarily in the neighbouring garden during the period of unem- 
ployment. There cannot be any reasonable objection to that for one must 
earn to live. But it has been proved in this case that none of these employees 
had been in employment throughout the period of their non-employment under 
this Company. This Tribunal considering the facts and circumstances of this 
case, allows the two employees three months’ wages as compensation for the 
period of their non-employment. The manapement is_ directed to pay _ this 
amount within a month from the date of the operation of this Award. The 
employees shall present themselves to the Manager of the garden for employ- 
ment within a week from the date of the operation of this award. 


As to the remaining 12 employees, the Management’s position seems to be 
this : (i) the Management did not refuse employment to any, it was the majority 
cf the workers who objected to their employment; (11) they refused to sign an 
undertaking which other workers signed; (iii) two out of them joined but 
subsequently left on getting higher wages in the Risheehat Tea Estate; (iv) all 
stayed out on an inducement from the Union in the hope of getting handsome 
compensation for the period of unemployment; and (v) all worked in the 
neighbouring gardens during the period of unemployment. The Union of 
course denies the management’s case. Seven of these workers have deposed in 
this case. Of them P. W. 7 Lagha Mangar is a resident employee. He worked 
for about 11 years and was drawing a salary of Rs. 24-12 as per month at the 
time of discharge. He admits that the other workers opposed his employment 
when he presented himself for work on the reopening date. He did not work 
anywhere after the closing of the garden. He did not work in the 1 
Tea Estate. His wife is working here. Then he admitted that almost all the 
workers had to work elsewhere to make their both ends meet during the time 
the garden was closed. They worked in the Risheehat Tea Estate. P, W. 8 
Shri Dhanbir said that he was in service for the last 25 or 26 years and his 
wages were Rs. 29-4 when the garden was closed. He said that almost all the 
workers including himself worked for one in the Risheehat Tea Estate when 
their garden was closed. He said he refused ا٢‎ sign the undertaking for it 
contained objectionable clauses. Nothing has been said that they were given 
work and then subsequently left the service of the estate on getting higher wages. 
Nothing like that was suggested in their cross-examinations. It is now idle to 
argue that they resumed but subsequently left on getting higher wages _ else- 
where. It is now proved beyond doubt from the evidence of both sides as also 
from. the evidence of the Company’s Head Clerk, from the Manager’s letter, 
that on the reopening date, the majority of the workers signed an undertaking, 
offered by the management, and objected to these employees taken in, as they 
refused to sign. ‘These employees refused to sign the undertaking and worked 
for a short time elsewhere in the neighbouring gardens during the period of their 
long non-employment. It has not been proved in this case that any of them 
stayed out on the inducement of the Union Officials in the hope of getting 
handsome compensation from this Tribunal for the period of their non-emplov- 
ment. Any such suggestion appears to be childish and devoid of merit. It is 
too much to expect that these poor workers would be staying out on anybody’s 
advice in the hope of getting something in future from the Tribunal. 


Two principal points arise in this connection, namely, (1) whether these 
employees forfeited their claim to the employment on their refusal to sign the

নি 


undgrtaking offered by the Management on the reopening day. This takes us 
0705 more to the undertaking itself. It is in the form of a resolution adopted 
at a meeting of the workers (vide Ext. G.) English translation of which is 
admitted by the Head Clerk to be correct (vide Ext. G.1.). All the terms and 
conditions of this undertaking appear to be very harsh and objectionable, parti- 
cularly clause 7 which refers to the payment of wages and clause 8 which 
relates to the newly imposed duty to spy on others’ activities and to report to 
the Company. The ic হা is entitled, in certain circumstances, to get a 
signed undertaking from their employees. But then, the conditions of service 
10005 be those laid down in the Standing Orders. The Standing Orders appli- 
৫8016 to Tea Gardens including this one is Ext. 5. The objectionable clause 
Jo not appear in the Standing Orders. Therefore, the employees did nothing - 
wrong in refusing to sign this objectionable undertaking. One other point, 
though not raised in the Company’s written statement, is that the services of 
these employees were terminated by a notice when the garden was closed. And 
that was according to the Standing Orders. The notice in this case is Ext. E. 
The Union challenges it. Their contention is that no such notice was issued 
to the employees or given effect to by payment of proper wages mentioned 
therein. In this connectton, the accounts are the most relevant evidence to 
show that in fact, on the day the garden was closed sine die, according to this 
notice, all the employees including the monthly paid staff were paid their wages 
and notice pay. Nothing like that was even attempted in this case. The 
accounts have been withheld. The employees, who deposed in this case, were 
not asked in cross-examination that they were paid their wages when the garden 
was closed and their services were terminated. All the employees are resident 
iof the estate and according to the Standing Orders, are permanent employees. 
It is only reasonable that on the re-opening day of the garden, when some out- 
siders were taken in, the permanent employees should be offered employment. 
he management, who is the final authority to employ its labour force, adopted 
ah abnormal course in the case of these employees. They did listen to the 
objection of the majority of the workers to their re-employment and _ their 
oiherwise claim to work. The Management, it seems, was anxious at the early 
stage of this dispute, for a settlement and accordingly on the very day the garden 
reopened, the Manager wrote to the local Assistant Labour Commissioner for 
his intervention in the matter. The Assistant Labour Commissioner intervened 
and the Management agreed to take all the employees but subsequently backed 
out. They should not have done so. An employee, when out of employment, 
for no fault of his own, must live with his family. It is only natural that he 
should try to earn a living to make both ends meet. He would not certainly 
forfeit his claim to re-employment by doing so, particularly when the Manage- 
ment was not making any provision for him during the period of his unemploy- 
ment, which in this case is pretty long. The Management has failed to establish 
that these employees were in continuous service of the neighbouring gardens 
throughout the period of their non-employment here. Casual or temporary 
employment, as stated above, for earning a livelihood will not disentitle any 
one to compensation otherwise payable to him. The case of one emplovee is 
different. P. W. 4 Dawa Tshering was a school teacher (No. 9.) mentioned in 
the schedule to the order of reference. The management refused him employ- 
ment when the garden reopened. He is out of employment even now. But 
then, it is the Union’s case, and his evidence is that the school did not reopen 
with the reopening of the garden. When he approached the Manager, he told

him that the Management had decided to close the school. In these circum- 
। stances, he cannot be taken into service of the Company till the school ts not

The Company will of course employ him, or offer emoloyment to him, when
