DECISION. 


The subject matter ot this appeal relates to the question of retrenchment 
of 24 clerks and to some other matters referred for adjudication. These clerks 
are the employees of the Garden Reach Workshop, Ltd. (hereafter called the 
Company). The Company has a workshop doing the business of painting 
and repairs of inland and deep-sea cargo and passenger vessels calling at the 
Port of Calcutta. It. workshop was originally at Howrah and was removed 
to Garden Reach (Kidderpore) sometime in 1925-26 Messrs. Macneill & 
Barry, Ltd., are the Managing Agents of this Company, having their head office 
at No. 2, Fairlie Place, Calcutta. Most of the clerical staff of the Company 
are stationed at its workshop office at Garden Reach and some 40 or 50 clerks 
were stationed at the head office of the Managing Agents at No. 2, Fairlie 
Place, Calcutta. Between thg years 1940-45, the লন: had a strength of 
about 5,000 workmen under their direct employment an about 2.000 workmen 
under the contractors. In 1949, the strength of the labour torce was about 
7,500. But by reason of the fall in the volume of business the labour forse

Issue No. 1.—This issue relates to the question of retrenchment of 24 
permanent 01015. The Tribunal has held that the rctrenchment of these 24 
clerks was made for genuine trade reasons and was fully justified. This finding 
of the ‘Tribunal has been challenged by Mr. D. L. Sen Guptu on behalf of 
the workmen. His argument is (1) that the Management has failed to make 
out a case for retrenchment and (2) that in muking the retrenchments it Jid 
not act in a !ہم‎ fide manner. ‘There is no substance in either of these con- 
tentions. It is conceded that the strength of labour was reduced from 7,400 
to 4,000 in the beginning of 195]. Shri Harihar Chakravorty (P.W. 1) 
cxamined by the workmen admits that the number of workmen in 1945 was 
7.000 and now the number  چ‎ less than 5,000, Shri Nripen Das (P.W. 2) states 
that about 650 workmen were retrenched in 1951 and about 1,000 workmen 
left the services of the Company voluntarily in 1950. The reduction of labour 
force to almost half of the original number is thus admitted by the workmen 
themselves. The question is whether the retrenchment of such a large number 
of workmen in the workshop was due to shrinkage of work. The evidence of 
Mr. C. P. Davis, the Chief Accountant of the Garden Reach Workshop, is 
that stcel, timber and paintare the main materials used by the Company to 
carry out repair works. He has stated that the Company muaintains figures 
showing the amount of steel and timber ,¢consumed in the various 
years and that these figures show 0081 ¢ volume of work done 
in the workshop had very considerably * dropped in 1950. Ext. 
“B” is a copy of the report forwarded by Mr. Davis to Mr. 
Boyes on the 4th October 1950 showing the consumption of steel and 
timber during different periods in 1950. Similarly Ext. “G” shows shrinkage 
of repair works but they do not indicate whether there was any reduction of 
paint work. Mr. Davis admits that the Company has no figures showing the 
amount of paint used. Mr. D. L. Sen Gupta contends that even if there was 
decrease in repair works, there might have been incrcase in the work of paint- 
ing. -There is no force in this speculative argument, for Nripen Das admits 
that a large number of workmen had to be kept on enforced leave in 1950/51, 
before the date of retrenchment. The balance-shects of the Company (C-C9) 
fur the half year cnding 30th Se ber 1949, 30th September 1950 and 31st 
March 1951 also show losses and downward trend in the business of the work- 
shop though the balance-sheet for the half year ending 30th September 1951 
discloses some profit. Thus on an examination vf the evidence to which we 
have referred, there is no escape from the conclusion that there was shrinkage 
of work and the surplus labour had to be retrenched on grounds of economy. 
Now the question is whether there was any justification in retrenching these 24 
clerks. The Company’s case is that owing to shrinkage of manual work and 
heavy loss incurred, by the Company, during the previous years, retrenchment 
of the clerks, was necessitated on grounds of econdmy, and that the Company 
acted bona fide in reducing the strength of the clerical: staf. The contention 
of Shri Sen Gupta is that even if the retrenchment of labour be justified there

was no justification for retrenching these 24 clerks, and in support of this con-

this contention for Harihar Chakemvarty’s evidence is contradicted by the 
evidence of Mr. C. P. Davis and the balance-sheets (C-C9) of the ری سس‎ 


Mr. C. P. Davis in his evidence states that the bulk of the work of the clerks 
in the Garden Reach Workshop is of a routine nature, such ds requisitioning 
materials required for the technicians, booking of Jabour in accordance with 
information given by the foreman of the departments, recording attendance,

the workmen has decreased during the last 2 or 3 years, there has becn a

the overhead establishment by reason of the reduction of the workload in the

ing to the evidence of Mr C P. Davis, by a firm of efficient experts. The result

however, did not make drastic retrenchment. Only 24 clerks were retrenched 
after a thorough investigation. The Management cannot, therefore, be said to 
have been actuated by ulterior motives in making the retrenchment As the

Management in such circumstances had a right to determine the number to be 
retrenched We cannot, therefore, interfere with the award of the Tribunal 
on this issue and it is, therefore, affirmed

of the clerical staff were revised and the clerks were classified into three grades 
with imecremental scales, namely,—

(2) Grade B—Rs !10—7—180.

A flat increment of Rs 10) was also given to all the members 01 the clerical staff

The first paragraph of this circular shows that it was agreed“by the Manag- 
ing Agents that while the Company remains under their Management, the clerical 
staff of the company stationed at their head office at Fairlie Place will be paid 
the same salaries and dearness allowance as are paid to their own clerks and 
that they would be entitled to the benfit of leave attendance rules. The Manag- 
ing Agents ‘pave effect to this by extending the benefit of the combined grade 
to the clerks of the Company stationed at the head office—obviously in 
compliance with the terms of the first paragraph of Ext. H. The second para- 
graph clearly shows that there was a conditional promise, the fulfilment of 
which depended upon the feasibility of extending the benefit and not an agreement 
laying down conditions of » service, This paragraph clearly shows that the 
nature of the clerical work in tbe workshop § and in the main office was not 
considered identical. In view of the distinction maintained by the Managing 
Agents in the nature of work at the workshop and in the head office, they 
simply promised to give the same scales of salary and dearness allowance, it 
practicable. A distinction ts made in clear and unambiguous terms between 
the first and second paragraphs ; as a matter of construction, therefore, it is a 
contingent promise and not a contract embodying the conditions of service. 
Whether or not it was feasible to extend the benefit of the combined grade to 
the clerks stationed at the workshop depended entirely upon the decision not 
to extend of the Managing جارس ا‎ and if they have ultimately decided not to 
extend the benefit of the combined grade to the clerical staff at the workshop, 
the latter cannot claim the er as a matter of right on the basis of Ext. H. 
The award on this issue must, therefore, be affirmed. 


Issue No. 4.—This issue relates to the Pension Scheme of the clerical staff 
of the Company. At one time, the clerks of the workshop used to receive the 
same retiring benefits as the clerks of Messrs. Macneill & Company. It appears 
from Ext. D, that from May 1945, a new pension scheme relating to the Indian 
clerica) staff of the Garden Reach Workshopy, Ltd., was introduced and under 
that scheme the~clerks with more than 15 years’ service and less than 20 years’ 
service became entitled by way of pension to 1/68 of their salary ; 2/6th of 
their salary if their service was over 20 years anti below 25 years; 3/6th of 
their salary if their service was over 25 years and below 30 years and 4/6th 
of their salary if their service was over 30 years. Im or about March 1947, 
Messrs. Macneill & Company revised the Pension Scheme relating to their 
own clerical staff slightly improving the benefit and their revised Pension 
Scheme was adopted by the Major Mercantile Tribunal in its award. The 
revised scheme of Messrs. Macneill & Co., is slightly better than the Company's 
Pension Scheme in that the denominator is 5 in place of six but in other 
respects there is no substantial difference in the two schemes. The Pension 
Schemes ,) Messrs. Macneill & Co., and of the Garden Reach Workshops, Ltd., 
are fully set out in the award under appeal. The contention of Shri Sen Gupta 
is that the clerical staff of the Company are entitled to the same retiring bene- 
fits as are given to the clerical staff of the Managing Agents. Thare is no force 
in this contention. For, it appears from the statement in the last paragraph 

Ext. H. That the scale سب تر‎ applicable to the Garden Reach Work- 
shop staff was different from that applicable to the Macneill & Co.’s staff and 
that the question of difference was under review by the Directors. Appendix 
A to the written statement of the Company, dated the 16th January 1950, 
shows that the position was actually reviewed by the ار ود‎ Agents and on 
an examination of the whole position, they express their inability to alter the 
Garden Reach Workshop’s Pensions Scheme ant bring it, in line with their 
ows. In view of the fact that the Company his got its own scheme and the 
scaig authorised by the.Company is liberal, we do got think that any-chenge 
جا‎ warratited. The award on this issue 2908 theretote, be upheld.

Issue No. 8.——This issue relates to tiffin allowance. Admittedly, the 
Managing Agents, Messrs. Macneill & Barry, Ltd., pay annas 9 per day to every 
clerk employed by them at their head office and also to the Company’s clerks 
Slationed at their head office, but no such allowance is given by the Company 
to their clerks stationed at their Garden Reach Workshop. The Union 
demanded the same amenity for them also but the Tribunal has rejected the 
claim. Shri D. L. Sen Gupta has challenged this award and his contention 
is that the Tribunal should have made 170 distinction in the matter of tiffin 
allowance between the Company’s clerks stationed at the Managing Agents’ 
head office and their clerical staff stationed at the Garden Reach Workshop. 
We do not think that there is any force in this contention. According to 
Nripen Das (P.W. 2) no tiffin allowance had been given by Messrs. Macneill 
& Barry, Ltd., to their clerks employed at their Head Office up to 1949; but 
it appears that from 1950, they started giving annas 9 per day to every clerk 
employed by them’ at the head offie and this arrangement was confirmed by the 
Major Mercantile Tribunal’s award and is still continuing. Although the 
Company does not give any tiffin allowance to its employees at the Garden 
Reach Workshop, it maintains a canteen on non-profit basis since 1948. It 
supplies food at cheap rates and for running this canteen, the Company spends 
about Rs. 12,000 per year. Having got the benefit of the canteen, the clerical 
staff stationed at the Garden Reach Workshop cannot, in our opinion, claim 
a further benefit in the shape of tiffin allowance simply by the reason of the 
fact that the Managing Agents’ clerical staff or the Company's clerks stationed 
at the head office get the benefit of such allowance, when there is no cheap 
canteen maintained for those clerks. The conditions of service of the two 
companies are not the same. If the Managing Agents have extended the 
benefit of tiffin allowance to the Company’s clerks, stationed at the head office 
they have done so not in recognition of any rights of the Company’s clerical 
staff at the head office, but simply to maintain uniformity of treatment and 
to avoid heart burning and discontent. The Tribunal has rightly rejected the 
claim and the award is accordingly affirmed. | 


Issue No. 9.—This issue relates to travelling allowance and ferry pass. 
Originally the Company’s workshop was at Howrah. After the workshop was 
transferred to Garden Reach the Company allowed Ferry Pass to those clerks 
only who had been working at the Howrah workshop office, and who were in 
the Company's books at the time of the transfer of the workshop. In 1950, 
the ferry pass system was discontinued owing to Breakdowns in the Public Ferry

148 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Parr IA 
¢ 


سے سس سے سے جج سے جس ےج سے سے سس سہ سے کے سر کس سے سس گج سے گککک حجحہھہس-حتے_ وس چتے٣٠”-_ ٣‏ 0گ گ"'گ,۰' گ ‏ گگ ‏ ,کے جج زتن(مںزنںن'نںج 'گ ‏ گ ‏ ——— 


Services and this caused inconvenience to some of the clerical staff. There- 
fore, by a notice dated the 2nd May 1950, the Company, intimated to those 
old clerks that they would be given equivalent cash payment in lieu of ferry 
pass and this was given effect to from Ist June 1950. It was clearly stated 
in the notice that no clerk appointed thereafter and not holding a ferry, pass, 
would be entitled to this concession, The Union claimed that all clerks who 
do not reside in the locality shoufd be given travelling allowance of annas 
twelve per day. The Tribunal has rejected this claim, and in our opinion, 
rightly. The clerks who were employed at the Howrah baal ys were given 
free passes when the office was transferred to Garden Reach and later on they 
got money equivalent in the shape of travelling allowance because there was 
change in a conditions of their service. But the new entrants appointed 
after the Company’s transfer of the workshop to the Garden Reach had no 
right under the terms of their appointment to claim travelling allowance which 
were granted to old clerks in lieu of the ferry pass. If they accepted the 
appointment, it is a condition of their service that they should attend the office 
and for any expense incurred by them for attending their duty, they cannot 
claim to be recouped. The Tribunal has, therefore, rightly rejected the claim. 
We accordingly uphold the decision of the Tribunal on this issue also. 

We may notice here that it was faintly contended that the travelling allow- 
ance to old entrants at annas 9 per day is insufficient. It was conceded that 
the point was net raised in the written statement nor is there any evidence to 
support their contention. It must, therefore, be rejected. 


Issues Nos. 7 and 10.—These issues may be taken up together. Issue 
No. 7 relates to “ working hours for day duty and night duty clerks” and Issue 
No. 10 relates to “ public holidays”, The Tribunal has negatived the claim 
of the Union in respect of both these matters. The decision of the Tribunal 
is based on the appreciation of evidenee in the case and is concluded by find- 
ings of fact. It is conceded that an appeal can 116 on these issues only if there 
be a substantial question of law involved. @#bri D. L. Sen Gupta was unable 
to forthulate any question of law, much less a substantial one. The appeal 
on, those issu@s must, therefare, be held to be incompetent and dismissed as 
such. 

For the foregoing reasons the whole appeal is dismissed and the award on 
he issues discussed above is affirmed. We make no order as to costs.

1. Admission. 


1. The College is open to students of all communities and religious 
persuasions. 


2. Applications for admission should be made in the printed form soon 
after the publication of the University results. The form may be had 
from the College office on personal application or by sending a stamped 
envelope. 


3. ‘Students who have passed the Matriculation Examination in the 
lst or 2nd Division may be admitted to the College. Applications from 
the students passing the Matriculation Examination in the 3rd Division 
will also be received which will be considered if seats are available after 
admitting the students passing in the Ist or 2nd _ Division. Women 
students fulfilling the above conditions may also be admitted to the 
College’’. Students who have come with transter certificates from other 
Colleges may be admitted if their attendance and progress in studies at the 
College where they last studied are considered satisfactory. Plucked 
candidates ure required to produce the mark-sheet or the cross list. Students 
from other Universities or School Boards should submit their Matriculation 
mark-sheet und Migration certificate with their application.

NOTICE. 


‘APPLICATIONS are invited for admission to the next 
term of the Prince of Wales's Mulltary College, Dehra 
Dun, commencing in January 1956. 


Course.—The College provides a public school education 
for boys who wish to obtain commissions in the Army, 
Navy or Air Force. The educational training is designed 
to bring boys up to the standard of the Senior Cambridge 
School Certificate und the Qualifying Examinations for 
entry into the National Defence Academy. Compulsory 
physical training, games and parades ensure physica! 
fituess and smartness; while special attention is paid to 
the imparting of discipline, self-reliance and social train- 
ing to all cadets. 


. Admission.— Candidates for admission te the next term 
of the College which commences from January 1955, will 
have to quality at an Entrance Examimation to be held 
at Caleutta some time in 3rd week of September 1954 
tollowfd by an interview. 


Age limits.—Onandidates must have been born noi 
earher than 218 January 1943 and not later than 20th 
Janyary 1944. The age limits can m no 0889 be relaxed. 


Educational qualifications.—_No educational qualification 
is prescribed for admission to 0718 College but it is 
expected that the candidate should have rend up to 
Class VIT standard of a Secondary School. 


Fees.—The fees are Rs. 750 per term plus additional 
expenses of Rs, 400 (e.g., uniforms, pocket money, books, 
washing, ete.). The actual cost is ‘thus Rs. 2,300 per 
innym. A cadet spends 6 to 6 years at the College. 


Scholarships.—A limited number of scholarships _ ot 

1,000 per annum is awarded to the deserving cadets 

after admission to the College by the West Bengul 
Gjovernment.

ACT NO. XXX ‘OF 1954. 
THE SALARIES AND ALLOWANCES OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT 
A ৫ 


| [2274 May, 1954.] 
An Att to provide for the salaries and allowances of Members of Parliament. 


‘it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of the Republic of India as‏ سس 
follows :---‏ 


1. Short title and commencement—(/) This Act may be called the 
Salaries and Allowances of Members of Parliament Act, 1954. 


(2) It shall come into force on the first day of June, 1954. 
2. Definitions.—In this Act,— 


(a) ‘committee’ means a Committee of either House of Parliament, and 
includes a Joint Committee of both H@uses; 


(b) ‘member’ means a member of either House of Parliament, but does not 
include— 


(i) a Minister as defined in the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers 
Act, 1952 (LVIII of 1952); and 


(it) an officer of Parliament, as defined in the Salaries and Allowances 
of Officers of Parliament Act, 1953 (20 of 1953); 


(c) ‘new member’ means a member who takes his seat in either House of 
Parliament after the commencement of this Act and includes a 
member who is re-elected or re-nominated; 


(d) ‘period of residence on duty’ méans the period during which a 
member resides at a place where a session of a House of Parlia- 
ment or a sitting of a committee is held or where any other 


188 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Parr V 
১৬০২ 


business connected with his duties as such member is transacted, 
for the purpose of attending such session or sitting or for the -pur- 
pose of attending to such other business, and includes— 


(1) in the case of a session of a House of Parliament, a period of such 
residence, not exceeding three days, immediately preceding the 
commencement of the session and a period of such residence, not 
exceeding three days, immediately succeeding the end of the 
session, and 


(ii) in the case of a sitting of a committee or any other business, a 
period of such residence, not exceeding two days, immediately 
preceding the commencement of the business of the committee or 
other business and a period of such residence, not exceeding two 
days, immediately succeeding the conclusion of the business of 
the committee or other business; 


Explanation—A member who ordmarily resides at a place where a 
session of a House of Parliament or a sitting of a Committee is 
held or where any other business connected with his duties as 
such member is transacted shall, for the duration of the session 
or sitting or the time occupied for the transaction of other 
business (including the three or two days immediately preceding 
or succeeding), be deemed to reside at such place for the pur- 
pose of attending such session or sitting or, as the case may be, 
for the purpose of attending to such other business; 


(e) ‘term of office’ means,— 


(a) in relation to a person who is a member at the commencement of 
this Act, the period beginning with such commencement and 
ending with the date.on which his seat becomes vacant; 


(৮) in relation to a new member, the period beginning with the date 
when such member takes his seat in the House of the People or 
the Council of States, as the case may be, and ending with the 
date on which his seat becomes vacant. 


3. Salaries and daily allowances.—A member shall be entitled to receive 
a salary at the rate of four hundred rupees per mensem during the whole of his 
term of office plus an allowance at the rate of twenty-one rupees for each day 
during any period of residence on duty. 


4. Travelling allowances.—(/) There shall be paid to each member 
in respect of every journey performed by him for the purpose of attending a 
session of a House of Parliament or a meeting of a Committee or for the pur- 
pose of attending to any other business connected with his duties as a member, 
from his usual place of residence to the place where the session or the meeting 
is to be held or other business is to be transacted and for the return journey 
from such place to his usual place of residence— 


(a) if the journey is performed by rail, an amount equal to one second 
class fare plus one third class fare for each such journey, irres- 
pective of the class in which the member actually travels; 


(b) if the journey is performed by air, an amount equal to one and one- 
fourth of the air fare for each such journey; 


(c) if the journey or any part thereof cannot be performed by rail or 
air— = 
(1) where the journey or any part thereof is performed by 
steamer, an amount equal to one and _ three-fifths of 
the fare (without diet) for the highest class in the steamer for 

each such journey or part thereof; 


Part V] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 189 


(ii) where the journey or any part thereof is performed by road, a road 
milage at the rate of eight annas per mile for each such journey or 
part thereof. 


Explanation.—For the purposes of sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of this 
sub-section, the.expression ‘journey’ shall include the journcy from and to the 
railway station, port or aerodrome to and from the usual place of residence of 
the member or as the case may be, the residence of the member at the place 
where the session of the House of Parliament or a meeting of the Committee is 
to be held or where any other business is to be transacted. 


.(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), a member who 
performs a journey by road between places connected by rail or steamer, either 
wholly or in part, may draw the mileage allowance _ referred 
to in sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of sub-section (4) in place of 
the the travelling allowance which have been admissible to him if 
he had travelled by rail or steamer, as the case may be: 


Provided that the total amount of travelling allowance drawn by such mem- 
ber for the entire journey shall not exceed the amount which would have been 
admissible to him had he performed such journey by rail or by steamer, as the 
case may be. 


Travelling allowances for intermediate journeys —Where a member‏ ۔ 
absents himself for less than fifteen days during a session of a House of Parlia-‏ 
mem or a sitting of a Committee for visiting any place in India, he shall be‏ 
entitled to receive travelling allowances in respect of such journey to such place‏ 
and for the return journey—‏ 


(a) if the journey is performed by rail, equal to one second class fare for 
each such journey irrespective of the class in which the member 
actually travels; 


(b) if the journey is performed by air, equal to one fare by air for each 
such journey : 


Provided that such travelling allowances shall not exceed the total amount 
of daily allowances which would have been admissible to such 
member under section 3 for the days of absence if he had not so 
remained absent. 


Explanation—The provisions of clause (c) of sub-section (1) and of sub- 
section (2) of section 4 shall, so far as may be, apply to travelling allowances 


payable under this section as they apply to travelling allowances payable under 
that section. 


6. Free transit by Railway.—Every member shall be provided with one 
free non-transferable second class pass which shall entitle him to travel by any 
railway in India at any time, but nothing contained in this section shall affect the 


payment of any travelling allowance payable to a member under any other pro- 
vision of this Act. 


7. Allowances during short intervals between the termination of one 
session and the commencement of another session, etc.—Where the interval 
between the termination of one session of a House of Parliament or, as the case 
may be, one sitting of a Committee and the commencement of another session 
or sitting at the same place does not exceed seven days and the member con- 
cerned elects to remain at such place during the interval, he shall be entitled 
to draw for each day of residence at such place a daily allowance at the rate 
specified in section 3: 


190 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Parr V 


Provided that if the member leaves such place during the interval, his 
absence from the place shall be treated as absence during a session of a House 
of Parliament or a sitting of the Committee, as the case may be, and the provi- 
sions of section 5 shall apply accordingly. 


8. Amenities—A member shall be entitled to such medical, housing, 
telephone and postal facilities as may be prescribed by rules under section 9. 


9. Power to make rules.—(/) For the purpose of making rules under this 
section, there shall be constituted a Joint Committee of both Houses of Parlia- 
ment consisting of five members from the Council of States nominated by the 
Chairman and ten members from the House of the People nominated by the 
Speaker. 


(2) The Joint Committee constituted under sub-section (1) shall elect its 
Chairman and shall have power to regulate its procedure. 


(3) The Joint Committee constituted under sub-section (J) may make 
rules to provide for all or any of the following matters, namely :— 


(৫) the routes for the performance of any journey; 


(b) the manner in which fractions of a day shall be dealt with for the 
purpose of determining the daily allowance admissible for that day; 


(c) the travelling allowance admissible where a member is provided with 
free transit for the whole or any part of a journey; 


(d) the travelling allowance admissible where the place from which a 
member commences his journey or to which he returns is not his 
usual place of residence; 


(e) the form in which certificates, if any, shall be furnished by a member 
for the purpose of claiming any allowance under this Act; 


(1) medical, housing, telephone and postal facilities mentioned in section 
; and 
(g) generally for regulating the payment of daily and travelling allowances 
under this Act. 


(4) Any rules made under sub-section (3) shall not take effect until they 
are approved and confirmed by the Chairman of the Council of States and the 
Speaker of the House of the People and are published in the Official Gazette, 
and gone! publication of the rules shall be conclusive proof that they have been 
duly made. 


10. Validation of payment of certain travelling allowances.—Where a 
member is entitled to receive travelling allowance in respect of any journey 
performed by him by a railway before the commencement of this Act, he shall, 
notwithstanding the abolition of first class accommodation on such railway, be 
entitled and be deemed always to have been entitled to receive travelling 
allowance in respect of such journey at the rates admissible to him in accord- 
ance with the law then in force, as if the first class accommodation had not been 
abolished on such railway and as if the member had in fact travelled by _ first 
class and, accordingly, the payment of any travelling allowance to such member 
in respect of such journey at the aforesaid rates shall be deemed to have been 

validly made and shall not be called in question by any authority on the ground 
only that the first class accommodation had been abolished on such railway 
and that the member had not in fact travelled by first class. 


K. Y. BHANDARKAR, Secy.

The following Act of the Parliament of India received the assent of 
ne President on the 28th May, 1954 and is hereby published for general

ACT XXXII OF 1954. 


THE SHILLONG (RIFLE RANGE AND UMLONG) CANTONMENTS 
ASSIMILATION OF LAWS ACT, 1954. 


[28th May, 1954. ] 


An Act to assimilate certain laws in force in the scheduled areas to the 
laws in force wn the Khasi and Jaintia Hills District. 


BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of the Republic of India 
as follows :— 


1. | Short title and commencement.—(7) This Act may be callgd the 
eae (Rifle Range and Umlong) Cantonments Assimilation of Laws 
ct, 4, 


(2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government 
may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint. 


2. Definitions.—In this Act,— 


(a) “appointed day’? means the date appointed under sub-section (2) 
of section 1 for the coming into force of this Act; 


(b) ‘law’? means so much of any Act, Ordinance, Regulation, rule, 
order or bye-law as relates to any of the matters enumerated in 
Lists I and III in the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution ; 


(c) ‘‘scheduled areas’? means the areas specified in the Schedule. 


3. Assimilation of laws.—(/) All laws which immediately before the 
appointed day extend to, or are in force in, the scheduled areas shall on 
that day cease to be in force in the scheduled areas except as respects things 
done or omitted to be done before that day, and for the removal of doubts, 
it is hereby declared that section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 (X of 
1897) shall apply in relation to such cesser as it applies in relation to the 
repeal of an enactment by a Central Act. 


(2) All laws which immediately before the appointed day extend to, 
or ure in force in, the Khasi and Jaintia Hills District shall as from that 
day extend to and be in force in the scheduled areas. 


4. Removal of difficulties.—If any difficulty arises in relation to the 
transition under section 3 from one law or group of laws to another law 
or group of laws, the Central Government may, by order notified in the 
Official Gazette, make such provisions as it considers necessary for the 
removal of the difficulty.

ACT NO. XXXII of 1954. 
THE HIMACHAL PRADESH AND BILASPUR 


(NEW STATE) ACT, 4. 
[28th May, 1954.] 


An Act to provide for the formation of the new State of Himachal 
Pradesh by uniting the existing States of Himachal Pradesh and 
Bilaspur, and for matters connected therewith. 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of the Republic of 
India as follows :— 
PART I. 


PRELIMINARY. 


1. Short title and commencement.—(7) This Act may be called the 
Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954. 


(2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Govern- 
শান by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint in this 
ehalf, 


2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise 
requires,— 
(a) ‘“‘article’’ means an article of the Constitution; 


(b) ‘‘Assembly constituency’’ has the same meaning as in the Govern- 
ment of Part C States Act, 1951 (XLIX of 1951); 


(c) ‘‘existing States’? mean the States specified as Bilaspur and 
Himachal Pradesh in Part C of the First Schedule to the Constitu- 
tion immediately before the commencement of this Act, and 
“existing State’’ means either of the existing States; 


(6) “law’’? includes any enactment, ordinance, regulation, order, 
rule, scheme, notification, bye-law or other instrument having 
the force of law in the whole or in any part of either of the 
existing States; 


(6) ‘‘Order’? means an order published in the Official Gazette ; 


(1) ‘‘Parliamentary constituency’? has the same meaning as 10 the 
Representation of the People Act, 1950 (XLITI of 1950) ; 


(7) ‘‘sitting member’”’ in relation to either House of Parliament or in 
relation to the Legislature of the existing State of -Himachal 
Pradesh, means a person who immediately before the commence- 
ment of this Act is a member of that House or that Legislature, 
as the case may be. 


PART II. 
ForMATION OF THE New Stats or HIMAcHAL PRADESH. 


3. Formation of the new State of Himachal Pradesh.—As from the 
commencement of this Act there shall be formed by uniting the existin 
States a new Part C State to be known as the State of Himachal Prades 
(hereafter in this Act referred to as the “new State’’).

REPRESENTATION IN THE LEGISLATURES. 
Council of States.

allotted one seat to the new State in the Council of States. 


(2) The sitting member of Council of States representing the group 
of States comprising the existing States shall on and from the commence- 
ment of this Act represent the new State in the Council but the term of 
such sitting membér shall remain unaltered, that is to say, shall expire on 
the 2nd of April, 1958.

_410. Parliamentary constituencies of the new State and their delimita- 
tion.—(7) The new State shall, until other provision is made by law, consist 
of the following three Parliamentary constituencies, namely :— 


(1) the constituency of Bilaspur comprising the existing Stute of 
Bilaspur; and 
(22) the two constituencies into which the existing State of Himachal 
Pradesh has been divided. 
(2) The Delimitation of Parliamentary Constituencies (Part (' States)

11. Sitting members.—(/) The sitting members of the Ilouse of the 
People representing the existing State of Bilaspur shall on and from 
the commencement of this Act represent the Bilaspur constituency 
of the new State and shall be deemed to have been elected to the House of 
the People by that constituency. 


(2) Every sitting member of the House of the People representing a 
constituency of the existing State of Himachal Pradesh shall on and trom

name in the new State and shall be deemed to have been elected to the House

Legislative Assembly of the New State. 


12. Legislative Assembly of the new State—(Z) There shall be a 
Legislative Assembly for the new State. 

(2) The total number of seats in that Legislative Assembly which shall 
be filled by direct election shall be 41.

14. Assembly constituencies of the new State and their delimitation. 
—(/) The new State shall, until other provision is made by law, consist 
of the following Assembly constituencies, namely :— 

(;) the constituencies shown at the commencement of this Act in_ the 
Delimitation of Assembly Constituencies (Himachal Pradesh) 
Order, 1951; and تا‎ 

(ii) the constituencies into which the part of the new State comprising 
the existing State of Bilaspur shall be divided. 


(2) The President shall, as soon as may be after the commencement 
of this Act, after consulting the Election Commission of India, amend the 
Delimitation of Assembly Constituencies (Himachal Pradesh) Order, 
1951 so as to include therein the constituencies into which the part of the 
new State comprising the existing State of Bilaspur, shall be divided and 
the said Order as so amended, shall, until superseded, be the Order relating 
to the delimitation of constituencies of the new State. 


15. Members of the বলার Assembly.—(/) Every sitting member 
of the Legislative Assembly of the existing State of Himachal Pradesh 
representing a constituency of the said State shall, on and from the

the new Stute and shall be deemed to have been elected to the 
Legislutive Assembly of the new State by that constituency.

21. Construction of Act XLIII of 1950 and Act XLIX of 1951.— 
Any reference to Himachal Pradesh in the Representation of the People

by this Act shall be construed as a reference to the new State. 


22. Electoral rolls of constituencies.—(7) The electoral rolls of the 
constituencies of the existing States shall, on and from the commencement 
of this Act, be deemed to be the electoral rolls of the constituencies of the

revised or fregh rolls are prepared, in accordance with law. . 


(2) The electoral rolls of the Assembly constituencies into which the

into force immediately upon their final publication.

velates to any or both of the existing States.

24. Rules of procedure of the Legislative Assembly of the new State. 
—he rules as to procedure and conduct of business of the Leyislative 
Assembly of the existing State of Himachal Pradesh in force immediately 
before the commencement of this Act shall, until rules are made under

(XLIX of 1951) have effect in relation to Legislative Assembly of the new

PART IV. 
Courts. 


25. Court of the Judicial Commissioner for the new State.—As from 
the commencement of this Act,— 


(a) the Courts of the Judicial Commissioner for the existing States 
(hereafter in this Part referred to as ‘‘the existing courts’’) 
shall be amalgamated and shall constitute the Court of the 
Judicial Commissioner for the new State (hereafter in this 
Part referred to as ‘‘the new court’’); 


(6) the Judicial Commissioner and the Additional Judicial Commis- 
sioner, if any, for the existing State of Himachal Pradesh shall 
be respectively the Judicial Commissioner and the Additional 
Judicial Commissioner for the new State; 


(6) every person who immediately before the commencement of this 
Act, is an officer or servant of either of the existing courts shall 
be an officer or servant, as the case may be, of the new court 
deemed to have been appointed on the same terms and conditions . 
of service (or on terms and conditions as similar thereto as the 
changes effected by this Act permit) as were applicable to him 
immediately before such commencement: 


Provided that nothing in this clause shall be deemed to prevent the 
new court from altering the designation or the duties of any office 
or post; 

)4( the new court shal] have all such original, appellate and _ other 
jurisdiction as under any law is exercisable immediately hefore 
the commencement of this Act by either of the existing courts 
iu respect of any area forming part of the new State; 


(6) the new court shal] have the same powers to admit, suspend and 
remove advocates, vakils and pleaders and to make rules with 
respect to advocates, vakils and pleaders in the whole of the 
new State as are immediately before the commencement of this 
Act, exercisable by either of the existing courts: 


Provided that subject to any rules made by the new court in exercise 
of the powers conferred by this clause, any person who 
immediately before the commencement of this Act is an 
advocate, vakil or pleader entitled to practise in either of the 
existing courts shall be recognised as an advocate, vakil or 
pleader entitled to practise in the new court; 


(f) subject to the provisions of this Part, the law in force immediately 
before the commencement of this Act with respect to the practice 
and procedure in the Court of the Judicial Commissioner for 
the existing State of Himachal Pradesh shall, until varied or 
altered by o competent authority, apply in relation to the new 
court with such modifications as may be made by that court;

(9) the Judicial Commissioners’ Courts (Declaration as High Courts) 
Act, 1950 (XV of 1950) shall apply to the new court as if the 
new court were in existence at the commencement of that Act; 
and any other law in force immediately before the commence- 
ment of this Act relating to appeals to the Supreme (Court 
from the Court of the Judicial Commissioner for the existing 
State of Himachal Pradesh shall, with necessary modifications, 
apply in relation to the new court, 


(7) all proceedings which immediutely before the commencement ০01 
this Act, are pending in either of the existing courts shall by 
virtue of this Act stand transferred to the new court and shall 
be continued as if they had been proceedings instituted in that 


court; 


(i) any order made by either of the existing courts in any such 
proceedings as aforesaid shall for all purposes have effect, not 
only as an order of that court, but also as an order made by the 


new court; 


(j) references in any law to either of the existing courts by whatever 
name, shall, unless the context otherwise requires, be construed 
as references to the new court, 


26. Subordinate oourts.—All courts which immediately before the 
commencement of this Act were exercising lawful powers, authority and 
jurisdiction under-the superintendence and control of either of the existing 
courts in any’area forming part of the new State shall, until further 
provision is made by a competent legislature or authority, continue to 
exercise their respective powers, authority and jurisdiction in that area 
under the superintendence and control of the new court. 


PART V. 
ADMINISTRATIVE AND MISCELLANEOUS PROVISIONS. 


27. Existing authorities and officers to continue to function in the 
new State.—Save as otherwise provided in this Act, all authorities 
and all officers, judicial, executive and ministerial, who immediately 
before the commencement of this Act were exercising lawful functions in 
any area forming part of the new State, shall, until further provision is 
made by a competent authority, continue to exercise their respective 
functions as far as may be, in the same manner and to the same extent as 
they were doing before such commencement. 


28. Existing laws to continue.—Save as otherwise provided in this 
Act, all the law in force immediately before the commencement of this 
Act in any area forming part of the new State shall continue to be in force 
until repealed or amended by a competent legislature or authority. 


29. Power to construe laws.—For the purpose of facilitating the 
application in relation to the new State of any law made before thre 
commencement of this Act, any court, tribunal or authority may, subject 
to any express provision of this Act, construe the law with such alterations 
not affecting the substance as may be necessary or proper to adapt it to the 
matter before the court, tribunal or authority, as the case may be. 


Part V] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 201 


30. Existing taxes to continue.—A!] taxes, duties, cesses and _ fees 
whigh immediately before the commencement of this Act were being 
lawfully levied in either of the existing States or any part thereof, shall 
continue to be levied in the same manner and to the same extent and to be 


applied for the same purposes until other provision is made by a competent 
legislature or authority. 


31. Saving of the powers of the Central Covernment in_ relation to 
the Bhakra-Nangal Project.—Nothing in this Act shall be deemed _ to 
derogate from the powers of the Central Government to make such 
arrangements or to take such uction in relation to the Bhakra-Nangal 
Rroject as may, having due regard to the purposes of the Project, be 


necessary to ensure its proper administration and effective implementa- 
tion. 


32. Power to remove difficulties.—If any difficulty arises in giving 
effect to the provisions of this Act, the President may make such orders 
not inconsistent with the said provisions, as appears to him to be necessary 
or expedient for the purpose of removing the difficulty: 


Provided that no such power shall be exercised by the President after 
the expiry of one yeur from the commencement of this Act.

been residing in India ; 


(b) a person other than a citizen of India, holding a reputable dental 
qualification and employed for teaching or research in a dental 
institution situated in any of the States may be permitted, irres- 
pective of any considerations of reciprocity, temporary registra- 
tion in the State register of dentists for the period of his employ- 
ment or for a period of five years, whichever is shorter : 


Provided that he docs not practise the eee of dentistry for per- 
sonal gain and his application for registration is approved by 
the President of the Council.”

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Dentists Act, 1948 (XVI of 1948,) came into force with effect from 
the 29th March, 1948, in all the then Provinces of India. It has also been 
extended to the newly created Part C States, e.g., Himachal Pradesh, Vindhya 
Pradesh, and Bhopal. In consultation with the Government of Part B States, 
it is now proposed to extend it to all Part B States except Jammu and Kashmir. 


2. Under the existing Act Indian citizens who did not possess any recog- 
nised dental qualifications, but had been engaged in practice as dentists as their 
principal means of livelihood for a period of not less than 5 years prior to the 
commencement of the Act, had been allowed registration under the Act at the 


76 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 1, 1954 [Part VI 
শাস্তি SRE SE RR SE SESS ER ER AED পাপ 


time of first preparation of registers in States. Certain displaced person® who 
had migrated to India from Pakistan after the first preparation of the Registers 
and who did not possess any recognised dental qualifications but who had 
been engaged in the profession of dentistry for their livelihood in Pakistan 
claimed similar facilities for registration as were given to Indian citizens, Since 
it is not possible to accede to their request without amending the Act, it is pro- 
posed to amend the Act for the purpose. 


3. Under section 33(2) temporary registration was allowed for a period 
of 5 years if one had been engaged in practice as a dentist as his principal means 
of livelihood for a period of not less than 2 years during the five years prior to 
the commencement of the Act, but permananet registration to such persons is 
admissible only if they could puss within a period of 5 years after the com- 
mencement of the Act an examination which satisfies the requirements of the 
Council. Since enough training facilities for the dentists do not exist in the 
country many dentists who were temporarily registered under the Act could not 
qualify for permanent registration. In order to enable them to pass an exami- 
nation, it is proposed to give them more time to pass the examination. For this 
purpose the five year period is intended to be extended to 10 years. 


4. Under section 3(c) of the existing Act, 4 seats are available on the 
Dental Council of India to be filled by clection from among themselves by the 
heads of dental colleges in States which grant recognised dental qualification. 
Since there is only one dental college in India which grants dental 01-25 
the other 3 seats meant for the heads of Dental Colleges on the Dental 
Council of India have remained vacant. It is now proposed _ to 
fill the vacancies by throwing open the election to heads of dental colleges which 
train students fer recognised dental qualifications. 


5. Under the existing Act a foreign national is not entitled to registration 
even if he possesses a recognised dental qualification unless by the law and 
practice of the State or country to which such person belongs, persons of Indian 
origin holding dental qualifications registrable in that State or country are per- 
mitted to enter and practise the profession of dentistry in such a State or country. 
It is therefore, proposed on grounds of expediency and propriety to permit, 
irrespective of considerations of reciprocity, foreigners holding reputable dental 
qualifications who are employed for teaching or rescarch in dental institutions 
in the country, to have temporary registration for the period of their employment 
or for a period of five years, whichever is shorter, provided that such foreigners 
do not practise dentistry for personal gain. 


This opportunity is also being taken to make some other minor and _conse- 
quential amendments in the Act which have becn found necessary during the 
past 6 years since its enactment. 


AMRIT KAUR.

Dated the 27th April, 1954. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM. 


The extension of the Act to Part B States would involve expenditure from 
the Consolidated Fund of India and from the revenues of the Governments of

expefditure that is likely to be incurred from the Consolidated Fund of India 
is indicated in the following paragraphs. 


2. After the Dentists Act, 1948, is extended to Part B States, these States 
will become entitled to send two representatives each (one elected and one nomi- 
nated) as members of the Dental Council of India. Assuming that the State 
Governments will agree to bear the expenditure on the Travelling Allowance 
and Daily Allowance of the 7 members to bc nominated by them under clause (০) 
of section 3 of the Act, as is being done by the Governments of Part A States 
except Bihar, the estimated expenditure on the Travelling Allowance of the 
remaining 7 clected members from the Part B States would amount to Rs. 2,740

3. In addition to the expenditure on the Travelling Allowance and Daily 
Allowance, the Central Government will be responsible for meeting the expendi- 
ture on the election of 0110 member from each Part B State under clause (a) of 
section 3 of the Dentists Act, 1948. In view of the fact that the amount of 
expenditure on such elections in the States will depend on the size of the electoral 
roll and other local conditions in cach State and must vary from State to State, 
any estimate of such expenditure can only be tentative. In connection with a 
recent election to the Dental Council of India from the State of Madras, the 
actual expenditure amounted to Rs. 1,145. If we base our estimate on this 
figure, the cost of 7 elections in the Part B States may amount to Rs. 7,000 every 
five years.

(2) Speed and halting charge—When a rickshaw is hired the bearer shall 
ordinarily drive the same at 2 speed of not less’ than eight 
miles per hour. If a rickshaw after being hired is made to halt, halting charges 
shall be paid according to the scale laid down in the above fare table. 


10. Passengers to pay other charges.—Passengers shall pay the ferry and 
other charges while going to and coming from the railway station over and 
above the rates payable to the bearer of rickshaw. 


11. Maximum weight to be carried in rickshaws.—Passengers and luggage 
shall not ordinarily exceed 4 maunds in weight. It shall not be permissible to 
any bearer to refuse to ply except on reasonable grounds. 


12. Advertisement on rickshaws.—No advertisement shall be fixed at such 
places as to cover the number plate and fare table affixed to the rickshaw. 


13. Rickshaws to wait at stand.—The rickshaws while at rest shall wait at 
a stand fixed by the Commissioners for such purpose. 


14. Power of entry.—It shall be lawful for a Commissioner or any other 
person authorised in that behalf by the Chairman of the Commissioners at any 
time between sun-rise and sun-set to enter any premises in which any licensed 
rickshaw or other things used therewith are kept in order to carry out any of 
the provisions of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919 or these by-laws and 
the owner or occupier of the premises or his agent shall afford every facility for 
inspection by, such Commissioner or person. 


15. Tables of fares and distances.—The Commissioners shall cause to be 
prepared and kept, for sale to the public, printed tables setting forth the fares and 
distances at a price fixed by the Commissioners. 


16. Particulars of registers.—The following particulars shall be entered in 
the registers and licenses under the Calcutta Hackny-Carriage Act, 1919:— 


(A) Bearer’s license. 


(1) The number of the license. 

(2) The name, father’s name, place of abode, present address and age of the 
person to whom such license is granted. 

(3) The date on which the license is granted. 

(4) The number of rickshaw allowed to the bearer. 

(5) Photograph of the bearer. 

(6) The date of expiry of license, 

(9) A ک0‎ of the more important statutory provisions and by-laws 

affecting bearers of rickshaws. 
(8) Signature of the Registering Officer. 


(B) Rickshaw owner's license. 


(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 

(2) The name, father’s name and residence of the owner, the description 
of the rickshaw and the place where the rickshaw is kept. 

(3) The number of passengers the rickshaw is licensed to carry. 

(4) The date on which the license is granted. 

(5) Date of expiry of the license. 

(6) Signature of the Registering Officer. 


(C) Register of rickshaws. 


(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 
(2) Date on which the license is granted. 
(3) Name and father’s name of the owner. 
(4) Owner's place of residence. 
(5) Place wheg the rickshaw is kept. 
(6) House number. 
(7) Name and father’s name of the bearer. 
(8) Bearer’s place of residence. 
(9) Period of suspensicn.,, 
(10) Date of “renewal. 
(11) Duplicate license. 
(12) Duplicate ticket. 
(13) Photograph of the bearer. 
(14) Date of conviction. 
(15) Section of law. 
(16) Punishment inflicted. 
(17) Date of offence. 
(18) Offence. 
(19) Ownership transferred to. ere : 
(20) The number of persons the rickshaw is licensed to carry. 
(21) Date of transfer. 
(22) Signature of Registering Officer. 
(23) Remarks. 


17. Definition.—In these by-laws unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context— 
(a) “Commissioner” means a commissioner of the Budge-Budge Munici- 
Pality in the district of 24-Parganas; টি 
(b) “Rickshaw” includes a “cycle-rickshaw”.

for the preparation, publication and execution of 
projects for water supply, sewerage or drainage by 
municipal authorities, it is hereby notified for 
general information that the scheme for installa- 
tion of a stand-by electric pumping set at the 
River Side Pumping §tation of the Baranagar- 
Kamarhati Joint Water Works has been approved 
by Government, and that the particulars of the 
said scheme are as follows :— 


109) The s¢heme provides for installation of a 
stand-by electric pumping set at the 
River Side Pumping Station of the 
Baranagar-Kamarhati Joint Water- 
works 11) the existing valve room. This 
new pump will have the same capacity as 
that of the existing one and it wilt be 
utilised during emergency. Both the 
new and old pumps may also be run 
simultaneously as and when required for 
filling up the reserved tanks quickly. The 
pumping unit comprises of one electrically 
driven vertical motor pump having an 
output of 2,000 gallons per minute against 
a total head of 18 feet, the manometric 
suction head being 16°56 feet. The 
suction pipe will run over the staging of 
the existing jetty in the river. 


(b) The estimated capital cost of the scheme 
is Rs. 34,488. 


(৫) The estimated annual cost of main- 
taining the pump is Rs. 2,000. 

(d) The cost will be met by the Baranagar and 
Kamarhati Municipalities in their 

proportionate shares, 


265) The total annual charge to be inowrred by 
reason of the water supply and to: be met 
by the water rate is Ra. 2,000. 


(b) The percentage of such water rate on the 
annual value of holdings will be as 
follows :— 


(i) Baranagar Municipality—7 per cent. 
(ii) Kamarhati Municipality—4 per cent. 


(c) The average incidence of such water rate 
per head of the population will be as 
follows : — 


(i) Baranagar Municipality—Rx. 1-6-2. 
(ii) Kamarhati Municipality—Rs. 0-13-7, 


3. The scheme will be taken into consideration

signed before that date, will be duly

2. In calculating license fees, annas 8 or above in the total license fees for 
each drug shall be reckoned as a rupee while the amount below annas 8 shall be 
ignored. 

3. The vendor of a combined shop (ganja and opium) who does not 
take issue of more than one kind of drug in a month shall be treated as a vendor 
of a single shop [as mentioned in sub-rule (1) of rule 1] for the purpose of 
calculation of license fees. 

4, (a) The fee shall be paid on or before 15th of the month following that 
to which the issue of ganja or opium relates. 

(b) The Excise Commissioner may, in his discretion and by an order in 
writing, permit relaxation of clause (a) for good and sufficient reasons. 

5. The holder of the licence shall pay for due observance of the conditions 
and terms of the licence an advance equivalent to one month’s licence fee during 
the previous year before the commencement of his licence. 

6. This notification shall be deemed to have effect and to have always had 
effect on and from ist June 1954,

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 


ORDER. 


No. 3097Dis./D/8L-31/54.—23rd June 1954.—-Whereas under the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4055Dis/D/8L-20/52, 
dated the 22nd December 1952, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Manindra Cotton Mills of Cossimbazar, Murshidabad, and 
their workers represented by the $Manindra Mill Sramik Sangha 
of Cossimbazar, Murshidabad, regarding the matters specified in the schedule 
thereto was referred for adjudication to the First Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal, a 
complaint was filed before it against the said Company by Shri Anil Choudhury, 
a workman of the said Company alleging that the said Company had discharged 
the said workman concerned in such dispute; 


And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudicated 
upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State Government; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
filed by Shri Anil Choudhury against Messrs. Manindra Cotton Mills, Ltd., of 
Cossimbazar in connection with Government order No. 4055Dis./D/8L- 
20/52, dated 22nd December 1952 (Case No. 77/53). 


BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 
Suri M. C. BANERJEE, District Judge (Retd.), Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 


For the applicant: Shri H. Banerji, Vice-President of the Union. 
For the Company: Shri 5. P. Choudhury, Managing Director. 


AWARD. 


The proceeding in connection with which this complaint under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed was based upon Government 
order of reference No. 4055Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 1952. 


On 16th February 1953 Shri Anil Choudhury, a workman of the Manindra 
Cotton Mills, filed an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947, complaining that he was discharged verbally on 22nd January 1953 
while a proceeding between the Company and its workmen was pending before 
the Tribunal and without the permission of the Tribunal. It is further pleaded 
that the applicant was an active member of the Manindra Mills Sramik Sangha 
and that he has been wrongfully dismissed by way of victimisation and unfair 
labour practice for his trade union activities. The applicant, therefore, prays 
for reinstatement with full compensation. / 


The Company in its written statement stated that for some time before 22nd 
January 1953 and during the pendency of the proceedings before the Tribunal 
the applicant was attempting to instigate loyal workers of the Mill to take part in 


2242 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 | 1১4 I 


পাশ পপ মহ 


০ oe 


a strike and other subversive activities in spite of repeated warnings and that his 
superior having reported his aforesaid conduct to the Manager of the Mill, while 
he was doing the same act on 22nd January 1953 he left the Mill premises and 
did not join his duties in spite of repeated notices. The applicant thus’ volun- 
tarily terminated the contract of service with the Company. 


On 6th February 1954 the applicant filed a petition praying for leave to with- 
draw his application. The applicant is permitted to withdraw his application 
under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as prayed for. 


M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 


The llth June 1954. 


By order of the Governor, 
.لا‎ S. ۶۰ MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy. 


ORDER. 


No. 3102Dis./D/8L-31/54.—23rd June 1954.—Whereas under the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department order No. 4055Dis./D/8L-20/52, 
dated the 22nd December 1952, the industrial dispute between Messrs. Manindra 
Cotton Mills of Cossimbazar, Murshidabad and their workers represented by the 
Manindra Mill Sramik Sangha of Cossimbazar, Murshidabad, regarding the matters 
specified in the schedulé- thereto was referred for adjudication to the First 


Industrial Tribunal; 

And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal, 
a complaint was filed before it against the said Company by Shri Nagendra 
Sarkar, a workman of the said Company alleging that the said Company had dis- 
charged the said workman concerned in such dispute; 


And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudicated 
upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State Government; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
filed by Nagendra Sarkar in connection with Government order No. 4055- 
Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 1952 (Case No. 64/53). 


BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 
PRESENT : 
Suri M. C. BANERJEE, District Judge (Retd.), Judge First Industrial Tribunal. 
For the applicant: Shri H. Banerji, Vice-President of the Union. 
For the Company: Shri S. P. Choudhury, Managing Director. 


The proceeding in connection with which this complaint under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed was based upon Government 
order of reference No. 4055Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 1952. 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 2243 


সস 


On 28th January 1953 Nagendra Sarkar, a workman of the Manindra 
Cotton Mills, Ltd., filed a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Acty 1947, stating that he was discharged on 17th January 1953 while 
a proceeding was pending before the Tribunal between the Company 
and its workmen and that no permission was taken from the Tribunal for 
his discharge. It is further pleaded that this action of the Management was by 
way of victimisation and unfair labour practice, inasmuch as, the applicant was 
an active member of the Manindra Mills Sramik Sangha being a member of 
its executive committee. The applicant prays that he should be reinstated to his 
job with full compensation. 


The Company in its written statement opposed the application and denied 
that the action of the Management was by way of unfair labour practice or victim- 
jsation for trade union activities of the applicant. Through inadvertence an 
order of dismissal was served on the petitioner but the mistake was soon 
detected and before the filing of this application the petitioner was informed 
that he was suspended and not dismissed on the grounds as mentioned in the 
notice of discharge dated 17th January 1953. It is further pleaded that for 
some time past before 17th January 1953 the applicant was attempting to 
instigate the loyal workers of the Mill to take part in a strike and other sub- 
versive activities during the pendency of জা before the Tribunal. 
In addition, the applicant was also guilty of wilful insubordination and dis- 
obedience to the reasonable orders of the superior and other misconduct. The 
Company, therefore, prays that the application should be rejected. 


On the date of hearing on 4th June 1954 the parties filed a joint petition 
of compromise which appears as Appendix A to this award. n a perusal 
of the petition of compromise it appears that the terms thereof are reasonable 
and should be accepted. I, therefore, accept the petition of compromise in 
Appendix A and award accordingly. The petition of compromise in Appendix 
A shall form a part of this award. 

M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 
The 1117 June 1954.

For the applicant; Shri H. Banerji, Vice-President of the Union. 
For the Company: Shri S. P. Choudhury, Managing Director. 


The proceeding in connection with which this complaint under section 
33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed was based upon Govern- 
ment order of reference No. 4055Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 
1952. 


On 28th January 1953 Shri Amulya Roy, a workman of the Manindra 
Cotton Mills, Ltd., filed this complaint under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947, stating that he was discharged on 16th January 1953 while 
a proceeding was pending before the Tribunal and without the permission of 
the Tribunal. It is stated that the applicant was served with a notice of dis- 
charge on 16th January 1953 without any previous charge-sheet or scope of 
defence. The applicant is an active member of the Manindra Mill Sramik 
Sangha, being a member of its executive committee. The applicant States 
that the action of the Management in dismissing him was unfair and that he was 
victimised for trade union activities. 


The Company in its written statement states as follows سس‎ 


Through inadvertence an order of dismissal was served on the applicant but 
soon thereafter the said mistake was detected and before the filing of this 
application the petitioner was informed that he was’ suspended but not dis- 
missed or discharged. The Company denies that the action of the Manage- 
ment was unfair or by way of victimisation or unfair labouf practice. For some 
time past before he was placed under suspension on 16th January 1953, the 
applicant was attempting to instigate and incite the loyal workers of the Mill 
10 take part in a strike, and other subversive activities while the proceeding 
before the Tribunal was pending. In addition to the aforesaid misconduct the 
petitioner was guilty of other misconduct also, namely, wilful insubordination 
and disobedience of the lawful and reasonable order of a superior, wilful 
damage to the Company’s property by making false entries about damaged 
cloth, etc. In the circumstances the Company prays that this application 
should be dismissed. 


The parties were partly heard on 5th June 1954. Then the parties filed a 
petition of compromise. This petition of compromise appears as Appendix A 
to this Award. On a perusal of the petition of compromise it appears that the 
terms thereof are reasonable and should be accepted. I, therefore, accept 
the petition of compromise in Appendix A and award accordingly. The peti- 
tion of compromise in Appendix A shall form a part of this award. 


M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, First Industrial Tribunal.

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industria] Disputes Act,

BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL,

MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial‏ 7 :ب5 
Tribunal.‏ 


Appearances : 
For the workman: Shri Suprasanna Pal himself. 


For ‘the Company: Shri Daga, Secretary, Messrs. Hall & Anderson, Ltd. 


This application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act made by 
a discharged workman Shri Suprasanna Pal, whose contention is that he served 
the Company for about 32 years and that he was unreasonably discharged on 
notice, dated 26th March 1952, and that he was not paid any gratuity although 
workmen who were discharged later on were paid such gratuity. 


The original references out of which this present case has arisen were made 
under Government Nos. 2119Dis./D/11L-43(A)/52, dated 7th August 1952 
and subsequent Nos. 4391Dis./D/11L-246/53, dated 19th November 1953 
and 2498Dis./D/11L-43(A)/52, dated Sth September 1952 and subsequent 
No. 4392Dis./D/11L-246/53, dated 19th November 1953. 


AWARD. 


The petitioner fails to explain how the Company could be said to have 
violated section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act by discharging him by notice 
without paying gratuity. It is apparent that the petitioner’s termination of service 
fell in April 1952, whereas the Government made references—one in August 
1952 and the other in September 1952. So there had been no contravention 
of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act during the pendency of either of 
the reference cases. Therefore I find that the petition under section 33A is not 


maintainable and it is therefore rejected. 
MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 


District Judge, 


Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 12th June 1954. : 


By order of the Governor, 
D. S. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

AWARD. 


The proceeding in connection with which this complaint under section 
383A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was filed was based upon ern- 
rt order of reference No. 4065Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 
1952. 

Shri Anil Kumar Sarkar and 115 other workmen of the Manindra 
Cotton Mills, Ltd., filed an application under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act on 19th February 1953. It is pleaded by these workmen that 
the Company all on a sucden and without any previous notice or taking pre- 
vious sanction of the Tribunal locked out the applicants from work since 27th 
January 1953 and that this act of the Company was illegal and was in 
contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The applicants 
prayed for being taken back to work and for full wages for the period of 
their unemployment. 


The Company in its written statement states as follows: On 
2٦٦ط‎ January 1953 when a proceeding before the Tribunal was _pend- 
ing between the Company and its workmen, the workmen applicants along 
with others all on a ھت‎ left the Mill premises and went on strike ille- 
gally for reasons best known to them. The same workmen did not call at the 
time office or join their duties in spite of notices, dated 28th January 3 
and 12th February 1953, given by the Company to that effect. In conse- 
quence of the said illegal strike and the refusal of the workmen to join their 
respective duties in spite of notice the Company had to recruit new workmen 
and has been running the Mill since then with great difficulty. The Com- 
pany further states that on diverse dates in the month of March 1958 when 
some of the strikers amongst the petitioners expressed their regret for the 
suid illegal strike, they were allowed to join their respective duties fter 
u warning. The act of the Company is not illegal nor in violation of section 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The petitioners are not entitled to any 
relief as prayed for. 


It appears that 22 workers out of the applicants were re-employed by the 
Company and 33 other workers withdrew their case before the Tribunal. 
None of the workers appeared before the Tribunal on the date of hearing on 
3rd March 1954. On 4th June 1954 Shri H. Banerji, the Vice-]’resident 
of the Manindra Mills Sramik Sangha, appeared for the applicants und 
Shri S. P. Choudhury, Managing Director, appeared for the Company 
and both the parties stated that the case had heen amicably settled. A 1)01)- 
tion was filed by Shri H. Banerji on behalf of the workmen stating that the 
matter had been amicably settled and the workers did not press their oppii- 
cation under section 33A of the Act. 


It may also be mentioned that a “loch out’ does not come within the 
ambit of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act and 80 no permission 
under section 33 1s required for a lock out. The present application under 
section 934 of the [ndustrial Disputes Act*is, therefore, nut maintainable 
(1226. 1952 1..A.C., page 219 at page 22%, 1951(2) L.L.J., page 344]. 
The present application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act is, 


therefore, rejected.
