FINDINGS 


issue No. 4. The Association claimed reinstatement of Padma Bahadur 
with th arrear wuges and allowances on the allegution that he was 
appointed as a Durwan against a permanent vacancy and that he wus 
dismissed by a letter, dated 25th March 1953, without assigning any reason 
whatsoever. It stated that the discharge was unfair and illegal and 
againat the principles of natural justice. The Club denied this allegation 
and stated that he was employed on a casual basis, liable to be discharged 
without notice. His services were required till 28th March 1953 and he 
was discharged with effect from the next day. 


Padma Bahadur is absent. He has not taken any oath in this case. 
There is no oral evidence on either side on the point of issue. The 
Assoviation put in ext. 1, a letter addressed to the Secretary of the 
Association, dated 10th May 1953. It appears from this letter that one 
Lalbahadur was appointed in his place on and from 20th April last. It has 
accordingly been urged on behalf of the Association that the discharge of 
Padma Bahadur is unjustified for there was no ground for it. The device 
of discharging employees shortly before the expiry of the period of 
probation 1s adopted by the Club to avoid making them permanent, and 
Padma Bahadur was discharged with ulterior motive. The Club put in 
ext. “A’’, a letter of appointment of Padma Bahadur, dated 30th Octobar 
1952. This is signed by Padma BRoahadur himself. It shows that he was. 
appointed on a daily basis of Rs. 2 per day from Ist November 1952. 
The appointment is casual in nature liable to be terminated without notice. 
It has been urged on behalf of the Club that the appointment was purely 
casual and that in terms of the letter of appointment, the services were 
lerminated. Accordingly, no question of reinstatement with or without 
arrear wages, etc., can arise. I have found that this contention of the 
Club is sound. In the absence of any materials which substantiate the 
contention raised by the Association it cannot be said that Padma Bahadur 
was discharged for any ulterior motive. The whereabouts of Padma Bahadur 


2258 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 Part ] 


are not known. [1 is also not known whether he was at all agreeable to 
vontinue in service or that he offered himself for reappointment when the 
Club required a fresh Durwan. It is also not proved that a fresh “Durwan 
was appoiuted in place of Padma Bahadur as alleged in ext. 1. Accordingly, 
I find that the discharge of Padma Bahadur is justified and that in the 
circumstances of the case, he is not entitled to any compensation. 1 
answer this issue accordingly. 


issue No. 3. This relates to the formation of the Trust Board of the 
Provident Fund. The Association stated in its written statement that there 
is no representative of the members (i.e., employees) in the Trust Board 
of the Fund which is composed of the President, Honorary Secretary und 
Honorary Treasurer (vide rule No. 5). Ext. “C” is the Trust Deed contain- 
ing rules of the Provident Fund. Rule No. 5 lays down that the number 
of trustees of the Fund shall not be less than three and not more than five. 
The first trustees shall be (1) President, (2) Honorary Secretary and (3) 
Honorary Treasurer. Admittedly, the said three persona are continuing 
on the Board. The Association suggests that the Board shall he composed 
of two members of the Club and two members of the Association on behalf 
of the employees and that every decision of the Board must be ratified by 
all or at least majority of the members. It has been argued on behalf of 
the Association that it is desirable in the interest of the employees that 
there should be two of their representatives on the Board. This has been 
resisted on behalf of the Club. The reasons are that the Board is already 
formed and in the absence of any allegation of maladministration, etc., of 
the Fund by the trustees of the Board, the question of reconstruction wf the 
Board or removal of the present trustees does not arise. It must be con- 
ceded that the issue is not properly worded. It should have heen one for 
the reconstruction or reformation of the Trust Board of the Provident Fun. 
In any case, the dispute undoubtedly is regarding some representation of 
the employees on the Trust Board. It has been further contended on behalf 
of the Club that in the absence of the trustees, the Provident Fund rules 
cannot be changed, and that it is not practicable to have any representative 
of the employees in view of the ever changing Unions of Workers of the 
Club. The Club’s contention that this Tribunal] will not have any jurisdic- 
tion to vhange the rules of the Fund in the absence of the trustees requires 
scrutiny. The trustees as stated above are (1) the President, (2) Honorary 
Secretary, and (3) Hovorary Treasurer. But then they are different persons 
in the eve of law. So, it will not do to say that since the Club is a party, 
and sinee it 1s represented by the President himself (who was present at the 
hearing), the trustees may 3 considered to be present in the proceeding. 
No such inference is permissible in law. 


Question now is whether the rules can be added or altered in this case. 
This takes us once more to the deed of trust constituting the Provident bund 
‘ext. C), Rule 30 provides, ‘““The employer may in its discretion with the 
written concent of the Trustees by writing under their hands add_ to, 
alter or repeal any of the provisions of these presents but so that no such 
udditions or alterations shall affect the right of any member of the tund 
then accrued with respect to any funds then in the hands of the Trustees gr 
result in the employer acquiring any beneficial interest whatsoever in the 
funds of the Fund. All such additions and/or alterations shall durin 
such time as the Fund shall continue to be recognised as a recognised Fun 
within the meaning of the Indian Income Tax Act, be subject to 
the prior approval of the Commissioner of Income-tax having jurisdiction 
over the Fund.” It is suggested on behalf of the Association that since the 
employer who has the right to add to, alter or repeal any of the provisions 
of the Deed under the aforesaid rule is party to this reference, 48 
Tribunal is competent to give proper directions in the matter, for any 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 2259 
৯৬১ 


additions or alterations of the rule. This would in the nature of recom- 
mendation to the employer who will in due course, give effect to the same in 
accordance with the provisions of the said rule with the consent of <he 
Trustees and with the prior approval of the Commissioner of Income-tax. 
To my ind, this appears to be sound. This Tribunal has jurisdiction to 
adjudicate the dispute between the parties on this point. Rule 0 
already provides that the number of the Trustees shall be not less than 
three and not more than five. At present, the Trustees are three. ()ues- 
tion is whether it is desirable in the circumstances to raise the number of 
{rustees up to five by including representatives of the subscribers to ihe 
Fund. Since the Fund consists mainly of the contributions made by the 
subscribers to it, i.e., by the employees of the Club, it is desirable thut there 
should be some representative of the subscribers on the Bourd of Trustees. 
His presence on the Board is likely to remove all apprehensions regarding 
any mis-application or improper investment of the Fund. Rule 7 provides 
for appointment of anyone of the members of the Fund os Manager. This 
shows that the management of the Club at the time of framing all these 
rules, desired the close association of the members with the administration 
of the Fund. Any such assoviation of a member or members of the Fund 
for its administration at once removes all mis-apprehensions as to the 
improper use of the Fund. The Tribunal, therefore, thinks that there 
should be one representative of the subscribers on the Board of Trustees 
and the Board be reconstituted with such representative as one of the 
Trustees. The subscribers shall elect one of the members as their represen- 
tative within a month from the date of the operation of the award to the 
Boar at a general meeting to be held specially for the purpose and they 
shall\elect the representative every three year. Such Trustee shall hold 
office \tor a period of three years from the date of the constitution of the 
Board\ provided that the representative of the subscribers shall cease to he 
a Trustee to the Board on ceasing to be a subscriber and he may resign his 
office a notice in writing to the Board. The Tribunal recommends to thie 
Club to take effective steps in the matter of necessary addition and/or 
alteration of the rules with the consent of the Trustees and the approval 
of the Commissioner of Incoime-tax, West Bengal Circle, within a month 
from the date of the operation of this award. I decide this issue accord- 


ingly. 


issues Nos. 1 and 2. These two issues relate to (1) Standing Orders and 
(ii) Provident Fund Rules. The Standing Orders (ext. B) were certified oa 
the 10th September 1952 after due formalities. These orders came_ into 
force from {7th October 1952. The Association alleged that the Standing 
Orders have introduced a change in the (1) working hours, (ii) grace period, 
(iii) casual leave with pay and (iv) casual leave and claimed that the work- 
ing conditions, in connection wth these items, which existed before the 
introduction of the Standing Orders, he restored. The Club denied that 
there was any change in the Standing Orders but admitted that the working 
hours were fixed according to the requirements of the Club. Regarding 
the disputed items in the Standing Orders, the defence is only a denial of 
the allegation made by the Association. It has been urged on behalf of the 
Club that since there was no change made in the Standing Orders, the issue 
becomes infructuous and redundant. Jt is admitted in paragraph 4 of the 
written statement of the Association that previously there were no written 
Standing Orders of the Club and the Club Authorities all on a sudden passed 
: written Standing Order on 15th October 1952 and enforced them from 
16th October 1952. It would, however, appear from the Standing Ordess 
(ext. B) that they were certified on 10th September 1952 and brought into 
force from 17th September 1952. It is incorrect to say that the Club all on 2 
sudden passed those orders and thrust them upon the employees. In fact, 


2260 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JOLY 8, 1954 IParr [ 
প্র 


it is gathered that the Authorities of the Club were asked by the Labour 
Commissioner to have written Standing Orders at an early date. The 
Management, pursuant to the request, got the Standing Orders drafted for 
the first time in the history ‘of the Club and presented them to the Labour 
Commissioner for favour of ০6110686501), This was in due course discussed 
with the Association and was duly certified by the proper authorities. It 
would, therefore, be absolutely wrong to say that these orders were brought 
into existence all on a sudden and were imposed upon the employees without 
their knowledge. But it is now admitted that the working hours were 
changed in the Standing Orders. Formerly working hours were—weekdays, 

a.m. to 5 p.m. with one hour’s lunch recess from 12 to 1 p.m. 
Saturdays, 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Under rule 8 of the Standing Orders, these 
hours have been changed as follows :— 


Weekdays: 9 a.m, to 5 p.m. with half an hour’s lunch recess from 
12-30 p.m. to 1 p.m.; Saturdays: 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. 


The Club contends that this change was made to suit its requirements. 
Naturally, the Tribunal enquired the reasons for this change. No oral 
evidence was forthcoming on either side. During discussions, it was 
ascertained that formerly there was absolutely chaos in the working of the 
Club and that for the first time, the President has made a very strong 
endeavour to regularise the whole matter and proceeded in o businesslike 
way. As the work has increased, the working hours have been increased, 
but not to the extent of putting any undue strain on any member of the 
clerical staff. I could gather this much that the employees were satisfied 
with the recess now enjoyed by them under the Standing Orders. They 
want to revert to the old hour of attendance, numely, at 10 in the morning. 
The Club, of course, stands by the new hour of attendance at 9 a.m., but it 
was prepared ৮২৮ the time of argument to concede half an hour to the 
employees. I have fully considered the view points of both parties ard 
find that the working hours should be—Weekdays, 9-30 a.m. to 12-80 p.m. 
and from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. Saturdays, 9-30 a.m. to 1 p.m. These hours 
appear to be fair and reasonable. The Tribunal directs that necessary 
changes in the Standing Orders be made at once JHegarding the objections 
of the Association to changes made by the Standing Orders namely that 
grace period for late attendance which was 10 minutes per day, i.e., 60 
minutes in a week was changed to 10 minutes in a week (vide rule 9 of the 
Standing Orders), the Association complained that this change was unneces- 
airy and very harsh in effect, whereas the Club contents that any increase 
in the grace period will put a premium on unpunctuality and indolence. 4۴ 
is gathered that no employee is punished foy exceeding this grace period 
under the Standing Orders, 1.e., no employee was either shut out from work 
for being late in coming to office or even lost his dav’s pay for that. I 
think the grace period now allowed under the Standing Orders is not unduly 
harsh. Therefore, it does not call for any change. Regarding Casual 
Leave, the Association claims that it should be granted in addition to holi- 
days and other leave and that it should be with pay. Further, at present 
such leave is granted for two days at a time in place of three days before 
the Standing Orders were introduced. Casual leave is intended to be casual 
in nature and accordingly, there cannot be ordinarily any occasion for on 
application for any such leave for more than two days at a time. Cusual leave 
is never allowed in extension of holidays or other regular leave. Accord- 
ingly, the Standing Orders in this connection do not call for any revision 
or change. It has been urged on behalf of the Club that since there was 
no previous Standing Orders, there could not be any ‘Change’ in them 
when the present Standing Orders were certified and hrought into force. 
Strictly speaking, no such change was introduced in the present Standing

Orders in the sense that they differ from the previous one. But udmittedly, 
the present Standing Orders introduced changes in the conditions of servive 
and a@cordingly this can legitimately form the subject matter of an issue 
under the Industrial Disputes Act. The Club’s contention on this point 
therefore fails. 


Regurding the change in the rules of the Provident Fund the Associa- 
tion stated that the Provident Fund which existed before 1943 was dis- 
continued between 1943 and 1946. Tt was reintroduced on 1st October 1946 
for the clerical staft only and on Ist October 1948, the Provident Fund has 
heen tor the subordinate staff also. There were previously no rules and the 
present rules are departed from the س/0‎ ones (where they existed) in

rules under three heads: (1) Regarding the formation of the Trust Board; 
This has been dealt with in connection with issue No. 3, (2) Regarding 
nomination: The employees shall be at liberty to nominate persons for 
receiving full value of their Provident Fund dues after their death and 
the system of production of succession certificate should be abolished. (£)) 
The employees shall be entitled to receive full contribution of the Provi- 
dent Fund from the Club on completion of two years’ service. This claim 
has been resisted by the Club mainly on the following grounds: (1) Rules 
cannot be altered in the absence of the Trustees who are not before this 
Tribunal. (2) The staff consists mostly of the Anglo-Indians. The intro- 
duction of nomination system will prejudicially affect their interest; 
they 1016 likely to make improvident nomination in favour of strangers in 
preference to their family members. (3) Club's full contribution should 
only He earned by long and faithful service. It is, accordingly, undesirable 
that ap employee leaving after completion of two years of service should 
receive\ full Club’s contribution. I have discussed the first objection in 
connectyon with issue No. 3. For the very same reasons, I find that the 
rules can be changed although the Trustees have not been brought on 
records of this case. It is extremely unfortunate that this matter of the 
absence of the Trustees was not brought to the notice of the Tribunal at an 
early stage of the proceeding. The objections could have been easily met 
if it was pressed, ہ٥‎ it 18 always desirable that all questions affecting defect 
in jurisdiction should be pressed, at a very early stage of the proceediag. 
Regarding the Club’s objection to adopt the system of nomination in the 
Provident Fund Rules, it does not appear to be very convincing. Nomina- 
tion system is a common feature of ae Provident Fund rules. It is learat 
on enquiry that the permanent clerical staff consists of 28 members and the 
temporary or casual staff, which varies from time to time, consists of (0 
to 200 members. The latter is appointed purely on temporary basis. It 
is not known how many of the permanent staff out of this 28, are Anglo- 
Indians but a demand is forfhcoming on behalf of all that the rules he 
changed by adopting the nomination system so that in the event of an 
employee’s death hefore his retirement, his successors may get all the 
Provident Fund money without incurring any cost whatsoever. The demand 
does not appear to be an unreasonable one. The system of nomination can 
be made optional if in the opinion of the management of the (lub, the 
Anglo-Indian staff requires any special protection. Their nomination may 
be entirely optional. 411 subscribers will not have to make nomination at 
the time of joining the Fund. It would be left entirely to their discretion 
to make nomination or not. Under the existing rules, an amount up to 
Rs. 600 can be withdrawn without the production of a succession certificate. 
But any amount in execess of that can only be withdrawn on the production 
of a succession certificate. It ia accordingly recommended to the manage- 
ment of the Club that they should take effective steps for alteration of the 


2262 THE CAIXUTTA 04১21511115, JULY 8, 1954 (Pinr I 
Ee | 


existing rules particularly rule 20 of the Provident Fund rules making 
provisions for the subscribers of the fund to nominate their successors in 
the event of their death before retirement, so that their nominees mav 
withdraw the accumulation of the Fund where they exceed Rs. 50) without 
the production of a succession certificate. The provision for nomination 
may be as follows:— 


1. Every subscriber to the Fund may make o nomination § confering 
the right to receive the amount that may stand to his credit in 
the event of his death occurring before the amoant has Lecome 
payable, provided that a subscriber may modify a nomination 
once after giving written notice of his intention of doing so. 


2. Nomination shall save us hereinafter provided be in favour of one 
or more of the subscriber's family and shall be made in the 
prescribed form. If a subscriber nominates more nominees than 
one, he may apportion the amount that may stand to bis 
credit in the Fund amongst his nominees at his own discretion. 
If at the time of making nomination, the subscriber haa no 
family, the nomination may be in favour of any other person or 
persons, but if the subscriber subsequently acquires a family, 
such nomination shall forthwith stand cancelled. ‘The above 
provision should be inserted in the Club’s Provident Fund rules. 
The Club is to prescribe the form for such nomination ind it is 
advised that the form of the Goverhment Contributory Provideat 
Fund be adopted in this case. 


As to the third objection regarding the Provident Fund rules, namely, 
the employees would be entitled to receive full contribution of Drovident 
Fund from the Club on completion of two years’ service, I have carefully 
considered the view points of both sides. The provision in rule 22(b) of 
the Club’s rules is reasonable and fair. It is not that the Club had any set 
of rules before the present rules came into force which allowed the employees 
to have full contributions on the completion of two years’ service. ‘The Asso- 
ciation could not show any such rule. The payment of the Club's contri- 
bution was entirely in the discretion of the management and therefore it 
is idle to contend on behalf of the Association that the present rules had 
departed from the previous ones to a large extent. The employers’ contri- 
butions are usually paid for long and faithful service and the provision in 
the existing rules has given recognition to that well-established practice. 
The Tribunal finds nothing in favour of a change in’ the existing rules as 
desired by the Association. That objection, therefore, fails. ‘The 
Tribunal has indicated the relief which the emplovees are entitled to in thia 
case in discussing issues above. I make myeaward accordingly.

No. 3095Dis./D/8L-31/54.—23rd June 1954.-—-Whereas under the Govern- 
ment ‘Of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4055- 
Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated the 22nd December 1952, the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Manindra Cotton Mills of Cossimbazar,

Sangha of Cossimbazar, Murshidabad, regarding the matters specified in the 
schedule thereto was referred for adjudication to the First Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal, 
a complaint was filed before it by Shri Suren Das, Shri Anil Kumar Ganguly

AWARD. 


1. By order No. 2124Dis./D/13L-16/53, dated the 11th June 1953, the 
Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under section 
10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute between Shri 
Gobardhan Paul, 37/1, Canal West Road, Calcutta, Managing Director, Howrah 
Press, Ltd., and his employee Shri Jitendra Nath Pathak, 45/8, Muraripukur 
Road, Calcutta-11, regarding the matters specified in the schedule, to the Third 
Industrial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, by notification No. 592Dis./D/12L-5/52, dated the 23rd February 1953, 
for adjudication. 


2. After usual notices thé parties entered appearance. Shri Jitendra Nath 
Pathak filed his written statement of claim on 30th July 1953 and the Managing 
Director, Shri Gobardhan Paul, filed written statement on 26-11-53, and then 
Shri Jitendra Nath Pathak filed supplementary written statement on 26th 
December 1953. Thereafter the parties were asked to file their lists of docu- 
ments. The case was then fixed for hearing on 15th April 1954. As the 
employer was absent, the case could not be taken up for hearing on that day 
and the case was adjourned to 8th May 1954. On 8th May 1954, the employer 
obtained adjournment on the ground of death of a relation. The case was 
adjourned to 14th June 1954. The employer did not turn up on that date and 
accordingly the matter was proceeded ex-partes 


3,, The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of reference 
is as follows: — 


(1) Is Shri Jitendra Nath Pathak entitled to arrear wages amounting 
to Rs. 382-6-6 from Shri Gobardhan Paul, Managing Director, 
Howrah Press, Ltd.? 


DECISION. 


In support of his claim Shri Jitendra Nath Pathak has deposed before this 
Tribunal. He served in the Howrah Press, Ltd., for 6 years or so till January 
1952 as an Accountant on a slary of Rs. 35 per month. According to his case in 
the written statements, his employer, the Howrah Press, Ltd., had closed down 
its business; he had left service of his own accord at the end of January 1952, 
and then applied before the Labour Commissioner on 26th December 1952 
complaining non-payment of arrears of salary amounting to Rs. 382-6-6 pies for 
the period ending January 1952. It further appears that during the conciliation 
proceedings which followed on such complaint, the present Managing Director 
Shri Gobardhan Paul did not appear and thus the matter came to be referred 
for adjudication to this Tribunal. 


Under the present reference, an individual workman simply wants his arrear 
dues and seeks no other relief. In a case reported in 1952, L.L.J. (Volume I), 
page 550, it has been held that such a claim by a workman for recovery of 
arrears Of salary due to him would be appropriate under the payment of Wages 
Act. But as section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act appears to be no bar to 
investigation of such a claim by an Industrial Tribunal, the Tribunal not being 
a Court and the proceeding before it not being a suit, the matter is taken up for 
decision as it has been referred by the Government. 


On the evidence which is ex-parte, I find that a sum of Rs. 382-6-6 pies is 
due to Shri Jitendra Nath Pathak on account of arrears of salary up to January 
1952 from Howrah Press, Ltd., and not from Shri Goberdhan Paul personally. 
The Managing Director, Shri Gobardhan Paul, is to pay the said amount out of

assets of Howrah Press, Ltd., in his hands, if any, to the workman within 2 
months from the date the award becomes enforceable.

DECISION. 
Issue No. 1—Acting allowance. 


The Union demands that when an employee is to officiate in a superior post 
for more than fortnight, he should be paid 50 per cent. of the difference in paly 
and allowance between his post and superior post. The Company resists the 
claim. It is said that the demand for an acting allowance is incompatible, when 
a senior employee may likewise claim additional emoluments for performing the 
work of an absent junior, The Company further alleges that by temporarily 
taking over senior position, a junior employee obtains excellent opportunities to 
gain experience, undertake responsibility and show his ability thus enhancing his 


chances of promotion. 


Giving careful consideration to the matter I find nothing to resist claim for 
acting allowance. There seems to be no reason why in fairness an employee 
who officiate in a higher grade or post and thereby discharges duties of a more 
responsible nature or of a different character from those attached to his own 
post should not receive an acting allowance. The principle of payment of 
officiating allowance to an employee when he acts in a higher and more respon- 
sible post is well established. In a case like this it is the usual practice that 
where an employee acts in a higher appointment he takes the minimum of the 
higher scale and if his کی‎ pay is higher, he takes his present pay plus one 
stage in the higher grade. The acting allowance will be available only in case 
the period of acting is more than 14 days and not otherwise. In accordance 
with the said usual practice, I direct payment of acting allowance when the acting 
is for a period more than 14 days. No acting allowance will however be payable 
if the period of acting is not more than 14 days. 


Issue No. 2—Tiffin or tiffiin allowance. 


The Union demands that the employees should be provided with tiffin or 
tiffin allowance at the rate of Re. 1 and annas 12 to the clerical and subordinate 
staff, respectively. The Union alleges that before the Mercantile Tribunal the 
Manager of the said Company assured to give due consideration to such demand 
but nothing has been done in this respect since then. It is further said that 
the wages do not leave any margin for expenses towards the tiffin during office 
hours, and that unlike this Company, tiffin is being granted to employees by a 
good number of commercial establishments from both before and after the 
Mercantile Award. The Company opposes the claim. It denies having made 
any promise to the Tribunal in this respect. It is said that a reference to the 
award will show that provision for tiffin was entirely discretionary. The Com- 
pany gave due consideration to the matter and found that there was no justifica- 
tion for making any provision for such an allowance. The Company, however, 
admits in its written statement that tiffin or an allowance in lieu is provided by 


some large concerns. 


After giving careful consideration to the matters, I think time has come when 
something should be done for the employees in this respect. The matter came 
up for consideration before the Omnibus Tribunal under issue number 5 headed 
“Canteen and Tiffin” (vide award published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 4th 
August 1949). It was provided in the said award, “According to the scheme 
of our award, these are in the nature of ex-gratia concession. A request was 
made to the Company by the employees to make a grant and the Manager 
assured to give due consideration to it.” When, however, it is admitted that 
some firms have been giving tiffin or tiffin allowance to their employces, it 15 meet 
and proper that this Company should do likewise. The firms which have been 
giving tiffin or tiffin allowance may be large concerns but this Company too 18 
not small and has not pleaded incapacity to pay. When admittedly it has been 


fant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 2275 
ee 


making profit every year, I think the Company should not grudge small payment 
in the shape of tiffin allowance to their employees, more so when there is no 
canteen @rrangement. Considering what other concerns have been paying in this 
respect and the financial position of the Company, | allow annas 6 to the clerical 
7 and annas 4 to the subordinate staff as tiffin allowance for each working 
ay. 

Issue No. 3—Medical aid. 


The Union demands that the employees shalf be allowed effective and 
adequate medical assistance including doctor’s fees, cost of medicines, injections, 
patent medicines and charges for beds in the hospital and for operations. The 
Company alleges that it grants to the employees one month sick leave on full 
رم‎ and further two months’ sick leave on half pay and further concessions for 
continued sick leave with proportionate pay. It pleads further that the Com- 
pany is and has always been sympathetic towards its employees and has assisted 
financially when genuine cases of hardship have arisen due to sickness. In the 
circumstances it says that no direction should be given under this head. I agree 
that in view of the existing facilities, no further provision is warranted or called 
for. P.W. 2 Shri Jyotirmoy Samaddar admitted that no distinction is made 
between Anglo-Indian assistants and Indian employees who are given same 
medical aid. He also admitted that they get medical leave with full pay for one 
month and with half pay for two months. In the case of Caltex (India), Ltd., 
and their workmen reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 402, the Hon’ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal held that the maximum limit regarding the cost of medical 
assistance should not exceed one month’s salary including allowances in any one 
year. As this Company allows sick leave for 3 months of which one month 
with full pay and two mopths on half pay unlike Caltex (India), Ltd., which was 
granting 14 days’ sick leave with full pay, it appears that the employees of this 
নিস are better treated in this respect. I, therefore, make no ا‎ under 
this issue. 


Issue No. 4—Employees’ representatives in Provident Fund Trust. 


The Union has abandoned its claim under this issue as the trustees of the 
Provident Fund have not been made parties. No direction is accordingly made 
under this issue. 


Issue No. 5—Gratuity. 


It is agreed on all hands that this Company started Provident Fund for its 
employees in 1939 when the rate of contribution on either side was 4 per cent. 
The said rate of contribution, it is agreed, lasted up to 1945 and thereafter from 
1946 to 1949, the rate of contribution was 5 per cent. on either side. The 
matter at this stage came up for consideration before the Mercantile Tribunal 
under issue No. 3 headed “Retiring benefits and benefits on termination of 
service’. The award published on 4th August 1949, raised 5 per cent. contri- 
bution to 10 per cent. for the clerks and to 64 per cent. for the subordinate staff. 
The award also provided gratuity for uncovered period since 1939. The award 
m this respect laid down as below:— 


“The Provident Fund was started in 1939. To make up for the deficiencies 
for the past period, we award for the clerks a retiring gratuity at the 
rate of half month’s salary for each year of service up to the raising 
of the contribution to 10 per cent. calculated on the pay drawn 

ejust before the introduction of the award. 


Similarly for the subordinate staff we award 7 days’ pay for each year of 
service up to the tage of raising the contribution to 64% per cent. 
calculated on the basis of pay drawn just before the enforcement 
of the award. ‘The gratuities in both the cases shall be paid when 
provident fund money shall become payable.” 


2276 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 [Parr | 
SaaS 


Before this background the Union now demands that when employees of a 
good number of firms are being given double retiral benefits, there should be in 
addition to the contributory provident fund the following scheme of gratuity for 
the employees of this Company:— 

(1) In case of death of an employee while in service, or termination of 
service for reasons of illness, or old age or some other cause beyond 
control, or retrenchment or termination of service by the Company, 
ما‎ shall be-paid at the rate of one month’s salary for each year 
of service. 


(2) On resignation of an employee after 5 years of service or more 
gratuity should be paid at the rate of one month’s salary for each 
year of service. 


The Company resists the claim. It is said that these are long term schemes and 
should not be changed with every rise and fall in the fortune of the employer. 


On giving careful consideration to the matter, it seems that the Company’s 
contention is well-founded. In the present case not only the system of 
provident fund has been in vogue since 1939, but also the rates of contribution 
have been increased and there has been provision for the uncovered period by 
grant of gratuity under the award. In the case reported in 1951, L.A.C., page 
402, it has been held that contribution at 10 per cent. to the provident fund is 
liberal. In the circumstances, I do not think that I would be justified to prant 
dual benefit of gratuity as claimed by the Union so soon after the award. The 
Company may not have pleaded want of financial capacity to bear the burden, 
but this does not alone afford justification for adding to the scheme provided 
under the award in 1949 by grant of dual benefit of gratuity. In this view of 
the matter Union’s claim for double benefit of gratuity is refused. 


Issue No. 6.—Bonus. 


The claim relates to the year 1952. The Union demands three months’ 
salary as bonus to be paid out of profit of the year to all clerical and sub-staff 
of the Company. The Company opposes the claim. It is said that there 
would be no available surplus for such payment after meeting the prior charges 
on account of taxation, rehabilitation and replacement, fair return on working 
capital, etc. 


The Company is a British Company registered in England. At the hearing 
it has filed its balance-sheet and trading and profit and loss account for the yea 
ended 31st October 1952, only in respect of the Calcutta Branch along with 
Auditors’ letter (Exts. B and B1). These account papers (Ext. B) have been 
filed by the Company as confidential information under section 21 of the Indus. 
trial Disputes Act. In the Auditors’ report appended to the balance-sheet there 
is mention about a separate report, dated 30th January 1953. This latter report 
has not been produced and in its place the Company has produced a letter, dated 
rd May 1954 (Ext. B1), from the Auditors to the Company to show that the 
report in question which was addressed to the Managing Director of the Com- 
pany in Dundee contained “particulars of additions to assets, depreciation being 
written off, comments on work carried out by us (meaning Auditors), details 
of commission and bonus to staff, and information with regard to foreign 
exchange contracts but does not contain any statement or remark which, in any 
way, affects the correctness of the figures in the accounts”. Fronf this it is 
contended on behalf of the Company that the accounts submitted by it (Ext. B) 
are full and complete for the purpose of calculation of bonus. It is on 07৫ 
contrary contended on behalf of the Union that without the separate report which 
has been withheld by the Company, the document is not complete for the 
purpose and should, therefore, be taken with a grain of salt. In.view of the

Auditors’ letter, Ext. Bl, the balance-sheet, Ext. B, has been accepted in 
evidence, though the separate report has not been filed. As there has been, 
however’ controversy between the parties as to whether the amount shown as

Before entering into the controversy, it is necessary to state certain facts as 
are admitted or established in evidence. The establishment with which we are 
concerned consists of 32 clerks and 10 sub-staff. Their total monthly bills on 
account of salary amount to Rs. 4,902 (vide Ext. D). The Company has been 
paying one month’s salary as Puja bonus all along and it has paid such bonus to 
the staff for the year 1952. In addition to Puja bonus the Company paid in past 
few years a bonus called closing bonus after the close of the accounts of the 
Compuny’s business of a year not to all employees but to some according to its 
discretion. Such closing bonus was paid to all tlie employees for the first time 
for the year 1951 on the basis of 3th of their basic salaries. At the time each 
employee signed a statement to the effect that the payment was ex-gratia and 
would not form a term or condition of service. Be that as it may, the bonus paid 
as closing bonus, it appears, is nothing other than a bonus paid out of profit. In 
the present case too, the employees claim the bonus out of profit and it has been 
held by the Full Bench of the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal that, if there be avail- 
able, surplus after making provision for prior charges, the employees are entitled 
to ett bonus out of such available surplus. So the claim of the employees cannot 
be defeated merely because they made a signed statement that they would not 
claim, bonus while receiving payment of closing bonus for the ycar 1951. If 
there be available surplus, they are entitled to have it distributed as bonus as of 
right. The statement, Ext. E, shows that the amount under head “Commission 
and Bonus to the Staff” as noted in the balance-sheet, Ext. B, includes among 
others closing bonus for the year 1952 being a little more than a month’s salary of 
the entire clerical and subordinate staff. This would show that the Company was 
also cognizant of the fact that it could not avoid liability to pay bonus out of 
profit which it described as closing bonus when it made provision for more than 
one month’s salary in this respect. 


Now, let us turn to the controversies. As the Company has claimed the 
account papers, Exts. B and E, to be confidential information under Section 21 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, I have to refer to them in a general manner without 
disclosing any of the figures shown in them. This puts me to some handicap in 
dealing with the subject. The Company filed its own calculations in Ext. C 
showing that there would be no available surplus after meeting prior charges for 
distribution as bonus but a huge deficit to the extent of Rs. 56,225-10-3 pies. The 
Union on the other hand contends that if calculations be made on correct data and 
properly, there would be no deficit but a sufficient surplus left for payment of 3 
months’ salary as bonus for the year 1952 to all clerical and subordinate staff. 


Firstly, the parties are at variance regarding the amount of profit earned by 
the Company during the year 1952 under discussion. The Company contends 
that what amount was shown in the balance-sheet against head “Balance as per 
balance-sheet” is the profit of the year. It accordingly took the said figure in item 
No. (1) of Ext. C as constituting the profit. The Union on the other hand 
contends that the profit of the year would be the total of the two amounts shown 
in Ext. B, respectively, against the heads (1) “Balance as per balance-sheet” and 

| (2) “Commission and bonus to staff”. On giving careful consideration to the 
Matter, it seems that Union’s contention must prevail to a large extent. The 


2278 THE ০1604 GAZETTH, JULY &, 1954 [Parr J 


— eens, 


details of the commission and bonus to staff are to be found in the statement 
(Ext. E) filed by the Company. The first item in it is a very big sum said to be 
U.K. Office purchasing commission (more than enough to wipe out the deficit 
shown in Ext C). Nothing has been shown by the Company how it could be 
taken away to reduce the profit of the year. In my opinion this is clearly a case 
in which the Company cannot be allowed to reduce its profit by exclusion of the 
aforesaid commission. Then again the statement (Ext. E) shows that except 
three, commission was paid to European Officers though there was no contractual 
obligation to do so. The amount so paid without service agreement should not 
in my opinion be excluded from the profit to the prejudice of the workmen for the 
purpose of calculation of bonus. Only the amount of commission said to have 
been paid to three European Officers on the basis of service agreements may with 
some justification be excluded from the profit and nothing else. Then the state- 
ment (Ext. E) reveals that the amount under head “Commission and bonus to 
staff” as shown in the balance-sheet (Ext. B) includes Puja bonus being a little 
less than 2 months’ salary of the entire clerical and subordinate staff besides closing 
bonus for the year 1952 being a little more than one month’s salary of the entire 
clerical and subordinate staff, Though the evidence does not show that Puja 
bonus was paid beyond oné month’s salary for the year 1952, 1 think, that in the 
absence of evidence that whole of it was not spent, the Company should be 
permitted to exclude from the profit the whole of the amount shown as Puja 
bonus. So it comes to this that out of the amount shown as commission and 
bonus to staff, a sum more than Rs. 85 thousand would be available for inclusion 
in the profit. If this figure be added to the amount of item (1) of Ext. C, it will 
appear that even on the basis of Company’s calculation of prior charges as in items 
(2) to (7). there would be no deficit but sufficient surplus left for distribution as 
bonus corresponding to 3 months’ salary. Then again the Union contends that 
the Company’s figures regarding prior charges are inflated and Company’s calcula- 
tions faulty and that even if no portion of commission and bonus to staff be includ- 
ed in the profit, the Company's position will not improve materially and that there 
will be sufficient surplus left for distribution as bonus as claimed. It appears that 
there is good deal of substance in this contention except with respect to items (2) 
and (3) in Ext. C. 


As regards provision for income tax both in India and in U.K. as shown in 
items (2) and (3) in Ext. C, the Union’s contention cannot be upheld. The 
demand notice produced, supports that the amount shown as payable as income 
tax in India in item No. (2) of Ext. C was so really payable. As regards income 
tax in U.K., the amount has been claimed at ۱8 per cent. in item No. (3) of 
Ext. C. When the Company is an English Company registered in England, it is 
obvious that it has got to pay tax out of its profit earned in India to the Govern- 
ment in England. So when the profit to that extent will not be available, I find 
no reason why the Company should not get allowance for the income tax payable 
in ...تا‎ Company’s claim under these two heads is, therefore, justified. 


As regards provision for rehabilitation of plant and machinery as claimed in 
item (4) of Ext. C, the Union’s contention must prevail. It appears that the 
Company has claimed the values of plant and machinery not in accordance with 
those shown in the balance-sheet but on the basis of the Insurance figures. | 
think that the values of the plant and machinery as shown in the balance-sheet 
should have been taken for the purpose of calculating rehabilitation charges. If 
these values are multiplied by 2°7 and then divided by 15 as the Company did, 
the allowance permissible on this head would come to Rs. 23,752-4-3 pies. If 
the values of the plant and machinery on the contrary be accepted at the Insurance 
figures as shown in Ext. C, it is obvious that it would be appreciated value and 
so there can be no question of multiplying the said figure by 2°7 as the Company 
did. If without multiplying, the said value is divided by 15, the allowance under

this head would come to Rs. 24,333-5-4 pies in place of Rs. 65,700 as shown in 
Ext. C, 

Likgwise, as regards provision for rehabilitation and reconstruction of the 
buildings as in item (5) of Ext. C, the انی سی‎ has not taken the value of the

opinion the life of the buildings should have been taken to be 30 years in place 
of 27 years as in Ext C. 


Lastly, as to claim for interest under items (6) and (7) of Ext. C, I find no 
justification for such separate claim under different heads when the balance-sheet 
discloses no capital other than the one shown against item No. (6). So allow- 
ance can be had only on the amount of the capital as shown in item No. (6) and 
not in item No. (7) of Ext. C. Nothing has been shown by the Company to 
support the claim laid in item No. (7). 


If the prior charges be calculated on the lines as indicated above it will be 
found that there would be no deficit but sufficient surplus left for distribution as 
bonus corresponding to 3 months’ salary to all the clerical and subordinate staff as 
claitbed by the Union. Union’s claim for bonus is accordingly allowed. The 
Company is directed to pay the amount within one month from the date the 
award becomes enforceable. 


It may be added here that the fact that the Company paid one month's salary 
as Puja bonus for the year 1952 makes no difference in this respect when the 
present claim is for bonus out of profit. 


The provisions regarding acting allowance and tiffin allowance will be effective 
from the date the award becomes enforceable.

Industrial dispute between Messrs. Dunbar Cotton Mif's, Shyamnagore, 24-

PRESENT: 
Suri 9. C. MUKHERIJI, District Judge, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 


For the Union: Shri Arun Prokash Chatterji, Advocate. 


For the Company: Shri K. B. Basu, Counsel, instructed by Shri D. Basu 
Thakur, Solicitor of Messrs. Orr, Dignam & Co., Solicitors. 


By Government order No. 4307Dis./D/8L-2/53, dated the 12th November 
1953, the aforesaid dispute was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. The 
issues framed by the Government were the same as the issucs framed by this 
Tribunal. and they were as follows:— 


(1) Should the Dunbar Mills appoint cleaners for the purpose of getting the 
machines cleaned? If not, what should be the ا و ا‎ and circum- 
stances under which the workmen themselves should clean the machines? 


(2) Are the workmen entitled to receive any wages or compensation for the 
period during which the Mill remained closed on account of the workmen’s 
refusing to clean the machines? 


On receipt of the aforesaid reference, notices were issued on the parties. 
The Union filed its written statement on 12th January 1954 and the Company 
filed its written statement on 28th January 1954, and the case was heard on 
31st May 1954 and on the following dates. 


The case for the Union is that the workers were compelled to clean machines 
while in’ motion, that this involves a risk and is against the Factory Rules, that 
the Company should appoint special cleaners for the purpose, that the Company, 
locked out the factory from 14th September 1953 to 18th September 1953 
without any reference to the Works Committee, that the lock-out is illegal and 
unjustified and that the workers should be entitled to full pay and allowances 
for the period. 


The Company, on the other hand, contended that on 25th August 1953, the 
workers of the Mill surrounded the Manager’s office over their demand for Pujé 
Bonus and kept the Management confined from 9 a.m. to 2 a.m., that on the 
7th of September 1953 Company gave notice to the employces that no- bonu: 
was payable in 1953, that in order to coerce the Management in paying bonu 
the workers adopted a go slow policy and the workers of the entire Mil 
stopped cleaning machinery, that on 9th September 1953, Company gave noticc 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 4 228 | 


পপ 


informing the workers of the said condition, that on 12th September 1953 the 
Management was compelled to close the Mill until such time as it was assured 
of resumption of normal work by the workmen, that on 18th of September 1953 
Management received مو‎ assurance from the workmen for resumption 
of normal work and opened the Mill from 19th September 1953, and that in the 
circumstances, the closure was justified and the workers are not entitled to pay 
for the period. 


AWARD. 


Issue No. 1.—At present there is no dispute as regards cleaning machine. 
The Assistant Manager said that the present practice is that the blow room is 
actually stopped before half an hour of the closing time and the waste droppings 
are actually removed and the machines are cleaned fully, that this is done by 
the tenters who work on the machine. As regards carding department he said 
that the cards are cleaned while they are for grinding, i.e., the cleaning of the 
gearing and everything is done according to the number of cards we have to 
allot for grinding, say 2 or 3 cards per day and gearing and all that is cleaned 
at that time. Further he said that it is done daily according to programme 
when the gearing, the bottom box, the top box, the rollers, etc., are thoroughly 
cleaned and the machine is restarted. In the Ring Frame also the machine is 
stopped for about 4 hours and the gearing 15 cleaned. The top rollers and the 
spindles are also cleaned. Then in the Winding, this is cleaned when one 
complete beam is removed. In Warping when the beam is complete the 
cleaning is done. In Weaving also when the beam is complete and the new 
heam is being brought and tied on the loom, the cleaning of the gearing and the 
complete.cleaning of the 10901) is done. Apart from this the machines are also daily 
Sree once or twice according to the convenience of the workers as regards 
non-moving parts. Again on Saturday the general cleaning for about 10 
minutes is done throughout the Mill at the close of the shift. During argument 
the learned Lawyer for the workers accepted this method of cleaning and hence 
I direct that the machine will be cleaned according to this programme ١ 
future. 


The Management contended that no machine is cleaned while in motion. 
Labour Officer and the Assistant Manager stated this on oath and I believe 
them. There is no substance in the allegation that the workers are made to 
clean the machine while in motion. There is also no substance in the conten- 
tion that the employers should accordingly engage special cleaners for ۶ 
purpose. The learned Lawyer for the workers contended that there is a pro- 
vision for cleaner in the Textile Award and so cleaners should be appointed. 
But I agree with the Assistant Manager’s explanation that this cleaner means 
“bobbin cleaners.” Workers have not been able to examine a single witness 
to show that the cleaners are appointed in any mill for the purpose of cleaning 
the machine. I accordingly turn down the claim of the workers. 


Issue No. 2.—It is clear that the Management's contention that they do not 
compel the workers to clean the machine while in motion is right. ey have 
also proved that cleaning is generally done by stopping the machine by turn 
on each day. The Union is not very sure of its position as to when and in what 
circumstances they stopped the cleaning. They even complained during trial 
that they have not been paid for the work of cleaning and hence they have 
stopped cleaning the machine. But there is no such case in the written state- 
ment and there is no proof that they have ever been paid anything extra for 
the purpose of cleaning. The Labour Officer has said that he has examined all 
the past records and was satisfied that there was no such payment. 
Mr. Prodhan has said that for such cleaning after stopping the machine the 
time-raters’ pay is not deducted and the piece-raters are given average wage for 
the period the machine is stopped. The contention of the Management is that 


2282 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTH, JULY 38, 1954 [Parr 1 
ern nee ere eee 


the workers stopped cleaning prior to lock-out not because they were compelled 
to work with the machine while in motion but because they retaliated duc to 
the refusal of the grant of Puja Bonus. It appears from the Management's 
notice, dated 9th of September, that during the “past weck” the workers were 
not cleaning their machines. Each party tricd to interpret tthe word “past 
week” in its own way. But obviously in my opinion this means the week from 
4th to 9th of September. I do not agree with the contention of the learned 
Lawyer for the Union that the words “past week”” mean Monday to Saturday 
of the previous week when the notice is dated 9th of September which is a 
Wednesday. It is clear that there was a strong fight going on over the bonus 
issue and the leaflets were being issued out and the preparations were being 
made and on 25th the Management was actually kept detained. On 28th the 
Conciliation Officer wrote to the Management asking for their views 01) the 
question of bonus. It is stated on this document that on 26th he met the 
representatives of the Company and on 27th he met the Works Committee 
representatives and he is now seeking the views of the Company on the subject. 
The Company by its letter, dated 3rd September, denied its liability to pay 
bonus. This is the exact point of time from which the production in the Mill 
showed a decrease and till 12th it went on like that. That shows that the 
refusal to clean the machine started on the point when Company refused to pay 
bonus. It is also the evidence of the Labour Officer that the question of 
cleaners were never raised during these conciliation meetings and it was only 
raised for the first time and on the last moment on 12th, when production had 
fallen a great deal. The workers also deliberately commenced working on half 
pulley and thereby production was day to day reduced. The Company gave 
sufficient warning to the workers but even after this warning there was no 
improvement up to 5 p.m. on 10th. There was risk of the machine taking fire 
at any moment. So the Company was forced to close the Mill on 12th by 
notice, Ext. K. Thereafter there was conciliation meetings. On 18th there 
was a provisional agreement. The workers undertook to clean the machine as 
usual. This also shows that the demands for cleaner or for extra payment are 
an afterthought and there is no ground on which these new claims can be 
founded. In the circumstances the lock-out was justified and the workers are 
not entitled to pay for the period of “no work”. There is no reason why the 
employers will be compelled to pay in spite of “no work”, which was occasioned 
due to the fault of the workers. “This issue is answered in the negative. 


S. C. MUKHERJI, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed their

3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference are as follows :— 


(1) Whether the Company was justified in terminating the service of Shri 
Bima! Kanta Mukherji on charge of theft ? 


(2) Is he entitled to reinstatement on being acquitted by the law court? 
Is he entitled to any other relief? 


4. The case of the Press Employees’ Association representing the work- 
man, briefly stated, is as follows :—Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee joined this Com- 
pany as a compositor and ultimately rose to the position of a section-holder. He 
was at the time of dismissal and for a long period prior thereto, a member of 
the executive committee of the Press Employees’ Association. The majority of 
the employees of the Company were and are still members of the said Associa- 
tion. Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee in his capacity as a leading Trade 
Unionist in the said establishment was called upon on various occasions to 
represent the grievances and demands of the members of the said Association 
before the Company. For sometime prior to the incident referred to herein- 
after the relation between Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee and the Company and 
in particular the Manager thereof, namely, Mr. Marquis was greatly strained as 


2284 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 Par 1 


a result of the former having had to protest several times to the said Mr. 
Marquis against the latter’s attempts to speed up work in the said establishment. 


۹ 

On 8th May 1952 after the tiffin break at about 1 p.m., said Shri Bima! 
Kanta Mukherjee had left the establishment and was proceeding towards 
Chandni Chawk when he was seized bodily by two Durwans of the 5210 
Company near the New Cinema and was 1010 by the said Durwans that they 
had orders to bring him back to the said establishment and that he must go witn 
them. The said Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee protested against such high- 
handedness but the Durwans would not listen to him. In order to avoid 
creating a scene as well as out of curiosity, the said Shri Bimal Kanta Mukher- 
jee did not resist further and allowed himsclf to be taken back to the said 
establishment. 


Upon his arrival at the said establishment, the said Shri Bimal Kanta 
Mukherjee was taken to the said Manager and one of the Durwans produced a 
packet of types and declared that the said packet was found on the said Shri 
Bimal Kanta Mukherjee and that the said types were Company’s property. 
The said Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherji vehemently protested his innocence and 
denied that he had anything to do with the said packet or that the said packet 
had been found on him but nevertheless he was ordered by the said Manager 
to go to the Head Office of the said Company and shortly after his arrival there 
he was handed over by the Managing Director to the Police. 


Thereafter, on the basis of the Company’s complaint a prosecution was 
launched against the said Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee under section 381 of 
the Indian Penal Code and he was tried before Shri B. Banerjee, Presidency 
Magistrate, Calcutta. The said Magistrate found that the prosecution story was 
“destitute of truth” and honourably acquitted the said Shri Bimal Kanta 
Mukherjee by the order, dated 6th September 1952. 


On or about T3th May 1952 when proceedings against the said Shri Bimal 
Kanta Mukherjee were still pending before the said Magistrate, the said Mr. 
Marquis served a charge-sheet on the former accusing him of theft and asking 
him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from his employment for 
the said alleged misconduct. 


The allegation of theft is utterly false and there was no reasonable basis 
for the Management’s suspicion that any theft as alleged had been committed. 
The order of dismissal was mala fide, arbitrary, unjust and was against all 
principles of natural justice. 


The Association accordingly prays for reinstatement of the workman Shri 
Bimal Kanta Mukherjee and for payment of compensation to him for the 
period of forced unemployment. 


In reply’the Company submits as below :— 


The workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee was not promoted ؛‎ the 
position of section-holder but was a senior compositor at the time of dismissal. 
The employer denies that the workman was a member of the executive com- 
mittee of any Union or that he ever was a leading trade unionist or that he 
ever represented to the employer grievances and demands of the workers 
or that this employer was ever aware of any union. activity of the 
workman and further denies that due to attempt of Mr. Marquis, the 
Manager, to speed up work or for any other cause there was any strained 
feeling between the aforesaid workman and the Company or Mr. Marquis, the 
Manager, or there was ever any such occasion for the same. 


The employer denies the length of service as alleged and further denies 
that he was ever an assistant section-holder or that he was promoted about

five years ago to the post of section-holder and submits that he was last working 
as senior compositor. 


The employer denies that the workman was going towards Chandni Chawk 
and also denies that the Durwans ever told the workman that they had orders 
to bring him back to the Company. It is also denied that the workman 
allowed himself to be taken back just to avoid creating a scene and that the 
workman ever pleaded his innocence regarding theft of a packet of types as 
untruly alleged. 


On 8th-May 1952 at about 1-05 p.m. workers were going out of the gate 
for tiffin as it was recess period from 1 p.m. to 1-30 p.m. and the Durwan at 
the gate was conducting the usual search of the workers at the time of their 
exit. The workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee was going out when the 
Durwan placed his hand on the hip as the Durwan suspected something to 
have been concealed there. The Durwan, who was busy in carrying out

| The aforesaid two peons followed Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee who began

fhe agi workman wanted to drop something tied in a piece of cloth from under 
his dhoti but it was found out by the said two peons and brought along with 
the workman to the office of this employer. The bundle tied in a piece of 
cloth. was opened in presence of the said workman as also in presence of the 
Manager and other workers and it was found to contain lead types which 
belonged to the employer. Suspecting this to be a case of theft, committed by 
the workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee of the employer’s property, police 
was informed and the said workman was taken into custody. 


On 13th May 1952 a charge-sheet (Annexure “A” to the written state-

any explanation within 19th May 1952 and again on 20th May 1952 another

no explanation was submitted by the said workman. Thereafter on 2nd June 
1952 another notice (Annexure “C” to the written statement) was issued to 
the workman fixing 7th June 1952 for investigation into the charges and he 
was directed to remain present at the enquiry to take part in the proceedings. 
But the said workmen ignored the said notice and failed and neglected to appear. 
The employer thereupon held the enquiry, examined witnesses and 
decided to dismiss him for his misconduct on being fully _ satisfied 
about the reasonableness of their suspicion § regarding theft of lead 
types committed by Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee and he was accordingly 
dismiused with effect from 8th May 1952 which order was duly communicated 
to the workman on 9th June 1952 (Annexures “D” and “E” to the written 
statement). 


The employer denies that there has been any violation of the principles of 
natural justice or there was any malice or unfair labour practice or victimisa- 
tion in the step taken and in view of the reasonable suspicion of the offence 
committed by the said workman, the employer was perfectly justified in dismiss- 
ing the said workman from service in the interest of the industry and discipline.

The employer is aware of a criminal case which was prosecuted by the 
State against the aforesaid workman and besides arranging production of

In the circumstances, the Company submits that the claim of the Association

DECISION, 


In support of the case the Association has examined the workman concern- 
ed Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee besides proving document, Ext. 1. The Com- 
pany on the other hand has examined its Manager, D.W.1 Mr. J. H. Marquis, 
its Legal Adviser, D.W. 2 Shri D. M. Lahiri, the Durwan, D.W. 3 Shri Sitla 
Sahay Singh, the office peons, 10. W. 4 Shri Satyanarayan Singh and D.W.5 
Shri Raja Ram Singh, besides proving documents, Exts. A to H. 


The workman concerned Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee, the evidence shows, 
was a senior compositor in this Company and did not hold the position of a 
section-holder as claimed by him. His own evidence in cross-examination that 
his salary at the time of dismissal was Rs. 87 while the minimum pay of the 
section holder was Rs. 120, shows that he was not holding the position of section 
holder but was a senior compositor. The evidence shows that as such com- 
positor he had to handle lead types. He was dismissed for theft of a packet 
of lead types and for refusing and avoiding search on 8th May 1952. The 
evidence shows that on 8th May 1952 durimg recess hours commencing at 
1 p.m. when the workers were going out of the gate, the Durwan, D.W. 3, 
Shri Sitla Sahay Singh was conducting usual search of the workers at the time of 
their exit and when Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee was going out, the 0 
Durwan while passing his hand over his body during the course of search felt a 
hard substance on his hip and thus suspected something to have been con- 
cealed there underneath the dhoti. As the Durwan was busy in carrying out 
search of other workers rushing out of the gate and as the Standing Orders 
required formal search to be made in the presence of a witness, he asked the 
workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee to wait for thorough search. The 
Durwan became busy in searching other workers when Shri Bimal Kanta Muk- 
herjee slipped out of the gate unnoticed and started walking faster. The 
Durwan finding him going away called him back but Shri Bimal Kanta Mukher- 
jee ignoring the call of the Durwan continued walking faster. At that time two 
peons, D.W. 4 Shri Satyanarayan Singh and D.W. 5 Shri Raja Ram _ Singh 
happened to come to that place and the Durwan who was alonc at 
the gate requested them to follow and bring back Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee 
and of them D.W. 4 Shri Satyanarayan Singh, who was going ahead caught Shri 
Bimal Kanta Mukherjee on the Madan Street and then D.W. 5 also reached the 
place and seized him. It is admitted by Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee in the 
written statement as also in evidence that two peons caught him and brought 
him back. The evidence of these peons reveals that after Shri Bimal Kanta 
Mukherjee was caught, they requested him to accompany them to the gate and 
when he was unwilling to do so, they brought him back by force to the gate. 
Their evidence also reveals that after being caught, Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee 
attempted to drop a packet containing lead types from the hip underneath his 
dhoti. Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee admitted that he was forcibly brought by 
the two office peons to the gate of the Press and there they held out a packet 
containing lead types as having been recovered from him. He deposed, “On 
8th May 1952 while going out during recess hours at about 1-5 p.m. or so, the 


Part 1} THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 4 228T 


gate Durwan Shri Sitla Sahay searched my body, found nothing and let me go. 
Accordjngly I proceeded and came up to the Madan Street. It was near about 
the jufiction of Dharamtalla and Madan Street. I was going to purchase 
medicine for my ailing wife from the Drug Shop of one Mukherjee. I was 
caught near about the junction of Dharamtalla and Madan Street by Shri Satya- 
narayan Singh while another bearer named Raja Ram was coming towards me. 
After they caught me they told me that Saheb wanted me to go to the office. I 
said that | would be going after purchasing medicine. They did not listen to me 
and insisted on my coming forthwith. They then dragged me to the office on 
holding my right arm. I was brgught to the office ncar the gate. There a row 
was created and it was given out holding out the packet containing the lead types. 
that this was recovered from me. 1 was not given any opportunity to disown 
such 21158701011. I, therefore, kept silent.” His own statement as above lends 
support to the case of the Company. Unless he was asked by the Durwan to 
stop for thorough search and unless he slipped off contrary to the said direction, 
there would be no meaning for the two peons to chase him, to catch him and to 
bring him back by force. This fits with the case of the Company that he was 
asked by the Durwan to stop for a এ search and as he slipped off the 
other office peons who happened to come that side were asked by the Durwan to 
follow and bring him back. As regards the recovery of the packet containing 
the lead types, according to his own showing, it was there and the office peons 
who caught him and brought him held it out and claimed it to have been 
recovered from him. The fact that he did not protest and disown such allega- 
tion but on the contrary he kept silent would belie his suggestion that this was 
not recovered from ۰ e production of the lead types packet being 
contemporaneous with his production at the gate, it is highly probable that it was 
recavered from him. In view of the evidence given by the workman himself as 
also the circumstances, the suggestion of planting must be ruled out. No 
animus has been suggested or proved against either the Durwan or the two office 
peons. Only thing which was suggested during trial is against the Durwan 
that, he used to lend money to Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee and that there was. 
disagreement over such transaction. The allegations are afterthought, uncon- 
vincing and unreliable. The Durwan denied having ever Jent money to Shri 
Bimal Kanta Mukherjee. It is, therefore, not probable and natural that for 
nothing these people would plant the packet of lead types on his person and 
haul him up on a charge of theft falsely. They have no axe 10 grind. 

regards the Manager, no doubt a strained relation between him and the work- 
man his been pleaded and even if it is correct, it is not natural and probable 
that a man_ of his position would ask the Durwans and the office [৩0178 to 
incriminate Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee for theft by planting a packet of lead 
types. The witnesses may lie but not the circumstances. The fact that the 
packet was claimed to have heen recovered from his person at the same time 
he was brought to the gate together with the fact that Shri Bimal Kanta Mukher- 
jee remained silent and did not protest can leave no room for doubt that it was 
not planted but was recovered from his person. No doubt there has been dis- 
crepancy as to the exact situation where and how the packet had been kept 
concealed and where it was recovered, but these are minor matters which do not 
materially affect the broad case of recovery of lead types packet from him. 
The fact of acquittal of Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee by the Criminal Court does 
not necessarily mean that Management’s decision to the contrary is without basis. 
The scopes of enquiries by the Management and the Criminal Court are entirely 
different. The evidence of the Lawyer, D.W. 2 Shri D. M. Lahiri, shows that 
when Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee was produced before him, he questioned 
Bimal Babu about the incident to which he did not reply. This does not suggest 
in favour of Bimal Babu’s innocence. D.W. 2 denied having offered any 
inducement or promise to the workman to extort confession. In cross-exam- 
ination the workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee admitted that he had no 


2288 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 [Parr I 


eel 
enmity with D.W. 2. So, evidence of D.W. 2 cannot be brushed aside. Then 
the evidence of workman himself to the effect that from the gate he was not 
taken to Mr. Marquis but was_ taken straight to the Head Office at Mango 
Lane, Calcutta, and there produced first before Shri Lahiri (D.W. 2) and then 
before the Managing Director Shri A. P. Bhargava, who said forthwith “Shala, 
you shall have to undergo imprisonment for 6 months” suggests in favour of 
Company’s case that Bimal Babu had been caught red-handed with the packet. 
So, it cannot be said that the findings of the Management regarding the charges 
were not the possible views on the evidence and circumstances before it. 


There is nothing to show want of bona fides on the part of the Manage- 
ment. After Bimal Babu was caught with the lead types packet, the evidence 
shows that he was sent to the Head Othce of the Company andgfrom there the 
complaint was made and he was handed over to the Police. Then on 13th May 
1952, a charge-sheet was drawn up against him (Ext. A) and the workman 
admittedly received the said charge-sheet. Though he was directed to submit 
explanation to the charges, he did not submit any explanation to the same but 
wrote through his lawyer (Ext. B) on 19th May 1952 threatening the Company 
with contempt proceedings for proceeding against him as the matter was before 
the Police and Criminal Court. After receipt of such letter the Company again 
wrote to his lawyer on 20th May 1952 (Ext. C) asking for submission of explana- 
tion to the charges within the extended time. Notwithstanding this the workman 
did not submit explanation. Then on 2nd June 1952, the Company sent a notice 
to the workman (Ext. D) intimating that 7th June 1952 was fixed for hearing 
of the charges against him in the office of the Company at 11 a.m. In reply to 
the said notice his lawyer wrote on Sth June 1952 declining to attend the 
hearing as notified. On 7th June 1952 enquiry was held by the Management 
when the two office peons as also Abdul Jabbar, Raghunath Prasad were examin- 
ed and the statements were recorded by the Manager and signed by the witnesses 
(vide Ext. F). Then as a result of the enquiries, the Manager was satisfied 
and came to the findings in respect of the charges as he did and dismissed him 
by his order, dated 7th June 1952. The order was duly communicated to the 
workman. The Manager, it will therefore appear, acted in a perfectly bona fide 
manner and there was strict compliance with the principles of natural justice. 
The allegation of strained feeling between the Manager and the workman is 
unreliable. In the written statement the said strained feeling was alleged to 
have arisen out of the workman’s protest against Manager's general order to speed 
up work, while during trial the workman Shri Bimal Kanta Mukherjee (P.W. 1) 
stated in examination-in-chief that the said strained feeling arose as the Manager 
used to ask him to speed up work for 3/4 months before dismissal and as he 
could not comply with it. In cross-examination he stated that although Mr. 
Marquis wanted all the compositors to speed up work, neither he nor the 
Union protested against such direction of Mr. Marquis. The evidence of the 
Manager reveals that only when emergent orders came, he had to pass direction 
10 complete the work within the specified time and not otherwise. 1٦ will, 
therefore, appear that there could have been no strained feeling out of such 
direction, if any. As regards alleged Union activities, the evidence of the work- 
man himself does not suggest that he took any leading part in the Union, far 
less to the knowledge of the Management. The workman when questioned 
could not say whether there was an award in 1951 between the Prmting Presses 
and their workmen. He also admitted that after 15 workmen were retrenched 
in 1949, and when the matter relating to them was taken up before the Tribunal he 
took no step except taking the men to the Union. He might have been a member 
of the executive committee for about 3 years before dismissal but it does not appear 
that this had anything to do with the action taken against him by the Manage- 
ment. His claim that he went to the Manager to represent grievances of the 
workmen has been denied by the Manager. There cannot, therefore, be any 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1964 2289 


سے 


doubt that the action taken against him was not for his Union activities or from 
spirit of টিপ Regarding the workman’s complaint that the depart- 
mental proceedings should not have bcen started against him before conclusion 
of the criminal case, | find no substance in it, The Management has unfettered 
right to proceed against an employee, if it were otherwise, the Management 
would ceasc to function (vide February 1954, L.A.C., page 79). In the case 
reported in 1951 L.L.J. (Volume II), page 37, it has been held that the Manage- 
ment was under no duty to await the result of the prosecution in order to dis- 
charge its workmen for conduct subversive of discipline or to reinstate them on 
being discharged or acquitted in any such prosccution. The Company was, 
therefore, within its right in refusing to reinstate the workman after acquittal by 
the Criminal Court, for a prosecution may fail for a variety of reasons. Then 
again the scopes of the proceedings before the Tribunal and thc Magistrate are 
entirely different and have to be judged on different standards of evidence. So, 
on the evidence and circumstances, I find nothing to upset the decision of the 
Management. It is accordingly held that the workman is entitled to no relief. 
] award accordingly.
