02 DECISION. 
s, the Standard Vacuum Oil Company, Ltd. (hereafter called 

the patos i om head office called the Calcutta Territory 06 at No. 6, 
Church Lane, Calcutta. It has one oil depots called installations at Budge- 
Budge Chetla, Narkeldanga and other places in the suburbs of Calcutta. The res- 
pon ents, Amiya Bhusan Pal and Kamal Kanti Mukherjee, clerks, had been 


লা SSS ee — 
ی2‎ 25৮5 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 
۸ 4 


[Part BA 


posted at the Budge Budge installation in February 1949 and had been working 
there since then. On the 7th July 1953, however, the Superintendent of that 
installation ordered their transfer to the head office at Calcutta and asked them 
to report for duty there on the 13th July following. At that time proceedings 
between the Company and its workmen relating to a claim for bonus in which 
the aforesaid two clerks were also concerned were pending before the Third 
Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, and the said transfers were made without the 
permission of that Tribunal. On the 28th September 1953 they filed before 
that Tribunal complaints under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
(hereafter called the Act) against their transfer to the head office. The 
grounds ہہ‎ which their complaints were rested were (1) that by the 5810 
transfers the conditions of their service had been altered to their prejudice 
and (2) that the transfers were by way of victimisation. The Tribunal by its 
order, dated the 3rd April 1954, upheld the first contention, and so considered 
it unnecessary to go into the question of alleged victimisation. Against that 
order the Company has filed the appeal. We may at once say that the transfers 
to the head office has materially prejudiced them. We need not repeat th 

findings of the Tribunal on the point which were not challenged before us b 

Mr. Mullick appearing for the Company. The only point, therefore, to be con- 
sidered by us 1s whether the conditions of their service had been changed by 
those transfers. 


2. The Company has no Standing Orders for its workmen employed at 
the head office but it has Standing Orders governing the conditions of service 
of its workmen employed at the installations. Paragraph 19 of the said Stand- 
ing Orders runs as follows :— 


“Employees (meaning thereby the employees working at the installations) 
may be transferred from one department to another at the discre- 
tion of the Installation Superintendent.” 


The lower Tribunal held that this rule in the Standing Orders only covered 
the cases of inter-departmental transfers within the same installation but did not 
authorise a transfer from one installation to another or to the head office at 
Calcutta. We are of opinion that this interpretation of rule 19 is correct. 
The Tribunal, however, went on to hold that because of this rule the 
“inherent power” of an employer to transfer an employee from 017৩ place to 
another could not be invoked by the Company because of the rule of construc- 
tion that when the terms and_ conditions had been reduced to the form of a 
document, those cannot be allowed to be varied, contradicted, added to or subs- 
tracted from. This part of the judgment of the Tribunal requires close exami- 
nation. It must however be understood that we are called upon to decide the 
question of transfers from one establishment of the employer at one place to 
another establishment of_his at another place and not with the question of inter- 
departmental transfers in the same establishment at the same place and so our 
observations must be taken to be limited to that type of case which we have to 
consider here. 


3. The first observation which we would wish to make is that the existence 
of a power and its scope and exercise of it are entirely two different questions. 
Colourable exercise by the employer of his power to transfer a workman from 
one establishment of his at one place to another at a different place (e.g., 
when the transfer of a workman is ordered with a view to victimise him) can 
always be the subject of an industrial dispute, and can be investigated on a 
reference made under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. It can also 
be the subject matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Act, if made 
without the previous permission of the Tribunal where proceedings concerning 
that workman is pending, for it would be regarded to be by way of 
punishment and so would amount to a contravention to section 33(b) of the 
Act. In this case therefore there would be the necessity to remand the case 
for an enquiry into the workman’s case of victimisation if we had not agreed 
with the view of the Tribunal that by the transfer the conditions of service of 
these two workmen had been changed. 

۰ 


4. In considering the question whether a transfer from one place to another 
had effected a change in the conditions of service of a workman the following 
types of cases have to be ০0851061720, namely :— 

A. Where there gre standing orders, or the conditions of service have 
been reduced in writing ~nd— 
(i) those may either contain provisions dealing with transfers, or 
(ii) they may not. 
B. Where there are no Standing Orders at all or any other instrument in 
writing dealing with service conditions. 


The cases falling within B or A(ii) are of the same type. In those cases 
liability to be transferred from one establishment of the employer to another 
establishment of his at a different place by the employer or at his instance is an 
incident of service that is to say an implied condition of service and the workman 
concerned cannot successfully complain unless he can show that the transfer 
was made by way of punishment, and the element of victimisation would be 
cogent evidence thereof. The case of Standard Vacuum Employees’ Union 
versus The St4ndard Vacuum Oil Company, Calcutta (1953 L.A.C. 315) was 
of this type because in that case there was ho Standing Orders governing the 
clerical staff attached to the head office. In cases of the other type. namelv. of 


Part JA] 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1964 


the type indicated by A(i) above, two broad questions arise for considera- 
tion, namely :— 

(1) Whether the rules or provisions dealing with matter of transfer are of 
the fullest amplitude, that is to say whether they cover the wholé 
field of transfer, or 

(2) Whether they are not so. 

In the first it 15170901955 to say that those rules or provisions would be the 
only governing rules or provisions on the subject and there would be scope for 
the rule of construction noticed by the Tribunal. 


Thus in cases where there is a rule in the Standing Order governing all 
employees that no one is to be transferred by the employer or his agent 
without his consent or notwithstanding his consent beyond a certain radius from 
the place where he was last posted, or in cases where there is a special provision 
of a similar import in a written contract of service with a particular workman, 
that rule or provision would be considered to be of the fullest amplitude and 
would govern the whole field of transfer. Whether the rules regarding transfer 
are of the fullest amplitude or not would depend upon the construction of the 
Standing Order or the particular contract. 


We will now proceed to deal with the second type of cases. Where the 
rules or provisions, as the case may be, are not of the fullest amplitude the 
question is also a question of construction of the relevant rule or provision. 
But the correct approach in such cases in our opinion would be to see to what 
extent the special provision or rules in the Standing Orders have affected or 
curtailed the general power of transfer of the employer which is implied in 
every contract of service. In the light of these principles the case before us is 
to be considered. 

. We have already said that the liability to be transferred from one place 
to another by the employer is an implied condition of service of every employee. 
That necessarily implies two things, namely :— 

(i) it can be only taken away or curtailed or regulated in express terms 

and 


an 

(ii) that the power is only in the employer, which means that only 
the employer or a person either expressly authorised by him or one 
who can be said to have that authority impliedly, who can exercise 

that power. 
Thus a manager or a person in general control of the business or of the adminis- 
tration of the undertaking of the employer such as the body of directors, or a 
managing director, where the employer is a corporate body, would be taken to 
have the implied authority from the employer, but other officers more so sub- 
ordinate officers would not be taken to have the implied authority from the 
employer. 
6. The Standing Orders of the Company on the matter of transfer in our 
opinion is not of the fullest amplitude. They do not deal with or touch the 
power of the employer on that subject. Rule 19 is limited to the power of the 
Superintender.t of the particular installation and is_ strictly limited ٤٤ inter- 
departmental transfers in the particular installation. The case therefore is of 
the second type mentioned in the first sub-paragraph of paragraph 4 above. 
Rule 19 of the Standing Orders has to be considered in the light of what we have 
said in the last sub-paragraph of paragraph 4 above. It has not affected in 
any way the power of the employer to transfer an employee from one _installa- 
tion to another or from one installation to the head office. Thus the implied 
condition of service of the workmen concerned making them liable to be trans- 
ferred by the employer from the Budge Budge installation to the Calcutta head 
office remain unaffected by the said rule No. 19 of the Standing Orders. 
That rule only amounts to a delegation by the employer to the Superintendent 
of the installation to make inter-departmental transfers in the installation under 
his charge. Whether that express delegation was unnecessary or not need not 
be decided by us, but it is quite apparent that rule was made to remove all 
doubts that may be cast upon the Superintendent's power in the matter of 
inter-departmental transfers in_his installation. We do 1801 therefore agree 
with the reasons given by the Tribunal in that part of his decision. In_ the 
case before us however the orders transferring these two workmen from the 
Budge Budge installation to the Calcutta head office was made by the Superin- 
tendent of that installation, and not by the Manager of the Company at the 
head office or by any other person who could be said to have in him the authority 
so vested in the employer, but this important fact has not been noticed by the 
Tribunal. Thus in purporting to transfer them to a place outside the Budge 
Budge installation, the Superintendent of 006. Budge Budge installation had 
acted beyond his powers. Thus an unauthorised change in the condition of 
service of those two workmen had been made, the condition of service being 
that only the manager of the Company or a person who could be said to have 
the authority of the employer in this respect could order their transfer. As the 
transfers to the head office had, as we have already held, affected them 
adversely the complaint under section 33A of the Act is maintainable and it 
must also succeed on the merits and on the ground of want of power in Super- 
intendent. The result is that the order made by the Tribunal is maintained 
though on different grounds and the appeal is dismissed with costs which we

SCHOOL FINAL EXAMINATION, 1957 AND ONWARDS. 


The following shall be the Syllabuses of studies in the subjects mentioned 
below for the School Final Examination of 1957 and onwards :— 


Physics and Chemistry as an Elective Subject. 


The course shall include the following in addition to the courses on similar 
topics prescribed for General Science :— 


CHEMISTRY. 
I. (1) Scope of Chemistry ; (2) mechanical mixtures ; (3) solution ; filtra- 
tion, crystallisation, distillation, sublimation. 


II. States of matter ; physical and chemical changes ; conservation of mass, 
— illustrated by phenomena of (a) evaporation and sublimation, (b) burning and 
rusting. 20 


III. Lavoisier’s experiment on air. 
IV. Oxygen—(i) preparation by heating— 
(a) mercuric oxide, 
(b) potassium chlorate, 
(ii) properties and uses, 
(iii) meaning of oxides, 
(iv) elements and compounds. 
V. (1) Air—composition—air is a mixture. 
(2) Nitrogen—preparation from air by burning phosphorus—properties and 
uses, 


VI. Water—natural water ; hard and soft water ; purification of water by 
softening and distillation ; action of sodium on water ; electrolysis of water. 


VII. Hydrogen—preparation (from acids and metals)—Properties and 
uses. 

VIII. (1) Atoms and molecules ; (2) symbols and formulae ; 

(3) Elementary ideas of valency and of equations. 

IX. Acids, bases and salts (elementary ideas). 

X. (1) Forms of carbon—lampblack, charcoal, graphite and diamond ; 

(2) Carbon dioxide—preparation (by the action of acids on carbonates), 
properties ; carbonates and bicarbonates. 

XI. (1) Sulphur dioxide (by burning sulphur) ; 

(2) Sulphuric acid (by contact process) (omitting details of manufacture). 


XII. (1) Study of the following metals سے‎

Biology as an Elective Subject. 


It is assumed that the animal and plant studies will be integrated by frequent 
cross references and comparisons in the teaching of Biology. Questions may 
be set on the plants and animals as on biological and ecological sections. 


Natura! history, structure and physiology are essential but the  cellulor 
structure may be demonstrated, by microscope or projector. Personal observa- 
tions on living organisms may be made wherever possible but detailed study of 
cellulor structure is not necessary. Hand lens is sufficient. 


Stress should be laid on the common principles and processes of plants and 
animals. 


A.—GENERAL BIOLOGY. 


(a) Characteristic of living and non-living objects. Difference between 
plants and animals, and between living and non-living matters. 


(b) Interdependence of plants and animals, carbon and nitrogen cycles in 
nature. Utilisation of energy by living organisms. Movement and body heat 
with regard to energy. 

(c) Air, Water and Soil in relation to plants and animals. 


(d) Food substances—their preparation and _ utilisation, Enzymes and 
Vitamins. 

(e) A brief treatment of saprophytic and parasitic “modes of nutrition. 

(f) Classification of plants and animals. 


(g) Cell structure of plants and animals. Elementary knowledge of cell, 
differentiation into tissues and different types of cells in organs or tissues, cell 
divisions. 


(h) Evolution, heredity and general discussions on reproduction should be 
taught but no questions should be set from these. 


B.—PHYSIOLOGY (to be treated in a most elementary way). 


(a) Plant physiology—Absorption, transpiration, photo-synthesis, respira- 
tion, کو‎ geotropism, phototropism of primary roots and shoots. Experiment 
should be included. Ascent of dyes to be demonstrated. 


(b) Animal physiology—nutrition, respiration, excretion, regulation of body 
temperature. Brief account of brain and spinal cord, principal sense organs, their 
position and formations. Structure of eye and ear—simply treated. Circulation 
—its main features. 


(c) Life history—to be discussed briefly of the following types :— 


Spirogfra, mucor, moss, fern, amoeha, monocystis or hydra, cockroach or 
butterfly (or moth). 


(d) The general elementary structure and life history of the following :— 
(1) Animals— 


(i) External features of a fish (including gills), a toad, a lizard, and a 
mammal (rat or guinea-pig or cat or dog). 


(ii) Development of frog or toad from fertilisation to metamorphosis. 


(iii) Economic importance of house fly, mosquito and tapeworm. 
(2) Flowering Plants— 


(i) Outline of external morphologies of an herbaceous plant-Datura and 
Mustard. Stem, root and leaf to be treated with reference to their 
functions. 


Part IB] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 


(ii) Internal structures of these plants members to be studied from dia- 
grams. 


(iii) The parts of a flower and their functions, pollination and fertilisation. 
(iv) Kinds of fruits—dispersal of seeds and fruits. 


(v) Structures and germination of seeds (gram or pea, maize and castor 
seed). 


(vi) Short description with example of herbaceous perennials illustrating 
vegetative reproduction and storage organs. 


(vii) Characteristic features of the following trees and crop plants :— 


(i) Jack fruit, (ii) Banyan, (iii) Silk cotton, (iv) Cocoanut, (v) Guava, 
(vi) Mango, (vii) Paddy, (viii) Maize, and (ix) Jute. 


The abovementioned subject matter is to be treated very clearly and briefly 


(120 pages অন 8০০৯ to the point so that the young students can 
study them without further reference to higher books.

NOTICE. 


APPLICATIONS ore invited for admission to the next 
term of the Prince of Wales's Military College, Dehra 
Dun, commencing in January 1956. 


Course.—The College provides a public school education 
for sbhoys who wish to obtain commissions in the Army 
Navy or Air Force. The educational training is desi ed 
to bring boys up to the standard of the Senior Cambridge 
School Certificate and the quabiiying Examinations for 
entry into the National Defence Academy. Compulsory 
physica] training, games and parades ensure physical 
fitness and smartness; while special attention is paid ‘to 
the imparting of discipline, self-reliance and social train- 
ing ta all cadets. 


Admission.—Candidates for admission to the next term 
of the College which commences from January 1966, will 
have to qualify at an Entrance Examination to be held 
at Calentta some time in 3rd week of September 1954 
followed by an interview, 


Age limits.—Onandidates must have been born not 
earlier than 2186 January 1943 and not later than 20th 
January 1944. The age limits can in no case be relaxed. 


Educational qualifications.—No educational qualification 
is prescribed for admission to this College but it is 
expected that the candidate should have read up to 
Class VII standard of a Secondary School. 


Fees.—The fces are Rs. 750 per term plus additional 
expenses of Rs. 400 (e.g., uniforms, pocket money, books, 
washing, etc.). The actual cost is thus Ra. 2,300 per 
annum, A cadet sponds 5 to 6 years at the College. 


Scholarships.—A limited number of scholarships of 
Rs. 1,000 per annum is awarded to the deserving cadets 
after admiasion to ‘the College by the West Bengal 
Government, 


Applications.—Application on the prescribed form in 
duplicate which can be had on request from: the Assistant 
Secretary, Home (Defence) Department, Government of 
West Bengal, Writers’ Buildings, Calcutta, should be 
submitted so as to rench him on or before the 16th 
August 19654.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA. 


National Library, 


IN response to public opinion, the working hours of the 
Reading Rooms and the Lendi 5 Section at Belvedere have 
been extended with effect for the 16th August 1953. The 
revised working hours are specified below:— 


Reading Rooms— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—9 a.m. to 8 p.m. 
- Sundays and holidays—10 a.m. to 5 p.m. 


Lending Section— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—10 a.m. to 5 p.m. 
Sundays and holidays—l0 a.m. to 1-30 p.m. 


The Reading Rooms and the Lending Section will, how- 
ever, remain entirely closed on the following days of the 
year:— ‘ 


(i) Republic Day, tii) Independence Day and (iii) 
atma (thandhi’s Birth Day. 


Persons above 18 years of age are eligible to make use 
of the Library; which is a free lending Library open to 
any one residing in any part of the Indian Union. There 
is no subscription to pay but security in cash is essential. 


B. 8. KESAVAN, 
Librarian, 
Belvedere, Calcutta-27, the 6th March 1954 


THURSDAY, JULY 8, 1954 


PART VI.—Bills introduced in Parliament of India; Reports of Select 
Committees presented to Parliament; and Bills published before 
introduction in Parliament, 

HOUSE OF THE PEOPLE. 


The following Bill was introduced in the House of the People on 11th 
December, 1953 :— 


Bit No. 126 or 1952. 


A 88211 to ertend the jurisdiction of a University of any State in India to 
۱ ٦ শা ۰ ° ৬ 
-other State or States linguistically connected or for any other purpose 
and to provide for matters connected therewith. 


BE it enacted by Parliament as follows ;— 

1. Short title, extent and oommencoment.—(/) This Act may be called 
the University (Extension of Jurisdiction to other State or States) Act, 
19, 

(2) It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and 


Kashmir. 


(3) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, 
by notification in the Officiul Gazette, appoint. 


2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) ‘appointed vas means the date appointed under sub-section (3) of 
section 1, for coming into force of this Act. 


(9) ‘colleges’ includes educational institutions where classes higher 
than matriculation are conducted. 


(০) ‘jurisdiction’ means the University area in which all colleges 
affiliated to the university are functioning. 


(d) ‘extension’ means to extend the jurisdiction of any University 
beyond its own State jurisdiction. 


80 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 8, 1954 | Part VI 
লুল 


3. Extension of the jurisdiction of any University to other State or 
States.—For the purpose of this Act— 


(a) the jurisdiction of any Indian University shall extend to a ৮ or 
to the whole of any State or States on the mutual agreement of 
the concerned people of that part respectively ; 


(b) any University shall extend its jurisdiction to a part of other State 
aving linguistic affinity. 


4. Mixed jurisdiction of Universities.—In certain part or bilingual parts 
of any State more than one University can have or extend their jurisdiction 
on the basis of the mutual co-operation. 


5. Appointment of an advisory committee.—(7) The Government may 
for the purpose of advising aud assisting the University authorities in the 
discharge of their functions with regard to jurisdiction and other matters 
connected therewith, appoint such an independent or a joint advisory com- 
mittee as it may think fit for the whole of India or any part thereof, 


(2) The Education Ministry of the Central Government shall make rogu- 
lations with respect to the constitution and functions of any of the advisory 
committees appointed under sub-section (J). 


6. Non-interference in the Jurisdiction of University.—(7) No State 
Government shall have powers to interfere with the extension of the Un- 
versity jurisdiction save as otherwise expressly provided in any other enact- 
ment as from the appointed day. 


(2) No State Government shall have power to settle the jurisdiction of 
any University within the State except by the Advisory Committee consti- 
tuted by the Goyernment. 


7. Liability of the State Covernment to give help.—The State Govern- 
ments concerned are liable to provide all kinds of facilities and aid to the 
University and to colleges affiliated to any University as long as they aie 
functioning within the jurisdiction of the State. 


8. Transfer of some Colleges to certain Universities.—Save as 90106 
wise expressly provided in any other enactment the affiliation of all colleges 
whose managing bodies favourably decide under the jurisdiction of 
any University shall immediately before the appointed day be transferred to 
such a University whose jurisdiction is notified by the Advisory Committee. 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Many University authorities are anxious to extend their jurisdiction, 
other than their own States, in order to keep contact with their own 
linguistic areas. Moreover if University jurisdiction is settled according 
to the linguistic areas then the number of the Universities will be reduced 
than what they are today. This act will provide the best cultural atmosphere 
among various States. The present Bill gives effect to the proposals of 
many University Senates. 


SIVAMURTHI ۰ 


M. N. KAUTL, Secy.

SUPPLEMENT—Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the conditions of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 23rd June 1064, 


Summary.—During the week under report, there was rainfall in thirty-eight subdivisions. Weather was unfavourable in nine 
subdivisions. Sowing of Aus and Jute almost completed. Weeding of Aus and Jute vontinued in some subdivsions. Sowing of Aman 
continued. Prospect of standing cropa was, on the whole, fair. Fodder was reported to be insufficient in eight subdivisions. Cuttle- 
disease waa repo ted from five subdivisions. The wages of the labourer varied from rupee one to rupees three in different zubdivisions.

The Government of West Bengal in the Department of Labour, by Order 
No. 3511Dis./D/14L-2/53, dated 17th September 1953 and Order 
No. 3552Dis./D/14R-2/53, dated 21st September 1953, referred, under 
sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the 
industrial dispute between Howrah Municipality, Howrah, and its workmen 
represented by (1) Howrah Municipal Employees’ Association, Municipal 
Office, Howrah, (2) Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha, Municipal Office, 
Howrah, (3) Howrah Jalkal Karmachari Sangha, Dey Ghat Lane, Serampore, 
Hooghly, (4) Howrah Municipal Free Primary School Teachers’ Association, 
101, Rajballay. Saha Lane, Ramkristopore, Howrah, (5) Howrah Jalkal 
Mazdoor Union, post office Serampore, Hooghly, and (6) Howrah Municipal 
Workers’ Union, 101/3A, Brindabon Mullick Lane, Kadamtala, Howrah, to 
this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Notices were issued on all parties, who appeared and filed written statements 
setting forth their respective cases. 

The Howrah Municipality, in consideration of its size and importance, is 
the second municipal corporation in West Bengal with a gross annual receipt 
of more than rupees fifty lakhs and second only to the Calcutta Corporation.

In this present proceeding, the employees are represented by six separate 
Unions, as mentioned in the order of reference. The Municipal Employees’ 
Association, which was registered in 1924, represents all the employees. The

conservancy mazdoors are represented only by this Union. The Howrah 
Municipal Kurmachari Sangha, registered in 1949, represents the clerical and

and they claim to represent all employees, except the conservancy mazdoors 
and employees at the Waterworks, not being members of the clerical staff.

Presumably owing to the rise in the cost of living in the country, an upward 
revision of the wages of all categories of employees was effected by the Muni- 
cipality on 30th March 1946, to be effective from 1st April 1946. It is well 
known that at that time revision of wages were being made by all employees, 
including the Government, to off-set the general economic depression conse- 
quent on the rise of the cost of living. On Sth June 1947, the Government 
of West Bengal referred an industrial dispute between the Howrah Municipality 
and its employees represented by the Howrah Jalkal Karmachari Sangha to 
Shri N. C. Chakrabarti, District Judge, for adjudication. The award of this 
Tribunal was published by notification, dated 25th September 1947. This 
proceeding related to the dispute between the Municipality and its employees 
at its Waterworks at Serampore, and the award resulted in a revision of wages 
and other terms of employment to the advantage of the employees and were 
mainly based on an agreement between the Municipality and the Union by 
Order No. 777Lab., dated 7th November 1947, the dispute between the Howrah 
Municipality and their eomployees represented by the Howrah Municipal 
Employees’ Association was referred to Shri ৩. N. Modak, I.C.S. (Retd.), for 
adjudication. Before 1949, there were only two Unions functioning—one at 
the Waterworks at Serampore and the other the Howrah Municipal Employees’ 
Association for rest of the employees at Howrah. The dispute referred to Shri 
S. N. Modak involved all the employees of the Howrah Municipality, except 
those at the Waterworks at Serampore. The award in this proceeding was 
published by notification No. 888Lab., dated 23rd March 1948. By this award, 
the wages and other terms of employment and the conditions of labour of 
employees of all categories were revised to their advantage. The Howrah 
Municipal Karmachari Sangha, which claims to represent all clerical and other 
employees of the Municipality, excepting the conservancy mazdoors and the 
non-clerical employees of the Waterworks at:Serampore, was formed in 1949. 
This Sangha complained that the award of Shri Modak did not appreciably 
improve the conditions of. service of the clerical and other superior staff and it, 
therefore, submitted a charter of demands before the Municipal authorities on 
8th August 1949 for increased pay scales bY upgrading the maximum in respect 
of the employces who were not benefited by the award of Shri Modak. The 
Municipality and the Karmachari Sangha entered into an amicable agreement 
on 12th September 1949 over this charter of demands. This agreement result- 
ed in an upward revision of the basic wages fixed by Shri Modak on condition 
that no further demands should be made within three years next and these 
increments were made effective from 1st October 1949. On 7th November 
1949 the Government of West Bengal referred another dispute between the 
Howrah Municipality and all its employees represented by the Unions then in 
existence, viz., the Howrah Municipal Emplo ees” Association, the Howrah 
Jalkal Karmachari Sangha and the Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha to

সস 
Shri P. R. Mukherjee, District Judge. The award of this Tribunal was publish- 
ed in the Calcutta Gazette, Extraordinary, dated 27th July 1950. In this award, 
the increase in busic salaries settled by agreement between the Municipality 
and the Karmachari Sangha was accepted and awarded by the Tribunal, and 
decisions on other claims were also made. It was also awarded that similar 
increase in cmoluments should be given to other employees not represented by 
the Karmachari Sangha, if their Unions undertook not to claim a further 
increase in the next three years. The employees at the Waterworks at Seram- 
pore gave such undertakings in December 1949, and February 1951, and they 
were allowed amicable increase in their pay in consultation with their Unions. 


On 26th May 1952 the Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha forwarded 
a representation of its members to the Municipality for increasing the dearness 
allowance and for grant of house rent and compensatory allowance at the 
scales laid down by the State Government. Demands were also preferred by 
other Unions and all these Unions were advised by the Municipality to submit 
a consolidated charter of demands for its consideration. A Negotiating Com- 
mittee. was then formed by all the six Unions and this Committee placed before 
the Municipal authorities a consolidated charter of demands on 9th July 1952, 
consisting of 18 items, as shown in an appendix to the written statement of the 
Karmachari Sangha for fulfilment within six weeks." These demands were dis- 
cussed at several meetings of the Commissioners and _ finally by resolution 
No. 105, dated 7th September 1953, the Municipality sanctioned an increase 
in the dearness allowance of all categories of employees. It appears that this 
partial increase of the dearness allowance by resolution No. 105, dated 7th 
September 1953, was not accepted by the Unions and the Howrah Municipal 
Employees’ Association sent a notice of strike of the employees, specially the 
conservancy mazdoors with effect from 18th September 1953. It also appears 
that the workers at the Serampore Waterworks gave out a threat of strike with 
effect from 21st September 1953. The dispute was then referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication by an order, dated 17th September 1953. 


All the six Unions filed separate written statements and the Municipality 
filed separate written statements in reply to each of these written statements. 
There are some common items of demands preferred by the Unions, while there 
are other demands which are confined to only some categories of employees 
represented by one or the other of the Unions. The details of the claims and 
the Municipality’s reply will be considered at the time of the decision of the 
issues.

AWARD. 
Decisions. 

Most of the issues, viz., Issues Nos. 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 13, 15 and 17 relate 
to claims involving financial implications. The claims of dearness allowance 
as made would involve a recurring expense of about Rs. 4 lakhs only for the 
employees drawing basic wages of less than Rs. 50 per month. The claim of 
house-rent¢allowance and compensatory allowance at 10 per cent. of the-pay 
is another item which would involve a substantial sum. The annual basic 
wage and dearness allowance of the employees amount to about Rs. 324 lakhs, 
vide Ext. 1 and the major portion of this sum is basic salary. These and other 
claims, along with that of the revision of leave facilities imply financial obliga- 
tions on the part of the Municipality and it is necessary to enquire if the Muni- 
cipality has the capacity to bear imposition of any terms and conditions of 
service resulting in fresh pecuniary commitments. 


The Howrah Municipality is situated on the western bank of the Hooghly 
just opposite to the Calcutta Corporation on the eastern bank. The popula- 
tion of the city of Howrah is about 44 lakhs. The general outlook of the 


964 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 [Parr I 


municipal roads and drains are anything but satisfactory. This means that 
Howrah Municipality situated so close to the Calcutta Corporation has yet 
much to do in the matter of improving amenities to its rate-payers. 


The award of Shri 9. N. Modak, I.C.S. (Retd.), published by a Government 
notification, dated 23rd March 1948, was characterised before me by all the 
parties to this proceeding as a document of great learning showing a wise appre- 
ciation of problems confronting the Municipality and its employees. In this 
award, Shri Modak considered the financial condition of the Howrah Munici- 
pality in great details ahd was dismayed at its chronic pecuniary embarrass- 
ments. The learned Adjudicator observes as follows :-— 


“I have examined the statements of actual receipts and expenditure for 
the twelve months of the financial year 1946-47, and also for the 
nine months from April to December 1947. I have also gone into 
the Budget Estimates for the years concerned. In spite of a sub- 
vention of six lakhs of rupees granted by the Government and an 
advance of Rs. 1,41,000 made by the Government, the position 
is that at the best the income and the expenditure on the existing 
scale of wages and allowances are just balanced, and yet several 
bills of contractors still remain to be paid, and there are practically 
no resources which can be utilised for meeting at least some of the 
demands put forward on behalf of the employees for the purpose 
of improving their conditions.” 


The learned Adjudicator observes that the demands put forward by the 
employees should be met partially in the interest of justice and that at the same 
time the employees should realise and appreciate the position that it was 
impossible for the Municipality to find adequate fund all at once in order to 
meet their demands in full. Shri Modak suggested the following remedies for 
improvement of the financial condition of the Municipality :— 


1. The evil of under-valuation and under-assessment is to be eradicated 
and a proper valuation of holdings and proper assessment of municipal rates 
should be made. 


2. The State Government makes recurring grant of Rs. 6 lakhs every 
year by way of subvention, and it also advanced Rs. 1,41,000 by way of loan. 
The learned Adjudicator recommended for increased subvention and more 


loans for tiding over the crisis. 


3. It was also suggested that existing law which imposed fetters on the 
Municipality relating to realisation of taxes should be amended so as to afford 

ater freedom to the Municipality to im taxes and increase revenue. 
Finally the learned Adjudicator supported the claim of the Chairman of the 
Municipality made to the Government in the following matters :— 


(1) Immediate payment of the accumulated motor vehicles tax fund for 
seven years amounting to Rs. 24 lakhs. 
(2) Restoration of the motor vehicles tax grant annually. 


(3) Immediate payment of compensation for damage to the roads of the 
Municipality by heavy military traffic out of the subvention receiv- 
ed from the Central Government amounting to Rs. 8 lakhs. 


(4) Payment of additional subvention for a period of five years, besides 
the six lakhs already sanctioned.

(5) To make available to the Municipality additional sources of revenue 
from the following heads of taxes :—

(b) share of electricity duty tax collected at Howrah, 

(c) share of commercial sales tax collected at Howrah, 

(d) share of stamp duty on transfer of properties at Howrah, 


(e) enhancement of schedules of rates of license fees on trades and 
professions. 


It appears that the revision of emoluments of the employees 
made on ist April 1946 involved an extra expense of Rs. 1,49,176. 
By the intervention of the District Magistrate of Howrah in July 
1947, an increase of dearness allowance was made for the em- 
ployees which involved an extra expenditure of Rs. 2,63,490. These 
two increases account for a recurring increase of a little over Rs. 4 lakhs 
in the year. Revision of pay scales of the Waterworks employees made by the 
award of Shri Chakrabarty, dated 25th September 1947, increased the expendi- 
ture by Rs. 13,824. Then came Shri Modak’s award which involved a recurring 
expenditure of Rs. 5,93,460 in the year. As has been stated above, with effect 
from 150 Qctober 1949, there was a revision of the basic wages of the clerical 
and the superior grades of employees by agreement with the Howrah Munici- 
pal Karmachari Sangha, and this agreement was ratified by the award of Shri 
۶۲. R, Mukherjee, which was published on 27th July 1950. This revision caus- 
ed an extra annual additional expenditure of Rs. 1,77,000. The increase in 
emoluments allowed by the award of Shri P. R. Mukherjee was for the cate- 
gories of employees who, according to the Karmachari Sangha, did not receive 
sufficient increase of emoluments in the award of Shri S. N. Modak. The wage 
structure of the employees, as it appears today before us, is the consolidated 
result of the award of Shri N. C. Chakravarty in 1947, of Shri S. N. Modak 
in 1948 and Shri ۶. R. Mukherjee in 1950. These three awards involved an 
additional annual recurring expense of Rs. 7,84,284. 


It has been mentioned above that the Municipality by its resolution No, 105, 
dated 7th September 1953, agreed to make a partial increase of the dearness 
allowance of the various categories of employees, although this increase was not 
implemented in view of the reference of the dispute to the Tribunal. The 
learned spokesman for the Municipality admitted that the Municipality stood 
committed to this resolution. The proposed increments in dearness allowance 
would involve an extra expenditure of Rs. 1,08,000. The learned spokesman 
for the Municipality proposed before me that in spite of increases in the current 
demands of the consolidated rates and increase of income in other directions, 
it is not possible for the Municipality to bear any further financial burden by 
way of increase of emoluments or other amenities to its employees. The rise 
of establishment expenditure including dearness allowance and Provident Fund 
(actual) of the Municipality from 1943-44 is shown in Ext. F. This table 
appears to be as follows :—

Exhibit 1 shows the statement of essential expenditure as provided for in the 
budget of 1954-55. This appears to be Rs. 49,30,856, out of which establish- 
ment costs, including dearness allowance is Rs. 32,56,427 and Provident Fund 
contributions is Rs. 2 lakhs. Exhibit J shows the financial position of the 
Municipality in brief from 1943-44 to 1952-53. Exhibit H 1s the statement 
of outstanding liabilities of the Municipality as on 1st April 1954. It shows 
total liability of Rs. 44,36,750 and Exhibit G is the statement of outstanding 
loans showing a total loan of Rs. 29,26,685. Exhibit G shows addition to loan 
account almost every year since 1943 to 315 May 1953. The condition of 
the Municipality is, therefore, by no means prosperous. 


At the date of the reference, the Municipality was being run by the Com- 
missioners. By an order, dated 20th April 1954, the Government of West 
Bengal superseded the Municipality for a period of two years and by another 
order of the same date, appointed Shri-R. 5. Trivedi, I.C.S., as Administrator 
to perform the duties of the Chairman and the Commissioners. Exhibit K 
shows the copy of these orders. The order of the Government shows clearly’ 
that the fiancial condition of the Municipality was extremely bad. In paragraph 
(8) of this order, it appears that at the end of 1951-52, the Municipality's 
liabilities on account of current bills amounted to Rs. 9,52,170 against the 
closing balance of Rs. 4,70,740,.and at the close of 1952-53, the liabilities on 
account of current bills appeared to be Rs. 8,76,891 against a closing balance 
of Rs. 4,30,336. It further states that “not only does the current income of 
the Municipality fall short of its current expenditure, but its liabilities on current 
bills alone far exceed its closing balance. It is thus obvious that the finances 
of the Municipality are in an appalling state.” 


From what has been discussed above, it is clear that the financial condition 
of the Municipality in April 1954 was precarious, Paragraph (4) of the Gov- 
ernment Order in Exhibit K shows that there has been a steady deterioration 
in the collection of the outstanding balance of the consolidated rates of the 
Municipality. Paragraph (7) shows that the Commissioners utilised the 
Employees’ Provident Fund money for other purposes and the Municipality's 
eal debt to the Provident Fund amounted to more than Rs. 74 lakhs at the 
close of 1982-53. It is admitted by all the parties before the Tribunal that 
since the appointment of the Administrator, there has been an improvement in 
the collection of the consolidated rates. Even then, in view of what has been 
stated above, it cannot be denied that the financial condition of the Munici- 
pality is unsatisfactory and the Tribunal will have to proceed with caution in 
imposing an extra burden on it by way of increase of emoluments for the 
employees. I shall now consider the issues for the decision of this case. 


Issue No. 1—Revision of pay for. Teachers and Peons in Free Primary Schools 
and certain categories of workmen in the Howrah Waterworks at Seram- 


pore. 7 
This relates to the revision of pay for teachers and peons 11) the free 

primary schools, as claimed by the Howrah Municipal Free Primary Teachers’ 

Association and of certain categories of employees in the Howrah Waterworks

৯ সস 


at Serampore raised by the Jalkal Karmachari Sangha and Howrah Jalkal 
Mazdoor Union. 


There are 19 primary schools in the Municipality with 92 teachers and 19 
ons, There are 398 peons in the Municipality. The basic wage of the peons 
is Rs, 30—1—45. The Municipal Free Primary School Teachers’ Association 
claimed revision of this wage to Rs. 35-—-2—-75. I do not consider that there 
is any ground for creating a privileged class of peons for the primary schools and 
the claim for increase of their pay out of a large number of other peons employed 
in the Municipality appears to be unjustified. This claim is rejected. 


The Teachers’ Association claimed for increase of the basic salaries of the 
Headmasters and the Assistant Teachers. The present pay of the Headmasters 
and the Assistant Teachers are as follows :— 


Headmasters—Rs. 55—5—100—7—170. 
Assistant Teachers—Rs. 55—4—75—5—110. 
The demanded rates are as follows :— 
Headmasters—Rs. 70—-7—140—-10—200. 
Assistant Teachers—Rs. 60—5—100—-7—-107—-9-——170. 


It may be mentioned that the minimum qualification for the appointment of 
an Assistant Teacher is passing of the Matriculation Examination and that for the 
Headmaster is passing of the 1.A. Examination. It appears that in this Munici- 
pality there is one Headmaster and one Assistant: Teacher who are Graduates. 
Of the rest of the Headmasters, one is a 1.۸. senior trained, four I.As., three 
Matriculate Guru-trained, eight Matriculates, one non-Matriculate Guru-trained 
and one non-Matriculate non-trained. Of the rest of the Assistant Teachers, 
one is an I.A. trained, seven I.A. non-trained, four Matriculate Guru-trained, 
26 Matriculates, 14 non-Matriculate Guru-trained and 24 non-Matriculate and 
non-trained. It is the custom of the Municipality to pay the same basic salary 
to the Headmaster or Headmistress as Clerks of Class If. An Assistant Teacher 
gets a salary which is a little above the salary of a junior grade clerk, which is 
Rs. 45—3—75—5-——110. For a junior grade clerk also, the minimum qualifica- 
tion is passing of the Matriculation Examination. The dearness allowance as 
available to the employees of the Municipality under the award of Shri S. N. 
Modak is Rs. 22 for basic wages from Rs. 51 to Rs. 100 and Rs. 25 for basic 
wages from Rs. 101 to Rs. 250. An Assistant Teacher drawing a basic salary 
of Rs. 100 or less will get a dearness allowance of Rs. 22. Over and above this 
dearness allowance, he will get Government dearness allowance of Rs. 4 per 
month and a Government Development Grant Allowance of Rs. 7 to Rs. 13 
according to qualifications. Rupees 7 is available to a non-Matriculate non- 
trained teacher, Rs. 9 to a Matriculate and Rs. 13 to a Matriculate trained teacher. 
A Matriculation passed trained Assistant Teacher will get a total allowance of 
Rs. 39 per month. It appears that in the Calcutta Corporation, a teacher's scale 
is Rs. 60-—4—80—5—120. He gets in addition a dearness allowance of Rs. 35 
and house-rent of Rs. 5 In the case of a Headmaster, the Development Grant 
is Rs. 15 if he is Matriculation passed and trained. The total Government allow- 
ance of a Headmaster would be Rs. 19 in addition to the dearness allowance paid 
by the Municipality. The scale of the Headmaster in the Calcutta Corporation 
is Rs. 80—5S—150. In view of the qualifications of the existing Headmasters 
and the Assistant Teachers, it cannot be stated that they are more qualified than 
their compeers in the clerical services. The teachers enjoy more holidays and 
less period of work than that of the clerks. The working hour of the teacher 
is from 10-30 a.m. to 3 pine on week. days and from 10-30 a.m. to 1 p.m. on 
Saturdays; whereas a clerk has to work from 10-30 a.m. to 5 p.m. on week days 
and from 10-30 a.m. to 1-30 p.m. on Saturdays. A member of the clerical staff 


968 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY.,- JULY 10, 1954 {Parr I 


gets 35 holidays throughout the year excluding Sundays, whereas a teacher will 
get 85 holidays excluding Sundays. I do not consider that in these circumstances 
there is any justification for an increase of emoluments of the Headmaster or the 
Assistant Teacher of the Free Primary Schools of the Municipality, as claimed. 
I would, however, make an exception in the case of the graduate Headmaster 
and Assistant Teacher, in view of their qualifications. A Graduate Headmaster 
will get an extra allowance of Rs. 10 per month and a Graduate Assistant Teacher 
will get an extra allowance of Rs. 8 per month. 


The Howrah Jalkal Karmachari Sangha claimed revision of scales of pay for 
Shift-in-charges from Rs. 60—5—140 to Rs. 75—5—170 and of the Filter 
Supervisors from Rs. 55—5—100 to Rs. 60—5—150. The Howrah Jalkal 
Mazdoor Union demanded the revision of the scale of pay of the Electrician from 
Rs. 35 —2—45—-3—60 to Rs. 55—-2—63—-3—75 and of the Filter Supervisors 
to Rs. 65—5—150. Exhibit E is a chart filed by the Municipality showing the 
increase of basic salaries of these categories of employees. It appears that the 
Electrician was called an بات‎ Cleaner before 8th February 1951, on which 
date by resolution No. 192(23) [Ext. M(1)], the designation was changed to 
Electric Mistri. He is in charge of two dynamos of 110 volts each—one working 
at night and the other working in the day. Exhibit E shows that in 1946 the 
Electric Mistri had a fixed pay of Rs. 16 only and in 1949 after the award of 
Shri Chakrabarty, his pay was increased to the scale of Rs. 18—-4—-25. In 1947 
this was increased to Rs. 30 fixed and on 8th February 1951 by resolution 
No. 192(23), the pay scale was raised according to the directions of Shri P. R. 
Mukherjee to Rs. 30—2—45—-3—60. The resolution shows that the designa- 
tion of Cleaner was changed to Electric Mistri. In the same way, increase of 
salary was allowed to the Shift-in-charges, who were previously called Drivers 
and the Filter Supervisors who were previously called Filter Attendants. There is 
no doubt that all these categories of employees, specially the Shift-in-charges and 
the Filter Supervisors have to do very useful and responsible work in the Water- 
works. It is not, however, possible to take up increase of basic salaries of only 
these categories of employees in view of the fact that these categories also were 
considered at the time of the general increase of salaries in 1951, following Shri 
P. R. Mukherjee’s award and these increases were based more or less upon an 
agreed formula. In view of these circumstances, I do not consider that the basic 
salaries of these three categories of employees should be increased in the present 
proceeding, as there is no evidence of any special hardship in the matter of basic 
salaries in the case of these three categories of employees. Issue No. 1 is 
accordingly answered.

Issue No. 4—Retiring age. 


The Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha demands that the retiring age 
of the employees of the Municipality should be fixed at 60 years with the 
provision of one year’s extension at a time up to the age of 65 years. The 
present age-limit is 55 years with a provision of extension by one year at a 
time up to the age of 58 years, but this lies at the discretion of the authorities, 
who use it at their swect will and which is not always done in a judicious way. 
According to a Government circular, the retiring age of the school teachets 
has been fixed at 60 with a provision of extension up to 65 years. Recently 
the Commissioners of this Municipality have granted this facility to the 
teachers of the school under its management. The retiring age of the mazdoors 
and other sub-staff is also 60 years. The Karmachari Sangha also pressed 


Pani I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 973 


a een 


that this facility should also be extended to the rest of the employees. The 
claim of the retiring age of all employees irrespective of categories to be fixed 
at 60 years was also made by the Howrah Municipal Employees’ Association. 
The other Unions did not press for this claim. The Municipality opposed this 
claim. The present rule is that for employees other than mazdoors and 
school teachers, the age of retirement is 55, but their services may be 
extended by the Chairman by one year at a time up to the completion of fifty- 
eight year. I do not consider that any change in the rule is called for. This 
claim is rejected.

Issues Nos. 6 and 17—Day of rest of outdoor staff, or increased remuneration 
in lieu thereof, and overtime wages or other privileges for work on Sunday 
or holidays. | 


These two issues relate to the same claim and are taken up together for 
decision. 

It was claimed by some of the Unions that there should be a day of rest for 
the outdoor staff including the conservancy mazdoors, or they should be 
allowed increased remuneration for work done on holidays. This claim was 
opposed by the Municipality on the ground that the outdoor staff have been 
doing their work without any holidays in the week, in view of the nature of 
their work which admits of no holidays. It is stated that from the very nature 
of work done by these employees, the work must be performed from day to 
day without any break. The conservancy mazdoor is one of these groups of 
employees. If the Municipality is to give them permission to enjoy holidays, it 
will be required to employ additional hands on holidays and this will entail a 
great extra cost, which from the financial condition of the Municipality, it is not 
possible to impose upon it at the present time. Such a claim was also made 
before the learned Tribunal adjudicating on the dispute between the Calcutta 
Corporation and its employees in July 1948, as well as in May 1950, and the 
claim was‘rejected by both the Tribunals. I also consider that the claims made 
in the two issues cannot be allowed and it is rejected. 


According to rule 25 of the Provident Fund Rules of the Municipality, the 
Commissioners may, on the recommendation of the Chairman, grant from the 
revenues, at the time of retirement, to any servant who has subscribed to the 
Provident Fund and has rendered continuous good service for not less than 15 
years, an additional contribution at the rate of half a month’s pay for each 
completed year of service rendered by such servant, subject to a maximum of 
15 months’ pay, but not exceeding Rs. 5,000. The amount of the contribution 
shall be calculated on ‘the pay drawn by him at the time of retirement. This rule 
applies to members of the superior staff, i.e., those who are not in the labour 
statf or in the conservancy staff. 


Gratuity Rules for inferior service is on a lower scale, and is generally or 
the following lines :— 
After service of not less than five years but less than ten years—Three 
months’ pay. ۱ 
After service of not less than ten years but less than fifteen years—Fou 
months’ pay. 
After service of not less than fifteen years but less than twenty years—Five 
months’ pay. ? 
After service of not less than twenty years but less than thirty years—Six 
months’ pay. 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., TULY 19, 1954 975 


In the case of conservancy staff there is a provision for Fidclity Bonus and a con- 
servancy mazdoor who has never taken part in any strike or hartal shal] at the 
end of 15 years’ continuous and loyal service, be entitled to a Fidelity Bonus of 
Rs. 100 on the termination of his service. 


The Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha claimed that notwithstanding 
anything contained in the Municipal Rules regarding Provident Fund and addi- 
tional contribution or gratuity, all employees having 15 years’ continuous service 
at credit should be entitled to additional contribution or gratuity at the rate as 
laid down by the Municipality irrespective of whether they subscribed to the 
Provident Fund for 15 years or not. It is further clarified that the period of 
15 years’ continuous service should only be insisted on for entitling an employee 
to gratuity, and the question of the period of subscribing to Provident Fund should 
not be considered at all. 


The Howrah Jalkal Karmachari Sangha also claimed that notwithstanding 
anything contained in the Howrah Municipal Rules regarding additional con- 
tribution, all the employees having 15 years’ service at their credit should be 
entitled to the additional contribution or gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ pay 
for each completed year’s service at the termination of employment, irrespective 
of whether they subscribed to the Provident Fund for 15 years or not. 


The Primary School Teachers’ Association also made a similar claim, and 
demanded that the clog of subscribing to the Provident Fund for 15 years in 
sola one to get the benefit of gratuity or additional contribution should be 
removed. 


The Howrah Municipal Employees’ Association claimed that all sub-staffs 
and\ mazdoors, including conservancy mazdoors, who have been entitled to con- 
tribyte to the Provident Fund in 1946, and have put in 15 years’ service, should 
get the additional contribution at the rate of half a month's pay just like the 
superior staff, whether they have yet subscribed for 15 years or not. It is pressed 
that there should be one uniform system of gratuity for all categories of employees. 
At the present time, the superior staff gets the additional contribution at half 
month’s pay for each year of service after completion of 15 years of service with 
a minimum of 74 months’ pay and maximum of 15 months’ pay. The sub-staff 
gets compensation gratuity with a maximum of six months’ pay, and the con- 
servancy mazdoors get Fidelity Bonus with a maximum of Rs. 100 at 8 annas 
for one month’s active service. It is claimed that the award of Shri 5. N. Modak 
directed payment of additional contribution to the inferior staff in the same scale 
as to the superior staff. 


I shall consider the claim of the Employees’ Association separately. The 
claim of the Howrah Municipal Karmachari Sangha, Howrah Jalkal Karmachari 
Sangha and Howrah Free Primary School Teachers’ Association relate to the 
claim of the superior employees to remove the requirement of contribution to 
the Provident Fund for 15 years as a condition precedent to an employee being 
entitled to additional contribution or gratuity. Rule 25, however, imposes other 
conditions also, as for example, continuious good service for not less than 15 years. 
The claim of these three Unions that only 15 years’ service with the Municipality 
would be sufficient to entitle an employee to additional contribution or gratuity 
does not appear to be satisfactory. I do not find any ground for making an award 
in contravention of rule 25 of the Provident Fund Rules. The claim of these 
three Unions in this regard is rejected. 


As for the claim of the Employees’ Association that all sub-staffs and mazdoors 
including conservancy mazdoors, who have been entitled to contribute to the 
Provident Fund in 1946 should get additional contribution just like the superior 
staff, it stands on a different footing. It appears that the Provident Fund for 


976 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE HEXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 [Parr I 


রা 


the sub-staff and the conservancy 17182009915 was introduced in 1949 and the 
rule came into cffect from Ist April 1946, and these categorics of workers could 
contribute to the Provident Fund with effect from Ist April 1946. It is contended 
by the Employees’ Association that Shri Modak’s award observed that “in the 
case of those employees who have done service for 15 years or more, the provision 
regarding additional contribution under rule 25 of the Provident Fund Rules 
would come into operation, and the rules regarding Fidelity Bonus or the gratuity 
rules for inferior service would not be applicable”. The learned Adjudicator 
directed the Commissioners of the Municipality to put forward modified proposals 
and to submit those proposals to the Government for approval. The learned 
spokesman for the Municipality contended that although rule 25 would be 
applicable to the members of the sub-staff and the conservancy mazdoors who 
would contribute to the Provident Fund for not less than 15 years, it is not 
applicable to persons who have not rendered continuous service for not less than 
15 years and there is no question of these categories of employees being entitled 
to gratuity without making contribution to the Provident Fund for 15 years, as 
claimed by the Employees’ Association. It was further impressed upon me that 
the financial implication of the payment of gratuity according to rule 25 will be 
great if employees with 15 years’ service are allowed the benefit of gratuity even 
without contribution to the Provident Fund for 15 years. The argument of the 
learned spokesman of the Municipality is sound. There is, however, one genuine 
grievance on the part of the sub-staff and the conservancy mazdoors on this 
account. They could not contribute to the Provident Fund prior to Ist April 
1946, for no fault of theirs. They could not so contribute, because the Provident 
Fund system was not introduced among them prior to ist April 1946. Even if 
a conservancy mazdoor puts in continuous good service for not less than 15 
years, and contributes to the Provident Fund from ist April 1946, he will not 
get any additional contribution or gratuity only because he could not contribute 
to the Provident Fund for 15 years. It appears that the justice of the case will 
be met if the following provision be made by the Municipality in continuation 
of rule 25 to meet the cases of the sub-staff and the conservancy mazdoors who 
could not contribute to the Provident Fund before Ist April 1946. The provision 
should be made on the following lines :— 


If he rendered continuous good service to the Municipality for more than 
15 years since a date prior to Ist April 1946, and if he contributes 
to the Provident Fund since Ist April 1946, then the period of con- 
tinuous service prior to Ist April 1946 during which he could not 
contribute to the Provident Fund should be considered for the purpose 
of additional contribution, as the period wherein the worker contributed 
to the Provident Fund, and the additional contribution should be paid 
to him accordingly. The 5 should take sanction of the 
Government for the modification of the rule on additional contribution 
on these lines. No workman whose period of service terminated prior 
to August 1954 should get the advantage of this rule. The issue is 
accordingly answered.
