It is further stated by.this Union that the Munici a within the course of last 
six years have failed to submit any Provident Pui account and no general 
meeting of the Provident Fund has ever been called. 


The restriction to the advances of loans to the subscribers has been clarified 
by the Free Primary School Teachers’ Association, which stated that at present 
temporary advance from the Provident Fund is granted to the employees except 
that one-fifth of their own contribution is always retained by the Municipality 
and is kept in reserve. The Association states further that an employee should 
be entitled to draw his contribution in full at the time of his need, and the 
Chairman cannot be allowed to have any discretion in this matter. 


The point of view of the Municipal Karmachari Sangha and the Free Primary 
School Teachers’ Association on this point appears to be wholly unreasonable. 
The Provident Fund is created for the purpose of giving relief to the employee 
after his retirement, or his dependants, if unfortunately he is dead. The 
employees represented by these two Unions really seem to consider the Provident 
Fund account with the Municipality as if it were a current account in a bank. 
This \s not so, and the claim of these two Unions is rejected. 


As to the other claim in regard to the Provident Fund which is made by the 
Municipal Karmachari Sangha, Jalkal Sangha and the Teachers’ Association, 
there is no doubt that this claim is wholly justified. The Municipality has got no- 
right to use the employees’ Provident Fund money for any শি? other than 
that for which it is meant. I have mentioned above that the Government also 
have taken a very serious view of this matter. The utilisation by the Commis- 
sioners of the employees’ Provident Fund money was one of the causes of the 
supersession of the Municipality on 20th April 1954. It is awarded that the 
Municipality should supply, at the end of every year, a statement of the account 
of the Provident Fund money to each individual employee, and this account 
should be up-to-date. This issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 9.—Consultation with the Unions in the matter of appointment, transfer, 
promotion and dismissal of employees. 


It was claimed by the Municipal Employees’ Association, Municipal Karma- 
chari Sangha, Municipal Free Primary School Teachers’ Association and the 
Jalkal Karmachari Sangha that the Municipality should consult the Union in the 
matter of appointments, dismissals, promotions and transfers. The claim was 
opposed by the Municipality and it was stated that the question of promotion, 
punishment, etc., of municipal employees could not be decided in consultation 
with any Union as a matter of principle, but suggestions, if any, of the various 
Unions in such matters were always taken into consideration. I find that such 
a claim by the Unions was rejected by Shri 5. N. Modak in his award on 23rd 
April 1948 and also by Shri P. R. Mukherjee in his award on 27th July 1950. 
The claim of the Unions is virtually a right for interference with the management 
functions of the Municipality and cannot be allowed by this Tribunal. In con- 
formity with the awards of Shri Modak and Shri Mukherjee, it is awarded that 
the Municipality will not be bound to consult any Union in the matter of appoint- 
ment, promotion, dismissal or transfer of employees, or in any other matter, but 


978 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 [Panr I 


that if any Union make any suggestion to the Municipality on any of these 
matters, the municipal authorities may consider the suggestion in coming to a 
decision. 


Issue No. 10.—Creation of some Class I posts in the clerical grade according to 
the award of Shn P. R. Mukherjee. 


The Municipal Karmachari Sangha claimed that some Class 1] posts in the 
clerical grade should be converted into Class I posts in consideration of the 
responsibilities attached to such posts. It is also stated that such a recom- 
mendation was incorporated in the award of Shri P. R. Mukherjee, but the 
authoritics have not yet implemented the recommendation. It appears that in 
the terms of settlement between the Municipality and the Karmachari Sangha, 
there was an agreement that with a view to encourage efficiency and to provide 
some scope of prospects of higher pay, some of the existing Class II posts should 
be converted into Class I posts and such promotions should be made in con- 
sideration of the responsibility attached and efficiency needed in these posts and 
that men for these Class I posts shall be selected by means of a competitive test 
amongst the existing staff who have put in 15 years’ service in the Class I grade 
and are at least Matriculates. 


The Municipality in its written statement opposed this claim and stated that 
such Class I posts could not be created by the Commissioners without Govern- 
ment sanction and the Municipal Commissioners have no powers to create any 
posts without the sanction of the Government. It is further stated that the 
maximum salaries payable to the employees have been liberally increased so as 
to surpass even the previous maximum salaries payable to the employees of the 
Class I grade. It appears that there are four Class I clerks as against 167 Class 
II clerks. There are 30 posts carrying salaries higher than Class II and lower 
than Class I grades. It is not possible for this Tribunal to make any award as 
to which posts should be ¢onverted into Class I posts without a thorough con- 
sideration of the work done by all the clerical staff of the Municipality. The 
Municipality should be the sole authority to decide as to which the Class II posts 
should be converted into Class I posts and how many of such posts should be 
so converted. I had the advantage of hearing the arguments of both parties on 
this matter and from what I heard, I make a recommendation that the Second 
Clerk of the Assessment Department, the Second Clerk of the Engineering 
Department, the Second Clerk of the License Department and the Head Clerk 
of the Serampore Waterworks may be posted in Class I grade. It is for the 
Municipality to make a final decision on the matter. Any appointment to the 
newly-created Class I posts should be made in the manner as provided in the 
terms of agreement between the Karmachari Sangha and the Municipality and 
mentioned in Appendix B, Clause (V) of the award of Shri P. R. Mukherjee. 
This issue ig accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 11.—Supply of uniforms and outfits. 


It was complained by some of the Unions that employees who used to get 
uniforms and outfits did not get such uniforms and outfits in proper time. The 
learned spokesman for the Municipality stated that those employees who were in 
receipt of ۶۳۷ر‎ and outfits should continue to get them. I have nothing 
more to add. 


Issue No. 12.—Repairs of quarters. 


The two Unions of the Waterworks complained that the buildings and 
quarters at the Waterworks at Serampore were out of repairs. The Municipality 
in its written statement states that repairs to quarters have already been taken 
up and work order has already been issued. The Municipality has also adduced 


Parr I) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 979 


evidence on this point. O.P.W. 5 Shri Amulya Chandra Ganguli, Waterworks 
Overseer at Serampore deposed that repairs to the municipal quarters at Serampore 
were done by him at a cost of more than Rs. 5,000 and that the repairs to the 
quarters of the Shift-in-charges will be done this year and the assessment of 
repairs to the quarters of other officers will also be considered in this year and 
that the repairs to the engine room are in progress. He also states that cooly 
and durwans’ quarters have already been repairs. It is, therefore, clear that the 
Municipality is doing its best in the matter of repairs to quarters. This issue 
is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 13.—Personal allowance for messengers and store durwans of Water- 
works at Serampore. 


The Jalkal Karmachari Sangha claimed that as the messengers and the store 
durwans have to work extra time almost every day and as they have to work 
on Sundays from time to time, they should be paid a personal allowance of Rs. 10 
per month. The Municipality states in its written statement that the question 
of personal allowance raised by the Sangha was never raised previously and as 
this question could not be considered by the Commissioners, this demand could 
not be considered as a dispute between the parties, which have been referred 
to the Tribunal for decision. Appendix B to the written statement of the Howrah 
Municipal Karmachari Sangha shows the 18 items of demands that were sub- 
mitted to the Municipality by the Negotiating Committee on 9th July 1952. This 
charter of demands does not show the claim raised in this issue by the Jalkal 
Karmachari Sangha. It is, therefore, obvious that the Municipality could not 
consider this demand and refuse it and this demand should not therefore be 
consttued as the basis of an industrial dispute between the parties. 


On merits also this claim is unjustifiable. The messengers at Serampore 
get monthly tickets to come to the central office at Howrah. The store durwans 
are only one category of many durwans employed by the Municipality. There 
is no point in claiming extra remuneration by way of personal allowance for 
these two categories of employees only. This claim is rejected. 


Issue No. 14.—Re-instatement of (1) Upen Das, (2) Jagrup and (3) Garib. 


The Howrah Jalkal Mazdoor Union claimed for re-instatement of three 
dismissed employees, viz., (1) Jagrup, (2) Garib and (3) Upen Das. The Union 
by its application, dated 24th May 1954, withdrew the case of Jagrup and Garib 
from the Tribunal. It pressed only the claim for re-instatement of Upen Das 
before the Tribunal. 


It appears from the written statement of the Union that Upen Das was 
suspended on 25th November 1950 and was dismissed on 6th January 1951. 
It is also stated that Kanai Lal Chatterjee, Filter Supervisor, was also suspended 
on 25th November 1950. Both Upen Das and Kanai Lal Chatterjee were asked 
to explain their conduct which was duly done. On 6th January 195] Upen Das 
was dismissed from service, while Kanai Lal Chatterjee was transferred to 
Howrah from Serampore Waterworks. This dismissal order passed by the 
Chairman on 6th January 1951 was confirmed by the Commissioners after 
objection was taken by the Union on the matter on 2nd September 1952. It is 
claimed that the dismissal of Upen Das was unjust, unfair, illegal and invalid. 


In its written statement, the Municipality states that the present Board of 
Municipal Commissioners only confirmed the order of dismissal of Shri Upen Das 
by the previous Chairman and hence the allegations against the present Board 
are not correct. The dismissal orders took effect from 25th November 1950, 
and cannot be re-opened now under any circumstances and under the existing 
rules the person appointed in place of Upen Das has been already confirmed. 


980 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 [Parr I 


০০০০০০০০০০০ ০৭ ৯১০৯ 


It appears that by letter, Ext. D(1), the Superintendent of Waterworks asked 
for explanation of Upen Das and seven other persons including Kanai Lal 
Chatterjee, Filter Supervisor, why disciplinary action should not be taken against 
them for holding a meeting with the inferior staff of the Waterworks on tha 
verandah of Aldin House on Friday, the 27th October 1950, in the afternoon 
without any permission of the authoritics and further to show cause within two 
days why disciplinary action should not be taken against them for leaving their 
work without permission of their superiors while they were on duty, and thereby 
breaking the discipline of the factory. This letter was dated 31st October 1950. 
The explanation of the persons concerned is Ext. D(2). In this letter, all the 
persons jointly denied having held a meeting as alleged. Exhibit A is the report 
of the Superintendent to the Engineer on the matter. Exhibit A(1) is the detailed 
report of the Engineer to the Chairman of the Municipality regarding the holding 
of the meeting by Upen Das and others on 27th October 1950. This report is 
dated 11th November 1950, and in this report the Engineer characterises the 
explanation, Ext. D(2), of the workmen in question as untrue. The report of the 
Engineer shows that Upen Das, blacksmith, and Filter Supervisor Kanai Babu, 
took the lead in holding the meeting. Exhibit A(2), dated 22nd November 1950, 
is the order of the Chairman of the Municipality suspending Upen Das and Kanai 
Lal Chatterji and calling for their explanations why disciplinary action should not 
be taken against them for wilful disobedience. This explanation by Upen Das 
is Ext. B. In this explanation, Upen Das states that the order of the Chairman 
is vague, that it gives no instance of disobedience which is to be apace and 
that there is no charge of any offence against him and the order of suspension 
was unjustified. He requested the Chairman to withdraw the suspension order 
and to institute an enquiry on the spot over the matter. Exhibit C is the order 
of dismissal of Upen Das by the Chairman. This order shows that the explana- 
tion of Upen Das was not accepted as satisfactory and he was dismissed. Shri 
Kanai Lal Chatterjee, Filter Supervisor, was transferred from Serampore Water- 
works to Howrah, 


Shri Manick Lal Chatterji, the Superintendent of the Waterworks, deposed 
in this case. He resides within the Waterworks compound. He states in evidence 
that npn Das and others held a meeting within the Waterworks without ‘eae 
sion, that explanations were called for from Upen Das and others and that the 
Chairman was not satisfied with the explanation and Upen Das was dismissed. 
On a consideration of the matter, it appears that the dismissal of Shri Upen Das 
was made by the Chairman after proper enquiry on the charge on which he was 
asked to explain. Upen Das, it appears, was found guilty of holding meeting 
within the compound of the Waterworks without the permission of the authorities 
and the Chairman in consideration of his past record and the present lapse thought 
it fit to dismiss him. It appears that there is evidence to support the action 
of the Chairman of the Municipality and this Tribunal will not therefore interfere 
with such aetion. The decision of the Chairman does not come under any of the 
four exceptions detailed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal in the Buckingham 
and Carnatic Company’s Case (1952 L.A.C., 490). 


The claim of re-instatement of Upen Das is, therefore, rejected. The Union 
is not entitled to any relief in respect of this claim. The issue is accordingly 
answered. 


Issue No. 15.—Revision of existing grades of pay for drivers. 


The Howrah Municipal Workers’ Union states in its written statement that 
Overseers and drivers were previously put on similar gradcs and the employecs 
of these two categories were allowed to enjoy equal benefits in regard to pay scalcs 
and other privileges but that the system has been changed and the drivers are now 
put on lower grades than the Overseers. It is claimed that drivers and Overseers 


Pant 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 981 


should be in similar grades and the scale of wages of drivers should be revised 
accordingly. 


The Municipality in its written statement states that Overseers and drivers 
were used to be in similar grades and they enjoyed equal benefits and privileges 
a long time ago. Since then grades have been revised several times and the 
Conservancy Overseers have already received higher grades of salaries than the 
lorry drivers. The pay structure, dearness allowance, etc., were revised in con- 
sultation and agreement with most of the employees and those who objected 
had the matter decided by the Industrial Tribunal presided over by Shri P. R. 
Mukherjee. The conditions of service of the Conservancy Overseers are much 
different from the lorry drivers inasmuch as the Overseers have to attend office 
from 2-30 p.m. in the afternoon, besides their morning duty when they have to 
supervise the work of the methors, It is further stated that the wages of the 
drivers of this Municipality is even higher than what is paid by the Calcutta 
Corporation and that the demand for increase of wages is absolutely unjustifiable. 


It appears that a Conservancy Overseer has to attend the office at 4 a.m. 
and to supervise the work of the methors. He can leave office at about 11 or 
12 in the forenoon and has again to come to the office at about 2-30 p.m. and 
to work there up to 6 p.m. or as long as the Health Officer is in the office. It 
was pointed out to me by the Icarned dept for the Municipality that the 
lorry drivers work only for 6 hours in this Municipality as against 94 hours in 
the Calcutta Corporation and that the lorry drivers in this Municipality get the 
scale wages of Rs. 60—4—140, whereas the lorry drivers in the Calcutta 
Corporation get salary in the scale of Rs. 55—5—60—4—80—5—110. Exhibit 
E shows the scale of wages of drivers and Conservancy Overseers since 1946 and 
it shows, that there have been revision of salaries since then of these categories 
of employees several times since 1946. The plea that the lorry drivers should 
have the same salary as the Conservancy Overseer is without any substance, 
because the job of the lorry drivers cannot be equated to that of a Conservancy 
Overseer. The ھا‎ scale of the lorry driver should rather be compared to that 
of his compeer in the Calcutta Corporation. At this test, the lorry driver of the 
Howrah Municipality cannot make out a case for grievance. I do not consider 
that there is any point in the claim for a revision of the wage scales of the drivers. 


Issue No. 16.—Court expenses incurred by the lorry drivers for the Municipal 
cases. 


The Howrah Municipal Workers’ Union states in its written statement as 
follows : 


The lorry drivers of the Road Department of the Municipality are to carry 
rubbish on lorries accumulated on both sides of the road. For that reason, they 
are to drive the lorries sometimes in such a way that the police authorities do not 
consider that practice to be in keeping with the traffic rules. Besides that, due 
to other reasons beyond the control of the driver, the traffic police file cases against 
them and the drivers are required to spend money for court expenses. Except 
in special circumstances, the lorry drivers should not be considered liable for 
sich cases. If the authority does not grant any protection to its employees and 
does not take any responsibilities for the trouble, the result will be that the 
employees will not be able to spend their full wages for family requirements and 
iconsiderable portion of the same will be spent for municipal affairs. 


The Municipality in its written statement states as follows : 


The lorry drivers of the Municipality are bound by the statutory Motor 
Vehicles Rules and other laws in the discharge of their duties and if they infringe 
iny law, they are bound to be prosecuted for such infringement. the demand 


982 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 10, 1954 [Parr I 


of the Union cannot be conceded as it would be against public policy. The 
Commissiongs have adopted the practice of making some advances to the accused 
lorry drivers in the case of accidents if they so think proper after considering 
the merits of each case and after receiving application from them. If the drivers 
are acquitted in the criminal court, the expenses are borne by the Municipality, 
otherwise the same is recovered from the drivers. 


The plea of the Union that the drivers have to disobey the Traffic Rules in 
doing their duty is not acceptable. The drivers are to obcy the Traffic Rules 
without any doubt. In case of any infraction of the Traffic Rules, they will be 
prosecuted by the police and the Municipality cannot help in the matter. The 
learned spokesman for the Municipality informs me that the present system 
followed by the Municipality is that on the application of the driver in individual 
cases, the Municipality enquires into the matter and if the driver is not found 
guilty by the court, he is given all court expenses and also reasonable expenses 
for pleader’s cost. Nothing is paid if he 15 found guilty by the Court. This 
appears to be a very healthy practice. The Municipality should also follow the 
following principles in the case of accidents. If the کل"‎ ٣٦ on enquiry 
finds that the accident caused by the lorry driver was beyond his control, and 
the offence of the driver can be condoned, the Municipality will pay him the 
expenses of the case, being all court expenses and reasonable expenses for the 
pleader’s fees. If it is found by the Court that the accident was on account of 
any defect in the car, the Municipality should pay the court expenses and reason- 
able pleader’s fees to the lorry driver. 


M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, 
First Industrial Tribunal. 
The 15th June 1954.

Order.

No. Medl. 4953/2D-72/54.—8id July 1954.—In exercise of the power 
conferred by clause (d) of sub-section (1) of section 28 of the Dentists Act, 
1948 (XVI of 1948), the Governor is pleased to sanction the following 
rules proposed to be made by the West Bengal Dental Council providing 
for the creation of a Provident Fund for the benefit of the employees of 
the said Council and for opening of a Savings Bank Account for depositing 
the Provident Kund money with the post office and for the control and 
manauyement of such Fund. 


West Bengal Dental Council Provident Fund Rules. 


1. very whole-time permanent employee of the West Bengal Dental 
Council shall be entitled to the benefit of a 1770510615৮ Fund. 


2. The Fund shall consist of the employees’ subscription amounting 
to 64 per cent. of the monthly basic salary, an equal amount as the 
empboyers’ contribution, and the interest accrued thereon on investment 
in the Postal Savings Bank hereinafter reterred to as the Savings Bank. 


3. The President and the Registrur of the Council shall be the 
Trustees of the Fund. The Registrur shall, on behalf of the Trustees, 
operate the account in aceordanee with these rules. 


4. The management of the Fund shall be entrusted to a Managing 
Committee consisting of 4 members, namely, the President, the Rejris- 
trar and one member nominated by the subscribers. 


5. The Manaping Commitiee shall maintain an individual ledger for 
each of the subseribers in Form ‘‘A’’ (annexed herewith) and shall, when 
the Savings Bank has credited the account with interest, distribute the 
interest proportionately to each subscriber at the end of each ১৪৪৮, 
very subscriber shall satisfy himself as to the correctness of his account 
and shall sign a certificate in token of his acceptance thereof. 


6. Withdrawal of deposit.—(a) The total sum at the credit of a sub- 
seriber in the Fund shall be payable to him on the termination 01১ his 
service subject {o the right of the employers to deduct therefrom any sum 
due to themselves, provided that the sum dedueted shal] not exceed their 
contributions to the subscriber’s account in the Fund: 


Provided further that if a subscriber is dismissed or removed from 
service, the employers’ contribution for a period not exceeding two years 
may be withhold at the discretion of the Managing Committee. 


(b) On the death of any subscriber while in service, the amount at the 
credit in the fund shall be paid to his nominee or nominees in accordance 
with the nomination made hs such subscriber in Form ‘B’’ (annexed 
herewith). 


(c) A temporary advance subject to the following conditions may “be 
allowed by the Managing Committee to a subscriber, provided that he has 
been in service tor not less than two years, for expenses in connection 
with the illness of the subscriber or of any member of his family, marriage 
or funerals of any member of his fanily or religious ceremonies to be 
observed by the subscriber and the like:— 


(i) Advances so allowed shall not exceed the aggregate of fle sub- 
seribers’ subscriptions, and shall be recovered in 12 te 24 equal 
monthly instalments, from the first payment of a tull month’s 
লং] after the advance is paid, but no recovery shall be made 
from a subscriber while he is on leave other than leave on full 
pay. 

(21) When on advance is repayable in 12 instalments or more, an 
additional instalment representing interest caleulated to the 
nearest anna equivalent to 4 per cent. of the amoufit of advance 
shall be paid by the subscriber provided that two such additional 
instalments shall be paid when the advance is repayable in 4 
instalments. 


(011) When an advance has already been granted to a subscriber, a 
subsequent advance shall not be granted to him, except for 
strong reasons to he recorded in writing by the Managing Com- 
nuttee, unless at least 12 months have elapsed since the com- 
plete repayment of the last advance taken. 


7. The employers shall not be bound by, or রর any assignment 
or encumbrance executed or attempted to be created which affects the dis- 
posal of the amount to the eredit of a subseriber who dies before retirement. 


8. ‘The decision of the Managing Committee on all questions arising 
out of these rules shall be final. 
; ٠ 
9. These rules may at any time be modified by the employers but not 
so ag to affect prejudicially the interests of the subscyibers 2297 to the

COST OF LIVING INDEX. 
Asansol-Ranigunge Arca, 


A family budget thquiry was conducted during the period August 1951 to 
February 1952 at the Ranipenge-Asansol industrial area during which 2,145 
budgets were collected. Of these 1,638 were family budgets and 507 were 
singleman’s budgets 13 family budgets being rejected for internal discrepancy, 
1,625 budgets were accepted for tabulation. The weights used for the prepara- 
tion of the cost of living index for the area are thus based on the pattern of 
expenditure of 1,625 families of industrial workers employed in the registered 
factories in the area. 

The weights, i.e., the percentage of expenditure on broad groups of items of 
an average family for all industries combined and for all expenditure levels 
taken together are as follows :— 


Food es os 64°77 
Fuel and lighting as ক 4-01 
Clothing i নর 7°30 
Miscellaneous 7 Ke 21°46 
House rent و‎ চে 2°46 


Selection of items.—With a view to make the Cost of Living Index répre- 
sentative of the actual pattern of consumption of the workers employed in the 
area,wit is necessary to utilise as much of the weights as it is possible in the 
preparation of the index. But the difficulty arises on the subject of availability 
of price quotations at regular intervals during the whole year. Making a com- 

,promise it is necessary to lump the weightages of certain items with those of 

hers. This procedure has the advantage of not ignoring the importance of 
items which have actually been consumed. There are certain items like interest 
ontjoan, postages, sweeper, religious rites, ctc., whose weights cannot be utilised 
for the purpose of preparing the index as the price quotations for such items are 
not regularly obtained and the weights themsclves are very small and have 
therefore been left out. 

Number of jtems.—In all 55 items have been selected for the purpose of the 
index representing 87°98 per cent. of the total weightage of a standard budget. 

ese are distributed in groups as (i)“Food, (ii) Fuel and Lighting, (iii) Cloth- 
ing gv) Miscellaneous and (v) House Rent. Number of items in each group 
is Sh6wn below :— 


Food rs) 
Fuel and Lighting 7 5 
Clothing a ia 12 
Miscellaneous a ও 15 
_ House Rent a 7 1 


In the above group in general clothing includes footwear, miscellancous 
includes conventional necessities and intoxicants. House rent is inclusive of 
rents, taxes and repairs. 


The table below shows the distribution of weights in different groups as taken 
from the standard budget and the percentage of the cost of these items to the 
total cost of the items in the groups as shown from the standard budget.

Details of lumping ہے‎ 
(A) FOOD GROUP. 


(1) Weights of paddy, chira and muri have been lumped with that of rice 
as they are different forms of the same item and their prices vary directly. 

(ii) Weights of brcad and biscuit have been added to the weights of wheat 
and atta. 

(iii) Weights of tomatoes and other vegetables which are available in different 
seasons have been distributed over. the weights of (a) potato, (b) brinjal and 
(c) onion in the same proportion as the latter items bear to total in the group. 

(iv) Weight of curd has been added to the weight of milk and that of butter 
to ghec. : 

Items like kitchen garden products, dried fish,. pork, fowl have not been 
considered to be items of wide use as the proportion of expenditure on these items 
is very small. These are not either priceable nor thg price quotations are 
collected regularly. ‘These items have us such been dropped out.

Base Period.—Family Budget Enquiry in the area was conducted in the year 
1951-52. As the base period for Cost of Living Index should synchronise as 
far as possible with the period of Family Budget Enquiry the calendar year 1951 
has been selected as the base of the index. 

Periodicity Index figures will be compiled month by month from January 
1952. 

Price quotations.—Prices of consumers goods are obtaincd every weck from 
the appointed price collecting agents from four centres in the area, namely (1) 
Asansol, (2) Ranigange, (3) Burnpore and (4) Kulti. 

P The prices are collected from important retajl shops and markets in the 
reas. * 

Compilation.~-Prices of articles cntering in the compilation of gndex haves 
been collected every week from the four centres mentioned above since the 
beginning of 1951. Average prices of each article have becn calculated on 
the basis of these weekly prices for thg different centres separately. Annual 
Average.price of different articles in diffCrent centres have been calculated and 
finally.fhe average for all the centges have been further averaged to give annual 
average prices of the articles in the whole area. : 

Simple index, i.e., relative increase or decrease of price of each item com- 
pared to that of the base prite have been calculated. These relatives have then 
been multiplied by the corresponding weights to find out the group index. Each 
group index is again multiplied by the corresponding group weight as found m 
the family budget enquiry. Weighted average of the sum of such products is then 
calculated to find out the General Cost of Living Index. 


S. N. CHATTERJEE, 
Dy. Labour Commissioner.

Minimum charge.

per month per kilowatt of connected load or part thereof on the

(b) For motors consuming energy under rate A(a)(ii), A(a)(iii) and rate

4. The 16 workmen as named in the schedule to the order of reference 
were all employed in the ‘‘B”’ Ticket Department of this Company. They 
were retrenched on 9181 March 1953 on the ground of اق‎ absence of 
ores eke orders after offering one month’s salary in lieu of notice to 
all of ) 


The 14 workmen, who put in appearance, alleged among others by a 
joint written statement that they had reasons to apprehend that the 
retrenchment was nothing but 0 clever device adopted with improper 
motive and with a view to wean away the workers from trade union acti- 
vities. In making the retrenchment the Company did not observe the 
rule of seniority in service and this was an instance of unfair labour 
practice. In the circumstances, the workmen prayed for reinstatement 
and for payment of compensation to them for the period of forced un- 
employment. 


In reply the Company denied having acted mala fide in the matter or 
from any extraneous considerations and pleaded that the retrenchment was 
effected for_bona fide trade reasons due to total absence of Government 
orders, and that it had no connection whatsoever with workmen’s union 
activities. Besides, it is said that no question of seniority arose as all 
those who worked in the “B’’ Ticket Department were temporary workmen 
and as the said ‘‘B’’ Department was wholly closed down for want of orders 
for blank tickets from E. I. Railway for which it was opened. In the 
circumstances, the Company submitted that the claim of the workmen 
should be dismiased. 


DECISION, 
The onus to justify the retrenchment is upon the Company. It has 


examined its acting Manager, D.W. 1, Mr. C. ©. Duncan, its accountant, 
D.W. 2, Shri Deba Prasad Sen Gupta and the cashier, 1(. W. 3, Shri 37 6٥ 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 15, 1904 2367 
রা 
Behari Adak, besides proving documents, exts. A to F. On the other hand 


none of the workmen have deposed except VP.W. ہا‎ Shri Benode Behari 
Jana. 


The (‘ompany does 75 and binding works. It has a permanent 
ticket department called ‘‘A’’ Ticket Department in which printed tickets 
are manufactured. The operations in ‘‘A’’ Department comprise cutting, 
chopping, printing and packing (vide D. W. 1). This department has 
been in existence for supply of printed tickets to Messrs. R. 8. N, Co., Ltd., 
I.G. N. & R. Co., Ltd., S. P. R. T. & Co., Ltd., and McLeod & Co., Ltd., 
and other concerns (vide D, W. 2). 


Then an order for blank tickets was received in September 1950, from 
the E. I. Railway, it (ext. D) being the first order. ‘‘B’’ Ticket Depart- 
ment was so opened in September 1950, to execute the said order for blank 
tickets from KE. I. Railway, ‘The operations in this department (which 
was to produce blank tickets) were limited to cutting, chopping and 
packing. The 16 workmen named in the order of reference came tov jom 
service of this Company in the ‘‘B’’ Department and admittedly worked 
only in this Department. The evidence shows that they were the only 
employees in the said 13১? Department. 


After reveipt of the first order in September 1950, the evidence shows 
that 4 out of 16 workmen, namely, Shri Binode Behari Jana, Shri Khetro- 
basi Mohanti, Shri Hrishikesh Mohallik and Shri Provakur Seeain 
(serials 1 to 4 of the order of reterence) were appointed on ا111‎ September 
1950 for work in ‘‘B’’ Department for production of blank tickets and 
packing. P.W. 1, Shri Benode Behari Jana, who deposed in this case 
admitted in cross-exumination that he was so appointed for the first time 
on llth September 1950. The second order was received on 3lst March 
1951 (yide 1). W. 2) and it appears that in between May and July 1951 the 
remaining 12 workmen were appointed tor work in 43” Department. 
D.W. 1, who was then acting in the absence of the permanent Manager 
on leave, appointed these 12 workmen. Exts. A, Al and A2 are the chits 
showing these appuintments. These chits recite that the workmen were 
taken on temporary basis. D.W. 1 also deposed that when he appointed 
these workmen he distinctly told them that they were being taken on tem- 
porary basis and that when they would have no work for blank tickets, their 
employment, would ভা terminate. The remaining workmen were 
appointed by the permanent Manager, Mr. McKenzie. It is also in 
evidence that he tao appointed the workmen on purely temporary basis 5 
connection with production of blank tickets for E. I. Railway. It is, there- 
fore, apparent that none of the 16 workmen had served the Company for 
more than 2$ vears up to the date of retrenchment on 3let March 19538. In 
his evidence P.W, 1, Shri Benode Behari Jana in a way admits that they 
were taken on temporary basis. He also admits that they made petitions to the 
Company for being made permanent after putting in service for 11 months 
or so. It is 8180 admitted that when they claimed to be made permanent, 
the Company replied on 9th November 1951 and 12th December 1951 as in 
annexures 1 and 2 to the written statement of the Company. The Company 
reiterated in reply to the claim of the workers that they were recruited on 
a purely temporary basis for a temporarv contract which wae to last for a 
certain period only and as such they could not be confirmed and treated as 
permanent employees of this Company. The workmen were accordingly in- 
formed that they were to continue to be temporary, It appears that after 
such replies the workwen kept silent for long and then only in. January, 
1953, when they scented impending retrenchment, they moved the Labour 
Commissioner for taking fhe issue regarding permanency with the manage- 
ment. As a result the Labour Commissioner forwarded a copy of their, 


2368 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 15, 1954 [Paxr 1 


application on 8th January 1953 to the Company for its comments (vide 
ext. F). The Company forthwith replied to it on 9th January 1953 refuting 
the charges as per annexure 6 to the Company’s written statement. Thus it 
will appear that these workmen were not only recruited on temporary basis 
but also their claim for being made permanent was not acceded to by the 
Company at any time. The case of the workmen that they had left employ- 
ment of another Company on a promise of higher pay and permanency by 
this Company cannot be sustained in view of the facts and circumstances. 
No doubt the Standing Orders as awarded by the Tribunal for the Printing 
Presses provide for permanency after continuous service for 12 months, but 
this has no application to these workmen when they had been recruited 
expressly on temporary basis to Jast till duration of production of blank 
Ban eta, Besides when the Company up to the date of retrenchment did not 
concede their claim for permanency, it cannot be said that they auto- 
matically became permanent after service of 12 months. So, all these 16 
workmen, I agree, were temporary employees. 


According to the Company, retrenchment was effected due to total ces- 
sation of Government orders for blank tickets. There is no dispute between 
the parties that the Company had only one sillting machine. It is also not 


one 


That there would be no further order for blank tickets was confirmed by a 
letter (ext. 01) which the Company received in May 1953 directing it to take 
return of security money deposited hy it. So when the orders for blank. 
tickets ceased for which ‘‘B’’ Department was opened, it is inevitable that 
the 16 workmen who were appointed in the said ‘‘B’’ Department became 
redundant. The Company was ‘therefore justified to abolish the “73? 
Department and to retrench the 16 workmen. There is nothing to show that 
in making the retrenchment the management was actuated by al.y extraneous 
considerations. If the workmen had formed a new union, there is nothing 
to show that it had influenced action of the Company. The evidence and 
circumstances on the contrary clearly indicate that the retrenchment wan 
effected for bona fide trade reasons. I accordingly find that the retrenchment 
was justified. As to the grievance of P. W. 1 that the three workmen,— 
Haripada, Kalo and another hoy who were working in ‘‘B” Department 
have not been retrenched but retained in service, his own evidence in cross- 
examination shows that these are employees who were working in other 
departments of this Company before ‘‘B” Department was created and that 
they were transferred to work in ‘‘B’? Department after it was opened. 
So when they are permanent and when the evidence reveals that they are 
senjor to the 16 workmen retrenched, no grievance can be made about it. 


As to the relief, it appears that the Company offered one month’s salury 
«to the workmen retrenched in lieu of notice. As temporary workmen they 


Part [] THE CALCUTTA GAZUTTE, JULY 16, 1954 2369 


are entitled to no compensation. The Tribunal cannot, therefore, interfere 
in the matter. It is accordingly held that the workmen are entitled to no 
further relief. I award accordingly. 


As to the grievance of 4১, W. 1 that he did not receive the notice pay and 
other dues, it appears from the evidence that on his own requisition by 
postcard dated 3001, July 1953, the Company remitted the umount to him 
by telegraphic money order post on 918 July 1954 (vide postal money order 
yeceipt) and received back the acknowledgment due ext. K1. On 1۸۸ August 
1953 the Company also wrote to P.W. 1 intimating despatch of the money 
(vide ext. E2). P.W. 1 says that the signature in the acknowledgment, 
ext. 101), 1৪ not his and he had not received the money. If it is so, this is 
not the proper place to agitate the question. As the Company had sent 
the money by telegraphic money order according to the instruction of 
p.W. 1, and as the او ا‎ had received back the acknowledgment through 
post office in due course, the Company cannot prima facie be held liable. 
[ am, therefore unable to help P.W. 1 in this respect.

For the Company: Shri Gour Mohan Chakraborty, Manager of the

While the aforesaid dispute between Messrs. Sarbamangala Pure Oil 
Mills and their workmen referred to under Government order No. 1807Dis., 
dated 4th July 1952, was pending the present application was filed by one 
Shri Munnar Jeshwara, on the allegation that he hus been suspended from 
work since 27th October 1952 without permission from the Tribunal and 
he accordingly prayed for reinstatement with compensation. Notice of 
the application being served, the employer filed a written statement on 
27th November 1952, in which they contended that suspension as a security 
measure is not a punishment, and, therefore, the application under 
section 338A is not maintainable. 


AWARD. 


At the time of trial the petitioner did not turn up. Thereafter the peti- 
tioner came us a witness for the Company and said on oath that he 1s 
now in employ ef the Company when no dispute exists with them. In the 
circumstances, I hold in the first place that suspension by way of security 
measure is not a punishment and consequently there is no alteration of the 
service condition. Therefore, petition under section J3A is not maintain- 
able. On merits also there is no dispute as the petitioner has got his dues 
for the period of non-employment and has also been reinstated to his former 
post. So, I hold that no dispute exists and I award accordingly that 
application under section 33A 1s not maintainable, and on merits also no 
dispute exists. 


S. C. MUKHERJI, 
Judge,

Gazette on 6th August 1953. 


On 2nd June 1953, one Surendra Nath Sarkar filed a complaint under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, stating as follower: -— 


The petitioner has been working as a Compounder in _ the factory 
dispensary at 8, Hide Road, Kidderpore of Brooke Bend (India), 
Ltd., Calcutta, since Ist July 1944. The petitioner entered service 
of the Company on a salary of Rs. 60 per month and by vearly 
increments is now drawing Ks. 115 per month as basic salary. 
When the petitioner was first appointed and til! about 1947 when 
a doctor was appointed, the petitioner used to carry on the duties 
of the dispensary and was in charge of the dispensary. In about 
1947 when the said doctor left the service, the petitioner was in 
charge of the dispensary for one month. On 27th February 1953, 
the petitioner was charge-sheeted on false charges. An ¢xplanation 
was submitted on 2nd March 1953. The authorities wrongfully 
held that the charges were proved against the petitioner aud on 
8th March 1953 by a letter suspended the petitioner from service 
with effect from 110) May 19583. The petitioner is not being paid any 
salary or allowance. The Company had no right ہا‎ suspend the 
petitioner from service, and by so doing, they contravened section 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The petitioner, therefore, 
prays that the Tribunal may be pleased to adjudicate upon the 
complaint and pending adjudication, the petitioner may be 
reinstated on payment of all back arrears of salary and allowances.

পুর সপ সা 


The Company, in its written statement, opposed the applicution and 
stated as follows :— 


It is not a fact that the petitioner was ever entrusted with the duties 
and responsibilities of a fully qualified doctor, tor the simple 
reason that the petitioner being only a Compounder could never have 
been found competent to perform the duties of a doctor. The 
petitioner was not worngfully charge-sheeted. He wns given every 
opportunity to defend himself in the enquiry held against him in 
connection with the charge of misconduct. The evidence available 
in the enquiry has been more than satisfactory and sufficient to 
warrant the finding of guilty. By his gross misconduet, the 
petitioner has completely forfeited the confidence of the Company, 
and the Company was justified in its decision to dismiss the peti- 
tioner from its service. Pending sanction of the Tribunal for 
implementation of its decision, the Company has suspended him ae 
a security measure. The Company prays that the petitioner may be 
dismissed as being incompetent. 


On the date of hearing on 25th June 1964, the compluinavt 520 not 
appear. It appears that after the award of the Tribunal was passed on the 
original reference on 8th July 1958, the Company placed before the H-n’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal an application under section 22 of the Industrial 
Disputes Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, seeking permission of the 81177611965 
court to dismiss the applicant Compounder. Actually the t‘ompany had 
before this Tribunal an application under section 33 of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act in place of which the application under section 22 of the Industrial 
Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act was preferred. The Hon’ble Apyellate 
Court considered the Company’s application in Miscellaneous Case No, (-265; 
53 ond passed an order on 4th December 1953 granting permission to dismiss 
the Compounder. 15৮, A is a true copy of ‘that order of the lJeurned 
Appellate Tribunal. The application under section 388A is not, therefore, 
competent, as the Company has already received permiasion from ‘he Hon'ble 
Appellate Tribunal to dismiss the complainant. The application under sec- 
tion 383A is, therefore, rejected.

NOTICE. 


APPLICATIONS are invited for admission to the next 
term of the Prince of Wales’s Military College, Dehra 
Dun, commencing in January 1955. 


Course.—The College provides a public school education 
for boys who wish to obtain commissions in the Army 
Navy or Air Force. The educational training is designed 
to bring boys up to the standard of the Senior Cambridge 
School Certificate and the Qualifying Examinations for 
entry into the National Defence Academy. Compulsory 
রাঃ training, games and parades ensure physical 

tness and smartness; while special attention is paid ‘to 
the imparting of discipline, self-reliance and social train- 
ing to all cadets. 


Admission.— Candidates for admission to the next term 
of the College which commences from January 1955, will 
have to qualify at an Entrance Examination to be held 
at Calcutta some time in 3rd week of September 1954 
followed by an interview. 


Age limits.—Orandidates must have been born not 
earlier than 2186 January 1943 and not later than 2th 
January 1944. The age limits can in no case be relaxed. 


Educational qualificationé.--No educational qualification 
is prescribed for سس‎ be to this College but it is 
expected that the candidate should have read up to 
Class VIT standard of a Secondary School. 


Fees.—The«fees are Rs. 750 per term plus additional 
expenses of Rs. (e.g., uniforms, pocket money, books, 
washing, etc.). e actual cost is thus Ra. 2,300 per 
annum. <A cadet spends 5 to 6 years at the College. 


Scholarships.—A limited number of scholarships of 
Rs. 1,000 per annum is awarded to the deserving cadets 
after admission to tthe College by the West Bengal 
Government, 


Applications.— Application on the prescribed form in 
duplicate which can be had on request from the Assistant 
Secretary, Home (Defence) Department, Government of 
West Bengal, Writers’ Buildings, Calcutta, should be 
submitted so as to reach him on or before the 16th 
August 1954.

National Library. 


IN response to public opinion, the کہ‎ hours of the 
Reading ms and the Lending Section at Belvedere have 
been extended with effect for the 16th August 1953, The 
revised working hours are specified below:— 


Reading Rooms— 


Week days (including Saturdays)—-9 a.m. to 8 p.m. 
Sundays and holidays—10 a.m. to 5 p.m. 


Lending Section— 
Week days (including Saturdays)—10 a.m. to 5 p.m. 
Sundays and holidays—10 a.m. to 1-30 p.m. 
The Reading Rooms and the Lending Section will, how- 


ever, remain entirely closed on the following days of the 
year:— 
(i) Republic Day, (ii) Independence Day and (iii) 
Satatena handhi’s Birth Day. 


Persons above 18 years of age are eligible to make use 
of the Library; which is a free lending Library open to 
any one residing in any part of the Indian Union. There 
is no subscription to pay but security in cash is essential.

SUPPLEMENT— Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 30th June 1954. 


Summary.—During the week under report, there was rainfall in thirty-eight subdivisions. Weather was unfavcureble in five 
subdivisions. Weeding of Aus and Jute continued. Sowing of Aman continued. Transplantation of Aman commenced. Prospect 
of standing crops waa, on the whole, fair. Fodder was reported to be insufficient in nine subdivisions. Cattle-disease was reported 
from five subdivisions. The wages of the labourer varied from Rupee one to Rupees two and annas eight in different subdivisions.

3. Regulation of site of service.privies and 
service-urinals.—(1) No service-privy or service- 
urinal exceeding eleven feet in height shall be 
placed in the space required by this Act to be left 
ul the back of a building. 

(2) No service-privy or service-urinal situated 
in, or adjacent to, a building shall be placed aot a 
distance of less than six feet from— 


(i) any public building, or 0 

(ii) any building which is, or is likely to be, 
used as a dwelling place, or kitchen, or 
as a place in which any person is, or 28 
intended to be, employed in any manu- 
facture, trade or business. 


(3) No service-privy or service-urinal shall be 
constructed in any premises occupied by a masonry 
building, or without the special sanction cf the 
Commissioners in any other premises which are 
situated in اھ‎ street which has been sewered and 
has an adequate water-supply. 


(4) Every service-privy and service-urinal shall 
be detached m the inhabited portion of any 
building. 


4. Prohibition of construction of srvice-privy 
or service-urinal on upper 1008৮ of a building.— 
No aervice-privy or service-urinal shall be placed 
on any upper floor of a building. 


h. Models and type-plans.—Models and type- 
plans of service-privies and urinals approved by 
the Commissioners, with estimates of the cost of 
constructing service-privies und urinals in accor- 
dance therewith, shall be bept in the municipal 
office, and shall he open to inspection by any person 
at all rensonable times without charge; but no 
person shal] be hound to construct any service- 
privy or urinal in accordance with any such model 
or type-plan if such privy or urinal be constructed 
in accordance with these by-laws. 


6. Drains.—(1) A drain shall be provided for 
every Rervice-privy or service-urinal. 


_ (2) Such drain shall be constructed of some 
impervious material, and shall connect the floor of 
the privy or urinal— 
(a) with a drain communicating with a muni- 
cipal sewer, or 
(b) if permitted by the Commissioners, with— 
(i) an impervious cess-pool the contents of 
which can be removed by hand or by 
vacum gulley-pit emptying machine, or 
(1) a aoak-pit, as described in by-law No. 33(a) 
of the modgl ip Baik regarding privies, 
urinals and drains of water-carriage 
system, Or, 
(iii) a municipal*drain. 


7. Floor.—The floor of every sé@rvice-privy and 
every service-urinal shall— 

(1) be made of cement or other impervious 
material, or if the owner so desires, of 
glazed tiles, artifieial stone, or glazed 
sanitary ware; 

(2) be in every part at a height of not less than 
six inches above the level uf the surface 
of the ground adjoining the privy or urinal, 
and 

(9) be made with a fall or inclination of at least 
half an inch to the foot towards the drain 
specified in by-law 6. 


8. Walls.—The walls and roof of every service- 
privy, and the walls and roof (if any) of every 
service-urinal, shall be made of such materials as 
may by approved by the Commissioners: Provided 
that the entire surface of the walls 01 a privy below 
the plattorm shall be surfaced with cement, or other 
materials as specified in by-law 7(1). 


9, Platform.—(1) The platform of every service- 
privy or service-urinal shall either be plastered 
with cement or be made of some: watertight non- 
absorbent material specified in by-law 7(1). 


(2) In the case of service-privies or urinals with 
an outlet drain constructed in accordance with by- 
law 6(2) (b) (ili), the platform must be sloped 
towards the aperture with an inclination of ut least 
half an iuch to the foot. In all other cases detailed 
in by-law 6(2), the platform may, if so directed by 
the Commissioners, be sloped away from the 
aperture towards a drain communicating with a 
municipal drain or a drain connected with a muni- 
cipal sewer, 


10. Ventilation.—Every service-privy and ever 
service-urinal situated in, or adjacent to, a build. 
ing shall have an opening, of not less than three 
square feet in area, in one of the walls of the privy 
or urinal, as near the top of the wall as may be 
practicable and communitating directly with the 
open air. : 


11. Construction of privies.—(1) Every service- 
privy and service-urinal shall be provided with a 
movable receptacle for sewage. 


(2) The following provisions shall have eftect with 
regard to such privies, urinals and receptacles, 
namely : — 


(a) the space beneath the platform of the privy 
or urinal shall be of such dimensions as 
to admit of a movable receptacle for 
sewage, of a capacity not exceeding two 
cubic feet, being placed and fitted beneath 
the platform in such manner and position 
as will effectually prevent the deposit, 
otherwise than in such receptacle, of any 
sewage falling or thrown through the 
aperture in the platform: 


(b) the privy or urinal ghall be so constructed 
as to afford adequate access to the said 
space for the pufposes of cleansing it and 
of placing therein, and removing there- 
from, a proper receptacle for sewage ; 

(c) the said receptacle shall be water-tight, and 
shall be made of metal, well-tarred earth- 
enware or glazed stoneware, and shal] be 
of such construction and shape as the 
Chairman may consider suitable: 

(d) the door of the opening for the insertion and 
removal of the said receptacle shall be so 
made as completely to cover the said 
opening.

usual notices were issued to the parties for appearence and written stute-

that 0. MeKenzie & Co. (1919), Ltd., is an automobile engineering unit,

skfiied. The workinen were always subjected‘ to anfair labour practice und 
muny of the legitimate demands of the workers were rejected. ‘Lhq present 
dispute cropped up with the unwarranted and arbitrary dismissal of one 
Tatiruddin, an active member of the Union, on 29th June 1953. The work. 
nien demonstrated their protest and staged u stay-in-strike, troin the 
morning of 30th June 1953. At the intervention of the ‘police, the manage. 
ment agreed to discuss the whole matter with the workers and tuke back al] 
who wish to return to work. The workers thereupon came out yf the 
factory. Tafiruddin was denied admittance into the workshop on Ist July 
1953 and the matter was reported to the Labour Comniissioner 101 his settle. 
tient. Since the stoppage of work on 30th June 1953 was provoked by the: 
management, they were entitled to full wages for that period-ou SUth June 
1953. Hence the claim. 


In reply, the Company stated that Tafiruddin was asked 10. go along 
with Bimal Ghose, N. 0. Rout, N. Khan and Thakur to the Peuinavlar 
Motor Corporation, Ltd., on the 25th June and they went willingly or 
without any objection having been raised either verbully or in writing. On 
the 26th next, the Company received a complaint from the Works Manager 
of the Peninsular Motor Corporation, Ltd., about the behaviour ot the said 
employees and was informed that it would be necessary for the employees to 
come on the 27th June to complete the work in its workshop. (n the 27 
June the said employees did not return to the Peninsular Motor Corporation, 
Ltd., as they were required to do. Afterwards, all except Tafruddin returm- 
ed. Mr. 10. J. D’Cruz, the Works Manager, requested him io go to the 
Corporation, which he refused. Tafiruddin repeatedly disobeyed the orders 
of the Works Manager and the Sales Manager and refused to submit any 
explanation when called for. After repeated attempts to 10011 proper 
amends, Tafiruddin dectined to comply with the request of the Manager and 
accordingly he was dismissed on justifiable grounds after a proper enquiry. 
That was on 29th June 1953. Tafiruddin however entered the workshop on 
30th June and all the workers stopped work and did not do any work for the 
rest of the day. When the workers refused to go out of the workshop ৯ 
the closing time, the police was called to the workshop at 6 ».m. After some 
discussion, the workers were pursuaded to leave the workshop at 8-30 p.m. 
Qn Wednesday, the Ist July next, Tafiruddin again entered the workshop 
without any permission and a letter, signed by four workers, was sent to the 
Management for his unconditional reinstatement. The Company replied its 
inability to reinstate the worker, when the workers again s.oonel work from 
11-30 a.m. to 3-380 p.m. On the 2nd July next, the work started at 2-30 p.m. 
as the workers refused to give an undertaking at first and stopped work. In 
the said circumstances, the Company denied its liahility to pay any wages 
for the period of stoppage of work. . 


The issues are: 
(1) Whether Shri Tafiruddin is entitled to be reinstated. What relief 
is he entitled to. 
(2) Whether the workmen are entitled to wages for the period they 
stopped work. 
0 


Issue No. 1: On 12th October 1953, the Manager of the Company 
informed this Tribunal that Issue No. 1 has been settled out of court (ride 


Parr 1] THE CATCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22,4 2429 


সস 
Ext. ৮0). The Management proved the letters of "Taflruddin (11505, GF: 
C1 and C2) and recespt which he signed*on receiving payment m full gatis- 
faction of his claims (vide Ext. B). Tafiruddin was absent during healing. 
He did not take any interest in this case. «In _ hig letters ty the Assistant 
Labour Commissioner, Mr,.D’Cruz, the acting Worke Manuger, explpined 
the reasons for the dismissal of Tafiruddin. ‘The ,easons.wo doubt} support 
the order of dismissal on justifiable grounds. I have since verified by an 
enquiry from the learned representative of the Union this rea] oosition 
about settlement. Issue No. ] was not pressed for hearing by the parties. 
(vide Order No. 4, dated 5th June 1954, recorded in the Order Sheet). I, 
therefore, find that there is no outstanding dispute regarding this issue. 


Issue No. 2: This relates to wages for the period of stoppage of work ou 
30th June 1953. The Union claims that the workers ure entitled to full 
wages دہ‎ the strike was provoked by an unwarranted action on the part. of the 
Management over the dismissal of Tafiruddin. The Management denied 
its liability on the allegation that the stoppage of work was not provoked by 
any action on their side. 


It appears from the evidence of O.P.W. 3 Mr. E. L. D’Cruz, the acting 
Works Manager, that the workers worked up to 11 a.m. and were duly pid 
for that work. They did not work after that period having struck work out 
of sympathy for the dismissal of one Tafiruddin. Accordingly it is cuntended 
that they were not entitled to any wages for the rest of the day. Mr. 1)’Crusz 
said he wrote Ext. 1 which explains the facts that led to the diamiasal of 
Tafiruddin. Shri Kalipada Mandal, the only witness on the Union side, 4 
not speak anything regarding this. J have already stated above thit 
Tafiruddin is absent throughout this enquiry. The strike is admitted. 6 
is not possible on materials now on record to say that the strike war in any 
way provoked by any unwarranted action on the part of the Managument. 
The workers, soon after Tafiruddin forced his entry into the workshop, 
struck wotk and illegally stayed in the workshop after the closing time, till 
8-30 p.m. when they left only at the intervention of the police. The manage- 
ment agreed to discuss the matter of dispute with the workers. All the 
workers were taken in except Tafiruddin and again they struck work on the 
next two days. This will appear from the pleadings and not denied hy the 
Union. In this state of things, and in the background of what happened 
previous to the date of the strike, the Tribunal cannot but find that the strike 
was not justified. The strike is no doubt a legitimate weapon in the hands 
of the workers and the workers have inherent right to stop work, when they 
desire. But this right has got to be exercised only when all other avenues 
for peaceful settlement of the dispute have failed. Since 11) this 
ease the workers did not take any reasonable attitude in the matter of 
settlement of the dispute over the dismissal of Shri Tafiruddin, it cannot be 
said that the Management provoked their strike on 30th June 1953, aud since 
the strike was not provoked by the Management, the workmen are not 
entitled to wages for the period they stopped work on 30th June 1953. 1٤ 
decide the issue accordingly. This is my award.

In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Chowringhee Stores,

The industrial djspute existing between Measrs. Chowringhee Stores, 
Ltd., 35, Chowringhee Road, Calcutta and their employees as represented 
by the Chowringhee Stores Employees’ Union, 23/1, Ramtanu Bose Lane, 
Calcutta-6, regarding the matters specified in the schedule to the order of 
reference, has heen referred to this Tribunal for its adjudication. The 
reference was received in the office of the Tribunal on &th September 1943 
and usual notices were issued to the parties for appearance and written 
statement. Parties filed their written statement and 2lst June 1954 was 
fixed for hearing. 


The employees in their written statement stated that the Chowringhee 
Stores, Ltd., (hereinafter called the Company), is the largest and _ best 
equipped retail store in Caleutta with an authorised capital of 10 lakhs, but 
it carries on wholesale business on an extensive scale in Calcutta and deals 
with foodstuff, provisions, wines, etc. In 1947, it was converted into a 
private limited concern. The number of staff at present is about 50. Since 
after the formation of the Union, the employees’ grievances were numerous. 
It formulated their demands as follows :— 


(1) The present wages are exceptionally low. There are neither 
grades nor scales of annual increment. 


(2) There is no dearness allowance for employees, to meet the increased 
cost of living. 


(3) No Bonus. 

(4) Provisions for leave und holidays are irregular. 
(5) No Provident Fund or gratuity. 

(6) No security of service. 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 243] 


১ সস ্ 


Rules for appointment, discharge, dismissal “and retrenchment have 
never been framed. 


The Company, in reply, stated that its paid-up capital was Rs. 60,000. 
It did not carry on wholesale business in Calcutta. During the War-period 
the number of employees was increased to about 50, but due to trade 
recession there was less for the last few years. It denied that the employees’ 
condition was plightful. The wages paid were more than adequate and 
considering its financial position there could only be the question of 
retrenchment and reduction of wages. 


Regarding the dearness allowance it was included in the wages. Bonus 
was paid on profits. Owing to financial stringency and loss, the Company 
was not prepared to consider the question of Provident Fund. 


As to holidays and leave, it was the usual custom in the Shipping Industry 
not to allow holidays in the office on all public holidays. 


Regarding the increment it pointed out that certain increments were, 
in fact, given to the employees as and when the occasion permitted. 


Issues as per schedule to the Order of Reference are—(i) Dearness 
allowance, (i1) Bonus, (11) Holidays, (iv) Leave, (v) Provident Fund and 
(vi) Grades and scales of pay. 


Both parties filed a joint petition on 2186 June 1954, the day fixed for 
hearing of the case stating, that the dispute had been amicably settled. 
The terms of settlement contained in separate sheets of paper form 
Annexures 4481 and ‘‘B”’ to this petition. 


Heard Mr. S. Mehta, the Director and Attorney for the Company and 
Mr. Jiten Banerjee, Secretary for the Union. The dispute has been settled 
in terms\of compromise, which are fair and reasonable. They are accord- 
ingly accepted. The case is disposed of in terms of the agreement (marked 
Annexures 54872 and ‘‘B’’) which forms part of this award.

ORDER. 


No. 3335Dis./D/7L-38/54.—9th July 1954.—Whereas under the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 3303Dis./D/7L-17/52, 
dated the 28th November 1952, the industrial dispute between Messrs. Bengal 
Jute Mill Co., Ltd., Shibpur, Howrah and their workmen represented by 
Howrah Zilla Chatkal Mazdoor Union, 4, Nityadhan Mukherjee Road, Howrah 
and Howrah District Jute Mazdoor Congress Union, 64, Joybibi Lane, Ghusury, 
Howrah) in connection with the dismissal of the nine workers mentioned in the 
schedule! thereto was referred for adjudication to the First Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal 
a complaint in writing was made by Shri Udaynath Das, a workman of the said 
Company, before the said Tribunal, against the said Company, alleging that 
the said Company had dismissed the said workman concerned in such dispute; 


And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudicated 
upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State Government; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to publish 
the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A filed by Shri Udaynath Das, a 
workman of Bengal Jute Mill Co., Ltd., as represented by Howrah Zilla 


Chatkal Mazdoor Union. 
BEFORE THE FIRST INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 
PRESENT: 
SHri M. C. BANERJI, District Judge (Retd.), Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 


AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal referred under Government order 
No. 3303Dis./D/7L-17/52, dated 28th November 1952, the industrial dispute 


2436 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1964 [Parr T 
8S  سججججج بے 0کک "' ٌٛ5 ج  تس ُٗؤْٗ سس سکم‎ 1.  سیسٴسعےےجےےس‎ 
between Bengal Jute Mills Co., Ltd., Shibpur, Howrah, and their workmen 
represented by Howrah Zillah Chatkal Mazdoor Union to this Tribunal for 


adjudication. The award on this dispute was published in the Calcutta 
Gazette, on 16th April 1953. 


_On 4th March 1953, one Uday Nath Das, an employee of the Bengal Jute 
Mills Co., Ltd., applied under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
stating as follows:— 


On 30th December 1952, the petitioner was most arbitrarily asked to 
accept temporary ticket and work as ৪ temporary hand in the 
Batching Department, while he was employed in the Preparing 
Department as a permanent hand. The petitioner protested against 
such a mala fide act on the part of the Management and on that date, 
viz., 30th December 1952, the Company dismissed him from service. 
On 26th February 1953 the petitioner approached the Labour Officer 
of the Company with a letter from the Labour Directorate, but the 
Labour Officer did not give him any job and asked him to quit the 
place. The petitioner, therefore prays for reinstatement with full 
wages for the period of unemployment. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


Udaynath was not a permanent workman, but joined as 2 budli in the 
Preparing Department on 20th August 1951 and worked in the night 
shift 01] 26th November 1952, when the night shift was abolished. 
Thereafter he continued to work as a budli in the Preparing Depart- 
ment in the day shift. As there was no job available for him in the 
Preparing Department, the Company asked him to join the Batching 
Department on 29th December 1952, which he refused. He absented 
himself from work from 29th December 1952 and 85 never dis- 
missed by the Company. The workman was asked to report for duty 
and he did so on 26th February 1953, when he was again asked to 
join the Batching Department, as no work could be found for him in 
the Preparing Department. The Company _ never dismissed 11115 
workman, but only transferred him from one department to another, 
and this application under section 33A did not lie. 


The case was taken up for hearing on 23rd June 1954. On that date, the 
complainant was not present and no one appeared for him either. The Com- 
pany was represented by Shri J. Raman of the I.J.M.A. and Shri M. N. 
Chakrabarty, Labour Officer. Shri M. N. Chakrabarty, deposed on behalf of 
the Company and proved the Company’s case as made out in the written state- 
ment. It further appears that Udaynath reported for duty again on 30th March 
1953 and was employed by the Company and is still in the employment of the 
Company. I do not find that this workman was ever dismissed by the Com- 
pany. It appears that he refused employment from 29th December 1952 to 
28th March 1953. Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act was not contra- 
vened by the Company and the complaint under section 33A is incompetent. 
The application uffder section 33A is, therefore, rejected. 


M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 
The 25th June, 1954. 


By order of the Governor, 
D. ও. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

Management did not allow her to join. The petitioner made several 
representations to the Management but to no effect. The Company 
discharged the petitioner during the pendency of an adjudication pro- 
ceeding without the permission of the Tribunal. The petitioner, 
therefore, prays for reinstatement with full compensation for the 
period of unemployment.

The Company, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


The workman concerned went on leave for eight weeks from 17th Noy. 
ember 1952 to 110) January 1953. On 12th January 1953 906 
applied for extension of leave for two weeks, i.e., from 12th Janua 
1953 to 25th January 1953, which was granted by the Company 
Since 26th January 1953 when the workman was to rejoin her duties 
she remained absent without leave unauthorisedly. On 2nd May 
1953 the workman submitted a letter tendering her resignation from 
the Company. This letter of resignation was considered by the 
Company and on 50) May 1953, she was informed about the Com. 
pany’s acceptance of her resignation. Neither the workman presented 
herself for employment on 27th February 1953, nor the Company 
discharged her, as alleged. The workman terminated her service with 
the Company of her own accord, and as such, the allegation of throw. 
ing her into unemployment, is misleading. The Company has in no 
way contravened section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act and the 
application is incompetent. 


On the date of hearing on 23rd June 1954, the complainant was not present

pany. O.P.W. 1 Shri M. N. Chakrabarty, deposed on behalf of the Company, 
and the case was heard in the absence of the complainant.

The resignation letter submitted by Katoria is Ext. A. In the circumstances, it 
appears that the Company never dismissed the complainant and did not con. 
travene section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The application under 
تج‎ 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, is incompetent and is 
rejected.

The Government of West Bengal referred under Government. order

between Bengal Jute Mill Co., Ltd., Shibpur, Howrah, and their workmen 
represented by Howrah Zilla Chatkal Mazdoor Union to this Tribunal for

Gazette on (6th April 1953. 


On 2nd March 1953. Issuf, a workman of the Company, complained under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act stating that he was discharged by the 
Company on 23rd February 1953. It is further stated that the petitioner was 
not served with any charge-sheet, nor was he shown any reason whatsoever for 
the discharge. The applicant, therefore, prayed for reinstatement with full 
compensation for the period of unemployment. 


The Company, in its written statement, states that the workman has not 
been discharged by the Company, as alleged. He was on sick 168৮5 from 16th 
July 1952 to 21st February 1953 and resumed his duty on 22nd February 1953. 
It is further stated that the workman discontinued work from 12-54 p.m. on 
22nd March 1952 and remained absent without leave till 2nd March 1953 when 
he submitted an application praying for leave for the unauthorised period of 
absence. The question of issuing a charge-sheet did not arise as the Company 
never contemplated any action against the workman. The _ applicant has 
continued in the employment of the Company since 2nd March 1953 and has 
not been discharged, as alleged. The application under section 33A of the Act 
is, therefore, misconceived and should, therefore, be rejected. 


On the date of hearing on 23rd June 1954, the complainant did not appear. 
None appeared for him either. Shri J. Raman of the 1.J.M.A. and Shri M. N. 
Chakrabarty, Labour Officer, appeared for the Company. O.P.W. 1 Shri M. 
N. Chakrabarty, deposed on behalf of the Company. e case was heard in 
the absence of the complainant O.P.W. 1 proved the case of the Company.

the petitidn. The Company did not violate the provisions of section 33 of the

Industrial Disputes Act and if so whether it was justified or not and what 
relief ee B. Roy entitled to get from the Joint Steamer Companies as 
aforesaid. 


DECISION, 


In the present case there is no controversy that the petitioner B. Roy is 
a workman within the purview of the Industrial Disputes Act. I asked the 
lawyer on the side of the Company as to whether there is any challenge that 
the petitioner is a workman, within the meaning of section 33 of the Indus. 
trial Disputes Act. The learned lawyer replied that the Company does 1701 
and would not challenge that the Audit Inspector Shri B. Roy was a work- 
man within the purview of the said section. 


It is not the case that the employer asks the employee to join his duty 
at a particulfr station on transfer and that the employee refuses to go there. 
If that were the case certainly the ready answer would be that the employee 
should be dismissed summarily because 1t would be misconduct on the part 
of the employee. Before partition of India and the creation of Pakistan 
Shri B. Roy, an inhabitant of Dacea district, was holding service under the 
Joint Steamer Companies having their jurisdiction in Calcutta, Dacca, 
Barisal, Mongyer, Assam and other places in India. After the partition of 
India and the creation of Pakistan B. Roy continued to have the permanent 
residence in Dacen district and at the time of the partition he himself was 
holding service in Narayanganj in Dacca district. Under the law therefore 
he could be held to be a Pakistan national but the Company, ٤. 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 2447 
rr 


employér had no right to alter the service condition of thé employee Shri 
B. Roy simply because of his Pakistan nationality. Admittedly the Com- 
pany has got many employees of different nationalities, all serving 11) India. 
By the political partition of India B. Roy’s nationality may have automati- 
cally changed from British India to Pakistan but 1 do not think that the 
splitting of the Companies itself could create any alteration of setvice condi- 
tion affecting the employee Shri 13, Roy unless he gives his consent thereto 
exprensly or impliedly. When the Company was split up into Kilburn & 
Co. (India), 10 and Kilburn & Co. (Pukistun), 1১0.) B. Roy ought to 
have been given option to choose this or that Company. He was not given 
such option. On the other hand it appears clearly from the evidence that 
he was treated as an employee of Kilburn & Co. (India), Ltd. Therefore 
the order of transferring his Provident Fund Account trom India to Pakistan 
without the knowledge and consent of the employee Shri B. Roy was a clear 
alteration of service condition which is illegal and unjustified. To confirm 
the said illegal act, the Company was out to transfer Shri B. Roy to Kilburn 
& Co. (Pakistun), Ltd., and relying on the alleged dismissal order passed by 
Kilburn & Co, (Pakistan), Ttd., B. Roy was asked to make over charge to 
Mr. K. 1), Mookherjee of Kilburn & Co. (India), Ltd., in Caleutta. This 
discharge order is therefore illegal. 


From the evidence I find that after the discharge of Shri B. Roy, 
Kilburn & Co. (India), Litd., gave extension of service of a retired Audit 
Inspector and also appointed some new hands to cope with the Auditing 
work in Calcutta. This shows that B. Roy who claims to be the second 
oldest Audit Inspector of this Company hos been sacked without any justi- 
fication simply because he was unwilling to abide by the decision of 
Kilburn & Co. (India), Lid., made behind his back to the effect that his 
provident fun account and service should be transferred to Kilburn & Co. 
(Pakistan), 150, Therefore Shri B. Roy should be reinstated in his service 
under Kilburn & Co. (India), Ltd., and his Provident Fund Account must 
remain in India and the order of transferring the said Provident Fund 
Account to Pakistan is to be set aside. For the purpose of ‘“‘loss of earn- 
ing” compensation Shri B. Roy is entitled to get back wages to the extent 
of 4 months’ salary plus dearness allowance. The said amount shall be paid 
and he shall be reinstated within 15 days from the date of publication of 
the award in the Calcutta Gazette. 5

In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), filed by Shri Kalipada Mondal and other

arising owt of an industrial dispute referred under Government order

D/10L-124/53, dated 5th October 1953 (Case No. 5 of 1954).

For the Union: Shri Patit Paban Pathak, assisted by Shri Benoy Roy Choudhury,
