AWARD. 


This is an application by Shri Kalipada Mandal and other workmen 
employed by G. McKenzie & Co. (1919), Ltd., under the provisions of sectior 
33A of the fdustrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), for reinstatement 
This was filed on 8th January 1954. It is alleged among others that the 
petitioners were the permanent employees of the Company working in differen 
capacities with varied period of service. They were with others agitating ove! 
the demand of Puja bonus, and a charter of demands including the demand 101 
bonus was placed to the Company on 7th September 1953. The Company 
instead of meeting their demands, declared a lock-out on 6th October 1953 0 
false and baseless grounds and thereby throwing as many as 180 workmen ou 
of employment. The petitioners were not given any charge-sheet. In th 
meantime, the Company reopened the factory on 30th October 1953 and 06৪2 
to take in some workmen by selection. About 100 of the old employees wer 


Parr J] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1964 2449 


already taken in and a number of new recruits were also made. The petitioners 
repeatedly approached the Management for work but were refused. ence this 
application for reinstatement and for any other relief to which they are entitled. 


_ The Company contests this application and contends that this is not main- 
tainable inasmuch as the lock-out does not attract the provisions of section 33 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947). It denied having 
received any charter of demands from the workmen but stated that there was a 
demand for payment of Puja bonus. It explained fully its position that it was 
unable to pay Puja bonus as its financial position did not justify that. The 
matter was reported to the Labour Commissioner. While the Puja bonus was 
being considered by him the petitioners and other workmen without waiting for 
the result committed the following offences on the 6th October 1953 and during 
the pendency of the adjudication proceeding before this Tribunal. They com- 
menced, instigated and participated in an illegal strike, incited others to partici- 
pate in it, confined Mr. E. L. D’Cruz, the acting Works Manager, in the factory 
premises, between 9-15 a.m. to 2-15 p.m. and acted in a manner subversive of 
discipline. The petitioners were guilty of gross misconduct for which they were 
liable to be dismissed. The Management issued notices immediately after the 
strike without any effect. Mr. D’Cruz was rescued only with the help of the 
police. The Company had already filed applications under section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), for permission to dismiss these 
workers for gross misconduct. Some of the workmen admitted their guilt, 
expressed repentance for what they did and requested to allow them to work, 
The Management considering the merits of each case and in view of the repent- 
ing attitude of the workmen concerned, condoned their guilt where it thought 
fit and proper to do so and permitted them to resume their work. It also took 
new recruits purely on a temporary basis just to carry out its obligations. The 
allegation \that the selection of these workmen was unfair is false and denied. 
The condi of these petitioners were found unsatisfactory and therefore they 
could not be taken in before the decision of the Tribunal was known. 


DECISION. 
Points for decision are— 


(1) Whether the petitioners are entitled to reinstatement in service? 
(2) To what other relief they are entitled? 


This case was heard along with the Company’s three applications under 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. I have passed orders in the 
three cases 7 only three workers among the petitioners in this case to 
be dismissed.. The remaining petitioners mav therefore be taken as continuing 
in Company’s service. The question of their reinstatement, in the strict sense 
of the term, does not arise. The petitioners were refused work when they 
approached the Management after the factory reopened after a lock-out. It 
has been urged on the side of the Company that the declaration of lock-out does 
not attract the provisions of section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, 
as it does not attract section 33 of the Act. It is true that Jock-out does not 
attract section 33 of the Act but the question is not that. It is the refusal of 
the Management to provide the petitioners with work. That is the subject 
matter of dispute in this case. To my mind, this can legitimately come under 
sections 33 and 33A of the Act. Admittedly, the work was refused to these 
workers. Mr. D’Cruz said that all the workers approached the Management 
for work and those who signed the undertaking and expressed regret for their 
conduct were taken in. Apparently, the petitioners did neither of the kind, 
namely, signed any undertaking or expressed any regret. The Management 
justified its action on two grounds; (1) the service record of these persons are 
not good; (2) they were guilty of gross misconduct for which they merit 


2450 THE CATLUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 [Parr [1 
সিল CE TT a a ERENT ہے‎ 
dismissal. The Management did not show in which way the service records of 
these petitioners are bad, bad to the extent of keeping them permanently awa 
from work. None of them received any warning beforehand nor told in any 
proceeding that they were unfit for further service. Accordingly, this comes بج‎ 
8 surprise to everybody. Therefore, it cannot possibly be argued that these 
workers should not be provided with work because of their past records. ۲ 
appears that the Management issued charge-sheet against them. It is only a 
handful of them that submitted explanations. There was no enquiry aguinst 
the petitioners. 


Question now is whether the materials on record justify their dismissal from 
service for their alleged misconduct on 6th October 1953. I am not repeating 
the evidence that I have discussed in my order disposing of the connected three 
applications under section 33 of the Act. It is enough to point out here that 
the alleged strike of workers on 6th October 1953 is now established. It was 
over the demand of payment of Puja bonus. By itself, this is not an illegal act. 
This demand was followed by a refusal by the Company on the ground of loss, 
Then followed, by all accounts, a very regrettable «und ugly incident. The 
Works Manager, who happened to be in the factory at the time, was surrounded 
by the workers and was wrongfully kept confined there till he was rescued by 
the police. The illegality of this action is so patent that I do not consider it 
necessary to 01509058206 p.int further in this case. I have found the Manage- 
ment’s evidence on this point to be worthy of belief and that adduced on behaff 
of the Union is untrue. 


Question now is whether these petitioners excepting the three, namely, 
Subhash Roy, Madhusudan Rout, and Bimal Kumar Ghose, took any active part 
in this incident. On a scrutiny of the Management’s evidence, I have found 
that there is absolutely no reliable evidence to definitely connect the petitioners, 
excepting the said three, with this incident. On the other hand, there is good 
scope for reasonable doubt regarding the complicity of these persons in this act. 
Accordingly, in my opinion, all these petitioners cannot be dismissed; neither 
it is desirable in the interest of industrial peace that they should be dismissed. 
They will accordingly report themselves to the Company’s factory, for duty 
within 15 (fifteen) days from the date of the operation of this award, when they 
will be taken in and provided with work. The period of their absence, since 
6th October 1953 will be treated, as one on leave without pay. In my Judgment, 
they are not entitled to any other relief. Regarding the said three petitioners, 
the Company has got the Tribunal’s permission to dismiss them from service. 
This application is, therefore, allowed in part.

The closing balance of 1953-54 was Rs. 40,780 and for 1952-53 Rs. 57,037. 
Ext. D. is the notes of Audit of the accounts of the Naihaty Municipality 
for 1952-53. Audit notes for 1953-54 accounts are as _ yet not 
available. It shows that the cash balance of Rs. 57,037-5-3 on 31st March 
1953 was not sufficient to meet the entire liabilities of the municipality, which 
amounted to Rs. 86,920. There is a huge amount of unrealised taxes, which 
on 31st March 1953, amounted to Rs. 2,87,467. At the end of 1953-54, this 
amount appears to be more than Rs. 34 lakh. It appears that out of the 
unrealised balance in 1953-54, a sum of Rs. 2,46,251 was due from the E.I.R., 
the Government, the Hooghly-Chinsurah Municipality and some amounts are 
in dispute with the Mills, and that Rs. 1,22,858 were due from the rate-payers. 
Although the municipality will have its position improved when the dues from 
the Government, the Mills and the Railways are realised, I do not find that these 
amounts will be received in the very near future. 


The financial condition of the municipality, as shown by the Audit Report, 
Ext. D, is not satisfactory. The municipality cannot attain a financial equilt- 
brium until the large dues from the Railways, etc., are realised and the collec- 
tion of rates from rate-payers is improved. The Union submitted the wage 
scales of the employees of the Titaghur Municipality (Ext. 1), Kamarhatty 
Municipality [Ext. 1(a)], and the Baranagore Municipality [(Ext. -1(b)], 
and the dearness allowance paid to the employees by the Garulia 
Municipality (Ext. 2), and the Bhatpara Municipality [Ext. 2(a)]. 


2456 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 [Parr T 


It appears that the basic wage scales of the employees of the Titaghur Muni- 
cipality; Kamarhatty Municipality and the Baranagore Municipality are higher 
than that allowed by the Naihaty. Municipality. The dearness allowance paid 
by the Garulia Municipality, the Baranagore Municipality are also higher than 
that paid to the employees of the Naihaty Municipality. The municipality filed 
the basic wage scales and dearness allowance allowed to the employees by the 
Halisahar Munici ality (Ext. E), which is adjacent to the Naihaty Municipality 
and by the Garulia Municipality [Ext. E(1)], and by the Bhatpara Municipality 
((Ext. E(2)]. The scales of basic wages and dearness allowance of 18811521881 
is not better than those given by the Naihaty Municipality. Although the scale 
of dearness allowance allowed by the Garulia Municipality and the Bhatpara 
Municipality are higher than those granted by the Naihaty Municipality, the 
basic wage scales given by these municipalities are not more favourable than 
those given by the Naihaty Municipality. It is not possible to come to any 
conclusion from the wage charts of other municipalities without an overall picture 
of their financial position. The necessity of complying with a_ theoretical 
definition of “living wage” cannot transcend “financial limitations” (Report of 
the Central Pay Commission, page 32). 


In view of the financial condition of the Naihaty Municipality and also the 
fact that the basic wage scales of the municipality were revised by the Officer- 
in-charge on Ist March 1951, it is awarded that there should be no further 
revision or increase of the basic wage scales of the employees of the municipality 
at the present time. Issue No. 1 is accordingly answered. 


It appears to me that the dearness allowance paid by the municipality for 
the clerical staff receiving the minimum pay is only Rs. 22 and for the sub- 
ordinate staff getting basic wage below Rs. 35 is only Rs. 10. There should be 
an increase in the dearness allowance. It is awarded that for employees 
recciving basic wages below Rs. 35 per month, an additional dearness allowance 
of Rs. 5 shall be paid and for employees receiving basic wages of Rs. 35 per 
month or above, an additional dearness allowance of Rs. 10 shall be paid per 
month. This increase in the dearness allowance will be a substantial addition 
to the emoluments_of the employees and will, to some extent, relieve their 
hardship. I believe, the municipality will not be put to any difficulty for these 
increases in the dearness allowance of the employees. These ‘increases should 
be allowed to all employees who are parties to this proceedings, including the 
teachers. Issue No. 2 is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 3.—Whether the employees are entitled to any house rent allow- 
ance in lieu of free accommodation? 


The Union in its demand No. 5 states as follows:— 


“Some staff are enjoying housing or house rent allowance without any 
specific rate. The Union demands provision of free quarters to all 


employees, or in lieu house rent allowance at 10 per cent. of pay 
with a minimum of Rs. 10 per month for each employee.” 


The munitipality, in its written statement, stated that it could not concede 
to this demand. 


It appears that the Head Clerk and the Sanitary Inspector get free house 
accommodation. The compounder gets a house allowance of Rs. 8 and the 
two mid-wives get a house allowance of Rs. 15 each. No other employee gets 
any house rent or free house accommodation. The house allowance to the 
compounder and the mid-wives are given in view of the strenuous nature of their 
work and the free house accommodation to the Head 01161 and the Sanitary 
Inspector are given for the convenience of the municipality. I do not find any 
justification for this claim for other employces. I have not been shown any 
such practice prevalent in any municipality. This claim is rejected. 


part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 2457 


০ পপ স্পা উন 


Issue No. 4.—Whether a scheme of gratuity for the benefit of the 
employees should be introduced? 


In demand No. 7, the Union states as follows:— 


“On retirement or termination of service or on death of the employee, the 
gratuity money shall be paid ordinarily within three months at the 


latest to the person, or to his nominee, or legal heirs of the deceased 
in case of death.” 


The municipality, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


“The municipality introduced the scheme of provident fund about 50 years 
ago whereby the municipality contributes 64 per cent. Under the 
ছি financial position of the municipality, it cannot grant a 
urther contribution in the shape of gratuity, as demanded.” 


It appears from the statement of the Chairman of the municipality that the 
municipality has adopted a scheme of gratuity or additional contribution 
according to a scheme made by the Local Self-Government Department of the 
Government of West Bengal. The adoption of this scheme of additional con- 
tribution or gratuity by the Naihaty Municipality was approved by the Govern- 
ment. According to this scheme, the Commissioners may, on the recommen- 
dation of the Chairman, grant from the revenues at the time of retirement, to 
any servant who has subscribed to the Provident Fund and has rendered con- 
tinuous good service for not less than 15 years, an additional contribution at 
the rate of half a month’s pay for each completed year of service rendered by 
such servant, subject to a maximum of 15 months’ pay. The amount of con- 
tribution shall be calculated on the pay drawn by him at the time of retirement. 
Thcre is a condition that this payment is to be made if the funds of the muni- 
cipality so permits. In any case, I consider that the municipality should make 
this additional contribution to its servants on the terms as mentioned above at 
the time of\ their retirement. The municipality should be able to find the 
necessary fund for such payment and payment should not be refused on the 
ground of p یا‎ of funds. As the municipality has adopted this scheme, it 
js only proper that no objection should be raised against this retiral benefit, 
which is absolutely necessary in the interest of the retiring employees. This 
issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 5.—What should be the number of holidays that the members 
of the staff will enjoy in a year? Should any employee not allowed to 
enjoy a holiday be paid extra wages for work done on a holiday? 


In demand No. 11, the Union states as follows:— 


“Holidays as sanctioned by the West Bengal State Government as also 
other local holidays shall be allowed to all staffs. If the employee 
is required to work on such holidays, he shall be given over-time 
remuneration at the rate as mentioned in item No. 9 above.” 


The municipality in its written statement states that the demand is not 
understood and wanted a clarification on the point. 


At the time of the argument, the first part of the issue, i.e., what should be 
the number of holidays that the members of the staff will enjoy in a year was 
not pressed, as the municipal employees were enjoying all holidays as sanctioned 
by the Government for its employees. 


The Union pressed the second part of issue, where it 1s claimed that. an 
employee who was not allowed to enjoy a holiday should be paid extra wages 
for work done on holidays. The learned spokesman for the Union argued 
that there is set of workers who work without any holidays throughout the 
year. They are the Valve Inspector, Sanitary Inspector, Assistant Sanitary 


2458 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 [Parr ] 


Inspector, Water Works Inspector, Labour Supervisor and Motor Mechanics 
From the very nature of the work done by these employees, the work must be 
performed from day to day without any break. As for example, a conser- 
vancy mazdoor is one of such class of employees maintained by the municipality 
The conservancy mazdoor is not, however, involved in this proceeding. 7 the 
municipality is to give permission to the employees as mentioned above, or to 
a conservancy mazdoor to enjoy holidays, it will be required to employ addi- 
tional hands on holidays and this will entail a great extra cost, which from the 
financial condition of the municipality, it is not possible to impose upon it at 
the present time. Nor is it proper that the municipality should pay any extra 
wages to these categories of employees for work done by them on holidays. 
Such holidays do not exist for these employees, in view of the peculiar nature 
of the work done. Such a claim was also made before the learned Tribunal 
adjudicating on the dispute between the Calcutta Corporation and its employees 
in July 1948, as well as in May 1950, and the claim was rejected by both the 
Tribunals. I do not consider that these out-door employees should be given 
any holidays or paid any extra wages for work done on holidays. This issue 
is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 6.——What should be the period of probation? 

The Union claims that the probationary period of an employee shall not 
exceed six months in any case. The municipality states that it generally con- 
firms an employee appointed in a permanent vacancy ,after the completion of a 
ইলা period of one year. I do not consider that this rule requires any 
alteration. 


Issue No. 7.—What should be the rules of Provident Fund? 


In demand No. 14, the Union states that the Provident Fund should be 
extended to all employees in permanent service. The rate of municipal contri- 
bution towards an employee’s Provident Fund shall not be less than 8 1/3 per 
cent. of his salary, the employee being required to subscribe an equal amount. 
On retirement or termination of service or on death of an employee, the Pro- 
vident Fund money shall ordinarily be paid in full within three months at the 
latest to the person-concerned or to the nominee or legal heirs of the deccased 
in case of death. 


The municipality in its written statement states that the Provident Fund 
introduced by the municipality is based upon the Model Rules for the Manage- 
ment of the Provident Fund of the Municipalities and District Boards. The 
Union’s demand in this respect is, therefore, not understood. It appears, 
however, from the Union’s statement that they asked for increase in the 
employee’s contribution from 6+ per cent. to 8 1/3 per cent. This is a matter 
outside the scope of the order of reference. The municipality cannot concede 
to the demand made by the Union. The claim that contribution to the Pro- 
vident Fund should be increased from 64 per cent. to 8 1/3 per cent. on either 
side and that peons and durwans should be allowed to contribute to the Pro- 
vident Fund is not allowed, in view of the financial condition of the municipality. 
The superior-staff are enjoying Provident Fund for the last 50 years. The 
learned Chairman for the municipality informs me that payment to the Pro- 
vident Fund is made with the utmost despatch. No instance of avoidable 
delay in the payment of Provident Fund to the employees has been mentioned 
before me by the Union. It is awarded that payment of the Provident Fund 
to the employees should be made without any avoidable delay. This issue 13 


accordingly awarded. 
M. C. BANERII, 


Judge, 
First Industrial Tribunal.

PART VI.—Bills introduced in Parliament of India; Reports of Select 
Committees presented to Parliament; and Bills published before

COUNCIL OF STATES. 


The following Bill was introduced in the Council of States on the 6th 
Muy, 1954: 


Birt No. XI or 1954. 
A Mill further to amend thé Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of our Republic as 
follows: 


1. Short title and commencement.—(/) This Act may be called the 
Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1954. 


(2) It shall be deemed to have come into force on the Ist day of April, 
1984. 


2. Amendment of section 25A, Act XIV of 1947.—In sub-section (2) of 
section 256A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (hereinafter referred to as 
the principal Act), for the Haplunation, the following Ezplanation shall be 
substituted, numely سے‎ 


“Keplanation.—In this section and in sections 260, 25D and 25k, 
‘industrial establishment’ means— 


(1) & factory as defined in clause (72) of section 2 of the Factories 


Act, 1948 (XIII of 1948); or 


(2৮) a mine as defined in clause (7) of section 2 of the Mines Act, 
1952 (XXXV of 1952); or 


(iit) a plantation as defined in clause (f) of section 2 of the Plantations 
Labour Act, 1861 (T.XIX of 1951).” 


3, Amendment of section 259 Act X!V of 1947.—In the proviso to sub- 
section (J) of section 257 of the*principal Act, after the words “which a 
workman has under”, the words, figures and brackets “the Minimum ‘Wages 
Act, 1948 (XI of 1948) or any notification or order issued thereunder or’’ 
shall be inserted. 


82 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 [Part VI 
اہ تھی وی سد‎ eA gee کت‎ 
STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1953, provides for payment 
of lay-off compensation to workers in factories covered by the Factories Act, 
1948, and in mines coming under the Mines Act, 1952. Workers in planta. 
tions have, however, not been included in the Act. In view of the insistent 
demand of plantation workers, the question of extending the provisions 
relating to lay-off benefits to them was placed before the Meeting of the 
Industrial Committee on Plantations held at Calcutta in January, 1964, 
The Committee recommended that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes 
(Amendment) Act, 1953, relating to lay-off should be applied to the planta. 
tion industry with effect from the lat April, 1954, subject to the condition 
that none of the provisions of the Act derogated from the effect of any 
statutory notifications issued by Governments or of any agrezments or con- 
tracts entered into between the parties requiring the provision by employers 
of a minimum number of days of work or wages or compensation to workers. 
The Bill is intended to give statutory effect to the above recommendation, 


V. V. GIRT. 
New DEtui; 


The 28th April, 1954.

with the Statement of Objects and Reasons relating thereto, and the Bill 
and the Statement of Objects and Reasons are accordingly published for 
general information :—

A Bill to amend and codify the law relating to intestate succession among 
Hindus. 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of the Republic of India

CHAPTER I. 
PRELIMINARY. 


1. Short title and extent.—(7) This Act may be called the 1 10 
Succession Act, 4. 


(2) It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and 
Kashmir, ‘and applies ulso to Hindus domiciled in the territories to which 
this Act axtends who are outside the said territories. 


2. Application of Act.—(1) This Act applies— 


(a) to any person who is a Hindu by religion in any of its forms or 
developments, including a ‘Virashaiva, a Lingayat or a follower 
of the Brahmo, Prarthana or Arya Samaj, 

(b) to any person who is a Buddhist, Jaina or Sikh by religion, and 

(c) to any other person domiciled in India who 1s not a Muslim, 
Christian, Parsi or Jew by religion, unless it is proved’ that 
any such person would not have been governed by the Hindu 
law or by any custom or usage as part of that law in respect of 
any of the matters dealt with herein if this Act had not been 
passed. 


Explanation.—The following persons are Hindus by religion within 
the meaning of this Act,— 


(a) any illegitimate child both of whose parents are Hindus, 


(b) uny child, legitimate or illegitimate, one of whose parents is a 
Hindu and who is brought up as a member of the tribe, 
tommunity, group or family to which such parent belongs or 
belonged, and 

(c) any person who is a convert or re-convert to the Hindu religjon. 


(2) The expression ‘Hindu’ in any portion of this Act shall be construed 
as if it included a person who, though not a Hindu by religion, is, 
nevertheless, a person to whom this Act applies by virtue of the provisions 
contained in sub-section (2).

3. Definitions and interpretation.—(7) In this Act, unless the dontext 
otherwise requires,— 


{a) ‘agnate’—one person is said دا‎ be au ‘agnate’ (gotraja) of another 
if ne two are related by blood or adoption wholly through 
males; 


(b) “cognate’—one person is said to be a ‘cognate’ (bandhu) of another 
11 the two are related by ৮19০৭ or adoption but not wholly 
through males; 


(c) ‘full blood’, ‘half blood’ and ‘uterine blood’— 


(£) two persons are said to be related to each other by full blood 
when they are descended from a common ancestor by the sume 
wife, and by half blood when they are descended from a 
common ancestor but by different wives. 


(2) two persons are said to be related to each other by uterine blood 
when they are descended from a common ancestress but by 
different husbands; 


Eaplanation.—In this clause ‘uncestor’ ‘includes the father and 
‘ancestress’ the mother; 


(d) ‘heir’ means any person, mule or female, who is entitled to suceved 
to the property of an intestate under this Act; 


(6) ‘intestate’—a person is deemed to die intestate in respect of property 
of which he or she bas not made a_ testamentary disposition 
capable of taking effect; 


(f) ‘related’ means related by legitimaate kinship: 


Provided that illegitimate children shall be deemed to be related to 
their mother and to one another, and their Jegitimate descendants 
shall be deemed to be related to them and to one another; and 
any word expressing relationship or denoting a relative, shall 
be construed accordingly ; 


(g) ‘son’ includes a son adopted in accordance with the law for the 
time being in force relating to adoption among Hindus. 


(2) In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, words importing 
the masculine gender shall not be taken to include females. 


(3) For the purposes of this Act, the domicile of a Hindu shall be 
determined in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 6 to 18 
inclusive of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 (XXXIX of 1925). 


4. Over-riding effect of Act.—Save as otherwise expressly provided 
in this Act,— 


(a) any text, rule or interpretation of Hindu law or any custom or 
usage as part of that law in force immediately before the 
commencement of this Act shall cease to have effect with respect 
to any matter for which provision is made in this Act; 


(b) any other law in force immediately before the commencement of 
this Act shall cease te apply to Hindus in so far aa it tb 
inconsistent with any of the provisions contained in thig Act.

33. Full blood preferred to half blood.—Heirs reluted to an intestate 
by full blood shall be preferred to heirs related by half blood, if the nature 
of the relationship is the same in every other respect.

(a) suve as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, per camta and

35. Right of child in womb.—A person who was in the womb at the 
time of the death of an intestate and who is subsequently born alive shall 
have the same right to inherit to the intestate as if he or she had been born 
before the death of the intestate; and the inheritance shall be deemed to vest 
in such a case with effect from the date of the death of the intestate. 


36. Presumption of survivorship.—Where two persons have died in 
circumstances rendering it uncertain whether either of them, and if ৪0 
which, survived the other, then, for all purposes affecting succession to 
property, it shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the 
younger survived the elder.

(b) devolves upon a female heir, together with any of the male relatives 
specified in class I of the Schedule, and any one of such male 
relatives compels the female heir to take her share of the property 
of the intestate for separate enjoyment (which he is hereby 
empowered to do), 

the provisions of the Partition Act, 1893 (IV of 1893) shall apply as if there 
was a partition and as if he or she were the transferee of a share of a dwelling- 
house and the Thtestate’s family were an undivided one. 


Disqualification of heirs. 


38. Hermit, etc., disqualified.—A person who has completely and 
finally renounced the world in any of the modes set forth in sub-section (1) 
of section 32 shall be disqualified from inheriting the property of any of his 
relatives by blood marriage or adoption. 


39. Unchaste wife disqualified.—A woman, who after marriage, has 
been unchaste during her husband’s lifetime, shall, unless he has condoned 
the unchastity, be disqualified from inheriting his property:

ProvMled that the right of a woman to inherit to her husband shall not 
be questioned on the above ground, unless a Court of law has found her to 
have been unchaste as aforesnid in a proceeding to which she and_ her 
husband were parties and in which the matter was specifically in issue, the 
finding of the Court not having been subsequently reversed. 


40. Disqualification of centain widows remarrying.—The widow of a 
pre-decensed son, the widow of a pre-deceased son of a pre-deceused son, the 
father’s widuw and the brother’s widow shal] not be entitled to succeed as 
heirs, 1f on the date the succession opens, they have remarried. 


41. Murderer disqualified.—A person who commits murder or abeta 
the commission of murder shall be disqualified from inheriting the property 
of the person murdered, or any other property in furtherance of the 
00 to which he or she committed or abetted the commission of the 
murder. 


42. Convert’s descendants disqualified.—Where, before or after the 
commencement of this Act, a Hindu has ceased or ceases to be one by con- 
version to another religion, children born to him or her after such con- 
version und their descendanta shall be disqualified from inheriting the 
property of any of their Hindu relatives, unless such children or descendants 
are Hindus at the time when the succession opens. 


43. Succession when heir disqualified.—If any person is disqualified 
from inheriting any property under this Act, it shall devolve as if such 
person had died before the intestate. 


44. Disease, defect, etc., not to disqualify.—No person shall be 
disqualified from succeeding to any property_on the ground of any disease, 
defect or deformity, or save as provided in this Act, on any other ground 
whatsoever. 


Escheat. 


45. Failure of heirs.—If an intestate has left no heir qualified to 
succeed to his or her property in accordance with the provisions of this 
Act, such property shall go to the Government; and the Government shall 
take the property subject to 81] the obligations and liabilities to which an 
heir would have been subject. 


CHAPTER ITI. 
TESTAMENTARY SUCCESSION. 

48. Testamentary succession.—Any Windu may dispose of by will or 
other testamentary disposition any property, which is capable of being so 
disposed of by him, in accordance with the provisions of the Indian 
Succession Act, 1925 (XX XIX of 1925), or any other law for the time being 
in force and applicable to Hindus.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


This, the third instalment of the Hindu Code, seeks to amend and codify 
the law relating to intestate succession. The original draft of the provisions 
relating to intestate succession contuined in the Rau Committee’s Bill 
underwent substantial changes in the hands of the Select Committee which 
considered the Rau Committee’s Bill in 1948. This Bill follows to a large 
extent the scheme adopted by the Select Committee but takes into account 
the various suggestions made from time to time for the amendment of the 
Select Committee’s version of the Bill. In particular, special provisions 
have been included for regulating succession to the property of intestates 
governed by the Marumakkattayam, Aliyasantana or Nambudri laws 01 
inheritance. 


The notes on clauses explain in detail the various provisions in the Bill.

The 20th May, 1954.

Clauses 11 to 14.—-With respect to the other heirs, the scheme of this Bill 
follows the scheme of the Select Committee on the Hindu Code which found 
the Rau Committee’s enumerated heirs defective because the list of heirs was 
too large and no limit was set to the agnates or coynates entitled to succeed. 
That Select Committee also found the order of preference not satisfactory and 
did not like uniformity in succession to be broken in any case. Apart from 
the changes made in clause 10 and the Schedule, the present Bill follows the 
scheme of the Select Committee, the heirs being rearranged on vo more rational 
basis and relatives who are far removed from the intestate and persons who 
are not heirs at all, like Acharya and Sishya, being eliminated from the list 
of heirg. Further, certain persons have been grouped together for simul- 
taneous succession, like father and mother, brother and sister und so on. ‘The 
number of possible heirs of agnates and cognates is also narrowed down.

Clauses 16 to 25,—These clauses lay down special rules of succession in 
the case of male Hindus governed by the Marumakkhattayam, Aliyasantana or 
Nambudri laws of inheritance. <A departure has necessarily to be made in 
these cases because the laws applicable to these persous have always been based 
on the matriarchate while the laws in the rest of India are founded upon the 
agnatic family. These clauses ure based on a draft furnished by the Govern- 
ment of Madras. 


Clause 26.—The Rau Committee vested a Hindu woman with full rights 
over stridhana property and laid down certain rules of succession with respect 
to stridhana. The Select Committee on the Hindu Code incorporated the 
substance of al] these provisions in a separate Chapter headed ‘‘Woman’s 
Property’’ and provided that after the commencement of the Code, whatever 
property was acquired by a woman became her absolute property and devolved 
on her own heirs. Clause 26 follows the Select Committee’s draft and declares 
that whatever property is acquired by a Hindu woman after this law, it shall 
be her absolute property, and the term ‘‘property’’ مز‎ defined as comprehen- 
sively as possible for the purpose. 


Clauses 27 and 28.—Under the existing law, succession to stridhana 
property varies according as a woman is married or unmarried and according 
as she is married in an approved form or in an unapproved form. It also 
varies according to the source from which the stridhana came. The rules 
of descent again vary from school to school. Clause 27, however, evolves a 
new and uniform scheme of succession to a woman’s property and clause 28 
regulates the manner of distribution thereof. 


Clause 29.—This clause contains a saving with respect to properties in 
which a female Hindu has at the commencement of this law only a limited 
estate. 


Clauses 30 and 31.—See the notes to clauses 16 to 25. 


Clause 32.—Under the existing law, where a person enters into a 
religious order renouncing all worldly affairs, his action is tantamount to 
civil death and it excludes him altogether from inheritance. But if he 
acquires property subsequent to the renunciation, it passes to his spiritual 
heirs. This clause is in accordance with the existing law. 


Clause 33.—The illustrations given below explain the scheme of this 
clause. 


Illustrations. 


(i) A brother by full blood is preferred to a brother by half blood; but 
a brother by half blood succeeds before a brother’s son by full 
blood, a brother being a nenrer heir than a brother’s son. 


(%) A paternal uncle by half blood ia preferred to a Paternal uncle’s son 
by full blood, an uncle being a nearer heir than on uncle’s son. 


100 THK CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 22, 1954 [Part V1 


(৮) A full brother’s danghter’s daughter is preferred to a half brother’s 
daughter’s daughter but the former is not preferred to a_ half

virtue of rule 4 in section 14 is preferred although he is only

Clauses 34, 35 and 36.—These clauses are self-explanatory and are in 
accordance with the existing law. 


Clause 37.—Where any immovable property or any business devolves 
upon male and female heirs, this clause would enable the male heirs, if they 
so desire, to compulsorily buy off the share of the female heirs. 


Clause 38.—See the notes to clause 32. 


Clause 39.—Under the existing law, chastity during the life time of 
the husband is a condition precedent to the taking by the widow of her 
husband’s estate unless the unchastity hod been condoned by him. 


Clause 40.—The principle underlying this clause is that the widow is the 
surviving half of her husband and, therefore, when she remarries, she 
ceases to continue to be such. (Section 2 of the Hindu Widows Remarriage 
Act, 1856, also contains a somewhat similar provision.) As the law stands, 
remarriage disables a widow of a gotraja sapinda froin succeeding to the 
property of a male Hindu when on the date the succession opens; she has 
ceased to he the widow of a gotraja sapinda by reason of remarriage. This 
rule is being applied to the widows mentioned in the Schedule who ure the 
only widows now entitled to succeed. 


Clause 47,—A murderer even if not disqualified under Hindu law from 
succeeding to the estate of the person whom he has murdered is so dis- 
qualified upon principles of justice, equity and good conscience. The 
murderer is not to be regarded as the stock for a fresh line of descent but 
should be regarded as non-existent when the succession opens (51 T.A. 368). 


Clause 42.—Change of religion and loss of caste, which at one time were 
grounds of forfeiture of property and of exclusion from inheritance, have 
ceased to be so since the passing of the Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850. 
But that Act applies only to protect the actual person who either renounces 
his religion or has been excommunicated. Consequently, where the 
property of a Muslim converted from Hinduism hns pnssed according ٥٥ 
Muslim law to his descendants, Hindu collaterals cannot claim by virtue 
of fhat Act to succeed under Hindu law. This clause, therefore, lays down 
that the heir should be a Hindu when the succession opens. Reconversion 
after the succession opens will not, therefore, be possible and this restriction 
will in most cases remove any abuse of the provision contained in the clause. 


Clause 44.—Under the Hindu law, blindness, deafness, dumbness, want 
of any limb or organ, lunacy, idioey, leprosy and other incurable diseases 
disqualified a person from inheriting but the Hindu Inheritance (Removal 
of Disabilities) Act, 1928, declared that no person shall be excluded from 
inheritance on any of these grounds unless he was from birth a lunatic or 
an idiot. This clause seeks to remove all such disqualifications. 


Clause 45.—Hscheat as such 10৮7 not been unknown to Hindu law. 


_ Clause 46.—This clause confirms the existing law that a Hindu may 
dispose of by testamentary disposition any property which he is capable of 


so disposing of,

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Recruitment to the urban units of the Territorial Army has not so far 
been satisfactory, especially in the technical units. The Bill seeks to 
impose compulsory liability for enrolment in the Territorial Army for 
certain categories of employees, namely, Government servants and em- 
ployees of specified public utility concerns in selected age groups. It is 
proposed to utilize this lability to fill up deficiencies in the authorised 
atrength of the Territorial Army units. The Bill, if enacted, will also 
fucilitate expansion of the Territorial Army in an emergency. [Public 
utility concerns have been included in the compulsory enrolment scheme 
in order, to ensure that essential services continue to function in an 
emergency. 


The Hill seeks to provide the necessary legal basis for calling for parti- 
culars revarding age, calling up for inquiry and medical examination, of 
persons liable to be enrolled under the scheme, the registration and calling 
‘up of the persons considered fit for service in the Territorial Army and 
other ullied matters. 


MAHAVIR TYAGI. 


New DELHI; 
The 13th May, 194. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM. 


The scheme for the liability to compulsory enrolment of Government 
servants and certain categories of employees of public utility concerns 
involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India. The scheme 
ig ut present intended to enable Government to fill up “deficiencies in the 
authorised strengths of certain Territorial Army Units. The expenditure 
on the pay and allowances of the enrolled personnel and requirement of 
training officers, etc. will be the sume as for the normal authorised strength 
of Territorial Army Units. A small amount of expenditure may have to 
be incurred on the registration of personnel covered by the scheme for 
compulsory enrolment and on the administrative arrangements for their 


281] up, where necessary.

EXPLANATORY NOTES. 


The Territorial Army was constituted under the Territorial Army Act, 
1948 und commenced raising in 1949. When fully formed, it will be 
composed of combatant technical and administrative units. The personnel 
of the Territoriul Army are given periodical military truining. During the 
training period and when embodied for service, they are entitled to pay, 
allowances, etc., al the same rates us for corresponding ranks of the 
regular Indian Forces. 


MEMORANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION. 


The Bill which seeks to amend the Territorial Army Act, 1948, imposes 
a liability on all persons employed under the Government or in a public 
utility service, who have attained the age of twenty years but have not 
রা the age of forty years for compulsory military service. Having 
imposed a potential linbility for compulsory military service on all such 
persons, the Bill leaves most of the matters relating to administrative 
details for giving effect to the scheme, from the stage of requisitioning the 
services of such persons to the stage of their being actually called out for 
service in the Territorial Army, to be prescribed by subordinate 19618180101 
by the Central Government. For the successful implementation of the 
scheme, the powers to determine the circumstances under which the ser- 
vices of such persons should be requisitioned for the purpose of performs 
ing service in the Territorial Army, and the authorities by which the ser- 
vices of such persons should be requisitioned, to prescribe the standards 
of physical fitness and other qualifications of such persons, to prescribe 
forms for obtaining particulars from such persons, to lay down the proce- 
dure to be followed in holding medical and other examinations, etc., have 
been delegated to the Central Government to be prescribed by means of 
subordinate legislation, as it is not practicable for Parliament to lay down 
such details in- the Bill. Some of the powers delegated to the Central 
Government such as the power to determine the circumstances under which 
the services of persénus liable for compulsory military service in the Terri- 
torial Army should be requisitioned, etc., which may not appear prima 
fucte to be normal in character are really so if one has regurd to the fuct 
that in enactments relating to the Army, the Navy and the Air Force, 
it is not possible for Parliament to 7 down matters relating to such 
administrative details in the law itself. The proposed delegations are, 
therefore, normal. 


M. N. KAUL, Secy.

PART I—Orders and Notifications by the Governor of West Bengal, the 
High Court, Government Treasury, etc. 


GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
IRRIGATION AND WATERWAYS DEPARTMENT, 
NOTIFICATIONS. 


No. 7-1.—l7th July 1954.—In exercise of the power conferred by 
clause (5) of section 2 of the Bengal Development Act, 1985 (Bengal Act XVI 
of 1935), the Gtovernor is pleased hereby to declare the work of improve- 
ment constructed by the State Government, forming part of the Mayurakshi 
Reservoir Project, including the Bakreswar Canal and described in the 
schedule below to be an improvement work for the purposes of the said

No. 8-I.—17th July 1954.—Whereas, in the opinion of the Governor, 
the improvement work specified in the notification No. 7-I., duted 17th July 
1954, the full description and the object whereof are stated in Parts I and 1 
respectively of the schedule below, has increased and is likely to increase 
the profits from the produce from the agricultural lands, or to increase the 
outturn of such produce, within the area included within the boundaries 
specified in Part III of the said schedule; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred by section 3, read with 
section 4 and sub-section (1) of section 5 of the Bengal Development 
Act, 1935 (Bengal Act XVI of 1935), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
declare his intention to impose an improvement levy within the said area 
and to mention the period of fourteen days from the date of publication of 
this notification in the Calcutta Gazette to be the period for the submission 
of objections referred to in sub-section (1) of section 5 of the said Act.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
MEDICAL AND PUBLIC HEALTH DEPARTMENT 
Medical 
NOTIFICATION, 


No. Medl./5292/5M-10/54.—17th July 1954.—In_ exercise of the power 
comferred by section 33 of the Bengal Medical Act, 1914 (Bengal Act VI of 
1914), and in supersession of the rules and forms published with notification 
No. 2905Medl., dated the 6th July 1935, as subsequently amended, the Governor 
is pleased to make the following rules namely:— 


RULES. 
PART I. 
Definitions, 


1. An these rules, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or con- 
text— 

(a) “Council” means the West Bengal Medical Council. 

(b) “Form” means a form in the appendix to these rules. 

(c) “Member” means a member of the West Bengal Medical Council. 

(d) “President” means the President of the West Bengal Medical Council. 

(e) “Registrar” means the Registrar appointed under section. 14. 

) “Returning Officer” means the Registrar and includes any officer 
deputed for the time being by the Registrar to perform, or assist 
him in, his duties under these rules. 

(g) “Registered practitioner” means a person borne on the register main- 
tained by the Council under section 15: and “Registration number” 
means the serial number in the register, maintained by the Council 
under section 15 of the registered practitioners. 

(h) “Rule” means a rule of these rules. 

(i) “Section” means a section of the Act. 

(j) The expression “the Act” means the Bengal Mcdical Act, 1914. 


PART II. 


Appointment of members by nomination of the State Government. 
[Clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 4.] 

2. (1) At least sixty days before the expiry of the term of office of any 
nominated member, the Registrar shall draw the attention of the President to 
the approaching vacancy, and the latter shall forthwith report it to the State 
Government for necessary action to fill the vacancy.

(2) In the case of a casual vacancy for which a fresh nomination will be 
necessary under clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 10, the Registrar shall 
on receiving information that such a vacancy has occurred report the vacancy 
to the Presidemt forthwith and the President shall intimdte the same to the State 
Government, for necessary action for a fresh nomination. 


PART II. 


Election of members under clause (b) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) of 
section 4 


3. (1) In case of a general election, the Registrar shall, at least sixty days 
before the expiry of the term of office of the Council, request the Registrar of 
the University of Calcutta and the Secretary of the State Medical Faculty of 
West Bengal, as the case may be, to arrange for election of members under 
clause (b) or clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 4, in such manner as the 
Faculty of Medicine of the University of Calcutta or the Governing Body of the 
State Medical Faculty, as the case may be, consider convenient, so as to complete 
the clections in ample time before the end of the term of office of the Council. 


(2) When the elections have been completed the names of the persons 
elected with their addresses, qualifications and registration numbers, shall be 
forthwith reported to the President by the Registrar of the University of Cal- 
cutta in case the election is under clause (b), of sub-section (i) of section 4 
and by the Secretary of the State Medical Faculty in case the election is under 
clause (c) of the said sub-section: and the President shall report the same to 
the State Government for publication of the names in the Calcutta Gazette 
under section 7. 

PART IV 


General election under clauses (d) and (e) of section 4(1). 
The electoral roll. 


4. (1) For the purposes of a gencral election under clauses (d) and 
(e) of sub-section (1) of section 4, the Returning Officer shall cause to be 
prepared a draft electoral roll separately for each of the two 61600019164 under

The electoral roll under clause (d) shall be in form I: and the electoral roll 
under clause (e) shall be in the form of the Medical List, prepared under sub

(2) The date appointed under sub-rule (1) shall be notified by the Return-

(3) The draft electoral roll shall be kept open in the office of the Return- 
ing Officer for public inspection for a period of not less than fifteen days. Any 
claim for inclusion of a new name or any objection to any entry in the draft 
electoral roll shall be made in form II(a) or form 1100) or form II(c), as the 
case may be. Such claim or objection shall be filed within the said period wah 
shall be examined and decided by the Returning Officer and his decision sha 
be final. - 

(4) The draft electoral roll shall be corrected in accordance with the 
decision of the Returning Officer and the roll thus corrected shall be the final 
electoral roll for the election. In the preparation of the final electoral roll, 
registrations and restorations after the date appointed under sub-rule (1) or 
new qualifications or employment obtained after that date shall be disregarded. 
No person whose name is not included in the final electoral roll for the election 
shall be entitled to participate in the election. Changes of address after the 
final electoral roll has been prepared shall be disregarded.

(6) An elector, whose name is borne on the final electoral roll and who is

papers, shall be invalid. 


(8) After recording his vote or votes on the voting paper, the elector shall

by the elector or sent singly by post, to the Returning Officer. 


(9) Only one voting paper shall be enclosed in one identification envelope: 
and if two or more voting papers are enclosed in the same _ identification 
envelope, the identification envelope and the voting papers therein, shall be 
rejected.

fication envelope supplied with it, and any defect, e.g., incompleteness in the 
entries required on the identification envelope, or its receipt after the latest day 
and time notified under clause (d) of sub-rule (5) of rule 4 for its receipt with 
the proper voting paper, shall invalidate both the envelope and the voting 
paper enclosed.

thereon in which respect it does not fulfil these requirements. and make a 
separate bundle of the rejected envelopes in each batch and deal with them 
under sub-rules (3) to (5) of rule 7.

Scrutiny and counting of votes. 


7. (1) The Returning Officer shall attend for the purpose of scrutiny and 
counting of votes on the date and at the time and place notified under clause 
(6) of sub-rule (5) of rule 4: and on any such subsequent date, or dates as 
may be necessary to complete the scrutiny and counting. 


(2) A candidate may be present in person or may send a representative, 
duly authorised by him in writing, to watch the process of scrutiny and counting. 


(3) The Returning Officer shall show all identification envelopes, whether 
accepted or rejected, to the candidates or their representatives for examination 
of the propriety of their acceptance or rejection. Any objection taken to his 
decision of acceptance or rejection of any identification envelope shall be decided 
at once by the Returning Officer, and his decision shall be final. 


(4) The rejected identification envelope shall be placed in separate bundles 
for the two electorates, namely the electorate under clause (d) of sub-section 
(1) of section 4 and the electorate under clause (e) of that sub-section. The 
bundles shall then be sealed and kept in safe custody under rule 9. 


(5) The accepted identification envelopes shall be opened in the presence 
of the candidates or their representatives appearing under sub-rule (2), and the 
voting papers separated from the covers which will be kept aside from view. 


(6) As the voting papers are separated from the envelopes, the Returning 
Officer will proceed to examine the voting papers in convenient batches, to see 
whether the votes have been recorded in accordance with sub-rules (6) to (10) 
of rule 6. He shall record his decision “rejected” on every voting paper which 
is found to be defective in any respect and which he rejects, and indicate there- 
on, the ground of rejection very briefly. The remaining voting papers shall 
be deemed as accepted. 


(7) If any objection is taken to his decision of acceptance or rejection of 
any voting paper, such objection shall be decided by the Returning Officer at 
once and his decision shall be final. 

(8) The Returning Officer shall separate or cause to be separated the 
accepted papers from those that have been rejected and keep them in separate 
bundles. 

Declaration of the names of candidates selected.

with declare the first two candidates in the case of an election under clause (d) 
of sub-section (1) of section 4 to whom the largest number of valid votes have 
been given to be elccted. 

In the case of an election under clause (e) of sub-section (1) of section 4, 
if the poll has been taken for the election of five members under clause (a) of 
sub-rule (2) of rule 6, the Returning Officer shall declare the first five candi- 
dates to whom the largest number of valid votes have been given, to be elected 
subject similarly to the operation of sub-section (2) of section 4(vide rule 
10) and to the provision of sub-rule (2) of this rule; 

and if the poll has been taken for the election of nine members under 
clause (b) of sub-rule (2) of rule 6, he shall first separate the names of the 
candidates who are Graduates or Licentiates of the University of Calcutta, and

Disposal of election papers. 

9, On the completion of the election proceedings, the Returning Officer 
shall make into convenient bundles the nomination papers, the voting papers 
and the identification envelopes, seal each bundles, and make over these and 
all other papers, relating to the elections, to the Registrar, who will keep them 
in safe custody in his office till the next general election. 


Reporting to Government about information of choice under sub-section (2) 
of section 4, and the consequent vacancies. 


10. (1) If a person is a member elected under more than one of the 
clauses of sub-section (1) of section 4, the period within which he is required 
by sub-section (2) of that section, to inform the Registrar under which of the 
clauses he desires to be treated as elected, shall be upto 5 p.m. of the third day 
after the completion of all the elections under sub-rule (1) of rule 3 and sub- 
rules (1) and (2) of rule 8. If this third day be a holiday, the next working 
day shall be deemed to be the third day for the purpose. A choice once made 
by the candidate shall be final, and he shall not be permitted to withdraw or 
modify it later: and when he has not informed the Registrar of his choice 
before 5 p.m. of the date laid down above, he shall not be permitted to do so 
after that time. 

(2) On the expiry of the period mentioned in the foregoing sub-rule, the 
Registrar shall report to the President whether the person has informed him of 
his choice or not within the period, and the President shall forward the same to 
the State Government for taking the same into consideration, when notifying in 
the Calcutta Gazette under rule 11, the names of the candidates who are to be 
deemed as finally elected and nominated under the several clauses of sub- 
section (1) of section 4 


(3) When forwarding the Registrar’s report to the State Government, the 
President shall state what vacancies occur by the operation of sub-section (2) 
of section 4, and obtain the orders of the State Government, for taking action 
for filling up these vacancies in accordance with the provisions of Parts V and 
VI of these rules.

Publication of the names of members elected or nominated. 


11. The names of the members elected or nominated to fill the several 
seats under clauses (a) to (e) of sub-section (1) of section 4, excepting the 
seats that become vacant by the operation of sub-section (2) of section 4, shall

Similar notification shall be issued later in respect of the seats becoming

Finality of the decision of the State Government. 


12. (1) The State Government may, of its own motion or on objection 
made within three months from the date of the election, declare any election to 
the Council to be void on account of corrupt practice (e.g., bribery, undue 
influence, personation, publication of false statement) or any other sufficient 
cause, and may call on the electorate affected to make a fresh election within 
a pens date, and any decision of the State Government under this rule shall 
be final. 


(2) The decision of the State Government on any question that may arise 
as to the intention, construction or application of these rules, shall be final. 


Miscellaneous. 


13. If a registered practitioner having been elected or nominated as a 
member,, is found guilty of infamous conduct in any professional respect and 
his name is removed from the Register of registered practitioners, the Council 
shall declare his seat to be vacant. 


The President shall report the fact to the State Government and 076 
vacancy shall be filled in the manner laid down in Parts V and VI of these rules. 


14. A register shall be maintained in form VI showing the names of the 
members, elected or nominated constituting the Council on a general election 
under these rules and also subsequent changes till the next general election. 


PART V. 


Filling up of casual vacancies amongst members elected under clause (b), (c) or 
(d) of section 4(1). 

15. (1) When the office of a member elected under clause (b) or clause 
(c) of sub-section (1) of section 4 becomes vacant by his resignation or death 
or under sub-section (2) of section 4 or sub-section (1) of section 9, the 
Registrar shall forthwith report the vacancy to the President and under his 
orders thereon request the Registrar of the University of Calcutta or the Secre- 
tary of the State Medical Faculty of West Bengal, as the case may be, to elect 
a member in the vacancy within two months from the date on which the vacancy 
occurs, and intimate to the President the name of the person elected, with 
his qualifications, registration number, and address. 


The President will thereupon report the same to the State Government for 
notification in the Calcutta Gazette. 


(2) When such vacancy is amongst the members elected under clause (d) 
of sub-section (1) of section 4, an election shall be held in accordance with 
the same rules as laid down in Part IV of these rules for general election by 
the electoral body referred to in the said clause except that the period of pub- 
lication of the draft electoral roll [vide sub-rule (3) of rule (4)] shall not be 
more than 7 days. 


1046 THE CAIAUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 27, 1954 | Parr |] 
————— -_---تسسس جججچڑٹّ<ت ےس پچ سشہ سی‎ 


The programme of time for the several stages of the operation shall also 
be so arranged that the election may be completed within two months from the 
date of occurrence of the vacancy. 


PART VI. 


Filling up of a casual vacancy amongst members elected under clause (e) ہو‎ 
section 4(1). 

16. (1) When the office of a member elected under clause (e) of sub. 
section (1) of section 4 becomes vacant by his resignation or death or under 
sub-section (2) of section 4 or sub-section (1) of section 9, the Registrar shal 
forthwith report the vacancy to the President and the President shall thereupon 
determine in accordance with the provisions of clause (c) of sub-section (1) 
of section 10, the candidate or candidates who should be considered as having 
secured for the purposes of that clause, the maximum number of votes at the 
preceding election under clause (6) of sub-section (1) of section 4. 


(2) If there be only one such candidate, he shall be deemed to have been 
elected in the place of the outgoing member: and the President shal! forthwith 
report the same to the State Government for notification in the Calcutta Gazette, 


(3) If there be more than one such candidate having the same maximum 
number of votes at the preceding election aforesaid, the President shall appoint 
a time and place for making a selection by drawing lot, and cause notices to 
be issued by registered post to all such candidates with the same maximum 
number of votes, inviting them to be present either personally or by a duly 
authorised agent, at the time and place appointed by the President for the 
purpose, and the President shall cause the lot to be drawn in the presence of 
the candidates invited or their duly authorised agents as may be present, in such 
manner as he thinks proper. The candidate thus selected by 101, shall be 
deemed to have been elected, and the President shall report the election to the 
State Government for notifying the same in the Calcutta Gazette. 

(4) If on the happening of a contingency mentioned in proviso (iii) to 
Clause (c) of sub-section (1) of section 10, a bye-election becomes necessary, 
such bye-eclection shall be held in accordance with the same rules as laid down 
in Part IV of these rules for a gencral election by the electoral body referred 
to in clause (e) of sub-section (1) of section 4, 


PART VII. 
Election of Vice-President under Section 11B. 


17. (1) The election of the Vice-President shall be held at the first meet- 
ing of the Council at which the President shall preside. 


(2) The President shall invite the members present at the meeting to make 
their nomination for the office of the Vice-President in such manner as_ the 
President considers fit. Every nomination § shall be supported by another 
member present at the meeting as seconder: provided that no one member shall 
nominate or second more than one person. 


(3) If there be only one person so nominated, he shall be declared as duly 
elected Vice-President. 


(4) If there be more than one such person, the President shall proceed to 
take ballot in the following manner, namely— 
(i) A slip of paper shall be given to every member present %/1)0 shall 
write on it the name of the person he votes for, fold the slip and 
hand it over to the President. 


(ii) The President shall then count the number of votes secured by each 
nominec: and declare the member who secures the largest number 
of votes as the duly elected Vice-President. 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRY., JULY 27, 1954 1047 
লগ) লন 


(ill) If the largest number of votes be secured by two or more nominees, 
the President may either give his casting vote for any one of them 
who shall then be declared as the duly elected Vice-President: or, 
the President may make the selection by lot drawn in such manner 
as he thinks fit, and the person so selected by lot shall be declared 
as the duly elected Vice-President. 


PART VIII. 
Election of the members of the Executive Committee (section 11C). 


18. (1) The election of five members for the Executive Committec, as 
required by section 11C, shall be held at a meeting of the Council at which the 
President, or in his absence the Vice-President shall be the Chairman. 


(2) The procedure for nomination shall be the same as laid down in sub- 
rules (2) to (4) of rule 17 for the election of the Vice-President, with this 
difference that a member may nominate or second as many as five persons. 


(3) If there be only five person so nominated, all these five persons shall 
be declared as duly elected members of the Executive Committee. 


(4) If there be more than five persons so nominated, the Chairman shall 
proceed to take ballot in the following manner, namely:— 


(i) A voting paper with the names of the candidates nominated shall be 
given to every member present who shall put a cross mark against 
the name of the person he votes for, fold the slip and hand it over 
to the Chairman. 

(ii) The Chairman shall then count the number of votes secured by each 
candidate in the voting paper and declare the five with the largest 
number of votes as duly elected members of the Executive Com- 
mittee. 

(iii) When an equality of votes is found to exist between any candidates, 

‘ and the addition of a vote will entitle any of the said candidates 
to be declared elected, the determination of the person or persons 
to whom such an additional vote shall be deemed to have been 
given shall be made by lot to be drawn in the presence of the 
Chairman and in such manner as he may determine.

or caused to be felled or removed or caused to

in contravention of any of the terms and

be inserted.

No. 2083F./F/1S-8(30)/54.—2st July 1954.—In exercise of the powers 
conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution of India, the’ Gov- 
ernor is pleased to make, in supersession of all previous rules issued on the 
subject, the following rules for the regulation of reeruitment to the clerical 
establishment of the Secretariat and certain other offices: — 


RULES FOR THE 'REGULATION OF RECRUITMENT TO THE 
CLERICAL SERVICES OF THE SECRETARIAT AND CERTAIN 
OTHER OFFICES OF THE GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL. 


1. These rules shall apply to the clerical establishments of the West 
Bengal Secretariat and the offices included in (2) and (2A) of Schedule “C” 
to the West Bengal Public Service Commission Regulations, 1937. 


2. The clerical service of the Secretariat and the other offices is divided 
into two divisions—the Upper Division and Lower Division. 


Upper Division. 


3. Pay.—The Upper Division of the clerical service in the Sécretariat and 
the Board of Revenue is graded as follows:— 


(a) A time-scale of Rs.150—10-—-370—15—400 with an efficiency bar 
after the 12th stage. 


(b}: A selection grade of Rs. 400—20—500 attached to posts of “Senior 
Head Assistants”, the number of which is limited to 7°5 per cent. 
of the total number of permanent Upper Division posts (including 
Head Assistants) in a Department; provided that no pest of 
Senior Head Assistant shall be admissible unless there are more 
than one permanent Head Assistant in the Department. 


(c) A special pay of Rs. 60 per month is attached to posts of Head 
Assistants. 


4. Method of recruitment.—Recruitment to the Upper Division in the 
Secretariat and in the office of the Board of Revenue shall be as follows:— 


(a) 50 per cent. by direct rccruitment on the results of the competitive 
examination for recruitment to the West Bengal Civil Service 
(Executive) and allied services, 


(b) 50 per cent. by promotion from Lower Division. 


If as a matter of fact the proportion between the two categories is found 
to be uneven in any Department or in the office of the Board of Revenue steps 
should be taken to secure the correct proportion. After the proportion has 
been ‘secured, vacancies in place of direct recruits shall be filled up by direct 
recruitment and those in place of promotees by promotion from, Lower Division. 


Upper Division vacancies in other offices mentioned in Schedule “C” to the 
Public Service Commission Regulations to which these rules apply shall be filled 
by promotion’ from the Lower Division unléss othetwise expressly provided for 
in any existing departmental orders applicable to a particular office. 


Promotion from the Lower Division to the Up r Divivsidn will be made 
on the ground of merit. Unless other considerations are equal, seniority will 
not be taken into account. . 


Similarly, in the matter of selection of Upper 70151591017 clerks for posts of 
Head Assistants, merit shall be the deciding factor and the time spent in the 
Upper Division shall not be taken into account unlegs it is impossible to choose 
between two or more clerks on merit alone. 


Candidates directly recruited to the Upper Division shall be on probation 
for two years. ‘ 


Qualifications —For direct recruitment to Upper Division posts in the 
Secretariat and the office of the Board of Revenue the qualifications regarding age 
and academic fitness shall be the same as those laid down for admission to the 
West Bengal Junior Civil Service. 


Lower Division. 


6. Pay»—The Lower Division of the clerical service is graded as 
follows‘— ۱ : 
(i) In the Secretariat Departments, the Secretariat Record Room and in 
the, office of the Bogard of Revenuc— 
a time scale of Rs. 8 160—5—180 with efficiency bar after the 
12th stage. 
(ii) In the West Bengal Government Press and in the Pooling Section 
of the Port Office, Calcutta— 3 
a time scale of Rs. 55—-3——118—-4—130 plus a compensatory allow- 
ance at 10 per cent. of the basic pay.

9. (a) A Department of the Secretariat may promote any permanent 
clerk in a Directorate under that Department to a Lower Division post in the 
Secretarfat after considering the claims of all Assistants in the said Directorate 
who have readered permanent scrvice of not less than five years in that

of this 101৩ shall never excced 10 per cent. of the strength of the permanent 
Lower ‘Division posts of the particular Department.

(b) A Directorate may promote any permanent clerk in an office subordi-

nent service of not less than five years in the subordinate office; but the total 
number of posts so‘ filled from time to time in terms of this rule shall never

that particular Directorate. 


In both cases mentioned in'(a) and (b) above, consultation with the Public 
Service Commission will not be necessary.

APPENDIX, ' 


Rules and Syllabus for the examination for recruitment to the Lower Division 
Clerical Service. 


1. English.—Questions will be asked on the following:— 


(a) An exercise in composition ٤6 test a candidagte’s abilitics to write 
simple correct English. It may be an essay or the drafting of a 
report or a letter of about 400 words from points or 17081918918 ' 

‘ supplied. 

(b) To write a precis of a series of correspondence or a summary of 
diffuse passages. A candidate’s capacity for comprehension and 
expression is to be tested. 


(c) Translation from Bengali or Hindi, Urdu or Nepali, as the case may 
be, to English. 


(d) Correction of sentences. 
(e) Punctuation. 
(f) ‘Correct use of words and common phrases. 


2. Bengali (or Hindi, or Urdu, or Nepali).—Questions will be asked on 
the following: ; 
(a) An exercise in composition to test a candidate’s abilities to write in 
eer language. It may be an essay or a letter of about 400 

words. 


(b) To condense a prose passage of about 1000 words. 


%) Translation from English té Bengali or Hindi, or Urdu, or Nepali, as 
the case may be. 


3. General Knowledge.—The paper will consist of questions to test the 
extent of a candidate’s knowledge and his capacity to express himself correctly: 
on.matters of tcommon experience and current events and problems with special 
reference to India. Elementary knowledge of Indian istory and Indian 
Geography may also be tested. 


4. Elementary Mathematics.—There will be 3 parts as. set out below: — 
Part A—Arithmetic (40 marks). 


Vulgar and decimal fractions, ratio and proportion, practice Unitary 
method, percentages, averages, profit and loss, simple interest, square 
roots of whole numbers and decimals, areas and volumes of regular 
figures, simple problems relating to the above topics. 


Part B—Algebra (30 marks). 


Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, simple equation, H.C.F., 
L.C,M., fractions, simultaneous equations, involution, ovolution, 
factors, identities, graphs on simple equations, application of graphs 
to simple arithmetical and statistical problems. রর 


Part C—Geometry (30 marks).- 


Knowledge of the properties of angles at a point, parallel straight lincs, 
angles of triangle, conguency of triangles, simple properties relating 
to sidés and angles of a triangle, area of a triangle with given sides, 
properties -of the angles, sides and diagonals of parallelogram, 
rhombus, rectangle, square and trapezium. 


Properties of circles, i.e., angle subtended by an arc or chord at the centre 
of a circle is double that subtended at the circumference, angle in a 
semi-circle is a right angle, a tangent to a Gircle is at right angle to 
the radius at the point of contact, angle between chord and tangent 
equal to the angle in the alternate segment. 

Constructions, bisection of angles and straight fines, construction af per- 
pendiculars, parallels, triangles, tangents to circles, inscribed and 
circumscribed circles of triangle. | 


5. The standard of examination.—In order to qualify in the examinaffon 
a candidate must secure 40 per cent. of the full marks allotted for each of the 
papers I and II and 30 per cent. of the full marks allotted for each of the 
papers III and IV. 2: 
In allotting marks the following considerations will be made; 
(a) No credit will be given for merely superficial knowledge. 


(b) Deduction up,to 10 per cent. of the maximum marks may be made, 
* for bad handwriting and,for wrong spelling. 


Answers to questions in Papers I and III shall be made in English, those in 
Paper IV either in English or Bengali and those in Paper II in Bengali, Hindi, 
Urdu or Nepali as the case may be. 


The standard of Papers I and II will approximately be that of the Inter- 
mediate standard of the University of Calcutta and of Paper IV that of the 
School Final Examination of the Board of Secondary Education, West Bengal.

Wheres, in the opinion of the Governor,— 


(1) the rules of the Provident Funds of the 
Factory mentioned in the schedule below with 
respect to the rates of contribution are not less 
favourable to the employees therein than those 
specified in section 6 of the Employees’ Provident 
Funds Act, 1952 (XIX of 1952), and 


(2) the employees in the said factory are also in 
enjoyment of other provident fund benefits which 
on the whole are not less favourable to them than 
the benefits provided under the Employees’ Pro- 
vident| Funds Scheme, 1952, hereinafter referred to 
as the said scheme, in relation to the employees 
in any other factory of a similar character ; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 
17 of the Employees’ Provident Funds Act, 1952 
(XIX of 1952), the Governor is pleased hereby 
to exempt the factory mentioned in the schedule 
below from the operation of all the provisions of 
the said scheme و ا‎ to the following conditions, 
namely :— 

(1) The employer in relation to the factory 
(hereinafter referred to as the employer) shall 
within six months from the date of the publication 
of this notification, amend the constitution of the 
Provident Fund of the Factory in such manner as 
to ensure that— 

(a) The Provident Fund vests in a Board of 
Trustees ; 

(b) The Board of Trustees includes representa- 
tives of employees equal in number to the 
representatives of the employers in the 
Board.
