—The following agreement is published under 
section 42 of the Land Acquisition Act, I of 1894, 
for general information :— 


Agreement. 


Memorandum of agreement made this 17th day 
of July 1954 between the Associated Aesby Indus- 
tries Ltd., 2, Company Registered under the 
Indian Companies Act 1913, and having its 
registered office at 22, Strand Road, Calcutta-l 
and factory at 81, Akshoy Kumar Mukherjee Road, 
Baranagore, (Calcutta-86) (hereinafter called 
“‘the Company’’) of the one part and ‘‘the Gover- 
nor” of the State of West Bengsl (hereinafter 
called the Governor) of the other part. 

Whereas for the purpose of the extension of 
factory and for construction of Metal yard and 
quarters for the staff and workers, the Company 
has applied to the Government of West Bengal 
for the acquisition under the provisions of the 
Land Acquisition Act, 1894, of the pieces or 
parcels of the lund containing 0-57 of an acre or 
thereabout situated in the village of Naopara, 
police-station Baranagore, in the district of 
24-Parganas and more particularly described in 
the schedule hereto and delineated in the plan* 
hereunto annexed. 

And whereas the said Government of West 
Bengal, being satisfied by an enquiry held under 
section 40 of the said Act, that the proposed 
acquisition is needed for the aforesaid purpose 
and that the said work is likely to prove useful 
to the public, has consented to acquire on behalf 
of the Company the pieces or parcels of the Jand 
hereinbefore described. 

And whereas the said Government of West 
Bengal has required the Company under the 
provisions of section 41 of the above mentioned 
Act to enter into the agreement with the Governor 
hereinafter contained. Now this Indenture 
witnesseth that it is hereby agreed and declared 
as follows : 

1. On demand the Company shall and will 
pay to the said Government of West Bengal all 
and every compensation in respect of the said land 
tendered, * paid or awarded or to be tendered, 
paid or awarded by the Collector under the Land 
Acquisition Act, 1894, or by Court to which a 
reference under part III of the said Act may be 
made, or by the Court or Courts to which an 
appeal from the award of the said Court may be 
preferred and all costs, charges ond expenses of 
the proceedings in the aforesaid Courts or other- 
wise incidental to the proposed acquisition or 
payable in respect thereof under the provisions of 
the said Act. 

2. On demand by the said Collector the obli- 
gations of the Company under the last preceding 
clause not being thereby limited, the Company 
shall and will deposit with the said Collector 
such sum or sums of money as in his discretion the 
said Collector muy in anticipation estimate to be 
necessary for the purposes mentioned in the last 
preceding clause. 


3. On payment by the Company of all demands 
under the foregoing first clause, or, in the discre- 
tion of the said Government of West Bengal (on 
deposit by the Company of all estimated amounts 
as provided in the second clause), but not before 
possession shall have been taken under the 
provisions of the abovementioned Act, the 
Governor shall make over possession of the said 
land to the Company and shall execute and do

6. Should the said construction and extension 
not be completed and fully equipped in all respects 
ready for use within the period stated in the last 
preceding clause or within such further period as

the said Government of West Bengal or should the

or cease to be required for the purpose or purposes

and in any such case, the said Government may 
summarily re-enter upon and take possession of 
the said land together with all buildings thereon, 
whether such buildings were erected before or 
after transfer of the land to the Company, and 
thereupon the interest of the Company in the 
said land and buildings shall absolutely cease ond 
determine. 

7. On taking such possession, the said Govern- 
ment may sell or otherwise deal with the said 
land and buildings as it may think proper: 

(i) Should the said Government sell the land 
with the buildings the said Government 
after deducting the expenses incurred 
in connection with the said taking of 
possession and with such sale shall pay 
the proceeds to the Company. 


(ii) Should the said Government decide-not to 
sell the land and buildings, the said 
Government shall retain the said land and 
buildings thereon in which case the Gov- 
ernor shall repay to the Company the 
market value as on the day of re-entry 
of all the buildings erected by the Company 
and all sums received from the Company 
in respect of all and every compensation 
as provided in the foregoing first clause 
(less the statutory allowance of 15 per 
cent. and less any amount received on 
account of trees and buildings which are 
not in existance at the time of resump- 
tion), but will not repay any sums paid 
and received on account of costs, charges 
and expenses. 


(iii) Should the said Government decide to sell 
the buildings only upon such sale, the 
Governor shall, after deducting the ex- 
penses of taking possession and selling, 
pay the balance of the proceeds of sale to 
the Company, together with the sum 
received from the Company in respect of 
the compensation for the Jand (less the 
statutory allowance of 15 per cent. and 
less any amount received from the Cum- 
pany on account of trees and buildings 
which are not in existance at the time of 
resumption), but will not repay any sum 
paid and received on account of costs, 
charges and expenses. 


8. The public shall be entitled to use the 
benefit of the acquisition on the following terms: 


(1) The Company shall admit annually 2 
apprentices for free training in various 


processes at their works. The first batch 
of apprentices shall be taken in within 
3 months from the date of making cver 
the possession of the land. 


(ii) The apprentices shall be nominated by the 
Director of Industries, West Bengal, or 
such other officers os may be authorised 
by him. He shall be assisted by a 
representative of the firm in makiny the 
nomination, 


(iii) The duration of training shall be one year 
and each apprentices shall be paid an 
allowance of Rs. 40 p.m. during the period 
by the firm. 


(iv) The Company shall submit periodical pro- 
gress report of the apprentices and shall 
grant certificate of proficiency to them 
who complete training sutisfactorily. 


(v) Any adverse report against an apprentice 
shall be brought to his notice forthwith, 
and the report together with the explana- 
tion, be submitted to the D.I. who shall 
suggest the disciplinary action, if any, 
to be taken in consultation with the 
authorities of the Company. 


(vi) In recruiting staff the Company shall give 
preference to the apprentices trained 
under this Scheme.

ANNEXURE. 


in the matter of an industrial dispute between the “Swadhinata” of 33, 
Alimuddin Street, Calcutta-16 and Shri J. C. Cupta, Keeper of the

Hart J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Third /ndustrial Tribunal.

gaban Pathak.

AWARD, 
1. By order No, 1088)Dis./1/181.-14/53, dated the Ist April 1953, the 


Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Tndustrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial dispute 
between the “Swadhinata”’ of 33, Alimuddin Street, Calcutta-16, and Shri 
J? C. Grupta, Keeper of the East Knd Press of 199, Park Street, Calcutta 
and their workers represented by Bengal Provincin] National Trade Union 
Congress, 59B, Chowringhee Road, Caleutta-20, regarding the matters 
specified in the schedule, to the Third Industrial Tribunal constituted under 
section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, by notification No. 592Dis. [- 
D/120.-6/52, dated the 24rd February 1953, for adjudication. 


2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance und filed their 
written statements. Shri J. C. Gupta also filed a supplementary written 
statement on 30th May 1953 in answer to the allegations of the ‘“‘Swadhi- 
nata” against him. The pleadings were completed on 30th May 1953. The 


2522 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 (Parr J 
پچ سہمممچےہ مہہ ژشلیہسآت٣ ںا ا ں ںہ کس ٹک سس تس تک ہےر‎ শীল লি 
parties were thereafter direeted to file their lists of documents and after 
several udjournments the hearing Was concluded on 1011) June 1954 &nd the 
award was reserved. 


3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference are as follows :— 

(1) Who is the actual employer of the discharged workers named below 
—‘‘Swadhinata’”’ or Shri J. C. Gupta, Keeper of the Kast End 

Press? :— 
(1) Shri Matilal Dhar, (2) Shri Mani Dhar, (8) Shri Sabdar Gani, 
(4) Shri Nirod Kushari, (5) Shri Sudhansu Biswas, (6) Shri 
Sushil Ghosh, (7) Shri Suryya Singh, (8) Shri Manoranjan 


Chakraborty. 
(2) Reinstatement and/or compensation of the said discharged 
workers. 


4. The newspaper ‘‘Swadhinata” began to be printed at and published 
from Ganasakti Printers, Ltd., at 33, Alimuddin Street, since 17th October 
1952. Before this it used to be printed at and published from East End 
Press at 199, Park Street, from 9th February 1951 to 16th October 1952. The 
eight workmen named in the order of reference are press workers who last 
worked at the aforesaid East End Press up to 16th October 1952 and received 
their dues up to that date. The dispute arose out of termination of their 
employment with transfer of printing and publication of the aforesaid paper 
from Ganasakti Printers since 17th October 1952. 


The eight workmen represented by Bengal Provincial National Trade 
Union Congress alleged that they were employed by the ‘‘Swadhinata” and 
last worked under it in Kast Knd Press up to 16th October 1942 and there- 
after when the paper began to be printed and published from Ganasakti 
Printers from 17th October 1952, the Management of the ‘‘Swadhinata” 
declined to employ them. 


The ‘‘Swadhinata” denied having ever employed the eight workmen and 
suggested that Shri J. C. Gupta, Keeper of the East End Press, had 
employed them. Shri J. C. (iupta in his turn denied having ever employed 
the workmen or having had any connection with them at any time. 


DECISION. 


Issue No, 1.—In support of their case, the workmen have examined 
P.W. 1 Shri Matilal Dhar (Serial No. 1 in the schedule to the order of 
reference), P.W. 2 Shri Manindra Kumar Dhar (Serial No. 2 in the 
schedule to the order of reference), P.W. 3 Shri Nirode Ranjan Kushar 
(Serial No. 4 in the schedule to the order of reference) and the then Press 
Manager of Kast Hnd Press, P.W. 4 Shri Narayan Chandra Kushari, bg- 
sides filing 15:65, 1 and 2. The Management of the “‘Swadhinata”’ on the 
contrary has examined the Supervisor of Ganasakti Press of Dacres Lane, 
D.W. 1 Shri Nirmal Chandra Das and a member of the Board of editors 
of the ‘‘Swadhinata”’, D.W. 2 Shri Bangeswar Koy besides proving 11566. A 
to A5, B to B39, C, D and H to H3. Shri J. C. Gupta in his turn has 
himself deposed (D.W. 3), besides proving letters Exts. E, F and ۰ 


The workmen alleged that they were employed by the ‘‘Swadhinata” 
from 1945 till 16th October 1952 at different presses beginning from Gana- 
sakti Press of Dacres Lane and were last employed at East End Press since 
it resumed publication on 9th February 1951, while the ‘‘Swadhinata” 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, 1111:۳ 29, 1954 25238 


denied having ever employed them at any time or in any press or in Kast 
End Press and suggested that Shri J.C. Gupta, Keeper of the East Ind 
Press, was their employer. It has heen said on behalf of the ““Swadhinata” 
that the paper had of has no press of its own and had or has no direct con- 
nection with the printers’ staff, as it used and uses to get its printing done 
on payment of printing charges to the presses concerned. Shri J. C. Gupta

his political creed is opposed to the one of the Communists whose organ

The workmen did not allege that they were ever employed by Shri

be construed to have been employer of the workmen. It, therefore, follows 
that neither the ‘‘Swadhinata” nor Shri J. C. Gupta was the employer of 
the workmen. I answer the issue accordingly. 


Tt will not be out of place to mention here that when the workmen did

The Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred 
the industrial dispute between National Carbon Company of India, I.td., and 
their workmen to this Tribunal by order No. 218-Dis./1/101-74/52, dated 
5th February 1962. This Tribunal was then presided over by Shri A. Das 
Gupta. The award of Shri A, Das Gupta was published in the Calcutta 
(Grazette on 2181 August ۰ 


On 10th July 1952 Badri and six other workmen applied under section 
838A of the Industrial Disputes Act and stated as follows : 


Might persons were working on mix platform operation since the intro- 
duction of piece-rates in 1948. The Company tried to reduce the number 
of workers on the mix platform in 1950 on the plea of altered job condi- 
tions, but at the intervention of the Labour Commissioner, the Company 
had to maintain the original number of people. In the month of March 
1952, during the pendency of the proceedings before the Tribunal, the Com- 
pany forcibly reduced two men on the plea that some jobs were eliminated. 
In the month of July 1952, the Company foreed these six men to do some 
of the jobs which were eliminated in the month of March while reducing 
hands. Under the circumstances, the applicants pray for maintenance of 
status quo and for compensation. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows :— 


The application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
Shri Badri Singh and others is not maintainable, as the application does not 
refer to any change in the condition of service prejudicial to the applicants. 
There has heen no contravention of section 33 of the Act and the present 
application under section 33A of the Act is incompetent. The Company 
submits that the number of men required for manutacturing mix is not 
fixed; it varies depending upon each grade of mix manufactured and the 
amount of mix required per hour. Gang-rates were first set in mix manu- 
facturing operations in 1947, and not in 1948, as alleged and these rates were 
based on six. men. Due to changes in the mix formulations and the type 
and quality ‘of materials used and due to the addition of some other opera- 
tions, the number of operators in the gang was increased to 8. The night 
shift since its inception, always worked with six men, as less mix is required 
at night. In 1950, the Company reverted to the simple formulation pre- 
viously used and therefore 7 operators were required in the gang. Accord- 
ingly, the eighth operator was removed from the gang and given alternative 
employment, but this led to a labour dispute. At the Union’s request, the 
Labour Commissioner, Government ot West Bengal, intervened. In the 
course of his investigutions, the Labour Commissioner ascertained that the 
simplified formulation was only an interim measure and the Company 
intended to revert to the more complicated formulation immediately upon 
receipt of certain critical raw materials, which at that time, were in short 
es Ife, therefore, suggested that to avoid difficulties, the Company 
should allow-the eighth operator to remain in the gang for day shift opera- 
tion during the interim period. The Company agreed to this request. In 
February 1952, the mix platform was reorganised and certain mechanical 
equipments introduced, the sum-total of which improved efficiency and 
lightened work-load. In view of these changes, the gang-rate was 1¢-studied 
and it was decided that the Company would balance the number of men at 
gaug-rate as six for both day and night” shifts. This change 
was put into effect on 6th March 1952, and operations on_ these 
basis continued up to 30th June 1952. During this period, the Company 
received no complaints from the operators about the gang-rates or the work- 
load. The output was as expected and from the check-up of the attitude

হা 
and éarnings of the operators, the rates were absolutely fair and the work- 
load im line with their earlier efforts. The job-study for this gang-rate was 
carried out in February 1952, the month when the factory achieved an all- 
time high production, Since that time, the tactory output has decreased. 
Consequently, the اوس‎ of mix required has proportionately reduced. 
The result has been that the gang of 6 operators produced sufficient mix in

is as follows:— 


(1) Dearness allowance with date of giving effect thereto.

India Electric Construction Co., Ltd., Employees’ Congress (hereafter described

DECISION. 


The parties have not adduced any oral evidence. They rely on the annex- 
ures to their respective written statements. Besides, the Company filed certain 
documents which have been marked Exts. A to T, while the workmen filed a 
copy of letter, dated 24th May 1947, marked Ext. 1. 


Before entering into the controversies, it is necessary to state the facts lead- 
ing to the dispute as are either admitted or established in evidence. The British 
India Electric Construction Co., Ltd. (hereinafter called the Company), like 
the Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and Bridge & Roof Co. (India), Ltd., is 
under the Managing Agency of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co., Ltd., and its 
head office is located in Calcutta and is in the same building in which the offices 
of its Managing Agents are located. Its factory and office are situated at 6 
and 14, Mayurbhanj Road, Kidderpore, Calcutta. The Company took over 
electric workshop of Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co., Ltd., The latter owns 
major shares of the Company. The Managing Agents have the power of 
appointing Company’s staff and fixing their remuneration. 


In December 1946, the Managing Agents decided to reorganize the staff and 
on 14th January 1947 introduced with retrospective effect from 1st January 
1947 mew grades and scales of wages as per Annexure “A” to the written 
statement of Employees’ Congress. 


In February 1947, the Managing Agents introduced the scheme of dearness 
allowance linked to the middle-class cost of living index on the lines of the 
scheme of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce. This was made applicable to 
the general, clerical and subordinate staff of the Company employed both at the 
head office and at the factory (vide Annexures A4, B, C and Cl ٠ت‎ the 
written statement of the Employees’ Congress). The Company went on pay- 
ing dearness allowance at the Bengal Chamber of Commerce’s rates to the 
seneral, clerical and subordinate staff employed both at the head office and at 
the factory up to July 1948. From August 1948, though the Company has 
been giving higher rates of dearness allowance to these employees at its head 
office as per Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme consequent on further rise 
in the costs of living index, it has refused to extend this benefit to its employees 
at its factory but has continued to pay latter at the old rates based on the living 
index of 311-32 as stated in paragraph 4. In the circumstances the above 
categories of workmen at the factory claim that the scheme of dearness allow- 
ance of Bengal Chamber of Commerce in its entirety and not piecemeal con- 
stituted a condition of their service and should be implemented. 


In the meantime the award of the First Engineering Tribunal appointed in 
October 1947, to which the Company and its workmen were among other 
parties, was published in the Calcutta Gazette on the 3rd July 1948. The said 
Tribunal noticed the fact that many of the engineering concerns who were

members of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce were paying dearness allowance

Though the said Tribunal did not accede to the general claim of the workmen 
of all the engincering concerns who were parties to the reference for dcarness

“This award will not affect adversely any other kind of existing advantages 
which the employees of a firm may be enjoying in excess of the 
benefits given by this award, unless an express provision has been 
made in this award concerning such advantage.” 


Shortly after the publication of the First Engineering Tribunal award, the 
Company to pay from August 1948 dearness allowance at increased rates beyond 
the costs of living index group of 311-32 as provided in the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce’s scheme (vide Annexure “B” to its written statement) but con- 
tinued to pay dearness allowance to these workmen of the factory at the old 
rates as paid for July 1948, which was lower than the one admissible under the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme _ with incrcase in costs of living, but 
higher than what had been fixed at first by the First Engineering Tribunal and 
subsequently by the’ Second Engineering Tribunal (vide statement Ext. R). 


Consequent upon this, the Enployees’ Congress, formerly known as [16 
British India Electric Construction Company Employees’ Union with registered 
No. 1138, made a representation on behalf of the factory workmen con- 
cerned to the Labour Commissioner, West Bengal, by their letter No. PB/ 
DRN/52/11/48, dated the 26th November 1948 (Annexure “D” to 1176 
written statement of the Employees’ Congress). The Iectter was signed hy 
D. N. Bhowmick for General Secretary of the Union. The Labour Commis- 
sioner wrote to the Works Manager of the Company on 25th February 1949 
regarding the Union’s demand by Annexure “C” and the Works Manager 
replied to it on 11th March 1949 by Annexure “D”. 


Then there was the award of Second Engineering Tribunal on 31st August 
1950, fixing higher rates of dearness allowance than those in the award of the 
First Engineering Tribunal. This second award also made reservation § as 
follows:— 

“Where a more liberal policy is already being pursued as regards dear- 
ness allowance, we shall direct that the existing scale of dearness 
allowance, whether based on the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme or anything else, shall not be reduced”. 


In the meantime the workmen of the Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., under 
the same Managing Agents being put to identical position raised a dispute which 
was ultimately referred on 6th February 1951 to the Tribunal presided over by 
Shri S. K. Niyogi for adjudication. The workmen claimed that after such 
reference the Company as well as the Managing Agents assured them that, the 
award that would be made between the Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and their 
workmen would be the determining factor in respect of the dispute with this 
Company and as such advised the workmen to await the award of that case, to 
which the workmen agreed. 


The said Tribunal of Shri S. K. Niyogi made its award on 27th July 1951. 
There was an appeal filed against it. The appeal was decided on 16th October 
1952. It was reported in 1953, L.A.C., page 93. The Indian Galvanizing 
Co., Ltd., has been directed to pay the clerks employed at the factory dearness 
allowance according to the scales of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce with 
retrospective effect from August 1948.

Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2535 


On the basis of the decision of the Hon'ble Appellate Tribunal in the said 
case,vthe workmen of this Company revived their old claim with regard to 
dearness allowance as they had same dispute as that of the workmen of the 
Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., based on similar set of facts and as the Company 
assured that the decision in that case would be the guide in the matter of the 
dispute with this Company. 


The Employees’ Congress on behalf of the workmen presented a charter of 
demands on 19th January 1953 to the Labour Commissioner and the Works 
Manager of the Company (vide Annexure “F” to the written statement of the 
Employees’ Congress). On 21st July 1953 Shri Bimal Chandra Sinha and 
others made similar demand to the Works Manager for payment of dearness 
allowance according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale with arrears 
(Annexure “G”). On 19th August 1953, General Secretary of the Employees’ 
Congress again wrote to the Labour Commissioner in the matter (Annexure 
“G 1”). On 25th August 1953 another letter was written to the Labour Com- 
missioner (Annexure “G 2”). A series of representations in respect of dearness 
allowance were thus made by the Employees’ Congress on behalf of the work- 
men. In the circumstances the Government made the present reference on 26th 
October 1953 to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


Behind this background the workmen represented by Shri Bimal Chandra 
Sinha and others and by the Employees’ Congress contend that the general, 
clerical and subordinate staff of the factory are eligible to be paid from August 
1948 dearness allowance on the lines of Bengal Chamber of Commerce linked to 
the cost of living index. The Company resists the claim. 


As preliminary objection it has been urged on behalf of the Company that 
as the workmen have not terminated under section 19(6) of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act, the award of the Second Engineering Tribunal which is still operative 
and binding on the parties, their claim for higher rates of dearness allowance 
than those in the award of the Second Engineering Tribunal cannot be sustained. 
The objection is without substance. In the present case the claim has been laid 
not simpli citer on the basis of the awards but as a condition of service and 
protected by the awards. So, no question of termination of the award on the 
part of the workmen arises. It was rather necessary on the part of the Com- 
pany to do so if it wanted to avoid the liability. 


Likewise, the contention of the Company that when the claim is laid on the 
basis of the awards of the First and Second Engineering Tribunals, the remedy 
of the workmen lay not on the basis of a fresh reference but by way of implemen- 
tation of the award under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes Act cannot be 
upheld. When nothing could be shown that the reference by the Government 
has contravened the provisions in section 10 of the Act, it is obvious that the 
Tribunal cannot go behind it and has got to adjudicate upon the reference. 
Besides the claim, it has alrcady been seen, has been laid as service condition 
and as protected under the awards. So the question before this Tribunal is 
not one of implementation of an award under section 22 of the Industrial Dis- 
putes Act but one of construction whether the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme of dearness allowance was a service condition of the three categories of 
workmen named in the order of reference and whether the said service condi- 
tion was protected under the awards. So, I am unable to uphold any of the 
preliminary objections raised on behalf of the Company. 


Now as to merits, the Company alleges that in the past they adopted 
several schemes in the matter of dearness allowance which were abandoned 
having been found unsuitable and laterly it adopted the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce scheme of dearness allowance up to a certain stage not permanently 


2536 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 {Paar J 


Oa ae এ 


but provisionally in order to see how it works on actual application. After the 
said scheme was tried for some time, it became evident that the said scheme was 
also unsatisfactory and the additional burden was too heavy for the Company 
to bear. The Company could not, however, forthwith stop payment according 
to the said scheme as the question of dearness allowance was then a spccific 
issue before the First Enginecring Tribunal to which this Company 9110 its 
workmen were among others parties. After the First Engineering Tribunal 
made its award, the Company discontinued from August 1948 payment accord- 
ing to Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme which was on trial by their cir- 
cular No. OTJ., dated 21st August 1948 (Annexure “B” to the Company’s 
written statement). It is said that in doing so the Company did not curtail the 
then existing advantage in the form of dearness allowance, nor did it adversely 
affect any workman. For, at the time of the award of the First Engineering 
Tribunal the Company was paying dearness allowance at the rate ot 70 per 
cent. of the basic salary on the first hundred rupees, 35 per cent. on the next 
one hundred rupees and 174 per cent. on the remainder to the general and 
clerical staff and at flat rate of Rs. 43 per month to the subordinate staff and it 
paid at the said rates to these categories of employees at the factory in July 
1948 and that though with further increase in the cost of living index the Com- 
pany did not pay higher rates of dearness allowance it has however been paying 
dearness allowance at the aforesaid rates to the aforesaid categories of the 
employees at the factory from August 1948 and these rates are much higher 
than those awarded by the First Engineering Tribunal and subsequently awarded 
by the Second Engineering Tribunal. So it is said that the Company is not 
liable to pay according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme beyond 
these rates which are the existing rates. After giving careful consideration to 
the arguments advanced on either side and having regard to the annexures and 
the exhibits on record and the decision of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tri- 
bunal in the case of Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and their workmen reported 
in 1953, L.A.C., page 93, I find nothing to resist the claim of the workmen. 
After the decision in the case of Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and their 
workmen, it is too late in the day for the Company, to contend that it did not 
adopt the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance beyond 
the rates at which it had paid in July 1948 and has been paying since August 
1948. The notice which Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co., acting as the Managing 
Agents of the Company issued on 18th February 1947 on the subject of 
dearness allowance to the clerical and subordinate staff of the Company is on 
identical terms with the one noticed by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal 
in the case of Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and their workmen. This notice 
was construed by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal as having given whole 
of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance to the 
clerical staff with whom the appeal was concerned. Said notice also applied 
to the subordinate staff as specifically mentioned therein. The Managing 
Agents gave benefit of the above notice to general staff by their letter, dated 
24th July 1947, with retrospective effect from March 1947 (vide Annexure 
10, Ext. 1). It further appears that these three categories of workmen employed 
both at the Head Office and the factory were paid dearness allowance from 
March 1947 up to July 1948 according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme. It also appears that in between March and July 1948 the cost of 
living index exceeded 300 and the Company paid dearness allowance at the 
higher rates corresponding to such increase in the cost of living index figure as 
contemplated in the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme. So the Company's 
contention that they adopted the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of 
dearness allowance up to cost of living index figure of 300 only cannot be 
sustained. On similar facts and circumstances the Hon’ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal construed the notice, dated 18th February 1947, as showing that the 
Company offered payment of dearness allowance according to the Bengal 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2537 


এ) সস ہے‎ oe 


Chamber of Commerce scheme lihked to the middle-class living index ‘figure as 
publishtd by that body and the clerical staff accepted it as a condition of their 
service. It was further held that the scheme conferred on the employces an 
advantage from the time it was introduced into the conditions of service, for it 
entitled the employees to an automatic increase with exact precision, in the 
amount of dearness allowance, with the rise of the cost of living index. It was 
also held that this advantage they were enjoying as of right at the time when 
the award of the First Engineering Tribunal was given. All these equally 
apply in the present case to gencral, clerical and subordinate staff employed at 
the factory of this Company. 


The Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal also held that dearness allowance 
according to the scale of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce was at the time of 
the First Engineering Tribunal “an existing advantage” and that it came within 
the saving of the award of the First Engineering Tribunal. So it is too late in 
the day for the Company to say that under the award of the First Engineering 
Tribunal what was protected was not whole of the Bengal Chamber of Com- 
merce scheme of dearness allowance but the highest rates of dearness allowance 
which the Company paid up to July 1948. 


From August 1948, it is said by the Company that the position has changed. 
The Company declined to follow the Bengal Caamber of Commerce scheme of 
dearness allowance any further with the rise of the cost of living index beyond 
the rates of dearness allowance at which they paid to these categories of staff 
for July 1948. Then while the Company was paying from August 1948 at the 
old rates but different from the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme, the 
award of the First Engineering Tribunal lapsed on 31st March 1949 with the 
expiry of one year from the date it came into force. Then payment of dear- 
ness allowance by the Company to these categories of staff however continued 
at the 010 rates but different from the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme. 
These rates which are the existing rates from August 1948, are 70 per 
cent. of the basic salary on the first hundred rupees, 35 per cent. on the next 
one hundred rupees and 174 per cent. on the remainder for the general and 
clerical staff and a flat rate of Rs. 43 per month for the subordinate staff. So 
the position at the time of Second Engineering Tribunal was that these categories 
of workmen of the factory were not actually receiving dearness allowance 
according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme from August 1948 but 
at different rates which were lesser than the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme but greater than those awarded by the First Engineering Tribunal. Then 
my attention has been drawn to the observations in the award of the Second 
Enginecring Tribunal that what was pointed out to that Tribunal was that the 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance was actually being 
applied to the Head Office of some engineering concerns (and not 10 the 
factory). From all these it is contended on behalf of the Company that the 
award of the Second Engineering Tribunal, which is operative and binding on 
the parties could have at best protected the existing rate of dearness allowance 
which the Company was then paying and not Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme of dearness allowance for these categories of employees at the factory. 
On careful scrutiny it, however, appears that such contention cannot be sustained. 
When these categories of employees have been found eligible to be paid 
dearness allowance according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme as a 
condition of their service and when further it has been found to be within the 
saving of the award of the First Engineering Tribunal on the analogy of the case 
of Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., it is obvious that claim of dearness allowance 
according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme must be deemed to have 
been protected by the award of the Second Engineering Tribunal, although they 
were not then actually receiving dearness allowance at that rate and although only 
case of the employees of the Head Office of some engineering concerns having 


2538 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 (Parr | 
--س بت پووٛپپچپ یی ''و‌'مسی  --.--.۔۔'۔'.۔'ڈھڈآژژ سی :شش صن .-..تٹ۲۲.ی:].۳سشیث ٹک س“سیيپتے‎ 
then been paid at the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allow. 
ance was brought to the notice of the said Tribunal and not of the en\ployees 
of the factory. Having regard to the reservations made in the award of 0116 
Second Engineering Tribunal and having regard to the facts and circumstances 
of the case, | am of opinion that the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of 
dearness allowance to which these categories of employees at the factory were 
eligible as a condition of their service and which came within the saving of the 
first award was protected by the award of the Second Engineering Tribunal 101 
them. So I find no reasonable answer on the part of the Company why it should 
refuse to accede to the demand of general, clerical and subordinate staft employed 
at the factory of the Company to higher dearness allowance under the Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce scheme, more so when they have been paying dear. 
ness allowance at higher rates according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme to the same categories of employees at their Head Office. I, therefore 
find that these categories of employees at the factory are entitled to be paid 
dearness allowance according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme linked 
to the rise in the cost of living index. 


As to the objection of the Company that the workmen having not raised the 
present dispute before the Second Engineering Tribunal to which the Company 
and their workmen were parties, they cannot now agitate the matter. am 
unable to sustain it. When it has been found by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal in the case of Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., that the existing advantage 
in the shape of Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance was 
within the saving of the award of the First Engineering Tribunal, such advantage 
of being paid dearness allowance according to the scheme of Bengal Chamber 
of Commerce must be presumed to have continued till the matter of dearness 
allowance came up again for adjudication before the Second Engineering Tri- 
bunal. So, there was nothing for these workmen to agitate at the time, it having 
been an existing advantage as a condition of their service and it having been 
protected by the award of the First Engineering Tribunal. The contention of 
the Company that under the award of the Second Engineering Tribunal what was 
at best protected is not the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness 
allowance but the rates of dearness allowance which the Company was then pay- 
ing to these catégories of employees being 70 per cent. of the basic salary on the 
first hundred rupees, 35 per cent. on the next one hundred rupees and 174 per 
cent. on the remainder for the general and clerical staff and a flat rate of Rs. 43 

er month for the subordinate staff cannot be sustained. The award of the 

econd Engineering Tribunal, it has already been seen, must be deemed to have 
protected the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance for 
those who were eligible to the said scale of dearness allowance. 


Likewise the plea of the Company that the workmen have waived _ their 
present claim cannot be sustained. It has already been noted that as soon as 
the Company refused to pay from August 1948 dearness allowance according 
to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme and in place it continued to pay 
at the old rates of July 1948, complaint was made by the then Union on behalf 
of the workmen and it was repeated until reference was made to this Tribunal 
for adjudication. There was no doubt lull intermittently and for long period 
in between 1950 and 1952, but the explanation for it offered by the workmen 
is that they were awaiting result of adjudication upon identical dispute with the 
Indian Galvanizing Co., Ltd., and their workmen under the same Managing 
Agents. It was natural that when similar issue was raised, its result should be 
awaited by the parties. In the circumstances it cannot be held that the claim 


was waived. 


Now, as to the question raised by the Company as to who comes within the 
scope of the present reference, the Government order makes mention of three 


Part 1 | THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2539 
ee স্পা 


categories of employees of the factory, namely general, clerical and subordinate 
staff. There is no dispute betwecn the parties that clerical and subordinate staff 
are all ‘workmen who would be bound by the award in this case. As to the 
general staff, the Company alleges that all of them are not workmen within the 
meaning of the Act. The circular of the Managing Agents attached to Ext. 1 
defines who are general staff. There is no evidence before this Tribunal showing 
the duty of the different employees grouped under the head “General Staff”. 
The workmen represented by Shri Bimal Chandra Sinha and others apparently 
in answer to the query from the Company wrote to the Assistant Secretary to 
the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, on 28th December 1953, 
after the reference, to the effect that by general staff they mean and include those 
who have got to do manual and clerical work as distinct from the exclusive 
clerical staff. According to them general staff does not include supervisory staff. 
So, I agree with the Company that the award in this case would apply only to 
those of the general staff who are workmen within the meaning of the Act and 
to none else. 


As regards claim of the workmen represented by Shri Bimal Chandra Sinha 
and others and by Employees Congress that the above categories of employees 
who have joined service since August 1948 should also get dearness allowance 
according to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale, I do not agree. In 
respect of the new entrants after July 1948, there cannot be any question of 
their pre-existing rights being protected under the awards of the First and 
Second Engineering Tribunals. It has already been stated that the Company 
declincd to implement the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness 
allowance from August 1948. So these new entrants cannot claim Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance as_ their condition of 
service beyond the rates at which they are being paid. So, only those workmen 
of the above three categories who joined service before August 1948 be entitled 
to get dearness allowance according to the scheme of the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce to the full extent linked to the cost of living index and none else. 


\ 

৯৪309 the contention of the Company that when dearness allowance is 
being paid to the subordinaté staff at a flat rate and not on percentage basis, 
their case does not come within the scheme of Bengal Chamber of Commerce, 
I am unable to uphold it. From different annexures appended to the written 
statements of the workmen and the Employees’ Congress, it appears that 
though the subordinate staff was being paid at a flat rate, it was being paid on 
the basis of the cost of living index figure of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce 
scheme as it varied from time to time, the flat rate being the lowest of the then 
particular cost of living index group. Annexure A2 of the written statement 
by the workmen reveals that the subordinate staff was paid dearness allowance 
at a flat rate of Rs. 25 per month for March 1947 on the then cost of living 
index group. Annexure A3 to the same written statement shows that it was 
paid at the rate of Rs. 31 per monthon different cost of living index group. 
Annexure A4 shows payment at the rate of Rs. 34 per month on the index 
group of 281 to 290. Annexure A6 shows payment at the rate of Rs. 37 
per month on the index group of 291 to 300. Annexure AS shows payment 
at the rate of Rs. 43 per month at the index level 300 to 332. It has already 
been noted that subordinate staff is being paid at this rate of Rs. 43 from 
August 1948 notwithstanding rise in the cost of living index group since then. 
It is, therefore, apparent that in the case of the subordinate staff too, the Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce scheme of dearness allowance linked to the cost of 
living index figures was adopted and they are eligible to it. 


The Company also alleges that due to its precarious financial condition it 
it unable to pay in future higher rates of dearness allowance according to the 


2540 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 ۱1! یں‎ ] 
س۹ت ژث ہچ کٗٗە پگ )6ی6س ٹپیٹ -ے-.۔ںٍں+ەسٔث-ہةےے‎ ییسٰٔپسىپپ-پ‌-٠.--ٹژککسگچہخىًٛٔپسسسسپسىس+ے+‌ً]ععُەۃە۔‌-‎ 
Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme or the arrears from August 1948, being 
the excess over what had already been paid. 


The capacity of the employer to pay is an important factor in determining 
the amount of dearness allowance but the present case is not one for fixation 
of dearness allowance but for dearness allowance said to have been offered and 
accepted as a condition of service and protected by the awards. So the ques- 
tion of capacity of the employer to pay cannot, strictly speaking, arise in this 
case except regarding claim for the past (that is, the arrears) which has arisen 
out of peculiar circumstances of the case and about which accounts have already 
been settled. Likewise, Company’s claim for limitation of the amount of 
dearness allowance to two-third of the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme 
beyond the index group of 332 from which the Company stopped payment on 
account of precarious financial position of the Company cannot be upheld; as 
otherwise it would in effect allow the Company to go back upon what they pro- 
mised as a condition of service and enable it to pay dearness allowance according 
to the existing scale as in vogue since August 1948 without legally terminating 
the existing contract. The case of Powells, Ltd., and their workmen reported 
in 1952, L.A.C., page 334, cited by the Company in this respect has no appli- 
cation to the peculiar facts of the present case. This is not a case where 
dearness allowance is being fixed but one where it is claimd as a condition of 
service and protected by the successive awards of the Engineering Tribunals. 
So, I am of opinion that the various categories of the employees at the factory 
with whom we are concerned are entitled to be paid dearness allowance accord- 
ing to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme so long the service conditions 
are not changed or the operation of the award does not come to an end. 


As regards the claim to accumulated arrears from August 1948, this stands 
on a somewhat different footing. Ordinarily this would have been allowed in 
full to the workmen. But having regard to the precarious financial condition 
of the Company and also the larger interests of the employer and employees 
themselves, 1 must jold that this should not be allowed in full in the present 
case. If the additional burden of entire arrear dues be now imposed on the 
Company, it will be too heavy for the Company in its present financial strin- 
gency to bear and may lead to its collapse, thereby throwing out all its workers 
out of employment. This is an eventuality which should be avoided by all 
means as the goose that lays golden eggs has to be preserved and not killed 
outright. It appears that the paid-up capital of the Company is Rs. 5 lakhs 
while it had incurred a loss of Rs. 3,46,940 between July 1949 and June 1953. 
It was further alleged that the accounts for second half of 1953 would reveal 
a further loss of half lakh, thus total loss exceeding 4 lakhs. Then it appears 
that if these three categories of staff at the factory have got to be paid in full 
their arrears dues from August 1948 till June 1954, the total amount of arrears 
being the excess over what had already been paid would come to Rs. 2,32,435. 
This would increase the total loss to more than 64 lakhs thereby wholly wiping 
out the paid-up capital. So, if the arrears are allowed from August 1948, the 
Company cannot obviously bear the burden and would likely close down there- 
by producing more evil than good. I think, this is a position which will be 
conducive to-well being neither of the Company nor of the employees. So, 
considering all the evidence and circumstances I think, it will be fair and equit- 
able if the Company is directed to pay the arrears of dearness allowance accord- 
ing to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme being the excess over what had 
already been paid from the date of the present reference, that 15 from 26th 
October 1953. The Company is accordingly directed to pay such arrears from 
26th October 1953 up to June 1954 within two months from the date the award 
becomes enforceable. The Company is also to pay dearness allowance accord- 
ing to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scheme from July 1954 onwards এ]

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
Shri Hiraman Shresta. The workman Shri Hiraman Shresta was discharged from 
service on 20th June 1953, on the ground of misconduct during the pendency of 
the reference made by Government order No. 1455Dis./D/10L-91/53, dated 
30th April 1953, before this Tribunal. Hence the complaint under section 33A 
by the workman. He alleges that he was a member of the Works Committee 
elected by the workers and was Assistant Secretary of the Union. The Company 
therefore, by way of victimisation discharged him on false charges. The Com- 
pany opposite party denies all these allegations and pleads that it acted bona fide 
in the matter. 


The point which therefore arises for determination in this case is, whether 
the discharge is justified. 


DECISION. 


In support of the case the petitioner has deposed (P.W. 1). The opposite 
party Company on the other hand has examined its night shift Chargeman, 
D.W. 1 Shri Gopal Chandra Banerjee, the Electrician, D.W. 2 Shri Jahed Ali, the 
Fitter, D.W. 3, Shri Pasupati Maity and the Welfare Officer, D.W. 4 Shri Biswa 
Nath Dutta, besides proving documents, Exts. A to E. 


The workman Shri Hiraman Shresta after cross-examining D.W. 1 left the 
Tribunal and took no further part in the proceeding. Thereafter the proceeding 
continued in his absence under rule 15 of the Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 
1947. 


The petitioner Shri Hiraman Shresta was an operator who was on duty in the 
night shift on the 10th of January 1952. In that night he was put to work on 
Lathe Machine. He admittedly came to duty late by 15 minutes having 
reached at 8-15 p.m. in place of 8 p.m. The Chargeman condoned his late 
coming and allowed him full attendance as he had claimed to have attended the 
Works Committee meeting before. Thercafter Shri Hiraman Shresta seported 
to the Electrician, D.W. 2, that the machine in which he was to work was out 
of order. D.W. 2 in turn brought it to the notice of the Chargeman, D.W. | 
and requested him for a helper to help him (D.W. 2), to repair the machine. 
D.W. 1 accordingly directed the Fitter (D.W. 3) to help the Eelectrician to 
repair the said machine. The Chargeman also put the workman Shri Hiraman 
Shresta to idle-time pending repair of the machine. After about 45 minutes the 
machine was brought to order by D.W. 2 and D.W. 3. They found that the 
machine was intentionally jammed by putting it on gear. They accordingly 
mide complaint about it to the Chargeman (as per Annexures “A1” and 
“A2” to the written statement of the Company). When _ thereafter 
Shri Hiraman Shresta was told that the machine was brought to order and he was 
to resume duty, he took D.W. 2 to task why they had repaired the machine so 
quickly. Shri Hiraman Shresta then resumed his duty after two hours, that 1s, 
at 10 p.m. and worked up to 1 a.m. The evidence shows that during this period 
his output was very low as he produced only 3 VB-27 Pistons in place of normal 
output of 44 Pistons. 


After recess break from 1 a.m. to 1-30 a.m. when the Chargeman went on 
his usual round to wake up the workmen and to ask them to resume duty, he 
(D.W. 1), found Shri Hiraman Shresta sleeping outside the factory. He awoke 
him and asked him to go to duty and then left for other workers. Thereafter 
when the Chargeman was out on his second round at about 1-45 a.m., he found 
Shri Hiraman Shresta sitting at the same place where he was previously found 
sleeping along with two other workmen, who were on idle-time. The Charge- 
man again asked him to go to his duty but Shri Hiraman Shresta did not carry 
out his instructions. The Chargeman found him on his third round, 15 or 20

minutes later, sleeping there. He awoke him and asked him to go to duty.‏ 
Thereafter the evidence shows that the Works Manager came on his round at 3‏ 
a.m. when he found Shri Hiraman Shresta sleeping outside the factory during his‏ 
duty hours. The Chargeman was asked by the Works Manager to explain why‏ 
Shri Hiraman Shresta was absent from his machine. The Chargeman accord-‏ 
ingly made report (Annexure “B” to the written statement). On these tacts a‏ 
charge-sheet was issued to the complainant on 15th June 1953 (Ext. 00).‏ 
He was charged for intentional tampering with the machine, insubordination and‏ 
gross negligence in the performance of duty (Ext. C). The workman submitted‏ 
explanation on the reverse of the charge-sheet on 17th June 1953. He admitted‏ 
that after there was break for tiffin at 1 a.m., he had fallen asleep as he had no‏ 
sleep previously and that somebody had awakened him at 3 a.m., and that he‏ 
was then called by the Works Manager and was questioned whether he was‏ 
sleeping. In his deposition he also admitted of having been questioned whether‏ 
he tampered with the machine. As regards production he admitted that he‏ 
produced 34 Pistons in place of normal output of 44 Pistons during work from‏ 
p.m. to 1 a.m. Although he denies having been thrice called by the Chargeman‏ 10 
to go to duty after recess hour was over, the evidence of the Chargeman is that‏ 
he awoke him and asked him thrice to resume duty. There is nothing to show‏ 
why the Chargeman would depose falsely against him. This is not a new case‏ 
either as it finds mention in the charge-sheet itself that the Chargeman had told‏ 
him thrice to go to work after the tiffin bell. Then the evidence of the Electri-‏ 
cian and the Fitter (D.W. 2 and D.W. 3), read with their report shows that the‏ 
machine was purposely jammed by putting it on gear. Further evidence of‏ 
D.W. 2 that when Shri Hiraman Shresta was asked to resume duty he took thenr‏ 
to task why they repaired the machine so quickly confirms this. Shri Hiraman‏ 
Shresta was admittedly questioned by the Works Manager whether he tampered‏ 
with the machine. These would suggest that in order to find an excuse for‏ 
sleep 106 had purposely put the machine to gear and thus jammed it. P.W. ٤٥‏ 
eviderice that he helped in the repair is denied by D.W. 2 and D.W. 3. Their‏ 
denial \is supported by circumstances. The evidence also shows that after‏ 
explanation was submitted an enquiry was held. The workman admits that after‏ 
he had submitted explanation, the Works Manager questioned him in his office.‏ 
Annexute “E9” is the proceeding of the enquiry which shows that Shri Hiraman‏ 
Shresta was asked to cross-examine the witnesses if he liked and to produce‏ 
witnesses, if any, in, support of his explanation. It appears that he had declined‏ 
to do so. So his evidence to the contrary before this Tribunal cannot be‏ 


accepted. 


In view of the evidence and circumstances before the Management, it was 
justified in holding that the charges were established. The action against him, 
it will therefore appear, took place in normal and natural course and had nothing 
to do with his alleged Union activities. I am, therefore, of opinion that the dis- 
charge was justified. The complaint must accordingly fail. 


I award accordingly.

AWARD. 


This application relates to the Government Order of Reference No. 4055- 
Dis./D/8L-20/52, dated 22nd December 1952, over صد‎ industrial dispute 
betwecn Manindra Cotton Mills, Ltd., and their workmen represented by 
Manindra Mill Sramik Sangha. The award on this dispute was published in

On 27th January 1953 Sontosh Goon, a permanent workman of the Com- 
pany working in the capacity of a Sizer, applied under section 33A of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947, stating that he was served with a charge-sheet con- 
taining false allegations on 29th December 1952 and was discharged on 8th 
January 1953, without taking permission of the Tribunal. It is further stated 
that the petitioner is an active member of the Manindra Mill Sramik Sangha, 
being the Treasurer of the same, and that he was, therefore, victimised by the 
Company. The~petitioner prays that he should be reinstated with compensa- 
tion for the period of unemployment. 


The Company, in its written statement, states that through inadvertence, the 
order of dismissal was served on the petitioner on 8th January 1953, but very 
soon thereafter, the mistake was detected and before this application under 
section 33A was filed by the petitioner, he was informed that he was suspended 
and not dismissed or discharged on the grounds referred to in the notice, dated 
8th January 1953. The Company states further that for some time before the 
petitioner was placed under suspension, he was attempting to instigate and illeg- 
ally incite loyal workers of the Mill to take part in a strike and other subversive

سسجت 


activitics during the pendency of the proceeding before the Tribunal. He was 
also guilty of other misconduct, viz., wilful insubordination and disobedience 
to the lawful and the reasonable order of his superior, habitual negligence or 
neglect of work, etc. The petitioner was not, therefore, entitled to any relief, 
as prayed for. 


On the date of hearing on 4th June 1954, the parties filed a joint petition 
of compromise, which appears as Appendix A to this award. On a perusal 
of the compromise petition, it appears that the terms thereof are reasonable 
and the petition should be accepted. I, therefore, accept the compromise 
petition in Appendix A and award in accordance with the terms thereof. The 
compromise petition in Appendix A shall form a part of this award.

AWARD. 


Issue no 2.—Whether durwans are entitled to overtime pay? 


The Britannia Biscuit Company has factories in Calcutta, Delhi and Bombay. 
In Calcutta the factory was situated at Dum Dum. Since January 1952, the 
Company commenced erection of a new factory at Behala by way of shifting 
its factory from Dum Dum. As a consequence several durwans had to be 
detained at Dum Dum and some were posted at Behala during the said transi- 
tional period. The contention of the durwans is that usually as a service con- 
dition they would get one day’s weekly off but because of this removal of the 
factory from Dum Dum to Behala they had to work on the off days also (17 
off days in 17 wecks) but the Company has not paid any extra amount for this 
overtime work. The durwans contend that now the normal situation has been 
restored and they do not work more than 8 hours a day as before. 


On behalf of the Company it is urged that durwans enjoy better service 
condition in other respect than other workmen in the factory, such as “ leave”, 
and therefure durwans cannot claim extra payment for overtime work and that 
the overtime work is not a frequent incident so far as the durwans are concern- 
ed and that for this special overtime work the durwans should not get anything. 


In the evidence I find that when the durwans were put to overtime work 
as aforesaid the Management assured them that for this overtime work, the 
claim of the durwans would be considered by the Management. There is no 
challenge of this allegation made by the durwans. It is admitted that for fire 
brigade training work durwans were paid separately. Everybody should have 
some fixed hours of work. It is not at all fair that the Management should 
not pay any extra allowance to the durwans for the special overtime work 
obtain¢gd from them by the Management during the factory removal period. 
That Overtime work was not confined to a day or two only or at intervals but 
it was & regular prolongation of actual duty period for a reasonably long period 
of time, say 17 days. In these circumstances my opinion is that the durwans 
who rendered such overtime work during the said transitional period are to 
be paid \an extra allowance at the flat rate of Rs. 15 per head for the entire 
overtime ‘period and the said payment is to be made by the Company within 
a week from the date of the publication of the award. 


Issue No. 3.—Whether men employed in the Paper Cutting Section should be 
considered as semi-skilled ? 


In this factory there is a section called Machine Section, e.g., where mixing, 
kneading, etc., are done. There is another section called Packing Section where 
the finished biscuits are packed in tin and cardboard boxes and suitably labélled. 
In the Biscuit Factory packing is also an important work. If the lining inside 
the boxes and the padding therein be defective, the whole biscuits would be 
spoilt within a short time and there will be greater breakage. 


The Unions contend that the (Paper Cutting Section men) paper cutters 
should be paid wages at par with that of the Machine Section men inasmuch 
as the works done by both the sections are almost of equal nature and that 
these involve equal amount of risk and require equal amount of skill. 


From the evidence I find that previously the Paper Cutting Section had 
several accidents but the incidence of such accidents is now rare as the workers 
have become much experienced in handling the paper cutting machines. At 
the desire of both the parties I inspected the paper cutting machines and mixing 
machine in operation in the Behala Factory of this company in the presence 
of the representatives of both the parties. Jn the Paper Cutting Section I 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1904 [Parr 1‏ 2552 
...می تسچ ہہ ہے ہے جےہ شس جج Sn‏ 


found 3 machines, 2 of which are of modern type, They require less amount 
of skill in handling them. I think an ordinary cooly can operate thew, easily 
and do the work of paper cutting like the workmen who are doing that work 
for a long time. But the old type machine is really difficult to operate on the 
part of a new man unless he is trained for a fairly long time. The workmen 
operating the old type paper cutting machine and the men operating the mixing 
machine in the Machine Section appear to me to be equally skilled and trained 
and in my opinion there should not be any distinction between the two regard- 
ing their wages and allowances. I find that the old type paper cutting treadle 
machine men should be considered as semi-skilled. There is no satisfactory 
evidence that any reliable expert was ever engaged by the company to evaluate 
the jobs of the paper cutting machine men compared with those of the Machine 
Section men. So I have no hesitation in coming to the conclusion that the 
old type paper cutting machine (treadle machine) men should be considered 
as semi-skilled in view of the evidence adduced and also of what I have per- 
sonally seen with my own eyes at the local inspection. 


Issue No. 4.—Whether discriminatory tactics have been employed in the cases 
of Santosh Mondal, Vice Department, Narayan Mistry, Fitter and Bijoy 
Chandra Das, Carpenter. What relief are they entitled to? 


The Unions gave up the cases of Santosh Mofdal, and Narayan Mistry. 
The case of Bijoy Chandra Das, Carpenter, alone has been canvassed at the 
hearing. His case is that he has been working in this factory for the last 44 
years as a Carpenter and he was appointed at a salary of Rs. 35 per month 
and now he gets only Rs. 46 per month plus Rs. 35 as dearness allowance 
whereas one Bachan Singh who is not superior to him in any respect has been 
recently appointed by the management to do the same nature of work at a 
salary of Rs. 100 per month and it is contended that this discrimination 
between Bijoy Chandra Das and Bachan Singh should be done away with. 


The contention of the management is that Bachan is not a ordinary carpenter 
but he is a joincr and he can make furniture which Bijoy Das cannot do. 
From the evidence I find that Bachan Singh was a joiner in the Engineering 
Firm of Britannia Building Co., and as head mistry of that firm he did the 
works of panelling joinery and other skillful works in the Behala factory of 
this Biscuit Company when the aforesaid Engineering Company constructed 
the new factory at Behala. Thereafter Bachan Singh has been appointed as 
a Carpenter in this Biscuit Company. It is the option of the company to decide 
whom it will appoint as a special joiner or carpenter and on what wages. It 
is not a case of discrimination between two workmen working in a factory. 
Bijoy Das was in service from before. Bachan Singh was not in service at all 
when these wages were settled. Moreover from the evidence of Bijoy Das I 
find that a carpenter like Bachan Singh could not be available at Jess than 
Rs. 100 as monthly salary at the time when Bachan Singh was selected for the 
post. In these circumstances I hold that the contention of Bijoy Chandra 
Das is unfounded and that no discriminatory tactics have been employed by 
the company in the matter of appointment of Bachan Singh as a Carpenter at 
a higher wages than those of Bijoy Chandra Das. 


Issue No. 5.—Whether suspension of Abdul Aziz during pendency of concilia-

to? : 

Abdul Aziz was suspended by the Manager as per Company’s order, dated

Abdul Aziz explained that on the date in question he was booked his own

It appears from the evidence that Abdul Aziz was an Office bearer of the 
Union and the Union also selected him as a member of the Committee to deal

Abdul Aziz would create a breeze over this defect in the egg served out to 
him. The Company has not produced its papers to show that Abdul Aziz was 
not booked for his meal on that day, although Abdul Aziz had clearly stated 
in his reply to the charge that he was not taking share of any meal booked by 
another person and that the meal concerned was booked in his own name. 
There was some debate no doubt between Abdul Aziz and the canteen Super- 
1১01, and it is admitted that on the report of the said canteen Supervisor this 
charge-sheet was framed against Abdul Aziz. I find no satisfactory evidence 
on the side of the management to show the ground of charge No. 1, in Ext. D. 
As regards charge No. 2, there is no tangible evidence as to what exact language 
Abdul Aziz used towards the said canteen Supervisor upon which the canteen 
Supervisor reported to the Mnagement that Abdul Aziz’s conduct was arrogant 
and insulting. Charge No. 3, falls to the ground because it is now clear from 
the evidence that Abdul Aziz went up to the counter of the canteen where 
every person has the right to go on business. Abdul Aziz also went there on 
business, viz., to enquire how and why the defective egg was supplied to him. 
The charge that Abdul Aziz went inside the kitchen is entirely incorrect. As 
amatter of fact Abdul Aziz did not go inside the kitchen. The next part of 
the charge is that Abdul Aziz has no right to argue with the canteen staff. 
Ordinarily people do not move the higher authority on each and every point 
0 grievance. I do not think that Abdul Aziz committed such wrong by

“We the canteen men misappropriate the things at the cost of the work- 
men taking meal in the canteen”, 


and that by “insinuating” remark I meant that Abdul Aziz used such expres- 
sions as— 
“Aisa Nahi Bardast Karega, Adha Egg Dia” 


I cannot agree that this can be said to be an insulting one. But with regard 
to the insinuating remark there are some circumstances which should be 
referred to. It appears from the evidence that one Durga Babu 15 the 
maternal uncle-in-law of this canteen Supervisor. When the canteen Super- 
visor was asked in cross-examination as to what Durga Babu was to him, the 
canteen Supervisor got much annoyed and refused to answer the said question 
and on the other hand went out of his way to argue with the cross-examiner 
that the question was irrelevant. Subsequently it appeared from the evidence 
that the said Durga Babu is an employee in the Head Office of this company 
and it also emerged in his evidence that canteen 19 run by a contractor and 
that the said contractor is no other than the brother-in-law of the said Durga 
Babu. Therefore the canteen Supervisor has some interest in the canteen 
affairs which a person having no relationship with the contractor would not 
have. In guch circumstances it is probable on the part of the contractor's 
relation Mohon Babu (canteen Supervisor) to find fault with anything spoken 
regarding the canteen affairs. The Labour Officer and the Manager ought to 
have been careful enough to have it from the canteen Supervisor as to what 
exact word Abdul Aziz had used on the basis of which the canteen Supervisor 
reported that Abdul Aziz made “insinuating and insulting” remarks to him. 
Remark cannot be held to be insulting and insinuating simply because the com- 
plainant says that the remark was so. It is a matter of judgment. The canteen 
Supervisor who happens to be the relation of the canteen contractor may find 
insult and insinuation in every word used regarding canteen affairs, but unless 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2555 
S888 IS 


the Labour Officer and the Manager had known the exact words used, it was 
simply ,difficult and impossible on their part to decide or judge whether those 
words were really insinuating or insulting. 1 remember that in a session trial 
the prosecution witness deposed that the accused in the murder case made 
extra judicial confession of his guilt. When I asked the witness to reproduce 
the exact words used by the said confessing accused, the witncss said that the 
accused uttered “pup pup Maha pup” and nothing else. The jurors could not 
spell out any confession of guilt from the said utterance. The principle laid 
down in the old case of Queen vs. Shoobjan, 10 B.L.R., page 332, is still the 
Jaw on the point. It was held there that the court should not accept merely 
the conclusions at which witnesses deposing to a confession, themselves arrived 
at from the answers which the accused gave to the questions put by them and 
that the answers themselves are the relevant materials. In the order of suspen- 
sion (vide the bottom of the charge-sheet) the period of suspension is said to 
be 4 days and not 5 days as stated in Annexure “A”. In the evidence also 
Abdul Aziz admits that he was suspended for 4 days. In the standing Orders 
maximum period of suspension is said to 4 days only. So I think that the 
statement in Annexure “A” is mistaken and it is held that the suspension is not 
a violation of any clause of the Standing Orders. 


In the Standing Orders there is no express provision that the management 
has any right to suspend without pay or allowance. But there is a provision 
to the effect “if however, the order is rescinded, the worker shall be deemed 
to be on duty during the full period of suspension and shall be entitled to the 
same wages as he would have received if he had not been suspended”. From 
this it has been argued that as the suspension order was not rescinded by the 
management as a result of the enquiry, the employee was not to be deemed 
to be on duty during the whole pcriod of suspension and shall not be entitled 
to the wages for the period. I think from this provision لا‎ the Standing 
Order, the employee cannot be legally deemed to be not on, duty during the 
period ۵٤۲ suspension. The deeming provision cannot be interpreted in that 
way. 0 admitted that Abdul Aziz has not been paid anything for the said 
period of| 4 days of suspension. I have followed in several cases the principle 
1910 ای‎ in Warburton vs. Taffvale Railway Company (1902), 18 T.L.R., 
Page 420:— 


“where an employer is entitled to suspend an employee and withhold his 
wages during the period of suspension, the employee is entitled to 
wages during the period of suspension if he is dismissed at the end 
of that period” and it was held in that case that “the suspended 
employee was in Company's service during the suspension period”. 


So it follows that even if the company has power to suspend under the Stand- 
ing Order, relation between the parties was not suspended. The contrary view 
was however taken in Wallwork vs. Fielding (1922), 2 K.B., page 66; where 
it has been held that where there is a power to suspend the suspension order 
suspends for the time being, the contract of relation between the parties on 
both sides and therefore the employer is relieved of in performing his part of 
the contract, viz., to pay the wages. In the latter case the said case of 
Warburton vs. Taffvale Railway Company, does not appear to have been 
referred to. 


The Standing Order provision cannot be interpreted in the way as has been 
done by the representative of the Company. The Standing Order provides 
that “if the suspension is rescinded, the worker shall be deemed to be on duty 
during the full period of suspension”. This provision cannot be construed 
that if the suspension is not rescinded, the worker shall not be deemed to be 
on duty during the period of suspension. The maxim expressio unius excrusio 


2556 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 (Parr ] 


alterius is one that requires to be watched (per Justice Wills, 1887-19 Q.B.N. 
page-400 at page-406). The interpretation that the worker shall‘ not be 
deemed to be on duty if the suspension order is not rescinded cannot be said 
to be an inevitable corollary of the state of affairs which is specifically provid. 
ed for in the Standing Order on the basis of the said “deeming” provision. If 
the said “deeming” provision (in case the suspension order is ultimately 
rescinded) in the Standing Order be treated as a proviso the principle laid 
dlown in West Derby Union vs. Metropolitan Life Assurance Society, 1887, 
A.C. page-697, would appear to be applicable in this present case. There it 
was observed— 


“That if the language of the enacting part of the statute does not contain 
the provisions which are said to occur in it, you cannot derive the 
said provision by implications from a proviso”. 


I am of opinion that there is no satisfactory evidence that Abdul Aziz made 
any insulting or insinuating remark to the canteen Supervisor, Shri Chatterjee. 
On the other hand it seems to me that Shri Chatterjee was hypersensitive and 
because of his relationship with the Canteen Contractor he was ready to smell 
insult and insinuation from anything whatsoever, concerning the state of affairs 
of the Canteen. The canteen Supervisor is not a superior officer to Abdul 
Aziz. So the remark alleged to have been made by Abdu! Aziz towards the 
canteen Supervisor must be clearly shown by evidence to be grossly abusive 
language, otherwise Abdul Aziz cannot be held to be guilty of misconduct for 
which he would be punished by suspension under the Standing Order. The 
mere fact that Abdul Aziz got much annoyed because of the defective egg 
being served to him and that he indulged in loud voice over the said affair in 
the Cantecn cannot be said to be a riotous or disorderly behaviour or “any act 
subversive of discipline”. It has been remarked in a foreign case that in these 
days a much greater laxity of language is permitted than what was the case 
many years ago. In that case the words which Mr. Gill 00590 ا٥‎ Mr. Finnerman 
were found to be abusive language and it was observed that the use of such 
words “particularly when used by an employee to the man supervising him in 
his work, 1.e., to the man who 13 representing in the disciplinary sense the 
employer—amounts to misconduct”. In the present case, the canteen Super- 
visor was not a person. supervising the work of Abdul Aziz nor was this 
canteen Supervisor a superior officer to Abdul Aziz. So tHe present case is 
distinguishable from the case of Mr. Gill vs. Finnerman. 


It is the contention of the Union that Abdul Aziz was suspended by the 
management when the conciliation proceeding was pending before the Con- 
cilliation Officer and that the suspension order was passed without any permis- 
sion from the Conciliation Officer. It is contended that under the Govern- 
ment notification Labour Officer is also ex officio a Conciliation Officer. 
Such notification has not been produced here before me. There is a 10110 
purporting to have been addressed by the Labour Officer to the company in 
the matter of an Industrial Dispute. The suspension order was dated 10th 
June 1952. The letter of the Labour Officer (Ext. 6) is dated 19fh June 
1952. Frdém this letter it does not appear that Britannia Biscuit Company was 
informed of the said proceeding prior to the date of this letter, on the other 
hand it appears that the representative of the Union was asked to see the Labour 
Officer on 21st June 1952. So this letter is irrelevant. But there is another 
Jetter Ext. 6(a), dated 9th May 1952, by which Labour Officer asked the 
representative of this company to see him for joint discussion on 30th May 
1952. That was a letter regarding “Grievances of the workers”. So it would 
appear, if I am to assume that the Labour Officer was a Conciliation Officer 
that the suspension order was passed after the Conciliation Officer had began 
and before it terminated. I am not in a position to hold that the “Labour

সস এ 
Officer ‘was a Conciliation Officer, I cannot conclude that this suspension was 
in contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. I have already 
come to the conclusion that the suspension order with the forfeiture of the 
wages during the suspension period was an unjustified order and it should be 
set aside and Abdul Aziz should be paid his wages and allowance for the said 
period of four days suspension and accordingly I direct that the Company ۷١ 91121] 
pay the said amount to Abdul Aziz within a weck from the date of publication
