Issue No. 7.—Revision of standing orders. 


The Union has made out a case in the written statement that the Standing 
Orders should be révised in such a way as to meet the following demands:— 


(1) After three months’ service all workmen should be made permanent. 
without discrimination. 


(ii) In cases of recruitment workmen’s nominees should get first prefer- 
ence. 


(111) In cases of discharge and retirement, workmen should get gratuity~ 
at the rate of one month’s wages for each year of service. 


(iv) Whenever there is any involuntary unemployment, the workmem 
should be paid full wages. 


(v) In cases of misconduct, there must a _ bi-partite enquiry before: 
punishment is awarded. 


The Company contends that these revisions as prayed for should not be 
granted and that the suggestions are unreasonable. 


Let me now discuss the points one by one. 


Point\ No. (i).—It is absurd that after three months’ service all workmer 
whether probationer or temporary or casual should be made permanent without 
discrimination. In the previous Award (see Calcutta Gazette, September 27 
1951), the Union raised the contention with regard to fixation of the proba- 
tionary period only and the Tribunal observed that the existing practice should’ 
not be disturbed inasmuchas it has been “asserted by the Factory Manager, 
Mr. Garratte that the praqbationary period according to the practice of the 
company never exceeds three months”. In the Standing Order there is no 
period stated with regard to probationer. It may be that in this company 
probationers are made permanent ordinarily after three months’ satisfactory 
probation but if any rule is to be laid down in the Standing Order it should 
be in line with what has been accepted in the majority of cases. My experi- 
ence is that in majority of cases 6 (six) months’ probationary period is laid down 
as the qualifying period subject to the condition that the probation during this 
period must be satisfactory and that the employer should be the person to 
decide whether the probation has been satisfactory or not. In this present 
case I direct that similar rule, i.e., 6 months’ probationership to the satisfaction 
of the employer, is to be adopted. 


Point No. (ii).—This prayer of the Union is not reasonable. It will make 
the factory something more than “closed shop”. In America “all Union” or 
“closed shop” are not looked-upon with favour in all the States. It is fair that 
the shop should be an open one. It is not reasonable to make the factory @ 
family shop of the present workmen. So this prayer is rejected. 


Point No. (iii).—Gratuity was claimed in the previous adjudication also 
but it was turned down by the Tribunal as there is a Provident Fund System 
since 1939. In these circumstances I do not think it fair to impose an addi- 
tional burden upon the finance of the company by providing for compulsory 


2558 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 [Part ] 


তপন পপ ES EP ee اہ‎ 
\ 


payment of gratuity as suggested by the Union. Of course this does not 7 
that in a proper case arising out of a discharge of a workman, the Tribunal জা] 
not be in a position to Award gratuity in addition to Provident Fund in the 
case of individual worker. 


Point No. (iv).—No revision is called for in view of the fact that there 
has been recently legislation on this point which governs this company as well, 


Point No. (v).—This point was raised to some extent in the previous 
adjudication (see Calcutta Gazette, September 27 1951). There is no such 
demand for a bi-partite enquiry was made. The direction given in the said 
award is what is called for by natural justice. A departmental enquiry against 
the employee is always held by the employer as a domestic Tribunal. What 
is required is that the enquiry should be fair and impartial but it is not neces- 
sary to have the charges investigated by an outsider. During such enquiry the 
employer has to play the role of both the prosecutor and the judge. I find 
that in Boards Miscellaneous Rules, governing the Government servants, there 
is a provision that in exceptional circumstances the Enquiring Officer may 
permit the respondent, i.e., the employee proceeded against, to be represented 
by a lawyer or a recognised agent. That is one thing, but what is demanded 
by the Union in this present case is a different one. However, I concede that 
there should be a rule to the effect that in case of enquiry in a charge of miscon- 
duct, the management in suitable cases should give the concerned employee 
opportunity to be represented by either a lawyer or by a competent officer of 
the Union to which the concerned employee belongs, because it has been 
experienced in some cases that all workmen are not intelligent enough to defend 
themselves unaided by a competent person. Therefore under the issue “Revi- 
sion of Standing Orders” I direct that a like rule as stated above should be 
incorporated in the Standing Order. 


Issue No. 1.—Whether it is possible for the canteen to offer food at rates 
cheaper than those prevailing at present? 


The Unions Contend that although the Company spends a decent sum every 
month for the purpose of running a cheap canteen for the benefit of the wogk- 
men, the beneficiaries do not get due amount of benefit as the present contract 
system takes away a good deal of the wherewithal. So the Unions suggest 
that the contract system should be dispensed with and the management should 
pay the money which it is now spending every month for the purpose of 
canteen to the committee of workmen who would themselves run the canteen. 


On behalf of the Management however it is contended that so much money 
would not be required for the purpose of having cheaper meals and snacks 
if the contractor is dispensed with and therefore the Company suggest that tea 
and snacks should not be subsidised by the Company and that the company 
is prepared to give a subsidy of Rs. 750 per month and also free use of canteen 
equipment, newspaper, electricity, coke, soap and gas and it is made a condi- 
tion by the company that the workmen themselves should be self-serving, so 
that the strength of the canteen servants may be appreciably reduced. ‘The 
suggestion made by the management is not accepted by the Unions. It is 
evident that as the contractor takes a good slice out of the subsidy given by 
the Company every month for the purpose of the canteen, workmen are not 
in a position to have meals at a cheaper rate as they expect. Recently it has 
been held by the Labour Appellate Tribunal in Calcutta in the case of Burn 
Labour Union vs. Burn Co., 1954, 1. L.L.J., Page 774, “That it is for the com- 
pany to bear a substantial part of the cost of running the canteen, so that the 
workers may have the benefit of having healthy food at a cost lower than at 
which it should be obtained outside”. In that case the Tribunal directed the 


pant T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2559 
পোপের a ER TO ET 


the company to bear the following expenses which are not to be taken into 
account in fixing the cost of the Hotel meal to be charged to the workmen. 


(i) Cost of utensils including cooking vessels, plates, glass and other 
articles, which would be necessary to serve meals to the workmen. 


(ii) Cost of furniture. 
(iii) Cost of coal, fuel and electricity. 
(iv) Salary of the cooks and of the canteen staff. 


My decision is that if the workmen form a committee for the purpose of the 
catering which is now done by the contractor and if the expenses as set forth 
above are made by the Company without the same being charged to the work- 
men towards the cost of the meals or snacks, there is the possibility for the 
workmen to have food from the canteen at rates cheaper than those prevailing 
at present. I do not think that what the company now spends for the purpose 
of running the canteen is inadequate or that the company is not sharing a good 
art of the overall cost of the canteen from its own pocket without charging 
the same to the workmen. : 


Issue No. 6.—Bonus for the periods 1950-51 and 1951-52. 


In the previous adjudication there was a demand for bonus but it was not 
for any specific year. The said reference was made by an order, dated 10th 
March 1951. In the award already referred to, the adjudicator remarked— 


“The demand is not for bonus for any specific service year, or in respect 
of past years, in which there have been profits, but for the future 
| and irrespective of the Company’s future profit or loss.” 


The ie therefore rejected the demand for bonus. 


The Appellate Tribunal however observed— 


“That\ the workmen claimed bonus for the year 1949-50 and for future 
years at the rate of four months basic wages, and that the Tribunal 
did not consider the claim for the year 1949-50, but simply turn- 
ed down the claim for future years.” 


The Appellate Tribunal allowed bonus at one month’s wages in addition to what 
have been paid by the Company, i.e., two months, in all three months’ wages. 
The Appellate Tribunal held that the claim for bonus for future years has been 
nghtly turned down by the Tribunal. The claim for additional bonus for the 
yar 1950-5] is challenged by the Company on the ground that this claim 
has been made long after the closing of the accounts for that year and there- 
fore the closed account cannot now be re-opened and additional bonus cannot 
therefore be paid to the workmen. In respect of the additional bonus for the 
year 1951-52, the contention of the Company is that there has been no profit 
for that year and therefore the claim is untenable. It is admitted that this 
company has been paying bonus every year at 2 months’ wages regularly and 
that such bonus has been paid even for the year 1951-52, although there has 
been no profit in that year. So it is now contended on behalf of the workmen 
that 2 months’ wages as bonus fall as service condition and what the workmen 
how claim is profit-sharing bonus. It is admitted on both 51005 that the 
pinciple to be followed has been laid down in Rastyiya Mill Case that the 
taim for bonus is to be decided on the available surplus profits of the parti- 
cular year under claim. Quegtions have arisen whether the workmen’s claim 
lr bonus for future years in the adjudication proceeding before Shri 9. K. 
Niyogi, as aforesaid can be treated as a claim for bonus for the year 1950-51, 
Whether the initial allowance under section 10(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act 


2560 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 [Parr 1 
7০০৮০৮০০০৮৮ شیج ے چ جج ‌چچںےںسں سس‎ 
is a measure of Rehabilitation cost and whether the said amount of deduction 
is called “statutory depreciation”, whcther the fair return on the reserve used 
as working capital or on the amount of reserve representing accumulated 
profits converted to bonus share should be 2 per cent. or 4 per cent. All these 
questions come up for decision. 


It appears from the evidence that the accounts for the year 1950-51 were 
closed at the end of March 1951 and that notice of the share-holders’ meeting 
was given in August 1951 and the meeting was held in September 1951, but 
the demand for extra bonus for the year 1950-51 was made sometime between 
May and October 1951. In July 1951, the workmen received the bonus (paid 
by the Company amicably). At that time also there was no claim for extra 
bonus for the year 1950-51. So it is evident that the claim for additional] 
bonus for the year 1950-51 is a belated one, and therefore it is untenable. 


Regarding alleged “statutory depreciation” under section 10(2)(vi) of the 
Income-tax Act, I think that the allowance or deduction provided in the said 
clause is not called depreciation or rehabilitation charge, it is simply an allow. 
ance or deduction. What is not taxed for the income-tax and is excluded from 
the calculation of the tax cannot be said to be depreciation, although for the 
purpose of the income-tax Act it may be so called in common parlance for 
equalising the incidents of income-tax amongst the profit carners, as a class. 
Such deduction as is provided under section 10(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act 
may be fair and reasonable because if such deduction is not allowed the assess- 
ment against the Company which started business with machineries purchased 
at a time when the price had shot up immensely high would be extremely hard 
as compared with the assessment made against the Company which has been 
Carrying on the business with the help of machineries purchased before 1940, 
i.e., when the price was very low. But for the purpose of assessing the avail- 
able surplus profits in order to decide whether any bonus is to be paid to the 
workmen for any particular year, the above consideration as indicated in 
section 10(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act would be irrelevant. The Company 
has submitted a chart which is marked Annexure “A”, showing available surplus 
profits for the years 1950-51 and 1951-52. The Company has also submitted 
a chart showing the addition and elimination of the machineries which is mark- 
ed Annexure “B” and a chart marked Annexure “C” showing the analysis of 
calculation on the basis of the case of Ruston and Hornby (India), Ltd. vs. 
Their workmen, reported in 1, L.L.J, page 400. The initial deduction made 
by the income-tax authorities under section 10 has not been adopted as a 
(statutory) depreciation in Annexure “A” submitted by the Company. The 
bonus at 2 months’ basic wages which have been already paid by the company 
has been added back in this calculation. This process is not justified. In my 
opinion the bonus which has been paid and which has_ been shown in the 
balance-sheet as costs of production and upon which Income-tax remission has 
been obtained cannot now be added back in order to get further deduction (by 
way of income-tax) thereon. So if this item of “adding back” is excluded the 
result will be that in the year 1951-52, the deficit would be Rs. 2,56,000 instead 
of Rs. 2,63,000 as shown in this statement and that the available surplus profit 
in the year 1950-51 would work out as Rs. 1,05,000 instead of Rs. 92,000 as 
shown in the statement. Much criticism has been levelled by the Unions 
against the item “donations” (Rs. 6,636) for the year 1950-51 and (Rs. 8,207) 
for the year 1951-52. It appears that in countries where trade and commence 
have developed immensely, the manufacturing and commercial concerns make 
huge donations for public utility on charitable” purposes and therefore these 
small donations should not be made grievance of by the Unions. Public ۳٢ 
tutions cannot thrive unless some donations are made by the solvent companies 


Part 11 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2561 


It has been contended on behalf of the Unions that huge stock in trade 
worth several lakhs has been shown in the balance-sheet of the Company for 
the year 1951-52 and it is contended that almost the entire surplus profit has 
been invested by purchasing this stock by way of forestalling. It has been also 
argued on behalf of the Unions that the balance-sheet would show that although 
huge amount of reserve profit has been spent by awarding bonus shares to the 
shareholders, the Company in the same breath borrowed Rs. 21,45,336 from 
the Chartered Bank. It has been further contended that the factory continued 
at Dum Dum till the end of 1952 financial year, and that the Behala factory did 
not commence working until March 1952 when Dum Dum factory ceased to 
exist ; and therefore it is contended that the costs of erection of the factory at 
Behala should not be taken into consideration as expenditure in carrying on the 
business which earned the profit for the year 1951-52 and as a matter of that 
the depreciation allowed for the said costs of construction of Behala factory 
should be excluded while calculating the available surplus profits for 1951-52. 


The money invested in the stock-in-trade which remains at the end of the 
year 1951-52 is not liquid asset in the hand of the company. So in order to 
show available surplus profits in that year it is unfair on the part of the Union 
to point to the said stock-in-trade and argue that there lies a huge amount of 
profit money and it should be available for distribution as additional bonus to 
the workmen. The stock-in-trade may be floating asset as opposed to fixed 
asset, but stock-in-trade is not liquid asset. Liquid assets are those which are 
represented by cash or those that can easily be converted into money, such as 
“cash in hands, cash in bank, gilt-edged securities and bills receivable”. The 
stock-in-trade cannot be sold immediately by the company for paying bonus to 
the workmen. There is no knowing whether immediate sale of the stock-in- 
trade would result in profit or loss. 


The \question is whether the Behala factory which was under construction 
during the year 1951-52 and which did not commence (i.e., to make) produc- 
tion during the said year can be said to be “used for the purpose of the busi- 
ness” within the meaning of section 10 of the Income-tax Act. Similar ques- 
tion arose in the case of Liquidators of Pursa, Ltd. vs. Income-tax Commis- 
sioner, A.IL.R. 1954, Supreme Court, page 253: it was held there— 


“that in order to attract the operation of clauses (v), (vi), (৬11), the 
machinery and plant must be such as were used in whatever sense 
that word is taken (whether active or passive user) at least for a 
part of the accounting year. If the machinery and plant have not 
at all been used at any time during the accounting year, no allow- 
ance can be claimed under clause (vii) in respect of them and 
the second proviso also does not come into operation.” 


It appears from the analysis of available surplus profits (Annexure C) that the 
depreciation for 1951-52 has been excluded from the amount of depreciation 
claim. So it cannot be said that the company included the depreciation in 
respect of Building and Machineries installed at Behala, for the purpose of 
running business and earning profit for the year 1952-53 and onwards. The 
said annual depreciation for the year 1951-52 in respect of the said Building 
and Machineries may be claimed by the Company as allowable deduction on 
account of the passive user of the same for earning profit for the year 1952-53. 
When the Company has already excluded the said debatable depreciafion of 
the building and machineries erected and installed at Behala (so far as the 
profits of the year 1951-52 are concerned), I find no reason to reduce deprecia- 
tion amount over again in the way as suggested by the Union. So my con- 
clusion is that the Company really suffered loss for the year 1951-52, and 


2562 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 {Part T 


therefore the Company cannot be saddled with a further burden in the shape 
of extra bonus in addition to two months’ wages already paid as bonus for that 
year. In the result I hold that the claim for extra bonus for the years 1950-51, 
and 1951-52 is to be rejected. 


The Company contends that 4 per cent. should be paid as fair return on 
the bonus share money which has been utilised as working capital whereas the 
Unions contend that the said return should not exceed 2 per cent. I have gone 
through several rulings on this point and it appears that in the majority of the 
cases 4 per cent. was given as fair return for the accumulated profit used as 
working capital after the said amount had already been declared to be the 
property of the share-holders by virtue of assignment of bonus shares to them. 
So I conclude that in this present case also fair return on the money represented 
by the bonus shares should be at 4 per cent.

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act,

AWARD. 


The original reference out of which this case has arisen was made under 
Governnjent order Nos. 2894Dis./D/4L-34/52, dated 29th October 1952 and 
4394Dis./D/4L-16/53, dated 19th November 1953. 


This is an application made by the employee Shri Kalipada Ghosh, under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act for reliefs against the employer’s 
order of dismissal passed during the pendency of the original case, without 
obtaining any permission of the Tribunal. 


The employer Popular Transport Service filed written statement but did not 
contest the case at the hearing. The original case mentioned above was in 
respect of the dispute between the Popular Transport Service and their work- 
men represented by Bus Workers’ Union, 249B, Bowbazar Street, Calcutta, 
and the issue was whether the termination of unemployment of Shri Madhu- 
sudan Das, (2) K. C. Dey, (3) Nanilal Bagchi and (4) Chintaharan Shaw is 
justified and whether the said workmen are entitled to reinstatement and/or 
compensation. Petitioner was a member of the said union at the time of his 
dismissal. So he was concerned in the dispute in the pending reference case. 


The petitioner was a bus conductor in this Company, viz., Popular Transport 
Service, for about 7 years. His daily wages were at Rs. 2-8. From the 
evidence I find that he was dismissed from service in November 1952 without 
assigning any reason for the dismissal. No charge-sheet was given to him. 
He denies allegations which the Company made against him in the written 
statement. He says that after his dismissal he could not procure job anywhere 
except that he did casual work for a day or two in a month here and there. 


Under the Labour Law the recognised principle is that workers shall pot be 
discharged “without adequate cause’. In the present case there was no cause 
whatsoever except that the petitioner happened to be a member of the Union. 
So it was a case of clear victimisation. Hence my award is that the dismissal 
is set aside and it is directed that the petitioner be reinstated in his job and 
he be paid compensation equivalent to two months’ wages at the daily rate as 
he had been receiving prior to his dismissal. The reinstatement and the said

eae رسس ۲ح جج‎ ee TPA a 


payment be made within a week from the date of publication of the award in 
the Calcutta Gazette.

AWARD. 


This is an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act made 
by the employee Panchanan Dey, whose case is that during the pendency of 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 2565 


the original case under Government order Nos. 2894Dis./D/4L-34/52, dated 
29th Qctober 1952 and 4394Dis./D/4L-16/53, dated 19th November 1953, 
the employer, viz., Messrs. Popular Transport Service, dispensed with the 
services of the petitioner without assigning any reason except that the petitioner 
happened to be a member of the Union. The petitioner was a conductor and 
he served the Company for about two ycars at the rate of daily wage of 
Rs. 2-8 per day, The Company filed written statement denying that 
Panchanan Dey was an employee of the Popular Transport Service, but the 
Company did not appear at the hearing. The original case also was disposed of 
ex parte as the Company did not appear. I find no reason to disbelieve the 
evidence of the petitioner. It appears from the evidence that the petitioner has 
been dismissed from service without any notice and without giving any reason 
for the dismissal and that the evidence shows that the dismissal was due to the 
fact that the employee happened to be a member of the Union. So the dis- 
missal is to be set aside and it is directed that the petitioner shall be reinstated 
and he shall also get unemployment compensation for a period of two months at 
the rate of the daily wage which he had been receiving from the Company at 
the time of his dismissal. The payment shall be made within a week from the 
date of publication of the Award.

AWARD. 


The Original reference out of which this case has arisen was made, under 
Government order Nos. 2894Dis./D/4L-34/52, dated 29th October 1952 and 
4394Dis./D/4L-16/53, dated 19th November 1953. 


This is an application made by the employee Shri Satya Charan Sadhukha, 
under section 33۸ of the Industrial Disputes Act for reliefs against the 
employer’s order of dismissal passed during the pendency of the original cage, 
without obtaining any permission of the Tribunal. 


The employer Popular Transport Service filed written statement but did not 
contest the case at the hearing. The original case mentioned above was رز‎ 
respect of the dispute between the Popular Transport Service and their workmen 
represented by Bus Workers’ Union, 249B, Bowbazar Street, Calcutta, and the 
issue was whether the termination of সা رٹ‎ ran of Shri Madhusudan Das, 
(2) K. C. Dey, (3) Nanilal Bagchi and (4) Chintaharan Shaw is justified and 
whether the said workmen are entitled to reinstatement and/or compensation. 


The petitioner was a member of the said Union at the time of his dismissal. 
From the evidence | find that the petitioner was a driver in this Company, i.e. 
employer Popular Transport Service, for about six years. His daily wages were 
at Rs. 5. In November 1952, he has been dismissed from service without any 
charge-shect or without any reason being assigned. ‘There was no notice ol 
dismissal. The allegations made against the petitioner in the written statement 
of the employer have been denied by the petitioner on oath. The petitione: 
says that since his dismissal he was able to procure casual job here and there 
for only 2 or 4 days in a month. 


I find from the evidence that the petitioner was concerned in the dispute iz 
the original reference case because he was also a member of _ the 
said Union which represented the cause of “the workmen” who Wert 
the parties in the said proceeding. So it is a clear violation 0 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The greatest importance is toda) 
attached by Labour Law of the country to the reasons for termination of th 
contract of employment. In this present case there was no reason assigned fo 
the said dismissal, therefore the dismissal must be set aside, and the petitione 
should get reasonable compensation for loss of earning. My award is that thi 
petitioner be reinstated and he be paid one month’s wages at the rate of Rs. -

per day as compensation and the reinstatement "and payment of the said

AWARD. 


The original reference out of which this case has arisen was made unde: 
Government order Nos. 2894Dis./D/4L-34/52, dated 29th October 1952 anc 
4394Dis./D/4L-16/53, dated 19th November 1953. 


2568 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JT LY 29, 1954 [Pawr 1] 


This is an application 71805 by the employee Shri Sasht Kumar Dutta under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act for relicfs against the em oyer’s 
order of dismissal passed during the “pendency of the “original case, without 
obtaining 80 ‘permjssion of the Tribunal. 


The empleyer Popular Transport Service filed written statement but did not 
contest the case at the hearing. The origirfal oase mentioned above Was in 
respect of the, dispute between the Popular Transport Service and their workmen 
represented by Bus Workers’ Union, 249B, Bowbazar Street, Calcutta¥ and the 
issue was Whether the termination of کت‎ of Shri Madhusudan Das 
(2) ×× C. Dey, (3) Nanilal Bagchi and (4) Chintaharan Shaw is justified and 
whether the said workmen are entitled to reinstatement and/or compensation. 


Shashi Kumar Dutta the present petitioner was a conductor in the Popular 
Transport Service and he was also a member of the said Union before his 
dismissal and as such he was concerned in the dispute in the referenc® ease. 
He has been dismissed from service on 12th February 1953 without assigning 
any reason whatsoever and no charge-sheet was given to him. He denies that 
he made short collection of fair from passengers or that he made any defalcation 
or that he left the service of his own accord. The employer made these alle$a- 
tions as abovementioned against him in the written statement but there is no 
evidence in support thereof. So the denial of the petitioner is sufficient 
answer to the allegations made against him. I find no reason to disbelieye the 
evidence of the petitioner. Petitioner says that he could not procure any job 
anywhere and he has been ssitting idle. Petitioner says that he served this 
Company for about seven years. So I find that the application succeeds, The 
accepted principle of Labour Law in this country is that a worker shall جا‎ 
discharged without ‘adequate cause”. He may be discharged or dismissed ah 
the ground of misconduct or for any “adequate cause,” e.g., trade reasons. In 
the present case there was no cause given for the dismissal. So my award ‘is 
that the order of dismissal is set aside and that the petitioner be reinstated in 
his job and he be paid compensation for loss of earning equivalent to two 
months’ daily wages at the rate as he was receiving prior to his dismissal and 
reinstatement and payment of compensation be made within a week from the 
date of publication-of the award. .

PART V-—Acts of the Parliament of India assented to by the President 
and Ordinances promulgated by the President 


GOVERNMENT OF INDIA. 
Ministry of Law. 
ORDINANCE No. 8 oF 1954. 
THE INDIAN INCOME-TAX (AMENDMENT) ORDINANCE, 1954. 
Promulgated by the President in the Fifth Year of the Republic of India. 


An Ordinance further to amend the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, to provide 
for the assessment or re-assessment of persons who have to a substantial 
extent evaded payment of taxes during a certain period. 


WHEREAS Parliament is not in session and the President is satisfied that 
circumstances exist which render it necessary for him to take immediate action; 


Now, THEREFORE, in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of 
article 123 of the Constitution, the President is pleased to promulgate the follow- 
ing Ordinance :— 


1. Short title and commencement.—(1) This Ordinance may be called the 
Indian Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance, 1954. 


(2) It shall come into force at once. 


2. Amendment of section 34, Act XI of 1922.—During the period of 
Operation of this Ordinance, section 34 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, 
Shall have effect as if after sub-section (1), the following sub-sections had been 
inserted, namely :— 


“(1A) If, in the case of any assessee, the Income-tax Officer has reason to 
believe— 


(i) that income, profits or gains chargeable to income-tax have escaped 
assessment for any year in respect of which the relevant previous 
year falls wholly or partly within the period beginning on the Ist 
ae نو تر‎ 1939, and ending on the 318٦ day of March, 

946; an 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 20, 1954 = [Parr V 


(ii) that the income, profits or gains which have so escaped assessment 
for any such year or years amount, or, are likely to amount, to 
one lakh of rupees or more; 


he may, notwithstanding that the period of eight years or, as the 
case may be, four years specified in sub-section (1) has expired 
in respect thereof, serve on the assessee, or, if the assessee Is a 
company, on the principal officer thereof, a notice containing all 
or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice under 
sub-section (2) of section 22, and may proceed to assess or re- 
assess the income, profits or gains of the assessee for all or any of 
the years referred to in clause (i), and thereupon the provisions of 
this Act [excepting those contained in clauses (1) and (111) of the 
proviso to sub-section (1) and in sub-sections (2) and (3) of this 
section] shall, so far as may be, apply accordingly : 


Provided that the Income-tax Officer shall not issue a notice under this 
sub-section unless he has recorded his reasons for doing so, and 
the Central Board of Revenue is satisfied on such reasons recorded 
that it is a fit case for the issue of such notice: 


Provided further that no such notice shall be issued after the 31st day of 
March, 1956. 


(1B) Where any assessee to whom a notice has been issued under sub-sec- 
tion (1A) applies to the Central Board of Revenue at any time within 
six months from the receipt of such notice or before the assessment 
Or re-assessment is made, whichever is earlier, to have the case to 
which the notice relates settled, the Central Board of Revenue may, 
after considering the terms of settlement proposed and subject to 
the previous approval of the Central Government, accept the terms. 
of such settlement, and, if it does so, the assessment or re-assessment 
shall be made accordingly and shall be final and conclusive in so 
far as it relates to matters covered by the settlement.” 


RAJENDRA PRASAD, 
President. 


K. Y. BHANDARKAR, Secy.

HOUSE OF THE PEOPLE. 


The following Bill was introduced in the House of the People on the 18th 
May 1954 :-— 


BiLL* No. 24 oF 1954. 
A Bill to provide for the constitution of an Auxiliary Territorial Force. 
BE it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of our Republic as follows :— 
1, Short title and extent.—(1) This Act may be called the Auxilitary 
Territorial Force Act, 1954. 
(2) It extends to the whole of India. 


2. Definitions.—In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires,— 


(a) ‘camp’ means any place established under section 4 as a camp where 
any body of persons enrolled under this Act is for the time being 
undergoing training; 

(b) اس‎ means the Auxiliary Territorial Force constituted under this 

ct; 

(c) ‘enrolled person’ means a person enrolled in the Force under this Act; 

(d) ‘prescribed’ means prescribed by rules made under this Act; 

(c) ‘superior officer’ means any officer, junior commissioned officer or 
7 0005 officer of the regular Army or of the Territorial 

10705, 

(6) all words and expressions used in this Act and not defined but defined 
in the Army Act, 1950 (XLVI of 1950), or in the Territorial 
Army Act, 1948 (LVI of 1948), shall have the meanings 1957 
pectively assigned to them in the said Acts. 


3. Constitution of the Auxiliary Territorial Force.—There shall be raised 
and maintained by the Central Government in the manner hereinafter provided 
a force to be designated the Auxiliary Territorial Force. 


১৮০০৮ রহ 
*The President has, in pursuance of clause (3) of artigle 117 of the Constituti 
of India, reeommended to the House of the People the یھ تر‎ of the Bil 


106 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 [Part VI 


4. Establishment of camps.—The Central Government may establish» uch 
number of camps for the purposes of the Force as it thinks fit and may ciose 
down or re-establish any such camps. 


5. Enrolment.—Any citizen of India may offer himself for enrolment as a 
member in the Force; and may, if he satisfies the prescribed conditions, be 
enrolled by the prescribed authority for such period not exceeding five years 
and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed. 


6. Duties of enrolled persons.—No enrolled person shall, by virtue of 
being a member of the Force, be liable for military service, but subject thereto 
an enrolled person may be called upon at any time to undergo such training as 
may be prescribed, and while undergoing such training shall perform such duties 
and discharge such obligations as the prescribed authority may, by general or 
special order, direct : 


Provided that where an enrolled person has, during the period of his enrol- 
ment, undergone training at least once after being called upon for the purpose, 
any further training shall be at his option, and if any enrolled person fails to 
attend at any place for subsequent training when called upon to do so, he shall 
not be deemed to have committed an offence within the meaning of clause (i) of 
sub-section (1) of section 8. 


7. Discharge.—Every enrolled person shall be entitled to receive his dis- 
charge from the Force on the expiration of the period for which he was enrolled, 
but any such person may, prior to the expiration of that period, be discharged 
from the Force by such authority and subject to such conditions as may be 
prescribed. 


8. Offences and 19672816865. 01) If any enrolled person commits any of 
the following offences, that is to say,— 


(i) without sufficient cause fails to attend at any place when duly 
required to do so; or 


(ii) while in camp on duty— 
(a) absents himself from the camp without leave; 


(b) uses criminal force or uses threatening or insubordinate language to 
a superior officer or assaults a superior officer; 


(c) disobeys any lawful command of a superior officer; 


(d) neglects to obey any standing, general or other orders by the officer 
commanding the camp; 


(e) uses criminal force ئ‎ or assaults any enrolled person or any 
person subject to the Army Act, 1950 (XLVI of 1950), or any 
officer or person enrolled under the Territorial Army Act, 1948 
(LVI of 1948); 


(f) escapes from lawful custody; 


(g) knowingly does any act which is prejudicial to the maintenance 
of good order or military discipline in camp; 


he shall be সর summarily by order of the prescribed authority 
with fine which may extend to fifty rupees or in default by being 


confined to barracks for a term which may extend to seven days. 


(2) Any fine imposed by order of the prescribed authority under sub- 
section (1) may, on application made in this behalf by the prescribed authority 
to a magistrate having jurisdiction in the place where the enrolled person 
resides or has a place of business, be recovered in accordance with the provi- 
sions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), as if it were 
a fine imposed by such magistrate.

9, saLiability for causing loss of or damage to Government property.—If any 
enrolled person wilfully or negligently causes loss of, or damage to, any pro- 
perty of the Government, the রি authority may, after giving that person 
an opportunity of being heard and after making such inquiry into the matter 
as it thinks fit, make an order requiring him to make good the loss or damage 
within such time as may be specified in the order or within such further time 
as may be allowed by the prescribed authority in this behalf, and where the 
amount thereof as determined by the prescribed authority is not paid within 
the time allowed, it shall, on application made by the prescribed authority to

required by or in pursuance of any rule made under this Act to attend at any 
place, a certificate purporting to be signed by the prescribed officer stating that 
the person so required to attend failed to do so طز(‎ accordance with such 
requirement shall, without proof of the signature or appointment of such officer, 
be evidence of the matters stated therein. 


11. Power to make rules.—(1) The Central Government may, by notifi- 
cation in the Official Gazette, make rulgs to carry out the purposes of this Act. 


(2) In particular, and without prejudice to the pita of the foregoing 
power, such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, 
namely سس‎ 

(a) the authorities by which, the manner in which, the period for which, 


and the conditions subject to which, any person may be enrolled 
under this Act; 


(b) the training, discipline, duties and obligations which an_ enrolled 
person has to undergo, observe, perform or discharge under this 
Act; 

(c) the authorities by which, and the conditions subject to which, any 
enrolled person may be discharged; 


(d) the manner in which, and the conditions subject to which, an enrolled 
person may be called out for training or duties; 


(e) the allowances or other remuneration payable to enrolled persons; 
(f) the determination of authorities for the purposes of this Act; 

(g) the officers by whom certificates may be signed under section 10; and 
(h) any other matter which under this Act is to be or may be prescribed. 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The object of the scheme is to inculcate a sense of discipline among the 
members of the public by giving them elementary military training. Military 
training is imparted in camps which are set up at convenient places both in 
urban and in rural areas. All able-bodied male citizens between the ages of 
18 and 40, except serving and ex-personnel of the Territorial Army, ex- 
servicemen and ex-cadets of the National Cadet Corps, are eligible to join the 
Auxiliary Territorial Force which does not carry any liability for compulsory 


military service. 


108 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, JULY 29, 1954 [Parr VI 
১১০০১০০০০০০ ১১১ 

The Bill seeks to provide the legal basis for the imparting of traim.g and 
lays down the broad principles for the establishment of training camps and for 
the exercise of disciplinary control over the trainees while in the camps. All 
other matters of administrative details connected with training, remuneration 
payable to trainees, issue of stores, etc., will be regulated by means of rules to 
be framed under the proposed law. 


MAHAVIR TYAGI. 


New DELHI; 
The 4th May, 1954. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM. 


The formation of the Auxiliary Territorial Force, originally called the 
Auxiliary Territorial Army, involves expenditure from the Consolidated Fund 
of India. At the rural camps, the trainees are provided with free rations and 
tented or other accommodation for the period of training. Trainees in urban 
camps are not required to stay in camp, but they are entitled to a small 
refreshment allowance. All trainees are given an out-of-pocket allowance of 
Rs. 5 on completion of training. A rural camp 1025 hitherto been of one 
week’s duration and in urban camps, training has been given for 3 hours pcr 
day for two weeks. In future, it is proposed to increase the duration of the 
rural camp to 10 days and of an urban camp to 20 days. Each camp 175 
intended to train about 480 persons. 


2. The cost of training will vary from year to year depending on the 
number of persons to be trained. It is estimated that the expenditure involv 
in a rural camp will be about Rs. 9,000 per camp and 10 an 
urban camp Rs. 5,000 106: oa This amount 00998 170 take 
into account the pay and allowances of the training teams which are provided 
by the Army out of its existing resources. 


3. As an experimental measure, 36 camps were set up in 1953-54 and 
financial provision necessary for similar camps and training has been included in 
the Defence Services Estimates for 1954-55 under Demand No. 12 and voted 
by the Parliament. An extract from the Explanatory notes to the Defence 
Services Estimates is enclosed. 


AN EXTRACT “FROM THE EXPLANATORY NOTES TO THE DEFENCE SERVICES 
ESTIMATES FOR THE YEAR 1954-55. 


The Territorial Army was constituted under the Territorial Army Act, 1948 
and commenced raising in 1949. When fully formed, it will be composed of 
combatant, technical and administrative units. The personnel of the Territorial 
Army are given periodical military training. During the training period and 
when embodied for service, they are entitled to pay, allowances, etc., at the 
same rates as for corresponding ranks of the regular Indian Forces. 


Commencing from the year 1953-54, a new organisation given so far the 
name of Auxiliary Territorial Army has been formed. All able-bodied Indian 
male citizens between the ages of 18 and 40 years are eligible to join (115 
organisation. Training in these Forces consists of drill without arms, ele- 
mentary field engineering and physical training, etc. 


Parr VI] 11115 CALCUPPA GAZETTE, TULY 29, 1994 104) 


MEM#@RANDUM REGARDING DELEGATED LEGISLATION IN THE 
AUXILIARY TERRITORIAL FORCE BILL, 1954 


The broad features of the scheme, namely, the constitution of the Auxiliary 
Territorial Force, the establishment and closure of camps (both rural and 
urban), the e~ o.ment of citizens of India as members of the Force, the com- 
mission of c:f21ces by members of the Force and the penalties to which they will 
be liable are laid down in the Bill itself. With a view to a succesful imple- 
mentation of the scheme, the powers to provide matters of administrative 
details, such as the prescription of the authorities by which members of the 
Force may be enrolled, the manner in which, the period for which, and 116 
conditions subject to which, such persons may be enrolled, the training, dis- 
cipline, duties and obligations which such persons may undergo, observe, pet- 
form or discharge, the manner in which, and the conditions subject to which, 
such persons may be called out for training or duties, the allowances or other 
remuneration to be paid to such persons, the conditions subject to which such 
persons may be discharged, etc., have been delegated to the Central Govern- 
ment to prescribe by means of subordinate legislation, as it is not practicable 
for Parliament to visualise, at the moment, the actual working of the scheme 
and to lay down in the 13111 itself all the necessary details. Some of the 
powers delegated to the Central Government such as the powers to appoint 
authorities by which persons may be enrolled and to prescribe the training, 
discipline, duties and obligations which such enrolled persons may undergo, 
observe, or discharge and the allowances to be paid to such enrolled persons 
etc., which may not appear prima facie to be normal in character are really 
so if one has regard to the fact that in enactments relating to the Army, the 
Navy and the Air Force, it is not possible for Parliament to lay down matters 
of administrative details in the law itself. 


M. N. KAUL, Secy.

BY-LAWS. 


By-laws framed for the control of the erection of buildings and 
material alterations and addition to buildings within the 
Kalimpong Municipality as required by the Governor of 
West Bengal under order No. M.3R-5/51(ii), dated 29th 
February 1952, issued in exercise of the powers conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 328 of the Bengal Miunici- 
pal Act, 1932 (Bengal Act XV of 1932). 


Part I—Definitions. 


Definitions. 1. In these by-laws unless there is anything repugnant in 
the subject or context,— 


(a) the word “base”, as applied to a wall, means the 
underside of the course immédiately above the 
footings of the wall; 


(b) “nogging” means lime or cement concrete, or brick- 
work in lime or cement mortar, which is filled in 
between the frames of iron or wood in a framed 
building; 

(c) “party-wall” means a wall forming part of a building 
and used or constructed to be used for the support 
and scparation of adjoining buildings belonging to 
different owners or constructed or adapted to be 
occupied by different persons, and 


(d) “topmost storey” means the uppermost storey in a 
building, whether constructed wholly or partly 
in the roof or not, and whether constructed, used 
or adapted to be used for human habitation or not.

(2) If the said engineer or oversecr certifies that the site is 
not secure as aforesaid, or that the stability or security of any 
hillside, bank or property would be threatened by the proposed 
building, or that the addition of protective works is necessary, 
and if the Commissioners consider that the site ought 
nevertheless to be approved and permission to execute the work 
a = granted or that the said protective works need not be 
added, 


the Commissioners shall refer the matter to the Engineer 
appointed under section 494 and shall deal with the applica- 
tion in accordance with his decision. 


(3) If protective works have to be added as aforesaid to 
any site, permission to execute the work shall not be granted 
until the necessary protective works have been constructed 
and have received the written approval of the Commissioners. 


Part I]i—Buildings generally. 


3. Every building erected or re-erected must have such 
structural and architectural features as to prevent the building 
being in the opinion of the Commissioners at a meeting, un- 
sightly or unsuitable to its surroundings. 


4. No building, other than a dwelling house, shall be 
erected or re-erected in the vicinity of dwelling houses without 
the written sanction of the Commissioners, 


5. No. building shall be erected or re-erected in any 
locality if, in the opinion of the Commissioners at a meeting 
certified in writing,— 

(i) the locality is so crowded with buildings that the 
sanitation thereof is or will be prejudiced; 


(ii) the building is intended to occupy so large a space 
as not to leave one-third of the whole area as open 
space within the compound; 


(iii) the building, either by reason of the nature of its 
construction and location or by reason of the 
uses to which it is intended to be put, is likely in 
any substantial degree prejudicially to affect any 
existing building in the locality— 

(a) by diminishing any advantage it enjoys on account 
of its situation or otherwise; or, 
“{b) by reducing its market valuc. 


5A. No building shall be erected or re-erected in which 
the rooms are in the opinion of the Commissioners placed 
back to back without proper ventilation. 


6. The Commissioners shall make full compensation to 
the owner for any damage which he may sustain in  conse- 
quence of being debarred by-law 4 or by-law 5 from re- 
erecting a building. 


7. Except in special sites, where in the opinion of the 
Commissioners, the conditions are such that the provisions of 
this by-law may be relaxed, no building, the annual valuation 
of which is estimated from the plan to be Rs. 180 or more, 
shall be erected without providing for decent servants’ 
quarters which must be proportionately big and commensurate 
with the maximum requirement of the possible number of 
inmates which such building is capable of housing. 


8. (1) Except in special sites where, in the opinion of the 
Commissioners, the conditions .are such that the provisions of 
this by-law may be relaxed, the height of a building shall be 
regulated by the width of the surrounding open space in the 
same holding plus the width of the road or roads, if any, in the 
following manner, namely :-— 


(i) if such width in any direction be twenty fect or less 
the height of the building shall not exceed 
fourteen feet in that direction; 


(ii) if such width in any direction be over twenty feet, 
but under twenty-cight feet, the height of the 
building shall not excecd twenty-three feet in that 
direction; 

(iii) if such width in any direction be twenty-eight fect 
or over the height of the building shall not exceed 
thirty feet in that direction;

(2) In every case in which the provisions of clause (1) are

9. The floor or lowest floor of every building erected or 
re-erectcd from the ground level must be constructed at such 
level as will admit of— 


(a) the construction of a drain sufficient for the effectual 
drainage of the building and placed at such level 
as will admit of the drainage being led into some 
drain at the time existing or projected, and 


(b) there being a ventilated air space of at least six inches 
in depth between the underside of the floor joists 
and the ground level. 


10. A building shall not be placed over any drain, except 
with the written permission of the Commissioners. 


Part IV—Masonry buildings and framed buildings generally. 


11. The foundation of a masonry or framed building 
must rest on solid ground or rock subject to the minimum of 
2 feet 6 inches below ground level and 3 feet where soil is 
not at all rocky. In all cases the-depth of the foundation pro- 
posed shall be spported by calculations of accepted engineer- 
ing principles to be verified and passed by the municipal 
Engineer or Overseer. 


12. (1) The projection of the bottom of the footings of 
each side of such wall of a masonry or framed building must 
be at least one-fourth of the thickness of the wall at its base. 


(2) The height from the bottom of such footings to the base 
of each wall must be at least two-thirds of the thickness of the 
wall at its base. 


(3) Except where the foundation is a rock, the bottom of 
such footings shall not be less than three feet below 005 
ground level. 


(4) When a wall is built on rock, footings may be omitted 
if the surface of the rock is properly cleaned and stepped to 
receive the first course of masonry. 


13. (1) The external and cross-walls of a masonry or 
framed buildings of onc or two storeys must may be built of— 


(a) stone or concrete brick bedded in cement mortar; 


(b) timber or iron framings covered with corrugated 
or plain iron, or plankcd, or with metal lath and 
plaster : 


Provided that if any of the said cross-walls are intended 
for partitions only and do not support any wall in 
the upper storey, they may be built of | timber 
framing planked with boards or corrugated iron or 
metal lath and plaster.

15. The party-walls of a masonry or framed building must 
be built of stone or brick bedded in lime or cement mortar for 
their full height, and, if the Commissioners so direct, must be 
carried up, of a thickness of not less than nine inches, above 
the roof, flat or gutter to such a height as will give a distance 
of at least eighteen inches measured at right angles to the slope 
of the roof above the highest part of the roof, flat or gutter. 


16. (1) Every wall of a masonry or framed building must 
دای‎ a damp-proof course at or above the level of the ground 
oor. 


(2) Such damp-proof course may consist of sheet-lead, 
asphalt, slates laid in cement, vitrified bricks or any other 
durable matcrial impervious to moisture. 


17. (1) The roof of every masonry or framed building must 
be constructed of corrugated or plain iron, lead, slates, tiles or 
ferro-concrete : 4 


Provided that with the written permission of the Commis- 
sioners, any such roof may be constructed of shingles securely 
attached to a frame of iron or timber. 


(2) The rise of the roof shall not in any case be less than 
one-eighth of the span in the case of a roof with corrugated or 
plain iron, lead, slates or tiles. 


18. The floors of every masonry or framed building must 
be constructed to bear safely the maximum load to be carried, 
such load being taken in the case of planked floors in dwelling 
houses as not less than sixty pounds per square foot including 
the weight of the floor. 


19. (1) All beams and girders in a masonry or framed 
building must be supported by a breadth of stone or other 
solid substances sufficient to secure their stability. In the case 
or stone walls, bed plates of steel, stone slabs or concrete slabs 
are to be provided undcr the bcams to distribute the direct load 
and guard against crushing. 


(2) The bearing of a beam or girder on a wall shall not, 
without the sanction of the Commissioners, be 1655 than three- 
fourths of the thickness of the wall. 


20. All iron posts, girders or joists or other iron work 
used for the support of any portion of a masonry or framed 
building must be of such quality and strength as are approved 
by the Commissioners. 


21. If the roof or walls of any building arc, in the opinion 
of the Commissioners, in an unsightly condition they may by 
written order direct the owner to repair, paint or colour-wash 
such part of the building as they may direct within a period to 
be specified in the order.

Part V-——Ferro-concrete buildings. 


22. (1)The foundation of ferro-concrete building must 
rest on a solid ground or rock. 


(2) The depth of foundation for ferro-contrete buildings 
ue be to the satsifaction of the municipal Engineer or 
verseer. 


(3) The spread of foundation wall bases shall be 50 
designed that the intensity of uniform pressure on soil does not 
exceed half ton per square foot, except in the case of solid 
rock, in which case the allowable pressure will be determined by 
the municipal Engineer or Overseer. 


(4) The external and cross-walls ' of ‘a ferro-concrete 
building not carrying any load except its own weight may be 
built of timber of iron framing covered with corrugated or 
plain iron sheets, metal lath and plaster, planked or ferro- 
concrete walling of not less than three inches thick. 


(5) The party or end wall of a ferro-concrete building must 
be built to such a height above roof level as may be required 
by the Commissioners. 

(6) Every wall of a ferro-concrcte building cxcept those 
constructed entirely of cement concrete must have a damp-proof 
course at or above the level of the ground floor which may 
consist of sheet lead, asphalt or slates, stones or vitrified bricks 
laid in cement or any other durable matcrial impervious to 
moisture, 

(7) The roof of a ferro-concrete building may be of re-inforced 
concrete laid to a fall of at least 1 in 150 and be sufficiently strong 
to carry a load of 40 pounds per square foot excluding its own 
weight. If plain or corrugated iron or lead sheets, slates or 
tile roofing are used the rise should in no case be less than one- 
eighth of the span.

No. 1920M.P. /2R-13/1953.—26th July 1954.— 
Whereas Messrs. Vishnupur Electric Supply and 
Industrial Development Company, Limited, 
licensees of the Vishnupur Electric License, 1950, 
have moved Government for making certain tem- 
porary amendments in the terms and conditions of 
the said license so as to suitably modify the require- 
ments contained in the proviso to clause 11 thereof, 
providing for maintenance of part time supply daily 
for ten hours and a half, namely, between 6-30 
a.m. and 5 p.m. local time, for a period of two 
years from the commencement of supply, specially 
during the months of November, December, Janu- 
ary and February ; 


And whereas in the opinion of the State Govern- 
ment, public interest permits the making of such 
temporary amendments in the said terms and 
conditions ; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by clause (b) of sub-section (3) of section 4 
of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), 
the Governor is pleased, after consultation with the 
local authority concerned, namely, the Adminis- 
trator of the Vishnupur Municipality to direct that 
the said license shall have effect as if for the pro- 
viso to clause 11 thereof, the following proviso had 
been substituted, namely :— 


“Provided that for a period of two years from 
the date of commencement of supply, the 
supply may be discontinued for a period 
not exceeding ten hours and ao half per 
day during specified hours, with the per- 
mission of Government previously obtained 
in writing.’’ 


This notification shall have effect and shall be 
deemed always to have had effect as if it had been 
issued on the 2nd April 1954. 

By order of the Govertedér, 


P. M. DAS GUPTA, Dy. Secy.

The cost of Living Index Number for Asansol. 
Ranipanj area has increased during the month of 
June 1994 by 1 point to 99. The important 
changes in the price quotations during the month 
are us follows:— 


There has been some fall in the prices of Rice, 
Atta, Dal, Mustard Oil, Spices, Dhoti, 
Sarees and Tobacco, while there has been 
a rise in the prices of Ghee, Vegetuble 
cooking material, Vegetables, Fish, Tea’ 
Coal, Cowdung cake, Shirting, Coating, 
Blouse, Frock, Vests, Gamcha and Pan. 


Corrigendum.—The Food Group Index for May 
1954 should read as 90 instead of 81 and the Generu] 
Tndex should read as 98 instead of 92 as published 
in the Calcutta Gazette, dated 15th July 1964.

Agriculture 
RESOLUTION No. 6405Agri. 
Calcutta, the 25th June 1954. 


The Governor is pleased to reconstitute the 
West Bengal Agricultural Research Committees, 
which was last reconstituted by Government 
resolution No. 4107Agri., dated the 30th May 
1951, with the following members :— 


(1) The Minister-in-charge, Department of 
Agriculture and Co-operation—President. 

(2) Dr. J. N. Mookerjee, D.Sc., lately 
Director, Central Building Research 
Institute and formerly Director, Indian 
Agricultural esearch Institute, Delhi. 

(3) Dr. B. C. Guha, D.Sc., Ghosh Professor 
of Applied Chemistry, Calcutta Univer- 
sity. 

(4) Dr. J. C. Sengupta, D.Sc., Principal, 
Presidency College, Calcutta. 

(6) Dr. H. N. Roy, D.Sc., Professor of 
Protozoology, School of Tropical Medi- 
cine, Calcutta. 

(6) Shri I. B. کا‎ M.Sc., L.Ag., 
Retired Physiological Chemist, Agricul- 
ture Department, Government of West 
Bengal and lately Assistant Agricultural 
Commissioner with the Government of 
India. 

(7) Dr. L. C. Sikka, B.Sc. (Agri.), Assoc. 
IDRI1, Ph.D., Milk Commissioner-cum- 
Administrator, Haringhata Centre. 

(8) Secretary to the Government of West 
Bengal, Department of Agriculture and 
Co-operation (er officio). 

(9) Director of Agriculture, 
(ex officio). 

(10) Director of Veterinary 
Bengal (ez officio). 

(11) Principal, West Bengal State College of 
Agriculture (ez officio). 

(12) Principal, Bengal Veterinary College (ez 
officio). 


West Bengal 


Services, West 


2. The Director of Agriculture, West Bengal, 
will act as the Secretary to the Committee. 


3. The members will hold office for a period 
of three years or until further orders. 


4. Government reserve the power to add to the 
number of members, if necessary. 


5. The Committee shall have powers of 
appointing sub-committees to deal with special pro- 
blems or matters and to appoint to such sub-com- 
mittees mersons who may not be members of the 
Committee. 


6. The Chairman shall have powers of inviting 
persons with expert knowledge or specialised 
experience to attend meetings of the Committee 
and participate in its deliberations. 


7. The functions of the Committee will be to 
advise Government on all matters relating to 
research in the sphere of agriculture, animal 
husbandry and veterinary science, to review from 
time to time the results of research undertaken by 
the organisations under the Department of 
Agriculture and Co-operation, to advise Govern- 
ment on schemes of research to be taken up by 
such organisations, to advise Government on 
schemes of research by other bodies and institu- 
tions for which grants from the State Government 
are requested, to examine schemes of research 
proposed to be aubmitted to the Indian Council of 


Agricultural Research and similar organisations 
of the Government of India and to assist the 
department in maintaining contact with research 
workers and_ scientific organisations outside 
Government. : 


Order. 
ORDERED that a copy of this resolution be for- 
warded to all members of the Committee for 
information. 


ORDERED also that the resolution be published in 
the Calcutta Gazette for information. 


By order of the Governor, 
K. SEN, Secy.

Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 265Dis./D/10L-

Leipzieg Chemical & Engineering Works, Ltd., 12 and 13, Pran Krishna

was referred for adjudication to the Fourth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal a 
complaint was received from Shri Gurdayal Singh, an employee of the 5910 
Company, against the said Company before the said Tribunal alleging that the 
said Company had discharged the said employee concerned in such dispute; 


And whereas _ in exercise of the টি conferred by section 33۸ of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudicat- 
td upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State Govergment; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
Act filed by Shri Gurdayal Singh against Messrs. Leipzieg Chemical and 
Engineering Works, Ltd., for contravention of section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act under Government order No. 265Dis./D/10L-131/52, dated 
24th January 1953 (Case No. 216 of 1953). 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 


PRESENT : 
Suri ও. C. MUKHERJI, District Judge, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 


For the Union: Shri Panchanan Bhattacharji. 
For the Company: Shri N. K. Mukherji, Advocate. 


While the dispute referred to this Tribunal by Government order No. 265Dis./ 
D/10L-131/52, dated 24th January 1953, was | ge the present applica- 
tion under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act was filed by the petitioner 
Gurdayal Singh on the allegation that he has been discharged illegally on 6th 
October 1953 without any charge-sheet and without payment of his ۶ج‎ 
wages. 


The notice of this application having been served on the Company the 
latter filed a written statement on 26th December 1953 by which they contended 
inter alia that the opposite party never discharged the petitioner from service. 
On the contrary, he absented himself and joined in the strike, that there was no 
violation of the provisions of section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act. They 
also contended that they are entitled to agitate the fact that the petitioner join- 
ed the strike and cemmitted misconduot and on that ground the Company is not 
liable to reinstate the worker. 


The only point for decision is: Whether there is any contravention of 
section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. If so, whether the applicant is 
entitled to reinstatement and on what terms? 


Part I] THE CAISUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 2633 


No question of reinstatement arises as according to the contention of the 
cmployer the applicant iis still in their service and may gy ot to duty on any 
day. There is, therefore, no violation of the provisions of section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act and as such the present petition is not maintainable. 


The petitioner contended that he has been discharged on 6th October 1953 
and in support of this allegation he has examined himself and one witness. 
Both of them said that on 6th October 1953 the applicant went at the gate of 
the Company, but he was not allowed to enter and was told that he has been 
discharged. It appears that the employee absented himself on Ist and 2nd of 
October but was present on 3rd and Sth, 4th being a Sunday and thereafter he 
was absent throughout. His story that on 2nd October 1953 he fell ill and he 
applied for leave along with a medical certificate on that date and thereafter he 
came to join on 6th of October 1953, is palpably false. The Manager said that 
on 6th he suddenly absented himself and did neither verbally apply for leave 
nor filed any medical certificate or any application for leave. In view of the 
state of the record in the hazira book I am prepared to accept the statement of 
the Manager in preference to the statement of Gurdayal Singh. On 7th, how- 
ever, there was a strike and the Manager says that on that date he was found 
picketing at the gate requesting the workers not to join work. Company 
admits that they were not regular in payment of wages and on this particular 
occasion they made a default but the workers having failed to appreciate the 
financial difliculties of the Company went on strike. This is palpably the 
reason why Gurdayal Singh absented himself from that day onwards. Subsequent 
to this there was an incident over an assault of a worker Debendra Mondal. It is 
said that after assault Debendra Mondal was made to sign a chit and Gurdayal 
Singh was amongst the party that obtained the signature of him. The evidence 
shgws that Gurdayal Singh was there though he did not take part in obtaining 
the chit. However, that Gurdayal Singh is one of the strikers is beyond dis- 
pute. On 1st of November Company issued notice to the workers asking them 
to join work. A notice was served on Gurdayal Singh also asking him to 
join and the Manager says that he personally served this notice on Gurdayal 
Singh and when he refused to accept it, it had to be put up on the notice board. 
I have no reason to 019090110৬5 the statement of the Manager on this point 
although tt was vehemently contended that the notice was concocted. That 
being so, it comes to the same thing whether it be a fact that Gurdayal Singh 
was locked out with effect from 7th October 1953 or whether it be a fact that 
he voluntarily absented himself from duty from 7th October 1953. In any 
case, if he voluntarily absented himself then he has no cause of action, and if 
he was locked out, still in that case also the Company having asked him to 
rejoin and he having failed to comply with it, he has still no cause of action 
against the Company. In either case there will be no violation of the provi- 
sions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act and the present application is 
not tenable. The Company, however, wrote his name in the muster-roll only 
in the months of November and December. Company filed its written state- 
ment on 26th December 1953 and thereafter from 1st of January they have dis- 
continued his name from the register. In my opinion, the position remains the 
same as it stood on 26th December 1953 and the discontinuance of the name 
does not by itself show that he was discharged. Manager under the pressure 
of cross-examination said that he had discharged him from January 1954 
but in his  examination-in-chief he has_ clearly, stated that the 
Company has never discharged this worker. In any case his reinstatement 
being a settled fact, the only question is whether in the circumstances the worker 
can ask for any compensation. I think he cannot ask for any compensation as 
he has failed to report to the Company when called. It is admitted that he 
never wrote to the Company that he has been illegally dismissed. On the other 


2634 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 [Parr I 


» 


hand, Manager personally served a notice to him asking him to rejoin even 
after his pee in the strike. But he failed to comply with it. That 
being so, he has no cause of action for compensation either. 


SUBODH CHANDRA MUKHERIJI, 


Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 13th July 1954.

D. S. ۶۰ MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

ANNEXURE. 

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Bengal Iron and 
Brass Foundry & Co., 5/8, Canal East Road, Calcutta-4, and their

Appearances :

AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. 2989Dis./D/10L-89/53, dated 10th August 1953, referred an industrial 
dispute existing between Messrs. Bengal Iron and Brass Foundry & Co., 5/8, 
Canal East Road, Calcutta-4, and their workmen represented by Engineering 
Mazdoor Panchayat, 59/B, Kankurgachi Road, Calcutta-11, regarding the 
matters specified in the schedule to the order of reference under sections 7 and 
10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), to this Tribunal for its 
adjudication. 


The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 17th August 
1953 and usual notices were issued to the parties for appearance and written 
statements. Both parties appeared and filed written statements in the case in 
due course. 


Part I] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 2635 


The Union in its written statement alleged that the Company was a private 
concern of Shri Lalit Mohan Kundu, a big merchant and an industrialist. The 
Company manufactures various machinery parts but the wages structure and 
other benefits of the workmen are very low and compare very unfavourably wit 
those of the other engineering industries in Calcutta. The workmen formed a 
Union in 1952 but the Company did not accept it in good grace. It asked the 
workmen not to join the Union and forced them to sign a blank paper. Having 
failed in its attempt to crush the Union, it declared a lock-out on 17th 
February 1952 and discharged all the workmen on the plea of “no work”. 
That matter was settled on the intervention of the Labour Commissioner and. 
the factory was reopened from 6th November 1952. The Company however 
did not implement the agreement and refused work to five important members 
of the Union. The Union placed a “Charter of Demands” on 29th December 
1952 and the Management began to harass the workmen in every possible way. 
The Company dismissed Shri Ratan Maity and Nemai Bag, Vice-President and 
Secretary of the Union and the Company declared a lock-out on 23rd April 
1953. Conciliation failing, the Union’s demand for minimum basic wage, 
dearness allowance, leave and holidays and service condition were referred to 
this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The Company, in its reply, stated among others, that it was a very small 
concern, established in 1356 B.S. and was still running at a loss. It alleged 
that it never declared a lock-out any time but that it was compelled to lay off 
or retrench the workmen on account of sheer paucity of work. On 22nd April 
1953, Nemai Bag, one of the employees, was dismissed and the other employees 
at once stopped work putting the management to a loss of several hundred 
rupees. That was the casting day and the furnace was heated, but no casting 
was done. On the next day, the Management had to dismiss those employees 
who struck work and carried on the work with the remainder of the workmen. 
There was no lock-out on 23rd April 1953 and the entire body of workers was 
not discharged. Regarding the demands for scales of wages, it stated that it 
was fair and that it never resisted the amicable settlement of the demands of 


the employees. 
The issues as per schedule to the order of reference are— 
(1) Minimum basic wages. 
(2) Dearness allowance. 
(3) Leave and holidays. 
(4) Service condition. 


DECISION. 


The case was taken up for hearing on Ist July 1954, the day fixed for its 
hearing. Both parties were present. The Company filed a signed statement 
informing the ‘Tribunal that its business was completely closed and _ the 
artnership was dissolved from 4th October 1953. In view of the admitted 
act that the work was completely stopped for a long time, and the alleged fact 
nat coe business was closed, the Union did not press the issues in this reference 
or hearing. 


I am satisfied after hearing both parties that the business was completely 
closed for a long time and that the partnership was dissolved. There is no 
work at present and no possibility of any in near or distant future. The 
Company is not employing even a single workman for a long time. Accord- 
Ingly, the Union is justified in not proceeding with the hearing of the issues in 


2636 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 {Parr 


eee eeEeEeEeEeEeEeEeEESESESEE=E——E—=—{—=—ETE=_E__@_ @_ 
this case. After all, no useful purpose would be served by deciding’ scales of 
wages, etc., for the workmen of a Company which is not in existence. In these 
circumstances, a report that no dispute regarding the issues in the case between 
the parties is submitted to the Government. The reference is disposed of. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


M. N, GAN, M. N. GAN,

Industrial dispute between Messrs. Hindusthan Motor Works, Ltd., 49

BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 
Suri 9. C. MUKHERIJI, District Judge, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
For the Union: Shri P. K. Sanyal, Advocate instructed by N. R. Roy, Pleader 


For the Company: Shri S. K. Bose, Counsel instructed by 91011 K. P 
Mukherjee, Advocate of Messrs. Khaitan & Co., Solicitors. 


By Government order No. 3736Dis./D/10L-148/53, dated 8th Octobe: 
1953, the aforesaid dispute was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. The 


Part হু] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 2637 


ٌَو وی ےرسود صےٛدکصود صوحہ -جدوں سسحت سج ےد - Sc a OR TO A‏ 


issu’ framed by the Government was the same as the issue framed by this 
Tribunal and it was as follows :— 


(1) Puja bonus for 1953. 


Notice of the reference having been served on the parties, the Union filed 
its written statement on 11th December 1953 and the Company filed its written 
statement on 9th January 1954. 


The case for the Union is that it was a condition of the service of the work- 
men of the factory that they should be paid an annual bonus every year at or 
about the time of Pujas irrespective of profit and loss of the Company, that in 
pursuance thereto the Company had paid bonus during the years 1948-51 
although the factory remained closed for six weeks in 1951, that in 1952 the 
factory was closed from 7th of April till August but still the Company paid 
Rs. 5 as bonus to all workmen irrespective of their period of service in the 
year, that the abovenamed Company having carried on their work 107 full 
swing from October 1952 till September 1953 the workmen are entitled to one 
month’s pay with dearness allowance as Puja bonus for the year 1953. 


The Company, on the other hand, contended that it was never a condition 
and/or stipulation express or implied that any bonus will be paid irrespective of 
profit and loss of the Company or at all, that the workmen are not entitled to 
any bnnus or Puja bonus or any bonus in any form or any ex-gratia payment 
as the Company is making loss consistently and has yet to pay 1 crore and 
20 lakhs of rupees to build up its depreciation funds. 


AWARD. 


The case was taken up for hearing on 6th July 1954 and on subsequent 
dates. During discussion the learned Counsel for the Company as a measure 
of gesture offered to pay 5 days’ wages for bonus for the year in question on 
the understanding that this will not act as a precedent to the workmen. During 
discussion it was also settled that 5 days’ basic wages only will be paid, that it 
will be paid to all workers temporary or permanent, that the qualifying period 
of service for being entitled to bonus, will be six months ending on the date of 
reference, i.e., 8th October 1953. The learned Advocate for the workmen and 
the workmen themselves agreed to this proposal. I am glad to note that the 
workmen were trying wholeheartedly to show increased production of cars since 
the time of the last Tribunal and they have appreciated the gesture on 
the part of the Company. I, therefore, make my award in terms of the said 
Offer as accepted by the workmen and I hope that the employer and the 
employees should now advance hand in hand for the mutual benefit. The 
matter rests here but it will not act as precedent on the question of bonus. 


S. C. MUKHERJI, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

AWARD. 


Issue Nos. 1 and 2. 


Under section 554 of the Bengal Municipal Act, the Municipality 
itself is not superseded. Under section 553 of the sad Act the State
