Now I come to the question whether the present dispute between Modan 
Mohan Banerjee and the municipality is an individual dispute and if so 
whether the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide the matter under the I] ndus- 
trial Disputes Act. 


The matter has been made highly complicated by the conflicting deci- 
sions of the Supreme Court and the Full Bench of the Appellate Tribunal. 
The Supreme Court decision was in December 1952 and the Full Bench 
decision of the Appellate Industrial Tribunal was in February 1953. In the 
Full Bench decision of the Appellate Industrial Tribunal, there is no 
reference to the Supreme Court’s decision. Presumably it was not pub- 
lished before the Full Bench of the Appellate Tribunal gave this decision 
or the 20th February 1953. The Appellate Industrial Tribunal or any 
Industrial Tribunal is not a body to decide any question of law. These are 
administrative bodies and they are concerned with ‘‘the question o* policy, 
ae law; of special advantage, not legal mandate.” Holmes observed as 
ollows :— 


“The true grounds of decision are considerations of policy, and of 
social advantage and it is vain to suppose that solutions (২১7) be 
attained merely by logic and the general propositions of law 
which nobody disputes’. 


2644 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1984 [Paar I 


SSS Re Nc 


It has been held by Allahabad High Court in Kashi Iron Foundry" we. 
State of U.P., 1964, F.J.R., page 428— 


“That the conclusion reached by the Appellate Tribunal] is the decision 
7 the গা miei body and cannot properly be described as 
6 aw’ at a ae 


So the intricate question comes up in view of the conflict between the 
Appellate Tribunal Full Bench decision and the Supreme Court decision, 
which decision is to be followed by me? I think so far as the decision on a 
point of law is concerned the decision of the Supreme Court prevails over 
the decision of the Appellate Tribunal, Full Bench decision and sv tar as 
Labour Law as dintinguished from judicial or statutory law in concerned 
the Industrial Tribunal should follow the directions of the Appellate 
Tribunal Full Bench decision as the Supreme Court decision is silent on 
such point. 


Ludwig Teller says— 


“In Labour Law as in other branch of the law, the process of judicial 
law making has been proceeding with rapid pace for the 
reasons :— 


(1) The questions presented for judicial determination are so novel, 
(2) That my involve so patently considerations of publie policy that 
it is difficult to hide their underlying drives,”. 


Labour Law as is developed by the Labour Tribunals by their decisions 
may be illustrated thus— 


(Such law. is not law in the real sense as observed by the Allahabad High 
Court already quoted.) 


For example, principles to be followed by the Tribunal in adjudicetien of 
disputes arising out of retrenchment have been settled by the Appellate 
Tribunals. Similarly they have laid down the law that— 


“a sit down strike is illegal, that in settling the amount of dearness 
allowance payable by the Company to its employees—the con- 
sideration to bear is the present day condition of the Company 
and reasonable expectations of the future, that if an award has 
been made between the parties under the Industrial Du:ispvutes 
Act, it should be tried for a sufficiently long time before any 
change can be effected in the terms thereof; that the rule of 
“manifest in justice and unfairness’? only—as applied by Civil 
Courts to decisions of domestic Tribunals—should not govern 
the powers of Industrial Tribunals in judging the orders ol the 
Managements regarding employment and non-employment and 
the charges of the Management will not avail if there is— 


(i) want of bona fides, 


(ii) or it is a case of victimisation or violation of the principles of 
natural justice, 


(iii) or there is a basic error of fact, 
(iv) or there has been a perverse finding on the materials; 


that the ordinary rwe is to order reinstatement of the employee if his 
dismissal is found to be unlawful; that a workman shall not be discharged 
without ‘‘adequate cause’ and that the greatest importance is to be attached 
to the reasons for termination of the eontract of employment. These are 
directions on points of ‘‘Labour Taw” given by the Appellate Tribunals

۔۔چٰىپیچجْْپْمْمُہٗ]‌‌ ‌ یہی ہہوپپسِِسرستمب]ژیکلًدأسؤژؤ ‏ کک کےٍیٹی۔ُکفبتتسسس سژچچً چ۰ چرچ جےہجخجچج ہش رہہ ے سس سےںے__ے٭-_ژسے_ _ءة6ے6ےںں‌ے سے ے سے 


from time to time. The High Court or the Supreme Court will not interfere 
with the above or similar prmciples of 09090 Law” as Jaid down by the 
Appellate Tribunal. Judicial Tribunals always regard legal rights and liabi- 
lities as pre-existing, because they are bound by fixed stundards; they only do 
what is according to law. But Administrative Tribunals which act upon 
policy and expediency, themselves dictate what is politic or expedient. The 
same idea has also been expressed by John Dickinson in his book on 
“Administrative Justice’ and the “Supremacy of Law”. The Courts 
however will decide whether the Appellate Tribunal’s interpretation of any 
provision 01 the section of the Act 1s correct or not, or whether Appellate 
Tribunal has exceeded its jurisdiction or illegally refused to exercise the 
jurisdiction vested in it. I think, whether a dispute is an Industrial Dis- 
pute or not—is a question regarding the basic fact upon which the jurisdic- 
tion of the Tribunal depends and it involves the question of ‘orrect inter- 
pretation of the definition clauses in section 2 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. So on such jurisdiction point of law the decision of the Supreme 
Court is final. The Supreme Court has decided in the case of Shri D. N. 
Ranerjee vs. Shri P. R. Meokherjee— 


“After all—whether there is an industrial dispute at all—is for the 
Gtovernment primarily to find out, for it is only then that it has 
jurisdiction to refer. Moreover it is not every case of an indus- 
trial dispute that the Government is bound to refer. They may 
refer some but may not also. It is a question of expediercy’’. 


(Reported in A.I.R. 1953, Supreme Court, page 58.) 


In view of the above decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court I need not 
decide whether the dispute referred to me by the Government is an indus- 
trial dispute or not. I must assume that the dispute referred to me by the 
Government is an industrial dispute. The above quoted decision of the 
Supreme Court disposes also of the question whether the dispute in the present 
case is an individual dispute or not. In the result my award is that the dis- 
charge of Shri Modan Mohan Banerjee is not justified and that he is to be 
reinstated. The reinstatement is to be made within a week from the date 
of publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette. 


As regards compensation for loss of earning I cannot but consider the 
fact that issue of ante-dated receipt was an improper act, although such 
practice was going on in this municipality for a long time without anybody 
attempting to prevent or restrict it. So in my opinion Shri Modan Mohan 
Banerjee is not entitled to get any compensation for loss of earning for the 
period of unemployment besides what he has received as suspension allow- 
lance under the order of the Administrator.

—— _ —_—=_=_[[_=__[_[[=#=[QV[T[L_L_lQlEU]E—LRLL___SSSESSESESEEESSSSSSS eee 


employer entered appearance. The three workmen filed a joint written 
statement of claim. The Firm in reply filed its written 
statement. The pleadings were completed on Ist April 1954. Shri Ram 
Jatan Lohar though duly served with notice did not put in appearance. 
The parties were directed to file lists of documents and then the dispute 
was fixed for hearing. The first date of hearing was fixed on 28th June 
1954. The employer was ready but the representative of the three workmen 
filed a petition for time. 00 the petition the hearing was adjourned 
to 9th July 1954. On that day the workmen did not take any step. The 
case Was thereafter adjourned to 10th July 1954, but the workmen did not 
turn up. Accordingly the dispute was heard ex parte under rule 15 of the 
West Bengal Industrial Disputes Rules, 1947, and the award was reserved. 


3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows :— 


(1) If the discharge of the following workers was justified and to what 


relief in the way of reinstatement and/or compensation they are 
entitled— 


(a) Shri Nirapada Dutta, (b) Shri Ram Jatan Lohar, (c) Shri Nazir 
Ahmed, (d) Shri Provat Porel. 


4. It was alleged that the workmen were discharged. The Firm on the 
other hand contended that they were not discharged but they ceased to 
attend their duty without assigning any reason and refused to join when 


asked to do so. In the circumstances the employer submitted that the 
workmen were entitled to no relief. 


DECISION. 


The Firm examined one of the partners, D. W. 1 Shri Kedar Nath 
Jayswal and one of its employees, D.W. 2, Shri Shew Prasad Shaw, besides 
roving attendance register, Ext. A. From the evidence which is ez parte, 
I accept the employer’s version of the case. The evidence reveals that the 
four workmen named in the order of reference along with others absented 
without any leave or justification from 3rd January 1953. The evidence 
further reveals that they were found loitering round the factory premises 
and were sent for but none of them did turn up for duty. It further appears 
that they refused to come even when requested. In the circumstances, I 
accept the employer’s version that the workmen must be deemed to have 
voluntarily abandoned their service of this Firm. The result is that they 
are not entitled to any relief. I award accordingly.

The parties have not adduced any oral evidence. They rely on the

documents which have been marked Exts. A and B (00120877081),

re a rae 


Te Union demands one month’s pay as bonus for each of 1951 and 1952 
ag payable in the year 1953 for all categories of workers including the clerks. 
The Company resists the claim. 


There is nothing to show that bonus for the year 1951 was payable in 
1963. 1065 Union’s claim for bonus for the year 1951 cannot, therefore, 
be entertained as being a claim for past bonus. It has been held by the 
Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal that bonus can be ullowed from the profits of 
the year from which it is claimed and that it is not possible to reopen the 
accounts for previous years. The claim for 1951 must, therefore, fail. 


) 

As regards 1962, claim for it ia maintainable as being pavable in th 
year 1953. Angus Engineering Works, whose workmen oe کس‎ 18 : 
separate engineering establishment situated within the general precincts of 
the Angus Works and adjacent to the Angus Jute Works. The Angus Jute 
Works is also operated as separate establishment. Both these establish- 
ments are separate units and are owned by the Angus Co., Ltd., which is 
the parent Company. The main business of the parent Company is the 
manufacture of jute which it does from Angus Jute Works. Besides, the 
parent Company also handles agency work. 


The Angus Engineering Works, it appears, has since the war been mainly 
and primarily engaged in the manufacture of jute mill machinery and 
spare parts required for the industry as a whole. As the demand for them 
began to wane since cessation of hostilities, the Angus Engineering Works 
has of late undertuken manufacture of tools and appliances of brass metals 
said to be as a measure to avoid retrenchment of existing staff following 
reduction in orders and recession in trade, due to jute mills no longer requir- 
ing the former type of obsolete machinery and spare parts and their plants 
for modernisation. The engineering Works, it further appeurs, has been 
started in 1932 and has ever since maintained separate accounts. It further 
appears that in the past when bonus was claimed in 1948 and in 1950, the 
Company filed its profit and loss account to show the trade position of the 
Engineering Works. In the present case too the Company have filed a 
profit and loss statement for the year ended 3lst December 1952 as annexure 
to their written statement. The said profit and loss statement was prepared 
by Messrs. Lovelock Lewes, Chartered Accountants. It shows a loss of 
Ra. 10,018 for the year ended 3186 December 1952 in question. The Union 
obtained inspection of the account books maintained in the Works. I am 
told that as many as 55 separate account books were shown to the Union 
representatives during such inspection. The Union after such inspection 
could suggest nothing definite against the correctness of the figures in the 
statement of profit and loss account filed by the Company with its written 
statement as above. Vague allegations or suggestions are no proof. If this 
statement can be accepted for the purpose of bonus, the claim of the work- 
ment cannot obviously be entertained there having been no profit for the 
year 1952. Thus finding their position untenable, the Union as a last resort 
filed a petition during trial on 25th June 1954 that the Angus Engineering 
Works had no separate existence in law and that it was integral and indivi- 
sible part of the Angus (o., Ltd., and as such the balance sheet of the 
Angus Co., 140.) should ءا‎ the guide for the purpose of the bonus. The 
Company on the other hand contends that when the different units carried 
on ا ارس‎ different business, the Engineering Works doing manufacture 
of implements while the Angus Jute Works doing jute businers and the 
third unit doing a different kind of business the workmen of the Engineer- 
ing Works are not entitled to share the profit, if any, made hy the major 
undertaking namely, the Augus Jute Works, to the earnings of which they 
had in no way contributed. I think the contention of the Company must

সস 


prevail. It has been well settled that employees of one establi ent 
are nat entitled to share in the profits to the earning of which they have not 
contributed. Therefore, Company's contention that the profits as may 
appear in the Company’s over ull balance sheet can in no way be shared by 
the workers who have not, contributed to its earning is well founded. Even 
if it is othcrwise, the balance sheet of the parent Company, Ext. A marked 
‘confidential’, although reveals a profit would leave no surplus but a huge 
defieit after deduction of the prior charges as admissible under the Full 
Bench Formula. The calculation according to the Full Bench Formula 
has been given by the Company in Ext. B. This would show that there 
would be no surplus left for distribution as bonus but 4 huge deficit. So 


the Union's claim for bonus for the year 1952 cannot be sustained in any 
view of the matter, 


I award accordingly.

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
workman Shri Ramadhar. He has been doing refuelling work in this Company 
at the Calcutta Air Port at Dum Dum. On 4th September 1952, he com- 
plained of having pain in the stomach. He was examined by the Medical 
Officer of the Company and sent to the Medical College for admission with a 
letter of introduction. He could not, however, get admission in the Medical 
College. According to the Company, the workman was not heard of since he 
had been sent to the Medical College and before he came to resume duty on 
17th August 1953, after 10 months. The workman on the contrary alleges 
that failing to get admission in the Medical College, he had been under the 
treatment of Dr. Satya Ranjan Mukherjee of Dum Dum Cantonment from 9th 
September 1952 to 11th September 1952. He then went home and was there 
for about 10 months. On 17th August 1953, he reported for duty with a 
chit written in Hindi purporting to be a certificate of a Kaviraj (Ext. C), under 
whom he was alleged to have been under treatment at home for the period of 


2654 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1964 [Part I 
গগন হল 


10 months during which he had been absent without leave and without intima- 
tion to the Company. He also produced at the time another medical certifi- 
cate from Dr. Mukherjee of Dum Dum showing treatment for 3 days from 90 
to 11th September 1952, Ext. C1. The workman was not permitted to resume 
duty pending cnquiry against him. 


Behind this background the Company issued a charge-sheet (Ext. D) on 
28th August 1953. The workman was charged for absence without leave and 
without offering to the Company reasons for his absence for a period of 10 
months. The workman submitted explanation to the said charge on the 81 
August 1953, Ext. A. Then an enquiry was_ held on Ist September 1953. 
Ext. F is the proceeding of the said enquiry. The questions put to the workman 
and the answers he gave to them were recorded as also the statements of the 
persons referred to by the workman. As a result of the enquiry the workman 
was found guilty of the charges framed against him. The management directed 
that workman’s two years’ normal salary increments be withheld and that the 
workman be permitted to resume duty on 17th September 1953, and that he 
would, not get any pay for the preceding period from 4701) August 1953 to 16th 
September 1953 when he was not allowed to join work pending enquiry. 


This took place during the pendency of a reference made by Government 
order No, 2150Dis./D/15L-13(A)/53, dated 12th June 1953, before this 
Tribunal. Hence the complaint under section 33A. 


The workman alleges that the punishment inflicted upon him is unjust and 
unfair and should, therefore, be rescinded. The Company on the other hand 
contends that there was no justification whatever for his absence without leave 
and without intimation. The management therefore maintains that it was 
justified in imposing the punishment in the interest of discipline. It is said 
that the employee has rather been treated leniently. Besides, the Company 
alleges that as the workman was not concerned in the original dispute, the 
application under section 33A is not maintainable. 


DECISION. 


I find no justification whatever on the part of the workman to absent for 
such a long time without previous permission and without any intimation to the 
Company. Even if he had obtained permission from the Superintendent, 
Mr. Cole, for going home, there was no justification on his part to continue to 
absent indefinitely without any intimation and without leave. No doubt the 
Company did not write to the workman to resume duty but this did not 
exonerate the employee from applying for leave or from obtaining permission 
from the Company for continuing indefinitely at home. Even if the medical 
certificate of the Kaviraj be genuine about which there is no proof this does 
not show that his disease was anything serious. The certificate speaks of 
stomach trouble. According to the workman, he was having sometimes loose 
৪৮901 and sometimes hard stool and this was his ailment for which he was 
absent at home for about 10 months. This is no excuse whatever for his not 
intimating the Company or for his not applying for leave. The workman's 
explanation that he was too weak to engage in correspondence with Dum Dum 
Installation is anything but satisfactory in view of his own evidence disclosing 
the nature of his ailment. The Superintendent, Mr. Cole, is not here but 15 
now at Madras. His letter (Ext. D) however shows that the workman did not 
obtain permission from him before leaving for home. In view of the evidence 
and circumstances, I find nothing to interfere with the action taken by the 
management. I agree that the workman had been dealt with rather leniently. 


Part I] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 2655

As to the preliminary objection of the Company, it appears that the workmen 
of the ¥nstallation to which the complainant belongs were no party 10 the 
dispute over bonus which was the subject matter of the previous reference. It 
further appears that these workmen obtained their bonus and granted signed 
receipts of having accepted the amount paid by the Company in full satisfac-

concerned in the previous dispute. So, section 33 cannot be said to have been 
contravened. I, therefore, agree with the Company that complaint under 
section 33A is not maintginable. So the application must fail both on merits 
and on law. 


I award accordingly.

There had been an Award by a Tribunal and on the said _ basis the wage

“That the basic ve of the lower grade staff which are on an average

index of 180 and slightly above what it would be at the living cost 
index of 100 points”, 
and it has been also argued that the Madras Tribunal gave awards in respect of 
the same categories of the lower grade staff in Oil Companies (I.D. 52 of 1951 
and I.D. 2 of 1952), by which the basic pay of the lower grade staff of the 
Standard Vaccum Company in Madras was fixed at Rs. 50 in the minimum. So 
the present contention of the workmen is that the differents categories of the

“Shri Swaminadhan appearing for the Company (Standard Vacuum) con- 
ceded that if there be any employee of these two categorics getting 
less than what the employees doing similar jobs in the Burmah

We think that Shri Swaminadhan has taken a very reasonable 
attitude. We accordingly direct that the members of the service 
and security staff of this ا یٹ‎ doing the same or similar jobs 
shall be put on the same footing as those of Burmah Shell 
Company”. 


If this be the view in that case, I think it is all the more reasonable that simila. 
view should be taken in the present case and that the members of the lower 
grade staff now in question should be put on the same footing as those of the 
lower grade staff of other department of the selfsame Standard Vacuum Com- 
pany; otherwise there would be serious discontent amongst the workmen in 
these two different departments of this Company. So I am of opinion that the 
grade and scales of wages accepted with regard to lower grade staff (vide Ext. 
A), of the other department should be the grade and scale of wages in respect 
of the lower grade staff now in question.

scale of wages effect was given from Ist January 1953, although the agreement 
was signed in June 1953. In these circumstances I hold that the above wage 
scale which is now being awarded is to take effect from Ist January 1953. As 
regards adjustment and fitting in, I am of opinion that the adjustment in item 
“C” in Ext. 1 (clause 1, a and b) should be applicable as regards lower grade 
staff scale of wages in the present Award, i.e., that all salaries will be increased

AWARD. 


overnment of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. کے ری ای‎ 53, dated the 14th September 1953, referred an indus: 
trial dispute existing between The Calcutta Jute Manufacturing Co., Ltd, 
93, Narkeldanga Main Road, Calcutta and their workmen represented by 7 
Calcutta Jute Manufacturing Workers’ Union, 95, Narkeldanga Main Road,

Calcutta, regarding the matters specified in the schedule to the order of refer- 


ence under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 
1947), to this Tribunal for its adjudication. 


This was received in the office of this Tribunal on 18th September 1953 
and usual notices were issued to both parties for appearance and written state- 
ments. Both parties filed written statements in due course. 


The three issues as per schedule to the order of reference are— 


(1) How many permanent posts in the Mill are lying vacant and should 
He filled up immediately. (a) How are they to be filled up and by 
what time. | 


(2) Whether the registered Badlis are entitled to any kind of allowance, 
or benefits. If so, what. 


(3) Whether the termination of services of Shri Jogen Prosad Sharma was 
justified. (a) What reliefs he is entitled to. 


The parties in a joint petition filed on 24th April 1954 informed the Tri- 
bunal that issue Nos. 1 and 3 as mentioned in the schedule to the order of 
reference have been amicably settled. The terms of settlement are mentioned 
in the attachment (Annexure “A”). 


Regarding the second issue, the Union stated that the registered Badlis were 
formerly granted a weekly allowance of Rs. 2 but the practice was _ discon- 
tinued some time in 1950. The Union submitted that the practice should be 
re-introduced and the registered Badlis be paid Rs. 4 per week while not in job. 


The Company in its written statement contended that the issue was not 
maintainable in law. The registered Badlis, when not actually employed, are 
merely employment seekers and as such they are not workmen within the 
meaning of the Industrial Disputes Act. The origin of the system of paying Rs. 2 

r week to the registered Badlis was traced back to war years when they were 
supplied with foodstuffs at concessional rates which were ex gratia. After the 
First Jute Tribunal Award, these concessions were valued at Rs. 2 per week. 
Since the publication of the Second Jute T ribunal Award, all Mills gradually 
stopped this payment. The last Badli in this Mill receiving Rs. 2 under the 
old system was absorbed in the permanent cadre in October 1951. The badlis, 
when they are not employed, are not entitled to any allowance or benefit much 
less, at the increased rate of Rs. 4 per week as claimed by the Union. 


FINDINGS. 


Issue No. 2. 


Neither party adduced any evidence. Heard representative for the Union 
and learned counsel Shri Bose and learned representative of the I.J.M.A., 
Shri Ghosh on this issue. Shri Bose relied on a case reported in 1953 L.A.C., 
page 440 of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of India (Nellimorla Jute 
Mills Co., Ltd., and another vs. their workmen) and contended that the 
Hon’ble Tribunal held in the case that the Badlis were not workmen under the 
Industrial Disputes Act and as such they were not entitled to any benefit. The 
facts as stated in the pleadings appear to be identically the same as in the case 
under report. Further, there is no rebuttal of the Company case that the last 
badli in the Mill receiving Rs. 2 under the old system was absorbed in the 
permanent cadre in 1951. The system of paying cash ~ value of concessional 
foodstuffs was purely a war time measure and there is no justification for con- 
tinting the same. That being the position, the Union can hardly justify its 
claim on any ground. The position of law as pointed out by the learned coun- 
sel for the Company is clear. The registered Badlis are not workmen of the 


2664 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 [Par I 


Mill save and except when they are actually taken in for work. The Mill 
no doubt maintains a register for Badlis and whenever there is occasion to 
engage temporary hands, they choose those whose names appear on the regis- 
ter and for the purpose of giving every one a fair chance, they follow the 
practice of employment by rotation. The badlis are employment seekers and 
not workmen of the Mill. Therefore, they are not entitled to get any allowance 
or benefit as a matter of right. I answer the issue accordingly. This is my 
award, 


The joint petition of compromise filed by the parties on 24th April 1954 
and its Annexure marked “A” do form part of this award.

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. The Indian Press, 
Ltd., 93A, Dhurmatatla Street, Calcutta, represented by the Culeuita 
Printing Press Owners’ Association, 32, Upper Circular Road, Calcutta and 
their workmen represented by the Press Employees’ Association, 249B, 
Bowbazar Street, Calcutta. 


BEFORE THE SECOND INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT: 
SHRI M. N. GAN, Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances: 


For the Company: Shri Nalini Kanta Mukherjee, Advocate with Shri N. N. 
Mukherjee, Advocate, Director, Indian Press, Ltd., and Shri S. Bose, 
Superintendent, Calcutta Printing Press Owners’ Association. 


For the Association: Shri N. D. Manna, Counsel with Shri K. K. Guha and 
Shri Indu Bhusan Sirkar. 


AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order 
No. 3123Dis./D/13L-34/53, dated the 17th August 1953, referred an indus- 
trial dispute existing between Messrs. The Indian Press, Ltd., 93A, Dhuramtalla 
Street, Calcutta, represented by the Caloutta Printing Press Owners’ Association, 
32, Upper Circular Road, Calcutta and their workmen represented by the Press 
Employees’ Association, 249B, Bowbazar Street, Calcutta, under sections 7 and 
10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), to this Tribunal for 
its adjudication. 


The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 26th August 
1953 and usual notices were issued to both parties for appearance and written 
statements. Both parties filed written statemens in the case. 


In the written statement filed on behalf of the employees, the employees 
among others stated that the Indian Press, Ltd. (hereinafter called the Com- 
pany), Calcutta, is a large famous and prosperous printing and publishing 
house in India having its head office at Allahabad and principal branches at 
Calcutta, Patna, Lucknow and other principal towns in India. It employs about 
130 employees in its Calcutta branch alone. In 1948, there was an industrial 
dispute between the Company and its workmen regarding grade, scales of pay, 
dearness allowance, Provident Fund, security of service, etc., which was 
referred to Shri A. Das Gupta, Judge, Industrial Tribunal for his adjudication. 
It was settled on the basis of an agreement between the parties and the Award 
was published in the Calcutta Gazette on 11th May 1948. In 1950, another 
dispute was referred to the same Tribunal who made an Award which was 
published in the Calcutta Gazette on 1st March 1951. The Company did not 
implement the award and took recourse to underhand and questionable methods 
to deprive the workers of their legitimate dues. A written representation of 
their grievances was put before Shri H. S. Ghose, Director-in-Charge, on 28th 
November 1953, which however was not attended to. Thereafter, at the 
intervention of the Assistant Labour Commissioner a séttlement was made on 
16th January 1953. A Memorandum of Settlement was drawn up that day 
and signed by the parties. The agreement was to take effect from Ist April 
next. That however was not implemented and the employees on 4th June 


2668 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 [Parr I 


লস یو‎ ea উস سے مصحف‎ wae 


1953 moved the Labour Commissioner for immediate implementation, of the 
terms of settlement. The Company failing to win over the employees on its 
side took recourse to methods of threat, coercion and victimisation. On 30th 
June 1953 it served notices on 27 employees terminating their services with 
elfect from 1st of next month and placed them under suspension from imme- 
diate effect pending the approval of its action by the Labour Commissioner, 
The retrenchment was malafide, unnecessary, and made for ulterior purpose. 
Hence, this reference. 


The Indian Press, Ltd. (hereafter called the Company) denied the allega- 
tions of the employees and stated that it sustained heavy losses in the past due 
to acute trade depression, dearth of work and unhealthy competition in market 
and the loss of several publications. There was also considerable fall in the 
number and vaiue of orders for several years past. The Company, however, 
continued to keep the workmen in employment and expecting improvement in the 
situation in near tuture. | Unfortunately, there was no bright prospect in the 
business in Calcutta. The Head Office accordingly wrote to the Calcutta 
branch on 20th April 1953 and sent a copy of the resolution dated 16th May 
1953 asking it to adopt immediately such measures of economy as considered 
necessary in view of the gradual deterioration in its financial position. 


The Head Office was unable to feed the Calcutta branch with orders as it 
did in the past and ran into debts to the extent of over sixty thousand rupees. 
The Calcutta branch instead of closing down the business completely thought 
it necessary to effect retrenchment of staff which it considered surplus to its 
requirements in view of the fall in work. It accordingly, decided to retrench 
27 members of its staff from different departments out of a total strength of 
91 and served notices on all of them terminating their services from Ist July 
1953. As conciliation proceeding was pending, it did not discharge the said 
employees immediately but placed them under suspension with effect from 15 
July 1953 as a security measure and in the interest of industry. In effecting 
the retrenchment in the Calcutta branch, the Company followed the normal rule 
of “Last come first go” as far as practicable. It has also filed an application 
undér section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act to this Tribunal for permission 
to retrench the said staff immediately. 


The Company admitted that the two previous disputes referred to in the 
employees’ written statement were adjudicated in the Tribunal and two awards 
were made on 11th May 1948 and Ist March 1951. The first award was fully 
implemented while the last was implemented in part due to stay order issued 
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India against the decision of the Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal. It admitted having been a party to the Memoran- 
dum of Settlement dated 16th January 1953 and said that it implemented the 
terms fully for some time but due to financial instability and loss, it revoked 
the agreement by a notice, dated 4th June 1953. It is only for that that the 
employees approached the Labour Commissioner for implementation of that 
scttlement. It pleaded that it was unable to carry out its obligations in view 
of its continued loss particularly in the Calcutta branch which had proved to 
be an uneconomic unit in the whole concern. Regarding the proposed retrench- 
ment and alleged suspension of the employees, it stated that both were justified 
in the circumstances of the case. 


The issues as per schedule to the order of reference are— 


(1) Whether retrenchment is necessary? If so, to what extent? 


(2) Whether the orders of suspension on the 27 workers are justified? 
What relief are the workers entitled to ?

FINDINGS. 


Issue No. 1 The Company justifics its action for retrenchment on 
economic grounds. It is stated that acute trade depression and consequent 
dearth of work resulted in substantial loss. The loss was duc to (i) trade 
depression; (ii) dearth of work (shortage of business); (iii) unhealthy com- 
petition; (iv) loss of several publications. In view of the substantial loss, the 
Head Office instructed its Calcutta branch to economise its expenditure as best 
as possible. The Board of Directors adopted a resolution to that effect and the 
Calcutta branch reacted promptly by issuing notices terminating the contract 
of employment of the 27 employees from various departments. In doing so, 
it alleged that it adopted a course which was less harmful to the business and 
to the employees in general. The choice was between closing the Calcutta 
business completely and retrenching the surplus staff. It decided to do away 
with the surplus staff and asked for necessary permission from this Tribunal 
in view of the fact that the adjudication of a dispute between the parties was 
pending before it. The Company further stated that in selecting the personnel 
departmentwise for retrenchment, it followed the well-known principle “last 
come first go” as far as possible. The defence of the Union is that the com- 
pany was actuated by motives of victimisation and other ulterior motives, in 
making this retrenchment. It was not necessary for there was no shortage of 
business. The Company did not fulfil its obligations towards the employees 
under the two previous awards and an agreement of settlement and carried 
out the threat to curb the Union activities by rooting out the evil elements from 
the staff. There were no genuine trade reasons for this retrenchment and the 
action was far from bona fide. In fact, the defence was a complete denial of 
the Company’s case. 


The onus of proving the necessity for the proposed action is on the Com- 
pany. The management has produced its accounts, its Balance-sheets for 
several years and all relevant files and registers in this Tribunal to show that 
the business in the Calcutta branch had been gradually deteriorating since 1948 
and that it sustained heavy losses in the year ending 3151 March 1953. It has 
proved abstracts and extracts from books of accounts and registers, showing 
considerable fall in the number of orders, both Hcad Office and local, and also 
showing loss of several publications in the relevant period. It examined wit- 
hesses including its Manager in support of the above and explained away the 
inconsistencies sought to be made out by the Union. The management no 
doubt has prima facie right to decide its labour force. It is not bound to incur 
any uneconomic expenditure merely to keep the certain number of workmen 
engaged. It has also the right to apply its capital in the manner it considers 
best. 


Question now is whether a case of retrenchment has been made out, namely, 
whether the management has been able to establish a case of loss in business 
and dearth of work which alone would justify the retrenchment proposed in 
this case. The next point is whether in the matter of retrenchment, the 
management had acted bona fide. If both these elements are established, the 
management is the sole judge to the number to be discharged by way of 
retrenchment. If the action is not bona fide, in that case the Tribunal must 
scrutinise the number and uphold the retrenchment of such number as it thinks 
to have become surplus. The principal point is no doubt the loss in business 
during the relevant period. The Balance-sheets of 1948 to 1953 (Ext. C to 
Ext. C5) show the gradual deterioration in business profits. Profits in 1951 
amounted to about Rs. 8 thousand. In 1952, it was Rs. 10 thousand and in 
the relevant year ending 31st March 1953, loss of the Calcutta branch amount- 
ed to Rs. 50 thousand. The Balance-sheets have not been challenged in the 


2670 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 {Part ] 


written statement and after a very searching examination during the hearjng of 
the case in the Tribunal, the learned representative for the Union could not 
point out any error in them. An endeavour was made to attack the company’s 
accounts as disclosed in the abstracts filed (Exts. E, El, F, G. H.) mostly on 
what appear to be speculative and unsubstantial grounds. It succeeded in find- 
ing a mistake in the total or alleged inconsistencies in the two statements which 
however were successfully explained on .behalf of the company. Apart from 
raising suspicion here and there, the Union had failed to show that the accounts 
particularly the Balance-sheets relied on by the Company on this point are 
substantially incorrect. The main criticisms about the Company’s accounts 
advanced on behalf of the Unon are: (i) The accounts are not strictly proved; 
(11) not kept in regular course of business; (iii) no statutory presumption of 
correctness in case of Balance-sheet. The learned representative had apparent- 
ly lost sight of the provisions of Rule 14 of the Industrial Disputes Act Rules 
in this connection. The Tribunal may accept, admit or call for evidence at 
any stage of the procceding before it and any such manner as it thinks fit. 
Accordingly, the question of proving the accounts strictly according to the pro- 
visions of the Indian Evidence Act, particularly under section 34 of it, does not 
arise. It has not been shown that any of these accounts are not kept in regular 
course of business for in that event, the evidentiary value of the accounts will 
certainly be less than what it otherwise should be and a Balance-sheet of 
accounts prepared by auditors who certify them according to the provisions of 
the Indian Companies Act can of course be shown to be inaccurate and not 
reliable in the case. But unless that is done to the satisfaction of the Tribunal, 
the Balance-sheet may be looked upon, for our present purpose, as prima facie 
evidence in this case. No question of presumption eitherway arises. In the 
next place, the learned representative for the Union has urged that the entire 
accounts of the Company including the Head Office and its other branches be 
taken into consideration to decide whether the Company had sustained loss in 
a particular year. This is no doubt true in deciding the question of bonus 
payable to the workers. It would be entirely begging the question, if we treat 
the Company with its Head Office and branches as one unit, one undertaking, 
as suggested by the learned representative for the Union in deciding whether the 
Calcutta branch is running at a loss in a particular year. After all, the manage- 
ment has the freedom in the matter of incurring an uneconomic industrial ex- 
penditure in any of its branches or departments. The Tribunal cannot reason- 
ably interfere with the management’s discretion in that matter. The Tribunal 
would be wrong if it takes the entire account of the Company including its 
Head Office and other branches into consideration in deciding the issue whether 
the Calcutta branch is running at a loss. That contention is unsound as the 
Calcutta branch maintains its separate accounts and separate Balance-sheet 
which are prepared every year, as it should be, for the consideration of the 
Board of Directors and the Shareholders. Accordingly, that criticism of the 
accounts on behalf of the Union should fail. The only evidence forthcoming 
on the Union’s side on this point is that of P.W. 6 Shri Kumud Behari Dey. 
He said that the Calcutta branch does work worth about 50 thousand rupees 
month and makes a profit of rupees 10 thousand out of it. In 1954, calendars 
were printed of the value of one lakh fifty thousand rupees. The evidentiary 
value of this is nil for the witness admits that he said this by impression. It was 
his guess work. There is no corroboration on this point. Coming as it does 
from a biased person, an employee to be retrenched, in this case, this evidence 
leaves no impression on the Tribunal as against the entire accounts of the 
Company placed for scrutiny before it. The learned representative for the 
Union did his best at the hearing of the case. He left no stone unturned in 
the matter of scrutiny of accounts but since he had not the help from an earlier 
inspection of the accounts (which was not asked), some of the grounds taken 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 4 2671 


appeag to be of merely speculative character. We are not unmindful of the 
difficulties of the employees in the matter of accounts, for ordinarily they do not 
get any access to the Company’s accounts, neither they are taken into confidence 
by the Company in these matters. Naturally, mat become suspicious and 
when the accounts are produced and shown to them in the Tribunal, they 
assailed almost every possible expenditure either as unduly heavy or as 
incorrect. That unfortunately happened in this case. The Union did not 
gave any idea of their points of dispute regarding the Company’s accounts either 
in the written statement or in any petition of objection filed subsequent to that. 
The Company produced all the books of accounts, registers and files, relevant 
for the purpose of this enquiry and made suitable abstracts for proper apprecia- 
tion of the points at issue. While the Union assailed some of the abstract 
accounts, it did not place its finger on any portion of the Balance-sheet and 
said that it was incorrect. The Union did not succeed in saying that the Com- 
pany had concealed any of its income from the Balance-sheet or has dishonestly 
diverted it with some ulterior purpose. It has been said that a commission was 
paid in a year of loss. This has been explained. It has not been shown that 
it is an unusual feature in the Company’s business and that it was incurred only 
in the year under review. It is in the next place said that paper worth rupees 
77 thousand 7 hundred and 32 was used in the relevant year which showed 
that the volume of work was greater than accounted for in the Balance-sheet. 
It has been explained on the Company’s side that this figure shows only the 
quantity of paper purchased and not consumed in the year in question. One 
cannot possibly make a reasonable guess from any such criticism of accounts. 
It is in the next place contended that the position of factory labour charges 
was going high whereas the average monthly volume of work, i.e., printing was 
going down. This was taken from Ext. El as an instance of inconsistency. 
At the same time, it has been contended that the only reasonable conclusion 
a Tribunal should draw is that the volume of work must have increased along, 
with the increase in labour charges. It appears that the factory labour charges 
was 26 per cent. in 1951, 29°25 per cent. in 1952 and 28 per cent. in 1953, 
whereas the monthly volume of work on an average in 1951 was 38 thousand, 
in 1952, 35 thousand, in 1953, 31 thousand. O.P.W. 1 Shri J‘ N. Bose, 
Assistant Manager, has explained that the labour charges have gone high in 
recent years and that due to unhealthy competition in the market and increased 
cost of materials, the printing charges in this particular concern, which is 
admittedly to be a quality press, are much higher. Accordingly, there could 
not be any such inconsistency as has been sought to be mde out from Ext. 1: 
A lot of comments was made on expenses under heads “Out Printing and 
Binding”. It has been suggested that this shows that the Company has acted 
dishonestly in getting a part of the work done outside at an enormous cost and 
not in their own concern by the employees. Nothing has been shown from 
this that the accounts or for the matter of that the Balance-sheets are incorrect. 
It has been explained by O.P.W. 2 Shri Mukherjee that printed matters are 
sometimes finished outside. P.W, 6 Shri Dey has explained this in his deposi- 
tion. He said that we had no employees to do this sort of work in our Press. 
Only such work as could not be done in the Press was done outside only to 
put a finishing touch to the printing work as for example, mounting a calendar 
after it was printed. O.P.W. 1 Shri Bose emphatically said that no portion of 
printing work was done outside. The Company had a temporary binding shop 
at Tangra and the casual labour charges paid for that shop was kept separate. 
That explains the casual labour charges paid in the accounts. As to binding 
charges, the Press had no binding department before and that it was done out- 
side. Jt has not been shown that departing from its previous practice, the 


Company has with’a view to defeat the just claim of the employees in pending 


2672 TOK CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 [Parr 1 


disputes, adopted a new measure in the particular year. The learned rrepre- 
sentative for the Union referred to Ext. 14, Bill Book and Ext. 17, Job 
Registrar and Ext. 18, Daily Allocations Book, and tried to show that regard. 
ing the volume of work, there was an inaccuracy noticed in the Bill Book. 
O.P.W. 3 Shri Mitra, the Estimator and outside representative who maintains 
these books, has explained it away saying that only so much of the work as was 
finished by the time 1185 shown in these accounts and that they do not give 
any idea of the total value of the work. As I have already said above, that 
much of the criticism levelled against the Balance-sheet and the Company’s 
other accounts, was based on suspicion. Suspicion is no substitute of proof. 
Accordingly, even if the Union can succeed in establishing a suspicious 
circumstances here and there in the accounts placed before the Tribunal, -that 
would not serve their purpose namely to show that the accounts were substan- 
tially unreliable and that the Balance-sheet was wrong. After all, the Company 
does not gain anything in preparing a false Balance-sheet for the purpose of 
effecting this retrenchment in this case. It has been said on more than one 
occasion in course of hearing of the case that Shri H. S. Ghose, the Director 
in charge of the Calcutta branch, is a good and reasonable man, who was 
always on the employees’ side and that it was the Head Office people who had 
prevailed upon him in doing this mischief to the employees. It was sought to 
be made out in this case by Shri 1. B. Sircar and Shri Mantu Choudhury that 
the Company never fulfilled its obligations towards its employees and that the 
two previous awards and a settlement, amicably made between the parties, 
were not implemented. The Manager’s evidence, on the other hand is (and 
that is corroborated by Shri I. B. Sircar, Secretary of the Union) that the 
award of 1948 was fully implemented, and that the award of 1951 was partly 
implemented due to stay order issued by the Supreme Court of India, in an 
appeal against that award and that the settlement was also partly given ০96 
to. It was only when the staggering loss became known to the Board of 
Directors that they changed their minds and pleaded inability to continue tp, 
give effect to the terms of settlement. The Calcutta branch took action only: 
when it was instructed to do so by a letter and a resolution of the Board of \ 
Directors (vide annexures to the Company’s written statement). Therefore, 
-in all probabilities, the management here could not even dream of manipulat- 
ing its accounts at a time when it was entering, into, in a spirit of conciliation, 
a solemn agreement, with its employees and when all disputes for the time 
being did not exist. Further, a Company as in this instant case, could not 
risk its reputation in the market by publicly proclaiming its loss in business. 
Judging by all reasonable standards, the ‘Tribunal fails to appreciate the 
criticism of the Balance-sheet from the Union side. The loss to the extent of 
rupees fifty thousand in the year ending 31st March 1953 in the Calcutta 
branch has been established. In addition to that, the debt amounting to about 
rupees sixty thousand due to “Sundry Creditors” is also disclosed in the 
Balance-sheet. O.P.W. 1 Shri Bose says that this debt remains unpaid over 
and above the loss indicated above. This is a substantial loss in the business 
and the management is no doubt justified in adopting measures of economy in 
_its expenditure in the manner proposed. The proposed retrenchment of 27 
employees will result in the reduction of expenditure amounting to Rs. 2,159 
per month, iie., Rs. 25,908 a year. The over-all financial position in the 
Calcutta branch does not show any improvement at present. The gloomy pros- 
pect of which O.P.W. 1 Shri Bose says (and that is the Company’s case in the 
written statement) still holds good. 


Next question is whether there is any real dearth of work as a result of the 
alleged trade depression and unhealthy competition in the market and loss of 
several publications as alleged. The Union's case is that there was plenty of

work for everybody, and that there was no employee who was surplus in any 
real sense. The alleged dearth of work was more fictitious, rather than 
real, and of the Company’s own creation, for the purpose of carrying out its 
intention “to root out the evil elements” out of the staff. This would be amply 
borne out by the admitted facts, namely, (i) refusal of work, i.e., publications 
on no justifiable grounds; (ii) overtime work; (iii) re-employment of retrench- 
ed staff and new recruits. It is, therefore, necessary to examine the evidence 
on this point. It would be wrong to do so, in complete isolation in disregard- 
ing the back-ground of the present distpute. The evidence of what happened 
_in the past regarding the previous disputes between the parties was given an 
undue emphasis on the Union's side. I have already referred to Shri I. B. 
Sircar’s evidence on this point. He is the Secretary of the Press Employees’ 
Union, a party to this dispute. He said that the two previous awards were not 
implemented. Accordingly a fresh list of demands was forwarded to the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner on 28th November 1952 (Ext. 2). This was 
followed by an amicable settlement between the parties even without the inter- 
vention of the Press Employees’ Union and the Labour Directorate. A Memo- 
randum of Settlement, dated 16th January 1953 (Ext. 3), was prepared which, 
among others, provided for payment of dearness allowance to some of the 
employees, who were not getting it, tiffin allowance for menial workers and 
arrears Of wages under the last award from April 1953. I recall the evidence 
of O.P.W. 1 Shri Bose who said that the awards and settlement were imple- 
mented and so much of the second award as stayed by the orders of the 
Supreme Court of India was not given effect to. In fact, it was admitted by 
the employees themselves that they were getting full dearness allowance under 
the award of 1951. Then came the directive from the Head Office due to dis- 
closure of substantial loss in the Balance-sheet of 1952-53. This was followed 
by revocation of the settlement (Ext. 3) and lastly, by this retrenchment in 
dispute. In one of its letters to Mantu Choudhury (Ext. E) the management 
took exception to his too frequent intervention, on behalf of the employees in 
general, in controversial matters, regarding the grievances of the employees. 
This letter has been interpreted as an open threat against the employees. All 
that it said that the management did not approve of the conduct of Mantu 
Choudhury playing the role of a self-styled leader of the employees, that it knew 
of the cxistence of a group of mischief-mongers and anti-social elements among 
the employees and that it was determined to root out the evil. At the same 
time, it assured that genuine Union activities would not 06 interfered with. 
This, according to the Union, is the background against which the evidence of 
dearth of work will be examined. First of all, regarding matters of pub- 
lications, the Company has admitted that there has been gradual loss in some 
publications. It has been sought to be made out on Union’s side that the 
management whimsically and with dishonest motive refused these publications 
and tried to connect it with the existence of labour dispute in the undertaking. 
The Union examined Dhirendra Kumar Dey, Manager of the fortnightly paper 
“CHITTARANJAN”. This was printed up to March or April 1953 in the 
Calcutta branch of the Indian Press, Ltd. Since then, it was discontinued. By 
letter (Ext. 1), dated 250) March 1953, Shri Dey said that Shri Bose, Assistant 
Manager, told him that he would not be able to make any arrangement for 
printing this journal due to existence of labour dispute in the Press. It was 
suggested to him in cross-examination that their bills were always in arrears. 
Shri Dey admitted that there was no letter to show that the management declin-

to the Labour Directorate on 9th July 1953 and 14th July 1953 (vide Exts. 12 
and 12A) was sought to be made out by the Union’s own document (Ext. 16). 
They have made their own calculations from the tariff rates. But it is not the 
tariff rates that always explain the value of work. Sometimes work was done 
at lesser rates. Accordingly, the alleged inaccuracies in these lists which were 
prepared from the registers for the purpose of the conciliation proceedings

Taken along with the evidence of Shri Bose, it establishes that there has been

a 50 per cent. reduction in the work in the relevant year. The retrencfument

urges that its action is justified. Existence of acute trade depression at the

sides and the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal finds that the 
Calcutta branch of this Company was running at a substantial loss due to acute 
trade depression and dearth of work in the relevant year. This would no doubt 
justify the proposed retrenchment and make the same necessary. 


Next question is whether in effecting the retrenchment as proposed, the 
Company acted bona fide. In view of the finding just recorded, the action 
does not prima facie appear to be mala fide. Economy in expenditure is ordi- 
narily the only way to prevent recurring losses.in a business. The management 
made this retrenchment with that end in view. It has already been noticed 
from the evidence discussed above that there has been about 50 per cent. reduc- 
tion in work due to fall in orders and necessarily some employees have become 
surplus to its requirements. It is not that the workload on the remaining staff 
has been unduly increased. No one speaks of it. The reduction of staff as 
proposed comes up to one-third of them. Therefore, judging by that test the 
action does not appear to be mala fide. The Union of course alleged that the 
entire move was actuated by motives of victimisation of the undesirable elements 
in the staff. The Union saw mala fides in every step taken in this direction. 
It relied on one of Company’s letters (Ext. 9E, addressed to Shri Mantu 
Choudhury) and on the evidence of P.W. 2 Shri I. B. Sircar and P.W. 5 Shri 
Mantu Choudhury in support of its contention that the Company never ful- 
filled any of its obligations to its employees, went back on its own agreement 
to settle current disputes and on flimsiest grounds discharged the employees. 
This has already been discussed. It would be sufficient if a review of the 
facts of the Labour Management Relations is made here. It is true that the 
two previous awards were not fully implemented. The reason was obvious. 
There was an appeal against the award of 1951 and the Hon’ble Supreme 
Court of India issued an order staying execution of the award in part. That 
stayed the hands of the management. The business was running at a loss and 

cut in expenditure was considered necessary in the interest of the industry. 
The settlement of 16th January 1953 made amicably between the parties 
without outside intervention given effect to for some time was finally revoked. 
The dismissal of 8 workers on 31st March 1953 consequent to the sale of 
machines, proved in this case not only by the agreement (Ext. Q) but by the 
evidence of P.W. 5 Shri Mantu Choudhury and P.W. 6 Shri Dhirendra Nath 
Das, discussed above, raised a dispute which also was amicably settled. The 
workers in a signed petition endorsed by the Assistant Labour Commissioner 
withdrew it and the dispute was closed. These do not show that the entire 
move of the management was motivated by something else than economic 
reasons. I have already discussed the letter (Ext. 9E). The management 
expressed its displeasure at the conduct of Shri Mantu Choudhury and said

that ahe undesirable elements within the staff was a menace to internal dis- 
cipline, so important in an industrial administration, and expressed its deter- 
mination to root out the evil. At the same time, it assured that the genuine 
trade union activities should not be interfered with. If Ext. E is to be taken 
as an admission on the part of the management, it must be read as a whole. 
Further no admission is conclusive. Accordingly, it must be read in the con- 
text in which it is used. It leaves no doubt in any reasonable mind that the 
management did not like Mantu Choudhury interfering too frequently in the 
management functions on behalf of the employees. He is not an official of the 
Press Employees’ Union which officially looks after the interest of the cmployees 
of this concern. He along with others were clected representative for a limited 
purpose, namely, to settle a dispute which was settled amicably. He was not the 
only representative of the employees but still he went on finding fault with the 
management in all matters affecting the employces in general. He would not 
even leave a closed dispute untouched. This naturally irritated the manage- 
ment and it came out with a reply in Ext. 9E. The action of the management 
appears to be bona fide but as Mantu Choudhury, one of the retrenched 
employees before this Tribunal has already incurred displeasure of the manage- 
ment and as there are good matcrials to show that some discrimination in his 
case was done, the Tribunal is justified in scrutinising the merits of the case 
of the proposed retrenched personnel. The Tribunal would be failing in its 
duty if it does not Jook into the case of the retrenched personnel in_ the 
circumstances stated above. 


The written statement, filed on behalf of the Union is unfortunately silent 
on many material points, and contains many unnecessary details, which could 
have been easily omitted. It is now contended on behalf of the workers that 
the well-known principle of “last come first go” was not followed 
in making this retrenchment. This does not find any place 11) the 
written statement. It is essentially a question of fact and it is 
imperatively necessary that it should be specifically pointed out. The 
Company was taken by surprise when the Union challenged its action 
on the aforesaid ground. Be that as it may, now that the both 51063 
have adduced evidence on this point, the question will be considered on its 
merits. ‘The Company’s contention is that the Block Department, Composing 
Department and Letter Press Department are running at a loss and that it has 
selected the personnel for retrenchment department-wise following the principle 
of “first come last go” as far as possible. The Union’s evidence reveals that 
(i) junior compositor is in service whereas a senior is selected for retrench- 
ment; (ii) only employee of a department has been retrenched and (iii) idle 
employees are kept in service. It is only in case of P.W. 5 Mantu Choudhury, 
that evidence has been given to show that his junior in the department con- 
tinues in service whereas he was improperly selected. No other evidence is 
forthcoming to show that any such unfair discrimination was made in making the 
selection. Evidence was however given to show that in some cases only 
employee of a department has been selected and that the favourites of the 
management who are idling away their time are kept in service. Further 
evidence is that some superannuated employees are continuing in service who 
should have been retrenched in terms of the Press Award, dated Ist March 
1951 (vide Government Publication, Major Tribunal’s Awards, March 1951 
p. 506). That shows that in case of retrenchment the superannuated employees 
should be first axed. Secondly, employees should be selected according to the 
“last come first go” principle as far as possible. Evidence is now given to show 
that Bafat Meah, Sudhamoy and Mutaleb are superannuated employees who are 
continuing in service. The age of retirement is 55. Here again, the Union’s 
written statement is silent on this point. O.P.W. 1 Shri Bose said that Bafat

whereas Mantu Choudhury was appointed on Ist November 1948, two years

whereas Narain Chandra was getting Rs. 57 + 22 per month. Judging by the 
length of service, Mantu Choudhury is undoubtedly senior to Narain. Question 
now is whether the two really worked in two different departments. Ext. 18

junior man was not given any complicated work. It is therefore abundantly 
clear that these compositors in the Hand Composing Department were employed, 
when necessary, on English-Bengali work. The Company could not prove 
that the two departments are water-tied departments, namely, that employees 
in one department are tied by the conditions of their service to that department 
alone and could not be employed in any other department. On the contrary, 
it has becn shown by the Company’s own document (Ext. 18) that Mantu 
Choudhury, a senior English Compositor, was given a senior Bengali Com- 
positor’s job. Unless the departments are water-tied, the normal rule of “last 
come first go” should be followed. The rule of “last come first go” has now 
been brought on the Statute Book by an amendment of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. [Vide Section 25(G).] The principle of retrenchment department-wise 
has been laid down in a very recent case by their lordships of the Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in Sudarsan Banerjee and others vs. 
McLeod & Co., Ltd. (1954, L.L.J., Volume ,ا‎ page 174). Since Mantu 
Choudhury who is a good senior English soar sea can do Bengali composi- 
tion work equally well, it is in the fitness of things that he should be retained 
in the service and not be selected for retrenchment. For good reasons, he 
seems to have been a headache to the management for his too frequent un- 
warranted move against the management for redress of the alleged grievances 
of the employees. But that should not be the reason why in the matter of 
retrenchment, he should be selected in place of junior man to him in service. 
I have considered the matter both subjectively and objectively from the point 
of view of the employer and the employee and considered it necessary to observe 
that the conduct of this employee was not always commendable. In the interest 
of discipline and industrial peace, he should not act as leader of the employees 
until he is elected as an official of the Press Employees Union or a Union of

Internal discipline is as much necessary for the establishment and maintenance

Evidence is now forthcoming that Anil Das Gupta, only distributor, Tara-

Issue No. 2.—The Company by a notice, dated 30th June 1953, suspended 
the 27 employees sought to be retrenched in this case for trade reasons, as a 
security measure and in the interest of industry. In the notice issued over the 
signature of the Manager, the workers werc told that the management wanted 
to retrench them as surplus hands. The notice however says: “As proceedings 
are pending before the Labour Commissioner,. West Bengal, for conciliation of 
certain matters, the Company is not able to give effect the above retrenchment 
forthwith, and it is necessary to seek the permission of the Labour Commis- 
sioner to discharge you on grounds of retrenchment with effect from 1st July 
1953. * ٠ * The Company hereby further informs you that on 
the grant of the permission referred to above, you will be paid one month’s 
wages in lieu of notice and you shall collect your Provident Fund dues. You 
shall receive your wages up to the period ending 30th June 1953 between the

hours 4—40-30 p.m. and 5-30 p.m.” This order of suspension is challenged 
on merits as also on point of law. The Union contends that there was no 
necessity for retrenchment, a point which has been decided in connection with 
Issue No. 1. It further contends that in suspending the employees without 
permission, the Company openly contravened the provisions of section 33 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act inasmuch as the order was illegal. The Company 
justifies its action on the allegation that the retrenchment is necessary for trade 
reasons and inasmuch as it cannot carry out its decision immediately in view 
of the ban of scction 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. It placed the employees 
under suspension with immediate effect as a security measure. O.P.W. 1 Shri 
Bose said that the management had to take recourse to this method in the 
interest of industry as also in view of the prohibition of section 33 of the Act. 
In due course, the Company applied for permission to the Conciliation Officer 
and thereafter to this Tribunal when the dispute was referred to it. Suspcn- 
sion is very different from dismissal. When a man is suspended from the office 
he holds it, it is merely a direction that so long he holds the office, he must 
not do anything in the discharge of his duties in the office. It has been held 
repeatedly that ‘suspension is neither dismissal nor discharge from service. 
This order of suspension cannot be interpreted as one altering the conditions 
of service. In the notice the Manager makes it abundantly clear that the 
measure was not adopted by way of punishment to anybody but that was 
necessary inasmuch as the previous permission of the Tribunal is required to 
give effect to its decision to retrench them. Accordingly, in my opinion, this 
order of suspension is no violation of the provision of section 33, Industrial 
Disputes Act and accordingly it is not illegal. 


Question is whether it is at all necessary. The 27 employces sought to be 
retrenched in this case include machinemen who work on the machine and 
the apprchension of the management that their continued presence in the work- 
shop is likely to disturb the internal discipline and peace and the safety of the: 
machineries docs not appcar to be unreasonable. In the opinion of the 
Tribunal, the action of the management in suspending the workmen pending 
the permission of the Tribunal is justified. This takes us to the last part of the 
“issue namely what relief the workmen are entitled to. The case of Mantu 
Choudhury stands on a different footing. It has been found that his selection 
for retrenchment has not been proper. He cannot therefore be retrenched. 
In due course, he will go back to duty. Question now is whether he is entitled 
to any unemployment relief for the period since the date of suspension about 
a year ago. He is still out of employment and is presumed to have suffered 
a lot at least financially during this period. The Company, on the other hand, 
has suffered substantial loss in its business and is still running at a loss. The 
entire blame for this long period of unemployment does not rest with the Com- 
pany for certain fortuitous circumstances are partly responsible for this long 
delay in disposal of this dispute. At first, it was pending before the Conciliation 
Officer, then it came up before this Tribunal for adjudication. Taking every- 
thing into consideration, the Tribunal finds that ends of justice would be made 
af Shri Mantu Choudhury is paid six months’ wages as unemployment relief in 
this case. That he is going back to work is no doubt a substantial relief. He 
will report to the Manager in the office for duty within 15 days from the date 
of the operation of this award. He will be paid his dues under this award 
within a month from the date of the operation of this award.

titled to has been causing some anxiety. It is only after anxious consideration 
that the Tribunal finds that they should get substantial relief from the Company 
for losing their employment for no fault of theirs. The Company is duty 
bound to provide them suitable retrenchment compensation on the termination

Choudhury’s formula appears from a letter of the Deputy Labour Commis- 
sioner, dated 17th July 1953, to the Manager and the Director of the Indian 
Press, Ltd. This is annexure to the Company’s written statement. Shri 
Mantu Choudhury has disowncd this statement contained in this letter whereas 
Shri J. N. Bose stands by it. He said that it was dictated by the Deputy 
Labour Commissioner, a responsible officer, in the presence of both parties. 
In view of the denial which comes from Shri Mantu Choudhury, the maker of 
this statement and formula and in view of the fact that he was not authorised on 
behalf of the employees to make or accept that offer and in view of the further 
fact that the employees did not approve of this action of Shri Mantu Choudhury, 
this cannot be accepted as a basis for granting of compensation. The standard 
of compensation, not its minimum, has now been incorporated in section 25(f) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act. This act came into operation on 24th October 
1953, a date subsequent to the date of retrenchment in this instant case. So 
strictly speaking, the provisions of this Act do not apply to the facts of this 
case. I think the ends of justice will be made if the following retrenchment 
reliefs are paid to the employees in this case:— 


(1) Notice pay.—One month’s wages in lieu of notice. This is conceded 
by the Company in the notice of retrenchment itself. 


(2) Provident Fund dues.—This is conceded also in the same place. 
The employees shall get full Provident Fund accumulations up to 
the date of retrenchment namely their own contributions and the 
Company’s contributions together with interest. 


(3) They will be paid for unpaid leave, if any, due under the Factories 
Act. 


(4) 15 (fifteen) days’ wages for each completed year of service. This 
of course includes pay and dearness allowance, both at the rate 
last drawn by the employee. 


Regarding the re-employment of the retrenched workers, I think it is now 
provided for in section 22(f) of the Industrial Disputes Aci. In this case, the 
employees were paid some interim. relief on their application under an 
“Interim Award” of this Tribunal, dated 6th November 1953, published in the 
Calcutta Gazette on November 19, 1953, Part I, page 3805. Those payments 
will be adjusted in the final award. The payments under this award shall be

made within a month from the date of operation of this award. I answer this 
issue accordingly. This is my award.

The industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Changrahandha Rice 
Mills, Ltd., post office Changrabandha, district Cooch Behar, and their em- 
ployee Shri Kartik Chandra De Sarkar, post office Changrabandha, district 
Cooch Behar, as specified in the schedule, has been referred to me under 
Government order No. 5091Dis. /D/111.-809/53, dated 30th December 1955, 


for adjudication. 
SCHEDULE. 


(1) Whether the dismissal of Shri Kartik Chandra De Sarkar is justified 
and whether he is entitled to reinstatement and/or compensation. 


(2) Whether he is entitled to a payment of Rs. 515 as his arrear due? 


Part 1 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 5, 1954 2683 


AWARD. 


After the evidence was taken on both sides and arguments were heard, 
the parties have come to an amicable settlement and a joint petition has 
been filed stating the terms of the said settlement and they moved me to puss 
on Award in terms of the said settlement. 


It appears from the evidence that the Rice Mill in question had its slack 
season from the month of June. So, although Kartik Chandra was appoint- 
ed as a permanent workman (Driver of the Engine) at a monthly wage of 
Ra. 120, the Management without giving notice of termination of the 
service of the said workman insisted on his going to Darbhanga and work 
there in a Mill under the Managership of Jamuna Prosad Babu who is also 
the Managing Director of Messrs. Changrabandha Rice Mills, district 
Cooch Behar. This was the origin of the trouble between the employer and 
the employee. I find that the terms of settlement are fair and equitable on 
both sides. So, the said compromise is recorded and an award is hereby 
passed accordingly in terms of the said settlement which shall form part of 
the Award. 


MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 


Judge, Siath Industrial Tribunal.

The following shall be the syllabus of studies in the subject mentioned 
below for the School Final Examination ہ‎ 1957 and onwards :— 


Physiology and Hygiene as an Elective Subject. 


Candidates are expected to renlise the gieat need for study and practice 
of hygiene in a country with low longevity, high incidence of preventuble 
diseases, low working capacity and high incidence of maternal and infunt 
mortality. They are expected to possess u conception of physiological +68

1. Definition ot hygiene. Its scope, its bearing on individual wnd

2. Growth of the body trom birth—heredity—environment—acquisition of

skeleton (bones, joints), thorax and abdominal cavities with contents, muscles, 
fat, heart and blood vessela—nerves—brain—different cella for different 
functions.

—path of food—distribution inside body—assimilation—storage—wnaste 
products.

SUPPLEMENT—Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 21st July 1954. 


Summary.---During the week under report there was rainfall in thirty-seven subdivisions. Weather was unfavourable in 
eleven subdivisions. Weeding of Aus and Jute still continued. Transplantation of Aman continued. Harvosting of Jute and Aus 
commenced in West Dinajpur and Cooch Behar. Prospect of standing crops was, on the whole, fair. Fodder was reported to be insuffi- 
cient in ten subdivisions. Cattle-disease was reported from one subdivision. The wages of the labourer varied from rupee one to rupees 
three in different subdivisions.

DIRECTORATE OF AGRICULTURE, 
WEST BENCAL. 


laleutta, the 30th April 1954. 


Third Forecast of Wheat Crop of West Bengal 


for 1953-54, 


[Note.—The figures of last year except for those 


ot Darjeeling district as shown in this fore- 
cast have been taken from the last year’s final 
forecast and are based on the results of sample 
survey conducted by the State Statistical 
Bureau, West Bengal. The figures for this 
ear and the figures of Darjeeling district for 
ast year shown in this forecast are based on 
the reports received from the stuff of the 
Directorate of Agriculture, West Bengal. ] 


ree ee 


Season.—The weather conditions were favour- 


wbhle in all the districts except 24-Parganas and 
Malda. 


Area and yield.—101,100 acres are estimated to 
be under Wheat this year compared to 107,900 
acres and 106,400 acres reported respectively in the 
corresponding and in the final forecast of last 
year. The total outturn of Wheat crop for the 
State as a whole is estimated at 36,200 tons this

No. Medl.6661/1N-30/53.—29th July 1954.— 
The following amendments which have been made, 
with the previous sanction of the Governor, by 
the West Bengal Nursing Council, under sub- 
section (1) of section 32 of the Bengal Nurseg Act, 
1934 (Bengal Act X of 1934), in the regulations 
published under notification No. 550Medl., dated 
the 7th February 1938, as subsequently amended, 
are hereby published under sub-section (2) of that 
section, for genera] information :— 


Amendments. 


(1) In regulation 42 of the said Regulations, 
after clause (J) relating to the register of regis- 
tered nurses, add the following clause :— 


“(K) A general part for Public Health 


Nurses holding Diploma in Public Health 
Nursing (D.P.N.) recognised as a higher 


qualification under the Indian Nursing 
Council Act, 1947, 

(1) After sub-clause (ii) of clause (2) of 
regulation 44 of the said Regulations, add the 
following sub-clause :—

No. 3719Dis./D/10L-76/54. — 28th July 1954. — Whereas under 076 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 3617Dis./D/10L- 
131/53, dated the 25th Se tember 1953, the industrial dispute between Messrs. 
Clyde Fan Co., Ltd., Rai Bahadur Road, Behala, Calcutta, and their workmen 
represented by Clyde Fan Workers’ Union, 574, Diamond Harbour Road, 
Calcutta-34, regarding the matters specified in the schedule thereto was 
referred for adjudication to the First Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said First Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the State 
Government its award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby 
to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto.
