statement setting 


The Union, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


The Clyde Fan Co., Ltd., is an electrical engineering concern, undertaking 
manufacture and repair of all kinds of electric fans, and having its factory and 
head office at Rai Bahadur Road, Behala, and its city office at Chowringhee, 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 2715 
সপ পপ পা 
Calcutta, employing about 130 workmen. The Union of the workers under 
the name and style of Clyde Fan Workers’ Union was formed in October 
1952. The Union submitted a charter of demands to the Company on 30th 
January 1953. On 16th June 1953, the Company issued a notice of retrench- 
ment of some 44 workers. There was a talk of settlement of the dispute over 
retrenchment and retrenchment of workers way, therefore, postponed till 016 
Union succeeded in assessing the financial position of the Company. There- 
after on 25th August 1953 workmen, numbering 50, were discharged, by way 
of retrenchment, in two notices. The workers launched a stay-in-strike from 
25th August 1953 and the Management declared a lock-out on 12th September 
1953, and the workers came out of the factory. The Union prays for an 
award directing the Company to reinstate all the 50 workmen mentioned in the 
schedule to the order of reference and to pay full compensation for the period 
of forced unemployment to these workmen. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


This Company is one of the smallest unit amongst the fan manufacturing 
concerns. The Company, however, pays to its workmen wages and _ other 
amenities, which are quite reasonable, in consideration of the status and paying 
capacity of the Company. The Company is not aware of the formation of the 
Union. The Company has been passing through financial difficulties, suffering 
losses for the last few years, which were fully known to the workmen. Some 
outsiders, posing themselves as Union leaders, put in a charter of demands, 
making unreasonable claims. These leaders have no knowledge of the trade 
condition of the fan industries, specially of this particular concern, and_ tried 
to put pressure upon the Company to accept those demands. The Manage- 
ment tried its best to come to terms with the Union, but failed owing ؛‎ the 
adamant attitude of the Union leaders. When it was found that the Company 
could no longer carry on with its surplus staff, the Company had no _ other 
alternative than to issue a notice of retrenchment of 44 workers. The matter 
of retrenchment of the abovementioned 44 workers was taken up by the Labour 
Directorate at the initiative of the Union. The Assistant Labour Commis- 
sioner, however, suggested to stop retrenchment for the time-being, pending 
enquiry into the financial position for the year 1952 and up to June 1953. 
Accordingly, retrenchment was stopped, pending scrutiny of the books of 
accounts up to June 1953, by a Chartered Accountant. In view of the deterio- 
rating financial condition of the Company, and also due to uneconomic 
production, and also considering the critical financial position to which it had 
arrived due to continued losses, the Company in order to save the Industry from 
ruin, issued a notice on 16th June 1953 to retrench 44 workers. On _ the 
report of the Chartered Accountant as made under the instructions of the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner, it was revealed that in 1952, the Company 
had suffered a further loss of Rs. 37,000 and odd, and that there were also 
losses up to June 1953. Considering the above facts, the Company decided 
that 50 men were surplus to requirements. The Company, therefore, issued 
notice on 23rd August 1953 to retrench 50 workers to save the Industry from 
total ruin. In doing so, the Company acted bona fide with the sole object of 
survival of the Industry. It followed the principle of “last come first go” on 
department-wise basis as far as practicable, keeping in view maintenance of 
efficiency. The workers were on strike on and from 24th August 1953. 
The strikers remained in the factory premises throughout day and night and 
confined the Works Manager without allowing him to go out of 
the factory premises. They 9150 interfered with the entry of 
the Secretary, Accountant and other office staff into the factory. The 
Assistant Labour Commissioner was duly informed of the situation. At a 
Tripartite Conference held before the Assistant Labour Commissioner on 28th

and ali disputes pending between the parties up to date. Terms of settlement 
are stated hereunder: 


2. Terms of settlement.—(a) The Company will start the factory with 
effect from the Ist July 1954. 


(b) Work of the factory will be started with 28 workers on seniority basis 
on category-wise from Annexure A enclosed. A list of workers who will be 
en now is given in Annexure “B” and they will be employed by ihe 
2nd week of July for regular work. During the 0150 week of July the Company 
will cleanse and repair the machineries for the purpose of starting work as 
stated in clause (a). 


(c) The workers will be employed according to seniority on department 
basis. Company will now start work with those sections which are absolutely 
necessary. Other departments will gradually be opened, Department, if any, is 
found unremunerative or unnecessary will be discussed as per clause (j) 
mentioned below. 


(d) Thereafter, as and when required, further employment will be made 
from amongst the old employees on senority basis. 


(e) Workers will be দা on departmental-wise on piece-rate basis as 
per Annexure “C” enclosed. Those workers who cannot be employed on 
piece-rate basis due to the nature of job will be employed on daily-rate basis. 


(f) A complete list of the workers on seniority basis is enclosed herewith 
and marked Annexure “A”. Those workers who are involved in criminal 
cases are shown therein with an asterisk sign. The Company will be employing 
gradually persons other than those who are involved in the the criminal cases. 
After the disposal of the criminal cases, those workers, if acquitted, will be 
employed on the seniority basis without making any distinction as stated above. 
But those workers who will be convicted will forfeit the claim of employment. 


(g) There will be no claim of compensation whatsoever for workers 
concerned in this dispute as well as the workers who were discharged due to 
closure of the factory. 


(h) If any worker does not report to work when required within ten days 
from the receipt of the letter asking him to join the work, he will forfeit his 
claim of employment and next person in seniority will be offered the vacancy. 


(i) Apprentice up to 5 in number, if and when required, may be employed 
from old apprentices according to efficiency. 


(j) The Union assures all co-operation to see that the Industry may prosper. 
The Company also assures sympathetic consideration with regard to the legiti- 
mate grievances of the workers. 


Both the Union’s representative Sri Patit Paban Pathak and Management's 
representative Sri N. Das Gupta, Advocate, will discuss from time to time over 
matters concerning labour and management and try to arrive at a settlement in 
case of dispute, if any. 


(k) The Company assures that so long as entire complement of workers are 
not absorbed, no over-time work will be done except in urgent Cases. 


(1) Those of the workers who will volntarily give up ‘claim of service in the 
Company will be granted both employer’s and employee’s share of contribution 
in Provident Fund standing at their credit together with leave wages, if any, 
earned up to the days they actually worked.

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
Shri Kamala Kanta Mukherjee. He was a permanent clerk in the Weaving 
Department. During the pendency of the reference made by Government 
order No. 1059Dis./D/7L-37/53, dated 30th March 1953, before this 
Tribunal, the complainant was given a charge-sheet on 7th September 1953 
for dishonesty in connection with employer’s property. The complainant 
submitted explanation to the charge on the next day (8th September 1953). 
Thereafter the Manager of the Mill recorded order to the effect on 12th Sep- 
tember 1953, “After full enquiry my decision is that you should be dismissed 
but until the permission of the Tribunal has been obtained you will continue 
to be suspended.” Thereupon the present complaint was filed on 3rd Novem- 


Ber 1953. 


The complainant alleges that section 33 has been contravened. The 
Company on the other hand contends that section 33 has not been contravened 
and that the complaint is accordingly not maintainable. The preliminary 
objection as aforesaid is heard. 


DECISION. 
It is contended on behalf of the complainant that the order of suspension 


without pay for an indefinite period amounted to punishment and thus section 
33(b) of the Act has been contravened. The Company on the other hand 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 2727 


contends that suspension pending permission from the Tribunal cannot be 
regarded as a punishment. I accept the contention of the Company and hold 
that the complaint under section 33A is not maintainable. The complaint must 
therefore fail. I award accordingly.

During the pendency of the proceedings before the Tribunal, the

sion of rates and that the additional jobs were parts of the original set up.

The Company, in its written statement, states as follows:— 


The complaint is not maintainable, as it does not refer to any change 
in the condition of service prejudicial to the applicants. There has been

the changing production requirements or conditions. Although it is alleged

by the Company, nor was any mention of these complaint received until 19th 
December 1951. The Company submits that a tew minor changes in the 
operations were made from time to time to facilitate running of Can 
machines. In the course of these changes, a number of old operations were 
eliminated and the overall workload of the machine operators was not 
increased. The Company submits that during the abovementioned 9} 
months period between 15th March 1951 and 19th December 1951, there 
was exchange of letters between the Management and the Union and there 
were a number of meetings held between the Disputes Committee of the 
Union and the Management. In neither correspondence nor meeting was 
there any objection to the piece-rates for can machine operations. On 
6th December 1951, a meeting was held with the Disputes Committee and 
the Management, which was specifically called to discuss the complaints of 

‘the Can Department, There were two representatives of the workers of the 
Can Department in this meeting. No mention was made during the course 
of this-meeting of any change in or objection to the piece-rates for can 
machine operators. The dispute was discussed at a meeting held between 
the Assistant Labour Commissioner, Government of West Bengal, repre- 
sentatives of the Union and representatives of the Management on 9th 
January 1952, wherein it was agreed that the Company would re-study the 
piece-rates and also would furnish the Union a statement of earnings of

the Company’s letter to the Labour Commissioner, dated 11th January

From the application under section 33A filed by the applicants, it 
appears that complaint is made by the applicants that some more jobs were 
added to the original set up of the workers since March 1951, some time 
betore January 1952. It is clearly stated that the workers made repeuted 
demands either to maintain the original set up or to revise the piece-rates 
in the light of new additional jobs, but the Company did not pay any heed 
to settle any of these demands one way or the other and took time and later 
on the workers were told that the dispute would be settled on 15th January 
1952. This statement clearly shows that the dispute in regard to additional 
1008 arose before 15th January 1952. As hus been mentioned above, the refer- 
ence of the dispute between the Company and the workmen to this Tribunal 
was made on bth February 1952. The inevitable conclusion is that any change 
of workload as complained by the applicants was made before the date of 
the reference. It cannot be said therefore that the action of the Company 
was hit by section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. The present appli- 
cation under section 33A of the Act was, therefore, incompetent. 


Tt will be discussed below that even on merits the application has no 
substance. P. W. 1 Satyanarayan Roy stated that some new jobs have been 
introduced from the early months of 1952. They are as follows. The 
workers used to take the flux from a bottle and in January 1952, they were

in which case, the worker has to spend some time in mending the pipe. The 
pipe may burst in one day or in two months. The second alteration named

in 8, particular row of 8 machines there are only 2 Inspectors. Formerly

states that he used to get a rest of 45 minutes if and when the machine

The workers are not entitled to complain about the alteration of the job 
content, as 0৮ 1s a Management function to determine the job content and 
to change the content of jobs (vide Management functions under Collective 
Bargaining—Ludwig Teller, page 62). A similar decision has also been 
made by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal im the case of India 
National Coal Mines Workers’ Federation reported in 1953 L. A. C. 633, 
where it has been stated that it is prima facie Management function to 
direct a particular process in a particular colliery area, and the Tribunal 
could inftrfere only if it was exercised mala fide to the prejudice of the 
workmen. Charts Ext. D, D(1) and D(2) showing the earnings of the can 
machine operators in January 1952, February 1952 und March 1952, show 
normal income for the can machine operators and the plea that job content 
waa altered by the Company to the prejudice of the workinen concerned in 
February 1952 is without any basis. The application under section 3۸ 
is devoid of any substance and is rejected.

ANNEXURE, 


in the matter of a complaint under section 33۸ of the Industrial Disputes 
Act filed by Sri Anil] Kumar Biswas against Waverley Jute Mills in 
connection with Covernment order No, 1059Dis./D/7L-37/53, dated 
the 30th March 1953. 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 
Suri J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal. 


Misc. 0856 No. 202 of 1953 under Section 33A of the InduStrial Disputes Act. 


Shri Anil Kumar Biswas -. Petitioner, 
versus 
Waverley Jute Mills .. Opposite party. 
For the petitioner: Shri P. Ghosh, General Secretary, Jute Workers’ 
Federation. 


For the opposite party: Shri M. M. Ghosh, Dy. Labour Adviser, I.J.M.A., 
assisted by Shri. T. Janki Raman. 


AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Shri Anil Kumar Biswas. The complainant was working in the opposite 
party Company as a permanent clerk in the Weaving Department. uring 


2734 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 (Parr 1 
SS کک‎ ٠‫... ہےے۔۔٭ؤجصجسدپیصصےوےےے-ح‎ 


the pendency of the reference made by Government order No. 7 
7L-37 /53, dated 30th March 1953 before this Tribunal, the complainant was 
charge-sheeted on 7th September 1933. The complainant submitted ex- 
planation to the charges on 8th September 1953. Then on 12th September 
1953, the Manager of the Mill recorded an order to the effect as below :— 


‘After full enquiry my decision is that you should be dismissed but 
until the permission of the Tribunal has been obtained you will 
continue to be suspended’’. 


On the basis of the said order the present complaint was filed on urd Nov- 
ember 1969. 


The complainant alleges that section 33 of the Act has been contravened 
by the aforesaid order. The Company by a written objection contends that 
section 39 has not been contravened and as such the complaint is not main- 
tuinable. The preliminary objection as aforesaid 19 only heard. 


DECISION. 


It is contended on behalf of the complainant that suspension without pay 
for an indefinite period amounted to punishment and so section 38(b) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act has been contravened. The Company on the 
other hand contends that the order of suspension pending permission from 
the Tribunal cannot be regarded as a punishment. It is now well settled 
that suspension pending permission from the Tribunal is not punishment. 
It cannot also be contended that by such action a new condition of service 
has been imposed. I, therefore, find that the complaint is not maintain- 
able and must be rejected. I uward accordingly.

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between Messrs. India Mould-

AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by its order No. 
$376Dis. /D/10L-135/538, dated the 4th September 1953, referred an indus- 
trial dispute existing between Messrs. India Moulding & Galvanizing Works, 
33, 34 and 36, Dasarath Ghosh Lane, Bamungachi, Howrah and _ their 
workers represented by the Howrah District Engineering Mazdoor Federa- 
tion, 63, Dasarath Ghosh Lane, Howrah, regarding the matters specified 
in the schedule to the Order of Reference under sections 7 and 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), to this Tribunal for its 
adjudication. 


The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 9th September 
19538 and usual notices were issued to both parties for appearance and written 
statements. Both parties filed their written statements in due course. In 
its written statement, the Union stated that the Company employed about 
36 workers and earned huge profits in course of its seven years of existence. 
The workers formed a Union and became a constituent member of this 
Federation and placed a Charter of Demands to the Management on 17th 
February 1953. The Management closed down the factory on 1061) June 
1953 without any previous notice. The closure of the factory was illegal 
and made with a motive to victimise the workers. Hence this case. 


The Company in its written statement alleged that on 1061) June 1953, 
the workers gave an ultimatum that they would stop work unless their 
demands of 13th March 1953 were immediately granted. As it was not 
possible to concede the demands in the near future, not to speak of answering 
them then aud there, the workers left the factory and did not return, The 
workers themselves were responsible for the deadlock. 


The jssue as per schedule to the order of reference is: 


(1) Whether the sudden closure of the factory by the Management on 
13th June 1953 is justified? To what relief are the workers 


entitled ? 
FINDINGS. 


6th July 1954 was fixed for hearing of the case. The Federation repre- 
senting the workers was absent. Qn the application of the Company for 
presenting a petition of compromise in the case, the hearing was adjourned 
till next day. On 17th July 1954, the Mazdoor Federation was again found 
absent. In fact, the Federation officials have long ceased to take any active 
interest in this case. Its long and unexplained inaction in the matter of 
this dispute shows that no dispute is outstanding between the parties. In 
fact, a batch of workers and the Company filed a joint signed petition of 
compromise in this case. In the absence of Federation officials, I enquired 
of the workers regarding the terms of settlement. I was satisfied that the 
settlement, so far as it goes, is bona fide and the terms are fair and as such 
they muy be accepted. It further appears from the petition that no Union 
of workers is now in existence. This is corroborated by the long silence 
and inaction on the part of the Federation. The dispute has been amicably 


2736 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 {Part I 
—————————————————— ee 


settled. The Management promised compensation and the entire dispute 
was now at on end. The settlement as presented is accepted. There is no 
outstanding dispute in this: case and it is awarded accordingly. 


The joint petition along with the petition of compromise do form a part 
of this award. 
M. N. GAN, 


Judge, Second Industrial Tribunal.

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Mahaluxmi Cotton 
Mills, Palta, 24-Parganas and their workers as represented by the 
Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Workers’ Union, Palta, 24-Parganas and 
Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Mazdoor Union, Paita, 24-Parganas, 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT: 
Suri J. N. MAITRA, Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal. 


Present Jor the Company: Shri N. Das Gupta, Advocate. 
Present for the Workers’ Union: Shri Jugannath Pandey. 
Present for the Mazdoor Union: Shri Patit Paban Pathak. 


AWARD. 
1. By order No. 2100Dis. /D/8L-23/58, dated the 9th June 1953, the 


Goverament of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred under 
section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Acl, the industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Muahaluxmi Cotton Mills, Palta, 24-Parganas and their workers 
represented by the Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Workers’ Union, Palta, 
24-Parganas and Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Mazdoor Union, Palta, 24-Par- 
ganas, regarding the matters specified in the schedule, to the Third Indus- 
trial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, by notification No, 592Dis./J)/12L-5/52, dated the 23rd February 
1958, for adjudication. 


2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed writtdn 
statements—the Company filing written. statement of claim while the 
Unions filing written statements in reply. The pleadings were completed 
on 7th December 1953. The parties were thereafter directed to file their 
lists of documents. After adjournments, the hearing was concluded on 
" 28rd June 1954 and the award was reserved. 


3%. The matters of dispute as stuted in the schedule to the Order of 
Reference are as follows :— 
(1) Whether the Company should be allowed to curtail the basic wages 
of workmen which are in excess of the wages fixed for such 
workmen by the Cotton Textile Tribunal award. 


(2) Whether the dearness allowance of the workmen which are in 
excess of the dearness allowance fixed by the Cotton Textile 
Tribunal award should be curtailed? 


(3) Whether the Attendance Bonus should be abolished? 


(4) Whether the Company be justified in discontinuing C Shift or in 
retrenching other workmen from any of the shifts, no matter 
whether the issues as framed above are answered in the atftir- 
mative or negative? 


DECISION. 
Issues Nos. 1 and 2, 


The parties have not adduced any oral evidence. They rely on the 
annexures to their respective written stutements. Besides, the Company 
filed documents which have been marked Exts. 1 to 16(a), on dispensing 
with formal proof. 


This is a dispute raised by the Company unlike the usual one which 1s 
raised by the workmen. To appreciate the controversies between the parties 


| 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1964 2739 
১ _- ہجو‎ 


it is necessary to state certain facts, which are either admitted or estab- 
lished in evidence, leading to the dispute. Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills (here- 
inafter culled the Company) wus incorporated in 1924. The Company is n 
gmall unit amongst the textile concerns haying only 171 looms and 6,136 
spindles. Messrs. H. Dutta and Sons, Ltd., were the Managing Agents. 


The Major Cotton Textile Tribunal’s award to which the Company and 
its workmien were parties was published in the Calcutta Gazette on the 4 
August 1948. In the said award the Company was described in Table K(2) 
as an uneconomic unit. The Company was, however, paying from before 
the award, higher basic wages than those fixed in the award. It was also 
paying higher dearness allowance in most of the cases under three heads, 
such us, dearness allowance, ration allowance ond attendance bonus than 
those seltled by the award. The award according to the Government 
order was to remain in operation for one year from Ist August 1948. Thus 
the award lapsed on the 9186 July 1949. 


The Company had its entire current account with Messrs. Calcutta 
Commercial Bank, Ltd. In September 1948, the said Bank closed its doors 
and two of the Company’s Directors who were the ea officio Directors as 
nominees of the Managing Agency Company were arrested and prosecuted 
an connection with the bank fraud case. The Company removed their names 
torin its Board of Directors. 


Then on 23rd November 1948, the Company applied under section 153 of 
the Indian Company’s Act before the Hon’ble High Court for sanctioning 
৪০1)61)1 of arrangement as between the Company and its share-holders and 
unsecured creditors. A Special Officer was appointed by the Hon’ble High 
Court, Calcutta, and the Company was managed by a Board of Directors 
subject to supervision and control of the said Special Officer. 


On 116) July 1949, a scheme of arrangement under section 153 of the 
Indian Company’s Act was passed by the Hon’ble High Court, Calcutta, 
and in December 1949, a new Board of Directors under the provisions of the 
scheme was elected and since then it has been managing the affairs of the 
Company. 

On 14th September 1949, an agreement was entered into between the 
Company and Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills Workers’ Union. The agreement 
comprised 15 items. It provided amongst others for increment in the basic 
wages und dearness allowance of all workmen and for payment of Puja bonus 
ed to two months’ basic wages in the manner indicated therein (vide 
“xt. 

Subsequently, a dispute arose between the Company and the workmen 
out of non-payment of Puja bonus fully according to the aforesaid agreement. 
There was a strike over it by the workmen. The dispute was ultimately 
referred to Shri G. Palit for adjudication. He made his award on 19th 
July 1951. There was an appeal against the said award. The Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal on the basis of the agreement, etc., declared that 
Puja bonus was a coudition of service of the workmen and accordingly 
directed payment of two months’ basic wages (vide 1952 L.A.C, page 375). 


Against the said decision the Company moved the High Court. The 
Hon’ble High Court set aside the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal 
regarding the quantum of bonus and remanded the matter to it for the 
determination of the quantum of bonus. The matter is since pending decision 
before the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal. Thus in addition to the 
asic wages and dearness allowance which the Company has been paying, 
the Company has been found to be under obligation to pay Puja bonus as 
a condition of service.

The Company claims that what it has been paying in the shape of basic 
wages and dearness allowance is the highest amongst textile concerns in 
West Bengal. 


It is said that the textile industry has been passing through crisis and 
the Company is one of the mills which have been hard hit. It has no working 
capital of its own since September 1948. It works on borrowed capital for 
which interest of Rs. 12,000 per month approximately is to be paid. 


As a result of the continued depression in the business, there has been a 
heavy fall in the prices of cotton stock in hand as held by the Company under 
the quota allotted by the Government and the Company has suffered huge 
loss on that account. 


Then Government controlled Provident Fund Scheme has been brought 
into operation since November 1952. As a result there has been increase in 
Company’s contribution (vide Ext. 9). Then the State Insurance Scheme 
has also been made operative since January 1952, imposing additional 
burden on the Company (vide Ext. 12). In December 1952, the Govern- 
ment issued a notification restricting the production of dhotis and the said 
notification has been enforced from January 1958. Since the Company’s 
mill was manufacturing dhotis mostly, it has been incurring additional loss 
in having to give effect to the Government circular (vide Exts. 10 and 11). 


The Company could not pay its unsecured creditors according to the 
scheme of arrangement under section 153 as sanctioned by the Hon’ble 
Court; they could be paid only two instalments. 


In the circumstances as the Management found that the re-organisation 
of the mill by reducing number of the workmen to its minimum require- 
ment and revision of their wages and other emoluments by reducing the same 
in order to run the industry on economic basis was absolutely essential, it 
thought it advisable to discuss the matter with the Union and accordingly 
wrote a letter to the Union on 12th January 1953 inviting the Union repre- 
sentative for discussion of the matter to find out ways and means to save the 
industry (Annexure B to the Company’s written statement). The Union 
representatives did not respond to دن‎ Saar aces invitation. 


As the Directors of the Company did not want to shoulder responsibility 
of incurring additional losses they decided at a meeting held on 30th January 
1953 to close down the C shift with a view to try if the liability could be 
partially set off and the mill as a whole not paralysed. The workers were 
notified on 818۲ January 1953 of the Company’s intention to close down 0 
shift with effect from 16th February 1953. 


Upon such notice the Union wrote to the Management on 4th February 
1953 challenging its action as mala fide. The Company then by a letter, 
dated 12th February 1958, placed all matters before the Assistant J.ahour 
Commissioner (Annexure C to its written statement.) In it, it made an 
alternative suggestion provisionally to keep the closure of C shift in abeyance, 
if the mill employees agreed to a cut of 10 per cent. of their total earnings 
in the interest of the survival of the mill. 


In the circumstances, the Company said that it had got two alternatives, 
either to run the mill on economic basis limiting its expenditure to its hbarest 
minimum as far as possible or to close down or to put it into liquidation. 
The Management in the mutual interest of the Company as well as of its 
workmen asked the Union representatives to accept the wages as fixed by 
the Cotton Textile Tribunal’s award, being the wages which were being 
followed by all cotton industries in West Bengal and to agree to the discon- 
tinuance of C shift due to enforcement of dhoti restriction order by the 
Central Government and also technical and economic grounds. As the con-

cilmgtion did not succeed, the matter has been referred to the Tribunal for 
adjudication. 

Behind this background the Company during trial prays for reduction 
of the existing wages and dearness allowance to those in conformity with 
the award plus the additional benefits which the workmen were in enjoyment 
since the award and before the agreement, dated 14th September 1949. In 
other words the Company wants to revert to the position as to wages and 


dearness allowance as existed prior to the agreement, dated 14th September 
1949. 


The two Unions representing the workmen—Mahaluxmi Cotton Mill 
Workers’ Union (hereinafter called ‘‘Workers’ Union’’) and Mahaluxmi 
Cotton Mil] Mazdoors’ Union (hereinafter called ‘‘Mazdoor Union’’) resisted 


the claim by separate written statements though virtually on the same 
grounds, 


The Company contends that the agreement, dated 14th September 1949, 
was obtained by coercion and is not therefore binding and of any effect. 
The Company further alleges that all the Mills have been paying salary and 
dearness allowanve according to those in the award and the hips bias of this 
Company have no special circumstances in their favour to get higher pay 
and dearness allowance than those in the award. Besides it is said that the 
Company's financial position has since become very precarious. It is said 
that from about the time of the agreement, dated 14th September 1949, 
there hus been serious deterioration in the financial position of the Company 
which makes it impossible on the part of the Company to bear the additional 
burden imposed under the agreement. The Company further says that 
though the basic wages and dearness allowance which they were paying 
prior to the agreement were higher and for which there is no justification, 
still the Company is agreeable for industrial peace to pay those wages and 
dearness allowance which they were paying immediately before the agree- 
ment, though according to the decision of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal and the High Court, they shall have to pay Puja bonus in addition. 


The Company points out that the award of the Cotton Textile Tribunal 
recognised that the Company was an uneconomic unit. My attention has also 
been drawn to the observations in the uward at page 162, paragraph begin- 
ning with the sentence ‘‘A question arises as to whether a workman can be 
paid beyond his producing capacity...’’ and ending with the sentence “... 


The minimum occupational wage has a close connection with the industry 
itself’’. 


It has also been pointed out that after the award Government set up an 
Expert Committee on Cotton Textile Industry of West Bengal by the resolu- 
tion, dated 23rd September 1949. The Committee so appointed submitted 
its report on the 8th June 1951. At puge 2 of the said report it was recog- 
nised that the Cotton Textile Industry in this State was passing through 
a crisis. The Committee accordingly refrained from suggesting any scheme 
as contemplated by the Government resolution and recommended that the 
acheme laid down 1n the award might continue at least for some time more. 
It was observed that the Cotton Textile Industry in West Bengal must be 
kept alive and that millions must be clad and unemployment problem must 
not be allowed to worsen. 


The two Unions on the other hand contend that there was no coercion 
by the workmen in the matter of the agreement, dated 14th September 
1949 and that the agreement is binding on the parties and still holds good 
as it has not been terminated under section 19(2) of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. It is further said that what is being paid as wages and dearness 
allowance after the agreement, dated 14th September 1949, is not adequate 
or fair and that the goal which has been fixed to be fair wages in the case

of Associated Cement Companies reported in 1959 14. A. C., page 683,,has

regarding Cotton Mills aud as a result the wages and dearness allowance fixed 
by the award regarding Cotton Mills have remained stationary and ure far 
below than those obtaining in the Jute Mills and Engineering concerns. In

There is no dispute between the parties that the wages which the Com- 
puny was paying to the workmen at the time of the award and before the 
agreement, dated 14th September 1949, were higher than those in the award. 
These wages are tu be found in statements, Ext. 16 and Ext. 1008), As

the dearness allowance. There is also no dispute between the parties that 
the sum total of payments under these three heads constituting the 
dearness allowunce was in most causes higher than that fixed us dearness 
ullowance in the award, and that the sum total was lesser only in few cases. 
It is agreed by both sides that after the award in 1948, the Company granted 
a flat _increment in the attendance bonus in all cases by two annas per head 
per working day and as u result the sum total paid under these three heads 
constituting the dearness allowance im all the cases became higher than that 
in the award. The amounts of dearness allowance as used to be paid after 
the award and before the agreement, dated 14th September 1949, are to be 
found in the statements, Exts. 16 and 16(a). Thus basic wages us also 
dearness allowance which the Company were paying after the award and 
betore the agreement, dated 14th Septinber 1949, were according to both 
sides higher than those in the award. The total emoluments which the 
employees were drawing were consequently higher than those allowed under 
the award. The increase in the amount of dearness allowance by the flat 
increment in attendance bonus after the award, was to the tune of 
Rs. 2,752-12-0 pies per month (vide Ext. 16). 

After this there was further increment both in basic wages and dearness 
alfowance by the agreement, dated 1411) September 1949, Ext. 14. The 
total increment was to the extent of Rs, 4,523-6-74 pies per month, Ext. 
16(a). The excess payment by the Company in terms of the Textile award 
was however to the tune of Rs. 7,815-15-9 pies per month (ride Mxt. 14.) 
এটি the Company's prayer for reverting to the position betore the agreement, 
dated 14th September 1949, is allowed there would be a saving of Its. 4,528 
and odd per month. Besides, the agreement, dated 1461) September 1949, 
also stipulated for Puja bonus to the extent of two months’ basic wages in 
addition to the increment in wages and dearness allowance. Thus the 
agreement undoubtedly imposed heavy additional burden on the Company.

The agreement which the Company in a way seeks to nullify took place on 
14th September 1949 when the industry was undisputedly passing through 
a crisis. The award regarding Cotton Mills according to the Government 
order was to remain operative for a period of one year from lst August 1948. 
The award therefore lapsed on the 3lst July 1949. After it so lapsed the 
agreement came into being on 14th September 1949. 


Shortly before this the Calcutta Commercial Bank closed in September 
1948. With such closure all the liquid assets of the Company amounting 
to Rs. 7,44,708-11-11 pies became blocked leaving the Company without any 
capital. The Mills were also mortgaged for Rs. 10 lakhs. The Company 
has therefore to pay heavy interest for the mortgage aos also for the borrowed 
capital consequent on the Bank’s closure. 


Thus placed the Company applied under section 153 of the Companies 
Act to the Hon’ble High Court on 23rd November 1948. The scheme was 
sanctioned by the Hon’ble High Court on llth July 1949, that is, two 
months before the agreement. As pS terms of the High Court scheme, 
arrears of Income-tax kept unpaid by the then Managing Agents had to be 
.انس‎ Besides, the company was to pay the unsecured creditors their 
principal and interest in full out of the profit and so long their claims were 
not paid in full it was directed that no dividend should be paid to the 
share-holders. 


The Company was thus apparently passing through a crisis before the 
agreement. In this state when the Company was carrying on on horrowed 
capital with high rates of interest, it appears that a notice was served on 
25th August 1949 on the Company by the workmen threatening strike from 
15th September 1949. Then the agreement in question took place on 14th 
September 1949. The Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal] held when the matter 
as to Puja bonus went on appeal that the immediate motive on the part 
of the Company to come to an agreement was termination of the threatened 
strike by conceding the demands made by the Union (vide 1952 I. A. 0. 
870 at page 376). 

The agreement in question among others provided for further increase 
in basic wages hnd dearness allowance and also for Puja bonus. As 8 
result of this agreement, the rates of basis wuges and dearness 
allowance as existing at  =present came into’ operation. These 
rates are undisputedly the highest amongst the textile concerns of this State. 
Exhibit 3 is a statement which shows that the average expenditure on 
account of wages, etc., per loom in this Company was higher than that 
incurred in other Textile concerns from 1950 to 1953. 


The question of coercion in the matter of agreement raised by the 
Company is not very material here. Wibether the agreement was obtained 
by coercion or not, it will suffice to state here that un agreement like the 
present one is not absolutely sacrosanct in an Industrial Tribunal and this 
can, be modified or varied if exigencies of situation so require. 


It has been held in the case of Bank Line (India), Ltd., and their work- 
men reported in 1954 L.A.C. 330 at page 348, ‘‘An agreement or settlement 
arrived at a conciliation proceedings is absolutely binding oa the parties 
thereto (section 18 of the Industrial Disputes Act). But other agreements 
betweeti employer and workmen in relation to wages and other conditions 
of service are not absolutely sacrosanct in an Industrial Tribunal. An 
Industrial Tribunal can refuse to give effect to them or modify them at the 
instance of either party when adjudicating upon a reference.”’ 


In the present case when the agreement was not arrived at in a concilia- 


tion proceeding, it is obvious that it is not absolutely sacrosanct. So the 
contention of the Unions that the Tribunal cannot go behind the agreement

SS 22 পি 
in question cannot be sustained. Section 1962) of the Industrial Disputes Act 
has no upplication to agreements other than those arrived at in conciliation 
proceedings. So the agreement in question is no bar to Company’s claim for 
reverting to the rates of wages and dearness allowance paid prior to its 
execution, 


lt further appears that since the agreement in question, financial posi- 
tion 01 the Company haa deteriorated and that additional obligatory burdens 
have been imposed on the Company which under the law it has got to 
discharge. The balance-sheet for the year ending 30th June 1950, Ext. 
15(a), tollowing the agreement in question, shows a loss of Rs. 50,290 and 
odd. So the Company could not pay the unsecured creditors according to 
the scheme under section 153 as there was no profit. In the financial years 
ending :)011) June 1951 and 1952, respectively, there was of course profit 
which enabled the Company to pay the unsecured creditors interest in two 
۰َ 0 according to the scheme but huge amounts remained yet to be 
cleared. 


The uext financial year ending 30th June 1953, it appears, was very 
bad year for the Company. There was a great drop in the gross profit pri- 
marily due to stiff decline in the selling price of cloth following an acute 
slump in the cloth market since October 1952. In this state additional 
burdens cume to be imposed on the Company. The Government-sponsored 
Provident Fund Scheme was introduced during the period and became 
operative with effect from November 1952. Under the scheme the Com- 
pany, which had so long to contribute 6} per cent. of the basic pay of the 
employees, has now to pay contribution not only on basic pay but also on 
allowances. The net effect has been an increase of about Rs. 12,373-7-3 pies 
on the annual Provident Fund contributions to the employees [vide Ext,

Besides, Government introduced Employees’ State Insurance Scheme in 
January 1952. It appears that as a result the Company has been burdened 
annually with a sum of Hs. 6,000 approximately though the Company has 
to maintain its medical expenses intact (vide Ext. 12). 


Then came the dhoti control order by the Government. It came into 
operation from December 1952. Under it the Company was allowed to

sheet also shows that the Company incurred a loss of R. 2,21,162-10-8 pies. 


Then just as capacity to pay on the part of the employer is an important 
factor in determination of the amount of dearness allowance so also in the 
matter of assessing the basic wages above the minimum. Though a Com- 
pany has no right to exist if it cannot pay the minimum wages to its workers, 
still it cannot be said fairly that the Company cannot legitimately seek 
for reduction of the existing wages to a level higher than the minimum when 
it is faced with extraordinary circumstances beyond its control. 


Considering all these, I think that situated as it is, the Company can 
legitimately claim to revert to wages and dearness allowance as prevalent

Issue No. 4. 


The Company wants to clouse down C shift for the purpose of economy 
and buna fide trade reasons following Government’s order restricting dhot: 
production from December 1952. The Unions opposed the claim. It is 
contended by the Unions that it is not an industrial dispute and cannot 
therefore form a subject of adjudication. I am unable to uphold 
the contention. Industrial dispute has been defined as to mean 
any dispute or difference between employers and employers or 
between employers and workmen or between workmen | work- 
men which :s connected with the employment or unemployment or the 
terms of employment or with the conditions of labour, of any person. In 
the present case, by the proposed closure there would be unemployment of 
some of the workmen. It is, therefore, obvious that the dispute raised by the 
Company in this respect is connected with the employment or unemployment 
of the workmen. I, therefore, hold that the Tribunal is competent to adju- 
dicate in the matter. It appears that the dhofis constituted 80 per cent. 
of the production of this Mill before the Government order restrictin 
production of 18908 was passed. Under the said Government order whic 
is effective from December 1952, the Company was permitted to manufagture 
only 60 per cent. of dhotits manufactured during April 1952—March 1953. 
Asa result of this restriction the Company had to cut down its 1/81۲ produc- 
tion, which, I am told, has gone down to 30 per cent. as against 80 per cent. 
of the production previously. Thus a prima facie case for discontinuing the 
C shift has been made ot. The Unjons could show nothing that such 
proposal of the Company was actuated by mala fides. The Mill has been 
running at a loss and its financial condition is precarious. Dhoti contro 
order diminished necessity for employing full complement. These facts by 
themselves go to show that the proposed «closure is bona fide. In the circum: 
stances, I find nothing wrong in the proposal of the Company to discontinut 


the C shift. The Company is accordingly granted permission to discon. 
- anue the C shift. 


As regards retrenchment of the workmen, it is for the Management to 
fix the number and choose its personal and not for the Tribunal to do ৪০. 
these are Managem ent’s functions and initiation must therefore be left wit 
it. Business must be run by persons vitally interested in the conduct of th 
business. Managment’s right to retrench is undisputable and the Tribuna 
can intervene only if in exercise of such right, it has not acted bona fide 
With these observations, I leave the matter here.

above step was taken by the Company several representatives of the 
employees were called to conferences and the facts and figures were also 
discussed in the said meetings. A lawyer representing the Union was also 
present in the said conferences. It has been argued on behalf of the Union 
that the lawyer unaided hy an expert could not understand anything from

no evidence that the said lawyer failed to understand as is attributed to 
him by the Union representative in this Tribunal. So my conclusion is 
that the closure of the factory with effect from 14th October 1952, was 
justified. It has been held in Associated Rubber and Plastic Works and 
their workmen, 1954, 1 L.U.J., page 182: 


that “an employer has the right to close the business, and that where the 
Management intimated the closure of the Factory and also ter- 
minated the services of the workmen there cannot be any question 
of lock-out. As the Management has the right to ace down 
the business there can be no question of reinstatement and the 
question of compensation would arise only when the closure is 
proved to be mala fide’’. 


An apparent closure is to be held a lock-out: 


‘if an employer shuts down his place of business as a means of reprisal 
or as an instrument 91 coercion, or as a mode of exerting pressure 
on the employees, or, generally speaking, when his act is what 
may be called and act of belligerency, there would be a lock-out. 
If on the other hand, he shuts down his work because he is un- 
able to sell the goods he had made or because his credit is 
exhausted or because he is losing money, that would not be a 
lock-out. In order to avoid a shut down, being called a lock-out, 
1 is not necessary that the shut down should be permanent”. 


(Reported in Shri Ramchandra Spinning Mill, Pandalapaka versus 
State of Madras and another, 1953, 1 L.1T..J., page 216.) 


It has been held by the Appellate Tribunal in the case of British India 
Steam Navigation Company, Ltd., versus S. Salvedore and 45 others, 1954, 
1 L.L.J., page 769: 


“it 1s absolute right of the owner of a business or undertaking to close 
it سر‎ the act of the owner in closing the business or his 
undertaking is bona fide”’

‘under the Constitution a citizen has the right to carry on any business

The reference was received in the office of this Tribunal on 17th Auguat

The Mazdoor Panchayat, in its written statement, in the connected case

was a private concern of Shri Lalit Mohan Kundu and manufactures various

break the Union by forcing the workers to sign a blank paper. Having 
failed in its attempt to do so, it declared a Jock-out on 17th October 1952. 
The matter of dispute was however resolved on the intervention of Miss R. 
Dutta, Conciliation Officer. The factory re-opened in terms of settlement

Compang ৪1] on a sudden without assigning any reason declared a lock-out

The issues as per schedule to the Order of Reference are—

(2) To what relief are the workers entitled ? 


FINDINGS. 


Issues Nos. 1 and 2. 


They relate to stoppage of work on 23rd April 1953. But the Mazdoor 
Panchayat in paragraph 19 of its written statement stated that the Company 
all on a sudden declared a lock-out and discharged all the old workers of 
the factory. The Company denies this case and alleged that it did not 
lock-out the factory on that day but in fact four or five workers attended 
their work on that day. 


_ Question now is whether it was a case of lock-out. [89119 No. 1 as framed 
in the Order of Reference supposes that it was a case of lock-out. Lock-out 
has been taken as established in the case. Ordinarily, it is not permissible

for ২ Tribunal to go behind the Order of Reference in order to ascertain 
whether a different state of things existed or not. In that way, the question 
whether the stoppage of work was really a lock-out or not does not arise. 


But since both parties have adduced evidence on this point, one alleg- 
ing the lock-out and the other denying it, it is desirable in the interest of 
industrial peace, to see whether in fact it was a lock-out or not. Shri 
Gobardhan Maity, Head Moulder, deposed in this case on behalf of the 
Mazdoor Panchyat and Shri Lalit Mohan Kundu has examined himself on 
his own behalf and on behalf of the Company. The Company has filed its 
Attendance Register of the relevant dates and some other documents also 
relevant to the matter of dispute. Curiously enough, the Mazdoor Panchayat 
has not said a single word in its written statement explaining the circum- 
stances that led to the alleged stoppage of word on 23rd 41311 1953. Shri 
Gobardhan Maity ig one of the 13 workers who were discharged from 
service by notice (Ext. C) on 22nd April 1958 and nothing untoward 
happened on that day. In fact, they did not know anything about the dis- 
charge of Nemai Bag, one of the Union officials, on that day. Nemai came 
to work the next morning and was stopped at the gate. The other workers 
entered the workshop, waited at the gate and were finally turned out by 
the police. It was at that time that they came to know that the factory 
was locked out. No one was permitted to do any work. He believed that 
this action was taken by the Company for their Union activities. In cross- 
examination, he admitted that 22nd April 1953 was a casting day but there 
was no casting on that day. He admitted at the same time that the furnace 
was lighted, that is to say, there was every preparation for doing the cast- 
ing on a casting day. He has not said a word why the casting was aot 
done. Nemai, according to this witness, came with him to the Tribunal. 
Shri Lalit Mohan Kundu has given another version of the incident that took 
place on 22nd April 1953 and 23rd April 1953. He said that the workers 
attended as usual in the morning of 22nd April 1953 and worked up to 
12 o’clock. About 3 or 34 tons of iron and 14 tons of hard coke were put 
into the furnace which was heated. Then at about 1 o’clock, the workers 
declined to do the casting on the plea that Nemai Bag was wrongfully dis- 
charged. Nemai was absent from duty and was dismissed on that ground 
in the afternoon of 218٤ April 1953. Thirteen or 14 workers out of a total 
20 or 21 struck work over that issue. This at once put the Company to a loss 
of Its. 800 and it was only with the help of other menials, durwans and 
sarkars, that he could put out the heat and save the furnace. Te at once 
informed the Jabour Commissioner about the incident. Shri Gobardhan 
Maity admitted that Nemai was absent for three days before 22nd April 1953. 
He corroborated the fact of absence of Nemai as deposed by Shri Lalit Mohan 
Kundu. Shri Kundu further said that 18 or 14 employees who struck work 
on the previous day did not attend on the 23rd April. After waiting for 
some time, he discharged those workers at 9 in the morning and admitted 
4 or 5 other workers who came for work. Police was called at about midday 
when the discharged workers came in a body and rushed into the workshop 
and created disturbances within it. The police pursuaded the workers to 
leave the factory. Thereafter, the work was stopped from 24th to 3rd May. 
The work was completely suspended till that period. Then from the 4th May 
till 3rd October, the work continued but not as before. The work was com- 
pletely stopped for dearth of work. Shri Kundu has in the connected case 
also filed a signed statement to the fact that the business had to be closed 
down purely on financial grounds resulting from dearth of work. The 
partnership business was also dissolved. Accordingly to the Panchayat, 
there was no work since 23rd April 1953. This is partly correct as would 
be borne out by the evidence of Shri Kundu, corroborated by the Attendance 


2764 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 [Part I 


উস উস) ০০০2 ০০5০ ০5 বস্তি PTL

Register (Ext. D). Exhibit D shows that there was no complete stoppage 
of work on 23rd April 1958. In fact, some attended and were paid half day’s 
work, although due to disturbances created by the discharged workers, the 
remaining workers could not do any work. ہ1‎ these state of things, the 
Tribunal is more inclined to accept the Company’s story in this case and 
finds that there was no lock-out as alleged by the other side. Lock-out is 
defined in section 2(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act. It received authori- 
tative interpretation from the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the 
Presidency Jute Mills Company Limited wersus Presidency Jute Mills 
Employees’ Union, 1952, L.A.C., page 62 and in Colliery Mazdur Congress, 
reported in 1952, L.A.C., page 219 at page 223. “If there is refusal of work 
connected with some dispute between the employer and his workmen in that 
case a lock-out takes place.”’ The evidence in this case does not establish 
that the Company refused work to the employees in connection with the 
dispute between 1৮ and its workmen. It is true that some workmen were 
discharged and some workmen attended. That does not amount to lock-out. 
Assuming for argument's sake, though not conceding, that it was a lock- 
out, the further question is whether it is justified. This takes us to the 
consideration of the same evidence which need not be repeated. The sudden 
strike of some of the workers on the casting day put the Company to a loss 
of several hundred rupees. Not only that, there was the danger of damaging 
the furnace as well. The Management viewed the situation with grave con- 
cern and dismissed those workers who were responsible for the strike and the 
consequent loss to the Company. It is not for the Tribunal to go into the 
propriety of the question whether such dismissal was right or not. It is this 
dismissal that eventually led to the lock-out. On a consideration of the 
facts and circumstances of the case against the said background, the Tribunal 
finds that the action of the Company, in stopping the work, is fully justified, 
The Panchayat did not make any attempt either by examining Nemai Bag 
who was present during trial or by calling the police who admittedly came 
to this factory on the day of the occurrence to stop the disturbances to say 
that the story now told by the Company was untrue. The Tribunal, there- 
fore, finds that the action of the Company is fully justified and accordingly 
the -workers are not entitled to any relief in this case. The issues are decided 
accordingly. This is my award.

was not entitled to re-instatement or any compensation.

By order No. 4685Dis./D/ 11L-12/53, dated the 7th December 1953, the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, referred the abovementioned 


Pant 1] THE CAITLCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 2759 


০০০০ 


dispute to me for adjudication regarding the matters specified in the schedule 
to the said Order of Reference. : ٦ 


Schedule. 
(1) Should there be increments for the year 7 


AWARD. 


The workmen make out the case that the Company was started in 1925 
in a low beginning when the workmen would get remuneration of Rs. 8 to 
Rs. 10 per month and that in 1940, the Company was made a public limited 
concern and that its 0 have won good market and that the Company 
has paid not less than"20 lakhs of rupees as dividend to the share-holders while 
the paid capital was only Rs. 14 lakhs, and that in June 1950, the Company 
granted lavish increment of pay to the General Manager by Rs. 1,000 per month 
and to the Sales Manager and Factory Manager by Rs. 500 per month with 
effect from 1949 January, but the workmen are not being given any increment 
in their wages in spite of the agreement followed by an award of 1948 incor- 
porating the said agreement. The workmen demanded increment of wages on 
the basis of the scale of pay in the said agreement and Award of the Tribunal, 
and the Tribunal gave an Award which was published in the Calcutta Gazette 
in November 1951. There was an appeal by the Company and the Award of 
the Tribunal was upheld. Thereafter the workmen again made a demand for 
increment of wages in the year 1951. The Company pleaded financial difficulty 
and the Union accepted the plea of the Company and gave up the demand for 
that year. The Company however granted increment in wages in the year 
1952. The Company however contends that the trading profit of the Company 
in the year 1952 was nil and that in the years 1950, 1951, and 1952 the 
Company made little profit and therefore the present demand for further 
increment for the year 1953 is unjustified and that on the other hand, the 
circumstances of the Company call for reduction of the wages. 


The Company all along contends that the Award of 1948 by which scale 
of wages with annual increment was framed on the basis of agreement between 
the Company and the Union (workmen) is no longer binding as under the 
law, it was in operation only for one year. The next contention is that the 
present circumstances of the Company and its future prospect do not warrant 
any more increment in the wages and that on the other hand, reduction of wages 
by way of revision would be the proper step. 


It is not denied that late ০৬ M. Bose was the founder of this business and 
that at present the members of the said Bose family are the executive and 
administrative heads of the private Limited Company. Shri J. M. Bose is the 
General Manager, Shri A. M. Bose is the Sales Manager, Shri B. P. Bose is 
the Factory Manager, Shri D. Bose is the Technical Advisor, Shri A. Bose is 
the Assistant Manager. They are the persons whose salaries have been 
increased by the Management by leaps and bounds so much so that the same 
has been the cause of great discontentment amongst the workmen who now 
demand the increment as outlined in the scale of wages in the Award and 
Agreement of 1948 should be given effect to so far as the year 1953 is con- 
cerned, particularly when the business fetched profit in that year. Under the 
law the Award of 1948 is no longer binding upon the parties. The question is 
whether the agreement upon which the said Award was based is still binding 
or not. It was an agreement effected not during the conciliation roceeding 
but after the reference was made by the Government to the Tribunal for adjudi- 
cation. Section 19 of the Industrial Disputes Act does not speak anything 
about such an agreement. The Award of 1948 was the said agreement to which 
was added the command of the Tribunal. It was like a consent decree of a 


2760 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 [Paps 1 


= 


Civil Court in which case the agreement remains challengable under the law of 
contract, although as a decree it is not challengable except on the ground of 
fraud. But collective agreement in the domain of Industrial Disputes should 
not be treated as an agreement binding for ever. So we find in section 19 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, that there are provisions for putting an end to such 
agreement effected during conciliation proceeding or even to the Award passed 
by a Tribunal. I am of opinion that the same principles should be applicable in 
the case of an agreement effected during the pendency of the reference and 
forming the basis of the Award. In the previous adjudication proceeding 
before Shri G. Palit, the Management کت‎ intimated in the written statement, 
copy of which was given to the "Union that the said Award or agreement of 1948 
was no longer binding upon the Company. Enough gme has elapsed since 
then It is therefore too late now to contend that the agreement of 1948 is 
still binding under the law. So in the instant case we have to consider whether 
the circumstances prevailing at present would favour the idea of increment in 
wages as envisaged in the scale of wages in the said agreement. One thing 
appears to be implied in every such agreement regarding wage scale involving 
annual increments, viz., that the agreement is subject to the proviso that the 
financial circumstances of the Company should be favourable otherwise it is 
absurd to expect that the Company should be obliged to allow increment in 
wages annually even though the financial position is awfully bad. 


The Award of 1948 has spent its force and the agreement on which the said 
Award was based has also been put an end to long ago because the Management 
gave notice of its intention by Ext. E which is dated 3rd June 1953. At the 
same time we cannot be forgetful of the fact that it was an agreement arrived 
at bona fide and that the Company also took a long range view of the circum- 
stances which were material for the purpose of coming to the conclusion regard- 
ing scale of wages and annual, increments. If the Company can now show 
that the circumstances which followed the said agreement of 1948 and which 
are likely to come out in the near future are unfavourable, certainly the Tribunal 
should hesitate to place the burden of the annual increment upon the shoulder 
of the Company. In 1950 the Company raised similar contention and in 1951 
also the said contentions were persisted in before the Hon’ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal, although the Directors in the General Meeting held on the Ist 
September 1953, remarked in the balance-sheet report : 


“Since its very inception, this Company has been yielding very satisfactory 
results right up to 1951”. 


In 1952, the gross profit amounted to Rs. 41,554 and after appropriations the 
amount of profit carried over was shown as Rs. 4,472. For the year 1953 no 
certified balance-sheet has been produced but in the Chart Ext. I it is noted that 
the statement regarding the year 1953 also, was complied from the Company’s 
balance-sheet, and 21 uncertified typed statement described as “Provisional 
balance-sheet as at 31st December 1953” was produced by the Company. The 
said document could not therefore be admitted in evidence. I am not impressed 
by the contention made by the Company that in the near future there is no good 
prospect of handsome profit simply because there has been recent competition 
in the market and as the price of the finished products have been reduced by the 
Company for the purpose of competition with the rival concerns. It has not 
been shown that there is no prospect of handsome profit in the near future. It 
seems that the amount of profit after appropriations in respect of the year 1953 
has been shown at Rs. 79,670. It appears from the balance-sheet of 1952, the 
Company has invested more than 3 lakhs of rupees in Bank Deposits. Con- 
sidering all these circumstances I am of opinion that the annual increment fall- 
ing due in the year 1953 as per agreement forming the basis of the Award of 


Parr [] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 12, 1954 276] 


io should be allowed by the Company to the workmen concerned and I 


award accordingly. 
Dictated and corrected by me. 
M. L. CHAKRAVATTI, MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 
District Judge. Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal.

PART I[A—Orders and Notifications by the Government of India republished for general information. 


IN THE HONOURABLE LABOUR APPELLATE TRIBUNAL OF INDIA, 
CALCUTTA. 
Appeal No. Cal.-31/54. 
The 46 workers of National Tin Box Mfg. Co., C/o Dr. S. K. 


Bose, 141A, South Sinthee Road, Calcutta-2 ۰ Appellants, 
versus 
Messrs. National Tin Box Mfg. Co., 36-C, B. T. Road, 
Calcutta Respondent. 


oe 6 
In the matter of an appeal against the award, dated 15th December 1953, and 
» published in the “Calcutta Gazette”, dated 7th January 1954, made by Shri 
M. N. Gan, Judge, 2nd Industria! Tribunal, West Bengal, in respect of an 
industrial dispute between the above parties. 
Calcutta, the 9th July 1954. 
PRESENT : 
Suri R. C. MITTER, Chairman. 
Suri L. K. JHA,: Member. 
Appearances : 
For the Appellant: .ا .لا‎ Ghorai (Secretary of the Union), B. Ash (Lawyer). 
For the Respondent: Shri Mukherjee (Lawyer), Shri Krishna Ch. Auddy 
(Lawyer). 
State: West Bengal. 
Industry: Tin. 
DECISION. 

A reference relating to a dispute between National Tin Box Mfg. Co. and 
their workmen represented by the National Tin Workmen’s Union was made by 
the West Bengal Government for adjudication by the Second Industrial Tribunal, 
West Bengal. This reference was made on the 6th July 1953. After the | 
reference was received by the Tribunal, Shri H. N. Ghorai, Secretary of that 
Union, appeared for the workmen along with a lawyer Shri B. Ash. For the 
Company a practising lawyer Shri Mukherjee was engaged and he was assisted 
by Shri Krishna Chandra Auddy. On the 8th September 1953, an application 
purported to have been made by some of the workmen, was filed before the 
Tribunal in which it was stated that the workmen desired to be represenged by 
Dr. S. K. Bose, who had no connection with that Union of which the workmen 
were members but was the President of another Union called the National 
Tin Box Mazdoor Union. This application was set down for hearing in the 
presence of all concerned. The Tribunal went into the matter and observed 
that it was a second attempt to bring in Dr. Bose and also observed thus :— 


“I do not know how far this desire is genuine. If they really desire any 
change they should approach the proper authorities for that. This 
Tribunal, in the fact and circumstances stated, is unable to help 
them in this matter, nor think it desirable to do so.” 


On the 4th December 1953 about threc months later a joint petition of 
compromise was filed by the Company and the National Tin Workmen’s Union, 
who were entitled to represent the workmen &t that time. The petition was 
accepted after hearing and the passing of the award was reserved. On the next 
day the award was made in the following terms :— 


“I accordingly make an awaatl in terms of the compromise filed in this 
case. The joint petition for compromise and the petition contain- 
ing the terms of compromise do form part of the award, which 
are marked Annexures A and B, respectively. Thus the award 
was on consent of parties, the consent being given by persons who 
had till then the right to represent the workmen and the Company.” 


An appeal has been filed and Dr. Bose has appeared before us in support 
of the appeal. It is incompetent because of the provision of clause 2 of section 
7 of the Industrial Disputes Appellate Tribunal Act, as the award as expressly 
stated was made with the consent.of parties. It is, therefore, dismissed but 
without costs. 

R. C. MITTER, Chairman. 
L. K. JHA, Member.

PART II—Advertisements, Notices 


Procedure regarding sending Manuscripts for publication of Advertisements, Notices, etc., in 
the “Calcutta 08791060975 (Part I1). 


1. Manusoripts should be properly edited and complete in ۱٢٤۸٤ 


2. Manuscripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. The name of the signatory should be type- 


‘written below the signature. 


3. Manuscripts intended for advertisement in the next issue of “‘Caloutta Gazette’ shall be received by Publication 
Sales Office at New Secretariat 88881017785, 1, Hastings Street, Calcutta, up to 11 a.m. on Saturday and at Head Office 


at Allpore up to 12 moon on Monday. 


4. All costs shall be paid In advance and deposited along with the Manusoripts. 


5. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressed to 
WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE. 


(PUBLICATION BRANCH), 


SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING

Financial Memorandum are accordingly published for general information:— 


(To BE INTRODUCED IN THE COUNCIL OF STATES.) 
Bill No. XIV of 1954. 
A Bill further to amend the Drugs Act, 1940. 


Be it enacted by Parliament in the Fifth Year of the Republic of India as 
follows:-—— 


1. Short title —This Act may be called the Drugs (Amendment) Act, 1954. 


2. Amendment of section 3, Act XXIII of 1940.—In section 3 of the 
Drugs Act, 1940 (hereinafter in tms Act referred to as the principal Act),-— 
(a) for clause (5), the following clause shall be substituted, namely:— 
“(b) ‘drug’ includes— 

(i) all medicines for internal or external use of human beings or 
animals and all substances intended to be used for or in the 
treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease in human beings 
or animals other than medicines and substances exclusively 
used or prepared for use in accordance with the Ayurvedic or 
Unani systems of medicine; and 

(ii) such substances (other than food) intended to affect the 
structure or any function of the human body or intended to 
be used for the destruction of vermins or insects which cause 
disease in human beings or animals, as may be specified from 


time to time by the Central Government by notification in the 
Official Gazette;”; 


(৮) after clause (b), the following clause shall be mserted, namely: — 


“(bb) ‘manufacture’ in relation to any drug includes any process or 
part of a process for making, altering, ornamenting, finishing, 
packing, labelling, breaking up or otherwise treating or adopting

16.” Substitution of new Chapter for section 34 in Act 350111 of 1940.—For 
section 34 of the principal Act, the following Chapter shall be substituted, 
namely :— 


“CHAPTER V., 
MISCELLANEOUS. 


34. Offences by companies.—(1) Where an offence under this Act 
has been committed by a company, every person who at the time 
the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible 
to the company for the conduct of, the business of the company, as 
well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence 
ane shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accord- 
ingly: 


Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any such 
person liable to any punishment provided in this Act if he proves 
that the offence was committed without his knowledge or that he 
saa all due diligence to prevent the commission of such 
offence. 


(2} Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (J), where an 
offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is 
proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or 
connivance of, or is attributable to any neglect on the part of, any 
director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such 
director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed 
to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded 
against and punished accordingly. 


Explanation.—For the purposes of this section— 


(a) ‘company’ means a body corporate, and includes a firm or other 
association of individuals; and 


(b) ‘director’ in relation to a firm means a partner in the firm. 
35. Publication of sentences passed under this Act.—(1) If any person 


is convicted of an offence under this Act, it shall be lawful for the 
court before which the conviction takes place to cause the offender's 
name, place of residence, the offence of which he has been con- 
victed and the penalty which has been inflicted upon him, to 
be published at the expense of such person in such newspapers or 


in such other manner as the court may direct. 


(2) The expenses of such publication shall be deemed to form part of the 
costs relating to the conviction and shall be recoverable in the same 
manner as those costs are recoverable. 


36. Magistrate's power to impose enhanced penalties ——Notwithstanding 
anything contained in section 32 of the Code of Criminal Pro- 
cedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898) it shall be lawful for any presi- 
dency magistrate or any magistrate of the first class to pass any 
sentence authorised by this Act in excess of his powers under 
section 32 of the said Code. 


37. Protection of action taken in good faith —No suit, prosecution or 
other legal proceeding shall lie against any person for anything 
which is in good faith done or intended to be done under this 
Act.”

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Drugs Act, 1940, which provides for the regulation of the import, 
manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs and prescribes the standards of 
quality of drugs, has been in force since April, 1947. In the light of the 
experience gained in the tle of the Act during the last seven years, it is 
proposed to make certain amendments in the Act. 


The term ‘drug’ as defined in the Act at present does not cover chemical 
contraceptives and insecticides. It is proposed to extend the scope of defini- 
tion of the term so as to cover such of the contraceptives as well as insecticides 
as may be notified by the Central Government from time to time in the Official 
Gazette, so that their standards may be controlled where necessary. It has 
further been found necessary that with a view to maintaining uniformity 
throughout the States the power to make rules under Chapter IV with respect 
to the manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs, which is at present vested 
in the State Governments should be entrusted to the Central Government. 


There have been complaints that the penalties provided in the Act for the 
contravention of the provisions thereof, are inadequate. The penaltics pro 
vided in the Act are being enhanced so as to make them deterrent. Oppor- 
tunity has also been taken to make certain other minor amendments. 


AMRIT KAUR, 
New DELHI, 
The 10th May, 1954. 


FINANCIAL MEMORANDUM. 


Section 5 of the Drugs Act, 1940 provides for the constitution of a Board 
(called the Drugs Technical Advisory Board) to advise the Central Govern- 
ment and the State Governments on technical matters arising out of the 
administration of the Act. Clause (2) of section 5 lays down the composition 
of the Drugs Technical Advisory Board. It is inter alia Hae ید‎ to make 
certain amendments in section 5(2) of the Act which will result in the mem- 
bership of the Board being increased by two. One of the additional members 
will be the Drugs Controller, India. As the meetings of the Board are held at 
Dethi which is the headquarters of the Drugs Controller, India, no expenditure 
will be incurred on his travelling allowance or daily allowance for attending the 
meetings of the Board. The other additional member will be elected by the 
Pharmacy Council of India. Assuming that one meeting of the Board is held 
in a year it is estimated that there will be an additional expenditure of about 
Rs. 400 per annum on his travelling allowance and daily allowance.

THE DARJEELING AND KURSEONG MUNICIPAL 
(PORTERS) (AMENDMENT) BILL, 1954. 


A 
BILL 


to amend the Darjeeling and Kurseong Municipal (Porters) 
Act, 1883. 


Wuenrras it is expedient to amend the Darjeeling and Sen. Act V 
Kurseong Municipal (Porters) Act, 1883 for the purpose and of 1883. 


in the manner hereinafter appeuring ; 


It is hereby enacted in the Fifth Year of the Republic of 
India by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows: — 


1. This Act may be called the Darjeeling and Kurseong 
Municipal (Porters) (Amendment) Act, 1954. 


2. Yn the Darjeeling and Kurseong Municipal (Porters) 
Act, 1883 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act), for the 
expression ‘‘coolie’’ and the expression 4500০01558১ wherever 
they occur, the expression ‘tmazdoor”’ and the expression 
‘‘mazdoors’’ shall respectively substituted. 


8. Referentes to the expression ‘“‘ooolie’’ and the 
expression ‘‘ovolies’’ in any register kept, license granted or 
badge delivered under the said ‘Act, shall be construed as 
references to the expression ‘‘mazdoor’’ and the expression 
‘‘“mazdoors’’ respectively. 


1097 


1098 


THE CALCULIYLA GAZETTE EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 12, 1954 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Darjeeling and Kurseong Municipal (Porters) Act, 1883 (Ben. Act V 
of 1883) was enacted for the purpose of registration and control of labourers 
employed as porters and dandiwallas; and the word “‘coolte’’ has been used 
throughout the Act to signify such labourers. 


The Government of India in the Ministry of Labour have, however, by a 
Resolution, dated the 27th May, 1950, decided that the word ‘“‘coolie” should 
no longer be used in official correspondence and have requested the State 
(Jovernments to substitute the term ‘‘mazdoor’’ for the term ‘‘coolie” in case 
it occurs in any State enactment. 


This Bill seeks to implement the above decision. The change in nomen- 
clature is not intended to affect the present position of the workers as regards 
pay or allowances or pension in any way.

The 21st July, 1954. Member-in-charge.
