STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


It is well-known that the cattle of West Bengal are very poor in quality, 
both in respect of milk yield and draft. 


A scheme for the improvement of livestock has been in operation in 
relected areas of Bengal since 1936. The object of the scheme ib to grade 
up the indigenous breed of cattle both for increased milk production and for 
draft purposes. 


Experience has shown that the value of the work is lost unless it is 
concentrated in specified regions where an adequate number of stud bulls 
are put in with the simultaneous elimination of scrub bulls. Difficulties 
have. been experienced in implementing the scheme as envisaged above, 
specially in the matter of the voluntary castration of scrub bulls which is 
eo necessary for the success of the scheme. The Government has, there- 
fore, for some time, been feeling the necessity for suitable legislation to 
surmount these difficulties. The present Bill has been drafted with this 
object in view. Certain other States have already enacted legislation on 
similar lines.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Private forests in West Bengal are controlled under the West Bengal 
Private Forests Act, 1948 (West Ben. Act XIV of 1948). 


2. The operation of this Act has disclosed certain lacunae. It has 
also become evident that the punishment provided under the Act has not 
heen sufficiently deterrent to prevent the owners of private forests from 
Violating the terms and conditions of approved working plans, 


38. Recently, many of the owners of private forests have shown a 
tendency of over-felling of the forests in vivlation of the approved working 
plans. Many of them have also failed to submit working plans for approval 
under the Act. The private forests, which constitute valuable national 
assetg,“Were therefore in serious danger of rapid exhaustion and deprecia- 
tion. 


4. Tha Governor, therefore, promulgated an Ordinance, namely, the 
West Bengal Private Forests (Amendment) Ordinance, 1954, on the 27th 
July, 1954, to amend the West Bengal Private Forests Act, 1948, so ns 
to remove the lacunae in the law and to provide for a more deterrent and 
effective punishment for the violation of the law. 


5. The main provisions of the Ordinance are as follows :— 


(a) it provides for cases in which the owner of a private forest has 
failed to submit a working plan and where no approved plan 
exists. In such cases the owner or any person acting on his 
behalf may not fell or remove any timber from a private forest 
without the prior approval of the Regional Forest Officer; 


(b) it makes clear that felling or removal of timber from a private 
forest is a punishable contravention of the prescriptions of tne 
approved working plan; 


(c) it makes it permissible to inatitute a prosecution against the owner, 
without prior notice, where the offence takes the form of tbe 
unauthorised felling or removal of timber; 


(d) #t enhances the punishment to imprisonment extending up to three 
months or fine extending up to rupees one thousand or both. 


6. As the risk of the rapid exhaustion of the private foreats 1ھ‎ 
y-ersists, the Bill seeks to enact the provisions of the Ordinance.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 
1+ is considered necessary to amend the West Bengal Evacuee Property 
Act, 1951 (West Ben. Act V of 1951) for the following purposes, namely :— 


(2) to empower the Evacuee Property Management Committee to lease 
or let out at a time any property which has vested in it for a 
period up to 5 years if it 1s situated in an urban area and for a 
period up to 10 years if it is situated elsewhere; and 


(2) to provide that all sums payable to the Committee shall, without 
prejudice to any other mode of recovery, be recoverable as arrears 
of public demand. 


The Bill has been framed with the above objects in view.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Mayurakshi Reservoir Project bas made turther progress and it has 
been possible, during this kharif season, to supply water tor irrigation over 
a large tract of areu. In the past available water from this Project ‘was 
supplied free of charge to the cultivators so that utilisation of the watey for 
the purpose of increasing agricultural production could be demonstrated to 
them. This Project involves a capital expenditure of the order of rupees 
sixteenecrores and is being financed by loan from the Government of India 


which the State Government is required to repay. The use of the water. 


means very substantia] additional income to the cultivators. It is necessary 
therefore that all cultivators to whom water can be supplied should pay an 
irrigation rate so that the loan to the Government of India may be repaid 
from the revenues. At the present kharif season the Governor promulgated 
an Ordinance, namely, the Bengal Development (Amendment) Ordinance, 
1954 (West Ben. Ord. VI of 1954), by way of amending the Bengal 
Development Act, 1935 (Ben. Act XVI of 1935), so as to intpose a 
compulsory levy, at a rate not exceeding Rs. 10 per acre per season on the 
occupiers of the irrigable areas of the Project where supply of canal water 
can be fully assured. It is now proposed to replace this Ordinance by an 
Act of the Legislature. 


CALCUTTA, 


The 13th August, 1954. AJOY KUMAR MUKHERJI, 
Member-in-charge. 


By order of the Governor,

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Government had been viewing with increasing concern the working of 


[Part IVA 


the West Bengal Board of Secondary Education for some time past. 


The 


Fr eee لت ہے‎ ed TT et সা সাপ een nn ae 
Printed and published by the Superintendent, Government Printing, West Bengal, 


episode gn connection with the School Final Examination of 1954 marked 
the climax of a series of irregularities and acts of mismanagement committed 
by the Board. It was therefore necessary and expedient to undertake a 
reorganization of the Board and pending such reorganization it was consider- 
ed essential and urgent in the public interest that the Board which had 
proved incompetent and inefficient should be superseded and some temporary 
arrangement made for control and management of secondary education in the 


State. 


As both Houses of the Legislature of West Bengal were not in session at 
the time, the West Bengal Secondary Education (Temporary Provisions) 
Ordinance, 1954 (West Ben. Ord. 111 of 1954) was promulgated. As the 
continuance of the supersession of the Board is likely to be necessary until 
the constitution of the Board is suitably re-organized, it is proposed to enact 
the Bill to replace the Ordinanre.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


It is considered necessary to give relief to every person who transferred 
any land by sale for maintaining himself and his family during the period 
of distress between the Ist day of January, 1951 and the 30th day of Novem- 
ber, 1953, for any consideration, the amount or value of which does not 
exceed Rs, 250 by directing restoration of such land on re-payment of the 
consideration together with interest and certain other sums by instalments 
and to provide tor matters ancillary and incidental thereto. 


The Bill has been framed with the above objects in view.

_ বুট is considered necessary to amend the West Bengal Estates Acquisi- 
tion ون‎ 1963 (West Ben. Act I of 1954), for the following purposes, 
namely :— 


(i) to provide for the vesting of all the estates, tenures, under-tenures

9 
(iii) notwithstanding the provisions of section 12, to provide— 

(a) for ad-interim payments to an intermediary whose estates and 
interests have vested in the State, of such amounts and at such 
times, as may seem to be reasonable; and 

(b) for an annual ad-intertm payment of the approximate net annual 
income of the interest of an intermediary in case it is held 
under a dona fide trust or other legal obligation for an 
exclusively charitable or religious purpose without reserva- 
tion of any pecuniary benefit to any individual;

section 6 and sub-section (2) of section 61 to 33 acres; and 


(vi) to provide for certain consequential matters.

service as would have made him or her eligible 
to receive the medal of the same class, such turther 
distinguished service shall be recognised by a Bar 
to be attached to the riband by which the medal 
is suspended and for every such subsequent 
distinguished service an udditional Bar টা be 
added. For every such Bar, a replica of the medal 
in miniature shall be added to the riband when 
worn ulone, 


এ Ifa recipient of the medal of any of the 
three classes shall aguin perform such distinguished 
service as would have made him or her eligible for 
the award of a medal of a class different from the 
one already received, such further distinguished 
service shall be recognised by the award of another 
medal of the appropriate class. 


10. The miniature medal which may be worn 
on certain occasions by recipients shall be half the 
size of the medal, and a sealed pattern of the said 
miniature mwnedal shall be deposited and kept. 


11. The President may cancel and annul the 
award of the medal to any person and thereupon 
the name of such recipient in the Register ol be 
erased and the recipient shall be required to 
surrender the medal; but, it shall be competent for 
the President to restore the decoration when such 
cancellation and annulment haus been withdrawn. 


12. The notice of cancellation or restoration in 


every case shal) be published in the Guzette of 
India.

By-laws under section 527(70) of the Calcutta 
Municipal Act, 1951, regulating the disposal 
of the articles brought with thé dead body to 
the burning ghats, burial grounds or other 
places fer the disposal of the dead. 


(1) The nearest relatives of & deceased person 
accompanying his corps to a burial or burning 
ground or other place tor the disposal of the dead 
or presént ut the time of burial, cremution or dis- 
posal of the dead body and particularly the person 
signing the Register of Deuths ay un informant, 
shall cause all clothes, bedding and other artjcles, 
excepting ornaments, which are carried with the 
dead body or the bier, to be destroyed to the’ 
satisfaction of the Sub-Registrar of the said 
burial or burning ground or other place for the 
disposal of the dead. No such article shall on any 
account be permitted to be taken out by apy 
person from the burning or burial ground or other 
place for the disposal of the dead. 


(2) Bulky articles, such as cots, biers or 
carriages in whith the dead body is borne to the 
placea for the dispusal of the dead shall, if not 
destroyed, be thoroughly disinfected by the etatf 
of the Corporation, whether the dend body carries 
infection or not, to the satisfaction of such Sub- 
Registrar. <A charge shall be payable for meeting 
the cost of such disinfection as the Corporation 
msy from time to time fix. 

(3) Any such person desirous of making a 10 
of new or unused clothing, bedding or ath 
articles brought with the dead body to priests, 
barbers, domes or similar other persons shall bring 
the same in such a manner as not to be in euntact 
with the dead body or the bier and may give away 
the same with the permission in writing, in a 
form to be prescribed by the Commissioner fer the 
said gel gd of the Sub-Registrar of the said 
burial or burning ground or other place tor the 
disposal of the dead. The decision of the Sub- 
Registrar that the clothing, bedding or other 
article proposed to be given away is or is not new 
or unused and has or has not come in contact with 


the dead body or the bier, shall be final. 


(4) Every person found guilty of a breach of 
any of the foregoing by-laws shall be punishable 
with a fine which may extend to fifty rupees.

ORDERED that a loan of Rs, 6,000 (Rupees six 
thousand only) be sanctioned provided it does not 
exceed 50 per cent. of the nett value of the assets 
of the applicant-firm in the industry to be offered 
as security against the loan, after deducting all 
encumbrances thereon existing at the time when 
the application was made. e loan is also sub- 
ject to the following conditions :—

jointly by Shri Hrishikesh Mondal and 
Shri Gunadhar Mondal, partners of the 
said firm of Bharat Iingineering Corpora- 
tion, in the form to be drawn up by 
Government for the purpose; 

(3) That interest should be charged at the rate 
of 6} per cent. per annum payable with 
each instalment on the balance of the un- 
paid principal ; 

(4) That if the instalments with interest there- 
on are, however, paid promptly on the due 
dates or within fifteen days thereafter 
interest will be accepted at the rate of 6 
per cent. per annum instead of 6} per 
cent per annum; and 

(5) That the entire amount of loan with interest 
thereon should be repaid in five equal 
annual instalments of Rs. 1,200 (Rupees 
one thousand two hundred only) each plus 
interest; the firat instalment being repay- 
able on the first anniversary of the date 
of payment of the loan.

NOTIFICATIONS. 


Subject :—Transaction of Treasury cash business by 
the Bank on Covernment holidays. 


No. TM /474.—9th August 1954.—A question has 
been raised as to whether the Branches and Pay 
Offices of the Imperial Bank of India which conduct 
cash business of the Treasury should transact such 
business on days on which the treasury concerned 
remains closed on account of Government holidays. 
With a view to obviate the working difficulties in 
incorporating Government transactions in accounts 
of the next working day following holidays it has 
been decided by the Government of West Bengal 
that the Bank should not be allowed to carry on 
Government transactions on the days on which the 
treasuries remain closed. 


All Treasury Officers and Sub-Treasury Officers 
in West Bengal should note the above decision. 
The Manager, Reserve Bank of India, Calcutta, 
may also communicate the above decision of Gov- 
ernment to the Branch Manager of the Imperial 
Bank of India in West কজন which conduct cash 
business of the treasuries. 


{Government of West Bengal, Finance Depart- 
ment, Audit Branch, letter No, 2175F., dated 29th 
July 1954, file No. TM/1-44 of 1953-54.]

Subject:—Estate Duty. 


No. TM/475.—12th August 1954.—All Treasury 
Utticers and Sub-Treasury Officers in West Bengal 
and the Manager, Reserve Bank of India, Calcutta, 
are hereby informed that for the purpose of accom- 
modating receipts and charges on account of 
Estate Duty the following new heads of account 
have been opened :-— 


Receipts. 
Major head; ‘‘V—Estate Duty’’. 
Sub-major heads: (1) ‘Estate Duty on Agricul- 
tural Land’’. 
(2) “Estate Duty on property other than Agri- 
cultural land’’. 


Charges. 


Major head—‘'5—Estate Duty’’. 


2. Money deposited with the Government by a 
person for the purpose of paying estate duty in 
advance should be provisionally credited under a 
distinct head ‘‘Depgsits towards payment of Estate 
Duty” in section ‘‘P—Deposits and Advances— 
Part I Deposits bearing interest—B—Other 
Deposits’’. 

3. The nomenclature of the major heads ‘‘IV /4- 
Taxes on Income other than Corporation Tax’’ has 
been changed io ‘‘IV/4-Taxes on Incomes other 
than Corporation Tax and Estate Duty’’. 


4. The Transactions in respect of Estate Duty 
are ‘‘Central’’ und should be treated accordingly in 
the accounts.

(2) Ministry of Finance (Revenue Division) Circu-

dated 11th March 1954 and (3) Ministry of Finance 
letter No. 1(110)-B/58, dated 28th March 1954, filed 
in BI.TKI-I.T-84-7 of 1954-55. }

The Associated Battery Makers Workers’ Union, which will be mentioned 
hereinafter as the Union, in its written atatement states as follows. 


The Company oume into being some six yeyry ago. From its very 
inception, the Company started payment of one month's wages, by way 
of bonus, on the occasion of the Durga Puja every year. Puja bonus was 
paid irrespective of profit or loss on the trading of the Company. This 
Paja bonus has become a part of wage payable on the occasion of Durga 
Juju. The amount of the bonus has been invariable and at one month’s 
basic pay. The payment of the bonus has never been governed by attend- 
ance, efficiency, production, behaviour or conduct, length of service, or 
profit or loss. In 1958, the date for payment of this bonus was not noti- 
fied to the workmen by the Company and this gave the workmen cause 
of apprehension whether the Company was out to withdraw the bonus. 
Thereafter the Union wrote to the Management demanding the payment of 
the Puja bonus. It was thereafter settled between the parties ihat the 
Company would pay one month’s basic pay as advance, pending decision 
by a Tribunal on the issue of Puja bonus. Jt was also agreed that the 
amount paid by way of advance would be treated as puja bonus, if the 
decision of the Tribunal was in favour of the workmen and in case, the 
decision was against the workmen, the Company would be entitled 10 
recover the advance in instalments. One month's basic pay by way of 
adviunce was thereupon paid to the workmen towards the middle of October 
1953. The workmen are entitled to Puja bonus equivalent to one month's 
pay in 1953. The Union, therefore, prays that an award may be made for 
payment to the workmen of Puja bonus at one month’s basic wage and 


to set off this bonus against the advance payment made to the workers in 
October 1953.

DECISIONS. 


issue No. 1. 


At the time of the hearing of the case, nobody appeared for the Asso 
ciated Battery Makers (Eastern) Mazdoor Congress, the case of the Unio: 
is that from its very inception, the Company started payment of bonus a

Evidence was adduced by both parties in support of their statements. 
P. W. 1 Shri Sukhdeo deposed for the Union and Mr. EK. J. Goode, Labour 
und Welfare Officer of the Company, deposed for the Company. Docu- 
ments Exts. A to H were also marked for the Company. 


It appears from the evidence on record that the present factory was 
erected by Messrs. Chloride Electrical Storage Company (India), Ltd., 
during the year 1945-46 and they worked it up to 91781 December 1949, by 
which date, the present Company purchased the factory und assets of 
Chloride Electrical Storage Co. (India), Ltd., and started operations on 
Ist January 1950. O.P.W. 1 Mr. Goode was in the employment of Messrs. 
Chloride Electrical Company (India), Ltd., since January 1949. It appears 
that in 1949, there was a lock-out of the factory from the end of May to 
the middle of October and on Ist January 1950 when the present Company 
took over the factory, it employed all the workmen of the old Company 
on their application to it, except those who were dismissed at the time of 
the lock-out by the previous Company. It, therefore, appears that Messrs. 
Chloride Electrical Storage Co. رس‎ Ltd., carried on operations for 
ubout four years from 1945-46 to the end of 1949, and the present Company 
has been operating the factory since the beginning of 1950. P.W. 1 
Sahadeo’ Bari states that he has put in 9 years’ service, obviously meaning 
that he has been serving in the factory since ita inception under the previous 
Company. His evidence is that Puja bonus was 1eceived by the workmen 
in 1948 and from 1900 to 1952. He also states in evidence that the workers 
demanded Puja bonus for 1949 and that there was a strike and lock-out 
in that year. He further states that the durwans of the Company who 
were in the employment of the Company at the time of the lock-out, got 
the Puja bonus in 1949, but the other workmen did not get this bonus. 
OP.W. 1 Mr. Goode states in his evidence that in 1949, there was 2 
demand by the workers for Puja bonus to previous Compuny, but it was 
refused on the ground that- there was no profit in that sear. He also 
stutes that no payment of any bonus was made to the durwans in 1949. 
This witness states that the present Company earned a profit in Lio, 
1991 and 1952, and Puja bonus was paid in those years. In 1953, there was 
no profit. Ext. A is a statement filed by the Company stating that 
there were profits in 1950, 195! and 1952 and one month’s basic pay 0. 
bonus was paid in or about October in those years. This statement also 
shows that in 1953 there was loss incurred by the Company. .)ہا‎ B ہد‎ 
a certaificate from Chloride Electrical Storage (Co. (India), Ltd., showing 
that no ez gratia payment on account of the Puja festival was made by 
the Chloride Electrical Co. (India), Ltd., during the calendar vears 1947 
and 1049. This fact is, however, admitted by the Union. According to the 
Union, the system of payment of bonus was started in 1948 and there was 
no payment in 1949. The statement of P.W. 1] that bonus was paid to 
the Durwans in 1949 is disproved by Ext. B and the evidence of O.P.W. 1

amount or form establish any precedent for the future. The letter then 
embodies conditions showing how the amount of bonus wil! depend upon 
the number of days worked by an individual workman. Exts. I} to 1()8( 
are the balance sheets of the Company for the years 1950, 1941, 1952 and 
1958, In 19450, the Company made o gross profit of Rs, 7,88,801 and odd 
and a nett profit of Rs. 51,636 and odd. In 1951, the Company made 
a gross profit of Rs. 18,27,085 and odd and a nett profit of Rs. 6,86,870 
and odd. In 1952 there was a gross profit of Its. 4,89,997 and odd and 
a nett profit of Rs. 4,038. in 1953 there was a gross profit of Rs. 77,861 
and aa and a nett loss of Ks. 3,387,243. It, therefore, appears that the 
Company 00 Punja bonus in 1950, 1951 and 1952 when it had some nett 
profit, although this nett profit varied from year to year und in 1983, 
there has been a nett loss of more that Rs. 3 lakhs. 


The learned spokesman for the Union stated that Ext, C issued by 
Chloride Electrical Storage Company (India), Ltd., on 29th September 
1948 when the er-gratia payment, by way of bonus, was first made by the 
Company, created an agreement between the Company and the workmen, 
as it was stated that the payment was to be made in time for the puja 
holidays. J do not find any such agreement to be embodied in this docu- 
ment. There ia a clear statement that this payment will be made only 
on the understanding that it does not esablish any: precedent for the future. 
The learned spokesman cited the decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal 
in the case of Muhaluxmi Cotton Mills, reported in L.A.C., 370, and urged 
that on the evidence on record and agreement between the employer and 
the workers for payment of Puja bonus at one month’s basic wage had 
been established. The Hon’ble Tribunal enunciates the principle of a 
customary Puja bonus as follows :— 


“Puja bonus is a bonus claimed by the workers as a matter of right, 
payable by the employer at a special season of the year, namely, 
at the time of the annual Durga Puja. This right is not based 
on the general principle that labour and capital should share the 
surplus )اہ(‎ after meeting necessary prior charges, but it rests 
on agreement between the employer and the workers. That 
agreement may be either express or implied, and where not 
express, past practice may lead to an inference of implied 
ngreement. But for nnplying an agreement, the practice must 
he unbroken and for a sufficiently lonz peried to exclude the 
hypothesis that payments had been made out of bounty. It is 
not possible to say, in general terms what should be the length 
of the period. That would depend upon circumstances of each 
particular case, but the fact that the payment had been made 
even in a year of loss would be an important factor on the 
question as to whether the payments were mere acts of bounty 
or an obligation on the part of the employers. When the right 
is established, the next question would relate to the amount. 
Where the rule for determining the amount is expressly laid 
down or can be inferred, the rule is to be followed. Where 
there is no definite rule or none can be found, the agreement 
founding the right cannot he disregarded in an Industrial 
Tribunal, as in Courts of law on the ground of vagueness. The 


2814 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 1954 [Parr 1 


Industrial Tribunal must hold that the workers are entithd to 
a reasonable amount as a term of employment and determine 
the amount, when a claim is made for a particular year ond 
for that purpose the amount paid or rate at which payments 
were made in the last years, would be a guiding factor.’ 


It must, therefore, be shown that there hus been the practice of pay- 
ment of Puja bonus in an unbroken manner and for 0, sufficiently long period 
10 exclude the hypothesis that payments had been made out of bounty. The 
fact that the payment had been made even in a year of loss would be an im- 
portant factor on the question as to whether the payments were mere acts of 
bounty or an obligution on the part of the employers. The learned spokesman 
for the Union drew my uttention to the fact that the Puja bonus was paid 
by the Company in each of the years 1950, 1951 and 1952, in spite of the 
fact that in these years, the nett profit of the Company ranged from 
Rs. 4,000 and odd to about Rs. 7 lakhs. It is to be pointed out that all 
these years were years of profit, though of varying amounts. None of 
these years was a year of loss. If the payment of the bonus had been made 
in a year of loss, that would have been an important evidence in support of 
an obligation on the part of the employers to make the payment. No such 
conclusion can be derived from varying amounts of profit. The learned 
advocate for the Company cited the decision of the Hon’ble Appellate 
Tribunal in the case of Calcutta Electric Manufacturing Co., Lid., reported 
in 1952 (II) L.L.J., 324. The workers in this case claimed that the 
Company had been paying them Puja bonus, irrespective of the state of 
accounts for several years and this bonus had thus become a condition of 
service. The Tribunal found that bonus was paid by the Company only 
from 1941-42 to 1947-48 and no principle was discernible upon which such 
bonus was paid and that such payments as were made were insufficient to 
establish a customary right to bouns. The claim of the workers to bonus 
was refused_jn these circumstances. In that case, payment of bonus for 
six yeirs successively wads not considered sufficient to establish the 
customary character of the bonus. In the present case, the Company paid 
the bonus only for three years 1950, 1951 and 1952, which were years of 
profit. The previous Company worked for four years and paid the bonus 
only in 1948. No bonus was paid in 1949. It is, therefore, clear that 
payment of bonus for the three years under the present Company and for 
one year under the previous Company cannot be considered to be sufficient 
to create a customary character of the payment so as to prove that this 
payment was a condition of service. The learned advocate for the Company 
also referred to the cases reported in 1963 L.A.C., 257, and 1053 14805 
261, pressing that no Tribunal should ignore, the Full Bench formula and 
grant bonus in pursuance of indefinite notions of social justice and there 
must be a foundation of prosperity in the year before a Tribunal is justified 
in granting bonus. The Full Bench ease referred to is Millowners’ case, 
reported in 1952 L.A.C., 433. In these circumstances, it is decided that 
there is nothing to show that the workmen were paid Puja bonus by the 
Company as a condition of service, and that the payments made in 1990, 
1951 and 1952, had acquired a customary character. In view of the fact 
that there has been loss to the Company in 1953, the workmen are not 
entitled to any bonus for tht year. The result is that the claim of the 
workmen for bonus for 1953 is rejected. That heing so, the question as to 
whether the amount which the Company have advanced to their employees 
should be treated as bonus does net arise. This advance was made by the 
Company to the workmen on their application in accordance with the terme 
of the notice dated 12th October 48 ae E(3)], which makes the 
advance recoverable in eight equal instalments. Ext. F is the receipt

regarding this issue. The preliminary objection taken by the Company in

Issue No. 3. 


This relates to the retrenchment of 55 workers mentioned in the list 
enclosed with the order of reference. The retrenchment is admitted. The 
learned representative for the Union relied on the observations of their 
lordships of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in Biswamitra Press, 
1952 L.A.C., p. <0 at p. 33 and contended that the onus of proving 
the necessity fur the retrenchment is on the management. ‘If the manuge- 
ment fails to establish it, its case would end there. If however 
the management is able to estublish un case of retrenchment, either on the 
ground of rationalisation, economy or other sufficient causes, the next ques- 
tion to be considered would be the extent of retrenchment. Here the matter 
has to be considered under two sub-heads, namely (i) whether the action of 
the management in retrenching the workmen in bona fide and (ii) whether 
in determining the extent of retrenchment, it acts partly on the extraneous 
considerations or on improper motives. It is only when the management 
is influenced by extraneous considerations or improper motives, the Tribunal 
must scrutinise the matter with great cireumspection and must confine the 
nuwber of retrenchment within the limits of actual requirements.’’ I re- 
called 119 evidence discussed in connection with the previous issue. 
Shri Mazumdar, the Factory Manager, is the only witness examined in this

describing them as temporary workers in full satisfaction of their claims as 
against the management. These receipts taken on typed forms presented

claiming compensation or relief in addition to that received by them at the

The Company justifies its action on the ground of sheer necessity due to

No. 3803Dis./D/7L-37/54.—3rd August 1954.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4740Dis./D/7L- 
32/53, dated the 12th December 1953, read with its addendum No. 47Dis./D/ 
7L-32/53, dated the 7th January 1954, the industrial disputes between the

sented by Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ Union, 1, Joy Bhattacharyee Lane,

dated the 12th December 1953, were referred for adjudication to the Sixth 
Industrial Tribunal; 

And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal 
a complaint in writing was received from Shri Lalu Mondal and Shri Abdul, 
two workmen of Lohia Jute Press, 28, Barrackpore Trunk Road, Calcutta-2, 
one of the said Jute Presses, against the said Jute Press before the said Tribunal 
alleging that the said 8. had altered, to the prejudice of the said two

2822 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 1944 | 14471 1 


The original reference out of which this present application under section 
33A of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government 
order Nos. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 8th August 1952, read with 
addendum No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 10th November 1952, read 
with 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. 


The petitioners contend that they were not allowed to work on 4th April 
1954 and therefore they pray that the employer may be directed to com- 
pensate for the loss of earning on 4th April 1954. 


The contractor contends that the allegation of the petitioners is not correct 
and that 4th April 1954 was a Sunday and on that day the regular staff of the 
casual workmen in which category the petitioners are included, did no work. 


AWARD. 


The Wage Register produced by the witness for the contractor shows that on 
all Sundays during April 1954, the press was closed and no work was done and 
the Register also shows that the Jute Press was closed generally on Sundays. 
In these circumstances I am of opinion that the application under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act is misconceived. The representative of the 
petitioners prays that the Tribunal should at least make a remark in its decision 
that in future if work be available on Sunday, the same should be done by the 
regular staff and not by new hands or outsiders. I leave it to the discretion of 
the Contractor and I hope that the Contractor should not sow seeds of discontent- 
ment amongst the regular staff of the workmen generally employed by him, by 
engaging outsider on Sundays if the regular staff is willing to do work on 
Sundays also. As there has been no alteration of service condition nor there 
has been any punishment by not running the press on Sunday, the 4th April 
1954, the present application is rejected. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


M. L. CHAKRAVATTI, MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 
Judge. District Judge, 
Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal.

The original reference out of which this present application under section 
33A of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government 
order Nos. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 8th August 1952, read with 
addendum "No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 10th November 1952, read 
with 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. 


The petitioner's case is that he is a permanent member of the Jute Press 
Workers’ Union and that he was working under the Contractor Messrs. 
Bhuwalka - Co., Ltd. The said Bhuwalka & Co. Ltd. ۱.٤٥ 
sent a representative to conduct the case on its behalf. The  repre- 
sentative simply cross-examined the petitioner Ramjhalak. The petitioner’s 
case is that while doing duty he was wounded on 25th December 1953, and 
consequently he was confined in hospital for some time and that when on the 
14th January 1954, he attended the press to do work he was verbally told that 
he was discharged. His contention is that he has not been granted any leave 
with wages nor has he been paid the medical expenses which are due to him 
and that the contractor dealt with him unfairly because of the fact that the 
petitioner appeared as a witness in the original adjudication proceeding. 


AWARD. 


For the relief for the period of the petitioner’s incapability to work due to 
the accident he should move the Workmen’s Compensation Commissioner, His 
representative however says that such application is pending there. So the 
prayer for medical expenses and for wages during the period he was 
unable to work because of the accident cannot be entertained under the present 
application under section 33A. That part of the prayer is rejected. The 
contractor's representative says that the petitioner is always welcome to join 
his duty in the press. The petitioner states that when on account of accident a 
worker is confined in hospital, the Contractor pays the allowances to such work- 
man out of the amount which is paid by the Insurance Company. There is no 
denying the fact that the petitioner has been discharged on 14th January 1954 
without assigning any reason. So I direct that the petitioner be reinstated and 
he be paid in full his daily wages for the period from 14th January 1954 up to

সি 


the date of reinstatement plus sustenance allowance of 8 annas per day. Pay- 


ment and reinstatement shall be made within a week from the date of publica- 
tion of the award.

PINDINGS. 


Issue No, 1. 


This relates to bonus for 1951 and 1952. The Union claims bonus at 
the rate of 3 months’ basic salary and dearness allowance alleging that 
the Company had earned huge profits in the past, and was able to pay this 
claim. At the sume time it is stated that the employees received bonus 
at the rate of 2 months’ basic pay and dearness allowance in 1951, and at 
the rate of one month’s basic pay with dearness allowance, and one month’s 
basic pay without dearness allowance in 1952. The Company resisted 
this claim on the ground that it paid bonus amounting to two months’ 
basic pay and dearness allowance in 1951 which was substantial and 
adequate. It was paid in view of the fact that the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce scheme of pay had not been then adopted. In 10523 the 
employees entered into an agreement with the Company by which the 
difference he{ween bonus at the rate of two months’ basic salary and 
dearness allowance, and one month’s basic salary was incorporated into 
basic salaries and dearness allowance on the clear -understanding that 
bonus would be paid on this basis at the rate of one month’s basic salary 
only. The employees are not entitled to break this agreement, and on 
yroper accounting it would be found that they were not entitled to any 
ee at all for 1952. Taken along with these grounds the Company 
alleged that there was a very serious drop in business in Calcutta which 
could not permit them to pay any further bonus. 


It has been held in the Full Bench decision of the Labour Appellate 
Tribunal in the case of Mill Owners’ Association versus Rastria Mill 
Mazdoor Sangh, reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 433, that essentially the 
রা of bonus must depend upon the relative prosperity of the concern 
during the year under review, and that prosperity is best reflected in the 


2838 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 1954 [Parr T 


umount of the residuary surplus of profits. The claim for bonyg ia 
dependent on profits. Admittedly, the employees received two months’ 
basic pay and dearness allowance in 1951, and one month’s basic pay and 
dearness allowance along with one month’s basic pay without dearness 
ollowance in 1952. They claim at the rate of 3 months’ basic salary and 
dearness allowance in both those years. The question now is, whether 
this claim is admissible and can be allowed. So far as the claim for 1951 
is concerned, the management’s evidence is that the account for that year 
is already closed. That being so, the present claim is not admissible. 
The learned representative for the Company relied on the decision of the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal, reported in 1952, Vol. TI, L.L.J., page 183, 
in the case of Caltex India, Ltd., versus their employees, and contended 
that the employees having accepted that bonus for the past year, without 
protest, they could not now raise an industrial dispute for higher bonus 
in that year. Regarding the Company’s other objection to the claim, as 
mentioned above, it is now admitted on both sides that there was an ayree- 
ment’ between the Company and its employees under which new scales of 
pay were introduced with effect from the Ist August 1952. The Union, 
not being 9 party to it, contends that it is not binding on it. It is the 
Union’s case now that the Company fraudulently got up this agreement 
with their own people of the Staff Committee who represented the employees 
at the time. The Company’s position has been made clear in paragraph 4 
of its additional written statement in which it is stated, among others, 
that the suid new scales of pay, etc., were introduced at the special request 
of the employees through the Staff Committee. The Union was not 
registered at such date. Nevertheless the employees having accepted the 
benefit under that agreement are bound by it. At the hearing the learned 
Counsel for the Company asked the Tribunal to scrap that agreement since 
it is the desire of the Union to do so. The Company has now retraced it 
steps taken in the written statement and joined with the Union in rescind- 
ing that agreement. Since both sides have disowned that agreement, it 
can no more be pleaded as a defence to the Union’s claim of bonus. 
Further, so far as I have been able to find, there is no materials on record 
to show that the said agreement was made on the clear understanding that 
bonus would be paid on the basis of one month’s basic salary only. It 
is needless to refer to the Union’s evidence on this point, for, it is not of 
any real assistance in this case. Shri S. N. Ganguly, the Secretary of the 
Union, and the only witness on its side, did not say anything about the 
profits of the Company, and for obvious reasons, for it is the Union’s case 
that the Company’s account is a sealed book to them. It is not difficult 
to appreciate that position, for, usually the Union officials, or for the 
matter of that, the employees get no access to Company's books of 
accounts. The Company filed the balance sheet in a confidential cover 
with a request to treat the same as confidential. It is a private limited 
concern, and, accordingly, the Tribunal cannot disclose the contents of 
the documents in its award. The learned representative for the Union, 
who had access to these documents, did not prepare any chart according 
to the directions given in the Full Bench case mentioned above. The 
learned Counsel for the Company, however, has helped this Tribunal with 
charts showing calculations of bonus strictly according to the Full Bench 
decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. In 1951 the surplus profit 
available for distribution as bonus amounted to Rs. 10°50 lacs. The actual 
bonus paid was Rs. 1,30,912-3-9 (vide Ext. M1 and the revised calculations 
filed subsequently). In 1952, any modest calculation will show a deficit 
amounting to Rs. 82,895 or so. The rehabilitation expenses have not been 
taken into consideration (vide Ext. M). Rupees 71,199 18 shown as-commis- 
sion in that year earned by the Company. This is the income which 1s

uurelated to workers’ efforta. According to the Full Bench decision this 
shoul have been deducted from the surplus. But this was not done. It 
this was deducted, the surplus would have been further reduced. It,

bonus to its employees amounting (0 Rs. 1,09,999 only. That there has

The Company lost nearly 50 per cent. of its business since December 1950 
when Squibbs, an important firm, terminated its business. The Company 
has got some new firms since then, but that the work in Calcutta continues 
to be much less than what it was before. There has been a very serious 
drop in business of the Company. Mr. Lemmon’s evidence taken along 
with that of Mr. Dawnley leaves no doubt that there has been a recession 
in its business, This is due to various factors. The recent import restric- 
tions are one of them, Apart from alleging that the Company has 
incurred heavy expenditure, the Union did nothing to show that the 
Company’s balance-sheets are wrong, or that the charts prepared by them 
axe wrong. The Company had profits in both these years, profits in 1952 
being very small in comparison with that of 1951, and the previous years. 
The Company has already paid bonus to its employees. There was no 
protest when the bonus was paid in 1951. It is only after the Union came 
into existence that there was a fresh demand for further payment. The 
demand does not appear to be a reasonable one, in the circumstances of 
the case. The available surplus profits do not justify any further puyment 
on this account both in 1951 and 1952. I answer the issue accordingly. 


Issue No. 2.—Tiffin allowance. 


In claiming the tiffin allowance equal in amount to that paid to the 
Anglo-Indian employees, the Union alleges that the unfair and _indis- 
criminate treatment in this matter should go. At the same time it asked 
for a payment of a tiffin allowance at the rate of 12 annas per day for the 
subordinate staff, besides tea that is now being served free of cost. In 
this connection the Union alleged that the Company should run a canteen 
at its own cost for the benefit nnd convenience of all the employees. The 
Company was not agreeable to maintain any canteen, and it contended 
that the tiffin allowance was at oll times an ezr-gratia payment, and could 
not be claimed as of right. Considering the different habits of the 
different communities, the Company paid the Anglo-Indians at the rate of 
Rs. 1-8 per day, and the other employees, excluding the subordinate staff, 
at the rate of 8 annas per day, when in 1952 tiffin rooms were closed. 


Canteen ia not an issue for adjudication in this case. So it is left out 
of consideration. 


It is admitted that the tiffin allowance is not paid to new entrants, 
and 0180 to the subordinate staff. It is only paid to those employees, 
Anglo-Indians and Indians, who enjoyed the benefit before the tiffin rooms 


2840 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTR, AUGUST 19, 1954 {Pant | 


সস 


were closed in 1952. It is further in evidence that the Company provided 
mid-day meals for the Anglo-Indians staff only since 1941 when 0৮82 to 
transport difficulties under War conditions the Anylo-lndians could not 
leave office for their mid-day meal. In 1949 the other clerical staff ask- 
ed for tiffin allowance, due to increasing economic difficulties, of a small 
amount, necessary to purchase snacks, to which they were accustomed in 
the middle of the day, and the Company made necessary arrangements 
accordingly. Cash alles was paid since tifin rooms were closed ۰ز‎ 
1952. The employees were paid just the amount which was paid to the 
contractors for providing them with صظانا‎ before that. The Company, 
of course, denies unfuir treatment to its employees in this mutter. ‘The 
question now is, whether it is an ez-gratia payment as alleged by the 
Company. It has not been proved by the Union that it is a condition of 
service. On its own admission, the new entrants are not entitled ٤غ‎ it. 
The subordinate staff has never received it. This benefit was not allowed 
to the employees before 1949. Therefore, it is abundantly clear that it 
is not a condition of service which can form the subject matter for 
adjudication. It follows that it was in the nature of an e#-yratia payment 
throughout. In fact, in many industrial and mercantile concerns, this is 
never allowed to any employee, and it is considered to be a luxury, which 
the Government servants do not enjoy. The learned representative for 
the Company furnished extracts from several awards on this point. It is 
Ext. M. It appears that some respectable European business firms provide 
small tiffin to their employees; the payment was held by the Tribunals to 
be in the nature of “er-gratia’’. I was not shown any award of an 
Tribunal in which a different conclusion was arrived at. Be that as it 
may, this does not appear to be at all a matter, which in the circumstances 
of this case, can all the moment form a matter of dispute for adjudication. 
And as the Company has succeeded in establishing that there has been 
a very serious recession in its business in Calcutta, and it is passing 
through anxious and critical times at present, it is not necessary to make 
this tiffin allowance available to the subordinate staff, nor it is necessary 
to increase its amount to the rate claimed by the Union, I decide the issue 
accordingly. 


issue No. 3.—Retiral benefits. 


In short, the Union claims (1) Pension Scheme as under the Pension 
Scheme available at present; (2) Provident Fund in which the Company 
should make equal contribution with the employees, and (3) Gratuity at 
the rate of one month’s basic salary and dearness allowance for each complet- 
ed year of service with the maximum equivalent to 15 months of such salary 
and dearness allowance. The Company resists this claim on the allegation 
that the employees have a non-contributory Pension Scheme 09 an 
alternative to a Provident Fund. The so-called Provident Fund, which 
more .aptly should be termed a staff Savings Fund is in existence. The 
Company has always encouraged this fund and assisted it in some degrees, 
but at no time interfered with its operation. It is operated solely by the 
employees. It denies its liability to make any provision for payment of 
any Provident Fund and Gratuity. The staff Pension Fund Rules are 
Ext. J, and the Provident Fund Rules are Ext. K. It appears on perusal 
of the Provident Fund Rules and the Union’s statement that an employee 
on retirement gets a pension equivalent to 50 per cent. of the sulary last 
drawn by him after putting in 10 years of service. The normal age limit 
of retirement is 60 years. The Union wanta to maintain this scheme, 
and it has no grievance against it. This appears to be a very good 
provision indeed. The Provident Fund as it now exists, consists of (a) 
personal contribution, (6) Company’s contribution, and (c) accrued | 


Parr J] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, ATGUST 19, 4 2841 
১১ ১১১১০ 
interest. It is in evidence of P.W. I, Shri Ganguly, that the employees 
contrifute 2 annas in a rupee each month in the fund. Mr. Lemmon says 
that they assisted this fund by contributing about 10 per cent. of the 
employees’ contribution, ‘They have no control over tbhia fund. ‘lhe 
employees administer it. The question now is, whether triple benefits 
should he allowed in this case, as claimed by the Union. The Union’s 
claim does not appear to be, on the face of it, reasonable. It has not 
made out a cause that the present time is most opportune for having three 
retiral benefits, in pluce of two they enjoyed so long. Ounce again, it is 
necessary to record that the Company’s financial position, so far as the 
Culcutta branch is concerned, is not good. Its business position has been 
reduced by 50 per cent. since 1951. Accordingly, this 14 not the proper 
time, in which further retiral benefits should be consider or ullowed to 
the employees, Any further burden on its finances is likely to cripple the 
business und render the Oalcuttu branch un uneconomic unit, probably, for 
good, In fact it has not been shown in this case that uny comparable 
concern in the locality does pay triple benefits to its employees on retire- 
ment. Very few enjoy even two benefits at a time. One is, in many 
causes, found to be a sufficient provision as retiral benefit. The Tribunal, 
on 1 consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, does not 
consider it necessary to allow any further retiral benefit at present. 
answer the issue accordingly. 


Issue No. 4.—Procedure for disciplinary action. 


The Union suggests that if the Company wants to take any = disci- 
plinary action against an employee, it must give a chiarge-sheet setting 
out, the offence, fairly and legibly, and the employees concerned should be 
given un opportanity to defend himself, by the Union, before a Board of 
five! persons, of whom two will be nominated by the Union, two by the 
employer, and one by the Labour Commissioner. There should be = an 
appeal to the Labour Commissioner. The Company has framed its stand- 
ing orders, for its industrial employees, under the Industrial Employment 
(Standing Orders) Act, 1946, which ore now awaiting certification by the 
Certifying Offiver. Regarding its mercantile employees, the Company has 
introduced the scheme, as laid down in the Bengal Chamber of Cominerce 
Award of 1949, and adopted the Chamber's procedure, which is the model

of discipline concerning the employees. In fact, the Union did not succeed 
in showing that in any award a Joint Board including representatives of the 
Union ever conducted any enquiry into complaints against employees. The 
maintenance of internal discipline is a management function, and the 
management is responsible for if. It is only, in the fituess of things, that 
enquiries affecting such discipline, amongst its employees, should be made 
by persons responsible for the management of the business, and not by

Lubour Stafi—Rs. 40 plus cheap ration system (vide Ext. 11). 


Dearness allowance is not a matter of dispute in this case. It is only 
mentioned to show the total emoluments which the employees are getting 
under the settlement of August 1902. 


The suggested grades of the Union are as follows: — 

Departmental Heads—Rs. 250—10—330—15—450. 

14825 Grade Clerka—Rs. 150—10—400. 

4532? Grade General Clerks—Rs. 100—5—150—10—330. 
Non-clerical staff—Rs. 70—3—140. 

Carpenters—Rs. 90—3—100. 

Packers, Bearers, Durwans, Sweepera and coolies—Rs. 50—2—100. 


The other grades as suggested are more or less the same plus some extra 
allowance. It has been urged on behalf of the Union that the employees be 
given the above grades and scales of pay, or im the alternative B.C.C. scales 
in tote, or 1.0.1. grades, it being a comparable concern with Mesars. Martin 
& Tlarris Ftd. (the Company in this case). The Union has supplied 
different grades of the Volkart Bros. (vide Ext. 7), 17051 and Arsociated 
Companies (vide Ext. 12) and also the grades of salesmen in four Gom- 
anies, including the Volkart Bros. (Ext. 14). The Company on the other 
and very emphatically contends that it cannot be reasonably compared 
with Messre. 1.C.1., Ltd. or Messrs. Volkart Bros And although it is 
afflinted to the Bengal Chamber of Commerce, us one of ite constituents, 
it cannot afford to pay ita staff as generously as the Bengal Chamber of 


2850 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 1954 [Parr I 


Commerce, being only a very smal] concern. The Company submitted the 
following scales and Dearness Allowance current from lst January 1947:— 


Special Grade—Rs. 12-6-0, 

Clerical Staff(A)—Rs. 80—5—125. 

Clerical Staff (B)—Rs. 50-—3—80. 

Non-clerical staff Durwans, Peons and coolies, etc.—Rs. 30—1—~46.

Non-clerical—HRs. 15 per month. 


Besides above, ration at concession rates which was availed of by the 
majority (Ext, G). 


The Company also filed the grades and scales of pay of its comparable 
concerns in Calcutta, viz., Messrs. Bengal Chemical, Messrs. B. K. Paul, 
Messrs, Curex Laboratories, Messrs. Smith Stanistreet & Co., and Mesars. 
Albert David (vide Ext. H). 


The question now is, whether the existing scales of August 1952 be 
maintained, or the admitted scales of 1947 be examined with a view to see 
if it is capable of further improvement in its reconstruction. The Company 
uk stated above stood by the existing scales of 1952, introduced on the 
request of the employees in August 1952 before the Union came into 
existence. The Union, it may be recalled, wanted to scrap it on the 
allegution that it was an act of fraud on the side of the management. 
During the trial the Company in view of the Union’s attitude, towards the 
settlement, agreed with the Union that it should go. In these circumstan- 
ces, und in view of the fact that under the scheme of 1952 some of the 
employees were getting reduced emoluments, the existing scales of 1952 
are given up. It may be mentioned here that it was a part of the B.C. (0058 
scale applicable to the employees of this Company. 1).4- as per B.C.O. 
was paid ttong with these scales of pay. The Union's claim of the Bengal 
Chamber of Commerce’s scale, with higher gerade in teto now taken up 
during the hearing of the case, appears to be untenable. The grades of 
the Bengal Chamber of Commerce are many, and they are mentioned in 
the award of our Tribunal, published in the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 
8th February 1949. It has two departments, viz., (1) General and (2) 
Licensed Measurers Department. The scales are different in these two 
departments. There are as many as five grades of clerical staff in the 
Licensed Measurers Department commencing from Rs. 60 and rising up 
to Rs. 250. In the General Department there are five grades besides one 
for the typists, one for Sircars and motor drivers, etc. The pay commences 
from Rs. 60 and rises up to Rs. 230. For obvious reasons the adoption of 
the Bengal Chamber of Commerce’s scales in toto is neither feasible nor 
reasgnable. Shri S. C. Chakraborty in his award in Holmes Wilson’s 
case (vide Calcutta Gazette, dated the 27th July 1950) considered this 
point. In that case the very same argument as advanced in the present 
case was made. The learned adjudicator said that ‘‘while agreeing on 
principle that the Bengal Chamber of Commerce scale should be introduced 
there are some practical difficulties in copying out the various scales of 
pay there. The principal difficulty is that in the Bengal Chamber of 
Commerce case it was found that the employees were mostly matriculates.” 
On a consideration of the special circumstances of that case he laid down 
a lower grade for the non-matriculate clerks. This takes us to the con- 
sideration of the qualifications of the employees in the service of _ the 
Company. Mr. Lemmon, the Chairman of the Board of Directors, said 
that they did not prescribe any minimum qualification for appointment 


Parr 1) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 14 2851 


mene ১ ওলি 


us clerks. They had not to pass in any qualifying test like the Steno- 
grupmers. In the staff, there is one graduate only and there are about 50 
per cent. non-matriculates und an equal number of mutriculates. In the 
majority of lurge mercantile firms in Caleutta, the clerks -are more 
qualified. The majority ure matriculates. Sri Ganguly said in his cross- 
examination that he did not know the educational qualifications of the 
employees. He did not know if there was any gruduate among them. He 
could not say how many of them are non-matriculates. So, practically 
speaking, Mr. Lemmon’s evidence stands uncontradicated. We take it that 
the majority of the employees are non-matriculntes, and there is only one 
graduate in the whole staff. In reconstructing the wuge scales the quali- 
fications of the employees will have to be taken into consideration. The 
present capacity of the Company to pay is another point to be considered. 
D.A. may also be taken into account, although it should not be very much 
in the picture. In this connection it is worth while to remember the nature 
of business that is transacted by this Company, and the nature of work 
done by its employees. The Company, as zie appeur from Mr. Lemon’s 
evidence, is engaged in representation of foreign manufacturers, booking 
orders from the people of India which would be shipped direct to the Indian 
purchasers. It is a smal) organisation as it did not entail physical handling 
of goods. At all times they have to deal with changing pattern of 
trade and conditions. Mr. Lemon said that with the changing conditions, 
with higher emoluments paid: to the staff, the higher expenditure in all 
directions, it is no longer possible to carry on the business on a profitable 
basis, unless working on full capacity. Sri Ganguly said that the Company 
deals in medicines, butter milk, toilet, ete. Tt manufactures some medicines 
atid toilets, including Oatine cream. The two witnesses differ very widely 
when mentioning its comparable concerns. Mr. Lemmon said that Messrs. 
Sihith Stanistreet & Co., Messrs. Benga] Chemical, Mesars. Bengal Immunity 
ا‎ identical business with them. The nearest comparison would be with 
Médssrs. Smith Stanistreet & Co., Shri Ganguly, on the other hand, men- 
tiohed the Glaxo, the Volkart Brothers, the Imperial Chemical Industries 
andthe May & Baker as identical concerns. He said that the Sinith Stani- 
street & Co., was a manufacturing concern, but they do not deal in butter, 
milk, quinine, ete. Shri Ganguly could not say what pay scales are given 
to the employees of those concerns. Regarding the 1.C.1., 1t would appear 
from Mr. Justice Divatia’s award that the I.C.[. (India), 150. was a 
subsidiary of a huge business organisation, with 87 subsidiaries all over the 
world. I am told that the organisation hus now more han 96 subsidiaries, 
including one in India, al] over the world. The I.C.1. deals in heavy 
chemicale and its business amounted to several crores. By no stretch of 
imagination it can be said to he a comparable concern with this Company. 
The Bengal Chemical is reported to be making profits of more than 16 
lacs in a year. The Volkart Brothers is the chief Swiss firm in India. 6 
has got import and export business in cotton textiles, air conditioning 
plants, electrical goods and also Jute business. This is also not a com- 
parable concern. The principle rival of this Company appears to be Messrs. 
Smith Stanistreet & Co. If any comparison of_ pay acale is necessary, 
it must he made with Messrs. Smith Stanisteet & Co. The acales in 68۰ 
Smith Stanistreet are as below :— 


Rs, 60—23—100. 

Rs. 70—4—130. 

Peons—Rs. 30—1—40. 

Darwans and others—Rs. 30—1—45. 


I have anxiously considered the scalea and grades of pay for the emplovees 
of the Company. Considering the nature of work done by the employees, 


2852 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 19, 1954 = [Part I 


প্রসার 


and also their qualifications, I am in favour of modifying some of the 
existing grades. The special basic grade is meant more or less fr the 
Supervisory staff. It is desirable that its increment should be left for the 
present to the discretion of the management = The existing conditions will 
continue. The ‘‘A”’ grade clerks get a good start at Rs. 80. It has been 
suggested on behalf of the Company that this grade should be reconstructed 
with a lower pay at the beginning at Rs. 70) for the new entrants. The 
maximum should he raised to Rs. 130, in place of Rs. 125. The scale 
should be Rs. 70-——4—130, The employees had enjoved for Jong the henefit 
of a good start in ‘‘A’’ grade, and there is no justification why in recon- 
structing this grade a lower start should be given to the new entrants. At 
the same time, I am not unmindful of a higher maximum of this grade in 
comparable concerns of the locality. This grade should therefore be re- 
constructed as Rs. 80—5—130. So far as ‘‘B’’ grade is concerned, it has 
a very low start. In Holmes Wilson’s case mentioned above, a grade of 
Rs. 60-—3—90 was created. But in the Smith Stanistreet case, the corres- 
ponding grade is Rs. 60—24—100. It is desirable that the ‘‘B’’ grade 
should be reconstructed with a better start, and there should be a com- 
paratively higher maximum at the end. This should be Ra. 60—2§—105. 
So far as S.N.S. and subordinate grades are concerned, the Company’s 
suggestion is that the grade for the subordinate staff should be Rs. 80—1— 
35 for the labourers, Rs. 30—1—40 for the Peons and Rs. 30-——-1—45 for 
the Durwans. 

TI do not think that these grades require any such reyision, for, it is 
likely to create a discontent amongst different categories of the staff. 
Accordingly, only two grades should be reconstructed as follows :— 


٠“ ''ھ‎ grade—Rs. 80—5—150. 

‘““B”’ grade—Rs. 60—24—105. 

Regarding adjustments of the grade ‘‘A’’, os point to point adjustment 
was made in the case of the employees of this grade when it was originally 
created, no_question of further adjustment arises in this case. 


Regarding the ‘‘B’’ grade, as the minimum is raised, the question of 
adjustment will arise, I think, it would be fair if one increment in every 
three years’ service up to a miximum of five increments is allowed in fit- 
ting in the pay of an employee of thia grade. But he shall not get more 
than the maximum of the new grade in which he is fitted in (1952, Vol. I, 
L.L.J., page 16). A new grade was claimed in modification of the one 
in existence for the salesman. There is a substantial difference hetween 
the total emoluments that a salesman gets, as according to the Union and 
the Company [vide Exts. 13 and 14(a)]. In this connection, the Union 
proved Ext. 14._ I have considered the pay of the salesmen in Calcutta 
and outside, and I find that it does not call for any revision at present. The 
one other point conceded on behalf of the Company should be placed on 
record. The employees, both clerical and subordinate, used to get fret 
ration “concession till it was abolished. Since its aholition each member 
of the clerical staff is paid Rs. 10 per month, and each member of the sub- 
ordinate staff Rs. 5 per month in lieu of that concession. This will, of 
course, continue. I answer the issue accordingly. This is my award.

West Bengal Clvil Service (Executive and Judicial) and 
Allied Servicos Examination, January, 1955. 


THE following concessions in agé and fees aro adminsible 
to displaced persons pectin at the West Hengal Civil 
Service (Executive and Judicial) and Allied Services Exa- 
mination to be held in January 1955. 


The upper age limit is relaxable by three years for 
displaced persons in general and by six years for displaced 
persons belonging to scheduled castes and scheduled tribes. 


_ The application and examination fees muy be remitted 
in case of bona fide displaced persons who are not in a posi- 
tion to pay the prescribed fees. 


The above concessions will be admissible to such dis- 
placed persona only as arrived in india from Pakistan in 
1951 or thereafter. A person already in tho rmanent 
employ of Government will also be eligible for the conces- 
sions if he is a displaced person of the above category.

DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, 
WEST BENCAL. 


Calcutta, the 17th June 1954. 


Final Forecast of Tobacco Crop of West Bengal 
for 1953-54. 


Season.—The weather conditions have been 
favourable at the time of sowing in all the dis- 
tricts except 24-Parganns, Nadia, Malda and 
Darjeeling. During growth period of the crop the 
weather conditions have been generally favourable 
in all the districts except 24-Paryunas und Nadia. 


Area and yield.—The total area under Tobacco 
in the State of West Bengal has been estimated 
at 38,950 acres this year compared to 40,200 acres 
of last year. The total yield of Tobacco for the 
state as a whole is estimated at 10,820 tons this 
year compared to 12,800 tons of last year. 


I. Ntcotrana Rustica.—24,200 acres have been 
estimated to be under ‘‘Nicotiana Rustica’’ variety 


of Fobacco this year compared to 25,900 acres of 
last year. The total yield of this variety of the 
crop for the state as a whole is 7,070 tons this year 
compared ta 8,5%0 tons of last year. 


11 Nicotiana Tabacum.—(a) Virginia type 
of Nicotiana TabacumtThe area and production 
of the virgina type of Nicotiana Tabacum have 
been estimated at 300 acres and 70 tons respective- 
ly against nil of last year. 


(b) Other types of Nicotiana Tabacum.—14,400 
acres have been estimated to be under the ‘‘other 
types of Nicotiana Tabacum’’ this year compared 
to 14,300 acres of last year. The total yield of 
this variety of the crop for the State as a whole is 
estimated ut 3,680 tons this year compared to 
4,260 tons of last year. 


S. N. MUKHERJEE, 
for Director of Agriculture, West Bengal.

Bengal for 1953-54. 


| Note.—The figures of last year and this year 
as shown in the forecast are bused on the results 
of sample survey conducted by the State Statistical 
Bureau, West Bengal, except those of Darjeeling 
distriet and also acreage figure of Malda for last 
year. The figures of Darjeeling district for last 
year and this year and acreage figure of Malda 
district for last year are based on the reports re- 
ceived from the extension staff of this Directorate. ]

been favourable in all the districts except 24-Par- . 
gauss, Bankura and Malda. 


Area and yield.—133,100 acres have been 9861 
mated to be under Wheat in the State this year 
compared to 106,400 acres of last year.«The esti- 
mated total yield of Wheat for the State as a 
whole is 38,400 tona this year compared to 35,300 
tons of last year. The average yield per acre of 
Wheat Crop for the State as a whole is estimated 
at 7°86 maunda this year compared to 9:03 maunds 
of last year.

[Part IVA 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


By virtue of clauae (b) of section ¢ of the West Benpal Legislature 
(Removal of Disqualifications) Act, 1952 (West Ben. Act VI of 1962), a 
person shall not be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, 2 member 
of the West Bengal Legislative Assembly or of the West Bengal Legisla- 
tive Council bye reason only of the ۸۴ that he holds an office of 
profit undér the Government of India or the Government of a State 
which is not a wholetime office remunerated either by salary or by fees. 
This section, however, may not be sufficient for the purpose of affording 
protection against any disqualification as may arise under article 191(1)(a) 
of the Censtitution of India in the case of a person who, having become 
a membes of the Territorial Army or the National Cadet Corps, wishes 
to stand as a candidate for election to either House, or in tho case of a 
member of either House who wishes to become a member of the 
Territorial Army or the National Cadet Corps, inasmuch ox membership 
of either organisation gives rise to a liability for wholetime service, 
for continuous periods, when certain emoluments become payable by 
Governrfént, so that wholetime offices of profit would be held under 
Government for the time being. It is felt that in the larger interests of 
the country, to such disqualification should arise under article 19] (2)69) 
of the Constitiition of India in connexion with membership of either organisa- 
tion. ڈ1‎ case of Members of Parliament, Parliament bas made a law 
under ar te تد‎ (a) of the Constitution of India. Certain other States 
have also enacted laws more or less to the same effect, viz., Bombay, Madras, 
eed Pradesh, Bihar, Punjab, Orissa, PEPSU, Saurashtra and Madhya 

arat.., 


As similar disqualification may arise in connexion with the member- 
ship of the West ]iengal National Volunteer Force raised and maintained 
under the West Bengal National Volunteer Force Act, 1949 (West Ben. 
Act I of 4549) , it is also proposed to remove this disqualification. 


The present Bill proposes to amend the West Bengal Legislature 
(Removal of Disqualifications) Act, 1952, accordingly.

THE WEST BENCAL BLACK MARKETING 
(REPEALING) BILL, 1954. 


A 
BILL 


to repeal the West Bengal Black Marketing Act, 1948. 


It is کت‎ enacted in the Fifth Year of the Republié 
of India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows : ہے‎ 


Short title. 1. This Act may be called the West Bengal Black 
Marketing (Repealing) Act, 1954. 


Repeal of 2. The West Bengal Black Marketing Act, 1948, is 
hereby repealed. 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


In Ram Kissen vs. the State of West Bengal (56 C.W.N. 689) the 
Calcutta High Court held that the provisions empowering Government, at 
ita discretion, to allot cases under the West Bengal Black Marketing Act, 
1948 (West Ben. Act XXXII of 1948), to a Special Tribunal for trial were 
ultra vires article 14 of the Constitution of India and therefore void. 


2. The matter having been referred to the Law Revision Committee, 
it expressed the view that this provision was’ discriminatory inaSmuch as 
Government had ao discretion to prosecute persons guilty of breaché& of 
various Control Orders in different ways, namely, under the Essential 
Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946 (XXIV of 1946), which is a Central 
Act, and the West Bengal Black Marketing Act, 1948, which ig a Btate 
Act. The maximum punishment under the former Act is rigorous“imprison- 
ment up to three years, whereas the maximum punishment under the latter 
Act is rigorous imprisonment up to seven years. Thus persons of the same 
class and similarly situated and circumstanced could be dealt with 
differently. 


3. Quite apart from this, the Committee held the view that in the 
context of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, the West 
Bengal Black Marketing Act, 1948 is void to the extent of repugnancy by 
reason of article 369 of the Constitution of India. It, therefore, secom- 
mended removal of the ۲مھ‎ from the Statute Book. 


4, The West Bengal Black Marketing (Repealing) Bill, 1954, is thpre- 
fore being introduced.

3. Any Court which convicts an offender of an offence 
under section 379 or section 380) of the Indian Penal Code or 
of any offence whatsoever punishable with imprisonment for 
not more than two years, may, if no previous conviction is 
proved against him, and if it is of opinion that having regard 
to his age, character, antecedents, or physical or mental con- 
dition and to the trivial nature of the offence or to the exte- 
nuating circumstances under which the offence was committed, 
it is expedient so to do, release him after due admonition 
instead of sentencing him to any punishment. 


4. (1) Any Court which sentences an offender to 
imprisonment (not being imprisonment in default of payment 
of fine) for a term not exceeding six months for un offence 
pot punishable with death or transportation for life, may,

and if it is of opinion that having regard to his

order and tv compty with the provisions of section 6:

Provided further that if any surety refuses to consent to 
such variation, the Court muy require the offender to provide 
a new surety in place of the surety who so refuses; and upon 
the failure of the offender to do so, the Court may order the 
sentence to be executed. 


7. (2) If a Court which passes an order under section 4 
has reason to believe on the report of the Probation Officer 
or on information received that the offender has failed to 
observe the conditions of the bond, it may issue a warrant for 
his arrest or may, if it thinks fit, issue a summons to him 
and his surety or sureties, requiring them to attend before 
it at such time as may be specified in the summons. 


(2) When the offender is brought before the Court under 
arrest or appears before it in pursuance of the summons, the 
Court may either remand him to custody until the case is 
concluded or admit him to bail, with or without sureties, ٥ 
appear on the date which it may fix for hearing. 

(3) If after hearing the cuse, the Court is satisfied that 
the offender has failed to observe any of the conditions of 
the bond, it may forthwith— 

(a) order the sentence to be executed, or 

(b) where the failure is for the first time then, without 
prejudice to the continuance in force of the bond, 
impose upon him a penalty not exceeding fifty 
rupees. 

(4) If the penalty imposed under clause ا‎ of sub-section 
(3) is not paid within the time fixed by the Court or within 
any such further time as may be allowed by the Court, the 
Court shall order the sentence to be executed.
