STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Persons who are sentenced to imprisonment for periods not exceeding 
six months constitute about ninety per cent. of the total convict population 
of jails in this State. Imprisonment for short periods is not oa deterrent 
and it is difficult to bring to bear suitable reformative influences on these 
persons in jail. Sub-section (ZA) of section 562(7A) of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898) provides that when a person is convicted 
of theft, theft in a building, dishonest misappropriation, cheating or any 
other offence under the Indian Penal Code punishable with not more than 
two years’ imprisonment and no previous conviction is proved against him, 
the Court before which he is convicted may, under certain circumstances, 
instead of sentencing him to any punishment, release him after due 
admonition. It is now দা, to extend this provision to convictions for 
all offences punishable with imprisonment for not more than two years, 
whether under the Indian Penal Code or under any other law. 


Sub-section (7) of section 562(Z) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1898, empowers the Court before which an offender is convicted to release 
him on probation, under certain circumstances, instead of sentencing him 
at once to any punishment. There is, however, at present no provision for 
placing such released offenders under supervision during the period of 
probation. It is now proposed that when any Court sentences an offender 
for a term not exceeding six months, and no previous conviction is proved 
مو‎ him, it shall have power to release him on probation for a period 
of not less than one year and not more than three years, and to place him 
under supervision of a Probation Officer during the period. Provision has 
also been made in the Bill for appointment of Probation Officers. 


The reasons for the different clauses of the Bill are explained below: — 


Notes on Clauses. 
Clause 3. 


This clause is based on sub-section (JA) of section 562 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898. Under that section release on admonition is 
ermissible when a person is convicted of theft, theft in a building, 
سسجت‎ misappropriation, cheating or any offence under the Indian Penal 
Code punishable with not more than two years’ imprisonment. In clause 
3 of the Bill the scope of this provision has been extended to all offences 
punishable with not more than two years’ imprisonment, whether under 
the Indian Penal Code or any other law. 


Clause 4. 


Sub-clause سے رر‎ sub-clause is based on sub-section (4) of section 
662 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Section 562 of the said 
Code applies when the conviction is for an offence punishable with 
imprisonment for not more than seven years in case of persons not under 
twenty-one years of age, or an offence not punishable with death or 
transportation for life, in case of women and persons under twenty-one 
years of age. Sub-clause (2) of clause 4 of the Bill applies to any first 
offender, irrespective of age or sex, who is convicted of an offence not 
punishable with death or transportation for life and_ sentenced to 
imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months. While probation, 
which involves supervision by a Probation Officer for a_ considerable 
eriod, is not suitable in very petty cases, it is coneidered that it should 
a limited to cases where the offence is not so serious as to make a heavy 
sentence of imprisonment appropriate. The scope of the said clause of the 
Bill has, therefore, been restricted to cases in which sentence of imprison- 
ment for terms not exceeding six months is passed. 


Under the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 562 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1898, the power to release an offender on probation 
cannot be exercised by a Magistrate of the third class or a Magistrate of 
the second class, not specially empowered in this behalf. Under sub- 
clause (7) of clause 4 of the Bill, this power can be exercised by any 
Court. t is considered that when a Magistrate can be entrusted to 
sentence. a person to imprisonment, be may as well be empowered to 
release him on probation. | 


Under sub-section (2) of section 562 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1898, the offender enters into a bond with or without sureties. Under sub- 
clause (7) of clause 4 of the Bill it is obligatory to furnish at least one 
surety before an offender is released on probation. A surety will normally 
be a person who has influence or control on the offender and it is considered 
essential to have in every case a surety who can exercise his influence to 
ensure the good conduct of the probationer. The proviso to sub-clause (7) 
of clause 4 of the Bill is based on sub-section (J) of section 564 of the Code 
of Criminal Procedure, 1898. But whereas sub-section (7) of section 564 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, requires that the offender or his 
surety shall have a fixed place of abode or regular occupation, under the 
Bill both place of residence and regular occupation are prerequisites. Thie 


1164 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 19, 1954. (Pant IVA 


a a I SR SIO a nS TN 


extra precaution is necessary to ensure. that the power to release og pro- 
batton is exercised only in cnses where good result can be reasonably 
expected. 


Sub-clause (¢).—This sub-clause provides for supervision by a @reba- 
tion Officer whenever the Court relehses an offender. on probation. There 
is no such provision in section 562 of the. Code of-Criminal Procedure, 1898. 


Clause 5. 
Sub-clause (1).—This is analogous to the provisions of sub-seciion (7) of 
section 545 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 28. 
Sub-clause (2).—This sub-clause provides for enforcing the responsi- 


bility of the parents or guardians where they have contributed to the 
offence by negligence or otherwise. 


Clause 14. 


As the provisions in the Bill deal with the same matter as section 562 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, it is intended that in areas where 
٦ law is brought into force, it will replace section 562 of the said 

ode.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS, 


For the purposes of municipal taxution, the valuation of the properties 
in Calcutta (and Ifowrah) vested in the Commissioners for the Port ot 
Caleutta ig governed not by the Caleutta Municipal Act, 1951 (West Ben. 
Act ×1 of 1951) (which regulates the valuation of all properties for 
municipal] taxation in Calcutta and Howrah) but by the Calcutta Port 
Act, 1890 (Ben. Act III of 1890), under which the annual value of the 
suid properties is, generally speaking, fixed at five per cent. of the capital 
cost.: As most of these_properties were acquired or constructed in the mid- 
nineteenth century, when prices were very low, this works out greatly to 
the detriment of the revenues of the Corporation of Calcutta (and the 
Howrah Municipality), which would, under the normal procedure laid 
down in the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951, derive a far larger revenue 
from the taxation of Port properties than they do under the provisions of 
the Calcutta Port Act, 1890. 


2. In September, 1950, following prolonged discussions with the Cor- 
poration authorities, the Port Commissioners produced a scheme of assess- 
ment which has been accepted by the Calcutta Corporation. The agree- 
ment is expected to result in an aunual increase of over eleven lakhs of 
rupees in the amount of municipal taxes und rates payable by the Port 
Commissioners to the Calcutta Corporution alone. 


3. In order to give effect to the agreement referred to above it is pro- 
19860 to amend the Calcutta Port Act, 1890, in the manner shown in the 
Bill.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


While both the Houses of the Legislature were not in session there 
arose ferfain circumstances which rendered it necessary to amend the West 
Bengal Bergadars Act, 1950 (West Ben. Act II of 1950), by promulgation 
of two Ordinances for the following purposes, namely :— 


(i) to obtain powers for the Sub-divisional Magistrate or any other 
officers subordinate to him to direct restoration to cultivation of 
any land ج تا‎ bargadar who has heen evicted by the owner in 
cantravention of the provisions of the Act and to enforce the 
order forthwith ; 


(ii) to make such eviction-a penal offence, if it is effected after the 
cemmencement of the West Bengal PBargadars (Amendment) 
Ordinance, 1954 (West Ben. Ord. V of 1954); 


(iii) to limit the time during which an order made by a Board or an 
Appellate Officer for the termination of cultivation of any land 
by a bargadar shall be executed; and 


(iv) to provide for certain ancillary matters. 


The Bill seeks to enact the provisions of the said Ordinances.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Cinematograph Act, 1918 (II of 1918), as it stood immediately 
before the commencement of the Constitution of Ludia, dealt principally 
with two subjects, uamely :— 

(1) examination and certification of films as to their suitability for 

public exhibition, and 

(2) regulation of cinemas including their licensing. 

The first of these beCame a Union List subject after the commencement ot 
the Constitution of India. The second comes within the State List. The 
existence of both Union List and State List matters in the same enactment 
led to a certain amount of confusion and udministrative difficulty. DParlia- 
nent accordingly passed the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVIT of 1952) 
replacing the Cimematograph Act, 1918. But as Parliament had no power to 
deal with the second of the two subjects mentioned ubove, so far as it related 
tou Part A and Part B States, it left the provisions of the Cinematograph 
Act, 1918, unrepealed in this regard. 


The present Bill repeals the existing provisions of the Cinematograph 
Act, 1918, in so far as it relates to West Bengal. Tt deals with regulation 
of cinemas including their licensing.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Under clausé (৮) of sub-section (J) of section 554 of the Bengal 
Municipal Act, 1932 (Ben. Act XV of 1932), when the Commissioners of 
a municipahty are superseded, the Administrator appointed by the State 
Government exercises and perfotfms only such powers and duties of the 
Chairman and the Commissioners (whether at a meeting or otherwise) as 
are given by the provisions of the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932 or any rule 
or by-law made thereunder. As u matter of fact, however, the Chairman 
and the Commissioners exercise and perform various other powers and 
duties under the provisions of other laws also, such as the Calcuita 
Munjcipal Act, 1951 (West Ben. Act XXXIII of 1951) (in the case of 
the Howrah Municipality), the Bengal Food Adulteration Act, 1919 (Ben. 
Act VI of 1919), the Cattle-trespass Act, 1871 (I of 1871), the Bengal 
Vaccination Act, 1880 (Ben. Act V of 1880), etc., and the rules, by-laws 
and notifications issued thereunder. The Administrator should therefore 
be authorised to exercise and perform those powers and duties as well. 


To remove the lacuna in the existing legislation, as soon as it became 
apparent, an Ordinance was promulgated in April, 1954 (when both Houses 
of the Legislature were not in session) suitably amending section 554 ot 
the Bengal Municipal Act, 1932. 


Under article 213(2)(a) of the Constitution of India the Ordinance 
will cease to operate at the expiration of six weeks from the date of 
reassenjbly of the Legislature; this Bill is therefore being introduced to 
enact the provisions of the said Ordinance. 


I. D. JALAN, 
Member-in-charge. 


CaucutTra,

the said Act, I do hereby order that movement of 
al) sorts of cloths and yarns within two niles 
from the Pakistan border of this district be 
prohibited. The Indian citizens residimtg within 
the aforesaid area may, however, obtain their 
supplies of aforesaid commodities for their 
personal consumption only. The dealers having

have to keep accounts for each sale to bona fide 
customers and will also mention the names and 
addresses of such purchasers in the cash memos, 
ingued, enabling the Police Officers or any other 
officers authorised in this behalf to verify the 
aume at any time. B 2

On behalf of the Company (employer) none appears. Workmen and 
their representatives appear. Perused the record and heard the 
representative of the workmen. These workmen (Amulya, Gorachand 
and Md. Moslem) have been suspended by the employer pending 
permission from Labour Commissioner to dismiss them on ground of 
misconduct. Company’s case is that suspension was made as ‘‘security 
measures’. The standing order in the award (published in March 1991) 
is alleged to be the standing order (by adoption) of this Company. 
There 5৪ no provision to suspend without wages although there is provision 
to suspend. Prima facie suspension is not termination of service. So, 
ordinarily suspended employee may claim wages or subsistence allowance 
for the period of suspension. I am, therefore, of opinion that it is a fit 
case where interim relief in the shape of subsistence allowance should be 
granted. Ordered that the employer Company shall pay from the

in the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, filed by Shri Duryodhan against the 
Lister Antiseptics & Dressings Co. (1928), Ltd., in connection with an 
industrial dispute referred under Government order No. 1225Dis. /D/ 
11L-8/53, dated the 10th April 1953. 


BKEFORE THE THIRD [INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT ; 
Shri J. N. MAITRA, Judye, Third Industrial Tribunal. 


Misc. Case No. 47 of 1954 under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 


Shr} Duryodhan ee ae .. Petttioner, 
versus 


The 11۸٥٥ ×ئ‎ Antiseptices & Dressings Co. 
(1928), Ltd. -7- 7 7 


; Opposite Party. 
Prasent for the petitioner: Shri Duryodhan himself. 


Present for the opposite party: Shri P. K. Sanyal, Advocate. 


AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 984 of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
workman, Shri Duryodban. He was a bearer in the Bivlogical Department 
of the Company opposite party. He alleged that during the pendency of 
the reference made by (tovernment order No. 1226Dis./D/111-8/53, dated 
10th April 1953, the opposite party had discharged him on 28th January 
1954 without notice and without permission from the Tribunal. He accord- 
ingly prayed for reinstatement and for payment of compensation for the 
period of forced unemployment. 


The Company opposed the application. The Company denied that 
Shri Duryodhan was discharged on 28th January 1954 and pleaded that he 
wus temporarily appointed on the 8th April 1953, for a period of 10 months 
in connection with some definite ordera on the expresa stipulation that his 
service would terminate on expiry of 10 months without any notice and 
without any claim from him. The workman accepted the appointment on 
those terms. The work in connecion with which he was appointed was com- 
pleted before he was discharged but he had to be retained in service even 
after the completion of the said work as the period of his appomtment 
was not over. Tt was alleged that he was discharged on completion of the 
period of hia appointment on 9th February 1954 and not on 2811) January 
1954. Tn the circumstancea, the Company submitted that section 33 was not 
contravened and that the claim of the petitioner should be dismissed. 


The point which therefore arises for determination is, whether section 
33 has heen contravened and whether the discharge is justified. 


2902 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 1954 [Parr ! 


সপ সস সু 
DECISION, 

{fu support of his case the petitioner hus deposed (P. W. 1) and 
examined P. ৮. % Shri Kanai Lal Roy and P. W. 3 Shr Sukhdeo Juana. 
The opposite party on the other band re exumined the Superviser of the 
Biological Department, D. W. 1 Shri Jajneswur Banerjee and the Labour 
Welfare Officer, D. W. 2 Shri Bejoy Krishna Chakraborty besides proving 
the document, Ext. A. 


Workman Shri Durvyodhan (?.W. 1) admitted in his deposition that 
he was appointed in the month of Chaitra to work as a bearer in the 
13191921081 Department for which he put hig thumb impression on Ext. A. 
According to the petitioner, he was uppointed for G6 months on condition 
that he would be lable to be discharged without notice within that period. 
116 deposed further that after employment of six months, he was sent for in 
the office and was asked to afhix thumb impression in acknowledgment of 
having been given extension of four months, but he declined to do ৪০, 
The petitioner, however, admitted that he had served for 10 months and 
that on completion of 10 months, his employment ceased. Ext, A, in which 
the petitioner admittedly put his thumb-impression shows that he was 
appointed for definite period of 10 months and that his service would 
terminate on the expiry of said period without any notice or any claim from 
him, D. W. 1, who is Supervisor in the Biological Department also deposed 
that the petitioner was appointed temporarily for a definite period of 10 
months and that his employment was to terminate without notice on com- 
pletion of the said 10 months. ٢ have had nothing to discard the evidence. 
P. W. 2 and P. W. 3 have admittedly no personal knowledge regarding 
the terms of employment of the petitioner. So their evidence ia useless. 
The writer of the endorsement Ext. A, Biren Babu, is now in Pakistan on 
leave. In the endorsement (Ext. A) the period was originally written as 
six months and subsequently changed to ten months. Such change muat 
have taken placé when the petitioner affixed his thumb-impression at the 
time of appointment. For, it was the definite case of the Company that 
the petitioner was appointed for ten months. The petitioner on the other 
hand did not at all disclose in his complaint that he was appointed for a 
limited period far less for six months and then for 4 months. I ৪০ accept 
Company’s version that the petitioner was appointed for a limited period of 
10 months. When he was so appointed for a limited period of 10 months, it 
is obvious that his employment would automatically cease on the expiry of 
the said period. I a case like this I agree that section 33 is not attracted. 
Besides, in view of express terms of employment I find that the discharge 
without notice is justified. The complaint under section 33A must, there- 


fore, fail. I award accordingly. 
JITENDRA NATH MATTRA, 
Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal.

in the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, filed by Shri Upendra Nath Chatterjee 
and Shri Sushil Kumar Chanda against Messrs. Mahalaxmi Cotton 
Mills, Ltd., in connection with an industrial dispute referred under 
Covernment order No. 2100Dis. /D /8L-23/53, dated the Sth June 3. 


BEFORE THE THIRD INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAI,.

Mahalaxmi Cotton Mills, Ltd. ... re Opposite party

For the opposite party: Shri N. M. Das Gupta, Advocate. 


AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Shri Upendra Nath Chatterjee and Shri Sushil Kumar Chanda. These 
two petitioners were employed in the Mill’s Grain Shop as sales clerks and 
they were admittedly the last comers out of three of that category at the 
relevant time. By notice, dated 18th March 1954 (annexure to the Com- 
pany’s written objection) they were discharged from 16th March 1904 as 
being surplus to the requirement for paucity of work with offer to pay 
wages up to date, one month’s salary in lieu of notice and compensation 
equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for every completed year of service 
corresponding to the benefits as per Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 
1953. In the notice of discharge it was also stated that besides being the 
1841 comers they had reached the age of superannuation. The discharge took 
place during the pendency of a reference between the Company and_ their 
workmen before this Tribunal and without permission from the Tribunal. 
Hence the complaint under section 33A. 


Parr 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 1954 2007 


The case of the petitioners is as follows. The petitioners did not cease 
tu be clerks of the general category merely because they were employed 08 
anlea clerks in the Mill’s Grain Shop. If viewed as such, they were not 
last comers but were senior to some clerks employed in different sections 
of the Mill and as such principles of “last come, first go’? was violated. 
Then the petitioners did not superannuate but they were quite fit for work. 
The opposite party bore grudge against the petitioners on account of their 
tride union aetivities and thus discharged them. 


In the circumstances the petitioners alleged that their discharge was 
unfair, unjust and by way of victimisation. ‘Rhey accordingly prayed for 
reinstulement and for payment of compensation for the period of forced 
unemployment. 


The Company denied having discharged the petitionera on account of 
their alleged union activities and pleaded that it retrenched the petitioners 
bona fide on account of trade reasons. It was alleged that the petitioners 
were employed in this Company in their old age after retirement এ other 
-oncerns. They were employed exclusively for the Grain Shop as salesmen. 
Sales in the (drain Shop greatly declined and correspondingly there was much 
shortage of work in the Grain Shop and there was hardly sufficient work 
even for one salesman. In view of the paucity of work two salesinen became 
surplus to requirement and thus the petitioners, who were the last comers 
in the Grain Shop, were discharged. The other salesman who has been 
retained in service is senior to them. 


x other employee in their category was employed by the Company. 
Grait Shop is itself a different category not connected with mill workers. 
The petitioners had no connection whatsoever with actual work in the mill 
connected with the production. Other employees of the Company are all 
empldyed aa workmen in connection with production work. Besides, the 
vetitioners had superannuated, The petitioners were thus retrenched offer- 
ing the benefita as per Industria] Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1953. The 
management acted bonn fide in the matter. The Company was not aware of 
uny union activity on the part of the petitioners. There was no victimisation 
or unfair labour practice. It is thus said that the discharge was just and 
proper. In the circumstances, the Company submitted that the petitioners’ 
claim should be dismissed. 


The point which therefore arises for determination is, whether ‘he 
dischurge of the two petitioners is justified. 


DECISION. 


In support of their case, the two petitioners have deposed (P. W. 1 and 
[১ W. 2). The Company opposite party on the other hand has examined 
its Audit Assistants, D. W. 1, Shri Subodh Chandra Neyogi besides proving 
documents, Exts. A to Bl. 


The evidence shows that there was necessity of retrenchment of two out 
of three sales clerks in the Grain Shop at the relevant date. It appears that 
out of two items of controlled commodities, the workmen, who were mostly 
Bengalees, ceased to draw wheat ration and as a result sales declined greatly 
৪0 much ao that there was not even sufficient work for one sales clerk (vide 
8180 P. W. 1). Ext. A is a statement which shows the sales position from 
July 1947 to February 1954. It shows that the sales greatly declined at 
the relevant time. ‘The petitioners do not seriously dispute that there was 
necessity for retrenchment of two sales clerks at the time. All that they 


2008 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 1954 [Parr 1 


contest ix that they were not the last comers and should not have been dis- 
charged, They claim that the rule “last come, first go’? should have been 
determined by taking the whole clerical staff employed in the Mill and not 
on the basis of Grain Shop alone as has been done. I am, however, unable 
to sustain their contention. The two petitioners, Shri Upendra Nath 
(Chatterjee and Shri Sushil Kumar Chanda, it appears from their own evi- 
dence, had previously served in other concerns, P. W. 1 Shri Upendra Nath 
Chatterjee admittedly had worked in a Jute Mill and retired from service 
and has been getting pension from before he was employed in this Company. 
Likewise P. W. 2 Shri Sushi] Kumar Chanda had served under Agartala 
Raj Estate in Tipperah before he was employed in this Company. Thus 
both the petitioners according to their own showing were employed in this 
Company at an advanced age. The evidence further discloses that these two 
petitioners were taken and employed exclusively for the Grain Shop as 
sales clerks. Both the petitioners admitted in their deposition that they 
were employed from the time they were uppointed in this concern till they 
were discharged as sules clerks in the Grain Shop and nowhere else. Thus 
they being appointed and tied down to the Grain Shop as condition of their 
yervice, they cannot claim to be considered as along with other clerks 
employed in the Mill in connection with production. Their claim that they 
were first appointed us clerks and were then posted to the Grain Shop is 
afterthought and unreliable. Likewise their evidence that clerks from the 
Grain Shop were transferred for work in the Mill is afterthought and 
unreliable. The evidence of D. W. 1 shows that none from the Grain Sho 
was transferred for work in the Mill. His evidence reveals that & aye 
from the Accounts Department was sent to the Grain Shop to check the 
accounts and on completion of his work he reverted to his own departinent, 
This being the position and the petitioners being admittedly last comers 
out of the three clerks in the Grain Shop, I think, the rule of “last come, 
first go’? has not been violated. Apart from this they could not also point 
that any clerk employed in the Mill was junior to them. The evidence shows 
that Shri Animesh Chakraborty and Shri Arun Kumar Gupta, who are suid 
to be junior are in fact senior to both the petitioners. As regards allega- 
tion of victimisation the petitioners themselves in their deposiion gave direct 
lie to it. Both of them admitted that they had no union activity to their 
credit and that they were simply ordinary members of the Union, It is thus 
apparent that the Company acted bona fide in the matter of retrenchment 
So, having regard to the evidence and circumstances, I find that the dis- 
charge is hona fide and justified. It, therefore, follows that the petitioners 
ure entitled to no relief except those offered by the Company as already 
referred to. I award accordingly. 


Directed and corrected by me. 


J. MAITRA, JITENDRA NATH MAITRA, 
Judge. Judge, Third Industrial Tribunal.

2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed their written

parties were asked to file their lists of documents by 26th June 1954. The dispute 
was then fixed for trial on 2nd August 1954. 


3. The matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of reference 
are as follows :— 
If the discharge of Shri Panna Lal Ghosh was justified. 


If he is entitled to reinstatement and/or any other relief. 


4. The dispute arises out of termination of employment of Shri Panna Lal 
Ghosh. He was a Plane-man in the Machine Shop for about 44 years on a 
weekly wages of Rs. 23. He was laid up with an attack of typhoid from Ist 
April 1953, He alleged that for his absence on account of illness he had applied

of compromise is made a part of my award.

By Government order No. 695Dis./D/10L-2/54, dated 13th February 1954, 
the aforesaid dispute was referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. is was 
subsequently amended by corrigendum No. 2313Dis./D/10L-2/54, dated the 
4th May 1954. The issues thus amended were adoptcd by the Tribunal and 
they were as follows :— 

(1) What should be the rate of payment for the period of intermittent 
closure in the months of April and May 1953 ? 


(2) Whether the dismissal of Debendra Nath Das, Gopal Chandra Dutta 
and Panchanan Das is justified? To what relief are they entitled ? 


Notice of the reference having been served the Union filed its written state- 
ment on 6th March 1954 and the Company filed its written statement on 9th 
April 1954. 


The case for the Union is that in April and May 1953 the Company closed 
its Printing Department for 22 days, Canister Department for 314 days, and 
so on, that they all along refused to pay anything for the aforesaid forced un- 
employment, that on 13th June 1953 Panchanan Das and others were made to 
leave the factory and on 18th they received three letters from the management 
in which they were told that they had been dismissed for theft. 


The Company, on the other hand, contended that the workers already 
obtained 15 days’ wages and allowances as compensation for involuntary un- 
employment in the first half of the year 1953 in terms of the Award of the First 
Engineering Tribunal confirmed by the award made by the Tribunal on 24th 
February 1953, and that no further dispute can be raised on this point. They 
also contended that the said 3 workmen were caught red-handed during working 
hours for stealing a jack fruit from a house adjacent to the factory premises, the 
owners whereof immediately lodged complaint to the management, that the 
workmen were duly charged with the offence of stealing and were asked to submit 
explanation but they prayed to be excused, but as the offence was serious they 
had been dismissed on 13th June 1953. 


The case was taken up for hearing on 21st June 1954 and on following 
dates. 


AWARD. 


Issue No. 2. 


During discussion the parties agreed to certain terms as regards issue No. 2 
They were as follows: “The Company agreed to take back the workmen. On 
behalf of the Union Shri Panchanan Bhattacharji agreed that workers will rejoin 
if the 3 workers were given Rs. 100 in lump at the time they report to duty 
and the Company agreed to this proposal.” Hence I direct that the workers 
would report by Ist July 1954 and the employers would employ them and pay 
Rs. 100 in lump as compensation to the 3 workers to be divided cqually 
amongst them. 

Issue No. 1. 


It appears from the register of the companies that the workers have been 
actually paid 15 days’ wages and allowances as compensation for involuntary 
unemployment during the first half of the year 1953 in terms of the award of the 
First Engineering Tribunal as confirmed by the Award made by this Tribunal 
on 24th February 1953. The Union contended that the factory was closed 
without giving any previous notice and without payment for involuntary unemploy- 
ment. But the register disproves this fact. It further appears that notices have 
been served on the day previous and copy of the notices had been sent to the 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 54 2015 


পতন‏ 0چ ے 


ساےہ ow‏ ساس TY‏ یھو EL TEES‏ کیج چ۶ لد ےےےوس ACT‏ سے پمیک سے AN‏ مجع পি‏ 
٠ ۶ = =‏ ہی — ہے ebsites ০ম ত্য Tea‏ کے جم se eee‏ ہے کھج এপ তা‏ ہہ 


Labour Commissioner as well as to the Factory Inspector. I have no reason 
to disbelieve the statement of the Manager on this point. The notices that were 
pasted on the notice board, were torn off and have been produced and proved 
before this Tribunal. It was contended by the Union that these notices were 
concocted. But in the circumstances, the statement on oath of the Manager 
must previal against the statement on oath of the workers and I hold that the 
Union has failed to prove that the notices were concocted and that copies thereof 
were not sent to the Labour Commissioner or the Factory Inspector. It was 
next contended that the factory was closed in order to punish the workers who 
went to the Tribunal. But there is no reason to think like that. This could 
have been believed if the Manager had supplied the orders by getting the work 
done through other factories or outside agencies. But the Manager has denied 
this and the Union has failed to contradict him. In the circumstances, the lay 
off for want of orders is justified according to standing order rules and the pay- 
ment made according to Engineering Tribunal Award is proper. The Union, 
however, contended that on some days they were made to sit up to 2 or 3 hours 
and then given work for the rest of the day and were paid for half day on those 
days. ‘The Manager contended that this was done with the consent of the 
workers. But there is nothing to show that the workers gave consent and agreed 
to forego half day’s wages. According to the Major Engineering Tribunal there 
are 2 forms of involuntary unemployment and the other form of involuntary 
unemployment takes place when sometimes the time-rated worker is given only 
2 or 3 hours’ work on a particular day and he is then told that there is no further 
work for the day and he loses several hours’ wages. According to the view 
expressed by the Enginecring Tribunal it is proper that in such a case the workers 
should get full day’s wages and I direct accordingly that the employers should 
give full wages for the days they have paid to the workers half day’s wages during 
the nionths April and May 1953 as covered by this issue. 


S. C. MUKHERII, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (XIV of 1947), as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate 
Tribunal) Act, 1950, filed by a workman named Sorab of Suraj Jute Press, 
represented by Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ Union, 1, Joy Bhattacherjee 
Lane, Calcutta-3, against Suraj Jute Press, 1, Gun Foundry Road, 
Calcutta-2 (Case No. 34/33A/54).

CALCUTTA.

MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial‏ بمہبک5

For the Company : Shri N. K. Mookherjee, Advocate. 


For the Workmen: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee, Secretary, Cossipore Jute

AWARD. 


The original reference out of which the present application under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government, order 
No. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated 8th August 1952, read with addendum 
No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 10th November 1952, and No. 4740- 
Dis/D/7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. 


The petitioner Sorab who has been working in the Suraj Jute Press for 
about 2 years complained that he has not been made a member of the Provident 
Fund nor was he allowed toenjoy the medical facilities. The Company con- 
tends that the petitioner is simply a Badlee previously in the place of his father 
Fazal and at present in the place of a workman named Hadis. He 19 a press- 
man. I find from the evidence of O.P.W. 1 (Shibdas Nandi), that one Hadis, a 
pressman went on leave ہہ‎ the 3rd April 1953, and that from that moment 
petitioner Sorab was appointed as Badlee in his place. The witness also says that 
Hadis has not yet returned on expiry of his leave although his leave expired long 
ago and that Hadis has not applied for any extension of his leave. The witness 
also admits that the petitioner Sorab is a competent pressman. In these circum- 
stances it is highly reasonable that Sorab should be made permanent immediately, 
because he is giving service efficiently and because the workman in whose place 
he is acting-as a Badlee has left the job and has been overstaying although his 
leave expired long long ago, and there has been no prayer for extension of leave. 
But the question is whether this application is entertainable under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act. It has not been shown that according to the Stand- 
ing Order or any Award or any agreement Sorab automatically became per- 
manent on the lapse of some specified time or on the happening of any con- 
tingency. It is the discretion of the management to make him permanent or not. 
It cannot be said that the management has done anything in contravention of 
the provisions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, I therefore rejec- 
the' present application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act but I 
recommend to the management that the petitioner may be made permanent 
immediately as the workman in whose place he has been working for this Jong

tinte should be held to have left service and there is no bar to the petitioner being 
made pefmanent in the place of the said workman Hadis.

The case was fixed for hearing on 26th July 1954. As the parties are ready 
the case is taken off from the list of cases for fixing final hearing dates and is 
taken up on 17th July 1954, for disposal. Case is opened. On behalf of the 
Company the learned Advocate says that the petitioner has been working 
as a Badli in the place of Tarapada who has since died in April 1954, and that if 
petitioner puts in a year’s service after April 1954, ie., (date of death of Tara- 
pada Babu), petitioner would be automatically made permanent. 00 this 
understanding the present application under section 33A is not pressed by the 
petitioner. His case is that he ought to have been made permanent by _ this 
time and if it were so done he would have been automatically entitled to service 
card and to participate in the Provident Fund Scheme and to enjoy annual, 
casual and sick Icave and also to avail himself of the medical facilities accorded 
by the Calcutta Hydraulic Press Association. Obviously there is no contraven- 
tion of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act and therefore the petition 
under section 33A does not lie. But as the employer, Opposite Party, gives 
undertaking as aforesaid and as the petitioner on the basis of the said under- 
standing gives up further proceeding with the present application, the said appli- 
cation is disposed of in terms of the said understanding.

The petitioner Guidhar is a workman under the Jute Press Contractor Ram 
Kumar Bhawalka. He was working there tor 3 years. His case is that on the 
30th April 1953, he received injury while doing duty and consequently he was 
unfit for work up to 3151 August 1953. He demanded compensation for loss of 


earning during the said period but the contractor discharged him on the Ist 
September 1953, 


In the evidence the petitioner admits that he has since been reinstated in his 
job and that he does not remember the date on which he was discharged. The 
contractor’s representative produced the “Wage Register” which shows that the 
petitioner worked on 19 and 2nd September 1953, and remained absent for 3 
(three) days only in September 1953. In these circumstances I find that the 
petitioner could not substantiate his case that he was discharged on the Ist 
September 1953, or that on account of such discharge he could not do any work 
on the Ist or the 2nd September 1953. My conclusion therefore is that the 
হা has not come to the Tribunal with a true case, so his application is 
rejected.

AWARD. 


The original reference out of which the present application under section 
33A of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government order 
No. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated 8th August 1952, read with addendum 
No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 10th November 1952, and 
No. 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. 


Biswanath, Noormahammed and Jagadish have made this application under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act against their employer Shri Ram 
Kumar Bhawalka, Labour Contractor of Calcutta Hydraulic Press, and the allega- 
tion is that they are members of the Union and therefore the employer gave them 
only 70 hours of work since March 1954, whereas some newcomers, viz., Sanchi, 
Chunni, and Jagannath and others were given about 140 hours work a month 
(on reduced rate of wages) which the petitioners describe as “forced unemploy- 
ment on working days”. 


On behalf of the contractor Ram Kumar Bhawalka, his witness Shri Krishnaraj 
Singh states that Sanchi, Chunni and Jagannath are not newcomers and that they 
were previously working in the Central Hydraulic Press under this contractor 
Ram Kumar Bhawalka and when the said press was closed these men have 
joined the Calcutta Hydraulic Press under the self-same contractor. The 
difference in the carnings is due to the fact that these three men are engaged 
as Ghirniwallahs whereas the petitioners work as Tulandars. In Kutcha Press 
there is no fixed rate of wages. It is admitted by petitioner Noor Mahammed 
that when they work in Pucca Press they are paid at fixed rate of wages by this 
contractor. 1 do not think that there has been any alteration of service condition 
or any punishment under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. There is no 
evidence that the wage rate in the Kutcha Press was the same as in Pucca Press 
or that the wage rate of the Kutcha has becn reduced in the case of the petitioner 


Part T] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 1954 2925 


during the pendency of tho original case. The application under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act is therefore not maintainable; it is rejected.

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act 
filed by Shri Jagannath Terai against Messrs. Britannia Enginecring Co. Ltd., 
in connection with an industrial dispute referred under Government order 
No. 2574Dis./D/10L-80/52, dated 16th September 1952 . (Case 
No. 167/52). 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 
PRESENT: 

Suri 9, C. MUKHERIJI, District Judge, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 

For the petitioner: None. 


For the Company: Shri D. Basu Thakur, Solicitor of Messrs. Orr, Dignam 
& Co., Solicitors. 

While the dispute between the Britannia Engineering Company and _ their 
workmen referred to this Tribunal undcr Government order No. 2574Dis./D/ 
10L-80/52, dated 16th September 1952, was pending, the prcsent application 
under section 33A was filed by one Jagannath Terai on the allegation that he 
has been illegally discharged on 16th September 1952 without any  charge- 
sheet and that he should be reinstated with compensation. 


Notice of this application having been served, the Company filed its written 
statement on 2nd December 1952, in which it contended inter alia that the 
present application under section 33A is not maintainable in law, that on 
merits also the petitioner was inefficient in his work and irregular in attendance 
and unreliable for the job, and that he was given opportunities to correct him- 
self but as he was incorrigible he has been finally discharged on 16th of 
November 1952. 

AWARD. 


At the time of trial the petitioner did not turn up. Hence, prima facie, he 
has no dispute and I, therefore, make a “no dispute” award in his case. 


On merits also I have found that the petitioner is a helper to a mali of the 
Bunglow of the Foreman. He was not getting any Provident Fund, leave or 
any other facilities available to the workmen. The Officer, in whose garden 
he was employed, says that these malies are a sort of concession given to the 
Officers and the Officers have full control over their appointment and dis- 
charge and they have no connection with the Mill, as such I hold that 01115 
petitioner is not a workmen, and consequently, the application under section 
33A is not tenable. 


Again on merits also the petitioner was slack and absent from duty without 
leave. He was detected as silceping while he should have been on duty and he 
absented again thereafter without permission. Consequently, he was discharged 
by the Officer. Under these circumstances, it was not necessary 10 Issue 
charge sheet. As the offence was serious the Officer was entitled to take 
action then and there ard he was richt in discharging the petitioner.

~

A 0066 ۰ 
For the company: Shri N, K. Mookherjee, Advocate. 


For the worker; Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee, Secretary, Cossipore Jute 
Press Workers’ Union. 


The original reference out of which the present applications under sec- 
tion 83A of the Industrial Disputes Act have arisen was made under Govern- 
ment order No. 18۰ 1)111744162, dated 8th ap feel 1962) read with 
addendum No. 3062Dis./D/71-44/52, dated 10th November 1952, and 
No, 4740Dis./D/71-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. 


AWARD. 


The application No, 44/33A/52, ia to be summarily rejected ٥ 
from the petition itself it does not appear that any contravention of section 
38 of the Industrial Disputes Act has been committed by the employer. The 
petitioner claims that since July 1953 he and another Tulander “‘are seldom 
given work and that the employer should he directed to give him em ١1 -ج0‎ 
ment at par with other workmen’. He does not say that he has been 
dismissed or that any discrimination is done against him or that he is being 
victimised, It is admitted that the Jute Press where the petitioner works 
has its slack every week or fortnight and on some days all the workers and 
on some days some of the workers have to go back without finding any employ- 
ment due to paucity of work, available in the Jute Preas. The contractor 
has got no contro! over such situation. Admittedly the workers are not 
permanent, they are daily-rated 08808] workers but it can be said this much 
that they are regular although casual. So this application under section 33A 
which 18 numbered 42/33A/54, fails and it is rejected. 


On 4th June 1954, petitioner Nirohu filed another application under 
rection 33A, it is numbered 95. In this application he alleges that on 8th 
April 1954 he has been dismissed for his union activities by the employer, 
Fulchand Singh, Labour Contractor. The contractor Fulchand Singh denies 
that he dismissed the petitioner on 8th April 1964, or on any date. It 
لا‎ from the Attendance Register produced by Opposite Party witness 
that in March 1954, Nirohu worked only for a single day and in April 1954, 
also it was the same case with Nirohu. Opposite Party witness says that 
since 2nd April 1964, Nirohu did not attend the contractor’s premises for 


2986 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 26, 1954 [Parr ॥ 


ہم٤ا‎ 


doing work at all and that the contractor never discharged him. J, do not 
believe that if the evidence of Opposite Party witness No. 1 1s true, Nirohu 
would state in his application under section 33A that he has been dicsharged 
on 8th April 1954 and that on the other hand it was likely that he would steal 
a murch over the cuntractor and allege that since 2nd April 1964, he was 
discharged. This shows that although he was not given any work on the 2nd 
or on the 3rd April 1954, he did not give up attending the contractor's place 
of work for some days and that on the 8th April, he was asked by the con- 
tractor not to attend. Petitioner's evidence that he remained without em- 
ployment anywhere, for about 2 months after this discharge, has not been 
controverted by the opposite party. I find no reason to disbelieve the 
petitioner’s testimony that after suffering unemployment tor 2 months 
since the discharge, he found job as a casual worker in Shiva Jute Press. 
The wages which he gets there are Rs. 3-14 per day, whereas the Opposite 
Party, Fulchand Singh, used to pay him Rs. 4 per day including 8 annas per 
day as sustenance allowance. This discharge of the ভিলা was not on py 
such ground as scarcity of work but it was the result of victimisation on the 
part of the management. It is adinitted that the contractor does not main- 
tain any record showing the attendance of the workmen in case they go 
back without finding any employment on any day. ০21 is maintained 
simply of the work actually done by the workmen, It appears that the 
contractor wants to take advantage of his own omission to maintain record. 
Therefore he cannot now contend (because there is no record) that the peti- 
tioner did not at all attend since 2nd April 1954. In March 1964, also 
ور جا‎ wos not given more than one day’s work. If really petitioner 
1ad the mind to give up work under the contractor Fulchand, he would have 
certainly procured job elsewhere in the month of March 1954, and would not 
have come to Fulchand’s premises on the Ist April 1954, and then come to 
the Tribunal with the story that on the 8th April 1954, he has been dis- 
charged. I believe the evidence of the petitioner to be entirely true and 1 
find that his discharge is without justification. The employer ought to have 
made some effort to equalise the works amongst these regular casual workers. 
It appears that whereas some workers earned Ra. 20 in a moeth, some were 
given only a single day’s work during that month. It is nothing but dis- 
crimination. I therefore suggest that the contractor Fulchand should keep 
a record showing the daily attendance of all such workers irrespective of 
the question whether they find work or not on any particular date. But 
their attandance must be noted down in the register if there is attendance 
at all. It is therefore directed that Nirohu be reinstated and he shall be 
given work if and when such work will be available on fair distribution of 
available work amongst the regular casual workers whose names are there in 
the Attendance Register. 


Some token compensation should be granted in this case in favour of 
the petitioner. I therefore direct that the employer shall pay him Rs. 10 
as compensation for loss of earning during the period of his unemployment 
after discharge. The payment shall be made within a week from the date 


of publication of the Award in the Calcutta Gazette.

IN THE HONOURABLE LABOUR APPELLATE TRIBUNAL OF INDIA, 
CALCUTTA. 


Misc. Case No. C-175/54 (under section 23). 


Shri G. C. Bhattacharjee and 25 others, Calcutta—A pplicant, 
versus 
Messrs. Parry and Co., Ltd., Calcutta—Opposite party. 


PRESENT: 
Mr, R. C. MITTER, Chairman. 
Mr. L. K. JHA, Member. 
Appearances : 
For the applicant: Shri Jiten Banerjee, Secretary of the Union. 
For the opposite party: Shri J. N. Chatterjee, Indian Engineering 
Association. 
State: West Bengal. 
Industry: Miscellaneous. 


True copy of the order No. 3, dated the 18th July 1954. 


On 26th March 1954 the Company made an application before us for per- 
mission to retrench 26 workmen on grounds which we need not reiterate. 
That application came up for hearing on the llth June 1954. At that time 
it was stated by the Company that & of them had voluntarily resigned since 
the date of the application. The Company, therefore, confined its applica- 
tion to the remaining 18 workmen namied in the list which was annexure B 
to the Compuny’s petition. On that date we gave the Company the per-. 
mission to discharge those 18 workmen. Thereafter on the 2186 June 1964, 
the Company served a notice on those 18 workmen which purported to 
terminate their services with effect from the Ist April 1954. Those 18 
workmen have filed a complaint under section 23 before us and this is the 
complaint which we are to consider. 


There were two prayers to that application, namely, (a) for reinstatement 
and (b) for payment to them their wages for the period of their forced non- 
employment. Prayer (a) is misconceived; for the Company has already 
got the permission to discharge them. We however consider prayer (b) to 
be of substance in regard to wages for the period between the Ist of April 
1954 and the 2lst June 1954. 


It has been pointed out in several cases by this Tribunal that section 
22 imposes a ban in the matter of the termination of services of workmen 
and on other matters mentioned in that section. The ban, therefore, conti- 
nues till the permission ia obtained. It has been further pointed out that 
when considering an application for permission to discharge or dismiss a 
workman, the only function of the Tribunal is either to grant or to refuse 
the permission. It cannot, without the consent of the parties, impose any 
condition, much less cannot order the employer to terminate the services of 
the employee from a date fixed by the Tribunal. It is for the employer to 
choose the date from which their services are to be terminated after the ban 
had been removed by the Tribunal by giving the permission. This is what 
has been said in the case of Carlabad Mineral Water Co., Ltd. vs. Their 
workmen, 1953 I. A. C., page 114. 


The Company relies upon a passage in that judgment and contends 
before us that as it is left to the Company to choose the date of the termina- 
tion of the services of the workman concerned after permission had beeg 
given. It ean choose any date and that 0106 mpy be one even anterior to 
the date of the permission. So in this case it was right in terminatin 
their services retrospectively from the Ist of April 1954. We do not think 
that this contention is supported by the judgment delivered in that case. 
The passage relied upon cannot be divorced from the context or the facts 
of that case. There the Company had asked for permission to retrench a 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETLE, AUGUST 26, 1954 


ee eee পাপা পা শী سح جح‎ পিসি 


number of workmen. The lower Tribunal gave permission on the 30th 
August 1951 and in its order stated as follows; ‘The Company will be 
directed to effect retrenchment with effect from the Ist September 1951,” 
that is to say, from a date later to the date of the grant of the permission. 
Dealing with this part of the order this Tribunal held that the Tribunal 
was wrong in directing the Company to discharge the workmen from that 
date and the following observations were made, namely, ‘‘Where permis- 
sion is asked for the discharge of workmen all that the Pribunal is required 
to do is to accord the permission or withhold it. If it accords the permission, 
it has ne right to direct the Company to discharge them from a date fixed 
by it. The permission only removed the bar and it is for the Company 
to decide as from when the discharge 18 to be effected’. 


As long as the ban imposed by section 22 of the Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate Tribunal) Act or the corresponding section—Section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act remains the power of the employer to dismiss or 
discharge his workmen is restricted. The Supreme Court has pointed out 
in clear terms that a dismissal pending adjudication proceedings without 
permission is illegal (See Punjab National Bank, Ltd. versus Its workmen 


" 1964 1 1..A.C., p. 1). In this case before us, on the Ist of April 1954, 


proceedings between the Company and its workmen in which these 18 
workmen were concerned were pending and if the dismissal is allowed to 
be given retrospective effect from that date, it would go against the words 
and spirit of section 22. The interpretation we give to our judgment in the 
Carlsbad Mineral Water Co., Ltd.’s case is that after the ban had been 
removed the employer can choose the date of dismissal prospectively from 
the date of permission and cannot date it retrospectively. 


The 18 persons except Mr. G. C. Bhattacharji are entitled to get 
emoluments at the same rate they were getting immediately before their 
discharge from Ist April to the 20th June 1954 and we direct accordingly. 

The parties are agreed that Shri G. C, Bhattacharji had been working 
elsewhere on casual basis after the Ist April 1954 and that he had earned 
Rs. 48 during the period from Ist April to the 20th June 1954. He is to 
৫ his emoluments from that period at the said rate less Rs. 48 which he 

as earned elsewhere as aforesaid. 

As we have allowed in part the complaint of the workmen the Company 
must pay them costs which we assess at Rs. 50. 


R. C. MITTER, Chairman. 
L. K. JHA, Member.

IN THE HONOURABLE LABOUR APPELLATE TRIBUNAL OF INDIA,

Messrs. India Chemical Industries, Ltd., Calcutta .. Applicant, 
versus 
Shri Tapeswar Ahir .. Opposue party. 
PRESENT :

Mr. L. K. JHA, Member.

For the applicant: 

For the opposite party: 
State : West Bengal.

True copy of the order No. 13, dated 27th July 1954. 


This is an application under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate 
Tribunal) Act, 1950, for permission to dismiss a workman of the name of 
Mr. Tapeswar Ahir. He was a cooly on night duty from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. on 
the Sulphuric Acid Concentration Plant on the 151. April 1953. The charge against 
him is that he was sleeping while on duty on that date and did not notice the 
overflowing of acid Tank. Am application was made before the Industrial 
Tribunal under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for permission 
to dismiss him but that application proved abortive as the award was given and 
published before it could be taken up by the Tribunal. After the filing of the 
appeal before us, this application was made by the Company under section 22 
of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, for permission to 
dismiss him for the same misconduct. A copy of the Certified Standing Orders 
of this Company was placed before us. According to that Standing Order 
ee while on duty is minor misconduct for which the Company is only 
entitled to give a warning to the workman concerned. 


When this fact came to our notice we told the learned Advocate, Mr. S. C, 
Sen, who appeared on behalf of the Company, that we could not grant thé 
permission to dismiss him as asked for and desired to know whether the Company 
would be prepared to amend its application by substituting the prayer for warning 
for the prayer for dismissal. The Learned Advocate took time till this morning 
so as to enable him to take instructions from the Company. Neither he nor any 
representative of the Company has turned up up to now, when we are about 
to rise for the mid-day recess. In view of the Standing Orders, we cannot grant 
the Company permission to dismiss this workman and as the prayer in the original 
application stands unamended, the application must be dismissed with ০০৫ 
which we assess at Rs. 50 to the workman concerned who through his advocate 
appeared both yesterday and today. 


R. C. MITTER, Chairman’.

Procedure regarding submission of books. 


It 1s hereby notified that books fo: Classes VI and VII, and jin one 
volume for Classes VII and VIII or VII to X as the case may be, invited by 
the Board in notifications published in the Calcutta Gazette from time to 
time, tor approval as text-books in different subjects are to be submitted 
within the prescribed dates to the office of the Director of Public Instruc- 
tion, West Bengal (Text-book Committee Section), Block No. ہا‎ Second 
Floor, Writers’ Buildings, Calcutta-1, along with either chalans showing 
deposit of the requisite fees in the Reserve Bank of India or money order 
receipts showing that the requisite fees have been sent to the Board. It 
is desirable that authors and publishers in Calcutta and neighbouring areas 
should deposit the fees yn the Reserve Bank of India under the head of 
account—‘‘Secondary Education Fund” in T.R. Form No. 7. Under the 
head “‘Full particulars of remittance and of authority’ the following should 
be recorded :—‘‘Fee for submission of text-books for approval.’’ Authors 
and publishers living in mofussil may send the fees to the Finance Officer, 
Board of Secondary Education, West Bengal, by money order, stating 
clearly in the coupons the purpose for which they are remitted. No exten- 
sion of the last dates ہے‎ announced will be made.

SUPPLEMENT — Official Papers 
Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 


Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 11th August 1954. 


Summary.— During the eek under report there was rainfall in all subdivisions uf the State. Weather conditions were favour- 
able in twenty-four subdivimaons. Aman transplantation hampered m seven subdivimons. Fodder was reported to be insufficient in 
eighteen subdivisions and cattle disease was reported from two subdivinons. The wages of the labourer varied from annas fourteen 


to rupees two and annas eight during the week.

Forecast of Pepper Crops of West Bengal for 
1953-54. 


Season.—The weather conditions have generally 
been favourable in the districts except 24- 
Parganas. 


Area and yield.—Black pepper.—Black pepper 
is not reported to have been grown in any district. 


Long pepper.—The acreage and 
long pepper tor both this year and 
be tuken as practically ‘‘nil’’. 


Red pepper (chillies).—16,300 acres 
inated to be under red’ pepper this year compared 
to 16,200 acres of 1785৮ year. The total outturn 
of red pepper in terms of dry crop is estimated at 
8,400 tons this year compared to 9,000 tons of last 
year. ‘he average, outturn per acre of dry red 
pepper is estimated at 15-95 mds. this year com- 
pared to 16°17 mds. of last year.

CORPORATION OF CALCUTTA 
NOTIOE. 
Central Municipal و"‎ 0 the 3rd August 


Notice is hereby given for general information 
that the Corporation of Calcutta under powers 
vested in it in this behalf under section 36° read 
with section 356 of the Calcutta Municipal Act, 
1951 (West Bengal Act XX XIII of 1951), has by 
resolution, dated the Jlth June 1954, prescribed 
the alignment of a projected public street (marked 
Y A 13 on the plan) to a width of 14 feet from Y 
to A without affecting the masonry building stand- 
ing on premises No. 10B, Monoharpukur 2nd Taae 
and thereafter following the existing 20 feet width 
of a private street from A to B and again tapering 
down from 20 feet at B to a width of 14 feet at 
40357 so as to establish a connecting link between 
the said private street (marked X Y) and a 13 feet 
arm of Aswini Dutta Road in Ward 62. 


A copy of the plan prepared in this behalf may 
be seen in the office of the Chief Valuer and Sur- 
veyor of the Corporation any day during office hours 
on payment of usual fees.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The proposed legislation seeks to provide means for, the development of 
land in West Bengal by imposing betterment and capital ldvies in 18১০৬ of 
increased profits from and increase in the value of land résulting from the 
execution of development schemes and to provide for certain other matters 
ancillary thereto, 


e existing legislations in this field generally suffer from two principal 
defects :—firstly, they apply in respect of irrigation projecta only and, 
secondly, they are cumbrous in execution. Both these defects are sought 
to be removed by the present legislation by waking it applicable in relation 
to all development schemes and by providing for its comparatively easy 
working for the sake of administrative convenience. The Bill has been 
drafted with these ends in view. 


B. C. ROY, 
Member-in-charge.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


By the Cooch Behar ‘(Assimilation of State Laws) Act, 1960' (West Ben. 
Act LXIII of 1950), all laws, reluting to matters in the State List of the 
Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and which are in force in ۲۷ نا68‎ 
Bengal, have been extended to Cooch Behar to the exclusion of old Cooch 
‘Behar laws except that certain Cooch Behar Acts specified in Schedule I 
to the Act still continue in force with adaptations and the corresponding 
Acts in force in other districts of West Bengal specified in Schedule 1 
thereof do not apply to Cooch Behar. Thus there is still some difference in 
the laws in force in Cooch Behar and those in force in other districts of 
West Bengal. 


For the convenience of administration seventeen chhits of Cooch Behar 
were tra&sferred to the Jalpaiguri district with effect from the 27th June, 
1952. It is possible that some more chhits will be similarly transferred in 
future. The Cooch Behar (Assimilation of State Laws) Act, 1950, defines 
Cooch Babar as ‘‘the merged territory of Cooch Behar in the State of West 
Bengal.’”’ The chhits of Cooch Behar, even when transferred to Jalpaiguri, 
continue to be covered by the definition and a conflict arises in the appli- 
cation of,laws. To avoid this conflict it is necessary to amend the above- 
mentioned Act so as to provide that when a part of Cooch Behar is included 
in anothey district all laws specified in Schedule I of the said Act shall cease 
to be in fotce in that part and all laws specified in Schedule II shal] extend 
thereto. Hence this Bill.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The Caleutta Improvement Act was placed on the Statute Book as early 
as 1911. Under existing vircumstances and in the light of similar legisla- 
tion in other States, its provisions are considered to be restrictive and out- 
of-date. The need to revise the Act on modern Jines igs thus obvious. 


The present Act recognises only two types of improvement, schemes—a 
general improvement scheme (section 35) aud ua street scheme (section 39). 
In other States such as, the Uttur Pradesh, Madras and Delhi, there are 
eight types of improvement schemes. Tn this Bill provision has been made 
for five types of improvement schemes (elause 20). The scope of improve- 
ment achemes has been widened on the lines of analogous statutes in other 
States (clause 20). 


110 order to obvinte the diffeulty of appointing a retired Judicial Service 
Officer to be the President of the Tribunal, section 72 of the Act has been 
suitably amended (cluuse 40). 


The existing Act does not coutain any provision regarding appeals. 
This is because of a judicial decision which held similar provisions in the 
Bombay Improvement Act to be ultra vires. Accordingly, the provisions 
relating to appeals were embodied in an ad hoc Central legislation, 
viz., the Calcutta Improvement (Appeals) Act, 1911 (XVII of 1911). 
Under the advice of the Government of India the provisions of the Appeals 
Act of 1911 are proposed to be incorporated into the State Improvement 
Act (clause 42). 


To save time and unnecessary duplication of procedure, the Bill seeks 
to make sections 4, 5A and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (I of 
1894), inoperative in so far as the acquisition of land ter the Trust is con- 
cerned. This is in consonance with the law in other States سا‎ 76006)]. 
Under section 21505) of the Land 61410782657 Act, 1894, an additional fifteen 
per cent, on the market value of the land acquired is payable in_ consi- 
deration of the compulsory nature of the acquisition. This extra allowance 
is considered to be both iniguitous and burdensome in the case of lands 
acquired by the Trust which is a public body functioning for public benefit. 
Section 28 of the Lund Acquisition Act is therefore preferred to he amended 
by omitting sub-section (2) [elause 7O0(c)]. This is তা) conformity with 
other Acta and also the recommendation of the Local Finance Enquiry 
Committee. 


Section 49(7) ot the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, under which the whole 
of a house must be acquired at the option of the owner, is sought to be 
amended by clause 70Q) of the Bill so as to make the final decision on this 
question rest with the Court. This is intended to save the Calcutta 
Improvement Trust trom uunecessary expenditure of money on costly 
acquisitions, 


Other amendments are either verbal or procedural,

NOTIFICATION. 


No. 2180M.P./2R-5/53.—28th August 1954.—In exercise of the power 
conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution of India, the 
Governor is pleased to make, in supersession of all previous rules issued on 
the subject, the following rules regulating the recruitment and the conditions 
of services of apprentices in the West Bengal Government Press, Alipore, 
Secretary to the Governor's Press, Calcutta, and the West Bengal Government 


Press, Cooch Behar:— 


Rules for recruitment and conditions of service of apprentices in the West 
Bengal Government Press, Alipore, Secretary to the Governor's Press, 
Calcutta, and the West Bengal Government Press, Cooch Behar. 


1. The recruitment of apprentices in the West Bengal Government Press, 
Alipore, Secretary to the Governor’s Press, Caicutta, and the West Bengal 
Government Press, Cooch Behar, shall be made on the results of an cxamina- 
tion conducted by the Public Service Commission, West Bengal. 

2. Each year the examination shall ordinarily be held in the last week of 
July. 
The State Government shall communicate the number of apprentices to be 
recruited in a*year to the Public Service Commission which shall thereafter invite 
applications. 

3. Not later than the 15th June, a notification shall be published in the 
Calcutta Gazette and an advertisement shall be published in the local news- 
papers stating the number of vacancies in the various branches of the Presses 
and inviting applications for permission to appear at the next cxamination. 

4. Candidates must havé passed the School Final Examination of its 
equivalent and must not be less than 16 years and more than 20 years of age 
on the Ist day of July of the year in which the examinajion at which they 
intend to appear is held. With their applications, candidates shall be required 
to furnish certificates of passing the School Final Examination or its equivalent. 
They shall also furnish certificates of responsibility and character, written not 
more than one year prior to their date of application from two respectable 


ersons not related to them. 
Every application shall be accompanied by a Treasury reccipt or a Crossed 
Postal Order fer a sum of Rs. 5 which in no circumstances shall be refunded. 


2954 THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 1954 [Parr I 


বিউটি ০ তি ইত eee tt 


5. The total number of apprentices in the various Presses of the West 
Bengal Government shall be as follows:— 


(a) West Bengal Government Press, Alipore. 


(1) Reading Branch 7 6 
(2) Hand Composing Sectio 5 10 
(3) Linotype Section seg রর 2 
(4) Monotype Keyboard Section 2 
(5) Printing Machine Section 2

(b) Secretary to the Governor's Press. 
(1) Hand Composing Section 7 se 2 
(c) West Bengal Government Press, Cooch Behar. 

(1) Hand Composing Section and s. 2 


6. Candidates shall state in their applications in which branch of the Press 
they desire to be trained. If more than one branch is indicated, the order of 
preference shall be given. An apprentice shall not be transferred after appoint- 
ment from the branch in which he accepts initial appointment to any other 
branch. 


7. The examination shall consist of— 

(1) Test in English and Bengali with special reference to spelling and 
punctuation ; 

(2) Reading of English and Bengali manuscripts; 

(3) A paper on General Knowledge shall be set for all categories of 
candidates. Selected candidates shall be required to undergo a 
viva voce test at which their general suitability as well as their 
828 for reading English and Bengali manuscripts will be 
tested. 


8. The scale of pay for various classes of apprentices shall be 
Rs.50—2-—54. Apprentices shall be entitled to the usual dearness allowance 
sand other allowances admissible to the whole-time temporary Government 
servants. 


9. Prior to joining, a selected candidate shall be required to furnish a 
security deposit of Rs.100 in cash, to be forfeited by Government in_ the 
event Of his desertion or discharge as specified in clause 11 before completion 
of training. The security deposit shall, however, be refunded on completion 
of training period. 

10. Apprentices shall attend the Press for the full normal working hours 
fixed for the Press and shall in all respects be subject to the disciplinary rules 
in force in the Press. 


11. The period of apprenticeship training shall be three years. Any 
apprentice who is irregular in attendance, whose conduct is not satisfactory, 
or who does not show sufficient aptitude for the work, may be discharged at 
any time during the period of apprenticeship by the Superintendent, whose 
decision shal! be final. In the event of such discharge, security deposit as 
specified in clause 9 shall be forfeited. The discharge of an apprentice under 
these rules does not amount to a removal or dismissal within the meaning of 
the Bengal Subordinate Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1936. 


12. Apprentices at no time shall have a claim, as a matter of right, to 
any appointment under Government. 


13. Apprentices shall be required to undergo a test once a year during 
the course of their apprenticeship so that their progress can be ascertained. 
Final test shall be held by a Board of Examiners comprising inter alia 
representatives of Ben Association of Master Printers and Calcutta Printing 
Press-owners’ Association. Apprentices may have to undergo proper courses 
of instructions at a recognised printing institution at the discretion of the 
Superintendent. 


14. Certificates of Proficiency shall be awarded to all apprentices on 
successful completion of training on the result of final test. An apprentice 
may, if vacancies exist in the department in which he served the apprenticeship 
and if he has passed the test*and has good records of attendance and conduct, 
be absorbed in the temporary or permanent establishment of the Press. If no 
vacancy exists in the te ry, 01 permanent establishment on the termination 
of the period of apprenticeship, the apprentice will be discharged. In regard 
to the apprentices who have satisfactorily completed the full course of training, 
but cannot be absorbed immediately on completion of training, preference 
shall be given to them over outside candidates while filling up future vacancies 
occurring within the next twelve months. 


_ 15. Apprentices shall be given leave in accordance with the rules govern- 
ing the grant of leave to temporary Government servants. 


16. A selected candidate shall produce a certificate of physical fitness from 
a Presidency Surgeon or Civil Surgeon. 


By order of the Governor, 
N. DAS, Secy.

AWARD. 
Issue No. 1. 


_ The factory has been closed with effect trom Sth of December 1943 
without assigning any reason therefor. In the absence of any such reason 
none can suggest that the closure was justified. The closure was effected 
حا‎ Joint Receivers who purported to act under the order of the Ion’ble 

igh Court which was to the effect: ‘Joint Receivers will he at liberty to 
sun the factory if they think fit and proper. Joint Receivers will be at 
liberty to borrow further money at such rate of interest, etc., ete.’? Under 
this order Joint Receivers are entitled to run the factory us well as not’ to 
run the factory. Since the order was made by consent of the parties, the 
consequences arising ax a result of the action or inaction on the part of 
the Joint Receivers will at the first instanee be viaited on the Company. It 
is very peculiar that the workers have neither been dischniged nor laid 
off. Under the circumstances, ] hold that the Management ot Messrs Polar 
Electrical Engineering Company, Ltd.. was not justified in closing down the 
factory on the 5th of December 1953 and in keeping it closed, Joint 
Receivers purported tu act under the orders of the Hon’ble High Court. 
This remark cannot be applied to them. 7

in the original reference case. | find that in the abovementioned 
Annexure ‘3’ there is no mention regarding wages ۱ن‎ lieu of notige. It 
is now the settled law that an employee who is not given proper and 
valid notice terminating his services is entitled to get wages and dearness 
allowance for the notice period, i.e., one month. The Company admits 
that Bijoy is entitled to get his wages and allowance for the leave period 
due to him. It is admitted that Bijoy Gopal (Chakrabarty has already 
received his Provident Fund from the Company after the retrenchment. 
Provident lund was introduced, as I am told, in 1949. It is not proper 
tu pive uny ad-interim award directing the employer to make any 
payment of money or compensation to the employee before the hearing 
of the case in cases where such clann for money ia hotly contested by the 
employer. The Tribunal may grant ad-interim award if any such claim 
is supported by the settled law and if the facta giving rise to such 
cluim. are adnutted. So on this principle 1 conclude that the petitioner 
Bijoy Gopal Chakrabarty cannot be given any = ad-interim award for 
gratuity plus retrenchment relief both together at the same time, 
particularly in view of the fact that Bijoy Gopal was 67 years old ut the 
time of termination of his service and he had very little span of service 
life in anticipation at that time. As regards the period of gratuity the 
fact is admitted that in 1947 Provident Fund was introduced. The 
Company is willing to pay gratuity at the rate of 15 days’ wages 
including dearness allowance for each year of service under the Rupee 
Company fo the period prior to the introduction of Provident Fund. 
So 1 think that the petitioner may be giveu the following reliefs by the- 
ad-interim award, viz.— 


(1) One month’s wages and dearnesa allowances on account of notice 
period, 


(2) wagea and allowances due for the entire leave period due to 
Bijoy Gopal, and 

(3) gratuity for the period from the formation of Rupee Company 
up to the introduction of Provident Fund at the rate of 15 days’ 
wages and allowances, per year of service. 


It is admitted that Bijoy Gopal Chakrabarty has already withdrawn 
his Provident Fund which was due to him. Hence it is directed that the 
employer Mesars. T. E. Thomson & Co., Litd., shall pay the above items 
of money to the employee Shri Bijoy Gopal Chakrabarty as interim relief 
within 15 days’ from this date and if not paid the award shall be enforce- 


uble according to law.

2. After usual notices the pe entered appearance and filed their
