3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is us follows :— . 


Whether Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik is entitled to get Rs. 1,500 
in lump as gratuity money which the Management previously 
agreed to pay in writing but later on refused ? 


2986 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 1954 [Part ] 


DECISION. 


In support of his case the workman, Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik 
has deposed (P. W. 1) besides proving documents Exts. 1 und 2. The 
Company on the other hand has not adduced any evidence. 


Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik was a clerk in the Cash Departinent of 
this Company. He had joined service on 4 monthly salary of Ks. 65. At 
the time of termination of his employment he was drawing a basic salary of 
Rs, 130 and deurness alluwance of Rs. 108-4, in all Rs. 233-4 per month. 


In December 1952 the Company wanted Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik 
to retire from service on the ground of superannuation on a pension of 
Rs. 90 per month during his lifetime, besides his provident fund money 
including the Company’s share of contribution. On such proposal there 
was a discussion between the workman, Shri VPratulla Chandra Pramanik 
and the Managing Director of the Company. As ao result of the discussion, 
the Managing Director wrote to Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik on 30th 
December 1952, Ext. .ا‎ By Ext. 1 the Company intimated that i was 
agreeable to pay a lump sum of Ks. 1,600 as gratuity in heu of pensivn as 
requested by the workman, besides the provident fund money and salary up 
to the end of January 1953, if the workman retired from servire ot the 
Company by 9181 January 1953. The workman, the evidence shows, accord- 
ingly retired from service. The evidence further reveals that the Company 
did not, however, pay according to their letter, Ext. 1. Thereupon the 
workman submitted an application to the Labour Commissioner to intervene 
in the matter. The matter was accordingly tuken up for conciliation and 
at the instance of the Conciliation Officer the Company again agreed to 
pay the gratuity of Rs. 1,500 in 1160 of pension besides the full amount 
standing at the credit of the workman in the provident tund account in- 
cluding the Company’s shure of contribution. The Company accordingly 
wrote another letter, dated 3rd February 1953 (Ext. 2), to that effect to 
the workman. In accordance with the letter the Company paid the work- 
man the provident fund dues. It, however, failed to pay the gratuity of 
Rs. 1,500 as agreed upon. The workman again moved the Tabour 
Directorate. In course of the conciliation proceedings the Company stated 
that it withheld payment as since the agreement it came to its notice that 
the workman, Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik had divulged certain secret 
informations to.the Company’s ex-London Principals. The Workman 
denied having done so. The matter could not be settled and hence it was 
referred to for adjudication. 


The Company reiterates the same ground for withholding the payment‏ ے 
of gratuity to the workman but has uddueed no evidence to substantiate the‏ 
charge. The workman on the contrary denied on oath befure this Tribunal‏ 
that he had divulged any secret information to the Company’s ex-London‏ 
Principals. I have bad nothing to discard his evidence. The letter which‏ 
the Company wrote to the werkman (Ext. 1) makes mention of the workman‏ 
having put in loyal and good service. So the charge being without foun;‏ 
dation, the Company cannot go back upon its own promise, more so after‏ 
having induced the workman to retire from service. JT am, therefore, of‏ 
ppinion that the workman Shri Prafulla Chandra Pramanik is entitled to‏ 
get Rs, 1,500 in lump 4s gratuity money from the Company as agreed upon.‏ 
The Company is directed to make payment to the workman ag soon as the‏ 
award becomes enforceable.‏

industrial dispute, if has been held in the case of Swadeshi Cotton Mulls 
Co., Jid., Kanpur, versus Shri Ram Baran, reported in 1953 1..A.C., page 
139, that a dispute raised by a workman individually comes within the

SCHEDULE. 


(1) What should be the quantum of bonus for 1952? 
(2) Annual increment. 


Notices were issued on both parties, who filed written statements setting forth 
their respective cases. 


The Union, in its written statement, states as follows :— 


Messrs. Walford Transport, Ltd., is a public limited company engaged in 
automobile industry. Its main business are distributorship of some important 
and popular cars, trucks, etc., whose franchises are held by them, sale of some 
cars, trucks and allied motor parts, repairs of cars and trucks, Government con- 
tracts and manufacture of trailer and pindle hooks, etc. The Company had its 
head office, workshop and several petrol stations in Calcutta and 1885 got a 
branch at Gauhati. The Company has been earning good profits year to year. 
It has accumulated huge profits and paid dividends to the share-holders. This 
Company and their workmen were parties to the first and second Engineering 
Tribunal proceedings, and there was a third proceeding between this Company 
and its workmen before Shri S. N. Modak, I.C.S. (Retd.), regarding some issues. 
The Company has issued bonus shares to its share-holders. The repairing work- 
shop is very paying and is making huge profits every year. The Company has 
stopped annual increments from January 1953, without any reason. During the 
pujas, the employees used to get regular customary bonus as puja bonus of not 
less than a month’s wages. Such bonus they were getting at the same rate for 
a considerable number of years, irrespective of any profit or loss to the Com- 
pany. Suddenly in the year 1953, the Company offered 15 days’ wages as 
puja bonus to the workmen, who refused to accept the puja bonus as offered. 
The Union, therefore, prays for customary bonus and puja bonus for 1952, 
payable in 1953, to the extent of one-fourth of the total carnings of the workmen 
in the year, and a profit bonus at three months’ salary to these workmen who 
have completed a year’s service, and to others with less period of service at pro 
ruta basis. The Union also claims that automatic increments for 1953 be paid 
to all workers according to their grades. No one should be victimised 11) the 
grade increments by stoppage of increments for late attendance. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows :— 


The main activity of the Company is the purchase and sale of new auto- 
mobiles, which activity includes certain obligations imposed by the manu- 
facturers, such as facilities for repair, service and distribution of spare parts. 
This Company and their workmen were parties to the two omnibus Engineering 
Tribunal proceedings, whose awards were published in 1948 and 1950, respective- 
ly. These terms of employment were again scrutinised and confirmed by the 
decision of a fresh Industrial Tribunal set up by the Government of West 
Bengal, by Order No. 57Dis.-10L-65-61, dated 14th September 1951, and the 
award on this dispute was given by the Tribunal on 28th November 1951. 
Between 1947 and 1951, the employees had the benefit of three awards, and the 
terms now in force are those which have been laid down or confirmed in these 
three awards. Retrenchment was found necessary by the Company on financial 
grounds consistent with the volume of business_available, profit potentialities and 
consistent ability to spend money. Retrenchment of employees were made in 
1950, 1951, 1952 and 1953. During the War years, substantial additions were 
made to the Company’s strength of personnel, as there was additional work to 
do. With the end of the War, a large number of employees became surplus. 
These men were retained in service as long as it was possible to do so, in spite of 
the fact that the volume of business was progressively dropping. Instead of 
disposing of surplus staff all at once, the reductions were effected by stages to 


Part I] THE CAICUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 1954 2989 
৯ 


cause the minimum hardship. Reduction in expenses were effected not only by 
reducing staff, but also reducing other expenses in the establishment. The 
Company was floated in 1920, with a paid up capital of Rs. 20,00,000 and odd. 
During the early stages, it was engaged in transport business in Calcutta city. 
It had to face wave after wave of adverse business conditions, which resulted 
in abnormal losses which accounted for about 50 per cent. of the capital by 
1925. A financial crisis followed, to overcome which fully paid up shares of 
Rs. 10 each were written down to Rs. 2-8 each. Severe losses were again incurred 
in 1931 and 1932, and in July 1939, the paid up share value was again written 
down to Rs. 2 per share. The Company’s main source of income is derived. from 
the sale of new automobiles. ‘The workshops have always been a liability. The 
Company holds two main selling franchises, viz :— 


(a) General Motors India, Ltd., for Chevrolet cars, Chevrolet trucks and 
Buick cars. 


(b) Automobile Products of India, Ltd., for Hillman Minx, Humber and | 
Sunbeam-Talbot cars and Commer and Karrier trucks. 


The gross profit ratio is progressively declining. The Company has three main 
Departments—Workshops, Stores and Sales Departments. e workshop which 
employs the maximum number of men produce the minimum volume of business, 
while the Sales and Stores Departments employing lesser number of men_ brin 
the maximum volume of business. The present paid up capital is Rs. 10,00,00 
and odd. This is inadequate for the purpose of carrying on the Company’s 
normal business activities in spite of the fact that reserves built up from profits 
are also utilised. There is thus a shortage of liquid fund in the business, which 
accounts for substantial bank borrowings. 

The Company does not admit that annual increments are automatic. It was 
always understood that increments were at the discretion of the Management and 
depended upon the financial position of the Company. In 1951, the average 
number of employees was 387, of which 86 per cent. received increments and 
14 per cent. did not get it. In 1952, the average number of employees was 
344, of which 78 per cent. received increments, while the balance did not. In 
1953, there was no increments, as the earning capacity of the Company and the 
potential outlook did not warant it. The First Engineering Tribunal award laid 
down that bonus should be paid if there are comparable profits. There is no 
case for increasing bonus or the granting of automatic annual increments for 
the year 1953. The claim of the Union should, therefore, be dismissed with 
costs.

Issue No. 1. 


The Union in its written statement claim customary bonus as puja bonus of 
1952, payable in 1953, to the extent of one-fourth of the total annual carnings of

each workman and also profit bonus for 1952, at the rate of three monthe’ basic 
wages. In the written statement, it has been stated by the Union that the 
employees used to get regular customary bonus as puja bonus of not less than 
a month’s salary, irrespective of any profit or loss and suddenly in the year 1953, 
the Company offered 15 days’ wages as Puja bonus to the workmen, which offer 
was not accepted. At the time of the hearing, no claim for customary bonus 
was pressed and there is no evidence to conclude that there was the system of 
payment of a bonus of at least one month’s basic wages resting on an agreement 
between the employers and the workmen. No evidence has been adduced to 
show that an implied agreement was indicated by an unbroken practice for 
along period of payment of bonus at the time of the pujas, as claim- 
ed by the Union. The claim of customa bonus, therefore, appears 
to be of no substance. 1٢ will only be considered as to whether the employees 
are entitled to any bonus on the general principle that labour and capital should 
share the surplus left after meeting necessary and prior charges. 6 principle 
of ascertaining the quantum of bonus for the workmen out of the surplus profits 
has been enunciated in the Full Bench case of the Millowners’ Association, 
Bombay, reported in 1952 L. A. C., 433. At page 4 of the written statement 
of the Company, it appears that bonus was given by the Company to its work- 
men to the extent of one month’s basic wages out of the trading profits of the 
year 1943, 1944, 1945, 1946, 1949, 1950 and 1951, and bonus to the extent 
of two months’ basic wages was allowed out of the trading profits of 1947 and 
1948. In 1947, an additional bonus of half a month’s basic wages was given as 
Independence Day bonus. This statement also shows that out of the trading 
profits of the year 1952, the Company has made _proxi- 
sions for payment of Rs. 16,851 as bonus, being an amount 
equal to half a month’s basic pay. It, therefore, appears that 
the Company has already made provisions for payment of 15 days’ basic ay 
as bonus in 1953 out of the trading peed of the year 1952. ٥ 
workmen did not accept this payment and have made a claim before me for 
three months’ basic salary as profit bonus for 1952, in addition to the customary 
bonus, which has been dealt with above. P.W. 1. Shri Rakhal Chandra Sarkar,

with the balance-sheet, Ext. 1, for the year ended 31st December 1952, for the 
purpose of ascertaining the available surplus from which the claim of the bonus 
may be made. On a scrutiny of the balance-sheet, it appears that the available 
surplus formula is to be deduced in the following manner from the following 
data :-—

The Company, in its accounts for calculation of available surplus claimed the

Issue No. 2. 


This issue relates to the claim of annual increments of basic salary of the 
employees. The Union states in its written statement that annual increments of 
basic salary was a regular feature of this Company as a condition of service for 
the workmen, but the Company suddenly stopped annual increments from Janu- 
ary 1953, without any reason. It is also stated that employees are punished for 
late attendance by deducting salary or by stoppage of annual increments. The 
Union claimed the annual increments from 1953 to all workmen as per their 
respective grades in existence retrospectively from January 1953. * A further 
prayer was made that no one should be victimised by stoppage of the annual 
increments for late attendance. The Company in its written statement states 
that annual increments are not automatic, and it was always understood that 
increments were at the discretion of the Management and depended on the 
financial condition of the Company. The average number of employees in 1951 
was 387, of which 86 per cent. received increments and 14 per cent. did not 
get them. In 1952, the average number of employees was 344, of which 78 per 
cent. received increments, while the balance of 22 per cent. did not get any 
increments. It is further stated that in 1953, there was no increment, as_ the 
earning capacity of the Company plus the potential outlook did not warrant it 
and that in view of the reduction in gross profits, the claim of annual incre- 
ment in the basic salaries of the employees should not be allowed. 


It is the common case of both the parties that the Company and its workmen 
were parties to the proceedings of the two Major Engineering Tribunals of 
which awards were made in July 1948, and September 1950. In the first award 
of the Major Engineering Tribunal made in July 1948, grade scales of salaries 
were fixed for the clerical and the subordinate staff. The Company in its 
written statement admits that increments in the basic wages were granted in 1951 
and 1952. The evidence of P.W. 1 Shri Rakhal Chandra Sarkar shows that 
since 1947, the workers get increments in salaries according to their grade scales 
and that an unskilled worker got an increment of 1 anna per day and a skilled 


2992 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 1954 [Parr I 


and semi-skilled worker got an increment of 2 annas per day within their gyades. 
The witness also states that in 1951 and 1952, some workers were denied annual 
increments as a punishment for iate attendance. It is, therefore, abundantly 
clear that annual increments are being given as a condition of service and this 
has been denied in 1951 and 1952 by way of punishment for late attendance. 
The Company should, therefore, grant annual increments also in 1953. The 
learned spokesman for the Company stated that it was not possible for the 
Company to grant any annual increments in 1953, due to the unsatisfactory 
financial condition at the end of 1952. The balance-sheet, Ext. A(1) does not 
show such a financial condition as to permit the Company to stop the annual 
increment which was already a condition of service for the workmen. It was 
stated before me that the normal rate of increments would amount to Rs. 18,902 
in the year, whereas the result of the trading in 1953 shows a net profit of only 
Rs. 10,017 and odd. It a ery that the financial condition of the Company 
has deteriorated at the end of 1953, but there was no justification for the Com- 
pany to refuse the annual increment in the beginning of 1953. Following the 
principles enunciated by the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in the 
cases of Ganesh Flour Mills (1952 L.A.C., 172) and of Kanpur Omnibus 
Service, Ltd. [1953(1)L.L.J., 47], it is awarded that the Company shall pay 
annual increment which was due to the workmen in the beginning of 1953, with 
effect from the beginning of 1954 in the circumstances of the case. I do not 
order the retrospective operation for this part of the award, in view of the fact 
that if such an order was made, the Company would be put to embarassment. 
The increments due in the beginning of 1953 should be given with effect from 
the beginning of 1954. No further increments should be paid in 1954. This 
issue is accordingly answered. 


M. C. BANERJEE, 
Judge, First Industrial Tribunal. 
The 13th August 1954. 


By order of the Governor, 
D. 9. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy. 


ORDER. 


No. 4087Dis./D/15L-11/53.—25th August 1954.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 2046Dis./D/15L- 
9/52, dated the 31st July 1952, the industrial dispute between Messrs. Lalji 
Raja & Sons, Oil Mill Owners, Bankura and the workers employed 17 their 
three oi] mills represented by Shri Basanta Kumar Chakravarty, Shri Amulya 
Das, Shri Golak Bihari Singh, Shri Rampada Gorai, Shri Guiram Karmakar, 
Shri Ram Chandra Upadhaya and Shri Amulya Gorai, C/o. Messrs. Lalji Raja 
& Sons, Bankura, regarding the matters specified in the schedule to the said 
order was referred for adjudication to the Fourth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal, 
a complaint was filed before it against the said Company by Basanta Kumar 
Chakraborty and Tulsi Dasi, two workmen of the said Company alleging that 
the said Company had discharged the said two workmen concerned in such 
dispute; 

And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33۸ of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudi- 
cated upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State"Government: 


Parr I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 2, 4 2993 


Now,, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
trial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section 33A ef the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, filed by workmen Basanta Kumar Chakravarty and Tulsi Dasi in 
connection with the industrial dispute between Lalji Raja & Sons, owners 
of 3 Oil Mills in Bankura and their workmen referred under Government 
order No. 2046Dis./D/15L-9/52, dated 31st July 1952 (Case No. 80/53). 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT: 
SHRI 5. C. MUKHERIJI, District Judge, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 


For the Union: Shri Basanta Kumar Chakravarty. 
For the Company: Shri Mohan Lal Kumarji, Partner. 


While the aforesaid dispute referred by Government order No. 2046Dis./ 
D/15L-9/52, dated 31st July 1952, was pending the present application under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act was filed by Basanta Kumar Chakra- 
varty and Tulsi Dasi on 21st February 1953 alleging that they were permanent 
workmen of the above Mill, that the Company is refusing to give work to them 
without any justification, that they are accordingly entitled to compensation and 
reinstatement. 


Notice of the aforesaid dispute having been served the Company filed a 
written statement on 24th March 1953 denying the allegations made by the 
workers and asserting that Basanta Kumar Chakravarty has been laid off from 
3rd February 1953 and Tulsi Dasi was laid off from 17th January 1953, and 
that she has been working in the Sree Gouranga Oil Mill from 21st* February 
1953. 


AWARD. 


At the time of trial, however, the complainants withdrew their case. The 
petition of withdrawal, however, contains only the signature of Basanta Kumar 
Chakravarty. As Tulsi Dasi and Basanta Kumar Chakravarty made a joint 
application, and Basanta was looking after the case for them this application 
for withdrawal is, in my opinion, binding on both Tulsi Dasi and Basanta Kumar 
Chakravarty. Further with regard to Tulsi Dasi, O.P.W. 1 has proved that 
Tulsi Dasi has no dispute. She was laid off and she has been working in 
another Mill from 21st February 1953. I accordingly make a “no dispute” 
award both with regard to Basanta Kumar Chakravarty and Tulsi Dasi. 


৩. C. MUKHERII, 
Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 
The 13th August, 1954. 


By order of the Governor, 
D. S. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

PART IIl—Advertisements, Notices 


Procedure regarding sending Manuscripts for publicztion of Advertisements, Notices, etc., in 
the ‘Calcutta Cazette’’ (Part 11). 


1. Manuscripts should be properly edited and complete in itself. 


2. Manuscripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. The name of the signatory should be type- 
written below the signature. 


3. Manuscripts Intended for advertisement in the next issue of ‘‘Caloutta Gazette’’ shall be received by Publication 
Sales Office at New Secretariat Bulidings, 1, Hastings Street, Calcutta, up to 11 a.m. on Saturdayand at Head Office 
at Allpore up to 12 noon on Monday. 

All costs shall be pald In advanoe and deposited along with the Manuscripts.‏ ھ 


5. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressed to SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING 
PUBLICATION BRANCH), WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE. 


The Press shall not be held responsible for dolay In publication of any advertisement due to the non-observance of the

For the purpose of the concessions referred to above 
the definition of ‘‘Displaced person’’ will be as follows:— 


Definition. 


‘Displaced person’’ means a person ordinarily resident 
in the territories now comprising Pakistan, who 
has arrived from the said territory after the end 
of December 1950 in the Indian Union on account 
of civil disturbances or fear of such disturbances 
or the partition of India and intends to take up 
his permanent residence in the Union of India.’’ 


Note.—(i) ‘‘A displaced person claiming age concession 
must furnish with his application satisfactory evidence that 
he is 5 bona fide displaced person and came out to India 
after the end of Decomber 1950, e.g., refugee registration 
card or a certificate from a শসা officer or a Member 
of Parliament or State Legislature, in original.

Tribe claiming age concessions must furnish with 1018 
application a certificate in original from a gazetted officer 
or a Member of Parliamont or State Legislature belonging 
to the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, specifying the 
particular caste or tribe to which he claims to belong. 


(iii) A displaced person seeking remission of the applica- 
tion fee must furnish besides the evidence required under 
Note (i) above, a certificate (in original) from a district 
officer or a gazetted officer or a Member of Parliament or 
State Legislature to show that he is not in a position to 
pay the prescribed fee.’’

SUMMARY OF THE MINUTES OF THE PROCEEDINGS 
OF THE COMMISSIONERS’ 2459TH MEETING 
HELD ON THE 2ND AUGUST 1954. 


AT the 2459th Meeting of the Commissioners, held or 
the 2nd August 1954, the following business was 
transacted :— : 


1. Tender for the construction and supply of a 200-01 
crane—Five Year Pian.—The Commissioners sanctioned, 
subject to the sanction of Government, an order being 
placed with Messrs. C. H. Jucho, West Germany, for thc 
construction, supply and erection of a 200-ton crane at a 
cost of Rs. 15,23,687 exclusive of customs duty and inci- 
dental expenses, and for the supply of certain spares valued 
at Rs. 70,000 approximately, as recommonded by the 
Ohairman. 


2. Arrangement for leasing the Commissioners’ land and 
covered accommodation pending the finalisation of the new 
schedule of rent oharges.—The Commissioners approved the 
adoption, as an interim measure, of certain proposals 
recommended by the Chairman in connection with leasing 
out the Commissioners’ land and covered accommodation 
pending the finalisation of the new schedule of rent 
charges. 


3. Grant of compensatory allowance during leave pre- 
paratory to retirement and during the period of leave In 
exoess of four months.—The Commissioners decided, subject 
to the sanction of Government, to fall in line with Gov- 
ernment in the matter of payment of compensatory allow- 
ance during leave preparatory to retirement and during the 
period of leave in excess of four months to all new entrants 
appointed on or after the lst August 1954. 


4. Appointment of Labour Representatives.—It was 
decided to appoint Shri A. C. Banerjee and Shri Kali 
Mukherjeo, M.L.A., Labour Representatives as members of 
the Finance, Establishment and Traffic and tho Works and 
Marine Committees respectively. 


The Commissioners also sanctioned routine establishment 
proposals and routine proposals relating to exccution of 
works, purchase of matorial, remission of charges, grant 
of leases, etc. 


P. C, MITTER, 
Secretary.

OFFICE OF THE COMMISSIONER OF POLICE, 
CALCUTTA. 


ORDER. 


Whereas there is apprehension of the occurrence 
of rioting, affrays a other disturbances of the 
public trunquillity within the area in the schedule 
hereto (hereinafter referred to as the said area); 


And whereas, I, li. S. Ghose Chaudhuri, Com- 
wiissioner of Police, Calcutta, being a Presidency 
Magistrate, have been specially empowered by the 
State Government under notification No. 2010G.A., 
dated the Sth July 1954, to act under section 144 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V 
of 1898) ; 


And whereas, in my opinion, there is sufficient 
eround for proceeding under the said section for 
€.e immediate prevention of disturbances of the 
public tranquillity and of riots and affrays within 
the said area; 


Now therefore, in exercise of the power con- 
ferred by sub-section (i) of section 144 of the Code 
of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (Act V of 1898), read 
with sub-section (3) of the said section, I, the said 
H. S. Gthose Chaudhuri, Comniissioner of Police, 
Caleutta, do hereby prohibit from the 4th Septem- 
ber 1954 until further orders, any assembly of five 
or more persons within the said area, or the carrying 
of any lathis or other dangerous weapons or the 
domg of any act which is likely to cause a dis- 
turbance of the public ডে or a riot or 
an affray within the said area.

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


LABOUR DEPARTMENT. 


ORDER. 


No. ا کش‎ | 71-37 /54.—8lst August 1954.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Tabour Department, order No. 4740Dis. el 
7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953, read with its addendum 
No. 47Dis. /D/7L-32/53, dated the 7th January 1954, the industrial disputes 
between the Jute Presses mentioned in the list attached with the said order, 
dated the 12th December 1953 and their respective contractors and their 
workmen represented by Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ Union, 1, Joy 
Bhattacharya Lane, Calcutta-8 and Laksmi Jute Press Workers’ Union, 
29/10, Cossipore Road, Calcutta-2, regarding the matters specified in the 
schedule to the said order, dated the 12th December 1953, were referred for 
adjudication to the Sixth Industrial Tribunul; 


And whereas during the pendency of proceedings before the said Tribunal 
a complaint in writing was received from Shri Thakur Singh and three 
others, workmen under Shri Ram Kumar Bhaualka, Labour Contractor of 
Messrs. Caleutta Hydraulic Fress, 8, Clive Row, Calcutta, one of the said 
Jute Presses against the said Shri Ram Kumar Bhavalka, before the said 
Tribunal alleging that the said Contractor had altered, to the prejudice of 
the said four workmen, the conditions of service applicable to them imme- 
diately before the commencement of the said proceedings; 


And whereas in exercise of the powers conferred by section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the said Tribunal has adjudi- 
cated upon the said complaint and submitted its award to the State Govern- 
ment; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the Indus- 
(7181 Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby 1 
publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto;

1274 THE CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 7. 1954 | Parr I 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an application under section ھ33‎ of the Industrial Disputes 
Act filed by Thakur Singh and three other workers employed by Shri 
Ram Kumar Bhaualka, Labour Contractor of Calcutta Hydraulic Press, 
represented by 00981109018 Jute Workers’ Union, 1, Joy Bhattacherjee 
Lane, Calcutta-3, against the aforesaid employer, 8, Clive Row, 
Calcutta-1 (Case No. 114/33A/53). 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. 


| PRESENT; 
Suri MOTILAL CHAKRAVATT', District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 


Tribunal, 
Appearances.’ 
For the employer: Shri Krishnaraj Singh. 


For the workmen: Shri Panchanun Bhattacherjee, Secretary, Cossipore 
Jute Press Workers’ Union. 


The original reference out of which the present application under section 
383A of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government 
order Nos. 218UDis. He 7L-44 /52, dated 8th August 1952, read with adden- 
dum No. 3062Dis. /D/11.-44/52, dated 10th November 1952 and subsequent 
order No. 4740Dis. /D/71-32/53, dated 12th December 1953. 


AWARD. 


. The petitioners Thakur Singh and three others allege that since August 
1952, the petitioners are being paid reduced wages on the plea that they were 
working in the Autcha Press and not in the acca Press in which case they 
are to receive fixed rates of wages per day and also sustenance allowance as 
settled by an agreement arrived at, at the intervention of Hon’ble Dr. B. C. 
Roy. The petitioners therefore pray that the employer may be directed to 
pay the rates as confirmed in the First Tribunal Award ond also the susten- 
ance allowance for the period in question. The petitioners are the employees, 
of the Jute Press contractor Ram Kumar Bhuwalka. The said employer 
submitted his written statement and it is stated there that these petitioners 
work on daily rate basis and that they are getting their daily wages in full 
and there have been no reduction of any nature since August 1952 on the 

lea of installation of Kutcha Presses. At the hearing, however, Nam 

umar Bhuwalka did not appear. One Shri Krishnaraj Singh, who is a 
sub-contractor under the Contractor Ram Kumar [$buwalka appeared on 
behalf of Bhuwalksa and deposed os a witness. His case is that he used to 
et payment from Bhuwalka and when Autcha Press is worked the employees 
are paid not according to the practice of. fixed rates of wages per day but by 
distribution amongst them whatever is received by the sub-contractor from 
the Contractor Shri Bhuwalka and that the Auwtcha Press is working for 
about 14 years and he also states that in the Kutcha Press the remuneration 
ot the workmen varies according to their respective outturns and not accord- 
ing to hours of work. He admits that in Autcha Press sustenance allowunce 
is not paid to these workmen. The question is whether there has been any 
contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act by Bhuwolla, 
the employer of the petitioners. It appears from the evidence that the 
Autcha Press was not working at the time when Hon’ble Dr. Roy effected 
the settlement. Autcha Press has been introduced sometime in August 1982. 


Part |] THE CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPTEMBER 7, 1954 1276 


হু 


In the settlement of Hon’ble Dr. Roy, there was no such clause that the 
casual workers in which category the petitioners fall, shall be all hourly 
rated ; on the other hand the provision is that the hourly rated casual workers 
shall be entitled to get sustenance allowance over and above the fixed wages 
per day (of 8 hours), So if any casual worker (after the reference hus been 
made) is employed on work on job rate and in a Kwtcha Press I think 
there is no alteration of their service condition. Autcha 21988. is a new 
thing. There is no direction in the agreement that hourly rated casual 
workers shall not be employed on job rate. If the employer fails to pay 
fixed rate of wages to aisle rated casual worker it may said that the 
employer has violated the terms of the agreement and as a matter of that 
has made an alteration of service condition. In the instant case I hold that 
there has been no such contravention of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act simply because hourly cated casual workers who were doing work in 
"7 Press were employed on job rate after the reference, in a ۶۵ھ‎ 
ress. 


But the fact that sustenance allowance has been withheld from them 
biings the case within the mischief of section 33 in that it was an altera- 
tion of service condition of the hourly rated Casual workers. These workers 
were entitled to get the sustenance allowance according to the terms of the 
ayreement, although they were engaged in Kutcha Press on job rate. So 
T hold that the petitioners ure to get sustenance allowance at 8 annas per day 
for the days on which work was done by them since the beginning of Sep- 
tember 1952, and payment thereof be made within 10 days after the publica- 
tion of this Award. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 


M. L. CHAKRAVATTI, 
Judge. 
MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 
Judge, Sizth Industrial Tribunal.

No. 6494W.T.—3lst August 1954.—In exercise of the power conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919 
(Bengal Act I of 1919), the Governor is pleased to make the following by- 
laws pee the Kamarhati Municipality in the district of 24-Parganas, 
namely :— 


BY-LAWS. 


1. Appointment and duties of the Registering Officer.— Every rickshaw 
in the Kamarhati Municipality shall be annually registered by the Register- 
ing Officer appointed for registering hackney-carriages. 


2. Qualifications of the bearers.—Every person applying for a bearer’s 
license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officer— 


(a) that he is not less than 18 years of age; 


(b) that he knows how to drive and control a rickshaw and is in all 
. respects a fit person for such employment; 


(c) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, workshops, 
factories, offices and places in and around the town of Kamarhati; 


(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and distances 
prepared by the Commissioners; 


(e) that he knows the rules of the road and the signals used by the 
bearers and drivers of vehicles and by the traffic police. 


3. 00٥0ہ‎ ٥: of license.—There shal) be attached to each license issued 
to a bearer— 


(a) the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 
(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him; and 


(c) a printed table of fares and distances prepared by the Commissioners, 
for which no charge shall be paid by the bearer. 


4. Production of license, etc.—Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carry 
with him his license and shal] produce it when called upon to do so by the 
traffic police, any Commissioner, or other person authorised by the Commis- 
sioners. He shall exhibit the table of fares and distances on a prominent 
part of the vehicle. 


5. Condition of riokshaws.—(a) The body of the rickshaw shall be sound 
and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. 


(by The wheels ahal]l be rubber-tyred, strong and sound, so as to run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by properly 
fitted splash boards. 


۶ 
(c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and pro- 
perly riveted and free from ۶. 


(d) The iron supports at the back shall be properly curved and securely 
fixed on each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 


(e) The hood, apron and cushions shall be made of and covered with good 
cloth, canvas or other material approved by the Commissioners at a meeting. 


(f) The shafts shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and furnish- 
ed at the fore-ends with a ring-shaped mete#l support and connected by a 
collision guard. 


“z) The hood and apron shall be so fitted as to make the vehicle water- 
tight ঃ 


(8) Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps—one facing the front and 
one in the rear. 


(i) Each lamp shall have a red glass window in the back and shall be so 
placed that the او‎ from the window is visible from a point ten yards in 
the rear of the centre of the vehicle. 


(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle bars or cross 
bara on the cycle and it shall be so constructed that it can be operated by 
fingers and it can giye continuous ringing as and when necessary.

9. Prohibition of smoking, etc.—No bearer shall smoke while driving 
nor shall he muffle up his face in such a manner as to endanger the proper 
driving of his vehicle. 


10. Maximum 1080 to be carried in rickshaws.—Passengers and luggage 
shall not ordinarily exceed 4 maunds in weight. 


11. Speed and halting charge of rickshaws.—When ao rickshaw 1s hired 
the bearer shall ordinarily drive the same at a speed of not less than 
eight miles per hour. If a rickshaw after: being hired is made tw halt, 
halting charge shall be paid according to the scule laid down in the above 
fare table. 


‘12. Advertisement on rickshaws.—No advertisement shall be fixed on 
the body of the rickshaws without the previous permission of the Commis- 
sioners and it shall be fixed at such places as not to cover the number 
plate and the fare table affixed to the rickshaws. 


13. Rickshaws to wait at stand.—The rickshaws while at rest aball’ 
wait at a stand fixed by the Commissioners for such purpose.

at any time between sun-rise ahd sun-set to enter any premises in which any

out any of the provisions of the’ Calcutta Hackney-carriage act, 1919 or 
these by-laws und the owner or occupier of the premises or his agent shall 
afford every facility for inspéction by such Commissione? or person. 


15. Sale of tables of fares and distance.—The OMommissionarg shall 
cause to be prepared and kept, for sale to the public, printed tables setting 
forth and fares and distances at a price fixed by the Commissioners, 


16. Particulars of registers.—The following particulars shall be entgred 
7 the registers and licenses under the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 
910 ;— 


(A) Bearer’s license. 


(1) The number of the license. 


(2) The name, father’s name, place of abode, present address and age 
of the person to whom such license is granted. 


(3) The date on which the license is granted. 

(4) The number of rickshaws allowed to the bearer. 
(5) Photograph of the bearer. 

(6) The date of expiry of the license. 


(7) A summary of the more important statutory provisions and by- 
laws affecting bearers of rickshaws. 


(8) Signature of the Registering Officer. 


(B) Owner’s license. 


(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 


(2) The name, father’s name and residence of the owner, the description 
of the rickshaw and the place where the rickshaw is kept. 


(3) The number of passengers the rickshaw is licensed to carry. 
(4) The date on which the license is granted. 

(5) Date of expiry of the license. 

(6) Signature of the Registering Officer.

The manner in which the Committee will dis- 
tharge ita duties, is as follows:— 


The members will not visit the hospital indivi- 
dually; the Committee will form itself into groups 
of not leas than three members, each group in turn 
Will, according to a roster to be kept for the pur- 
pose, visit the hospital on a fixed day and at a fixed 
time in each month. In addition to these visits 
ut fixed times the members will pay unexpected 
visits to the hospital. Members while paying sur- 
rise visit should on arrival at the hospital imme- 
اہی‎ contact the Superintefident and in his 
absence his Deputy before entering the wards. If 
all the three members of the group are not present, 
the remaining members can yo round without the 
absentee or absentees, as the case may be. The 
members constituting the group should inspect the 
internal arrangements and offer such suggestions 
regarding the administration of the institution as 
they think proper. 


A visitors’ book will be kept in the hospital in 
which the recommendations of the Committee will 
be recorded. The Superintendent will note on the 
margin the action token on each recommendation 
with any other remarks or explanations that he 
may wish to offer. He will transmit a copy of the 
entries without delay to the Director of Beatin 
Services, West Bengal, for consideration. e 
Director of Health Services will take such further 
action as may seem necessary and will bring to 
the notice of Government any matter which he 
thinks sufficiently important. A copy of the 
entries should alao be sent to the Secretary to the 
Government of West Bengal, Medical and Public 
Tealth Department, for information. 


The Committee as a whole will meet at least 
Mee a quarter, review the reports of the visiting 
groups and discuss the remedial meagyres adopted. 

e Superintendent of the Nilratan Sirear Medical 
College Tospital should attend the meetings of the 

iiting Committee. 


The Committee will send copies of the resolution 
Passed ad, their quarterly meetings to the Secretary 
to the Government of West Bengal, Medical and 
Public ILealth Department, and also to the Diree- 
% of Tealth Services, West Bengal, who will sub- 

9 to Government a report of the action taken 
5۷ proposed to be tukepn on the points raised on those 
79801020208 ۱ 


The members will hold office for three years or 
until the next reconstitution of the Committee. 
Any member who fails to visit the hospital during 
three suécessive months without sufficient reason 
will automatically cease to be a member, Govern- 
ment will appoint a new member in his or her place. 
Visitors’ book should be submitted by the Superin- 
tendent to Government once every quarter for 
noting the names of habitual absentees. 


By order of the Governor,

LABOUR DEPARTMENT 


ORDER. 


No. 4119Dis. /D/7L-25 /54.—26th August 1954.—Whereas under the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 4798Dizs. / 
D/7L-58/58, dated the 18th December 1953, the industrial dispute 
between Messrs. Dalhousie Jute Mills, Vitd., post office Champdany, 
district Hooghly, and their worker Ali Khan represented by National 
Union of Jute Workers, post office Baidyabati, district Hooghly, regard- 
ing the matters specified in the schedule thereto was referred for adjudica- 
tion to the Sixth Industrial Tribunal; 


And whereas the said Sixth Industrial Tribunal has submitted to the 
State Government its award on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions of section 17 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased 


hereby to publish the said award as shown in the annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between Messrs. Dalhousie Jute 
Mills, Ltd., post office Champdany, district Hooghly and their worker, 
Ali Khan, represented by National Union of Jute Workers, post office 
Baidyabati, Hooghly. 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. ۱ 


PRESENT : 
Sugar MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, 
Judge, Sicth Industrial Tribunal. 


Appearances. 


For the Company: Shri S. C. Sen, Advocate, assisted by Shri A. Das, 
Deputy Chief Labour Officer. 


For the workman: Shri Pandey, Vice-President of the Union. 


Acting under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV of 1947), the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, by 
order No. 4798Dis./D/7L-58/53, dated the 18th December 1953, referred 
the aforesaid dispute for adjudication, to me regarding the matters 
specified in the schedule to the Order of Reference. 


SCHEDULE. 


(1) Whether dismissal of Ali Khan is justified? What relief he is 
entitled ۶ 


-Ali Khan, a durwan of Dalhousie Jute Mill, contends in the written 
statement-that he was suddenly called to the office of the mill on the 
25th May 1953 and informed that he was dismissed and that on the 
276) May, he went to the office to know the cause of his dismissal and 
that the Labour Officer intimated that the altercation with the Security 
Officer was the said cause and that on 28th May 1953, the Labour Officer 


3042 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 9, 1954 [Pani I 
FY 


handed over a charge-sheet ৮৮ 10 a.m. to Ali Khun and that it was dated 
25th May 1964 and that ×٢ was not signed or ‘endorsed by any officer 
und that on the 29th May, Al: Khan went to the Labour Office to submit 
his eaplanation to the charge-sheet, but the Labour Officer drove him out 
saying that no reply was needed and that since then Ali Khan was 
kept out of employment. His case in the written statement is that on 
the 25th Muy 19538, the Security Officer took him to task for not saluting 
him and that Ali Khan verbally explained and apologised but it was not 
accepted by the said Security Officer. 


The case of the Company, 2.e., Dalhousie Jute Mill is that on the 27th 
May 1953, when the Security Officer was driving & motor van towards the 
Northbrooke Mill past the gate of Dalhousie Jute Mill, he noticed that 
Ali Khan, a durwan, was inattentive ond he simply called him to 
‘“‘attention’’ and after returning trom Northbrooke Mill the Security 
Officer sent for the Hubilder and Jamadar of the Dalhousie Mill and 
thereafter Ali Khan also was sent for and that when the Security Officer, 
asked Ali Khan to mend his conduct otherwise he would be served with 
w warning, Ali Khan becume violently abusive and threntened to ussault 
the Security Officer, so much so that he had to be held back by the 
armed guard of the Security Officer. Thereafter Ali Khan was directed 
to go to the Labour Office and there Ali Khan again threatened to 
assault and shoot the Security Officer in presence of Havilder, Jamader 
and the Head Clerk. Then a charge-sheet was being drawn up against 
Ali Khan on that occasion and Ali Khan suddenly rushing out of the 
Labour Office, picked up a brick und attempted to assault the Security 
Officer, but he was prevented from the act by the armed guard and the 
Habilder. It is contended by the Company that thereafter the charge- 
sheet was drawn up and رای‎ to Ali Khan but the latter refused ta 
accept it. Ali Khan then guve a verbal statement in reply and it was 
recorded by the Head Clerk and in the next morning, .7.e., on the 28th 
May 1968, an enquiry was held and evidence given by the witnesses was 
recorded and that Ali Khan was given full opportunity to defend 
himself. Thereafter the Manager dismissed Ali Khan. It is alleged

DECISION. 


Four other employees whose termination of employment is in issue are 
(1) Md. Ayub, a Typist who was discharged by a notice on 3lst January 
1963, (2) Gulum Nubi Mullah, (3) M. H. Shirazee and (4) Daulat Ali Khan 
all Sarkars, discharged by notice on 26th February 1958. The Union’s 
case is that they were victimised and discharged for their Union activities 
although the management discharged them ‘‘under colour of retrench- 
ment’’. It is further stated that there was no diminution of work in the 
Yc me of business justifying the discharge, on the other hand, the work- 
load was increased, There was no genuine trade reason and the question 
of loss did not arise at all. Lastly, it is stated that in any case, 1f there 
be any loss, it was due to the Company’s mismanagement and bad handling 
of business. The Management justifies its action on the ground of economy 
necessitated purely by trade reasons for in the year in question, the Company 
suffered a huge loss in its business. 


The legal position is clear and does nét admit of any doubt. It has 
been held in the Biswamitra Press, 1952, L.A.C., page 20 at page 33 that, 
“It ix the prima facie right of the management to determine its labour 
agree and the management would be the best judge to determine the number 
a workmen who would become surplus on the ground of rationalisation, 
economy or other reason on which retrenchment can be sustained. Where 
in effecting the retrenchment, the management acts in a bona fide manner, 
the number retrenched by it ought to be accepted. The increase of work- 
lnad on the workmen retained would be an instance of extraneous consi- 
deration. Similarly, victimisation or unfair labour practice in effecting 
retrenchment would be instances of improper motive. When the manage- 

ent is influenced by extraneous considerations cr improper motives, the 
Tabunal mist scrutinise the matter with great circumspection and must 
confine the number of retrenchment strictly within the limits of actual 
requirements. If the question is answered in favour of the management 
and the extent of retrenchment determines in accordance with the princjples 
indicated obove, the next question would be the personnel who would fall 
under the acts. Other things being equal, the ‘‘last come must first go. 
If that rule has been departed from, the management must justify the 
departure....... "’,. Both parties stand by this decision although the learned 
representative for the Company wanted to tell the Tribunal on the authority 
of a later decision in Arezona vs. their workers reported in 1953 L.A.C. 
page 993 that, “‘when the retrenchment was bona fide, the Tribunal should 
ot interfere’. The matter was incidentally dealt with in a still later 
decision of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal reported in Sudarshan 
Bauerjee and others vs. Mcleod غ‎ Co., Ltd., 1958 L.A.C., page 702. Two 
things should be specifically looked into in adjudicating a dispute over 
retrenchment with are: (1) Whether a case for retrenchment has been 
made out, that is to say, whether the grounds for saying that their surplus 
has been made out by the employer: and (2) Even if such a ground has 
been made out by the employer, whether in the matter of retrenchment the 
employer had acted bona fide. A further point should also be considered, 


3050 THK CALCUTTA GAZKTTE, SEPTEMBER 9, 1904 [Parr } 
نین تہ ھت‎ ne Nee eee ere eR eC ne. 
۴ 
namely ,whether in discharging the workmen, the employer had followed 
the rule of “last come first go’’, or not. ‘Thut rule is not a fixed rule but 
it is the normal rule and if departed from by the employer, he must justify 
by evidence the departure made hy him. A statutory provision has bee 
made in the amended Industrial Disputes Act in which the procedure fo: 
retrenchment has been codified in section 2008) of the Act. 


We will now proceed to examine the question presented in this case iz 
the light of the observations of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribu 
mentioned above. The four employees have deposed in this case. Thet 
are P.W. 1, Md. Ayub, P.W. 2, Doulat Ali Khan, P.W. 3, Gulum Nab 
‘Mullah and P.W. 4 0. H. Shirazee. It appears from their evidence thai 
all of them are ordinary members of the Union which came into existence 
in January 1953. They said that they worked for the improvement of the 
Union and they were discharged for their Union activities. It would 
further appear trom the Union’s letter, dated 815৮ March 1958, which is ar 
annexure to the Company’s written statement in this case, that the Secretary 
of the Union informed the management about he formation of the: রন 
on that date. It is now admitted that the registration was made on ط201‎ 
March 1953 and this information was conveyed officially to the: manugement 
subsequent to that. An endeavour was made on the Union’s side to prove 
by the evidence of the employees concerned as also by a receipt (Ext. 5), 
dated 2nd January 1953, that the Union existed in January 1953. It ha 
not been proved in this case on the side of the Union that the management 
had any information about that before the official date on 3lst March 1953. 
Two facts emerged out of this enquiry and they are: (1) the executives of 
the Union are continuing in service even now; and (ii) the discharged em- 
ployees received very good certificates from the management. It has bees 
contended on behalf of the company that it would be the last person to و‎ 
good certificates’to the discharged people if they proceeded from any motive 
other than what is now stated to be. There was no extraneous reason 101 
proceeding against these employees. Ayub was served with a notice on 
3186 January 1953 and four others on 26th February 1953, £.৪.১ long before 
the registration of the Union and the official intimation was being given to 
the management. I am inclined to hold that these employees were 2001 
discharged for their alleged Union activities. Therefore the story of ٣1٥٢

not consider it necessary for the purpose of deciding this reference to go

from doing it. It is however not improper to say that the Tribunal considers 
for very good reasons that the employees who were taken over to this

M. M. শর Ltd. According to Mr. Seal (and he is the only com- 
petent person to speak on the side of the management in this case) these 
employees were retrenched department-wise as they were found surplus 
to requirements. The fact whether they had any junior still in the 
employment or not was not considered at that time. The learned 
representative for the Union contends that the management proceeded on 
a wrong basis and accordingly, the termination of services of these 
employees should be held unjustified on this ground alone. I think there 
are very cogent reasons for holding the wait view. The normal rule as 
has been laid down in the Biswamitra case reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 
20, is that other things being, equal, the Jast come must first-go. If there 
is any departure, the management will have to record ita reasons for that. 
In Sudarsan Banerjee vs. McLeod Company’s case, / 19538 L.A.C., 
p. 702 at page 712, their lordships of the Hlon’ble Labour Appellate 
Tribunal held as follows: ‘‘The whole clerical staff at the office should be 
taken as one unit. Then it should be divided into separate categories, 
Stenographers, Typista, Clerks and Sarkars. All workmen in_ the 
particular category do the same type of work and if the selection proceeds 
taking the affected department only to be the unit, there would be great, 
unjustice. A clerk who is comparatively senior and happens to be at the 
time of the proposed retrenchment in the affected: department where he is 
the juniormost amongst the clerks, will lose the benefit of his long service. 
Te POET ee Poe This on the face of it would not only be against the 
principle underlying security of service and the rules of social justice 
which is the foundation of the normal rule of ‘last come, first go’, 
different considerations may, however, apply where the departments are 
water-tight where, as we have already observed, a set of employees is tied 
down 60 a particular department, that is to say, where it is a condition of 
service—express or implied—that the employer cannot put him to work 
elsewhere.” Mr. Seal did not say that the departments from which these 
employees were selected were the most affected out of the whole office. Even 
assuming then that they were so uffected, the position would remain the 
same. On Union’s evidence it has been proved beyond doubt that there 
are juniors to at least three of the said employees in service. The case of 
Daulat Ali Khan is different. He according to the Union joined the

The management has not shown that these employees were appointed in 
the departments which were water-tight, namely the conditions of their 
service would not permit them to move them out of the department in 
any case. This being the position, the Tribunal finds that the termina- 
tion of their service by way of retrenchment is not justified. They are 
entitled to reinstatement. For reasons given above, the Tribunal finds

AWARD. 


The petitioner, an employee of Messrs. Sun Jute Press, alleges that 
he has been kept suspended for the last nine months although the 
employer’s application under section 33 for permission to dismiss him 
had been rejected by the Tribunal. He therefore prays that the 
suspension order may he set aside and he may be allowed to resume his 
job and that the employer may be directed to pay him full wages for the 
period of his suspension. 


The contention of the employer is that the petitioner was not int 
position to do any work during the period of suspension. On the other 
band he was applying for long leave because of his illness und therefore no 
question of compensation for loss of earning during the period of illness 
arises. 


It appears from the evidence thut in April 1958, the petitioner was 
on leave for one mouth and on the Ist May 1953, he was sent to Medical 
College for X-Ray examination. Doctor recommended three months’ 
leave and the Company granted him the said leave. Thereafter the 
Factory Inspector requested the Company to grant the petitioner leave 
with wages for two months more. Petitioner says that the leave expire! 
although his medical examination and treatment was not then completed | 
It also appears from his evidence that when he was insisting on having 
extension of leave, the company was not agreeable to grant him long 
leave {as the petitioner contends) and that on the other hand the 
Company framed a charge-sheet aguinst him and suspended him anid 
that after the section 33 proceeding was over and after the Tribunul had 
rejected the employers’ prayer for permission to dismigs the petitioner, 
the Company of his own accord granted two years’ leave_to the petitione’ 
“895৮ any wages. The position therefore is that the petitioner was

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
"1947 (XIV of 1947), as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate 
Tribunal) Act, filed by Kalika, an employee under Fulchand Singh, Labour 
Contractor of Messrs. Rallis India, Ltd., Jute Press, represented by Cossipore 
Jute Press Workers’ Union, against the aforesaid Jute Press (Case No. 177/ 


33A/52). 
BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. 
PRESENT : 
Suri MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District: Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 
Tribunal. 
Appearances. 


For the employers: Shri N. K. Mookherjee, Advocate. 


For the workman: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee, Secretary, Jute Press 
Workers’ Union. 


The original reference out of which this present ۰ئ00‎ under section 
33A has arisen was made under Government order Nos. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, 
dated 8th August 1952, read with addendum No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated 
10th November 1952, and subsequent order No. 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated 
12th December 1953. 


AWARD. 


The petitioner contends that he was an employee under contractor Fulchand 
Singh, Rallis India, Limited, and that he became ill and was granted leave ana 
when after recovery of illness, he came to the Press to do work, he was driven 
out by the said employer and that this took place during the pendency of the 
original case. 


The employer contends that he was not a party in the original reference 
case and therefore this application under section 33A does not lie. The 
employer further contends that the petitioner and other workers worked as 
Casual workers from time to time and the employer has got no permanent 
employee and that the petitioner was not driven out or discharged and that on 
the other hand he absented himself since 7th October 1952, and never reported 
for employment thereafter. 


Neither party adduced any oral evidence. It is admitted that the employer 
has got no permanent worker under him and that all the labourers including 
petitioner are labourers under this employer as more or less regular workers, 
although not permanent. The jute owners are called balers, they send their 
bales of jute to the Jute Press for pressing into bales and there is no regularity 
in the said transaction. Jute Press business is more or less a casual business 
depending upon the need of the jute balers and which in its turn is practically 


৪ TI) THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, St PTEMBER 9, 1954 3063 


A বদ SE EE ETT‏ گی 
পপ‏ 


a ৪ সা سے یں ' یں تک‎ ee পপর oe کر‎ 2 
nar ve ee Es পপি সপ ee ee eee . Ce ree ےہ سے ےہ‎ = ee সপ 


controlled by the jute market in Calcutta. The Jute Press has got some con- 
tractors under it and these contractors engage some labourers for pressing the 
jute into bales. There are different categories of these labourers. There is 
no work available every day and on some days these workers or some of them 
come and go back without finding any work to do. Petitioner Kalika says that 
he has been driven out and was not allowed to do any work but the employer 
says that due to paucity of work, the petitioner absented himself and did not 
report for work. Admittedly the employer keeps no record of the workers who 
attend and go back without finding work. He keeps records of only those 
labourers who are given work on days on which jute pressing is done. In these 
circumstances [ think that the contention of the petitioner that he was driven 
out or discharged is correct. I do not believe that after absenting himself since 
7th October 1952, the petitioner Kalika would come to the Tribunal on 10th 
December 1952 and make this application under section 33A of the Industrial 
Disputes Act against his employer. At the same time it is to be noted that the 
petitioner could not show that on 7th October 1952 or on the alleged date of 
discharge there was work available for him. It would be proper on the part 

the employer to keep a panel for the regular casual workers and note their 
attendance on dates if they really attend irrespective of whether on those days 
they got work or not. So my award is that Kalika is to be reinstated from the 
date on which he comes to work under this employer and that Kalika is to be 
given work by the Opposite Party Fulchand, Labour Contractor, if such work is 
available. In these circumstances already referred to it will not be proper to 
give any direction to the employer to compensate the petitioner Kalika.

In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (XIV of 1947), as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate 
Tribunal) Act, filed by Lakhan Ram, a workman of Shiva Jute Press, 
2, Kali Prasanna Singha Road, Calcutta, represented by Cossipore Jute 
Workers’ Union, 1, Joy Bhattacherjee Lane, Calcutta-3, against the aforesaid

SHRI MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial

For the Jute Press: Shri N. K. Mookherjee, Advocate. 


For the workman: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee, Secretary, Jute Press 
Workers’ Union. 


Sai 


The original reference out of which the present complaint under section 33A 
of the Industrial Disputes Act has arisen was made under Government order 
No. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated the 8th August 1952, read with addendum 
No. 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated 10th November 1952 and subsequent 
No. 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated the 12th December 1953. ۱ 


AWARD. 


The petitioner Lakhan Ram, an employee of Shiva Jute Press, alleges that 
on 16th October 1951, he met with an accident : injury in course of employment. 
He got some compensation from his employer under the Workmen’s Compensa- 
tion Act. His case is that the said compensation case was disposed of on 23rd 
March 1953 and as a result thereof the employer got disgusted against the 
‘petitioner and therefore dismissed him on 24th March 1953. 


The employer filed a written statement. There the Company, i.e., the 
employer, does not challenge these facts on the other hand it is there made out 
that the petitioner met with an accident and received compensation from the ' 
employer and that discharge was not in any way influenced by these facts. 


It appears from the evidence that Lakhan was a mate. His duty was to 
collect the coolies and carry on the work of pressing jute bales on days on which 
the press works. It would be playing Hamlet without Hamlet, if Lakhan who 
is the mate of the coolies in this press is said to be laid off on account of paucity 
of work, when the coolies themselves found work in the said press. The employer 
does not deny the fact of discharge but alleges that because of want of work 


Pins CT] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 9, 1954 3065 


স্পাই 


a - সর ও সপ শত সস ای ہے‎ RE সী শি পাপা সপ তত PSE TSE ২ ہے‎ 
পারের: ez. পি 


in the press he had to be discharged. I can not understand how the mate could 
be discharged on the aforesaid allegation. It appears from the evidence that 
ifter the discharge of Lakhan Ram who worked in the press for about 20 years, 
this Company engaged some new hands. I am convinced that the fact that the 
employer had to pay the compensation under Workmen’s Compensation Act to 
the papers enraged the employer so much so that immediatey after the disposal 
of the said compensation proceedings, the petitioner was summarily dismissed. 
It is nothing but victimisation and I am not at all impressed by the pleading 
that because Lakhan was not permanent hand or a monthly rated worker and 
because Lakhan was a casual worker therefore he had no lien on service for 
the morrow. As a matter of fact this petitioner was working regularly as a 
casual worker for many years in this press and he was the mate and his function 
was to collect the coolies for working in this press on days on which work is 
available. There is therefore some regularity in the work and attendance of the 
petitioner although he was a casual worker. The order of dismissal or discharge 
when there was work in this press which 15 still working, is unjustified and 
vindictive. It is set aside. € petitioner be reinstated and the opposite party 
Rhall give him job from the first available day, i.e., on which work would be 
available, on which the petitioner would be in attendance. 


For loss of earning for these days he shall be paid by the opposite party 
Rs. 20 as compensation. This payment shall be made within a week from the 
date of publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette.

shall be deemed to be false in 8, material respect 
if the average length of the hank in a bundle is 
less than 809 yards. 


V. (i) For all threads, (of cotton, wool, flax or 
silk) in units of 100 yards or less, a_ trade 
deacription of length shall not be deemed to he 
false in material respect unleas the length or 
weight in individual units, exceeds 10 per cent, 
of the average length or weight of the units in 
the smallest packet or box. In the case of 
threads in units of more than 100 yards, the 
length or weight in individual units shall not 
differ by more than 5 per cent. of the average 
length or weight of the ynit in the smallest packet 
or box. 


Provided that the total length or weight in a 
packet or box does not differ by more than 1 per 
cent. of the declared length or weight. 

(11) Two-folda sewing or darning thread other 
than such thread in the shape of skeins and balla 
er on cards, reels and paper tubes shall be 
considered as yarn.”’ 


J. N. DUTTA, Dy. Secy.

College.

age, examination passed, citizenship of India, an attested 
copy of certificate of physical fitness bearmg a date not

hours in Northern Circle in West Bengal. A monthly 
allowance of Rs. 25 will be givon during the practical 
training. During training period at the Indian Forest

granted. Selected candidates must execute Agreement

DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, WEST 
BENCAL. , 
Calcutta, the 2lst July 1954. 


Forecast of Miscellaneous Rabi Crops of West 
Bengal for 1953-54. 


[Note.—The figures of yield rates of the composite 
crops ‘‘Rabi fruits’, ‘‘Rabi vegetables’’ 
(other than potato), ‘‘Other Rabi food crops’’, 
“Rabi fodder crops’’, ‘‘Condiments and 
রা and “Other Rabi non-food crops’ as 
shown in the forecast represent the estimated 
outturn as percentages of their normal yields 

per acre. ] 


Season.—The weather conditions have been 
favourable in all the districts except 24-Parganas, 
Nadia, Hooghly, Howrah and West Dinajpur. 


« 


Area and yield.—Rali food crops.—The argas 
sown with different Rabi food crops are estimated 
ut 242,300 acres this year as against 211,800 acres 
of last year. 


Rabi non-food crops—The areas edwn with 
different Rabi non-food crops are estimated at 
14,900 acres this year as against 16,800 acres of’ 
last year. 


Rabi sunnhemp.—900 acres are estimated to be 
, under sunnhemp this year compared to 1,400 acres 
of last year. The total outturn of sunnhemp for 
the State as a whole has been estimated at 1,450 
bales this year compared to 2,600 bales of last 
year. The average yield per acre, of sunnhemp 
for the State as a whole is estimated at 1-61 bales 
this year compared to 1:86 bales of last year. 


S. N. MUKHERJEE, 
for Director of Agriculture, West Bengal.

Minutes of Dissent. 


= رم 

According to me,— 
The general principles in delimitin consti- 
tuencies of the Parliaments and/or the State 


Assemblies as enunciated by the Constitution, 
thes Delimitation Commission Act, and the prac- 
tice followed in forming of constituencies during 
last election are administrative units, contiguous 
aren and good communication and the uniformity 
of the population strength. The Constitution has 
provided that after each census a Commission is 
to be set up to delimit the constituencies in accord- 
ance with the change in the population figure and 
if necessary the constituency will have to be deli- 
mited anew. In our country the area of our 
constituencies are often large and communication 
are not easy, which generally makes it difficult for 
u representative to reach conveniently each anid 
every part of this constituency in order to nurse 
in properly and have closer contact with his elec- 
torate. In our country a new experiment is being 
made in Parliamentary democracy healthy deve- 
lopment whereof depends largely upon the 
ability of the representative to keep closer contact 
with the electorate and express their point of 
view correctly which is only possible if the 
representative has personal knowledge of the 
matter and the problem involved. Therefore it is 
absolutely necessary not to change the  consti- 
tuencies and as far as possible with each and every 
delimitation work. آ1‎ it becomes imperative to 
alter a constituency because of population varia- 
tion, special effort should be made in delimiting 
a constituency afresh to restrict its alteration to 
the minimum with the idea of keeping it to the 
limits of the old constituency. I have therefore 
atated below the items which I could not agree 
with the views of the Commiasioner with reason 
therefor,— 


Basirhat Parliamentary.—1 have been unable to 
uppreciate the reason for changing this  consti- 
tuency which hay also necessitate the change of 
the scheme of the entire parliamentary consti- 
tuency of the 24 Parganas. However if the Com- 
missioner’s proposal is to be accepted it is 
absolutely necessary and logically correct to form 
a constituency composed of Basirhat, Barasat and 
Bongaon sub-division and Dum Dum of Barrackpore 
sub-division. This delimitation will keep three 
sub-divisions of Basirhat, Barasat and Bongaon in 
tact and by inclusion of Dum Tum Seat to make 
up hecessary components it will also limit to the

existing constituency with minimum alteration aa 
necessitated by the alternative scheme. 


It will not basically alter the character of 
Barrackpore Seat which will have given up three 
seats to Calcutta North-West and Basirhat to 
Nadia may be added to it to make up the requisite 
numbers. 


State Assembly. 


Sonarpur Seat.—The demarcation line should 
be drawn along the Diamond Harbour Road as 
suggested earlier. I therefore sugyest that 
Union 12 of Bishnupur police station should be 
added to the Bishnupur Constituency and therefore 
rf necessary Union No. ] (Bowali) of Budge Budge 
police station may be taken away from Bishnupur 
und added to Budge Budge Seat. 


I suggest the alteration to the Joynagore, 
Canning and Mathurapur Constituencies in the 
following manner as they are more contiguous and 
convenient :— 


Joynagore—Joynagore police station (exclud- 
ing Unions 3 and 4) and Unions 1, 2, 3 
of Mathurapur.

ing Union 3) and Union Nos. 3 and 4 of

to 4 of Kakdwip police station. 


I cannot accept the manner in which Baruipur 
has been tagged to part of Mograhat with which it 
has very bad or practically no communication and 
1৯০ no economic relation. If Baruipur has to be 
tagged with any other part it should be with 
adjoining part of Joynuagore. 


Regarding Burdwan Constituency.—The origins] 
suggestion of the Delimitation Commission, viz., 
Burdwan ___ police station excluding Unions 
Nos. 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 is to be retained. Instead of 
that to tag Union 4 (Bandul) and Union ا‎

is the height of absurdity, because Union No. 4 is

of Khandaghosh and Union No. 6 is nearly twenty 
miles away. There is absolutely no communica-

and 6 are included in the Rurdwan Constituency,
