KAMAL KUMAR BASU, M.P., 
Associate Member. 


a 


If. 


We have carefully studied the Delimitation 
Commission’s revised draft proposals for delimita- 
tion of constituencies in West Bengal. We offer 
the folloiwng comments :— 


Calcutta. 


We have seen the State Government’s proposals 
for Assembly constituencies in this area, which 
ure already with the Commission, and we think 
that these proposals should be accepted for the 
following reasons. In our opinion the Comuiis- 
sion’s proposals show very wide variations in the 
number of people represented by each Assembly 
member in this area, although the average number 
should be in the neighbourhood of 104,974, which 
has been closely adhered to in the State Govern- 
ments proposals. In the Commission’s proposals 
while there are seats at 93,787, 94,341, 95,608, 
95,428, 96,215, 97,018, 97,608, 99,672, etc., there 
are also seats at 108,972, 109,479, 112,746, 
113,986, 113,598, 113,936, 114,599, 114,430, ete. 
It is, of course, noticed that the Commission has 
uvoided breaking up the municipal wards’ while 
a few wards have been broken up in the State 
Government’s proposals. In our opinion it is far 
more desirable, indeed in correct accordance with 
the direction of Constitution in this behalf, that 
the number of people represented by — each 
Assembly meinber in a constituency should be the 
same as far as practicable (if necessury, by break- 
ing up wards in forming the constituency) than 
thai there should be very wide variations in the 
number of people fram constituency 0٥ 
constituency in an attempt to ensure that 
wards are not broken up at all. It is true that the 
the Delimitation Act says that in forming the 
Constituencies regard should be had to the fact 
that administrative units are not broken up as far 
as practicable but this is only a factor to be 
taken into consideration whereas there ۹ 
8 positive direction in article 170(3) of the Consti- 
tion that in forming the constituencies the number 
of people to be represented by » member in an 
Assembly constituency shall be the same 


as fur ag practicable, and we consider that in 
the joint application of these two principles, one 
of which is mandatory and the other only recom- 
mendatory, the State Government are amply 
justified in placing a relatively greater emphasis 
on what the Constitution directs than what the 
Delimitation Act asks to be taken into considera- 
tion only. We notice that in forming the 
Assembly constituencies in Calcutta the State 
Government's proposals have ensured the closest 
pousible approximation to the ayeruge number of 
people per seat, and while it is true that ai few 
wards have had to be broken up in giving effect 
to this principle, we 150 notice that, in = such 
cases, the constituencies have been formed with 
complete wards plus the required portion of another 
ward which has been clearly described with 
reference to well-known street boundaries to which 
the people of the locality are admittedly accus- 
tomed. In a city like کسر کن‎ people are sel- 
dom familiar with the territorial extent of a muni- 
cipal ward, so that not much importance need be 
attached to the need for keeping a ward intact as 
the Commission has sought to attach. 


It is true that the Commission has avoided 
breaking up wards. But as the (Government of 
West Bengal have rightly pointed out, these wards 
are not well-known administative units like 
mufassal police stations. In fact they themselves 
are constituencies—and that even, very recently 
creuted—only for the limited purpose of munici- 
pal elections. The police stations even now cover 
different areas: the ration-areas, when they 
existed, were not vo-extensive with the, wards. 
There is no question of communication difficulties 
with regard to Calcutta constituencies. For these 
vurious reasons, no undue emphasis should be 
placed on the wards in delimiting Caleutta consti- 
tuencies and they may be broken yp when there 
are other important reasons for doing so. 


West Dinajpur. 


Gn the basis of the Scheduled tribe population 
of this district, only 1-17 or 1 seat is admissible for 
Scheduled tribes in this district. We, however, 
notice that the Commission has allotted a second 
seat for Scheduled tribes in this district whereas 
u similar seat admissible to the 24-Purganas district 
on the basis of its Scheduled-tribe population 
(0-57 seat=1 sent) has been withdrawn. It appears 
that the Scheduled tribe population in the parti- 
cular constituency of the West Dinajpur district 
in which the Commission has placed the second 
tribal seat numbers 31,207 whereas the Scheduled 
tribe population in the constituency in the Sandesh- 
khah area of the 24-Parganas digtrict where the 
State Government have placed a tribal seat is about 
20,000 only. It also appears that the Comnniission 
interprets section 8(2)(d) of the Delimitation 
Comuniission Act to mean that a tribal seat is to be 
located in the constituency in which the Scheduled 
tribe population is most concentrated, for which 
reason the Commission apparently considers that a 
second tribal seat in the Gangarampur constituency 
of the West Dinajpur district would be more justi- 
fied than in any constituency in the 24-Parganas 
district. We do not, however, think that Sec- 
tion 8(2)(d) of the Act is capable of the interpreta- 
tion placed upon it hy the Commission. In our 
opinion, section 8(2)(d) means that the tribal seat is 
to be placed in the areas or regions in which the 
tribal population is most concentrated irrespective 
of whether, in the particular constituency in that 
region in which the seat 1s placed, the concentration 
is not so heavy. If in the areas of the 24-Parganas 
district the concentration of tribal population is 
such that a tribal seat is justified in that region 
rather than in the West Dinajpur region, the tribal 
seat should be placed in the 24-Parganas district 
rather than in the West Dinajpur district irres- 
pective of the fact that in o particular constituency 
in the West Dinajpur district the tribal population 


1296 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE EXTRAORDINARY, SEPTEMBER 13, 1954, [Parr IA 
en 


may be higher than in any constituency in the 24- 
Parganas district, We accordingly think that the 
second tribal seat in the Gangarampur Constituency 
should be withdrawn from the West Dinajpur dis- 
trict and restored to the 24-Parganas district to 
which it properly belongs.

Murshidabad. 

We have no comments to offer on the Commis- 
sion’s proposals for Assembly constituencies in 
this district except 7 in one respect. In the 
Lajgola Constituency the Commission has taken 
unfons 3 and 4 of police-station Bhagabangola 
along with police-station Lalgola, but we suggest 
that unions 3 and 5 of police-station Bhagabangola 
be taken instead. ‘ Communications between unions 
3 and 5 are easier, apart from these two unions 
being more clearly contiguous. This is also the 
position in the existing constituency. Union 4 is 
better connected with the Bhagabangola Consti- 
tuency as the greater part of it is in the Char 
Kutibari (in the river Padma) which can be 
reached from the Lalgola Constituency only after 
passing through the Bhagabangola Constituency. 
Union 4 should accordingly be included in the 
Bhagabangola Constituency. 


Bankura, Burdwan and 24-Parganas districts. 


In regard to the above three districts, we have 
carefully considered the Commission’s revised 
draft proposals in the light of the State Govern- 
ment’s proposals which we have already supported. 
We stil think that the State Government’s pro- 
posals, which appear to have been drawn up on 
the basis of their adequate local knowledge about 
facility of communications and have ensured the 
closest possible approximation to the average 
number of people per Assembly seat, are much 
better than the Commission’s preposals and should 
accordingly be accepted. 


With regard to the Commission's revised pro- 

sals for Assembly Constituencies in the 

rjeeling, Jalpaiguri, Cooch Behar, Malda, 
Birbhum, Hooghly and Howrah districts, we find 
them generally acceptable.

Parliamentary Constituencies. 


We generally agree with the distribution of 
Parliamentary seats between the different districts 
as made in the Commission’s revised draft pro- 
posals. We particularly appreciate the Commis- 
sion’s difficulty in adhering to their original pro- 
posals under which the 24-Parganap district, in 
spite of heing entitled to 6 complete Parliamentary 
Constituencies on the hasis of 42 Assembly seats, 
was made to part with 2 Assembly seats in favour 
of Calcutta, 3 Assembly seats in favour of Nadia 
and 2 Assembly seats in favour of Midnapore, for 
completing the necessary Parliamentary Consti- 
tuencies in those regions. We now find that the 
Comission has had to abandon that scheme with a 
view to doing justice to the 24-Parganas district 
and also because the former Mahisadal Consti- 
tuency which would have extended acros» the Bay 
of Bengal was difficult to justify. We duly 
appreciate the considerations which weighed with 
the Commission in revising the original scheme. 


We do not, however, necessarily support the 
actual extent of the Parliamentary Constituencies 
as formed by the Commission. We recommend 
that the actual extent of each Parliamentary Con- 
stituency be redrawn in terms of the Assembly 
Constituencies in the Commission’s proposals 
which we have accepted and the Assembly Con- 
stituencies which we have recommiehded above in 
deviation from the Commissiof’s proposals.

IRRIGATION AND WATERWAYS 
DEPARTMENT 


RESOLUTION No. 4694-1۰ 
Calcutta, the 11th September 1954. 


In veiw of the occurrence of serious floods § in 
the northern districts of the State successively in 
the years 1950, 1952 and 1954 and in view of the 
consequent necessity of evolving a machinery at a 
high level for consideration of all matters of 
policy relating to flood relief, flood control and 
protection against flood and for  ensurin 
the expeditious implementation of approvec 
measures for the above purposes the Governor 6 
pleased to constitute a Board, to be known aa the 
West Bengal Flood Control Board, consisting of 
the following :— 


The Chief Minister—Chairman. 


The Minister in charge of the Irrigation and 
Waterways Department. 


The Minister in charge of the Works and 
Buildings Department. 


The Minister in charge of the Food, Relief and 
Supplies Department. 


The Secretary to Government in the I[rriga- 
tion and Waterways Department— 
Secretary. 


The Consulting Engineer, Irrigation and 
Waterways Department — Assistant 
Secretary. 

will be as 


2. The functions of the 10081 


follows :— 


(a) to assess the flood problem in the State 
and to deal with questions of policy ىا‎ 
connection with flood relief and measures 
for flood control and protection: 


(b) to arrange for the collection of the requ 
site data in accordance with an approves 
programms, 


(c) to evolve and organise a flood warning 
system in the State ; 


(d) to plan the necessary remedial measure? 


and to determine priorities ; 


Part |]

(e) to arrange for’ the implementation of 
approved schemes in accordance with an 
suthorised schedule: 


and 


(f) to arrange for the efficient maintenance of 
flood contro] works. 


3. -The Board shall meet as often as may be 
considered necessary by the Chairman. 


4. The Chairman shall have the power to in- 
vite such persons ws he may consider necessary to 
be present at uny meeting of the Board and _ to 
participate in its deliberations. 


5. The North Bengal Flood Inquiry Committee 
constituted by the Irrigation and Waterways 
Department Resolution No. 3-]., dated the 2nd 
April 1954, shall function under the general direc- 
tions of the West Bengal Flood Control Board. 


Order.—Orderod that the Resolution be  pub- 
lished in the Calcutta Gazette and that copies be 
forwarded to the members of the Board, to all 
departments of the State Government and to the

NOTIFICATIONS. 


Subject:—-Payment of loans and advances—Issue 
of authorities by the Accountant-Ceneral, 


No. T.M./478.—26th August 1954.—Under 
S. R. 447 of the Treasu Rules, West 
Bengal, Volume I, loans and advances requiring 
sanction of the Government are required to be paid 
under the orders of the Accountant-Gieneral. As 
a matter of practice, however, authorities from this 
office had been issued in many cases in the past on 
Government orders sanctioning allotment of 
funds even in the case of loans, viz., loans under 
Land Improvement Act, cattle purchase loan, etc., 


ns HE ee 


which were within the powers of sanction of 
authorities subordinate to Government. Since 
orders placing allotments cannot be treated as 


sanctions for the purpose of the aforementioned 
rule no authority from this office will be issued in 
such cases in future. Authorities; for payment 
will be issued by this office only in the case of 
loans and advances sanctioned by the severs! 
departments of the Government. 


All treasury officers in West Bengal should note 
the above for guidance.

AWARD. 


The Union claims for a bonus equivalent to 16 months’ wages for the 
year 1953, treating the accumulated reserves as a part of the profit for 
the year 1953, along with the trading profit for the relevant year. The 
issue that has been referred to this Tribunal for adjudication is as to 
the determination of the quantum of bonus for the year 1953, The 
financial year of the Company is from Ist April to the 3let March follow- 
ing. The question for decision in this issue is, therefore, the quantum 
of bonus payable by the Company for the year ended 3lst March 1953. 
The Company’s case is that they can pay bonus equivalent to 15 days’ 
basic wages, and no more.

Calcutta and the Bombay branches constitute the same Company, in 
calculating bonus, the balance-sheet of the Company as a whole, and 
not the balance-sheets of its branches, should be taken as the guiding 
principle. This principle has been enunciated by the Hon'ble Labour 
Appellate Tribunal in the case of Distillery & Brewery Workers’ Union 
versus Dyer Meakin Brewery, Ltd., Lueknow (1952 L.A.C., 464). The 
same principle has been Jaid dawn in Appeal cases Nos. Gal. 199 and

1951001) 1,147 page 613, and Appeal cases Nos. 53 and 54 of 1950, 
Indian Oxygen and Acetylene Co., 1۸١1, 1952 L.A.C., page 264, and 
Viswamitra Pregs and its workers, 1952 L.A.C., page 20. 1 is, 
therefore, decided that the claim of bonus of the workmen for the 
trading year ended 9181 March 1953 should be decided on the balance- 
sheet of the whole Company, and net on the balance-sheet of the Caleuttu 
branch alone, 


The statement of the Union that the Company paid Puja bonus 
equivalent to one month’s basic wage for the last 12 years or ao, hus not 
been pressed before me at the time of the hearing as the foundation of a 
eustomary bonus or as a condition of service of the workmen. The 
vidence of Shri J. 0. Biswas, clearly shows that the factory workers got 
more than one month’s basic pay as bonus about 3 or 4 ০78 ago. The 
Union claims bonus out of the reserves which were capitalised in 
October 1952, on the ground that these reserves were built out of the 
profit of the previous years on which the workers had a claim. The 
claim of a share of the reserves which were capitalised in 1952 hy way 
of bonua is of no substance. The Union can ء181٥‎ bonus only out of the 
trading profits of the year ended March 1958 to enable them to participate 
in the prosperity of the concern in the relevant year. There cannot be 
any right to bonus on consideration of social justice other than those 
incorporated in the Full Bench decision (1954 1..A.C., 257). This Full 
Bench decision is 11) the case of Mill Owners’ Association, Bombay 
(1952 L.A.C., page 438).

It has been stated before me at the time of the argument by the 
representative of the Company that one month’s basic wage for the 
Calcutta workmen would amount to Rs. 26,000 and one month’s basic 
wage for the Bombay branch would amount to Rs. 21,000. Rs. 47,000 
is the total monthly basic wage of the Bombay and the Calcutta branches. 
Considering, however, the large risk and uncertain prospect im the 
automobile trade, and that a higher rate of dividend than at 6 per cent. 
capital is justified, as has been observed by the Hon’ble Appellate 
Tribunal in the case of Metro Motors, reported in 1962(11) L.L.J., 206, 
I consider that the employees are entitled to 14 months’ basic 
wage, and no more, out of the surplus as found above. It is, therefore, 
awarded that the Company shall pay to the workmen bonus equivalent 
to 1 months’ basic wage for the year ended 918 March 1953. The 
employees shall therefore get bonus equivalent to 3/24th of the total 
basic wages earned by each of them during the year ended 3lst Mar¢h 
1953. This issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 2. 


The question for decision is, if the employees are eligible to get incre- 
' ments annually, and if so, what would be the rate of increment. In the 
written statement, the Union states that the workmen are covered by 
grades and scales of pay laid down by the award of the Major 
Engineering Tribunal and as subsequently modified by the agreement 
between the parties in November 1949. The Union further states that the 
Company violated the terms of the said award and agreement in_ not 
granting increment, in granting increment at lesser rate than prescribed, 
and in granting at intervals far in excess of one prescribed in the award 
and agreement. The agreement mentioned by the Union is set forth in 
the Annexure A to the Union’s written statement. It allows to all old 
members of the clerical staff who on the 3lst March 1949, had completed 
12 months’ service, and were drawing basic salary of less than HRs. 100 per 
month, an increment of 10 per cent of the basic pay. In other cases, the 
increments were to be given on the recommendations of the departmental 
heads. This increment was in lieu of the increment which normally 
should have been given on the Ist of April 1949. This increment was 
limited to the clerical staff of the Company. The Union im its written 
statement claimed for u revision of the pay scales of the clerical staff, and 
claimed the following scales :— 

A—Ks. 160—15—300. 

B—Rs. 110—10—200. 

C—Rs. 75—5—150. 

D—Rs. 70—4—130. 


Special grade—Hs. 160 and upwards. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 3109 
সপ 


The Union also claimed that the Company should compensate for 
increments wherever it was withheld or paid at lesser rate than provided 
for in the award and the agreement in the years 1948 to 1952, and also 
to pay the workmen increment as per scaies of pay mentioned above. 


The Company in its written atutement pleaded that the increment 
was not automatic, and it exercised its right as sud when necessary in 
withholding increment, and even refusing the same and that, by the 
agreement mentioned in the Union’s written statement, the position was 
further clarified. 1 is claimed that the workera by that settlement 
accepted a lump sum, and thus indicated that the increment was not 
automatic. The said agreement was still effective between the parties. 
The question of annual increment cannot be adjudicated upon. The 
Company states that in view of the financial position of the Company, no 
increment should be given. 


The Company and its workmen were parties to the First Major 
Engineeri Tribunal. The scales of pay with increments as fixed for 
the clerical staff by that award are applicable to the clerical staff of the 
Company. The four grades, A, B, and D for the clerical staff as 
fixed by the Firat Major Engineering Tribunal shall continue to apply 
to the clerical staff, and I do not find any ground for revising the scales 
of pay as claimed by the Union. The issue that was referred to this 
Tribunal does not justify revision of the grades and scales of pay as 
claimed by the Union. The claim for revision of the grades and scales 
of pay of the clerical staff is therefore rejected. It is awarded that 
the employees shall get increment annually as provided for by the First 
Major Engineering Tribunal. The Company is entitled to withhold 
increments for a justifiable cause. The claim of the Union that an 
award should be made directing the Company to compensate tor the 
increment wherever it has been withheld or paid at lesser rate cannot be 
allowed, as this claim is not covered by the issue referred to this 
Tribunal, There is no doubt that increments were refused on the Ist 
April 19538, and the Company’s plea is that increments were not 
automatic, and as the agreement mentioned in the Annexure A to the 
Union’s written statement was in force, no increment could be claimed. 
The agreement of November 1949, which merged in the award published 
by the Government notification No. 6236Lab., dated 7th December 1949, 
was not in operation for more than one year, and was not, therefore, still 
operative between “the parties. As there is no ground 60 refuse 
increment to any of the employees to whom the pay and scales are 
applicable, it is awarded that the clerical stuff and the subordinate staff 
who have not reached the maximum of their grades shall get increment 
৪৪ provided for in the scales laid down in the First Engineering Tribunal

By Government order No. 1212Dis./D/131-6/54, dated 24th March 
1964, the aforesanl dispute was referred to thig Tribunal for ndjadication. 
The issue framed by the (fovernment was the same as the issue framed by 
the Tribuna] and it was as follows: 


1. Whether the termination of service of Shri Oma Prasanna 
Bhattacharjee is justified? What relief he is entitled to? 


Notice of the aforesaid dispute having been served on the parties the 
Union filed its written statement on 9th April 1954 and the Company filed 
its written statement on 23rd April 1954. 


The case for the Union is that Shri Uma Prasanna Bhattacharji is only 
48 years and 11 months old and has a very strong constitution, that he was 
a first witness in a case before the Tribunal between the Company on the 
one hand and Makhan Lal Adhikari, an employee of the firm, on the other 
hand, that his evidence in the 0088 was considered by the management to 
be adverse to their interest and hence he had been often called a ‘fifth 
columnist”? by the Manager, who threatened to drive out all the fifth 
columnists from the office, that to this the worker mildy protested, but 
subsequently on Ist of December 1943 he was served with a notice which 
purports to put him 01) the pension list, that this discontinuation of his 
service was unjustified and prompted by ulterior motive aml he wus entitled 
to reinstatement. 


The Company, on the other hand, éohtended that it had × pension 
scheme under which an employee who has been in service not less than 5 
years would be entitled to pension and the Company has _ absolute 
right to put a man in the pension list, that the scheme had been a condition 
of service all along as the company in all good faith had the worker put in 
the pension list, that this is not a case of dismissal or retrenchment and 
as such no case of reinstatement arises. 


AWARD. 


‘I'he question that arises for decision at the outset is whether in ao case 
like this, the prayer for reinstatement is tenable. The law on the point 
is very clear. In the case of Bengal Chemica] & Pharmaceutical Works, 
Ltd., and their workmen, Shri S. N. Modak pointed out that apart from 
cases of ordinary discharge there may be cases of discharge under the 
circumstances of the closure of the concern, retrenehment, etc., where an 
Tndustrial Tribunal is entitled to exercise its power in the interests of 
social justice and peaceful industrial relations and may award suitable 
compensation such as an ordinary Court of Law would not be entitled to do 
(1949 ہا‎ 14. J., page 49). The present case is practically a case of refusal 
to employ a workman and as such it is an industrial dispute. The 
principles involved in cases in which there may be reinstatement has been 
discussed in the cases of Western India Automobile Association vs, Indus- 
trial Tribunal of Bombay and others in the following terms: “An indus- 
trial dispute may arise in any one of the 4 cases :— 


(1)... هو یہی‎ @eeencne Pes সকল নুসানুজর ল PASSES 2৯, ॥ 

کہ یب می می تو ہہت ٣ت‏ 

(3)...........An employer may dismiss a person or decline to employ 
him. This matter, as in the present case, raises o dispute as to 
non-employment. 


(4)........(See West Bengal Government, Publication of 1949, Federal 
Court Judgment, pages 4 and §). ۱ 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 $113 


SS সীল 


This is also the law in other countries. Tn Canadian Law, promotions, 
demotions, transfer, rehiring have been treated on the sume principle. (See 
Labour Relations and Precedence in Canada, page 264). 


In America also the law is the same (ade Ludwig Tellers—Luabour 
Disputes and Collective Bargaining, Volume TI, page 861), where it 8 
stated that Board has uniformly held that refusal to hire applicants for 
employment......... is an act of discrimination. In consideration of the law 
on the subject, 1, therefore, hokd that the present case comes within the 
purview of an industrial dispute and the only relief available to' such cases 
will be reinstatement and compensation. Company’s 0089 in the written 
statement with regard to the present workman is that the company has an 
absolute right to put a man in the pension list under the pension scheme 
which is a condition of service. This contention of the company can have 
no legs to stand upon in view of the statement of the Manager that pension 
rules submitted were never circulated in print. Under the Omnibus Press 
Tribunal to which the present employers were parties it has been laid 
down that under the standing orders all workmen shal] retire ordinarily 
on completion of 55th vear of their age. If any workman ie considered 
fit. even after completion of 55th year of his age he may, on his application, 
be given an extension not exceeding three years, provided no retrenchment 
is called for in the meuntime. No workman who 35 physically fit shall 
be made to retire. In the present case the worker is only 48 years 11 
months old according to his Matriculation Certificate and he appears to be 
quite fit. Company does not either controvert hia statement regarding his 
age or regarding his fitness for work. Company only says that 16 has an 
absolute right to put a man in the pension list umler the pension scheme 
which is a condition of service. But the alleged pension scheme is obviously 
against the standing orders and in order to prove the existence of such a 
scheme there must be definite and positive evidence that the scheme was 
in force in supersession of the standing orders. But the evidence falls far 
short of the mark. As an afterthought ‘Mr. Wilks wanted to say that it 
was circulated but he has failed to prove his statements by production of 
office records. In view of the case of the worker that he has been victimised 
by giving him early pension against the standing order, the onus lay heavily 
on the empioyers to show that the pension scheme was a_ condition of 
service and that the company acquired the right to retire people previous to 
hig attaining 55th year of age which is the age of retirement according to 
the standing orders. Appreciating this difficulty O.P.W.1 tried to change 
his case at the time of trial and said that this is a case of genuine financial 
stringency which has led to his retrenchment in consideration of the period 
of service of 17 yeors. But there is no iota of evidence to show that 
retrenchment was justified on the ground of economy. No such case was 
also put forward in the Company’s written statement and it was also 
asserted by the workers that no such case was put forward at the time of 
conciliation, So the company cannot take up this new position which is 
inconsistent with his written statement and his past conduct. Further to 
support this new case there is no evidence. That being s0, we are only left 
to accept the evidence of the worker that he has been put in the pension list 
because the evidence given by him in Makhan [Tal Adhikari’s case was 
not helpful to the Manager. Mr. Wilks admitted that Makhan Lal 
Adhikari’s case centred round the point whether or not charge sheets were 
delivered to him. Uma Prasanna was cited to prove delivery of charge 
sheet. But admittedly his evidence did not help the management. A 
perusal of the statement giveh by Uma Prasanna in that case read with the 
judgment of the Tribunal gives full support to this contention of the 
employee. He haa been put in the pension list because he has deposed 
against the company in Makhan Lal’s case. Even the list submitted by

The employee, Shri Sailendra Nath Mitra, in his written statement 
states as follows:— 


He joined the Company on Ist April 1932, on a salary of Rs. 35 per 
month as a Clerk-Typist in the Collection Department. He was promoted 
as an Accountant at the Calcutta Divisional Office in 1939 at a monthly 
salary of Rs. 80. He got substantial increments and in the beginning 
of 1953, his basic salary~ was Rs. 300 and his dearness allowance was 
Rs. 190) per month. In May 1952, he was placed in charge of commission 
bill copies with transmittal sheets, and he was doing work in connection 
with commission and other account works as and when asked for. He 
was doing his works satisfactorily under instructions of Shri G. Krishnan, 
Accountant, Mr, George Devlin, Administrative Officer, and Mr. D. J.

sent for him und asked him to submit his resignation, in default of whic!

service with immediate effect. Shri Mitra did not accept the salary as 
offered. It is complained that the Company lost confidence in 
Shri Mitra, because he followed Mr. Deog’s instructions regarding 

ayment of commission and he sold Company’s goods in 1946 under his 
etter head. It is pleaded that no proceedings were drawn against him 
before dismissal, and he was not given any opportunity of showing cause 
against the charge brought against him, and the principles of natural 
justice were not followed. It is, therefore, stated that the Company 
committed an unfair labour practice in dismissing him. 


The Company, in its written statement, states as follows :— 


Shri এ. N. Mitra, joined the Company on Ist April 1932 as a typist- 
clerk at a monthly salary of Rs. 36. Prior to July 1952 Shri Mitra was 
in the Accounts Office of the Calcutta Accounting Division, but on the 
2th July 1952 this was merged with the Head Office Accounts Depart- 
ment and Shri Mitra became redundant. Under a scheme of reorganisa- 
tion, Shri Mitra was assigned the duty of dealing with the calculation 
of Salesman Commission, and was made responsible to the Administrative 
Officer, Mr. Devlin, and the Accountant Shri Krishnan. The procedure 
is that the Salesmen enter their names on Sales Orders at the time these 
are prepared. Commission copies of the bills with transmittal sheets 
were then passed to Shri Mitra. Shri Mitra had to check the transmittal 
sheets and ensure that all bills listed therein were attached. He had 
then to compute the amount of commission earned by salesmen and 
enter these on each copy of the Commission bill. A proportion of

commission bills were received by Shri Mitra, which did not show on 
them the name of any Salesman as being responsible for the sale. This 
occurred more particularly in the case of service. Hilling where no 
commission is paid when the businees is obtained by the Service Department 
or direct without the intervention of a Salesman. In such cases, no com- 
mission was paid. It was discovered on examination of commimasion bills

Mitra had never had the approval of the Company or its officers. Under 
the circumstances, the Company prays that Shri Sailendra Nath Mitra’s 
prayer for reinstatement or compensation be rejected.

; ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of complaints under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, as amended by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 
1950, filed by Bikram Misra, Haripada Chakraborty, Ramji Singh, Indradeo 
Singh and Ramkailas, against Messrs. McLeod & Co., Ltd., Secretaries, 
Tea Districts Labour Association, Calcutta, Post Box No. 78, Calcutta, 
represented by Tea Districts Labour Association Employees’ Union, post 
office Naihaty, 24-Parganas (Case Nos. 179, 187 under section 33A of 
1952), 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL. 


PRESENT : 

Sunt MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 
Tribunal. 
Appearances : 


For the Company: Shri J. K. Ghosh, Advocate, instructed by Messrs. Orr. 
Dignam & Co., Solicitors. 


For the Union: Shri P. K. Sanyal, Advocate, assisted by Shri N. Roy, Pleader. 


When the reference case under Government order No. 1511Dis./D/9L- 
15/52, dated 29th May 1952, was pending in the Tribunal the employer, viz., 
McLeod & Co., Ltd., Secretaries, Tea Districts Labour Association, transferred 
five chalan peons from their Naihaty branch to Shahebganj branch. The 
Shahebganj branch is in Bihar. Reference case included among the disputes, 
the question of wage scale and dearness allowance of chalan peons in branches, 
viz., Asansol, Kharagpur and Naihaty in Bengal. Admittedly, no such dispute 
was then pending in Bihar in respect of chalan peons. The transferred chalan 
peons Ramji Singh, Indradeo Singh and Ramkailas are the petitioners under 
section 33A being the serial number 27 in the file of this Tribunal. The other 
transferred chalan peons, viz., Bikram Misra and Haripada Chakraborty are the 
petitioners under section 33A being the serial No. 25 in the file of this Tribunal. 
The case is involved in identical questions of fact and law and the evidence was 
being the same. These two cases were taken up together for hearing. The ques- 
tion is whether the aforesaid transfer of the chalan peons from Naihaty to Shaheb- 
-ganj during the pendency of the original case without obtaining any permission 
of the Tribunal is hit by section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act and whether 
the said transfer orders were by way of punishment of these chalan peons or had 
the effect of altering their service condition. 


AWARD. 


From the evidence I find that at the time of the transfer order there were ten 
chalan peons at Naihaty branch and that after these five petitioners were trans- 
ferred to Shahebganj the strength of the chalan peons at Naihaty came down to 
five. Subsequently, one Vandari has been promoted to the rank of chalan peon 
and, therefore, the total strength of chalan peons at Naihaty is now six. It 
also appears from the evidence that before these five chalan peons from Naihaty 
joined at Shahebganj on transfer there were only four chalan peons at that place. 
It also appears from the evidence that the work at Shahebganj is heavier than 
that at Naihaty and that at Shahebganj also the said branch was working with a 
shortage of three chalan peons at that time because those three were dismissed. 
Therefore, it is obvious that there were sufficient reasons for transferring these 
five chalan peons from Naihaty to Shahebganj at that time. It is not the 


3124 গু CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 [Paar I 
৬২২০-২১-২৯ 


suggestion of the petitioners that any discrimination has been made 8779087251 the 
chalan peons at Naihaty in the matter of selecting the personnel to be transferred 
to Shahebganj. It also appears from the evidence that chalan peons are trans- 
terred by the employers trom one place to another if and when necessity arises. 
It is admitted that some chalan peons were transferred from Nathaty to Asansol, 
from Naihaty to Lalmonirhat and from Naihaty to Kharagpur. Moreover the 
management has right to transfer the workmen from department to another or 
from one branch to another and such transfer can be challenged before a Tribunal 
only if it is shown that it is discrminatory and that it is mala fide and with the 
ulterior motive to victimize the workmen concerned. If there is no such guilty 
intention or object on the part of the employer, such transfer cannot be 
challenged simply because it has the effect of causing some disadvantages or 
injury to the workman under order of transfer. It has not been shown that 
these petitioners or any chalan peon at Naihaty had as their service condition 
any such term that they were not liable to be transferred to any place from 
Naihaty or to any place outside Bengal. The normal rule is as I have already 
observed that the management has the right to transfer a workman from 
from department to department or from one station to another and it has been 
held in several cases that such transfer does not amount to be a change of any 
condition of service within the meaning of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. 


When it is a fact that in Bihar no such reference case regarding the wage 
scale and dearness allowance of the chalan peons was pending, when these five 
petitioners were transferred from Naihaty to Shahebganj and when it is a fact 
that the reference case when pending in the Calcutta Tribunal has led to an 
award raising the wage scale of the chalan from Rs. 25—-1—32 to Rs. 30—1—45, 
and that the dearness allowance has been raised from Rs. 25 to Rs. 30 as the 
minimum, it goes without saying that the petitioners on being transferred from 
Naihaty to Shahebganj shortly before the passing of the said award were 
deprived of the benefit of the said prospective award regarding their wage 
scale and dearness allowance. It is however admitted that before this Calcutta 
Tribunal award was passed the wage scale and dearness allowance of chalan 
peons at Naihaty and Shahebganj were the same. But I have already held that 
these transfers were for sufficient and valid reason and that there Is no sugges- 
tion that these five chalan peons were discriminated against. If the employers 
had any such guilty intention in their mind to deprive the Naihaty chalan peons 
of the benefits under the prospective award in the said pending adjudication 
procecding the employer could have easily transferred the whole lot from 
Naihaty to this or that branch in Bihar. Moreover it is a difficult question to 
decide even if the employer makes any such transfer order with such object in 
view because I find that the court did not interfere with the actions taken by the 
persons for avoiding Estate Duty taking ই of the loop-holes in the said 
act. As for example, in 1950—2 K.B. page 429, Jenkins L.J. observed; 


“There is nothing unlawful in a scheme designed to minimise the incidence 
of duty by legal means.” 


In 1908—2 K.B. page 729, Farewell L.J. observed; 


“I know of no law which prevents a man from avoiding a duty which has 
not attached to the property in any way not forbidden by the Act.” 


In 1926—A.C. page 395, Lord Sumner observed : 


“The subject is entitled so to arrange his affairs as not to attract taxes 
imposed by the Crown, so far as he can do so within the law.” 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 4 3126 
eA ہت سس سس س‎ ROR OO aE NE SP nO گ‎  گ‎ TERR A aC De A ET 

My <Hnclusion is that these transfer orders were not hit by section 33 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act and, therefore, the applications under section 33A of the 
Industrial Disputes Act are hereby rejected. The Company’s circular Ex. A 
does not indicate that the transfer of any workman would depend on the consent 
or option of the employee concerned. The word “willing” in the said document 
I think means not consent but an element of compulsion. The wording was not 
a happy one but its meaning as interpreted above is clear. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

In the matter of an application for interim relief filed by one Shri J. M. Sen

Union, 7, Old Court House Street, Calcutta, against Messrs. May & Baker 
(India), Ltd., 7, Old Court House Street, Calcutta.

SHRI MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 
Tribunal, 
Appearances : 


For the workmen: Shri P. Ghosh, Secretary, Federation of Mercantile 
Emplayces’ Union. ' 


For the Company: Shri D. Basu Thakur, Solicitor, of Messrs. Orr Dignam & Co, 


3126 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 [Part 1 
৯৯৯১৯৯৯৯৯৯৯ 


_The original reference out of which this present application for ۰ interim 
relief has arisen was made under Government order No. 6012Dis./D/11L- 
293/53, dated 30th December 1953, and subsequent order No. 700Dis./D/ 
11L-293/53, dated 13th February 1954, 


J. M. Sen Gupta, has been suspended by the employer, viz., May & Baker 
(India), Ltd., by an order, dated 8th October 1953 and he was suspended with 
effect from that date “until further notice”. It is now said that the employer 
has recently filed a petition under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for 
permission to dismiss the said employee. The reference case as well as 33 
application both are pending. The employee Shri J. M. Sen Gupta now applies 
for interim relief as the reference case is not likely to be heard in the near 
future. He prays that he may be paid 4 of his wages per month from the 
date of his suspension order till final disposal of the reference case. 


On behalf of the Company it is contended that such interim relief cannot be 
granted by the Tribunal as the application section 33 of the Industrial Disputes 
Act is now pending and that the Tribunal cannot pre-judge the question as to 
whether the suspension order is justified or not. 


INTERIM AWARD. 


I do not think that the*granting of interim relief as prayed for at all depends 
upon the question as to whether the suspension order is justified or not. If it 
be law that even on the assumption that the suspension order was justified, that 
the employee under suspension is legally entitled to have some subsistence 
allowance apart from compensation for unemployment or loss of earnings jin 
case the suspension order be found in the final decision to be unjustified, there jis 
no bar to grant of such ad-interim relief and the only point for consideration 
would be as to what should be the quantum of such relief. In the reference case 
the issue is whether suspension is justified or not and what relief is 
the suspended employee entitled to. Therefore it indicates that the 
question of suspension being 22) or not and the question 
of compensation for the period of unemployment cannot now ০০ pre- 
judged, but the Tribunal has ample jurisdiction to decide if on the 
assumption that the suspension is justified any allowance is to be paid (0 the 
suspended employce until final decision of the case. This depends upon the 
state of law on this matter. If it is a settled law that even under justified sus- 
pension the employee is entitled to get some subsistence allowance I should hold 
that the petitioner J; M. Sen Gupta should get it as interim relief. 


It is obvious that he is now without any employment or earning and that he 
is hard to put to it and on account of want of funds for maintaining himself and 
his farnily during this suspension period. It is admitted that his contribution 
towards the Provident Fund amounts to Rs. 411 and that amount is payable to 
him even if he is dismissed in the long run. Regarding the state of the law, 
I think, the decision in the case of Wallwork vs. Fielding (1922) 2 K.B., page 
66 : “that suspension suspends for the time being, the contractual relation between 
the parties on both sides” was arrived at after distinguishing the case of Hanley 
vs. Pease (1915) 1 K.B., page 698, in which case therc was no power of sus- 
pension but only a power of dismissal; but in the case of Wallwork vs. Fielding, 
there was the power to suspend. In the present case there is no Standing Order 
and there is no suggestion that the employer is expressly entitled by any Standing 
Order or by any contract to suspend, and not only to suspend but also to with- 
hold the wages during the period of suspension. So I should réfer to the decision 
in the case of Warburton vs. Taffvale Railway Company (1902) 18 T.L.R., 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 3127 


০1১ come 


page 420. That case was not at.all referred to in the case of Wallwork vs. 
Fielding. In Warburton vs. Tafivale Railway Company’s case it was held that— 


“Where an employer is entitled to suspend an employee and withhold his 
wages during the period of suspension, the employee is entitled to 
wages during the period of suspension even if he is dismissed at 
the end of that period”: 


Jn view of this state of law on the subject and in view of the fact that there is 
nothing to show that the employer had authority to suspend or to withhold 
wages during the suspension period, it seems to be obvious that the employee is 
legally entitled to get subsistence allowance during the period of suspension. 
The claim for arrears of subsistence allowance from the date of suspension order 
up to this date cannot be maintained under this application for interim relief. 
Interim relief can be granted only from this date. It is ordered that the employer 
shall pay one-third of the basic wages and of dearness allowance to the petitioner 
per month as subsistence allowance during the period of suspension until the 
disposal of the reference casc or until further orders and that the first payment 
shall be made within the first weck of September 1954. 


MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 
District Judge,

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A by Shri Netai Chandra Karmakar, 
Assistant Secretary, Surgical Workers’ Union, alleging that during the pendency 
of adjudication proceedings before the Tribunal and in contravention of section 
33 of the Industrial Disputes Act, the Company, opposite party, declared lock-out 
of the factory from 11th May 1954. 

The Company, opposite party, by a written objection contended that the 
complaint was not maintainable as it was not made by the aggrieved workmen 
but by the Union. 

The point which therefore arises for determination is, whether the complaint 
under section 33A is maintainable. 


DECISION. 

The case was received by transfer from the Fourth Tribunal after the original 
reference was withdrawn from the said Tribunal and sent by Government to this 
Tribunal for adjudication. 

Section 33A enables only an employee, aggrieved by alleged contravention, 
to make a complaint in writing in the prescribed manner. It therefore, follows that 
a trade union or any person other than the aggrieved workman is not competent to 
make the complaint under section 33A. 1۱× the present case the complaint was 
made by Shri Netai Chandra Karmakar, Assistant Secretary of the Union, and 
not by the aggrieved workmen themselves. The complaint as it is, is, therefore, not 
maintaintable and must fail. I award accordingly.

INTERIM AWARD. 


This is an application of the suspended employee Surul Haque for interim 
relief during the pendency of his application under Section 33A. The original 
reference was pending when the employer after cay ase him made an appli- 
cation under section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act for permission to dismiss 
him on the ground of doing wilful mischief to the tray of the factory. In the 
Section 33 case my finding was that is was a case of accident and not of wilful 
mischief. The application under Section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act was 
rejected.

The employer has preferred an appeal against the said order of re¢‘ection. 
Appeal is pending before the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal. The aver 
also applied before the Appellate Tribunal under Section 22 for permission to 
retrench some employees including this petitioner, Surul Haque, and that appli- 
cation is still pending. After the award has been passed in the nt pies case, 
the employer preferred an appeal against the said award and the said appeal is 
also pending and im the said appeal an at ee prayed for stay of execution of 
the award but the prayer has been turned down. 


In Section 33 proceeding I also found the order of suspension of the peti- 
tioner for an indefinite period of time and without any allowance whatsocver 
to him, was nothing but punishment. On the basis of that finding it seems that 
the petitioner Suru! Haque applied for interim relief against the employer in 
the application under Section 33A. By an order, dated Ist July 1954, 1 have 
stayed the proceeding under Section 33A until the appeal of Section 33 proceed- 
ing is disposed of by the Appellate Tribunal. Thereafter the employee (peti- 
tioner) has made this present application for interim relief, viz., payment of 
wages or allowances during the pendency of Section 33A proceedings. The 

uestion is whcther such ad-interim relief can be granted by me at this stage. 

think that for the same reason for which I had to stay Section 33A proceed- 
ing, the present application also is to be rejected because if the ت۳"‎ succeeds 
and my decision that the suspension order in the circumstances of this case has 
been a punishment is set aside, the interim relief, if any, if granted at present, 
will also be affected. Moreover, I do not find any provision in the Industrial 
Disputes Act of 1947 for granting any interim relicf. “AWARD” as has been 
defined in the Act, means an interim or final determination by an Industrial 
Tribunal of any industrial dispute or of any question relating thereto; that is 8 
different thing altogether from interim relief as has been prayed for in _ this 
case. Moreover the claim for compensation as made in the petition undef 
Section 33A has been contested by the employer and therefore in view of the 
principles laid in A.I.R. 1953, Madras, page 420, the Tribunal cannot give any 
Award at this stage—money or compensation in favour of the petitioner until the 
claim is decided, and the said claim can only be decided at the time of final 
hearing of the case. It could be claimed by the Tribunal as a term of an 
interlocutory relief if such prayer were made by the opposite party or if suc 
interlocutory relief were prayed for by the petitioner in a proper case and if the 
Tribunal thought it proper not to grant the said prayer provided the opposite 
party were agreeable to do or pay something as consideration for rejection of 
the petitioner’s prayer. Suppose, plaintiff in a suit, prays for appointment of 
a receiver, in such a case the Court can put down certain terms. In a proper 
case it can appoint receiver, and it can also as an alternative case order 
defendant to pay something to the plaintiff ad-interim as a condition to rejection 
of the plaintiff's prayer. In the present case nothing of this kind has happened; 
therefore my opinion is that the claim for interim payment of compensation in 
the shape of wages and allowances, etc., is to be rejected. So the application is 
rejected.

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act by 
Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari, a Durwan attached to the Budge Budge Installation

of the Company. He has been living in Company's quarters eve® now. 
The complaint was filed on 8th June 1954, long after ter- 
mination of the proceedings before this Tribunal in respect 
of the industrial dispute between the Company, opposite party, and 
their employees relating to bonus for 1951, and during pendency of 
appeal against the award, the dispute was referred by the Government to this 
Tribunal for adjudication by order dated 12th June 1953. 


Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari was admittedly arrested by the Port Police on 
20th December 1953 on charges of theft of two sliding wrenches, two double 
ended spanners, one length of jute chord and one old paint drum from the Budge 
Budge Installation. Subsequently he was released on bail. The Company 
alleged that before this the complainant, Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari, had 
received warning on 22nd August 1953 for removing coal from railway wagon. 


On 19th January 1954 the Company, opposite party, admittely issued 
charge sheet against ‘Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari on charges of theft and mis- 
appropriation of the property in the circumstances as found by the police. Shri 
Man Bahadur Chhetari replied to the charges on 22nd January 1954. 


Thereafter on 25th January 1954 police sent up Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari 
for trial. On that day (25th January 1954), the award relating to the dispute 
between the Company and their employees regarding bonus was made and 
signed. 


On ist February 1954 the Company, opposite party, served a notice of 
enquiry regarding the charges on Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari. Then the award 
relating to the dispute between the Company and their employees was published 
in the Calcutta Gazette on 18th ene 1954. By the award it was found 
that the labour and security staff of the Installations at Budge Budge and other 
places to which category the complainant Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari admittedly 
belongs had received their bonuses for the year in question in 0011 and final 
settlement of their claim on the basis of settlement and that the reference was 
limited in its application only to the clerical and the subordinate staff and not 
to the labour and security staff of the Installations. 


On 19th February 1954 the Company held enquiry into the charges against 
Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari when the lawyer of Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari was 
present. On 25th February 1954 the officer holding the enquiry recommended 
dismissal of Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari. On the 8th of March 1954 101 
Manager of the Company passed order among others as below :— : 

“It is no longer possible for the Management to excuse and condone your 
action and, as such, I order that you will be dismissed from the 
Company’s service for misconduct with effect from March 10, 1954. 
Furthermore, your suspension from 19th January 1954 to 9th March 
1954 will be without pay.” 


The complainant alleged that in view of the aforesaid order his cause of action 
for the complaint under section 33A had arisen on 10th March 1954 as the pro- 
ceedings were still then pending and as the Company did not obtain permission 
from the Tribunal previously. 


On 16th March 1954 an appeal was filed on behalf of the workmen to the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal against the award. On 26th March 1954 the Presi- 
dency Magistrate, before whom Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari was being prose- 
cuted, discharged Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari of the charges brought against him

judgment). 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 4 3133 


০১-০০-১০০৬ 

On 8th June 1954 the present complaint under section 33A was filed by Shri 
Man Bahadur Chhetari before this Tribunal during the pendency of appeal 
against the award. On 26th June 1954 the Company made reply to the said 
complaint. On 3rd August 1954 the Company made application before the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal seeking permission under section 22 of the Industrial 
Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, to dismiss Shri Man Bahadur 
Chhetarl. The appeal against the award regarding bonus is admittedly pending. 


Behind this background, the Company, opposite party, contends that the 
complaint under section 33۸ is not maintainable. The preliminary objection as 
aforesaid was only heard at the request of the parties. 


* DECISION. 


After giving careful consideration to the arguments advanced on either side, 
I may straightaway note that Company’s objection should prevail. Although I 
agree that there is no time limit fixed for making a complaint either under 
section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act or under section 23 of the Industrial 
Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, it does not, however, mean that an 
aggrieved workman can make a complaint at any time at his pleasure. In the 
absence of any time limit, the complaint must be made within a reasonable time of 
the occurrence (vide 1954, L.L.J., Vol. I, page 676). In the present case the 
complaint under section 33A was filed on 8th June 1954 long after termination 
of the proceedings before this Tribunal. The award was published on 18th 
February 1954. So the proceedings in view of section 20(3) read with section 
17A must be deemed to have concluded on 18th March 1954. The complainant 
has given no explanation whatever in his application under section 33A for the 


inordinate delay. 

Then the original reference has been found applicable only to the clerical and 
subordinate staff and not to the service and security and labour staff of the 
Installations at Budge Budge and other places to which category the complain- 


ant, Shri Man Bahadur Chhetari, belongs. So he cannot be said to have been 
concerned in the original dispute. It being so, section 33 or as a matter of that 


section 33A is not attracted. 


Last of all, to avoid conflicting decisions and having regard to the fact that the 
complainant would have opportunity to vindicate himself in answer to the appli- 
cation of the Company under section 22 before the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal, 
apart from his other remedy, I think, I should not proceed with the complaint 


under section 33A even if it is otherwise regular. 


In this view of the matter, I think, that the complaint under section 33A must 
fail. 1 award accordingly.

Issue No. 4, 


The six workmen were laid off with effect from 19th March 1953. The 
workmen represented by Surgical Workers’ Union alleged that the workmen 
were laid off on extraneous considerations outside the domain of bona fide 
trade reasons. They accordingly prayed that the workmen should be taken 
back to their posts and paid full wages for the period they were laid off. 


The Company on the other hand alleged that owing to shortage of work 
ind for bona fide trade reasons it had to lay off the six workers and not on 
*xtraneous considerations. The Company accordingly submitted that the claim 
١۶ the workmen should be rejected. 


During hearing the learned representative of the workmen, however, sub- 
mitted that as the business was since altogether closed, he would not just then 
press for re-employment and that the workmen would be satisfied if they were 
ie involun unemployment relief at the discretion of the Tribunal with 
irection that if and when the business was re-started the workmen should be 
ken back according to seniority in service as and when necessary, The Com- 
any as a gesture of goodwill expressed that it had no objection to such grant 
f involuntary unemployment relief to the workmen and that it had no objec- 
ion to take back the workmen according to necessity as and when the business 
as re-started. In the circumstances, I proceed to award compensation to the 


ix workmen without going into the question whether the lay-off was justified 
r not. 


Exhibit D is a statement which gives service period and wages of the six 
borkmen laid off. Keeping in view the provisions of the Industrial Disputes

(Amendment) Act, 1953 and considering the length of service of ٥۷۴۲1 
and other relevant factors, | award compensation as below, which I think to be 
fair: — 


Rs. a. 
(1) Shri Netai Chandra Karmakar ১১:90 0 
(ii) Shri Netai Chandra Hazari .. 24 0 
(iii) Shri Palan Chandra Karmakar te fe. .۹( 
(iv) Shri Pasupati Dutta .. 84 Q 
(v) Shri Jitendra Nath Das .. 67 8 
(vi) Shri Fani Bhusan Mite .. 74 12 


The Company is directed to pay the compensation as aforesaid, within a 
month from the date the award becomes enforceable. The Company is also 
to take back the workmen according to seniority in service and according to 
necessity as and when it re-started business. e notice calling the workmen 
to resume duty should be served on the workmen through the Union. The 
issue is accordingly decided. 


Issue No. 2. 


Regarding Shri Dhirendra Nath Roy.—The Company alleged that he along 
with Shri Kamal Kumar Acharyya were dismissed for gross insubordination 
and indiscipline. It was said that they not only assumed violence but also 
incited other workers to resort to violence and illegal strike and threatened the 
Management with breaking the costly machineries. The Company further 
alleged that as a result of the illegal strike the Management suffered loss. 
Exhibit A is the copy of the charge-sheet brought against the workman Shri 
Dhirendra Nath Roy. Exhibit Al is the copy of the explanation which the 
workman Shri Dhirendra Nath Roy submitted on 28th August 1953 in respect 
of the charges brought against him. He admitted his guilt unequivocally and 
expressed regret. Thus on his own admission Shri Dhirendra Nath Roy was 
rightly dismissed for gross misconduct. Workman Shri Dhirendra Nath Roy 
has not also come forward in this Tribunal to challenge his dismissal. I, there- 
fore, find nothing to interfere. As he has, however, expressed regret, the 
Management is to consider whether it can take him back as and when the busi- 


ness is re-started. 


Regarding Shri Kamal Kumar Acharyya.—He has since been re-instated on 
his expression of regret. 


Regarding Shri Amulya Das.—The evidence of the Factory Manager, 
D.W.1 Shri Sakti Kumar Mukherjee shows that there was strike in the factory 
once on 21st March 1953 and the other on 24th March 1953. It further 
appears that the workman Shri Amulya Das not only stopped the machines and 
incited other workmen to strike on 24th March 1953, but was also responsible 
for stay-in-strike on that day. The evidence further reveals that he assumed 
violent attitude towards the Factory Manager and abused him. In the 
circumstances, Shri Amulya Das was forthwith dismissed by notice, Exhibit 1. 
In the said notice the broad facts which occurred on that day including the 
one stay-in-strike, inciting the workmen to illegal strike and causing financial 
loss of the Company were stated. Workman Shri Amulya Das (P.W. 6) 
virtually admitted in cross-examination that he along with others resorted to 
stay-in-strike on that day inside the factory. In his examination-in-chicf he 
also stated that he wanted re-instatement and compensation not only for himself 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1964 3137 


but also-for all the co-workers. This would confirm the evidence of the Factory 
Manager that it was he who had incited the workmen to resort to stay-in-strike. 
The evidence further reveals that he had also struck work on 21st March 1953. 
In the circumstances if the Company had not proceeded against the other 
workers but only against him, this would not show discrimination but because 
he was the prime mover. The Company was within its right to pick up such 
workman for disciplinary action. No doubt the workman was not afforded 
opportunity to offer explanation before dismissal, but no serious view can be 
taken of it in view of the workman’s violent conduct and illegal and criminal 
act which required immediate action. If there was no formal enquiry before 
such dismissal, no grievance can be made of it either. When the occurrence 
took place in presence of the Factory Manager, there was no scope for further 
enquiry. The evidence before this Tribunal reveals that the workman was 
really guilty of gross misconduct. I am, therefore, of opinion that his dismissal 
was justified. 


Regarding Shri Nepal Chandra Karmakar.—According to both sides there 
was no such worker in this Company. Both sides also agree that the 
would be Palan Chandra Karmakar. His case has already been dealt with 


under issue No. 1. 
Regarding Shri Pasupati Dutta.—His case has also been dealt with under 


issue No. 1.

ANNEXURE. 


In the matter of a complaint under section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
filed by Dukhbaran, a workman of Shri Fulchand Singh, Labour Contractor 
of Messrs. Rallis (India), Ltd., represented by Cossipore Jute Press Workers’ 
Union, 1, Joy Bhattacherjee Lane, Calcutta-3, against the aforesaid 
Company (Case No. 3/33A of 1953). 


BEFORE THE SIXTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL, 
CALCUTTA. 


PRESENT : 


SHRi MOTILAL CHAKRAVATITI, District Judge, Judge, Sixth Industrial 
Tribunal. 
Appearances: 


For the Company: Shri N. K. Mookherjee, Advocate. 
For the workman: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee. 


The original reference out of which this present application under section 33A 
has arisen was made under Government Order Nos. 2180Dis./D/7L-44/52, 
dated 8th August 1952, read with 3062Dis./D/7L-44/52, dated 10th Novem- 
ber 1952, and subsequent order No. 4740Dis./D/7L-32/53, dated 12th Decem- 
ber 1953. 


Petitioner Dukhharan claims that he is an employee of Jute Press Contractor 
Fulchand (Labour contractor of Rallis India, Ltd.) and that in August 1952, he 
has been discharged without any reason whatsoever. 


The employer, opposite party, contends that the petitioner was never a 
worker under him and therefore no question of discharge arises and it is 
further contended that this employer was not a party in the main reference case 


and that no summons was received by him in the said proceeding, 


Neither party adduced any oral evidence, 


3140 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1964 [Parr ] 


————————— a / سس‎ 


AWARD. 


It is admitted that all the workers under Jute Press Contractors are casual 
workers but these casual workers are more or less regular workers although not 
permanent hands. The contractor docs not give any record of the regular 
workers who come and go back without finding work on any day. I think it is 
highly proper and advisable on the part of the employer, opposite party, to keep 
a panel of the regular casual workers who come and go back after the attendance, 
due to paucity of work on any day. 1۱ find from the award that this opposite 
party, the employer, was a party in the main reference case and that he appeared 
and filed written statement in that proceeding. It has not been shown by the 
employer that the petitioner never worked under him. The employer has not 
produced this record to support his contention. As the employer did not pro- 
duce records I should 11010 that the petitioner’s case is true. It cannot be 
accepted that the labourer like the petitioner would be in a position to produce 
any document unless the said document is furnished by the employer. It is 
admitted fact that Jute Press works casually and that on some days thcre is no 
work at all and that on some days some of the regular casual workers have to 
go back without finding any work, as there is no work available. In spite of 
these it is quite reasonable to expect that the employer would give work to 
such regular casual workers if and when work is available and to enter their 
attendance in a register in case they go back without finding any work on any 
day. In view of the circumstances I direct that the employer is to reinstate the 
petitioner Dukhharan when the latter will attend for doing work and in case 
such work is available. The petitioner shall not get any compensation for the 


period of unemployment. 


MOTILAL CHAKRAVATTI, 
District Judge, 
Judge, Sixth Industrial Tribunal. 


The 14th August 1954.

D. S. P. MUKHERJEE, Jt. Secy.

Petitioner’s case is that he is a clerk in Shiva Jute Press and that he has been 
dismissed in December 1953. So he wants reinstatement and compensation for 
loss of earnings from the time of his discharge. 


The contention of Shiva Jute Press is that the petitioner was never an 
employee of Shiva Jute Press and that the said Jute Press never discharged him. 
In the evidence it is made out that the petitioncr is an employee of Shiva Jute 
Baling, Limited, which is a separate limited concern, It is admitted by the 
petitioner that there is a business named Shiva Jute Baling business. He also 
admits that Prithwish Moitra was a clerk in Shiva Jute and that on some 
occasions he and Prithwish Moitra received payment of the salarics on the same 
date, but they signed two scparate acquittance registers. Petitioner did not sign 
the register in which Prithwish Moitra put his signature while receiving his salary. 
Petitioner also admits that he signed in different acquittance register because he 
was paid his salary from the Baling Department. is case is that Shiva Jute 
Baling Department is a department of Shiva Jute Press and not a separate 
limited concern, but the “Certificate of Incorporation” and the “Certificate for 
Commencement of business” granted to Shiva Jute Baling, Ltd., which have been

The following shall be the syllabuses of studies in the subjects mentioned 
below for the School Final Examination under the Commercial Course of the 
new curriculum adopted by the Board. The date of introduction of the 
syllabuses will be notified later on: 

SCHOOL FINAL EXAMINATION. 
Business Method and Correspondence. 
۔‎ 1. Business—sub-divisions into industry, trade and commerce. 


2. Different methods of business organisation—individual proprietorship— 
Partnership—Joint Stock System—Kinds of Joint Stock Companjes—Memoran- 
dum of Association—Articles of Association—Prospectus—An elementary 
knowledge of Joint Stock Companies procedure—Directors—Managing Agent. 

3. Internal Office Organisation—Receipt of Letters, Money Orders, 
remittance, etc.—Cash Department—Accounts Department—Purchase Depart- 
ment—-Sales Department—Type Section—Despatch Section—Record Section— 
Functions of Secretary. 

4. Office procedure—Treatment of incoming letters—Letter Registe 
Docketting—Precis writing—Office Notes—Preparing replies—Preserving i, 
—Filing and Indexing. 

5. Commercial Correspondence—Characteristics of business letters—Draft- 
ing Of advertisements, announcements, notices and telegrams. 

6. Meetings—Notices—Agenda—Minutes—Filing of Returns. 

7. Various modern office appliances and labour saving devices. 


8. Usual business forms—Receipts, Payment WVouchers—Cheques—Pay-in- 
Slip—Invoice—Bills for goods supply—Debit and Credit Notes. 


9. Usual books and registers maintained in Commercial Offices—Cash Book 
—Ledger—Journal—Stock  Register—Bill Register, Employees Attendance 
Register and Service Records. 


10. Banks—Definition—Current A/C, Fixed Deposit—Call Deposit— 
Overdraft—Hypothecation of goods. 


11. Elementary knowledge regarding booking of goods by common 
carriers including rail, steamer and ship. 


12. Shares, Debentures, Negotiable Instruments. 

13. Provident Fund, Gratuity, Bonus, Co-operative Societies. 

14. Insurance—Fire Insurance—Marine  Insurance—Fidelity Guarantee 
Bond—Cash in transit insurance—Workmen’s compensation—Employees State 
Insurance. 

15. Usual business terms and abbreviations. 

N.B.—Only elementary (and not detailed) knowledge regarding above items 
arc required. 


Commercial Geography. 
1. (A) The Scope of Commercial Geography: man and his environment. 
Principal factofs of environment:— 
(a) Physical: geographical location, mountains, rivers, coast-line; climate, 
soil, -animals, vegetation, minerals, etc. 
(b) Non-physical : population, political and social organisation, religion, 
etc. Adaptation of man to his environment; effects of environment 
on the economic life of man. Examples from Indian conditions.

Shorthand and Typewriting. 
A. Typewriting. 
Full marks for typewriting examination will be 50 and the pass marks will 


be 36 per cent. Candidates will be tested in three different question papers as 
mentioned below:— 


1. Ist Paper—Speed Test. Marks—30. 


Condition of test:— 
(a) Minimum speed required—25 words per minute. 
(b) A passage of 250 words to be set. 
(c) Time allowed—10 minutes. 
(d) Re-write the passage, if it is finished before the allotted time is 
called out. 


2. 2nd Paper—Tabulation Test. Marks-——10 


Condition of test:— 
(a) Time allowed—15 minutes. 
(b) If the student finishes before the allotted time is called out he 
should hand over the answer paper to the invigilators who will 
mark the time thereon. 


3. 3rd Paper—Accuracy Test. Marks—10. 


Condition of test:— 
(a) Time allowed—15 minutes. 


(b) If the student finishes before the allotted time is called out he 
should hand over the answer paper to the invigilators who will 
mark the time thereon. 


4. Marking of Answer Paper : 
(a) 3 per cent. mistake is allowed; above that five words are to be deducted 
for each mistake. 
(b) Striking a letter or typing a line over another, ے1‎ overlapping will 
be counted as mistake. 


B. Shorthand. 


Full marks for Shorthand examination will be 50 and the pass marks will be 
36 per cent. One hour will be allotted for the examination. The question 
paper will include the following: — 


(1) 1st question—On theory. Marks—15. 


(2) 2nd question—A passage containing 100 words to be written in 
shorthand outlines. Marks—15. 


(3) 3rd question—A passage containing 100 words in Shorthand to be 
transcribed in English. Marks—15. 


(4) For neatness—5 marks.

BOARD OF SECONDARY EDUCATION, WEST BENGAL.

Calcutta, the 25th August 1954. 


The following shall be the syllabuses of studies in the subjects mentioned 
below for Classes VI, VII and VIII:— 


ALTERNATIVE HINDI. 
(59 marks paper.) 


Class VI. 


The simple letters (vowels and consonants) of the Devnagri Alphabet, 
Systematic training in the sounds of aspirates, w and a, @ and 4, হা, 9, @) 
Writing of the vowels and their matras and of the simple consonants. 
(Transcription from the Reader and also the blackboard تع‎ essential.) 
Reading from the first half of the Reader without conjunct consonants, in the 
first half of the year. Second half of the year: Conjunct consonants. Read- 
ing aloud from the Reader. Formation of easy sentences by the pupils with 
words from the Reader. Simple dictation. A text-book will be not more than 
40 pages (Imperial 16 mo—74”x54"). 


Class VII. 


Conjunct consonants continued. Reading aloud by the pupils to correct mis- 
pronunciation of werds, the principal objective being clear utterance. Easy 
conversation about familiar objects and actions and topics of the reading 
lessons. Practice in hand-writing and_ dictation. Easy written composition 
based on the reading lessons. Formal grammar shall not bé taught but pupils 
will be taught easy functional grammar from examples in the Reader (particu- 
larly nouns and their plurals; easy pronouns and adjectives; past and future 
tenses of verbs). A text-book will be not more than 50 pages (Imperial 
16mo—74"x54"). 


Class VIII. 


Development of previous work. Initial difficulties of mechanical reading 
should by now have been overcome. The pupils should continue reading aloud 
but some silent reading should be introduced. Comprehensive tests may be 
answered either in Hindi or in English, but reproduction of simple stories should 
be in Hindi. The use of words in their relation to other words should now be 
taught. Cases of nouns and pronouns, voices, other tenses of verbs, simple 
analysis of sentences should now be taught, based on the examples in the texts. 
Poems should be learnt by heart. Letters of a simple kind should be written by 
the pupils as their exercises in composition. Dictation of passages from the 
Readers, at least ten lines on each occasion. 


Supplementary Reading matter may be prescribed by the teacher; but such 
books should not be more difficult than the Reader. 


The text-book prescribed will not exceed 60 pages and should be of the same 
standard as that of Class V for Hindi-speaking boys (Hindi Compulsory).

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 
Subdivisional reports on the condition of weather, crops, etc., for the week ending the 1st September 1954. 


Summary.—During the week there was rainfall in all subdivisions oxcept Barrackpore, Barasct, Jalpaigum and Tufanganj. The 
weather conditions were unfavourable in fourteen subdivisions. Transplantation of Aman and harvesting of Aus continued. The 
conditions of the standing crops were on the whole fair. Fodder was reported to be insufficient in seventeen eubdivimons and cattle 
disease was reported from five subdivisions. The wages of the labourer vayed from annas fourteen to rupees two and annas eight dur- 


ing the» week.
