SUPPLEMENT TO THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 16, 1954 895 


DIRECTORATE OF ACRICULTURE, WEST 


BENGAL. 
Calcutta, the 14th July 1954. 


Forecast of Rabi Pulses (other than Gram and 
Tur) of West Bengal for 1953-54. 


[Note.—The figures of Mung, Mashkalai, 
Masur, Motor and Khesari for 
last yeur and this year except 


Darjeeling as shown in the forecast have been 
based on the results of sample survey and crop 
cutting experiments conducted by the State 
Statistical Bureau. The figures for both this 
year and last year of ‘“‘Other pulses” for all 
the districts and those of Mung, Mashkalai, 
Masur, Motor and Khesari for J)arjeeling 
district have been estimated by the Directorate 
of Agriculture, West Bengal. ] 


Season.—The weather conditions have been 
generally favourable for the cultivation and 
growth of the crops in all the ditsricts, except 
24-Parganas, Murshidabad, Bankura, Malda and 
West Dinajpur. 


Area and yield.—The total area under different 
Rabi Pulses (other than Gram and Tur, the fore- 
casts whereof are separately published) has been 
estimated at 1,182,800 acres thins year compared 
to 1,043,200 ecres of last year. The total outturn 
of different Rabi pulses for the State as a whole 
hag been estimated at 243,900 tons this year 
compared to 228,000 tons of last year. The 
average outturn per acre of different Rabi pulses 
for the State as a whole has been estimated at 
6:86 maunds this year compared to 5:95 maunds of 
last year. 


Mung.—34,600 acres have heen estimated to be 
under ‘‘Mung’’ this year compared to 37,600 acres 
of last year. The total outturn of the crop for the 
State os a whole has been estimated at 8,700 tons 
this year compared to 9,300 tons of last year. 
The average outturn per acre of the crop for the 
State ag a whole has been estimated at 6-87 
maunds this year compared to 6۰14 maunds 01 
last year. 


Mashkalat.—304,800 acres have been estimated 
tu be under ‘Mashkalai’’ this year compared to 
361,700 acres of last year. The total outturn of 
the crop for the State as a whole has been estimated 
ait 66,600 tons this year compared to 63,600 tons 
last year. The averuge outturn per acre of the 
crop for the State 98 a whole has been estimated 
at 6:94 maunds this year compared to 4°78 
maunds of last year. 


Masur.—315,400 acres have been estimated to 
be under ‘‘Masur’’ this year compared to 294,000 
acres of last year. The total outtutn of the crop 
for the State as a whole has been estimated ut 
66,500 tons this year compared td 62,000 tons of 
last year. The average outturn per acre of the 
crop for the State ag a whole has been estimated 
at 5:74 maunds this year compared to 5-74 
maunds of last year. 


Motor,—40,300 acres have been estimated to be 
under ‘‘Motor”’ this year compared to 40,500 acres 
of last year. The total outturn of the crop for 
the State as a whole has been estimaed at 5,400 
tons this year compared to 8,300 tons of last year. 
The averge outturn per acre of the crop for the 
state as a whole hag been estimated at 3.64 maunds 
this year compared to 5.59 maunds of last year. 


Ahesari.—432,100 acres have been estimated to 
be under ‘‘Khesari this year campared to 306,100 
acres of last year. The total outturn of the crop 
for the state as a whole has been estimated at 95,500 
tons this year compared to 84,100 tone of last 
year. The average outturn per acre of the crop 
for the state as a whole has been estimated at 6.01 
maunds this year compared to 7.48 maunds of last 
year. 


Other pulses.—3,500 acres have been estimated to 
be under “Other pulses’? this year compared to 
3,300 acres of last year. The total outturn of the 
crop for the state as a whole has been estimated at 
800 tons this year compared to 700 tons of last year. 
The average outturn per acre of the crop for the 
state as a whole has been estimated at 5.83 maunds 
this year compared to 5.91 maunds of last year. 


S. N. MUKHERJEE, 
for Inrector of Agriculture, West Bengal.

License, 1904.

the same respective meanings provided that in this license:

statutory modifications thereof; 


(ii) ‘the Government” shall mean the Government of West Bengal ; 


(521) the expression ‘‘the licensee’’ shall mean and include the Amta 
Electric Supply Corporation, Limited, ٥ company registered 
under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 and their permitted 
assigns;

the licensee shall maintain a continuous supply of energy for 24 hours

Provided that for a period of two years from the commencement of

Government obtained in writing.

following, be taken to mean and include the licensee, his employees,

20. Revocation.—(i) If the licensee shall in the opinion of the Govern- 
ment have failed to give such immediate and full information as 1s required

reasonable care have been prevented by the licensee, or if the licensee shall 
in the opinion of the Government fail to comply with any of the provisions 
of this license, or shall in the opinion of the Government fail to show 
satisfactory progress during any portion of the period of two years, specified 
in clause 6 of this license or if the general direction and control of the 
licensee shal] cease to be in the hands of the citizens of India the license 
may be revoked, 


(ii) In the event of the Government revoking the license for any of 
the causes specified in the sub-clause (i), the security deposit of Ra. 10,000 
made in accordance with clause 3 may in whole or in part be forfeited as 
the Government may decide and the decision of the Government as to both 
revocation and forfeiture shall be final and binding on the licensee.

THE BENCAL MUNICIPAL (SECOND AMENDMENT) 
ACT, 1954, 


[Passed by the West Bengal Legislature. } 


[Assent of the Governor was first published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
Eatraordinary, of the 22nd September, 1954.] 


An Act tu amend the Bengal Muntcipal Act, 1932. 


WHueERE«s it is expedient to amend the Bengal Municipal 
Act, 1932, for the purpose and in the manner hereinafter 
appearing; 


It is hereby enacted in the Fifth Year of the Republic of 
India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows :— 


1. (2) This Act may be called the Bengal Municipal 
(Second Amendment) Act, 1954. 


(2) It shall come into force immediately on the Bengal 
Municipal (Amendment) Ordinance, 1954, ceasing to operate. 


2. In clause (৮) of sub-section (7) of section 554 of the 
Bengal Municipal Act, 1932, for the words ‘‘or any rule or 
by-law made thereunder’’, the words ‘‘or any other Act or 
any Ordinance or any Regulation or any rule, by-law, order, 
notification or subsidiary legislation made under the provi- 
sions of this Act or such other Act or such Ordinance or such 
Regulation”’ shall be substituted and shall be deemed to have

West Bengal Act XXII of 1954 


THE WEST BENGAL SECONDARY EDUCATION 
(TEMPORARY PROVISIONS) ACT, 1954, 


[Passed by the West Bengal Legislature. | 


[Assent of the Governor was first published in the Calcutta Gazette, 
Extraordinary, of the 22nd September, 1954.] 


An Act to reorganize the administration of secondary educa- 
tion in West Bengal and pending such reorganization to’ 
supersede the Board of Secondary Education and certain 
other bodies and to provide for certain connected matters. 

WHEREAS it is expedient to reorganize the administra- 
tion of secondary education in West Bengal and _ pending 
such reorganization to supersede the Board of Secondary 

Education and certain other bodies and to provide for cer- 

tain connected matters; 

It is hereby enacted in the Fifth Year of the Republic 
of India, by ae Legislature of West Bengal, as follows :— 


1. (1) This Act may be called the West Bengal Secondary 
Kducation (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1954. 


(2) It extends to the whole of West Bengal. 

(3) It shall come into force immediately on the West 
Bengal Secondary Education (Temporary Provisions) Ordi- 
nance, 1954, ceasing to operate. 


2. In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant im 
the subject or context,— 

(a) ‘‘the Act’? means the West Bengal Secondary 
Education Act, 1950 7 . 

(6) ‘‘the Bourd’’ means the Board of Secondary Educa- 
tion established under the Act; 

(c) ‘‘Committee’”? or ‘‘Sub-Committee’” means any Com- 
mittee or Sub-Committee constituted under the 
Act, or any rule, by-law or regulation made 
thereunder ; 

(2) ‘‘the Executive Council’? means the Executive 
Council referred to in section 20 of the Act; 


(৪) ‘‘the President’? means the President of the Board. 


3. The State Government may, by notification in the 
Oficial Gazette, publish on order (hereinafter referred to as 
the Supersession Order) to be in force for such period as may 
be specified in the order and may by like notification extend 
such period. .

be constituted by him; 


(০) representatives of the Board on every body (statu- 
tory or otherwise) shall vacate their offices as such 
representatives and shall, whatever may be their 
wumber, be replaced by the Administrator.

allowances as may be fixed by the State Government. 


(4) The salary and allowances fixed under sub-section (4) 
shall be paid from the Secondary Education Fund referred 
to in section 44 of the Act,

‘sions of this Act, the State Government may, as occasion 
requires, by order, authorise any matter or thing to be done, 
not being inconsistent with the provisions of this Act which 
may be necessary for removing the difficulty. 


No suit, prosecution or other proceeding shall lie 
ayainst the Administrator, or uny person or body to whom 
the Administrator muy delegate any of his powers, duties 
or functions under the proviso to clause (b) of section 4, for 
anything done in pursuance of or in the execution of this 
Act or done in good faith or in intended esecution of this Act.

implying in any way the dissolution of the Board as a body 
corporate.

1954, shall, on the said Ordinance ceasing to operate, be 
deemed to have been issued, made, tuken or done under this 
Act as 1f this Act hud commenced on the 12th day of May, 
1954.

No. 56!0W.T.—10th September 1954.—The following draft of, by-laws, 
which the Governor proposes to make for the Bankura Municipality, in the 
district of Bankura, in exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of 
section 71 of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919 (Bengal Act ۱ of 1919), 
is published for the information of persons likely to be affected thereby. 


2. The draft will be taken into consideration on or after the 25th October 
1954 and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto which may be 
received. by the undersigned before that date through the District Magistrate, 
Bankura, shall be duly considered :-— 


BY-LAWS. 


1. Appointment and duties of the Registering Officer —Every rickshaw in 
the Bankura Municipality shall be annually registered by the Registering Officer 
appotnted for registering hackney-carriages. 


2. Qualifications of the bearers.—Every person applying for a_bearer’s 
license shall be required to satisfy the Registering Officers— 


(a) that he is not less than 18 years of age; 


(b} that he knows how to drive and contro! a rickshaw and _ is in all 
respects a fit person for such employment; 


(০) that he is well-acquainted with the principal streets, workshops, 
factories, offices and places in and around the town of Bankura; 


(d) that he has a thorough knowledge of the tables of fares and distances 
prepared by the Commissioners, 


(০) that he knows the rules of the road and the signals used by the bearers 
and drivers of the vehicles and by the traffic police. 


3. Contents of license.—There shall be attached to each license issued to 
a rickshaw bearer— 


(a) ‘the thumb mark or signature of the bearer; 
(b) a photograph of the bearer, to be supplied by him; and 


(c) a printed table of fares and distances abe hala by the Commissioners, 
for which no charge shall be paid by the bearer. 


4. Production of license, etc-—Every bearer of a rickshaw shall carry with 
him his license and shall produce it when called upon to do so by the traffic 
pglice, any Commissioner, or other person authorised by the Commissioner. 
He shall exhibit the table of fares and distances on a prominent part of the 
vehicle. 


5. Condition of rickshaws.—(a) The body of the rickshaw shall be sound 
and clean and all the boards strong and properly secured. 


(b) The wheels shall be rubber-tyred, strong and sound, so as ا‎ run 
smoothly and without rattling or shaking and shall be protected by properly- 
fitted splash boards. 


i. (c) The springs and axles shall be made of good metal, strong and properly 


riveted and free from rust. 


(d) The iron supports at the back shall be properly curved ٥4 securely 
fixed on each side, strong and of sound metal and free from rust. 


(e) The hood, apron and cushion shall be made of and covered with good 
cloth, canvas or other materials approved by the Commissioners at a meeting. + 


(f) The shafts Shall be of sound wood, strong, securely fixed and furnished 
at the Tore-ends with a ring-shaped metal support and connected by <a collision 
guard. : 


(g) The hood and apron shall®be so fittgd as to make the vehicle water-tight. 


, (h) Every rickshaw shall have two good lamps—one facing the front and 
one in the rear. 


(i} Each lamp shall have a red glass window jn the back and shall be’so 
placed that the light from the window is visible from a point ten yards in the 
rear of the centre of the vehicle. ; . 


(j) Every rickshaw shall have a bell affixed to the handle bars or cross bars 
on the cycle and it shall be so constructed that it can be operated by fingers and 
can give continuous ringing as and when necessary. *

9. Prohibition of smoking, ctc.—No bearer shall smoke while driving nor 
shall be muffle up his face in such a manner as to endanger the proper driving of 
his vehicle. 


10. Maximum load to be carried in rickshaws.—Passengers and luggage shall 
not ordinarily exceed four maunds in weight. 


11. Speed and halting charge of rickshaws.—When a rickshaw is hired 
bearer shall ordinarily drive the same at a spced of not less than eight miles 
per hour. If a rickshaw after being hired is made to halt, halting charge shall 
be paid according to the scale laid down in the above fare table. 


12. Advertisement on rickshaws.—No advertisement shall be fixed on the 
body of the rickshaws without the previous permission of the Commissioners and 
it shall be fixed at such places as not to cover the number plate and the fare table 


affixed to the rickshaws. 


13. Rickshaws to wait at stand.—The rickshaws while at rest shall wait at 
a stand fixed by the Commissioners for such ptrpesc. 


14. Power of entry.—It shall be lawful for a Commissioner or any Other 
person authorised in that behalf by the Chairman of the Commissioncrs at any 
lime between sun-rise and sun-set to enter any premises in which any licensed 
rickshaw or other things used therewith are kept in order to carry out any of 
the provisions of the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919, or these by-laws and 
the owner or occupier of the premises or his agent shall afford every facility for 
inspection by such Commissioner or person.

15. Tables of fares and distance—The Commissioners shall cause to be 
prepared and kept, for sale to the public, printed tables setting forth the fares 
and distance$ at a price fixed by the Commissioners. 


16. Particulars of registers.—The following particulars shall be entered in 
the registers and licenses under the Calcutta Hackney-carriage Act, 1919 :— 


(A) Bearer’s license. 


(1) The number of the license. 


*(2) The name, father’s name, place of abode, present address and age of 
the person to whom such license is granted. 


(3) The date on which the license is granted. 

(4) The number of rickshaws allowed to the bearer. 
(5) Photograph of the bearer. 

(6) The date of expiry of the license. 


(7) A summary of the more important statutory provisions and by-laws 
affecting bearers of rickshaws. 


(8) Signature of the Registering Officer. 
(B) Owner's license. 
(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 


(2) The name, father’s name and residence of the owner, the description of 
the rickshaws and the place where the rickshaw is kept. 


(3) The number of passengers the rickshaw is licensed to carry. 
(4) The date on which the license is granted. 
(5) Date of expiry of the license. 
(6) Signature of the Registering Officer. 
(C) Register of rickshaws. 
(1) The number assigned to the rickshaw in the register. 
(2) Date on which the license is granted. 
(3) Name and father’s name of the owner. 
(4) Owner’s place of residence. 
(5) Place where the rickshaw is kept. 
(6) House number. 
(7) Name and father’s name of the bearer. 
(8) Bearer’s place of residence. 
(9) Period of suspension. 
(10) Date of renewal. 
(11) Duplicate license. 
(12) Duplicate ticket. 
(13) Photograph of the bearer. 
(14) Date of conviction. 
(15) Section of law. 
(16) Punishment inflicted. 
(17) Date of offence. 
(18) Offence. 
(19) Ownership transferred to. 
(20) The number of persons the rickshaw is licensed to carry 
(21) Date of transfer. 
(22) Signature of the Registering Officer. 
(23) Remarks.

subject or context :— ‘ ‘ 


(8) “Commissioner” means a Commissioner of the Bankura Municipality 
in the gistrict of Bankura. 


(b) “Rickshaw” includes a cycle-rickshaw.

No. 6545¥For.—30th August 1954.—In exercise 
of the power conferred by the proviso to article 309 
of the Constitution of India, read with articles 313 
and 372 of the said Constitution and paragraph 19 
of the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950, the Gover- 
nor is pleased to make the following amendment in 
the Bengal Provincial Services Recruitment Rules 
published with the notification No. 7183A., dated 
the 22nd May 19830, as subsequently amended, 
namely :— 


Amendment. 


In item 17B of schedule III to the said rules, for 
paragraph (b) substitute the following :— 

‘*(b) Candidates having the following qualifica- 
tions may, at the discretion of the State 
Government, be selected for appointment 
direct to the service, namely :— 


(a) a degree in Forestry of a recognised foreign 
University or its equivalent, or 


(b) a Master’s degree, or an honours degree not 
lower than a second class in Mathe- 
matics, Physics, Chemistry, Botany, 
Zoology, Geology or Agriculture of an 
Indian or a foreign University, or a first 
class degree in Agriculture of an Indian 
or a foreign University which has no 
honours degree in Agriculture plus 
Associateship of the ' Indian Forest 
College, Dehra Dun. 


Candidates for appointment direct to the service 
should not و ام کی‎ be below 22 years of age nor 
‘above 30 years of age. The age fimit may, how- 
ever, be relaxed in the case of a candidate with 
exceptionally high qualifications or a candidate al- 
ready in the service of the Central or a State 
Government’’.

AWARD. 


1. By order No. 687Dis./D/11L-148/53, dated the 12th February 
1954, the Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, referred 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, the industrial 
dispute between Messrs. Lucky Glass orks, 242/2, Manicktola Main 
Road, Clalcutta-11 (Head Office—165, Lower Chitpur Road Calcutta) and 
their workmen represented by Jueky Glass Mazdur Union, 2422, 
Manicktola Afain Road, Calcutta-1l, regarding the matters specified in the 
schedule, (0 the Third Industrial Tribunal constituted under section 7 of 
the Industrial Disputes Aot, 1947, by notification No. 592Dis./D/12L- 
5/52, dated the 23rd February 1953, for adjudication. 


2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed their 
written stutements. The pleadings were completed on 28th April 1964. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file their lists of documenta by 
10th June 1954. Hearing of the dispute was then concluded, on 30th July 
1954 and the award was reserved. 


3178 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Part I 


১১৯ 
3. Ths matters of dispute as stated in the schedule to the arder of 
reference are as follows:— - 


(1) Puja bonus for 1953. 
(2) (i) Whether discharge of Shri Nirapada Biswas was justified. 
(ii) What relief is he entitled ۶ 


DECISION. 


[00 appreciate the controversy it 18 necessary fo state the facts leading 
to the dispute as are either admitted or established in evidence. 


The Lucky Glass Works is a proprietory business of Shri Khemjee 
Hansraj. It manufactures glasses. سا‎ its workmen were 
represented by Lucky Glass Workers’ Union. It presented a charter of 
demands whereupon as many as 21 issues including scales and grades of 
pay of the workers of different categories (Issue No. 3), dearness allowance 
(Issue No. 4), cheap food and free tiffin (Issue No. 5), special allowance to 
workers of departments said to be exposed to the risk of occupational 
diseases (Issue No. 6), city allowance (Issue No. 7), bonus (Issue No. 8), 
and free quarters or house rent allowance (Issue No. 13) were referred by 
Government of West Bengal, in the Labour Department, under order 
No. 838Lab., dated the 19th March 1948, for adjudication to the 
Industrial Tribunal presided over by Shri A. Das Gupta. The award 
which Shri Das Gupta made was published in the Calcutta (Gazette on 
26th June 1948. Among others Shri Das Gupta granted a higher pay 
scale, made provision for increments and allowed separate dearness 
allowance to each worker at a flat rate of Rs. 10 per month. As regards 
bonus, he sllowed on Company’s offer one month’s pay as bonus to the 
’ employees. 


After the award by Shri A. Das Gupta, there was an agreement on 
12th September 1948 (Ext. 1) between Lucky Glass Works on one hand and 
the Lucky Glass Workers’ Union on the other “in consideration of the fact 
that the Company would not be able to meet all the items awarded by Shri 
Das Gupta.’’ The award was accordingly adjusted on mutual agreement 
under 12 heads. The Union among others agreed to remain satisfied with 
an increment of Rs. 5 in place of Rs. 10 as in the award up to monthly 
wages of Hs. 80 (vide item No. 10), to work 48 hours in a week and 8 hours 
on Saturdays if required by the Company without demanding any over-time 
payment (vide item No. 8) and not to press claim for uniform as awarded 
(item No. 8). The Company on the other hand among others agreed “to 
pay to all workmen of the Company one month’s wages as bonus provided 
such worker has completed over 11 months’ service and to all others who 
have completed under 11 months and over 9 months’ service 75 per cent. 
of a month’s wages, and to those who have completed under 9 months and 
over 6 months shall receive 50 per cent. of a month’s wage” (Item No. 1 
of the agreement). 


The award of Shri Das Gupta on agreement, as aforesaid, by both sides 
and with intimation to the Joint Secretary to the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department (Ext. 2), was modified. It further appears 
that the agreement as aforesaid was also acted upon by the parties. 


Part 1] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 3179 


ee es ee ee ee ۴ ০৮ .یت ہے .لہ‎ 


eee,‏ ہے 


The, Company admittedly paid bonus from the time of the agreement 
without’ scrutinising the profit or loss till the financial year 1950-51. I+ 
admittedly pid such bonus at the rates as below and these are in 
conformity with the agreement and according to the rates agreed upon :— 


6 mouths to below 9 months—Half a month’s wages. 
Above 9 months and below 11 months—% month’s wages. 
11 months and above—Full wages. 

(Vide page 2 of the Company’s written statement.) 


Not having been satisfied with the agreement, dated 12th September 
3948, the workmen formed the present Union “Luck Glass Mazdur 
Union.” This Union submitted a new charter of demands. The Company 
on the other hand declared lock out and closed the factory from 22nd March 
1952. The factory remained closed till 24th September 1952, that is, for 
a period of 5 months and 11 days. As there could be no settlement in 
course of conciliation proceedings, the dispute was referred by order 
No. 822Dis.;0/11L-113/52, dated the 15th April 1952, to the Tribunal 
preaided over by Shri P. R. Mukherjee, for adjudication. As many as 
1] points including the question of lock out were referred to him for 
adjudication. All the issues including the one of lock out were settled on 
compromise except issue number 5 relating to dismissal of Sidheswar and 
others. Shri P. R. Mukherji gave his award on 22nd September 1952 on 
issues 1 to 4 and 6 and 7 on the basis of the terms of settlement and on 
issue 5 independently. The award was published in the Calcutta Gazette 
on 28rd October 1952. 


Under item No. (8) of terms of settlement it was stated: “The 
management further agrees to pay (as a special case) only to permanent 
workers who were in the rolls of the firm on the 20th March 1952, one 
month’s. salary for full 12 calendar months’ service or the proportion 
thereof as per firm’s rules to be paid before Puja holidays.” The 
Company admittedly paid the amount as aforesaid on the eve of the Puja 
in the year 1952, that is, during the financial year of 1951-52. The Union 
contended that this payment was a payment of bonus; while it was 
contended on behalf of the employer that the payment was in connection 
with lock out. The letter which the Union wrote in this connection and 
which was forwarded by the Labour Officer to the Company (Ext. E with its 
annexure) clearly supports-the employer’s version that it was a payment in 
connection with the lock out and not one relating to bonus. 


Subsequently dispute again arose. The employer closed ‘the factory 
again from Ist May 1969 to 8th July 1959. pon such closure and no 
settlement baving been possible in course of conciliation proceedings, the 
dispute was referred to me for adjudication under order No. 2067Dis./D/ 
117.-148/53, dated 8th June 1953. The parties came to an amicable 
settlement and there was an award in terme of the petition of compromise. 
Ext. 3 is the petition of compromise with terms of settlement. The award 
in this respect was published on 6th August 1953. 


Behind this background the present dispute was referred to me _ by 
order, dated 12th February 1954, for adjudication. 


The workmen represented by Lucky Glass Mazdur Union demand 
payment of Puja bonus for the year 1953 on the basis of the agreement and 
following payments on the eve of the Puja hitherto before. The Company 


3180 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr 1 
৯১ 


on the other hand resists the claim. It says that by the 
agreement, dated 12th September 1948, it did not agree to pay 12008 for 
all time to come. It is said that the bonus which the Company paid from 
the agreement onwards till the financial year 1950-51 was so paid er-yratia 
us a gesture of goodwill and thus the workmen cannot claim Puja bonus as 
of right. Then it is alleged that though the management did not pay 
any bonus for the year 1961-52, it being a year of loss, the workers did 
not prefer sny complaint or raise dispute on that score. Then there was 
no profit but huge loss in the year in question. In the circumstances, the 
Company submits that claim for bonus should be dismissed. 


After giving careful consideration to the evidence and arguments 
advanced on either side, it appears that the cluim of the workmen for bonus 
for the finaucial year 1952-58 must be upheld in view of the agreement. 
The circumstances surrounding the agreement can leave no room for doubt 
that by itein No. 1 of the agreement (Ext. 1) the employer unequivocally 
agreed to give to the workn:en bonus in terms and conditions as stipulated 
therein as service condition in consideration of the workmen having 
relinquished various benefits and amenities including increment in wages aa 
awarded by Shri Das Gupta. Therefore the said term in the agreement 
cannot be ireated as one for that year only. ere is no such hmitation 
expressed] in the agreement either. The fact that there has been payment 
of bonus irrespective of profit or loss (Ext. 1) from the time of the 
agreement till the financial year 1950-61 precisely according to terms and 
conditions as stipulated in item No. 1 of the agreement Ext. 1 would also 
leave no room for doubt that it was so meant, When the employer has so 
promised to pay bonus as a condition of service, the fact that there was no 
payment of tunus for the financial year 1951-52 would make no difference. 
It appears that the workmen did not claim bonus for that year under aa 
erroneour impression having got identical sum on the eve of Puja سا‎ the 
year 1952 on the basis of the agreement relating to lock out as in item 
No. 8 of the terms of settlement in the award by Shri P. R. Mukher}i 
(Ext. J). It will not be out of place to mention that when the dispute 
was referred to Shri P. R. Mukherji for adjudication, the cause of action 
relating to bonus for the financial year 1951-52 which according to practice 
was payoble on the eve of Puja did not arise and as such no such dispute 
could hnye been raised. 


Be that as it may, non-receipt of bonus for a particular year does not 
debar the workmen from claiming bonus for the subsequent year, that is, 
for the financial year 1952-53, when it is admissible to them aa a condition 
of service on the basis of the agreement, Ext. 1, irrespective of the 
question of profit or loss. So even if there was no profit in the year in 
question, the workmen would be entitled to bonus. 


Regarding Company’s allegation that there was no profit but loss in the 
years 1961-52 and 1952-53, the Company has not filed audited balance 
sheets but trial balance sheets prepared by their officers (Exts. A2 and A8). 
The balance sheets (Exts. A2 and 49) do not appear to have exhibited 
true state of affairs. There has been great variation in the trading results 
of these years, the percentage being 26 to 40 which does not normally 
happen. No explanation has been given why the accounts for these two 
years were not audited. It further appears that by way of reducing the 
profit heavy expenditure was shown on account of machinery, furnaces and 
factory. It is a private concern belonging to Khemjee MHanaraj. 
D.W.1, the Manager, stated that in 1953 the business was converted into 
a partnership one, but nothing has been filed to substantiate it. Jt seems 
that such ease has been introduced to find an excuse for inflating the 
capital in order to wipe out the profit, Before Shri A. Das Gupta, it was 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 3181 


stated that the business belonged formerly to Shri Ratan Singh Mulji 
(son-in-law of Shri Khemjee Hanaraj) and that it was subsequently acquired 
by Shri Khemjee Hansraj but nothing was produced to substantiate it. 
Qn the contrary, the account papers both prior to and after the alleged 
transfer which were then produced were found to stand in the name of 
Khemjee Hansraj. Shri Das Gupta did not believe the story of transfer 
and was of opinion that under such plea Rs. 2,60,000 was added to the 
accounts only to swell the capital outlay and thereby to make out a case 
that the proprietors were not getting a fair return for the money they had 
invested. Ife had also noticed that huge expenditure was noted against 
repairs of the furnaces year after year which could not be true. Shri Das 
Gupta was thus of opinion that the accounts were not properly kept or 
reliable. J am also of opinion that no reliance can he placed on the 
unaudited balance sheets for the yeurs 1951-52 and:1952-68. Even if there 
was no profit, it has already been noted that 5৮ would make no difference. 
So to be precise, I find that the workmen are entitled to bonus for the 
financin] year 1962-58 to be paid at the rates and conditions os noted in 
item No. 1 of the agreement. The payment is to be made as soon as_ the 
award becomes enforceable. 


Issue No. 2. 


The Union has examined in this respect the workmen concerned, Shri 
Nirapada Biswas PW. 1, and another workman P.W. 2, Shri 
Nizamuddin, besides proving Exts. 4, 5 and 5(a). The employer on the 
other hand has examined the General Manager D.W.1, Shri Sankar Dayal 
Agarwal besides proving Exts. B, C, Cl, D, D1 and F. 


Shri Nirapada Biswas admittedly joined this concern as delivery clerk 
on 19th September 1947 on a salary of Rs. 40 per month (vide Exts. B and 
D). He admittedly worked in that capacity up to August 1952 and as such 
delivery clerk his salary on gradual increments rose to Rs. 90 per month 
(ride Exts. B and D). From September 1952 he was admittedly employed 
both aa lorry driver and delivery clerk when his salary hecame Rs. 95 per 
month (vtde Exts. ہڈا‎ D and D1). He worked in these’ two 
rapracities up to 8th August 1953 when his service was terminated 
by the notice, dated 8th August 1953 (Ext. 4). By such notice 
he was told that his services were no longer required چنا‎ the 
management from 9th August 1953 and that he would be paid 
one month’; salary in lieu of notice in addition to his salary for 
the period worked, which he could take on any week day. Shri Nirapada 
Biswaan at once protested to such action by his letter, dated 13th August 
1858 [Ext. 5(a).] He complained that he was retrenched by way of 
victimisation on account of his Union activities as evident from the fact 
that a new delivery clerk had been appointed in the first quarter of 1953 
and another new delivery clerk was appointed just after his retrenchment. 
The Company replied to it by its letter, dated 17th August 1953 (Ext. T°). 
It was stated therein that he was working 08 a lorry driver and the number 
of trucks having been reduced he was retrenched and that the question of 
victimisation did not arise. In the reply nothing was however stated 
regarding necessity or otherwise of a delivery clerk. Before this Tribunal 
the Company pleaded in its writfen statement that it was a bona fide 
retrenchment for trade reasons. It was stated thaf the Company reduced 
the number of lorries from 4 to 2 and as such services of Shri Nirapada 
Biswns were no longer required and thus his employment was terminated, 
he being junior to other lorry driver. 

The onus to justify the retrenchment is on the employer. The emplover 
did not allege that there was no necessity for o delivery clerk. The 
employer’s Khatas from September 1952 up to the date of discharge

on 8th August 1953 (Exts. D and D1) show that Shri Nirapada Biswas was 
working as lorry driver-cum-delivery clerk and not exclusively as a lorry

from September 1952 up to the date of discharge os driver-cum-delivery

fn view of the evidence and circumstances, it is not unlikely that in

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 894 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
by Shri Niranjan Paul and four others. The complaint was filed 
originally before the Fourth Industrial Tribunal. On withdrawal of the 
majn reference from the said Tribunal and committal of the same to this 
Tribunal by the Government, the record of the case relating to complaint 


under section 338A was received by transfer from the Fourth Industrial 
Tribunal. 


The petitioners alleged that in contravention of the provisions of 
section 88 of the Industrial Disputes Act and during the pendency of the 
adjudication proceedings they had been suspended for an indefinite 
period. Hence the complaint. 


The Company opposite party denies having contravened the 
provisions of section 33 and contends that the complaint under section ۸ 
18 not maintainable as the order of suspension was passed by way of 
security measure pending permission from the Tribunal to dismiss the 
workmen. It is said that as a matter of fact it had made application 
before the Tribunal seeking such permission. 


The preliminary objection as aforesaid has been heard. 


DECISION. 


The copies of the orders served on the five petitioners clearly state 
that they are suspended pending permission from the Tribunal to discharge 
them. It further appears that as a matter of fact, after such order 
the Company opposite party applied under section 33 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act, seeking permission from the Tribunal to discharge ‘ia 
workmen. Such petition was filed on 1161) May 1954, while the present 
complaint was made on 17th May 1954. In the circumstances there can 
be no doubt that the order of suspension was not by way of punishment 
but 85 a security measure pending permission from the Tribunal. I, 
therefore, agree that there has been no contravention of section 33 by the 
orders in question. In the result, the complaint must be held not to be 
muintainable and must, therefore, fail. I award accordingly. 


Dictated and corrected by me. 
J. MAITRA, JITENDRA NATH MAITRA,

The Route Committee manages the service buses of route No. 5A on 
behalf of the Bengal Bus Syndicate. The Committee is guided by rules 
framed by it. It regularises the bus service of Route 5A, detailing the 
vehicles to run on each day along that route, drawing up the detailed 
timings and exercising certain amount of control over the conductors 
and drivers while on duty on the route. There are different route 
committees for different bus routes, and each committee maintains its 
separate staff. The Route Committee’s staff consists of starters, 
supervisors, sweepers, fine collectors, checkers and durwans. It appears 
that 38 buses ply in route 5A of Calcutta. These buses are owned by 
individuals and firms who are members of the Bengal Bus Syndicate 
which is an Association of the bus owners. The employees” of the 
Committee are members of the Rashtriya Bus Mazdoor Congress which 
was formed in 1949, The Union raised the dispute over the claims of the

employees as mentioned in the order of reference in January 1959. Ag

DECISIONS. 
Issues Nos. 1 & 2. 


There are at present 24 employees under the Route Committee, as 
mentioned in Ext. E, filed by the Company. The Union also filed 
statement of the employees in Annexure A to their written statement, 
which virtually’ tallies with the Ext. E, except that the Annexure A 
shows the name of one Durga Das in excess of the names in the Ext. E. 
There was no controversy over the matter. It appears on a study of 
the list that there ure 16 Starters and five Collectors, 3 Checkers, one 
Supervisor, one Durwan and bearer, one Sweeper, and one Clerk 
besides Shri B. D. Lambay, the Assistant Traffic Superintendent. It 
appears that the clerk Shri R. C. Ghosh is a part-time employee who 
works only for one day in a week. His permanent posting is as the 
Chief Accountant of the Bengal Bus Syndicate. The Starters, Checkers 
and Fine Collectors get the same scale of wages, and the minimum wage 
appears to be Rs. 51 as basic wage, and Rs. 27 as dearness allowance, 
making Rs. 78 in total. Shri Bhim Sen and Shri Nirmal Singh who are 
temporary checkers, get Rs. 50 as basic pay and Rs. 22 as dearness 
allowance, 7.¢., in all Rs. 72. Shib Dayal, tha sweeper, gets Rs. 36, and 
Kapildeo Singh, Durwan, gets Rs. 43. The part-time clerk is paid 
Rs. 56. The Union claims that since the workmen are poorly paid, and 
the Route Committees are maintained in the interest of the employees 
of buses of Routes Nos. 5 and 5A who earn huge profits, the employees 
should be given the scales of basic wages as mentioned in the Annexure C 
to their written statement. These claims are as follows: — 


Clerk—Rs. 100—5—165. 

Sturter, Fine Collector and Checker—Rs. 85—9—150. 
Supervisor—Rs. 95—5—160. 

Bearer and Durwan—Rs. 45—5—110. 

Sweeper—Rs. 40—5—105.

The claim of dearness allowance was as follows: — 
Rs. 31 for basic pay up to Rs. 50. 
Rs. 42 for basic pay up to Ra. 75. 
Rs. 50 for basic pay up to Rs. 100. 
Rs. 60 for basic pay over Rs. 100. 


The Union claims that every employee should be granted an increment 
in pay for every 2 years of past service over the starting minimum 
without prejudice to their existing wage, and that the claims of increased 
basic wage and dearness allowance should be allowed with effect from lst 
May 1952. 


The Committee states in its written statement that it maintains itself 
by the fixed subscriptions from the bus owners, and apart from these 
subscriptions, the Committee has no other source of income. The 
Committee further states that in view of the Government policy of 
plying their own buses in different routes, the position of private bus 
owners has become very unstable. It is further stated that although 
the wages of the employees are shown under two separate columns— 
basic pay, and dearness allowance—the wage structure of the employees 
has not grown up on 8) scientific basis, The Tribunal should only 
consider the total wages paid to the workmen. The Route Committee 
states that it has not the means to increase the basic wages and dearness 
allowance of the workmen, and that in view of the qualifications of the 
employees, and the nature of work done by them, the wages they are 
drawing should be considered reasonable and fair. The Committee filed 
before me the accounts for the years ended 3lst December 1953, and 31st 
December 1952, being Exts. F and F(1), with a view to substantiate 
the claim that the Committee has got no substantial financial resources 
to pay any more wages to the workmen. The learned Advocate for the 
Union raised objection to the item of expense for Ballygunge Fund as 
appearing in both the accounts, and argued that this was an unjustified 
expenditure which might be utilised for payments to the workmen. 
It, however, appears from Exts. G and H that this money has to be 
incurred by way of monthly rent for the Ballygunge Stand for the buses 
of the Committee. The expenditure was, therefore, necessary in the 
interest of the business. There is an item of contribution of Rs. 760 
of which Rs. 380 was paid to the Punjab Sports Club, and the other 
portion to the Deshabandhu Memorial Fund at Darjeeling. It appears 
trom the statement of the representatives of the Committee that this 
amount was realised separately from the bus owners with a view to make 
these contributions. I do not think that the accounts are open to 
objection in any way. 


The employees are mostly Starters, Fine Collectors and Checkers. 
There is one Supervisor who gets a higher salary than the Starters, ond 
there is one A.T.S. who gets a basic pay of Rs. 140 and dearness allowance 
of Rs. 65. The Company’s case is that the Starters, Fine Collectors 
and Checkers have got to do very simple jobs requiring little education 
except a little knowledge of reading English, and that the wages which 
are paid by the Committee are sufficient for these categories of workmen 
in view of the nature of jobs done by them, and the qualifications they 
possess. The minimum pay of the workers of the categories of 
Starters, Fine Collectors and Checkers appear to be Rs. 51 as basic pay 
and Rs. 27 dearness allowance. It appears that these employees come 
from the middle class of the society with some education. I consider that 
the pay and the dearness allowance which they receive are inadequate, and

০০০৯ 


call for a revision. The Government of West Bengal, by notification 
No. 5454Lab., dated 29th August 1961, fixed the minimum rates of wages 
ayble to employees in the Public Motor Transport in the State of West 
Hengal. In this notification the wages and dearness allowance of Cleaners, 
Assistant Mistries, Conductors and Drivers were fixed. It appears that 
in the Calcutta zone, the 08810 pay and the dearness allowance of 
Conductors holding license for more than five years were fixed at Rs. 45-8 
and Rs. 32-8, respectively, The minimum pay of Starters, fine Collectors 
and Checkers should be Ra. 55 per month, and the dearness allowance 
shoulfi be neur about the same as that fixed for the Conductors, and it is 
awarded that it should be at Rs. 32 per month. The minimum total 
wage of Starters, Checkers and Fine Collectors should, therefore, be 
Rs. 87 in place of Rs. 78 as at present. I do not consider that a graded 
scale of basic pay with automatic annual increments should be allowed 
for any category of employees employed by the Route Committee, in view 
of its financial condition. The clerk is only ao parti-time worker working 
only for one day in a week. No acale of pay and dearness allowance 
need be fixed for the post of the clerk under the Route Committee. In 
view of the fact that the minimum wage of Starters, Fine Collecors and 
Checkers, who constitute the bulk of employees of the Committee, and are 
virtually the representative group of employees, are being given an 
increment of Rs. 4 in their basic wage and Rs. 5 in dearness allowance, it 
is proper that all employees should be given these increments with a 
view to maintain the wage differentinl. It is, therefore, awarded that 
the basic wage of all employees under the Route Committee shall be 
increased by Rs. 4, and the dearness allowance shall be increased by Rs.'6 
per month. These increments shall be effective from the date of the

Issue No. 3. 


The Union states in the written statement that the hours of work of 
the employees are strenuous, aud the Union claims that under no 
circumstances the working hours should be more than 8 hours a day, 
without prejudice to the existing benefits where it is less, and this 8 
hours should include half an hour’s rest every day. The Annexure B 
to the Union’s written statement shows that the duty hours in the 
morning shift of the Starters, Fine Collectors and Checkers are from 7 
hours 87 minutes to 9 hours at the various stations, and in the evening 
shift the total period of duty varies from 9 hours to 10 hours 15 minutes. 
The Committee states in its written statement that the Starters are 
required to work 8 to 9 hours a day, and the Starters get enough rest 
when they are on actual duty. The Committee also relied on the 
agreement, Ext. D, between the Route Committee of Route Nos. 3 and 3A 
oe its employees in which 9 hours have been fixed as the normal period 
of duty. 


The Government of West Bengal have fixed the minimum rates of wages 
in respect of Public Motor Transport in the State of West Bengal under 
the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 (XI of 1948). Ext. C is a copy of the 
Notification No. 4455Lab., dated 29th August 1951, PM which the Govern- 
ment notified the normal working hours for the employees of the Public 
Motor Transport in the State of West Bengal. The notification 
No. 5454Lab., dated 29th August 1951, is one by which the minimum 
wages were fixed. It appears from this notification that the wages were 
fixed are for Cleaners, Assistant Mistries, Conductors and Drivers. It 
appears from the Ext. C that the Notification No. 5455Lab., dated 29th 
August 1951, fixed the normal working hours of these categories of 


part 7] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 3189 


——— ra re oe | 


employges for which the minimum wages were fixed under the Minimum 
Wages Act, 1948. By the Notification, Ext. C, the Government fixed 
the normal working hours constituting a normal working day and the interval 
for rest in accordance with the provisions of section 65 of the Motor Vehicles 
Act, 1939 (ITV of 1939). Section 65 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1989, 
prescribes the hours of work of the drivers, and it lays down that ‘‘no pergon 
shall cause or allow any person who is employed by him for the purpose of 
driving a transport vehicle or who is subject to his control for such purpose 
to work— 


(a) for more than five hours before he has had an interval] of rest of at 
least half an hour, or 


(b) for more than nine hours in one day, or 
(c) for more than fifty-four hours in the week. 


These hours of work were preseribed by the Government of West 
Bengal by the notification No. 5465Lab., dated 29th August 1951, for 
the categories of employees .in the Public Motor Transport for whom 
minimum wages were fixed, Under Rule 89 of the Bengal Motor 
Vehicles Rules, 1940, the period of rest has been defined, and it has been 
stated that ‘‘any time spent by the driver of a vehicle on or near the 
vehicle when it is at rest, when he is at liberty to leave the vehicle for 
rest and refreshment although required to remuin within sight of the 
cehicle shall be deemed to be an interval of rest for the purpose of 
clause (a) of sub-section (1) of section 65 of the Act.’’ It is in evidence 
that the work of a Starter is to note the hour of arrival and departure 
of buses, to note the late arrival of buses, and at one or two stations to 
collect fines. That being so, the Starters get periods of rest between 
the arrival of buses. In view of the fact that the nature of the duty of 
the Starters is such that they rannot be away from the station for any 
substantial period of time, I consider that the plea of the Committee 
that the Starters get enough rest when they are on actual duty is 
acceptable. It is, therefore, awarded that the employees of the Route 
Committee shall work up to 9 hours in one day, and 54 hours in the week, 
and not wore. The Bl دا‎ of work of the Starters and other 
categories of workers should be so arranged by the Committee that they 
are not engaged in duty for more than 9 hours in one day, or more than 
64 hours in a week. The issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 4. 


The Union states in the written statement that the workmen of the 
Company do not get any weekly holiday or any compensatory holiday or 
overtime wages for work on days which should have been holidays. 
The workmen claim one day’s holiday with full wages after every six 
days’ work, or alternate holiday for work on such a day or double wages 
for work on days which should have been holidays. In the written state- 
ment the Committee pressed that it was unable to accede to the claim of rest 
day in a week, as such a measure will entail additional expenditure 
which the Committee was unable to bear. In this connection, the 
Committee referred to the agreement between the Committee of Route 
Nos. 8 and 3A and its workmen (Ext. D) where it is stated that if the 
workmen wanted an off day, then the said day will be without wages. 


In this connection, I have ta refer to the Government notification 
No. 5455Lab., dated 29th August 1951 (Ext, C), again. In clause 3 of 
‘this notification, it is provided that every employee im Public Motor 


3190 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr I 
হা 


Transport shalt be allowed rest for one day in course of every seven 
days. Clause 4 provides that the rate of payment for work on a day 
of weekly rest shall be double the normal rate of basic wage and dearness 
allowance. I do consider that the same principle should be followed in 
regard to the employees of the Route Committee who are engaged in 
the same industry as those for whom these provisions have been mude by 
the aforesaid Government notification, Ext. C. It is, therefore, 
awarded that every employee of the Committee shall be allowed rest for 
one day in course of every seven days. The workmen are all monthly 
paid, Thére should be no deduction of wages for this off day. It is 
also awarded that if any workman is made to work on the day of weekly 
rest, he shall be paid for that day at double the normal basic wage and 
dearness allowance. The issue is accordingly answered. 


Issue No. 5. 


The Union states in its written statement that the Committee does 
not follow any rule in taking disciplinary actions, impositions of fines, or 
other forms of punishment. It is also stated that the action of the 
Management in this connection is arbitrary, and it very often puts the 
workmen to sufferings and financial loss. The workmen claim that no 
such action should be taken without issuing a charge-sheet specifying 
clearly the charges, without affording proper opportunity of defence, 
or without holding an enquiry in presence of he workman concerned 
and at least one trusted representative of the Union, consistent to the 
principle of natural justice. The Committee states that in taking 
disciplinary action and imposition of fines, the Committee follows the 
principles of natural justice as required by the decision of the Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal of India in the Buckingham & Carnatic case. 
In the circumstances, it is awarded that no workman of the Committee 
shall be punished for any alleged misconduct without giving the workmat 
concerned an opportunity of explanation. The workman shall be given 
a charge-sheet in writing, and he shall be given an opportunity for defend- 
ing himself at the enquiry, and in such an enquiry he shall be entitled 
to take the help of another employee who may be a member of the Union. 
The issue is answered accordingly.

AWARD. 


This is a complaint under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
by the workman, Shri Surendra Mistry. He is a permanent workman in 
the opposite party Company, working in its Mains Department since 1928. 
On 26th May 1954, a charge-sheet was issued against him to which he 
submitted explanation on 27th [May 1954. Thereupon the management 
held enquiry ond was of opinion that the workman was guilty of the charye 
brought against him. Then the Company issued an order suspending the 
workman pending permission from the Tribunal to dismiss him. Upon 
this the complaint has been made alleging that suspension for an 
unlimited period amounts to dismissal and as such section 35 has been 
contravened. The Company on the other hand conteds that it was no 
punishmnt and as such the complaint under section 33A is not maintainable. 


$194 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr I 


DECISION. 


The order upon which the complaint under section 33A has been lodged, 
clearly recites that the workman is suspended pending permission from the 
Tribunal to dismiss him. The Company also, as a matter of fact, made 
such an application under section 33, seeking permission to dismiss the 
workman, which is even now pending. In the circumstances, the sus- 
pension cannot be treated as a punishment. It is, therefore, obvious that 
section 33 has not been contravened. The complaint under section 33A is, 
therefore, not maintainable and must fail.. I award accordingly.

FINDINGS. 


Shri Balaram Singh was a Time sri ie in the Shifter Section, Spinning 
Department, in MiJl No. 1 of the Hukumchand Jute Mills. He entered 
service on the 186 July 1942. He was dismissed by an order of the 
General Manager, dated the 3lst January 1953, with effect from 5th 
Jauuary 1953, the date of his suspension for misconduct under clauses 
14(c)(i) and 14(c)(ii) of the Company’s Standing Order (vide Ext. 10). 
Shri Balaram Singh was transferred to the Calendering Department by 
an order of the Manager, dated 29th November 1952 (Ext. 1). He was 
informed by a letter, dated 9th December 1952 of the General Manager 
while on leave, that investigations had brought to light a number of 
ross irregularities amounting to dishonesty in his work as the Time 
کسی‎ in the Spinning Department. He was warned that this might 
lead to his dismissal. On 3rd January 1953, he was sent a charge-sheet 
in continuation of the previous letter giving details of the charges 
Thereafter, it is alleged by the management that he submitted his 
explanation, and that an enquiry was held into the charges, of which he 
was found guilty. He was dismissed, as stated above, by an order, 
dated 9136 January 1953. The Union, on behalf of Shri Singh, has 
bnpunged this order, mainly on the grounds of violation of the principle 
of natural justice, victimisation, unfair labour practice, basic error vf 
facts ond perverse findings. Both the parties adduced evidence in this 
pase, oral and documentary. Shri Singh’s evidence was adduced .o 
establish fhat (1) he did no more than his duty which was purely 
clerical in nature, (2) he was on leave op some of the dates mentioned 
in the charges, and (3) that his alleged mistakes were bona fide ones 


3198 THe CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Part ] 


a 9 
due to pressure of work. On the other hand, the Company’s évidence, 
sought to estublish that (1) Shri Singh deliberately disobeyed the orders 
of the management and (2) dishonestly committed irregularities in hig 
work. It has been urged on behalf of the Union that the management 
did not proceed bona fide in the matter, but on the contrary they tried 
to crush Shri Singh, an important office bearer of the Union, for his 
Union activities, particularly, for having obtained the sum of Rs. 7,000 
from Shri D. P. Goenka as compensation for loss of employment of hig 
brother Satyanarain Singh, who was dismissed by the Company. Ip 
cases of this description, the requirement of bona fides is essential. It 
is, therefore, necessary that the question of bona fides should be carefully 
one into in this matter. The leading case on this subject is that of 

uckingham and Carnatig Co., Ltd. versus their workers, reported 
in 1952, Labour Appeal Cases at page 497. It has been held in that cage 
by the Labour Appellate Tribunal that ‘‘It would thus be open to the 
Tribunal to examine the findings of the management on the charge of 
misconduct to assure itself that there is evidence to support the finding, 
and that the decision of the management is a_ possible view on the 
evidence before 97979 0 0كی۹ََ۹0ً‎ The result, therefore, is that the 
decision of the management in relation to the charges against the employee 
will not prevail, if— 


(a) there is want of bona fides, or 


(b) it is a case of victimisation or unfair labour practice or violation 
of the principles of natural justice, or 


(c) there is a basic error of facts, or, 
(d) there has been a perverse finding on the materials. 


If after scrutiny on the aforesaid lines it is found by the Tribunal that 
it ought not to interfere with the findings of the কেলি that ‘the 
charge has been proved, the Tribunal must next consider whether it 
should interefere with the punishment’’. 


The Company’s case, as has been put by Shri Ghosh, is that for 
some time the management was receiving complaints of irregularities 
and malpractices existing in the Time Keeping Section, and that the 
management appointed a special officer to enquire into them with a 
view to their removal. As a result of this enquiry, not only Shri Balaram 
Singh, but others also of the Time Keeping Section, and one of the 
Labour Office were found involved. Actions were taken against all of 
them, some tendered their resignation to avoid punishment while others 
were dismissed from service. One other was demoted, and in one case 
the increment of one clerk was stopped. Shri Ghosh accordingly 
contends that the move against Shri Singh was taken in usual course 01 
business in connection with the check enquiry into the existence of 
irregularities and malpractices in the department. He said that the 
transfer was made only to facilitate the confidential enquiry so that the 
books and registers might not be tampered with or removed. The 
Company had no information of his Union activities, there being so 
many Unions in the Mill, and accordingly had 700 good reason to 
victimise him in any way. The alleged payment of Rs. 7,000 by way 
of compensation as unemployment relief to his brother Shri Satyanarain 
was absolutely untrue. The management examined Shri 8. Mookerji, 
the Chief Accountant in the Head Office, Shri S. Ghosh, the Senior Labour 
Officer of the Mill, Shri N. R. Mupid, the Special Officer doing the 
check enquiry even now and Shri Mahiuddin, a mill hand. Shri Mookerji

said wat in October 1952, they received reports that malpractices 


were going on in the Time Keeping Section of the Mill. He was asked 
to go to the Mill to hold a check enquiry. On the 26th November

etc., in the Time Keeping Section. He had a talk with Shri Varma,

Shri D. P. Goenka, the Director of the Mill, who is alleged to have 
made the payment of Rs. 7,000 to Shri Singh for the loss of his brother’s 
employment was away in America as an official of the I.J.M.A., and 
returned to Calcutta on the last day of the hearing of the argument of

Union Shri Singh examined himself, and also examined Shri Kasi Singh, 
a Sirdar in the Mill, to show that both of them were now the

3200 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr I 


Se 
There was nothing in the written statement to show or suggest that the 
payment of that amount was made by Shri D. P. Goenka himself, and 
that at his residence at Calcutta, and not by any other person in the 
Mill Office where the deputationisis saw him. No other evidence is 
forthcoming to show that Shri Singh was an important official of the 
Union before his dismissal, or that he had ever taken any prominent 
part in Union activities, particularly, with the management. In_ the 
absence of this evidence, particularly, in view of the fact admitted by 
Shri Singh that absolute peace prevailed among the workers after the 
said payment, it was unthinkable that the management should take 
action against Shri Singh. If Shri Singh was really such an important 
Union official, and an agitator among the workers whom the management 
wanted to buy up to its side, the management would not have taken 
any steps at all against him far less steps to remove him from service. 
It appears from Ext. 1 that Shri Satyanarain Singh was retrenched in 
1948, and according to Shri Balaram Singh, the payment of Rs. 7,000 
was made in October 1951. The charges were drawn up in January 
1953. Looking at these dates, dne cannot reasonably say, that the 
action agarhst Shri Singh was prompted by any motive to victimise 
him for having received the money over a year ago in connection with the 
retrenchment of his brother, three or four years even before that. 
The action appears to be remote to support any inference of victimisation 
for payment of this money. It is, therefore, difficult to believe that the 
management proceeded in this cose with an ulterior motive against 
Shri Sing, or tried in any way to victimise him for his Union activities. 
On the contrary, it is reasonable to hold that the management proceeded in 
the matter in good faith.

the employee was on leave on the relevant dates mentioned in the 
charges. He placed emphasis on the point that the Manager who was 
solely responsible for carrying out the Standing Orders of the Company 
was nowhere seen in this case either in the framing of the charges or in 
holding the enquiry into them. It was his clear duty to be present in 
both, and not to relegate this important function to any other person. 
Further, some unknown gentleman or gentlemen signed on behalf of 
the Managing Agents of this Company, the written statement filed on 
behalf of the Mill in this case. He said that that was done in clear 
violation of the law and Standing Orders. Shri Ghosh in reply said that 
the Managing Agents under the Standing Orders have got specified 
duties to do. Under rule 15 of the Standing Orders, the Managing Agents 
shall be deemed to be employers within the meaning of the rules. The 
signing of the written statement by the Managing Agents is not, therefore, 
irregular, far less illegal. The Company by filing the written statement 
has taken the entire responsibility for it.

amoung to irregularities amounting fo fraud and dishonesty punishable 
ander Yule 140001) of the Standing Orders. During the argument 
Shri Ghosh, representing the Company, frankly said that in some cases 
Shri Sing was absent on leave. The non-reporting of earned leave is a 
serious matter, for it leads to granting leave where leave is not due. 
Now, this has to be considered on the background of evidence regarding 
the duties of the Time Keeper and that of the Labour Office. Further, 
whether the irregularities mentioned in the charge-sheet amount to 
fraud and dishonesty in connection with the employer’s property or 
business, as mentioned in rule 14c(ii) of the Standing Orders. We have 
an idea of what dishonesty and fraud mean from the definition given in 
pane 24 and 25 of the Indian Penal Code. Section 24 runs as 
follows :— 


‘Whoever does anything with the intention of causing wrongful 
gain to one person or wrongful loss to another person, is said 
to do that thing ‘dishonesty’.”’ 


Section 25 is: 
‘‘A person is said to do a thing fraudulently if he does that thing with 
intent to defraud but not otherwise. Where there is an inten- 


tion to deceive and by means of the deceit to obtain an 
advantage there is fraud’.’’ 


The charges in the instant case do not disclose the fact that 
Shri Balaram Sing committed these irregularities for the purpose of 
making personal gain or deriving any personal advantage out of them. 
There is no evidence adduced in this case on the side of the management 
to show what were the mulpractices regarding wage payments in the 
Time Keeping Section. There is no evidence, again to show or suggest 
that Shri Sing committed these irregularities and errors being bribed 
by the workmen concerned. Apart from a vague suggestion during the 
argument, Shri Ghosh did not lead any evidence to show that Balaram 
Sing was out for an advantage to himself or for a personal gain out of 
these irregularities. Further, I fail to see how these irregularities in 
the matter of not reporting earned leave, etc., can amount to dishonesty 
aud fraud in connnction with the employer’s business or property. It 
may be that the granting of earned leave unreported to the Labour 
Office may mislead the Labour Office to-~give it twice to the employees 
at the cost of the employer. In that way it has remote connection with 
the employer’s business or property. But then, one cannot, on proof 
of these irregularities alone, say that the employee guilty of committing 
them did so dishonestly and fraudulently. An employee is to be presumed 
innocent till his guilt is established beyond reasonable doubt. At least 
that seems to be the right spirit of the Standing Orders embodied in the 
rule 14. The management committed one fundamental error in finding 
Shri Sing guilty of misconduct under rule 14¢c(ii) without any evidence 
to show any act of deceit on his part in this case. No such inference 
can be drawn from the materials that have been placed before the 
Tribunal. As I have already stated above, both Shm Sing and 
Shri Ghosh, the senior Labour Officer, have said regarding the duties 
of the Time Keeper vis-a-vis the Labour Office in making employments 
in the Mill. Shri Balaram Sing says that his work, was clerical, notin 
attendance, sending requisitions for absent labour, complying with 
the instructions given in the employment pass, making calculations of 
Whges and preparing earned leave accounts. The Labour Office now 
deals with the appointment and leave of the labour employed in the

me to be this, that the management has acted on mere suspicion in 
dismissing Shri Balaram Sing on a charge of misconduct, when materials 
reveal only at the most that some irregulerities had occurred in his 
work. I am afraid, I am unable to accept the view point pressed so ably 
and emphatically by Shri Ghosh on behalf of the Company in this 
case. To my mind, the evidence placed before this Tribunal—it does not 
appear what evidence, if any, was placed before the Manager during 
the enquiry—does not support the finding made by the Manager in the 
enquiry into the charges against Shri Balaram Sing in this case, nor 
can ] say that the finding in dispute is the possible view of this evidence. 
Accordingly, the inescapable conclusion is that Shri Balaram Sing is not 
guilty of misconduct under rule 14c(ii) of the Standing Orders. He has 
committed some very serious irregularities in his work. This may amount 
to neglect of duty, a misconduct under the Standing Orders. 


To sum up the charges relating to cases Nos. 1 to 8 mentioned in the 
charge-sheet have not been established, but those relating to Nos. 9 and 
10 have been established. That being so, the action taken by the 
management in dismissing the employee is not fully justified. This 
takes us to the question of punishment. Is the punishment unduly severe 
and arbitrarily harsh P 


The employee had a clean record of service. His conduct as found 
in this case dovs not appear to be prima facie offensive. He has 
committed some errors of omission and commission, i.¢6., some irregularities 
only in his work. This might have been due to pressure of work, 
It 1s only in the background of the supposed existence of mal]practices 


part J] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 3209 


তি ৩০০০০০০০০০০ om: 


a a a a ee ডট ے+یووےجٗی‎ 
سیر‎ eee 


in theddepartment, that it comes within the mischief of misconduct, 
unishable under the Standing Orders. In this context, the punishment 
of dismissal from service, with consequent loss of all the benefits to 
which he was otherwise entitled, appears to be unduly harsh. The 
nishment of discharge will, in the circumstances, be adequute. 
Farther even if the action of the management in dismissing him from 
service on proof of some of the charges be found totally justified, which it 
18 not, the question of his reinstatement, which no doubt is the normal relief 
in such circumstances, has got to be examined with due care, and that 
hoth subjectively and objectively, both from the point of view of the employer 
snd the employee. The parties have admittedly lost confidence in each 
other. Shri Balaram Sing who said that he had direct approach to Shri 
(toenka, the all in all of the Mill, suspected his motives in dismissing him 
from service. 139 thought he was victimised for his Union activities. He 
می‎ nO More a persona grata with him. He was not an ordinary employee 
but a Time Keeper, who has some very important duties to do in connection. 
with the work of the labour force, employed in the Mill. The management 
entertained and even now entertains strong suspicion for his complicity 
in the malpractices said to be rampant in his department. His reinstate- 
ment would mean sending him back to his old post with all 
the benefits and privileges attached to it. The proper work in that post 
would depend to a large extent on what co-operation he gets from and 
renders to the management, and on the mutual trust and confidence. 
Both he and the management will find it difficult to carry on in the 
present atmosphere of distrust and suspicion. The justice of the case 
tequires the immediate creation of a harmonious relationship between 
the two. 1118 reinstatement in any view of the matter will have the 
spposite effect. The question of rcinstatement in the circumstances 
like this was examined by their lordships of the Hon’ble Labow 
Appellate Tribunal in Banaras Light and Power Co., Iitd., vs. Brizlidhar 
1952, L.A.C., page 248), after their decision in the Buckingbam and 
(arnatic Co., Ltd. rs. Workers of that Company reported in 1952, L.A.C., 
page 492. It has been held by their lord»hips in that case that, 
‘although, in case of wrongtul dismissal, the normal rule ia reinstate- 
ment, other things sare to be considered before making an order for 
leinstatement. Where it is clear, as in the instant case, that reinstate- 
went would not tend to promote harmonious relations between the 
parties but would have an opposite effect, the parties having lost 
confidence in each other, the order is not reinstatement but adequate 
,ompensation’’. In any view of this case, this Tribunal, on a considera- 
tion of the evidence and review of the whole position, comes to the 
conclusion that Shri Balaram Sing is not entitled to reinstatement. 
This finding however does not fully dispose of the issue. It now 
remains to be seen, what other relief, if any, the employee is entitled 
bo. Shri Ghosh on behalf of the Company, raised a short point here. 
Ho said that the issue of reinstatement, having been decided by this 
Tribunal, it is no more competent to adjudicate upon other matters 
connected therewith, having regard to the limited nature of the issue 
framed. This contention overlooks the provisions of section 10(4) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, which says that the Tribunal shall confine its 
uljudication to the points referred to it and matters encidental thereto. 


é 


lt is an established principle ef law that where a Court or Tribunal 
is called upon to decide o matter, it must decide the matter zn a complete 
way, in order that the rights of the parties may be settled. The Court 
or Tribunal, therefore, should give appropriate reliefs which would 


3210 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER. 23, 1954 [Parr ] 
০৭ 


flow from its findings (1954, L.A.C., page 5). This contention therefore 
fails. Shri Balaram Sing, however, is entitled to adequate cofmpensa- 
tion for loss of employment as envisaged in the aforesaid case. He hag 
put in a little over 10 years of service. He is allowed to get (i) one 
month’s total emoluments, at the rate last drawn, for each completed 
year of service; (11) Provident Fund dues including the Company’, 
contribution due to him; and (111) any earned leave due. 


The management should make these payments, less any amount 
wlready paid on this account within one month from the date of the 
publication of this award.

Mahammad and several others named in thé petition, all of the Packing 
Pepartment, where in consequence the production has fallen resulting im

reliefs, namely, their re-transfer to their original work, and for direction

National Tobacco Company of India, Ltd. On 24th August 1954 the Com-

withdrawn, and uo ‘‘no dispute” award is passed in this case. The agree- 
ment will form part in this award.

3. The matter of dispute as stated in the schedule to the order of 
reference is as follows :— 


(1) What should be the system of payment to the workers whether it 
should be direct payment or payment by the SirdarsP 


4. There was an agreement on 8th May 1952 between the parties in 
course of conciliation proceedings whereunder the Contractor, Shri Mohim 
Chandra De agreed to pay wages directly to the porters und not through the 
Sirdara as was the practice hitherto before. Then after one year, Shri 
Mohim Chandra Te stopped direct payment and restored the old system of 
parent of wages through the Sirdars from 25th May 1953. ence the 
dispute. 


The porters represented by the Calcutta Port Mazdoor Panchayet alleged 
among others that the Contractor Shri Mohim Chandra De should directly 
pay their wages and not through the Sirdars who made and were making 
illegal exactions besides realising ‘‘Bhaga’’ without doing any work or 
without supervising their work or without even remaining present at the 
site. It was said thai the Sirdars were sometimes employed by Shri Mohim 
Chandra De in his other works for which these porters were made to pay in 
the shape of “Bhaga’’ and other illegal exactions from their earnings. 


The West Bengal Mazdoor Congress on the other hand alleged that the 
Contractor, Shri Mohim Chandra De had engaged Sirdars through whom the 
porters were employed. It were the Sirdars who were to recruit, employ 
the porters and maintain their rolls. The Sirdars used to pay railway fares 
of the porters to and from their native places and they had to maintain the 
porters when they had no work and also to provide- other amenities to the 
porters. The contractor Shri Mahim Chandra Dey in his turn used to pay 
to the Sirdars the weekly bills uf the porters on the basis of the output of 
work and the Sirdar’s in turn used (0 distribute the money among the 
porters after deducting their Dasturi, commission and ‘‘Bhaga’’. These 
were charged by the Sirdars in consideration of the amenities they provided 
to the porters. If the system of direct payment be enforced, the responsibi- 
lity of recruitment, employment, maintenance, etc., should also pass on (0 
the Cantractor. 


The Contractor Shri Mohim Chandra De denied the relationship of 
employer and employees between himself on one hand and the porters on the 
other and pleaded that the porters were the employees of the Sirdars. It 
was said that the Sirdars were the sub-contractors and that Shri Mohim 
Chandra De had thus nothing to do with the porters. As, however, dispute 
arose between the porters and the sub-contractors known as Sirdars, Shri 
Mohim Chandra De had to intervene in the matter and came to an agreement 
as referred to. The agreement did not, however, work well. As a matter 
of fact, it operated to the detriment of smooth work, the Sirdars having been 
neglected and their status as employers having been in practice ignored and 
defied. The Sirdars legitimately and rightfully threatened Shri Mohim 
Chandra De with legal action for encronching upon their rights and hence 
the latter (Shri Mohim Chandra De) had to step aside in time. The Sirdari 
system has been in vogue for long past in view of the requirements of the 
trade, the casual nature of job, uncertainty about quantum of work and the 
floating nature of workmen. In the circumstances 1¢ was submitted that no 
obligation should be imposed upon Shri Mohimn Chandra De to make direct 
payment to the porters.

The settlement, dated 8th Mav 1992, it has already been noted, was arrived 
at in course of conciliation proceedings under the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Under section 18 of the said act such settlement is binding on the parties to 
the settiement. Section 19(2) lavs down among others that such settlement 
shall continue to be binding on the parties after expiry of the period as is 
agreed upon by the parties, until the expiry of two months from the date 
on which a notice in writing of an intention to terminate the settlement is 
given by one of the parties to the other party or parties to the settlement. 
In the present case nothing has been proved by Shri Mohim Chandra De
