As to the contention that no relationship of employer and employee 
existed or exists between Shri Mohim Chandra De on one hand 
and the porters on the other and ihus the settlement is bad and inoperative. 
I am unable to uphold it. Whatever might have been the position in the 
past and whether Shri Mohim Chandra De was the direct employer of the 
porters or not, it cannot be disputed in view of the terms im 
the settlement that Shri Mohim Chandra De, 1f he had _ not been 
the employer, had assumed the status of employer of the porters by the 
settlement and so long the settlement is not annulled according to Jaw, the 
relationship of employer and employee s0 assumed would continue to 
subsist. By the settlement Shri Mohim Chandra De assumed the status of 
a direct employer and relegated the Sirdars to the position of his employees. 
if they were not so before, as Supervisors under him for which the 
Sirdars would be entitled to get ‘Bhaga’ out of the earnings of the porters 
and nothing else. Then Shri Mohim Chandra De not only took upon himself 
the obligation to make direct payment to the porters but also agreed to pay 
the porters at an enhanced rate of wages. All these are consistent ouly 
with the character of an employer. So, in view of the terms of the settle- 
ment there can be no doubt that Shri Mohim Chandra De had assumed the 
status of direct employer of the porters. After having done so, he cannot 
now resile from that position without terminating the settiement in 
accordance with law. 


In this view of the matter the question whether Shri Mohim Chandra 
De or the Sirdars were employers of the porters before the settlement is not 
material, One can assume character of on employer if he was not লি 
previously. The present case is one such where Shri Mohim Chandra De 
had assumed such character of direct employer by the settlement if he had 
been not so before. As the settlement has-not been terminated according to 
law, he cannot either disown that the said character has been subsisting. 
It is accordingly held that Shri Mohim Chandra De is to continue direct

according to law.

The Issues as per schedule to the order of reference are— 


(1) Are the workmen entitled to receive from 15199199101, Ltd., any benefits 
for the period of services rendered by them under Messrs. M. M 
Ispahani, Ltd.? 

(2) Wages, scales and grades. 

(3) Dearness allowance. 

(4) Rates of contribution to the Provident Fund. 

(5) Whether the workers are entitled to Pujah bonus for 1953? 

(6) Procedure for discharge, dismissal or any other punishment. 

(7) Bonus. 


FINDINGS. 


Issue No. 1,—The Union’s contention is that the workmen are entitled to 
receive from the Ispahani, Ltd., benefits for the services rendered by them under 
the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., mainly on two grounds, namely, (i) there had been 
transfer of business by the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., to its successor the Ispahani, 
Ltd.; and (ii) there was continuity of service after the transfer. The company 
contests this claim, alleging among others, that it is altogether a separate concern 
and not a successor of the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. and that there is no transfer 
-of business from one to the other and lastly, the employees of the M. M. Ispahani, 
Ltd., are taken over after their services are terminated by that company aad 
accordingly, there is no continuity in service. The scope of enquiry, under this 
issuc, is clear though appears to be somewhat limited. Prima facie 
it appears to be nothing more than a mere declaration of a_ right 
without uny special reference to a claim. But the Union in its statement 
made it abundantly clear that the benefits which the employees are entitled to 
gel are in respect of length of service for the purpose of adjustment of salaries, 
retiral benefits, grades and scales, leave, etc. The issue, therefore, has got to 
be examined not only subjectively but objectively as well. Two different 
approaches to this question were suggested by the parties; the company’s approach 
is, what has been characterised as legal, whereas the Union’s is alleged to be a 
real and substantial one, based on well-established principles of social and 
‘economic justice, administered in the industrial courts, Necessarily the decision 
of this issue would depend on a close examination of the relevant facts in 
controversy, and also of the legal principles involved in it. 


The legal position advanced on behalf of the company may be summed 
up briefly as follows:— 


(1) This company, a limited one, was incorporated on the 15th September 
1947 under the Indian Companies Act and as such it was a separate 
legal entity from Messrs. M. M. Ispahami, Ltd., which was incorpora- 

ted on 19th December 1934. It was not a successor to the latter 
There could not be any transfer of one company to the other. 


(2) In the eye of law, the company came into existence only from the date 
of its incorporation and the sefvices of its employees must be taken 
to have commenced from that date. 


The learned representative for the company relied on a case reported in 
1953 L.A.C., page 557. The Union, on the other hand, did not so much dispute 
the theory of the sepurate legal existence of the new company but contended 
that there was transfer of business to this new company by the M. M. Ispahani, 
Ltd., and that there was m substance no terminatidn of services of the 
employees who were taken over to the Ispahani, Ltd. Their services continued 
without break, and accordingly, they were entitled to the benefit of pall get 
service. Shri Niren Dey, Counsel, appearing on behalf of the Union relied ০৪ 


Part I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 238, 1954 3225 


EEE OP ORME ہیں چچ ےش‎ Nene: 
——— পল পপ আর জপ পি শপ ১ পাপ পাপ AI AAS لج‎ 


a numer of cases. They are: 1953 L.L.J., page 14, Volume I, Bombay Garage, 
Industrial Court Reporter, July/December 1949 at page 1134, 1953 L.A.C., page 
67, Rallies (India), Ltd., Industrial Court Reporter, September/December 1952 
at page 453. He also distinguished the case, reported in 1953 L.A.C., page 
557, “The Arezona, Ltd.”, relied on by the company. Shri Dey distinguished 
the case of 1953 L.A.C., page 556, mainly on the ground that it was a case of 
proprietory concern, carried on in an assumed name, whereas this was the case 
of a limited company. Their lordships in the said case at page 553 at page 
556-7 considered the claim for payment of bonus and reported to have said as 
follows: “As the concern is a propretory concern carried on under an assumed 
name, we do not see how continuity of service can be claimed. The workmen 
were the employees of Zordon. After Gregory’s purchase, they became his 
employees only because he chose to retain the services of the workmen who 
had been working in the establishment. In the eye of law, their employment 
came under Gregory from the time when he became the sole proprietor.” 
This is the short report of the case referred to above. The ratio decendandi in 
that case do not appear very clearly from the shortness of the report. But the 
distinguishing facts are there. As it is a case of transfer of business from one 
man to another, the services of the employees of the one must be taken to have 
commenced from the date of the other’s purchase not because of the purchase 
but because of the fact that the latter simply desired their employees to be in 
service. The facts of the present case which will be shortly discussed are 
entirely different. So far as I have been able to follow, the leading cases on the 
subject are primarily (i) the case of Bombay Garage, a decision of the Bombay 
High Court, reported in 1953 L.L.J., Volume I, paage 14; (ii) a decision of the 
Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal reported in 1953 L.A.C., page 388, 
“Lalubhai Aminchand vs. Govindajeon Tikuloo”, (ii) a case of the Hon'ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal reported in 1953 L.A.C., page 553. The other cases 
relied on by Shri N. Dey are cases of the State Tribunals reported in the Indus- 
trial Court Reporters. Of them the case of Rallies (India), Ltd. reported in 
Industrial Court Reporter, September/December 1950 at page 449 is probably 
to the point. All these cases seem to follow the decision of Mr. Justice Tendolkar 
of the Hon’ble Bombay High Court in the Bombay Garage, Ltd., 1953, Volume 
I, L.L.J., page 14. In considering the claim for payment of gratuity based on 
the services rendered in the past under the predecessor company, Mr. Justice 
Tendolkar observed, “An employer cannot deprive his employees of the benefits 
that have accrued to them by reason of past services merely by transferring his 
business to another person or to another limited company. The work done by 
the employees primarily benefit the concern, although of course the owner also 
receives the benefit therefrom. In any case, therefore, where there is continuity 
of service, new employer is bound to take into account the services rendered 
by the workers to his predecessor-in-title and it was open to the respondent to 
award that for the purpose of gratuity, services rendered to the former employers 
should also be taken into account.” His lordship thereafter distinguished the 
case of the I.C.I. (India), Ltd., an award by Sir Divatia with these words, 
“In that award, Sir H. B. Divatia came to the conclusion that the services of 
the workmen were terminated before the I.C.I. (India), Ltd., took over the 
concern and there was no continuity of service. On this ground he held that 
the period during which the workers were in service prior to the time when 
Imperial Chemical Industries (India), Ltd., took over the concern should not 
be taken into account. ...... But even assuming that this decision was correct, 
that was a case in which on the facts the Tribunal came to the conclusion that 
there was no continuity of service and it has no application to the present case 
where the respondent has, in my opinion, rightly come’ to the conclusion that 
there was continuity of service.” That decision was followed, so far as I can 


See, in two decisions of the Labour Appellate Tribunal. This question came 
up before their lordships of the Labour Appellate Tribunal, in 1953 L.A.C.,

page 388, Lalubhai Aminchand, Ltd., in which it was held that, “The employers 
have contended that they cannot be saddled with the responsibility for paying 
gratuity for the past services of the employee with the predecessors of 015 
company, and they also contend that the scheme of gratuity envisages that 
the computation of gratuity shall commence from the date of the agreement 
which is 23rd July 1949. There is no substance in either of these contentions, 
This company is the successor of the previous firm and must accept responsibility 
in matters of gratuity for the past services of the employees with that concern; 
there was no break in service and employment continued with the successor 
firm...... and in the normal course the employees are entitled to the benefit of 
their past services with the previous firm in the computation of gratuity.” The 
decision of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the Arezona, Ltd., did 
not lay down a different principle of law than what was enunciated in the 
Bombay High Court case. The requirements of law, as laid down in the leading 
cases, placed before this Tribunal, would be satisfied, if it is shown that (i) 
there has been transfer of business from one company to the other (ii) and that 
there has been continuity of service of the employees of the predecessor 
company in its successor. There could not be any break in service. Now let us 
examine the facts of the present case in the light of the above. There are 
certain facts which are not in controversy. They are: that some of the

This and the documentary evidency reveal that the Ispahani, Ltd., is occupy. 
ing the same office building as M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. They are using the same 
telegraphic address, paying the same old Municipal Bills in the name of M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd. Mr. N. K. Seal’s explanation at page 10 of his deposition 
that “the mutation was not done inadvertently” does not appear to be satis- 
factory. Ispahani, Ltd., 1s doing the same business as was done by the M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd. Shri N. Dey’s evidence on the side of the Union and Mr. Arakai’s 
evidence on the side of the company would establish it. Ispahani, Ltd., is not 
only doing the same business in the same place on the same terms of brokerage, 
etc., but doing it with the same parties. Exts. 11, 14, N. Dey and Kasinath 
Das’s evidence would show it. Taken along with this, the admitted position of 
the company that they purchased furnitures, motor cars and immovable pro- 
perties including two houses of M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., would show that they had 
acquired sufficient assets of M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. Regarding the position of the 
employees, there was no change in work with the change in the name of the 
business. The services of the employees were not terminated by any notice or 
letter or verbally, neither they were appointed by any such letter, etc. This is 
admitted on both sides. The employees except the Muslim staff were not asked 
to go to Chittagong neither they did ask for a new appointment. They 
continued to receive the same salary and naturally they had an impression that 
they were in service of the same company and that there had been no break in 
the continuity of service. It appears from Ext. J that the M. M. Isphani, Ltd., 
had caused the new company to be incorporated as a limited company. On 
the company’s side, no serious attempt was made to prove the allegations made 
in its written statement. The company’s two important points of defence are: 
It has a separate legal entity and as such it cannot be made liable unless it 
admits its liability strictly according to law, ...ا‎ by any registered document. 
That would be begging the entire question and not properly appreciating the 
scope of the present issue. In fact, Shri Niren Dey made it clear during argu- 
ment that the issue really is “whether the present terms and conditions be on the 
basis of the past services”. The issue speaks of benefits or advantages flowing 
from the.past services. This is not related to any of the dues of the M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd., or any of their liability to the employees. Accordingly, that

contention does not appear to be at all tenable. Second important point of 
defence urged on behalf of the company is that there was already a break in the

dues when the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., removed its Head Office to Chittagong. 
Under certain conditions, an employee is entitled to get back his Provident Fund 
dues. So, receiving dues of the Provident Fund does not necessarily indicate 
the termination of the contract of employment. Further, it is nobody’s case 
that at that time the employees were told that their services under the M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd., were terminated by the fact of payment of the Provident Fund 
dues. There was some real difficulty in administering the Fund from its Head 
Office in Chittagong which is in a foreign State. There are difficulties of com- 
munication inherent between the two different States. It is not very unlikely 
for the employees to think, as they now say, that they received the Provident 
Fund dues because the Trustees thought it desirable to make the payment. 
No endeavour was made on the side of the company to show by production of 
the Attendance Register that there was really any break in service of the 
employees who were taken over from the parent organisation of M. M. Ispahani, 
Ltd., to that of Ispahani, Ltd. In fact, Mr. Seal admits that it was on the 
recommendation of Mr, M. A. Ispahani, the Director of M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., 
that their employees were taken over by the Ispahani, Ltd. After all, it was 
the work of one man, the man of destiny at that time. Mr. M. A. Ispahani 
was making over the services of the employees of Mr. M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., 
to his ownself, the Managing Director of the Ispahani, Ltd. The conduct of 
the Directors of the Ispahani, Ltd., did not raise even the faintest of suspicion 
in the mind of the employees. And Mr. M. A. Ispahani assured the employees 
that they would continue to receive the same care and attention from the 
management and enjoy the same conditions of service and privileges as under 
the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. Mr. Reza, another Director of the Ispahani, Ltd., also 
assured the employees including Shri N. Dey that they would enjoy the same 
rivileges as before. Mr. M. A. Ispahani and Mr. Reza do not deny this. 
Mir. Seal who was present at the Independance Day celebration where Mr. M. A. 
Ispahani is said to have given the assurance, docs not deny it. Mr. P. R. 
Mukherjee had no answer to this, but urged very emphatically that the state- 
ments of the Directors do not bind the company. A promoter had no right 
of indemnity against the company which he promotes before its incorporation. 
He further contended that in case of an assurance, one would have expected a 
letter from the Directors in this case. No such letter is, of course, forthcoming. 
Assurance was given verbally. Question is whether such an assurance is 
unlikely in the circumstances and in the background of the political changes 
taking place in the country. In the opinion of the Tribunal it was not. It is 
true that an admission is not conclusive. Neither it creates any title where law 
requires a deed for it. This argument on the facts and in the circumstances 
appears to be very little assistance in deciding the issue. Question is not that 
the issue is being decided on the evidence of this assurance treating it to be 
an admission of the party but that whether considering the entire evidence and 
circumstances an inference may be legitimately drawn in favour of the Union 
namely that the identity between the two concerns is so striking that an indus- 
trial tribunal administering social and economic justice would hold that for 
certain purposes and in the public interest, the past services under the one 
company should be taken as continuing for the benefit of the employees in the 
Other. That 1s the whole point. There are some important documents which 
also throw much light on the decision of this issue. They.are Ext. 11, a letter 
from the Ispahani, Ltd., signed by Mr. Reza, its Director, on lst March 1948, 
introducing the company to the old customers of Messrs. M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. 
Ext. 14 is another Ietter of the Ispahani, Ltd., dated 25th October 1948, signed 
by Mr. Reza and addressed to the Assistant Secretary to the Government of 
India, Ministry of Commerce, New Delhi, in which Mr. Reza_ described 
Ispahani, Ltd., as successor company to M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. Three certificates

(Exts. 8, 10, 10A) signed by Mr. Arakai, Director of Ispahani, Ltd., and Mr.

But it is inconceivable to believe that these documents would be placed before

customers in the market that they were doing the same business left to them 
by the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. They were holding themselves out to the Govern. 
ment of India, Commerce Department, as a successor to the M. M. Ispahani,

employees for obvious reasons placed their confidence and trust in the Directors 
of the company and were encouraged by their assurances and conduct. They 
received increments and bonus from 1948, facts which have not been denied 
by the company, speak volumes in favour of the continuity of service. As to the 
transfer of business from the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., to the Ispahani, Ltd., the strong 

int of Shri P. R. Mukherjee seems to be this, namely, that the M. M. Ispahani, 

td., continues even now to carry on business on a very small scale holding 
some immovable properties in Calcutta and accordingly, question of the Ispahani, 
Ltd., becoming its successor does not arise. Undisputed evidence on this (point 
however is that the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., still holds some immovable propérties, 
mostly house buildings, in Calcutta and collect their rents here. That does 
not mean that the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., is still carrying on business ‘on a Nery 
smiull scale* in India. To me, it does not appear to be a very important factor 
in the whole case. M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., holds half of the capital of the Ispahani, 
Ltd., a company which they brought into existence due to the political changes 
in the country. They sold on very favourable terms valuable immovable pro- 
perties and other assets to the new company, not for cash but against shares 
in the new company. The Directors were continuing at the helm of affairs 
of the new company. Even the Trustees on the Board of the Provident Fund 
remaining the same. ‘Transfer of business means handing over so many things 
essentially connected with it. The evidence in this case leaves no doubt in any 
reasonable mind that the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., transferred its business to the 
Isphani, Ltd., who continued it thereafter in the same place with practically 
the same resources and with the assistance of the same old staff. The old 
company received the benefit of the service of its employees in the same way 
as the new company is now getting from them. It is therefore only reasonable 
to hold that the employees of the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd., are entitled, to the benefit 
of the past services rendered by them to the said company while in the service 
of the Ispahani, Ltd. On a consideration of all these, the Tribunal is inclined 
to answer the issue in affirmative in favour of the Union. ' 


Issues Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 7.—They are taken together for they depend more 
or less upon the financial position and stability of the company. It would, 
therefore, be necessary to examine the financial position of the company as 
disclosed in the Balance Sheets filed in this case. 


The company pleaded loss in the year ending 31st March 1953, also in the 
next year as a defence to the claim arising out of this issue. The Union askec 
for the rejection of the plea on the ground that there was im fact no loss in the 
years in question. It alleged that there was really no Joss in business anc

that if there was any loss, it was due to the mismanagement of it. The loss 
disclosed in the Balance Sheet was fictitious, for the figures were cooked up 
and manipulated and the money was drained out in the interest of a foreign 
country. The Union inspected the books of accounts of the company and had 
sufficient opportunity to examine them carefully and closely. No _ written 
objection was taken to any particular item in the Balance Sheet. Necessarily, 
the criticism of accounts advanced on the side of the Union was more or less 
in the nature of mere speculation, and the figures suggested were nothing more 
than mere guess. The Balance Sheet for the year ended 3lst March 1953 is 
Ext. C. A request was made on behalf of the company to treat the informa- 
tion in this Balance Sheet as confidential, although other evidence was openly 
adduced on the entries in the Balance Sheet. Also oral evidence was given 
regarding the loss. Endeavour would, therefore, be made to accede to this request 
as far as possible. Net loss according to the Balance Sheet (Ext. C) was more 
than about seven lakh fifty thousand. In the previous year, there was profit 
amounting to about 23 thousand and odd. The Balance Sheet of the current 
year ending March 1954 has not been audited. Shri Seal, Director, said that 
the loss in the year ending 3lst March 1954 was not so much as in the year 
1952-53 but still they expected loss. He said, “Our business is so big that we 
cannot without going into examination of accounts say how much loss we 
sustained but it wil be a minus and not a plus”. The Union, as stated above, 
did not accept this Balance Sheet as true. It tried to prove that it was 
manipulated in its preparation to show loss. P. ۳۸۷ 7, Shri Kasinath 
Das, was the accountant of the Ispahani, Ltd. He was in_ charge 
of the department. He is also the Assistant Secretary of the Employees’ 
Union. Speaking about the Balance Sheet he said 11) cross-examina- 
tion, “In 1952-53, the Balance Sheet discloses a loss. The accounts 
have been manipulated. I was instructed to prepare false accounts which I 
ےکرک ھت‎ [ did not inform the management by writing any letter that I 
will not be able to carry out instructions in preparing the false accounts. The 
accounts previous to that are all correct. I never told the Income-tax Officer 
that our accounts were manipulated.” It was on this evidence the Union con- 
tended that the accounts were manipulated to show loss. As already stated, 
no genuine endeavour was made to show that any part of the Balance Sheet 
was particularly wrong or inaccurate or that any money had been wrongly 
diverted or any income concealed from it. The criticism of account on the side 
of the Union 1s, for obvious reasons, generally speculative in character. Doubts 
and suspicions are raised regarding almost every entry made in it. But usually on 
many occasions, such criticism 1s justified as the Union officials have no access to 
company’s books of accounts. Here in this case, the position is entirely different. 
The accountant in charge is the Assistant Secretary of the Union, making 
tadbir in this case. Not only some important information regarding 
the accounts but sime other official information was supplied before this 
Tribunal without the knowledge or permission of the executives of the company. 


Question is, therefore, whether Shri Das’s evidence is to be relied upon. 
In all probabilities, he, being one of the executives of the Union, will hesitate 
to carry out any such instructions of the management to prepare false accounts, 
for the simple reason that they might be used against the interests of the Union. 
Moreover, he seems to have a definite bias against the management, now that 
he had been relieved of his important position in the office. He has been 
transferred to the Tea Department, although on the same pay, where he holds 
a very minor position. It is not very unlikely for a man in this position to 
depose falsely against the management. He wants to serve two purposes by 
doing so; (i) he advances the claim of the Union in these matters and (11) brings 
discredit on the reputation of the company. It is very difficult to distinguish 
Shri Das as an accountant, entirely responsible for the maintenance and pre- 
paration of the accounts on which the Balance Sheet is prepared, from Shri 


3232 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr I 


Das, the Assistant Secretary of the Union, responsible for defending the cause 
of the employees, as against the employers. He thus plays a double role in this 
case. He breathes hot and cold at the same breath. He should not be, in the 
interest of justice, allowed to take an undue advantage of his own wrong. He 
must have clearly done wrong if he had prepared false accounts of a public 
limited company as he says he did under the instructions of his employers. 
In this vew of the matter, and in view of the fact that Mr. Seal definitely denies 
the allegation that the management instructed Shn Das to manipulate the 
accounts, the Tribunal finds that the story of manipulating accounts is totally 
untrue. 

There is no evidence on the Union side, barring the fact that the Ispahani, 
Ltd., carries on business transactions with a firm in London and with the 
Government of Pakistan to show or suggest that the company drains out the 
money, “through gross mismanagement and calculated fraud”, in the interest 
of foreign countries. The business of the nature that the Ispahani, Ltd., is 
doing can hardly be confined to the internal market. It must of necessity try 
for a foothold in the world market. That they did so only in the particular 
year, out of any design, to deprive the legitimate dues of the employees, remains 
to be proved in this case. Such allegations against the company’s accounts as 
are made in this case on behalf of the Union which the Union did not even 
care to prove by any reliable evidence, do not reflect any credit on it. After 
all, the use of strong and bitter words indicates a weak cause. The two other 
criticisms of the accounts are: (i) there has been an undue increase in the 
revenue items in 1952-53 showing that expenditure went unchecked, and (ii) 
that an advance of a huge amount of 13 lakhs 46 thousand rupees was made 
to the Jute Suppliers of which Mr. H. D. Nomani, the Director of this company, 
is a co-Director, was shown as unpaid in the year under review. In connec- 
tion with objection No. 1, the learned representative for the Union filed a com- 
parative chart showing the increase in the turnover in 1950 and 1953. He 
suggested thereby that in usual course there would be more profits in th 
years. The Balance Sheets, since 1948 to 1953, have been filed. It appears 
therefrom that in the year ending March 1950, the company suffered a loss 
amounting to 1 lakh 69 thousand and odd besides the huge loss sustained in 
the year ending March 1953. Total expenses as per “Profit and Loss Account” 
show a decline in the year under review. It was 28 lakhs 58 thousand and odd 
from 34 lakhs 17 thousand and odd in the previous year. Nothing was suggested 
while Mr. Seal was under cross-examination regarding this increase in the 
expenditure. Now increased turnover explains increase in the expenditure but 
does not necessarily prove that there will be more profits. The trend of general 
criticism of the company’s accounts is that the expenditure is excessive. I have 
found it very difficult to follow such criticism in the absence of materials to 
judge it. It is not possible to assess the reasonableness of the expenditure 
unless materials are forthcoming to show that expenditure in any comparable 
concerns is much less, or that the management has overstepped the limits of 
law in any matter. As to the allegation of mismanagement, apart from the 
fact that the company charged handling commission at 40 per cent. amounting 
to Rs. 1,585-2 as. in Ext. 12, in an invoice from the Director-General, Depart- 
ment of Supplies, Government of Pakistan, Karachi, there is nothing to show 
that the management did that work in an unbusinesslike way. Even there, 
the explanation was that they paid no commission for buying jute 
while they allowed some handling commission in due course of business 
to the purchasers. As to the objection No. 2, the advance of rupees 13 lakhs 
46 thousand to the Jute Suppliers, Ltd., Mr. Seal said that that was done in 
due course of business. The account not being settled was shown in the books 
of accounts as due. I fail to see how this can bring down the profit of the 
company, as is sought to be made out, in this case. So far as I have been 
able to follow, the criticisms are mostly speculative in form -and character and 
carry us nowhere. The accounts as shown in the Balance Sheet, in the opinion

of the Tribunal, should be accepted. That being so, the company is found 
to be running at a heavy loss. In course of five years of its existence, it had 
suffered losses in two years, including a very huge one in the year ending March 
1953. In the current year, the management is also expecting a loss, which may 
not be so big as in the previous year. But still it would also be a year of loss. 


Now let us examine the claims against this background of loss under the 
different issues, one by one. 


Issue No. 7.—This relates to bonus. It appears from the written statement 
filed by the Union that this refers to three bonus per year. The learned repre- 
sentative for the Union, however at the time of argument made the position 
clear. He said that he was now claiming a profit bonus only for the workers 
for the year 1952, 1.5. the year ending March 1953. Unfortunately, the learned 
representative did not file any chart drawn up according to the formula 
laid down in the Millowners’ Case reported in 1952 L.A.C., page 
433. Bonus to workmen is intended to enable them to participate in the pros- 
perity of a concern in the relevant year. There cannot be any right to bonus 
based on custom, or on consideration of social justice, other than are incorporated 
in Full Bench Decision. An order of payment of bonus in year of loss made upon 
the ground that it was paid in spite of loss, must be set aside (vide 1953, L.A.C., 
page 257). As there was no surplus profit or any profit in the year in question, 
available for payment of bonus, the claim shall fail. I decide the issue against 
the Union. 


Issue No. 4.—This relates to the rates of contribution to the Provident Fund. 
The Union wanted a contribution at the rate of 10 per cent. in place of 5 per cent. 
at present on the allegation that many comparable concerns are paying at that 
rate. In the view of the fact that the financial position of the company is far 
from stable, and that it is running at a loss, 1 consider it undesirable to increase 
the rate. The learned representative suggested that it should be increased at 
least up to 84 per cent. I do not consider present to be an opportune moment 
for increasing the rate of Provident Fund. I decide the issue accordingly. 


The two other issues (Issues Nos. 2 and 3) relate to wages scales and grades 
and dearness allowance. At present, dearness allowance is not separately paid. 
The wages include it. There are no scales and grades. The Company has filed 
lists of employees with their pay as an annexure to its statement. The Union 
has also claimed different grades and scales of pay, providing annual .increment 
in every case. It did not و‎ the Engineering Tribunal’s Award in this matter 
and alternatively it suggested, that for the present, an increase of 20 per cent. over 
the existing salary up to Rs. 200, 10 per cent. for those drawing above Rs. 200 
but below Rs. 350 and 5 per cent. for all drawing above Rs. 351 should be provid- 
ed. The wages of all the employees including the Directors’ remunerations suffered 
a cut to the extent of 10 per cent. as an economy measure. The cut is in force. 
It will, I believe, be restored as soon as the finances of the company would 
permit. Their lordships of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in Caltex 
(India), Ltd., 1952, L.A.C., page 402 at p. 408 held, “In Buckingham & Carnatic 
Mills case, this Tribunal pointed out that the influences of the first three and four 
factors cannot be appraised with precision and the important factors would be 
the capacity of the industry and the prevailing rate of wages.” Their lordships 
were dealing with the Fair Wages Committee Report in which it was stated that 
the following factors would be taken into consideration in fixing the wages: (1) 
productivity of labour, (ii) prevailing rate of wages in the same or similar occupa- 
tions in the same neighbouring localities, (111) level of national income, and 
(iv) the place of industry in the economy of the contry. The capacity of the 
industry to pay is the most important factor in deciding the wages scales. The 
Hon’ble Labour Appellaate Tribunal confirmed the above views in two more 
recent cases reported in 1954, L.A.C., page 18 and 1954, L.A.C., page 234. They 


3234 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 28, 1954 [Parr ] 


সু REET i iQ Tm 


held that for the purpose of seeing whether incremental scales should be given 
or not, the ability of the employer to pay is the relevant factor, As the burden 
on the employer would be increased, year after year, it is also necessary to consi- 
der whether it would have the ability to pay in future years, that is to say, the 
financial stability of the concern is also a relevant factor. Their lordships found 
that the financial condition of the company was not sound and it was in a very 
bad way. In those circumstances, the claim of the Union for incremental grades, 
retiring benefits in the shape of Provident Fund and bonus should not be allowed. 
I have considered the wages at present paid by the company and I have found 
that only in the case of 15 that the wages including dearness allowance fall below 
Rs. 61. I am told by the learned representative for the company that some of 
these employees are appointed on part-time work. That may so particularly in 
the case of Sweepers. At the most, the wages of these employees call for a 
revision and the company would do its best to make it Rs. 61 where necessary. 
Considering the fact that the company is facing a very critical time and has not 
the capacity to pay more, due to its unstable financial position due to loss, the 
Tribunal does not propose to fix any grades and scales of pay at present. The 
same remarks apply regarding the dearness allowance for it is now inseparable 
from the wages. I answer the issues accordingly. 


Issue No. 5.—This relates to a claim for Puja bonus of 1953. No bonus 
was paid in that year. This is admitted. 


The company resisted this claim on the ground that it never paid any 
customary bonus on the occasion of the Durga Puja since its incorporation and 
that it was not liable to pay any in view of the fact that it suffered a huge loss 
in that year. The Union however claims the same irrespective of the question 
of profit and loss, alleging that it was always paid at the rate of a month’s 
wages on the occasion of the said Puja by this company and by its predecessor, 
the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. A Puja bonus is different from ordinary bonus. It 
is paid irrespective of any profit and loss of the year. It is claimed as a matter 
of right, being a term of the employment. The right is based on agreement 
which may be either express or implied. The leading case on the subject of 
Puja bonus is Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills, Ltd., Calcutta, a decision of the Labour 
Appellate Tribunal of India reported in 1952, L.A.C., page 370. Their 
, Lordships of the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal observed in that case at 
page 374 as follows: “Puja bonus is a bonus claimed by the workers as a 
matter of right, payable by the employer at a special season of the year namely 
at the time of the annual Durga Puja. This right is not based on the general 
principle that labour and capital should share the surplus left after meeting 
necessary and prior charges, but it rests on agreement between the employer 
and the workers. That agreement may be either express or implied; where not 
express, past practice may lead to an inference of an implied agreement. But 
for implying agreement, the practice must be unbroken and for a sufficiently 
long period to exclude the hypothesis that payments had been made out of 
bounty. Jt is not possible to say in general terms what should be the length 
of the period. That would depend on the circumstances of each particular 
case, but the fact that the payments have been made even in a year of loss would 
be an important factor on the question as to whether the payments were mere 
acts of bounty or an obligation on the part of the employers. When the right 
is thus established, the next question would relate to the amount. ............ 5 
Unfortunately, the evidence on both sides on this point is very meagre. 2.۷۰ 
6 Shri Bose, Vice-President of the Union and an old employee of the M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd., said that they did not get any Puja bonus in 1953. They went 
on a deputation to the Director who regretted his inability to pay any bonus. 
He said further, ““We used to get Puja bonus and two bonus each year before 
that. We used to get Puja bonus every year, the payment was never stopped 
in any year. We used to get it at the rate of full one month’s salary without 


Parr I] THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 3235 
oh ee SSS eae 


deduction of Provident Fund. We got it in 1947 and 1948. It was paid 
irrespective of profit and loss made by the company.” In cross-examination, it 
was suggested to him that bonus was not paid because there was loss sustained 
by the company and that Puja bonus was paid previously when there were profits. 
He denied the suggestion. O. P. W. 1 Mr. Seal said that bonus was paid only 
on profits, on the occasion of the Puja in advance on the closing of account. 
It may be in one or two years that they paid bonus even when they suffered 
small loss. Payment of bonus was not a condition of service, it was not a 
customary bonus. It cross-examination, Mr. Seal said that he was not sure of 
the year but in one year two bonus were allowed to the employees. That was 
all the evidence regarding this issue. It struck me, at the time of argument, 
that the evidence was meagre and that it should be supplemented by further 
statements on both sides, if available. Pursuant to that, both parties filed 
statements. The company did so under protest. As it failed to assist the 
Tribunal with more materials particularly regarding the nature of payments made 
under the previous company, the statements of both sides were not taken into 
consideration in deciding the issue. Question now is whether the said evidence 
discussed above is sufficient to establish the right now alleged by the Union. 
It is a very important matter affecting the conditions of service. The evidence 
establishes the payment of bonus on the occasion of Durga Puja since 1948, 
1.۰, last five years. It was paid at the rate of one month’s wages at that time. 
It is admitted on the side of the company that bonus was paid even in a year 
of loss once or twice when the loss was very small. I do not think that, in this 
state of evidence, Puja bonus was paid at the uniform rate of one month’s wages 
a year, for a sufficiently long time and for an unbroken period. The Union did 
not make any endeavour to prove by evidence that the employees of the M. M. 
Ispahani, Ltd., who are now serving the Ispahani, Ltd., received the same bonus 
previously. I am afraid, that even that evidence would not have been sufficient 
in this case, for the claim in this case had been put forward on behalf of all 
the employees of Ispahani, Ltd., including the new entrants. It is not the case 
of the Union that the present staff consists only of the employees who served 
under the M. M. Ispahani, Ltd. That being so, the Puja bonus cannot be 
claimed as a condition of service in any circumstances on behalf of all the 
employees of the Ispahani, Ltd. After all, the payment of bonus for an 
unbroken period of five years only does not establish any right, much less a 
customary one, or show that it was a condition of service agreed on between 
the parties. The company’s objection must also be taken into consideration 
in deciding the question whether there was any implied agreement between them 
and their employees regarding the payment of Puja bonus. The company’s 
contention althrough was that the bonus was paid on profits, the payment of 
which was not stopped in a year of loss, when such loss was negligible. 
Examining the evidence in the light of probabilities keeping the principles 
enunciated in the Mahaluxmi Cotton Mills’ case in view, the Tribunal finds 
that the workers are not entitled to any Puja bonus in 1953. 


Issue No. 6.—This relates to procedure of discharge or dismissal or any other 
punishment. Both parties agreed to adopt for the purpose of this issue, the 
procedure laid down in the Bengal Chamber of Commerce Award. I accept 
their proposal and decide the issue accordingly.

DECISION. 


During the pendency of proceedings before the Lower Tribunal between 
the Company and its workmen, four persons were discharged, namely, (1) Shri 
Algoo, (2) Shri K. P. Bhaduri, (3) Shri Anath Nath Paul and (4) Shri P. N. 
Samanta. The first named person was discharged without notice with effect 
from ist September 1952 and the other three from the Ist November 
1952 after due notice. They filed complaints under section 33A_ of 
the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, before the Lower Tribunal. The Com- 
pany’s case against Shri Algdo was that he had absented himself for a long time 
and therefore, the Company*was justified in getting rid of his services. With 
regard to the three others, its case was that they were retrenched because with its 
dwindling business it undertook to reorganise its Jabour staff and these three 
persons were found to be surplus. The Tribunal held that there was no justi- 
fication for discharging Shri Algoo. He was given leave which he overstayed. 
Thereafter he joined and worked for six days and then absented himself again. 
During this period of his absence the Doctor of the Company examined him and 
gave him a medical certificate that he was down with Pneumonia. But this 
medical certificate was not taken into consideration and he was not taken back 
in the service of the Company. The Standing Orders of the Company do not 


176 


THE CALCUTTA 94821705119, SEPTEMBER 28, 1954 


1 خی‎ AG 


rovide for automatic termination of service, for abffence without leave. The 
مس‎ admitted that he was net charge-sheeted and therefore he had no 
Opportunity to explain his absence on the sccond occasion. The Tribunal 
ointed out that the Company by allowing him to join after he had overstayed 

is leave and to work for six days, had condoned his absence for the first period 
and his absence on the second occasion was due to the attack of Pneumonia. 
These findings are well supported by evidence and the Company has no case 
against him. The award made in his favour, is, therefore, upheld. 


The Tribunal held that P. N. Samanta was not a workman. In coming to 
that conclusion it relied upon his cross examination wherein he admitted that he 
was the Chemist-in-charge and Head of the Department, and that his duties were 
only of a supervisoty nature and that he had the absolute control in his depart- 
ment. On this state of the evidence, we think that the Tribunal was right in 
holding that he was not a workman. His complaint, therefore, does not lie. 
We ০ affirm the award made by the Tribunal also 90 far as he is 
concerned. 


There remain the two other persons, namely, K. P. Bhaduri and Anath Nath 
Paul. The Tribunal did not believe the Company’s case that due to reorganisa- 
tion made in view of its dwindling business, these two workmen had become 


surplus. But in the view that we are taking in this case, we need not express our 


opinion on that point. The fact remains, however, that many more workmen 
junior in service to them have been retained while these two persons were dis- 
charged. Shri Anath Nath Paul was a time-keeper and had put in 12 years of 
service. He says m his evidence that in 1946, the strength of the labour force 
was over 200 but it became gradually less and less, with the result that in 1951, 
a whole-time time-keeper became unnecessary. At that time he was given 
other duties in addition to his duty as time-keeper, namely, not only to record 
the attendance of the few workmen that were 1916 but also required to do other 
miscellaneous jobs such as despatching, etc. He further said that there were 
other employees who were much junior to him in service. In fact, it was proved 


@hat another clerk was appointed, only about 8 months before his discharge. The 


fact, that the Company in retrenching him has departed from the normal rule of 
“Jast come first go” without any justification, is sufficient for upholding the award 
of the Tribunal in so far as this workman is concerned. 


» There remains the complaint of the workman Shri K. P. Bhaduri. The 
Company first of all wanted to make out acase that his retrenchment was 
necessary because the business of the Company was not 10 a good position. 
Seeing that he--was a senior man with 14 years of service at his back, the 
Company wanted to get rid of him on the mere plea that he was suffering from 
Loucoderma and that the other employces and customers of the Company were 
afraid to have contacts with him. That was the main reason for his discharge. 
In the evidence it transpired that he was suffering from that disease since 194], 
shortly after-he joined this Company. That fact itself proves the hollowness of 
the defence of the Company, and no objection on that score had _ been 
taken by the Company for the last 13 years of his service. It is 8150 in 
evidence that no complaint was made to the Management on account of his 
said disease and there is also the expert opinion in the shape of a Doctor’s 
certificate that the disease was neither contagious nor infectious. There is also 
a Durwan in the service of the Company suffering from the self-same disease 
and the Company has not taken any action for getting rid of the services of that 
Durwan. These bcing the fact, we hold that in discharging K. P. Bhaduri, the 
Management was actuated by ulterior motives. We accordingly uphold this 
part of the award also. 7 

The result is that the workmen's appeal, namely, Cal-88/53, which is con- 
fined to P. M. Samanta is dismissed but without costs, and the Company’s Appeal 
No: Cal-92/53, which is directed against the award made in favour of these 
three other workmen, Algoo, Anath Nath Paul and K. P. Bhaduri, is also dis- 
missed but with costs, which we assess at Rs. 50. 


R. C. MITTER, Chairman.

PART II—Advertisements, Notices 


Procedure regarding sending Manuscripts for publication of Advertisements, Notices, etc., in 
the ‘Calcutta Cazette’’ (Part 88), 
1. Manuscripts should be properly edited and complete in itself. 


2. Manusoripts should always be typewritten on one side of the paper. Tha name of the signatory should be type- 
sritten below the signature. 


3. Manuscripts Intended for advertisement in the next issue of ‘‘Caloutta Gazette’’ shali be recelved by Publication 
Bales Office at New Secretariat Bulldings, 1, Hastings Street, Caloutta, up to 11 a.m. on Saturday and at Head Offies 
at Allpore up to 12 noon on Monday. 


All costs shali be pald in advance and deposited along with the Manuscripts.‏ ق 


5. Manuscripts and postal remittances shall be addressed to SUPERINTENDENT, GOVERNMENT PRINTING 
(PUBLICATION BRANCH), WEST BENGAL GOVERNMENT PRESS, ALIPORE. 


The Press shall not be held responsibie for delay In publication of any advertisement due to the non-observance of the 
instructions detalied above.

GOVERNMENT OF INDIA. 


North East Frontier Agency. 
Advertisement. 


APPLICATIONS are invited by the adviser to the 
overnor of Assam, Shillong, for a few temporary posts 
of Welfare Officers, Base Superintendents and Transport 
Superintendents in the North East Frontier Agency from 
Indian citizens and persons migrated from Pakistan with 
the intention of permanently settling in India or subjects 
of Nepal, Sikkim, Portuguese or French possessions in 
India. 1479 date for receipt of applications will be 25th 
September 1954. 


Applications must contain, inter alia, the following 
particulars :— : 


Name in full; Educational and other qualifications ; 
Age on Ist September 1954; Community; Home 
district; Experience; Aptitude for social and wel- 
fare activities in backward areas; Proficiency in 
sports; Whether bachelor or married; Details of posts 
held with present pay if still in service. 


2. Preference will be given to suitable serving officers 
from the following services of the State Governments who 
will be taken on deputation in the first instance:— 


(1) State Civil Service. 
(2) Police Service. 2 


(3) Excise Service. 


Existing officers of the North East Frontier Agency work- 
Ing in any executive capacity will alsa,be eligible. 


Selection will also be made from other suitable young 
mon possessing the required qualities. Such persons must 
graduates of recognised Universities and should not be 
Over thirty years of age. The ago limit can, however, be 
relaxed in case of bona fide refugees or candidate from 
Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes and also in case of 
ose who possess suitable administrative experience. 


8 Sorving officets will be on deputation for three 
70888 in the ‘first instance. The question of extension or 
Perinanent absorption will be ےت مہ‎ at the ond of that 
Period. All officers will be treated as on trial during the 

tat year of their service, 


THE CALGUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 68d 


4. S8enlority required.—Selection from the existing servi- 
ces will ordinarily be confined to officers with the minimum 
service indicated below :— 


(1) For posts of Welfare Officers—65 to 7 years 
seniority. 


(2) For posts of Base and Transport Superintendents— 
3 to 5 years’ seniority. 


6. Terms of service.— 


(a) Basic pay: (1) Welfare Officers (Gazetted posts, 
belonging to Central Services Class IT) in the 
scale of Rs. 250—250—300—(conf.)—25—400 

(£.B.)—400— (E.B.)—25—600—(E.B, )—25—750, 


(2) Base and Transport Superintendents (Gazetted 
posts, belonging to Central Services Class IT) ia 
the scale of Rs. 150—150—200—(conf.)-—10—260—. 
(E. B.)—10—300—124—375—(E. B.)—124—450. 


(b) Special pay: Special pay of 334 per cent. of basic 
pay subject to a minimum of Rs. 125 and a maxi- 
mum of Rs. 250 when posted in tribal areas. 


(c) Accommodation: Free accommodation of simple 
type on a fixed acale. 


Note.—The posts of Base and Transport Superintendents 
are anologous in functions to those of a Tahsildar or Sub- 
Deputy Collector of a plains district. The posts of Wel- 
fare Officers are equivalent to E.A.Cs. but the functions 
are those implied in the designation. 


6. Working conditions.—Service in the North East 
Frontier Agency calls for a high degree of physical fitness 
and the possession of special qualities of initiative, ima- 
gination, resourcefulness, and broad sympathy for and 
understanding of tribal peoples, and interest in the life and 
customs of primitive tribes. Officers will be required to 
serve in the forward areas in very difficult conditions, as 
communications are very poor and social amenities hardly 
exist. They will be expected to live among the tribes, learn 
their languages, study their manners and customs and win 
their confidence and trust. They would alao have to co- 
ordinate the activities of the various development depart- 
ments such as Agriculture, Engineering, Health, Educa- 
tion, etc., in these areas. Bachelors or married officers 
whose wives are also interested in welfare work will be 
preferred. Married officers with children will not be able 
to take their children with them to the forward areas 
but will have to make separate arrangements for their 
education, etc., at Shillong or elsewhere. 


7. Applications will be examined by a Selection Board 
oa appheants considered suitable will be called for 
interview. 


No travelling expenses for interview will be paid by this 
Administration, 


Selected candidates will be required to furnish a certi- 
ficate of physical fitness from a Civil Surgeon before they 
are appointed that they are fit for strenuous touring on 
foot in the hills.

PART VI.—Bills introduced in Parliament of India; Reports of Select 
Committees presented to Parliament; and Bills published before 
introduction in Parliament. 


HOUSE OF THE PEOPLE. 


The following Bill was introduced in the House of the People on the 
26th 10910270825 1954:— 


Brut No. 58 or 1953. 
A bill to preserve the milch and draught cattle of the country. 
Be it enacted by Parliament as follows :— 


1. Short title, extent and commencement.—(Z) This Act may be 
called the Anti Cattle Slaughter Act, ہج لا‎ 


(2) It extends to the whole of India. 


(3) 16 shall come into force at once. 


Z. ODefinitions.—In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in 
the subject or context,— 


(a) ‘cattle’? shall include cows, bullocks, their calves, he and 
she buffaloes and their calves; 


(b) “person” shall include any company or association or body of 
persons whether incorporated or not. 


3. Stopping of cattle slaughter.—No person shall kill or slaughter 
cattle either for food or for any other purpose either in a_ licensed 
slaughter-house or any public or private place and no _ person shall 
knowingly permit the use of any premises owned, occupied or possessed by 
him for any such killing or slaughtering. 


4. Penalty and procedure.—(Z) Any person who contravenes the 
provisions of section 3 and kills or causes to be killed or slaughtered 
any cattle, shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may 
extend to three years or with fine which may extend to one thousand 


rupe3s or with both. 


(2) The offence shall be cognizable and non-bailable. 


120 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 23, 1954 [Parr V] 


RP Sea 


STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


The directive in the Constitution of India for stopping cow slaughter: 
has remuined a dead letter so far. It is imperative to give effect to the 
pressing seutiments of the vast majority of people and of the unanimou: 
expression of the will of the Boats os expressed in the Constitution. 
Further, India being an agricultural country and being deficient in milk 
needs cattle. The cows and buffaloes and ihe bullocks provide these twa 
pressing needs. To meet this constitutional directive and for the 
preservation of draught and milch animals, it is necessary to take steps 
for stoppage of slaughter of cows, bulls, bullocks, he and she buffaloes and 
calves of these animals. Hence this Bill. 


U. M. TRIVEDI. 


M. N. KAUL, Secy.

An Act to amend the West Bengal Burgadars Act, 1950. 


WHERFas it is expedient to amend the West Benyal 
Bargadars Act, 1960, for the purposes and in the manner 
hereinafter appearing ; 


lt is hereby enacted in the Fifth Year of the Republic 
vf India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows :-— 


1. (1) This Act may be called the West Bengal Barga- 
dars (Amendment) Act, 1954. 


(2) It shall come into force immediately on the West 
Bengal Bargudars (Amendment) Ordinance, 1954, ceasing 
to operate. 


2. In sub-section (3) of section 12 of the West Bengul 
Bargadars Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the said 
Act), for the words ‘‘the months of Chaitra and Baisakh’’ 
the words ‘‘the month ot Baisakh’’ shall be substituted. 


3. After section 12 of the said Act and before the hexc- 
ing entitled ‘‘Supplemental.’’, the following section shall be 
inserted, namely :— 

“Effect of contraven- 2A. (/) Where the owner of

the West Bengal Sargadars (Amend- 

ment) Act, 1954, terminated or caused 

to e terminated, the cultivation of the

৮২-২২-২০০০ ০০০৭ 

The industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Hoare Miller & Co., Ltd. 
and the workmen as per schedule given below has been referred to this 
Tribunal under Government order No.  4583Dis./D/10L-85(B)/53, dated 
the lst December 1953, for adjudication. 


SCHEDULE. 


(1) Whether the workmen are entitled to receive any amount in 
addition to one month’s basic pay as bonus payable in 1953. 


AWARD. 


Original reference was in respect of the dispute between the Company 
and their workmen (employees in their Head Office), subsequently by 
corrigendum No. 995Dis./D/10L-85(B)/58, dated the 2nd March 4, 
the words ‘‘employed in their Head Office’’ were deleted after the worda 
‘fand their workmen’’. The result is that the dispute now falling for 
adjudication is between the Company on one hand and its workmen on the 
other. 

The Union contends on behalf of the workmen that the Company has 
been paying the annual bonus every year during the Puja time, equivalent 
to one month’s basic pay and dearness allowance and one year’s Provident 
Fund contribution, irrespective of any profit or loss and that this bonus 
is now 0 service condition by implied agreement. It is stated that in 
1958 such bonus for 1952 was payable and that the Company paid only 
one month’s basic wage and not dearness allowance and Provident Fund 
contribution. 


The Company contends on the other hand that bonus was never a 
service condition and that the Company by way of ‘‘good-will gesture’’ ۱ 
paid such bonus every year during Pujas and that in 1952, there was no 
profit, on the other hand there was sheer loss, still the Company paid the 
workmen (excluding the workmen of the Upholstery Factory in respect 
of whom separate reference has been نوا‎ one month’s basic wage as 
bonus for the year 1952 (in 1953). The Company gives a chart of the 
years in their written statement in which rate of bonus paid to its 
workmen is shown. This chart shows that in 1940, 1941 and 1943, only 
half month’s basic pay was paid as bonus and that in 1942, 1944, 1945 
and 1946, one month’s basic pay was paid as bonus. In 1947, 1948 and 
1951 one month’s basic pay plus dearness allowance was paid as bonus. 
In 1949, 1950 and 1952, one month’s basic pay plus dearness allowance 
plus one year’s Provident Fund contribution were paid as bonus. It is 
admitted that the payment is made every year for the immediately 
preceding years. Admittedly in 1951, there was peak profit made by 
this Company and therefore we find that for the said year bonus equivalent 
to one month’s basic wage plus dearness allowance plus one year’s 
Provident Fund contribution was paid to each workmen and that the 
said payment was made in 1952, 7.e., the following year. The balunce- 
sheet of the year 1952 produced by the Company shows that the gross 
profit was Rs. 3,57,918 after making aon allowance in the sum of 
Rs. 1,89,006 on account of depreciation during the said year. The 
Company has submitted a statement which is marked Annexure ‘‘A’’, 
which shows that after allowing deduction on account of depreciation, 
income-tax, rehabilitation, and 6 per cent. return on the paid-up capital 
and 4 per cent. on the working capital there has been deficit to the extent 
of Rs. 1,44,090. The Union did not challenge thig statement but its 
contention is that there has been un implied agreement_for payment of 
bonus equivalent to one month’s basic wage plus dearness allowanee 


Pant I] THE CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPT, 28, 1954 1373 
07777:7700 ee বলে 

plus one year’s Provident Fund contribution, and that this agreement is 
implied from the conduct of the Company because such payments were 
made ot least in the years 1949, 1950 and 1952 and that one mounth’s 
basic wage plus dearness were paid as bonus in 1947, 1948 and 1951. 
The question is whether from these several payments it may be held that 
there has been an implied agreement for paymnt of bonus equivalent to 
one month’s basic wage plus dearness allowance plus one year’s Provident 
Fund contribution. It is admitted that the Company has already paid 
one month’s basic wage for the year concerned. [ think that repeated 
payments of bonus amounting to one month’s basic wage for these long 
years have given rise to the implied agreement for payment of bonus at 
that rate. The payment of dearness allowance and Provident Fund 
contribution as part of bonus in some of the years does not unequivocally 
show that these were paid on the basis of any implied agreement. In 
some years dearness allowance was not paid as bonus, in sume years 
Provident Fund contribution was not paid as bonus. It has been held in 
Press Employees’ Association and the Statesman, 1954, 1 L.L.J., page 167, 
that— 


“The conditions of service of a workman are to be ascertained either 
on the basis of the Standing Order or on the basis of an 
agreement either expressed or implied’’. 


In that case it was also observed that— 


‘“‘As the payment of bonus in the past was only a gesture of good-will 
and was depending upon the trading result of the year, no 
implied condition could be inferred from the payment of bonus 
for years in which the Company incurred loss’’. 


It was held in Martin Burns, Ltd. vs. Workmen, 1953, 2 L.L.J., page 603, 
by the Appellate Tribunal that:— 


‘‘Where the Company has been paying two months’ basic wages as 
bonus to all workers irrespective of the trading results of the 
Company for over ten years, it must be held that payment of 
bonus has come to be an implied term of contract of service’’. 


Similar principles were also laid down in Muller Phipps, Ltd. vs. Workmen, 
1964, 6 F.J.R., page 171 and Mahalaxmi Cotton Mills case, 1952, L.A.C, 
page 070, It was observed in Mahalaxmi Cotton Mills case that— 


‘fan inference of implied agreement may be drawn from the past practice 
but the past practice must be unbroken and for a sufficiently 
long period to exclude the hypothesis that payments have been 
made out of hounty. It is not possible to say, in general terms, 
what should be the length of the period. That would depend 
upon cir¢umstances of each particular case’’. 


It was ulso observed in that case that— 

“the fact that the payment had heen made even in a year of loss 
would be an important factor on the question as to whether 
the payments were mere acts of bounty or an obligation on the 
part of the employers’’. 

In the present case it has not been shown that dearness allowance or 
Provident Fund contribution as bonus was ever paid in any year of loss. 
In the case of Union Drug Co. vs. Union, 1954, 1 L.J..J., page 766, it was 
held that— 

‘‘Period from 1945 to 1950 was not a sufficient long period for this 
purpose’’, 


1374 11) CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPT. 28, 1954 [Parr J 
টে ইসস ১৯৯ 


In view of the fact that in 1952 there has been loss and no profit it cannot 
be held that the Compary is bound to pay dearness allowance and Provident 
Fund contribution for one year in addition to one month’s basic wage as 
bonus, so J hold that the workmen are not entitled to receive any amount 
in addition to one month’s basic wage as bonus payable in 1953.

The industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Hoare Miller & ٥ہ.‎ 
[8.১ and their employees of the Upholstery Factory as represented by 
Hoare Miller (Manufacturing Division) Employees’ Union and Administra- 
tive Staffs Association, Upholstery Factory, Messrs. Hoare Miller & Co., 
Ltd., bas been referred to this Tribunal under Government order 
No. 6006Dis./D/10L-85(B)/53, dated the 380th September 1953, for 
adjudication. 


DISPUTE. 
Bonus for 1953. 


AWARD. 


It is admitted that the financial year of the Company ends on the 
۹18 December every year. It is also admitted that the present claim 
for bonus is a claim for the year 1952, which is alleged by the Unions 
to be payable in 1953. The Unions contend that the Manufacturing 
Pivision and the line staff have not been puid any bonus for the year 
1952, although such bonus has been paid to the workmen of the other 
departments and they claim this bonus as a service condition, based on 
long standing practice of paying such bonus at the time of the Pujas 
every year irrespective of any profit or loss arising to the Company. 
The Unions claim bonus as an annual bonus equivalent to one month’s 
total emolument, %,6.১ one month’s basic wages and dearness allowance. 


The Company on the other hand contends that this Manufacturing 
Division previously belonged to Messrs. Scott & Pickstock Company and 
that in August 1951, the said Manufacturing Division has been purchased 
by Messrs. Hoare Miller & Co. It is also admitted that in 1961 and 
1952, the Company paid bonus to the workmen of this Manufacturing 
Division also at one month’s basic wages and dearness allowance. In 
the written statement the Company contends that the said bonus was 
paid by way of ‘‘good-will gesture’? and that the workmen have no right 
to demand it and that the bonus which the workmen had in 195] and 
1962) ‘‘was unrelated to profit?’ and it was never meant to be a condition 
of service, and that according to the decisions in Mill Owners’ Association 
case, the workmen’s claim for bonus as a_ condition of service is not 
maintainable, 


The fact is admitted that in 1951 and 1952, Messrs. Hoare Miller 
Company paid bonus equivalent to one month’s basic wages and ۸۵ 
allowance to al] the workmen including the workmen of the Manufacturing 
Division and that in 14953, workmen’ other than those of the 
Manufacturing Division were paid one month’s basic wage as bonus, 
but the Manufacturing Division workmen were not pajd anything. It 
also appears from the written statement that when the matter was pending 
before the Labour Commissioner, the Company made some payment 
to the workmen of the Manufacturing Division by way of advance 
during the Puja time and it was understood that the said payment would 
be adjusted afterwards. When it is the Company’s own case that this 
bonus which was paid in 1951 and 1952 to the workmen of this 
Manufacturing Division ‘‘was unrelated to profit’? and when it is a 
fact that even after working of the said Manufacturing Division for only 
a part of the year, the Company was pleased to pay the workmen bonus 
for that year without any diminution, seem to suggest that the bonus 
wan paid as a service condition. In this connection we should also 


1376 THE CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPT. 28, 1954 [Parr ] 
এ সস 


consider the fact that Messrs. Hoare Miller & Co. gave a notice Ext. 1, 
to the staff of this Manufacturing Division at the time of the purchase of 
the concern, Messrs. Scott & Pickstock, Ltd. By that notice Mesars. 
Hoare Miller & Co. expressed that they were willing to offer the entire 
staf employed in the said department on terms identical with those 
which were being received at that time from Scott & Pickstock Company, 
Limited. It is clear from the evidence that the staff (wholesale) of the 
Manufacturing Division was tuken in by Messrs. Hoare Miller & Cu. 
after this purchase. The Company has also filed a statement Exi. A 
showing that Scott & Pickstock Manufacturing Division staff were paid 
bonus every year since 1944 up to 1951 and that before 1947 they were 
paid at 2 months or more and that since 1947, they have been paid at 
one month’s wages. It is admitted that in 1951 and 1952, they were 
paid at one month’s basic wages and one month’s dearness allowance. 
The payment of dearness allowance in 1951 and 1952 only in these 
circumstances cannot give any inference that it was paid as a service 
condition, but payment of one month’s basic wages since 1947, up to 
1951, methodically gives the reasonable inference that it was paid as a 
service condition. Considering all these circumstances I cannot but 
vome to the conclusion that the bonus as claimed by the Unions is an 
annual bonus and that it 1s a service condition based on implied agreement 
as laid down in Mahalaxmi Cotton Mills and other cases. It is 
contended in the evidence that for the year 1952 (which was otherwise 
payable in 1953), the Company did not pay any bonus to the workmen 
of the Manufacturing Division simply because in the year 1952, there 
was no profit in the said Manufacturing Division and that on the, other 
hand there was loss. When the Company admits in its written statement 
that the bonus which was paid was ‘“‘unreluted to profit’, I do not ,think 
that the question of profit or loss arises at all in this cuse.: The 
question is whether the bonus was paid as good-will gesture, or as service 
condition. There is nothing documentary to show that the practice of 
paying annual bonus since ‘1944 as is admitted by the Company in its 
own statement was paid as good-will gesture, on the other hand, this 
long standing practice of paying bonus annually irrespective of profit 
and loss gives rise of the inference that it was based on implied 
agreement, So the claim of the workmen for one month’s basic wages 
as bonus for the year 1952, payable in 1953 is quite just, reasonable 
and legal and it is binding upon the Company. So my award is that the 
Company shall pay one month’s basic wage to each of these workmen, 
less what have been already paid to them as advance during the concilia- 
fion proceeding, if such adjustment is due and if after adjustment 
anything is payable to the workmen the same shall be paid within 15 days 
from the date of publication of the award in the Calcutta Gazette.
