AWARD. 


The Government of West Bengal, Jiabour Department, by its Order No. 
A826Dis. /1D/10L-153/53, dated the 18th November 1953, referred an 
industrial dispute existing between Messrs. Crown Cork Manufacture Co. 
(Calcutta), 1, Umakanta Sen Lane, Calcutta-30 and their workmen 
represented by Crown Cork Workers’ Union, 67/7, Barrackpore Trunk Road, 
Calcutta-9, rewarding the matters specitied in the schedule to the Order of 
Reference under sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV 
of 1947), to this Tribunal for its adjudication. 


This was received in the office of this Tribunal on 2318+ November 1953 
and usual notices were issued to both parties for appearance and written 
atatements. Both parties filed their written statements in due course and 
the case was taken up on the day fixed for its hearing. 


The Union in its statement stated that the dispute related to the closure 
of the factory by the Management without any previous notice. On the 
12th September 1953, the workmen went to the factory gate as usual to 
resume their duties when they found a notice of the previous day informing 
that the factory would be closed from 14th September next due to depression 
in trade and curtailment of orders. This was strongly resented by the 
workers who went on a deputation to the Management. The Management 


1878 THE CALCUTTA GAZ. EXTRY., SEPT. 28, 18604 [Panw 1 


সপ 


agreed to settle the matter in consultation with their Labour Officer. In 
that meeting, the next day, it was found that the production had exceeded 
the preceding years in some cases. The matter was taken to the Labow 
Directorate for further discussion and settlement. But the matter howeve: 
was not settled. The closure was highly irrational and unjust in the 
following circumstances: (i) the factory was declared closed without any 
previous notice; (ii) the decision was taken by the Managemnt without any 
prior consultation with the workmen or their Union despite the fact that a 
Union recognised by the Management was in existence since 1948; (iii) 
on no previous occasion, out of 15 years of its existence, the Company 
declared closure of the factory on the ground of depression in trade and 
curtailment of orders; (iv) the closure could have been avoided as is done 
in other manufacturing concerns in times of slack season by putting the 
workers on to other jobs; (v) the action was taken indirectly to suppress the 
dernands of the workers for Puja bonus; (vi) the production cost was reduced 
from the beginning of the year; (vii) the Management did not produce 
relevant documents called for by the Union. The Union in the foregoing 
circumstances, pray for opening the factory, wages for the period of closure, 
Puja bonus and wages for the 10101) August and 26th January. 


The Crown Cork Manufacturing Co. (hereinafter called the “Company’’: 
in their stutement resisted the claim of the Union and stated that they 
had a very small factory employing only 20 workers. They are engaged in, 
the manufacture of crown corks used in aerated water bottles. The Company 
is engaged in manufacturing an auxiliary commodity only, its busines: 
depends on the business or sale conditions of aerated water. As the summer 
season is the penk season for consumption of aeruted water and cold drinks. 
there is naturally comparatively larger business .for crown cork during 
summer months. During the last {wo years, however, the position showed 
considerable deterioration due to ponent depression. For instance, in 198: 
the total sales came down to 190,700 grosses as compared to 273, 500 grosses 
in- 1951. In 1953, the position further deteriorated inasmuch as except for 
the four months of March, April, May and June—the peak period—the sales 
were negligible in January, February and again in July-August, The sales in 
July came down to 4,200 grosses and further went down to 700 grosses in 
August as compared to 39,000 grosses in April 1953. The Management 
tried their best to keep the factory running and with this end in view. 
they approached all the parties who had placed orders but from whom 
instructions had been received not to effect further despatches. Only when 
the Management realisd that parties were not prepared to issue instructions 
for effecting despatches owing to slump in business, that they decided to 
keep the workers on involuntary unemployment to overcome the crisis. It 
would appear that on 10th September 1953, orders to the extent 
of about 75,000 grosses were outstanding, but most of the parties had issued 
instructions not to effect despatches. The company had already stock of 
about 29,000 grosses It would not possible to keep the manufactured goods 
for a long time because they get rusty and as such it was not possible to 
keep on producing when the immediate prospects were very gloomy. The 
financial position of the Company had become very weak because of the 
continued depression in business. Goods worth ahout Ra. 38,000 were sold 
on credit during 1858 as the pariies were not able to make immediate pay- 
ment, There is little chance of recovering this amount. It is under these 
circumstances that the Management had to put up the notice for involun- 
tary unemployment. 


Dealing with the allegations of the Union. it stated that the notice of 
involuntary unemployment was put up on llth September 1953 during 


ment was proper. The factory re-opened from Ist January 1954. ৪ 
Company asserted that its action in laying off that workers was for hona 
fide trade reasons and was fully justified tn the circumstances in which it 
was placed. The workers were not entitled to any ا‎ ay for the period of 


unemployment except such benefit as was promised in the Company's notice, 
dated 11th September 1969. It filed several statements showing the position 
of stock, production and sale. 


The only issue is: 


Whether the closure of the factory is justified? To what relief are the 
workmen entitled ? 


FINDINGS, 


Shri Sing on behalf of the Company has urged that the matter of dispute 
is not closure of the factory, as it is stated to be, but putting the workers 
to involuntary unemployment for trade reasons. There is not much of 
real difference between the closure of the factory and putting the workers 
to involuntary unemployment in the circumstances of the case. Admittedly, 
there was complete stoppage of work in the factory from 14th September 
1963 till the end of that year. The factory re-opened on Ist January next, 
the 20 workers were laid off by the Management by a notice dated 11th 
September 19583 and nothing turns on the alleged difference between the 
closure of the factory and the stoppage of work in it due to involuntary 
unemployment. 


The Management of the Company justifies its action on the grounda 
very elaborately stated in paragraphs 2, 3 and 4 of its written statement 
filed in this case. Briefly stated the immediate grounds for laying off the 
workers are, depression in trade and serioue curtailment of orders as given 
out in the Manager’s notice, dated 11th September 1963, which forms part 
of the Company’s written statement in the case, It put all the 20 workers 
to involuntary unemployment with effect from 14th September 1953, 
initially for a period of two months. The Management stated in the notice 
that the workers would be recalled if the situation improved in the mean- 
time and that the workers would be paid the unemployment benefit at 
the rate 15 days’ pay as per Major Engineering Tribunals Award, 1948. 


The Union raised o dispute as soon as the notice was given and resisted 
the Company’s action as irrational and unjust mainly on the grounds 
atated at page 3 of its written statement. Their objections are mainly: 
(i) there was no previous notice; (11) Wnion was not consulted; (111) no 
such action was taken on any previous occasion when the workera were 
employed on other jobs; (iv) a false plea of depression in trade; (v) non- 
production of relevant documents in the conciliation proceedings and lastly 
(vi) the production cost was’ greatly reduced since the beginning of the 
year 1953. 


Shri Sing contends that all these objections are untenable for (i) they 
are contrary to facts: (ii) they are irrelevant and lastly (iii) frivolous. It 
is in evidence of the Management that a notice was hung up during working

Turning to the evidence of the Management on the trading and financial 
position of the business at the relevant date, namely, in the beginning of the 
month of September 1953, the Tribunal finds from the volume of corres- 
pondence that passed between the Company and its customers in Madras 
and Delhi (Exts. D to D9, E ںا‎ E4, F to F14, G to G6) that the customers 
had either cancelled their orders, wanted reduction in prices, wanted goods 
on credit and instructed the Company not to despatch the goods at present 
due to depression in the market. It would appear from Exts. B and G that 
the order received from the parties amounted to 75,000 grosses. Out of 
this, no reply from the customers came in respect of 17,050 grosses. 
Instructions received from the customers not to despatch goods in respect of 
39,<00 grosses. Credit was asked in respect of 4,100 grosses and reduction 
in prices wanted in respect of 11,350 grosses. The remaining orders were 
cancelled. In fact, the Company had suffered a losa for sale on credit 
amounting to Rs. 33,000 in 1953 alone. Exhibit A, a comparative state- 
ment showing production, sale and stock, is very helpful in this case. There 
was production for 12 months in 1951, 10 months in 1952 and 8 months in 
1953. The production fell from 277,276 to 149,981 grosses. Sales fell from 
273,600 to 145,282 in 1952 and there was the closing stock of 29,287 at the 
end of August 1953. Taken along with this, the fact that the production 27) 
the first half year of 1943 exceeded that of 1952 (which of course 18 not 
totally correct), there was sufficient justification for the Management to 
stop production for the time being just to completely ascertain the position 
of the market. The Company manufactures crown corks for aerated water 
bottles ond generally has good business during summer months when 
cold drinks are in great demand and this corks made of tina get rusty and 
are damaged if remain unsold for some time due to the climatic position 
of this place. Tt is in evidence of Shri Goenka and Shri Ganguly, the 
Proprietor and the Manager of the Company, that in view of this alarming 
market position, the Management decided to stop production for some time. 
‘Bhey did so after due care and caution and consulting the principal 
customera in the market. The Company has filed its Balance Sheets for 
1951 and 1952. Unfortunately they are not audited. They show that the

On a consideration of the evidence, the Tribunal finds that the action اہ‎ 
the Company in putting the ‘workers of the factory to involuntary unemploy- 
ment and thereby closing the work of the factory for the time being is 
justified. It is extremely unfortunate that the period of unemployment 
extended over two months, i.e., the period of notice under circumstance 
over which the Management had no control. That is however 0 matter 
which is not necessary to investigate in the present case. 


The Management told the laid off workers in their notice, dated 11th

except to those who have already withdrawn their dues This will be 04

As he Dundi and Manziu of the Boating Crew are not members of

‘‘Bonus payable in 1953" 


It is admitted that the claim is for bonus for the year 1952, as 
payable in 1953, and that this bonus is claimed as profit-sharing bonus. 
It is also admitted that since 1947, the Company did not pay any bonus to 
these workmen; therefore the workmen also did not claim bonus as a 
service condition on the basis of any express or implied agreement. The 
Company’s contention is that there was no sufficient surplus profit after 
meeting the prior charges, for distribution as bonus to the workmen and 
that in the year 1952, the Company met with a loss. Balance-sheets for 
several yeurs including the year 1952 have been produced by the Company 
and the Company has also filed a statement, marked Annexure A, showing 
the gross profit and the calculations of the prior charges which have been 
deducted from the same. From the gross profit annual depreciation to the 
extent of Rs. 1,85,000 have been deducted leaving Rs. 1,86,300 as balance, 
and after deducting the statutory income-tax and super tax and return at 
6 per cent. on the paid-up capital and also return at the rate of 4 per cent. 
on the working capital, a deficit of Rs. 5,833 has been shown. 


Workmen on the other hand contend that the iterhs “other expenses” 
and “repairs’? are not real things and that the return on _ working 
capital should not be more than 2 per cent. and further that the Company 
must prove by evidence that it really utilised Rs. 8,90,259 for running 
the business in the year 1962. 


The Company contends that if rehabilitation costs according to ۶ 
formula laid down by the Appellate Tribunal] in Mill Owners’ Assoriation 
case are deducted, the gross profit after deduction of the same rehabilita-

contention of the Company on this point has got substance as the figures 
in their statement, marked Annexure B would show. The cost price of

4 per cent, return on the working capital is not without authority. 
There are several rulings in support of the view that 4 per cent. would 
be fair return on the amount of reserve used or utilised as working

Direct proof on this point is extremely difficult to be adduced by the

The Engineering Association on behalf .of the Company resisted the

the factory was closed. The only point for decision is whether this

connected files that the Management applied under section 33 of the 
Industrial টা Act for permission to dismiss Shri Panchu Roy from 
service on 13th January 1954, three days before Shri Panchu Roy filed his 
জানিনা under section 383A of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is 
abundantly clear that the Management did not dismiss Shri Panchu Roy 
from service but only asked for permission of the Tribunal to dismiss him 
on certain allegations, among others, on the ground of his unauthorised

FINDINGS. 


Issue No. 1—Whether stoppage of production of the Mills is justified. 


The Tribunal made every endeaveur to bring the Management of the 
Company and the Official Receiver, now holding the assets of the Compauy, 
under orders of the High Court, before it দিত purpose of proper adjudi- 
eation of the issues, Unfortunutely, it did not succeed. The Company whe 
filed the written statement, and some papers from time to time contesting 
the proceedings before the Tribunal in the earlier stages, did not contest on 
the date of the final hearing. Probably it thought the whole thing {o be ৪ 
dead inatter, not worth paying attention any more. The Official Receiver, 
for reasons best known to ডি did not render any ussistance in the matter 
of adjudication of the dispute though he is concerned with one of the bigest 
cotton mills within the State, in which, on an average ostimate, 2,500 
workers were elmployed at the time the Mill stopped production. This 
regrettable attitude on the part of the Management had Created some very

The Tribunal. will proceed!'to the adjudication of the issues only on materials 
that are on ate récord. 


The financial reasons, stated to be the main ground for the stoppage of 
production due to loss in the business, have to be guessed from the informa- 
tion that the Munagement from time to time supplied to the Tribunal. 
There is nv other evidence on this account, Neither there is any material 
to show any basis for the grounds taken up by the Company in paragraph .22 
of its written statement, under the caption ‘‘the following ditional 
reasons tor stoppage of the production in the Miull’’. Apart from the 
‘Charter of Demands’’ presented to the Management of the Mill on 27th

points taken in paragraph 22 remain to be established.

(iv) and (v) Next claim is gratuity and notice pay as per recent Ordinance. 
This has been righily characterised by the learned representative for the 
Union to be the unhappy expression for compensation paid for retrenchment 
of workmen undet the Ordinance, now incorporated in the amended Jndus- 
trial Disputes Act. The claim is for retrenchment compensation. A question 
may arise as to the maintainability of this claim on the ground that the 
Company had not in so many words retrenched their employees. The total 
effect of the proceedings before the Hon’ble High Court in which the Hon’ble 
Court had directed the sale of the entire assets of the Company and to hold 
the same in the hands of the Official Receiver is that the Mill had been closed 
for good. It is reasonable to find that the services of the employees auto- 
matically came to au end and that when the Company by its notice (Ext. 1) 
forbade them not to register their attendance in the Mill. Virtually, the 
employees did not work or come ready for it after that date. Therefore, it 
is not unreasonable tq hold that their services were terminated with effect 
from that date, namely, from 22nd December 1953, and under section 
Q(iv)(oo) of the amended Industrial Disputes Act, retrenchment means the 
termination hy the employer of the services of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary 
action, but it does not include voluntary retirement, termination of service 
on the ground of continued ill-health or retirement on reaching the age of 
superannuation. There cannot be any doubt as to the legal effect of the 
termination of services of the employees under the above circumstances. 
They were retrenched and they were entitled to all the statutory benefits 
therefor. This retrenchment relief has been laid down in section 25(F) of 
the suine Act. In this case the employees were not given any notice of such 
retrenchment. Therefore, the employees who had been in continuous service 
for not leas than one year should get one month’s wages in lieu of such notice, 
Iam afraid, ] cannot accede to the request of the learned representative for 
the Union to pay at least three months’ notice pay in this case. It is no 
more a matter of discretion of the Tribunal, It has been expressly provid- 
ed in the Act. Further, the Tribunal would not bave been justified in allow- 
ing more than a month’s pay in lieu of notice, even if it had any discretion 
in the matter for there could not have been any possibility of doubt or 
mistake in the mind of the employees about the future when the Mill stopped 
its production. The employees under the same section be paid at the time of 
retrenchment, compensation equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for every 
سو رن‎ year of service or any part thereof in excess of six months. This 
holds good in the case of monthly and daily-rated staff and be paid out of 
the assets of the Mill.

between Messrs. Kusumike [ron Works, Ltd., 73, Jeliapara Lane, Salkia,

dated the 23rd February 1953, for adjudication. 

2. After usual notices the parties entered appearance and filed their 
written statements. The pleadings were completed on 15th May 1954. 
The parties were thereafter directed to file their lists of documents. The 
hearing was concluded on 27th August 1954 and the award was reserved. 


3. The matters of dispute us stated in the schedule to the Order of 
Reference are as follows :-— 


(1) Increment. 
(2) Grade system. 
(3) Bonus. 


3278 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 30, 1954 [Parr 1 
এশার 


DECISION. 


Issue No. 1.—Under this issue the Union demands a flat increment of 
Rs. 10 per month for all workmen with retrospective effect from January 
1954. The reasons for such demand are stated in paragraphs 6 to 12 of its 
written statement. The Company is an engineering concern ond it was a 
party to the awards of the Major Engineering Tribunals, The Union alleges 
that as by the award of the First Engineering Tribunal the minimum wages 
for the workmen were fixed at rate lesser by Rs. 10 than the ideal basic pay 
found admissible under the then conditions and as there has been no mnere- 
ment in the Jast three years, the workmen should be granted a flat incre. 
ment at the rate of Rs. 10 per month to make up the deficiency and 4s a step 
forward towards achieving fair and ultimately living wage. The Company 
on the other hand resists the claim. 


On giving careful consideration to the pleadings, evidence and the 
arguments advanced on either side, it appears that Union’s claim for incre- 
ment cannot be sustained. If by the demand the Union wants revision in 
the rates of minimum wages as fixed in the award of the First Engineering 
Tribunal, I think, this cannot be permitted only in respect of this Company 
as has been held in the case of Britannia Building & Iron Co., Ltd. versus 
their workmen reported in 1954 L.A.C., page 13. The fixation of wages is 
a long-term policy and wages cannot be made subjert 10 periodic revisions in 
a particular establishment as that will have the adverse effect of disturbing 
the equilibrium in the entire industry. So, there cannot be any reyigion. 
If the claim on the other hand means an ad hoc increment of Rs. 10 on the 
existing wages of the workmen, this cannot 2180 be sustained when admittedly 
there are no fixed grades and incremental scales already in existence in this 
Company. According to the pleadings, there are either no grades or scales 
in this টি There has been no increment in the last three years. 
Before this, Company granted increments only to deserving cases as shown 
in the statement, Ext. B, during the years 1947 to 1951. It will appear 
that there was no fixed rate or period fixed for increment. In the case of 
Union Druy Co., Ltd. versus their workmen reported in 1953 L.A.C., page 
714, it has been held that ad hoc increments should not be given when (a) 
there are no fixed grades and incremental scales already in existence, or (b) 
without fixing by adjudication settled incremental scales, when such scales 
are already in existence. In this view of the matter the Union’s demand in 
thia respect cannot be conceded. The issue is accordingly decided. 


Issue No. 2.—Under this head the Union demands a graded pay scale for 
different categories of workmen with provision for annual increment as 
shown, in Annexure C to its written statement. There the minimum wages 
have been shown assuming an increment of Rs. 10 over and above the 
miniinum wages as fixed in the award of the First Engineering Tribunal. 
Besides, the Gnion claims that for the purpose of fitting in into the grades 
every working may be given one increment for every two years’ past service 
in the Company without prejudice to the existing rates. In other words, 
the Union claims adjustment into the grades taking the past years of 
service into consideration. The Union alleges that similar concerns—Messrs. 
Sritannia Building & Iron Co., Ltd., and Messrs. Bridge & Roof Co. (India), 
Ltd.—have grades as shown in Annexure B of its written statement. So it 
৮৪ said that there is no reason why this Company should not provide pay 
scales for different categories of workmen. 

The Company resists the claim and I think for good reasons. The 
workmen of this concern, it appears, have not been classified into different ! 
eategories of unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled and highly skilled. It further

৬ জজ ےہ ہہ‎ eres ees ee ہے سے حوسیہ‎ 
0 SS ےت رت تر‎ ER PTT সী পি a 


পর CE جا سی‎ i Soc nc 
Se SP ৩০৯০৫ aera RR OF ۷ہ‎ SR সী 


appears that each workman iv this concern is paid according to bis capacity 
aud nathre of the job he performs (vide Annexure A to the written state- 
went of the Company). Annexure A no doubt gives designations of the 
different workmen but the designations cannot determine the 018৭ in which 
a particular workman is to be placed. Classifications of workmen into 
unakilled, semi-skilled and skilled can only be solved satisfactorily by 
scientific analysis of the type of work done by them with the assistance of 
expert opinion as has been held in the case of Britannia Building & Iron Co., 
Ltd., reported in 1954 L.A.C., page 11. So, in the absence of such classi- 
وروی‎ it is obvious that no pay scale can be laid down or adjustment can 
be made. 


Then it appears that there is no fixed scale for any category of workmen 
in this Company. The award of the First Engineering Tribunal did not fix 
the maximum but only the minimum for the unskilled and semi-skilled 
workmen. P ,W. 1, Shri Muni Lal Koyal, Secretary of the Union, admits 
that no maximum or minimum is fixed in this Company for skilled workmen. 
He also admits that no maximum is fixed for semi-skilled workmen in this 
Company. As regards his claim that a maximum is fixed for the unskilled 
workmen, Annexure A to the Company’s written statement bélies it. 
Annexure A, which the Company filed, shows the workmen only by desig- 
nations and from it it cannot be said who comes under what category. So, 
as there is no pay seale fixed nor classifications of workmen into skilled, 
semi-skilled and unskilled, ۲ think, no pay scale with provision for annual 
increment as claimed by the Union can be provided. The case of Britannia 
Building and Iron 00. Ltd., reported in 1954 L.A.C., page 11, cited by the 
Tnion has no application to the facts of the present case. The facts there 
were quite different. The workmen in that Company were placed in different 
categories of unskilled, semi-skilled and skilled on the basis of agreement 
between the Company and the Union. Then the Company had in existence 
an incremental scale for all the categories of workmen except the unskilled 
ones. Thus the facts were different. Then a pay scale can be provided only 
when the Company has not only present capacity to pay, but also its 
financial capacity can be counted in future. When the Company has been 
exining profit, it may have present capacity to pay, but one cannot be so 
sure about the future when it has no appreciable reserve fund. In this view 
of the matter, I am unable to provide a graded pay scale for different cate- 
gories of workmen with provision for annual increment as claimed by the 
Union. The issue is decided accordingly. 


issue No. 3.—The Union demands two months’ basic pay as bonus for 
the year 1952 payable in 18958, that is, for 1359 B.S., out of the surplus 
profit. The Company says that after deducting the prior charges, there will 
09 no available surplus for the workmen to justify their claim regarding 
honus. The سور‎ maintuins accounts according to Bengali year. The 
Company filed the hbalance-sheet for the year ending 30th Chaitra 1359 B.S. 
and made a petition under section 21 for treating the sume as confidential. 
I am, therefore, not permitted to disclose the figures from the balance-sheet. 
Admittedly there has been profit during the year in question. 


The parties have filed statements showing calculation of prior charges. 
There is no dispute between the parties regarding the amount of gross profit 
for the purpose of calculation of bonus. There is also no dispute regarding 
the amount of income-tax payable from the same. ‘The parties are, however, 
ut variance regarding the amount allowable under head ‘‘Return on paid-up 
capital’’, The Company claims that the return should be at the rate of 12 
per cent. The Union on the other hand coutends that it should be at the 


3280 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 30, 1954 [Parr 7 


rate of 6 per cent. I accept the Union’s version which is in accord with 1018 
Full Bench Formula. The reasons which the Company enumerated in they 
statement regarding calculation for a return at the rate of 12 per cen: 
on the paid-up capital are not convincing. Then there has also been 
difference hetween the parties regarding claim on working capital. The 
Union coutends that no deduction is permissible under the head ‘“Working 
Capital’? as there is nothing on the part of the Company to show that any 
reserve was employed as such. The Company on the other hand maintains 
that what amount has been sbown in their statement of calculation under 
the head ‘‘Working Cupital’? was arrived at on a computation as in the 
dacument marked ‘'X’’, and it should be accepted as the working capital 
and allowance should be made for it at the rate of 9 per cent, Union’s con- 
tention that to get an allowance, working capital has got to come from the 
reserve fund cannot be sustained. I accept Company's version of the amount 
of the working capital as shown on a calculation as indicated in the docu- 
ment marked ‘‘X’’. Huaving regarding to the nature of the working cupital 
said to have been employed, I think that a return of 3 ‘su cent. would be 
fair in place of 9 per cent. or 4 per cent. as ultimately claimed by the 
Company. Then another deduction has been claimed by the Company on 
account of extraneous profit. The Union said that no deduction is permis- 
sible on this score. 1 cannot uphold their contention. The Company is 
entitled to make deduction on account of interest which was extraneous 
profit, As regards claim for reserve for rehabilitation, the Company has 
adduced no evidence whatever. Company’s claim for allowance in this 
respect cannot, therefore, be sustained. 


The monthly bill in respect of wages of the workmen, I am told, would 
be about Rs. 6,000. Atter making due allowance for return on the ناوات‎ 
capital at the rate of 6 per cent., for working capital at the rate of 3 per cent. 
and giving due allowance for extraneous profit, it appears that there would 
be sufficient surplus left for distribution as bonus at the rate of two months’ 
basic pay as claimed by the Union. Union’s cluim for bonus at the rate of 
two months’ basic pay is accordingly allowed. The payment should he 
made within a month from the date the award hecomes enforceable. 


I award accordingly.

(1) Bonus for 1953. 
DECISION. 


The parties have not adduced any oral evidence. The Union filed ics 
comments regarding the balance-sheet of the year ending 30th June 1953 
(Ext. 1). The Company on the other hand has filed balance-sheet and 
other documents (Exts. A, Al, B, C, D and D1). 


The Union demands bonus at the rate of two months’ wages out of the 
profit of the vear 1952-53 (year ending in June 1963). It made such 
demand on 2nd September 1953. On 2nd October 1953 the Company 
pleaded inability to meet the demand. Hence the dispute. 


3282 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 30, 1954 [Panr | 


১ 6 mE aE Ee ےسئیکھی۔‎ Se সস 


The Company is a proprietory concern of Sri Kalidas Roy. It is ny 
engineering concern. Ita factory was established in August F936. 1 


inanufactures steam, water, gas and fire fittings as also cocks and valves. 
The case of the Union is as follows. 


Like other proprietory concerns, the accounts of this concern have been 
muapipulated by suppressing production and sale and by showing inflated 
expenses in the profit and loss account on possible and impossible heads, 
The profit has been reduced by catia the purchase price more and the sell- 
ing price less than what it should be, Proper scrutiny of the books of accounts 
and vouchers of the Company world on the contrary reveal available 
surplus from which the demand of the Union for bonus could be met. Ay 
the assets of the Company have all been purchased from the surplus profits 
of the Company of the past years, 00 deduction from gross profits on 
account of rehabilitation of machineries and buildings should be granted. 


The Company denies the allegations and pleads that after meeting tho 
prior charges there will be no surplus for payment of any bonus. 


The financial year of the Company ends on 30th June. The Company 
has filed balance-sheets of the two years ending 30th June 1952 (Ext. Al) 
and 1953 (Ext. A). The Company has filed a petition for treating the 
balance-sheet of the year ending 30th June 1953 as confidential. In the 
circumstances, I am not permitted to disclose the figures. It shows some 
profit. The Company has filed a statement showing calculation of 
available surplus according to Full Bench Formula (Ext. D): After 
meetin: the prior charges, it shows no surplus but a deficit. Ext. 1(1 shows 
how cost of replacement of buildings and machineries has been caloulated. 
The Union has virtually nothing to say against these items. Ext. 1 contains 
general comments of the Union regarding the balance-sheet of the year 
ending 30th June 1953. Ext. C is the reply by the Company to these 
comments. ٤ find nothing to discard the balance-sheet. Even if it goes, 
it is of no help to the Union. The Union has furnished nothing to justify 
its claim for bonus out of the profit of the year ending 30th June 1953. 
The allegations made by it are no proof. The Company has heen admittedly 
paying bonus linked with attendance for some years past and it has also 
paid in 1958 such bonus linked with attendance on the result of the financial 
7 ending 30th June 1963. This would show bona fide of the Company. 

e that as it may, when nothing has been proved to show that there would 
be sufficient surplus after meeting the prior charges. Union's demand for 


bonus for the year 1953 on the result of the financial year ending 30th June 
1953 must fail. 


I award accordingly.

DECISION. 


issue No. 1.—Both the Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation Mazdoor 
Union (hereafter called Mazdgor Union) and the Calcutta Electric Supply 
Workers’ Union (hereafter referred to as Workers’ Union), demand that 
the workmen of the Mains Department should be declared to come within 
the purview of the Factories Act, 1948, and should as such be held 
eligible to get overtime payment according to provisions in the said Act 
cal that with retrospective effect from Ist April 1949. The Calcutta 
Electric Supply Corporation, Ltd. (hereafter described as the Company), 
resists the claim. 


The Company is a limited Company with its registered office in the 
.کا .تا‎ It carries on the business of generation and distribution of 
electrical energy in the city of Calcutta, its industrial area and suburbs 
under different licenses under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (Act 1X 
of 1910). Under the Calcutta and District Consolidated License, 1946, 
its licensed area of supply extends to 546 square miles. It is a public 
utility Company and its profits are governed by the Electricity (Supply) 
Act, 1948, both as to amount and method of distribution. 


The Mains Department according to the Company has approximately 
1,950 workmen divided up at present into 67 gangs varying in number 
from 10 to 200 each as shown below. The attendance of the men in these 
gungs is recorded by the foreman in charge of each gang on the site.

It will appear that the Mains Department is responsible for opening

lighting. installing meter-boards und house services in consumers’ and

It is agreed on all hands that except 200 Emergency Depot staff, who 
work 48 hours a week, the workmen in the Mains Department work 46 
hours a week as follows سے‎ 


Mondays to Fridays—8 a.m. to 4 p.m. 
Saturdays—8 a.m. to 2 p.m. 


If the men are required to work beyond these hours, they are paid 
overtime rates calculated at “double time’ for all work in excess of 48 
hours per week or on Saturday afternoons, Sundays or public holidays 
since 1946. Before 1946, the workmen used to be paid ‘‘time and a 
half’? for all overtime. The first two hours per week of overtime for 
work on a weeh day in excess of 46 hours a week are, however, calculated 
at ‘‘time and ao half’’. Overtime rates are calculated only on 1১2,910 pay. 


The Factories Act on the contrary permits payment for overtime 
both on basic pay and dearness allowance. Under section 59(1) of the 
said Act, where a worker works in a factory for more than 9 hours or 
for more than 48 hours in any week, he shall, in respect of overtime 
work, be entitled to wages at the rate of twice his ordinary rate of .دہ جم‎ 
Section 659(3) of the Act defines “ordinary rate of wages’’ to 
mean basic wages plus such allowances including cash equivalent of the 
advantage accruing through the concessional sale to workers of food- 
yrains and other articles, as the worker is for the time being entitled to, 
mt dves not include a bonus. It is, therefore, obvious that overtime is 
admissible according to the Factories Act on the basis of basic salary and 
dearness allowance. 


The real dispute between the parties, as I find, is not that the 
workmen in the Mains Department should be classed as Factory Workers, 
but that dearness allowance should be consolidated with pay for the 
purpose of overtime payment. The issue as, however, posed, imposes 
limitation on the Tribunal in considering the said real dispute inasmuch 
as it has been linked with the applicability or otherwise of the Factories 
Act. The Industrial Tribunal is not the proper forum for a mere 
decision of the question, whether the workmen of the Mains Department 
come within the purview of the Factories Act and would have no jurisdic- 
tion to go iato it, had not the question of overtime payment 
giving rise to an industrial dispute been linked with it. As the issue 
stands, the workmen can get benefit only if they come within the scope 
of the Factories Act, aud not otherwise. It would have heen otherwise 
had not the question of overtime payment been so linked. Thus the 
Tribunal has no unfettered discretion in deciding the real dispute as 
already stated. It appears that the Unions, ا دوہ‎ the Mazdoor Union, 
are responsible for creation of such unenviable situation.

To come within the scope of the Factories Act, there must first be a 
factory. The word “Fuctory’’ has been defined under section 2(m) of 
the Factories Act to mean ‘‘any premises including precincts thereof, 
etc.”? The requisite of a factory is therefore ‘‘any premises includin 
xrecincts thereof.’’ The word ‘‘Premises’’ is defined in Murray’s Oxforc 

ictionary us ‘‘a house or building with its ground or other appurtenances,” 
The word ‘‘Precincts’’ is defined in the same dictionary وو‎ 
‘the space enclosed by the walls or other boundaries of a particular place 
or building’’ and ‘‘more vaguely, the region lying immediately around 
a place without distinct reference to تع‎ enclosure, the environs,” 
It 18, therefore, obvious that except when the workmen in the Muing 
Department ore employed in the Generating Stations or Sub-Stations 
having premises (as are factories under the Factoriea Act) for which 
occasions are very rare, the workmen cannot be said, in view of the 
duties enumerated, to be employed on the premises or within the 
precincts thereof. When they have usually to perform work on the 
roadside or in the premises of a consumer and other such places outside 
the Generating Stations or Sub-Stations, they would not come within 
the scope of the Factories Act. Merely because the Generating Stations, 
Sub-Stations and the roadsides are connected with one another with 
cables either overhead or underground, it cannot be said that these 
constitute one establishment. The street or public highway cunnot be 
accepted as premises of the Generating Stations or of the Sub- 
Stations merely because they are connected by overhead or underground 
cables. Premises implies some definite place with metes and bpunds 
and means the main ground or building with its ground or other 
appurtenances. The work in the Mains Department, it appeurs, is 
comparable to the one of the permanent way worker in a tramway or in 
the railways or of linesman of the underground and overhead section 
of the Post and Telegraph Department. None of them, 1 understand, 
is treated as factory worker, Jn a case where a workman in the employ 
of « Gas Company was in course of his employment engaged in muking 
a trench in the road-way, under which one of their gas imains 
was laid, at a distance of a quarter of a mile from the works where the 
yas was manufgctured, which works came within the definition of a ngn- 
textile factory, when he was injured by an accident out of and 
in course of his employment, it was held that the main was not a part of 
the factory and the man was not employed ‘about a factory’ and was 
not entitled to compensation (vide the case of Spacey vs. Dowlais Gas & 
Coke, Co., 54 W.R. 1388). In the present case the workers of the Mains 
Department are usually employed in open air outside the Generating 
Stations and Sub-Stations. The workmen in the Mains Department 
cannot, therefore, be said to be employed in the factory except when 
they are employed in the Generating Stations or Sub-Stations as are 
factories under the Factories Act. The occasions for such employment 
in the Generating Stations or Sub-Stations are very rare and there can 
be no dispute that when any workman of the Mains Department is 
employed in them, he would be a factory worker within the meaning of 
the Factories Act. 


It is contended on behalf of the Workers’ Union that when there were 
occasions in the past and would be so in future for employment of the

2০৪০ RE ویو‎ হাত ےمحبچچٹہہے‎ 


workmen of the Mains Department in the Generating Stations or Sub- 
Stations for laying or repairing cables and when as such they would be 
workers within the Factories Act, they should be regarded as factory 
workers for all time to come. In other words, it is said that once a factory 
worker, always, a factory worker. The Act does not, however, so contem- 
plate. Only when ے‎ worker is employed in a factory, he will be a factory 
worker provided other requirements are fulfilled and not otherwise vide 
section 2(1) of the Factories Act. Under section 2(1) of the Act, the word 
used 8 a نس‎ It is, therefore, obvious that when a worker ceased 
to be so employed in a factory, he could not continue to be a factory worker. 
Then again, merely because departure is noted in Princep Street, which 
is a factory, the workmen cannot become factory workers thereby. They 
can be factory workers only when they are employed in a factory and not 
otherwise. Section 79 of the Factories Act, relied upon by the Workers’ 
Unjon, is of no help. It lays down when a worker employed in a factory 
is enfitled ۱١ annual leave with wages. Merely because certain interruption 
in service is allowed to be disregarded for the purpose of computation of 
240 days or more, it cannot be said that a factory worker will not cease to 
be so notwithstanding employment outside the factory. 


For premises to be a ‘‘factory’’, it is necessary that in any part a 
manufacturing process is carried on. A ‘‘worker’’ has been defined jin 
section 2(1.) of the Factories Act to mean a person employed, directly or 
through any agency, whether for wages or not, in any manufacturing 
process, or in cleaning any part of the machinery or premises used for a 
manufacturing process, or in any other kind of work incidental to, or con- 
nected with the manufacturing process, or the subject of the manufacturing 
process. So the question which next arises for consideration is, whether 
the workmen in the Mains Departmént when employed outside the 
(ienerating Stations or sub-Stations are employed in the manufacturing 
process or in any kind of work incidental to or connected with the 
manufacturing process or the subject of manufacturing process. 
The words ‘manufacturing process’’ have been defined in section 2(k) of the 
Factories Act. It includes among others process of generating, transforming 
or transmitting power or for ا‎ altering, repairing, etc. Section 2(1) 
of the Indian Electricity Act defines ‘‘Main’’ to mean any electric supply- 
line through which energy is, or is intended to be, supplied by a licensee 
to the public. Section 2(g) of the said Act defines energy; section 2(f) 
defines electricity supply line; and section 2(1) defines service line. Section 
2(5) of the Electricity (Supply) Act defines generating station or station; 
section 2(7) of the said Act defines main transmission lines. 


On the basis of these it has been contended on behalf of the Union that 
the workmen in the Mains Department when employed outside the 
Generating Stations or Sub-Stations should be held performing duties 
within the meaning of the menufacturing process and in any case these 
would be work incidental to or connected with the manufacturing process 
or the subject of the manufacturing process. The Company on the other 
hand contends that their duties do not fulfil the requirements of section 2(1) 
and (m) of the Factories Act. It is said that these workmen have nothing 
to do with the process of generating and transforming and that their duties 
end just before process of transmitting power starts. 


The duties which the different gangs in the Maina Department according 
to the Company, are to perform have already been enumerated. I do not, 
therefure, recapitulate them here. In their written statement filed on 
20th August 1954 (styled Annexure ‘‘A’’), the Workers’ Union alleges,

After power is generated in the Main Power House, electric cables, 
both high tension and low tension, negative ond positive, ure to be 
attached on the Generating sets and these cables are thereafter joined to 
different distributing boards inside the main Generating Stution for 
carrying the electricity from the Generating Stations tv the distributing

are interlinked between themselves through such high tension cables, 
There are in Calcutta four such Power Stations which are interlinked

consumption. : 


Therefore, it will be seen from the above that the work of the Mains 
Department is not only transmitting and transforming power but also 
various other work which is included in the term of manufacturing process 
both inside the premises as well as in the precincta thereof.’’ 


The claim of the Unions that the workmen of Mains Department 
perform work of generation and transformation cannot be sustained. 
Only some of them it appears, work in transmitting power. Be that as it 
may, having regard to the duties the workmen im the Mains Department 
are to perform when employed outside the Generation Stations or Sub- 
Stations, I am of opinion, that these would amount to work incidental to 
or connected with the manufacturing process, I, therefore, agree with 
the Unions that this ingredient is fulfilled in their cose. But their 
employment outside the Generating Stations or Sub-stations cannot be 
said to be within any premises including the precincts thereof. The 
main ingredient of a factory would, therefore, be wanting. It has 
already been stated that merely because the Generating Stations or

central area of the town and Howrah. As the network expanded, it was

the Central Depot at Princep Street. In addition, an extra half hour 
each way was given for Howrah work on account of the old Bridge and 
its delays. This allowance was in effect of cash value and it was up 
to the employee to decide how he arrived at the job. A maximum of

Under the scheme as introduced from 10th May 1954, there has been 
improvement on the old system so far provisions have been made for 
allowance over 7 miles and under 2 miles. 


The Mazdoor Union demands walking allowance at the rate of one 
hour’s basic wage for each mile traversed and that with effect from lst 
Apri] 1949, 1¢ further claims that it should be paid as an overtime 
allowance. The Workers’ Union demands that the walking allowance 
should be paid at double the rates os in the case of overtime work. The 
Company resists the claims. 


The Mazdoor Union relies on the findings of Shri M. C. Banerji 
under issue No. 19 in the award between the parties published on 19th 
April 1951. The findings under issue No. 19 run as follows :— 


‘Issue No. 19—Compensation for reduction in road allowance of 
Mains Department workmen, 


This is in regard to the ‘‘walking allowance” peculiar to the Mains 
Department. An allowance at the rate of one  hour’s basic 
wage for each mile traversed by Mains Department workmen 
is allowed, if the worker has to report at the correct starting 
time at a distance from his normal depot. It takes the form 
of adding some hours to his daily time-sheet and, therefore, 
increases his emoluments while working in outlying areas. 
This allowance is not allowed in central areas in which case 
the emoluments are normal. The Company was agreeable to 
pay the actual travelling allowance involved in accordance 
with fares published by public transport concerns, and this 
issue was not seriously pressed by the Union at the time of the 
hearing.”’ 


From the uforesaid findings, it is urged on behalf of the Mazdoor 
Union that there has been award by Shri M. C. Banerji for payment of 
walking allowance at the rate of one hour’s basic wage for each mile 
traversed. The Company contends that there has been no such award. 


On giving careful consideration to the matter, I am unable to uphold 
the contention of the Mazdoor Union that Shri M. C. Banerji awarded 
walking allowance at the rate of one hour’s basic wage for each mile 
traversed. It appears that Shri M. C. Banerji has merely recorded 
what the Company was supposed to have heen giving as walking 
allowance at the time. From the admission as made before this 
Tribunal, it, however, appears that the Company was not paying at the

rates as noted by Shri M. ©. Banerji. The rates at which walking 
allowance was then being paid and which continued till 10th May 1954, 
had already been mentioned. So, there has been apparently a mistake 
by Shri M. C. Banerji while making mention about the rates contrary 
to the same. In any case, the findings under issue No. 19, I agree,

Union's claim for grant of walking allowance at the rate of one 
hour's basic pay for each mile traversed on the basis of the award of 
Shri M. C. Banerji cannot be allowed. Hod there been really such 
award, the remedy would be by way of implementation of the award. 


The walking allowance is admittedly calculated like overtime payment 
on the basis of basic pay only. Workers’ Union demands for payment of 
walking allowance on the basis of pay and dearness allowance, but 1 
find no sufficient justification in support of such demand. Likewise, 1 
find no justification for their demand for payment of walking allowance 
at double the rates as in the case of overtime work. If the time spent 
for reporting on the 109 is to be included in day’s work, the Company has 
rightly pointed out that it would lead to enhancement of the cost 
enormously which would compel the Company to resort to contrictor’s 
labour or to charge higher rates on the public for services. I think this 
is not desirable. The walking allowance has been introduced not by 
way of enhancement of pay but to compensate for the cost of journey 
as also for the time lost in the journey. As to the instance of journey 
to Mulajore cited by the Workers’ Union, the Company’s reply os given 
in its written statement repels the suggestion. 


Having regard to the cash value of the walking allowance as stated 
in Annexure “D”’ to the Company’s written statement, I think that the 
scale as has been brought into existence by the Company from 10th May 
1954, with modifications as below would serve the purpose of walking 
allowance fairly سے‎ 


Up to 3 miles, in place of $ hour’s basic pay, J think it should be jth 
hour’s basic pay each way. 


Likewise, in case of cver 7 miles, I think, in addition to fare to nearest 
tram stop and/or Railway Station, basic pay should be given 
at the rate of } hour’s basic pay each way for every 3 miles in 
place of every 4 miles. 


Thus to be precise, I maintain the scale as introduced from 10th May 
1954 with the modifications as above. The scale us modified would be 
operative as sven as the award becomes enforceable. I answer this issue 
accordingly.

As regards contention of the Unions that the workmen who have been 
excepted us aforesaid are also workmen within the meaning of the 
Factories Act, I am unable to sustain it. Section 2(1) of the Factories 
Act defines a ‘‘worker’’. There is nothing on record to show that the 
aforesaid men are employed in any manufacturing process or in cleaning 
any part of the machinery or premises used for a manufacturing process 
or in any other kind of work incidental to or connected with the 
manufacturing process or the subject of the manufacturing process. I 
am, therefore, unable to hold that they ure workmen within the meaning 
of the Factories Act. Merely because attendance of these workmen is 
reported in the premises of Central Stores as declared a Factory, or 
merely because they work in the said factory premises, it cannot be said 
that they are workmen within the meaning of the Factories Act. To 
become a worker within the meaning of the Act, their employment must 
be in any manufacturing process or in cleaning any part of the machinery 
or premises used for 0. manufacturing process or in any other kind of 
work incidental to or connected with the manufacturing process or the 
subject of manufacturing process. As it has not been shown that they 
are so employed, it is obvious that they cannot be accepted as workers 
within the meaning of the Factories Act. 


As to the date of operation, the Chief Inspector of the Factories 
has declared the Central Stores situated at 33, Syed Amir Ali Avenue, 
Calcutta, to be the Factory from the date of inspection, that is, the 13th 
May 1994. As to the claim of the Unions for making the decision 
operative from 186 April 1949, or from a date prior to the one on which 
it was declared a factory, I find no sufficient justification. I, therefore, 
maintain the direction that the Central Stores should be regarded as 
না with effect from the 13th May 1954. The issue is accordingly 
ecided.

section 33 and under section 383A have been heard together as the evidence 
18 the same and the question for decision is whether permission to dismiss 
should be given to the employer and whether the suspension order 
contravenes the provisions of section 34 of the Industrial Disputes Act aud

AWARD IN SECTION 33A PROCEEDINC. 


Admittedly the suspension order was made by the employer during the 
pendency of the reference case in this Tribunal without any permission 
being previously obtained from the Tribunal, The question is whether 
this suspension is a punishinent or not. 


It has been contended on behalf of the Company that this suspension 
pending the decision in section 33 proceeding is a security measure and it 
1g not a punishment. Iu industrial law which is social law the inter- 
pretation adopted in the Penal Code should not be followed. ‘‘In adminis- 
trative law the first caveat which the Judges have always to rai in mind 
is that the learning and the Jaw laid down on one statute is to be applied 
only with grent discrimination to cases urising under another statute.’ ا‎ 
may also refer to the remarks of Rajadhyaksha J, in I.L.R. (1947), Bombay, 
page 863. The word “‘punishment’’, I think, in section 38 has not been 
used with reference to the context of offence or guilt under the Penal Code. 


_In the present case Nitya Gopal has been placed under suspension 
without any allowance or wages of any kind. He has not been given even

subsistence allowance. In Ramdeo versus Patna Eleciric Supply Company, 
Ltd., 1954, 1? L.L.J, page 234: Vatna Tribunal has held that— 


mere statement that the employer by suspending the employee did‏ ۸ھ“ 
not intend to inflict a punishment on him would not prevent the‏ 
suspension being treated as punitive. The true significance of the‏ 
each‏ ل0ۃ order has to be judged with reference to circumstunces‏ 
individual case’’,‏ 


I fully agree with this view. There is no Standing Order in this Company 
and it has not been proved nor even suggested that the Company has got 
any authority to suspend the employee, or that the Company got any 
authority to withhold the wages or allowances of the employee during the 
period of suspension. There is no contractual authority to suspend nor 
there is any such power by any Standing Urder. So the case of Wallwork 
& Fielding, 1922, 1.K.B., page G6, is distinguishable. There the employer 
had the statutory right to suspend. In the case of Warburton versus 
Taffvale Railway Company, 1002, 18 T.L.R., page 420, it was held that— 


‘‘Even when an employer is entitled to suspend an employee and 
withheld his wages during the period of suspension, the employee is 
entitled to wages for the period of such suspension’’. 


In the fuce of the law as discussed above it cannot be said that suspension 
without allowance or wages is not uw punishment to the employee, It might 
be a security measure to restrain the employee, accused of serious mis- 
conduct from engaging in any work under the employer but I eannot 
imagine that withholding of wages or allowances is always a_ security 
measure. J am of opinion, in the circumstances of the case, that the 
suspension order, depriving Nitya Gopal Ghosh of even his subsiktence 
allowance, is nothing but اک ا‎ Therefore the suspension order 
under reference is hit by section 33 and as a matter of that the application 
under section 338A of the Industrial Disputes Act is maintainable.

Manindra Nath Dutt made an application under section 3۱۸ و"‎ the

parties have no dispute between them.

petition of compromise which do form a part of the award.

PART IA—Orders and Notifications by the Government of India republished for general information 


IN THE HONOGURABLE LABOUR APPELLATE TRIBUNAL OF 
INDIA, CALCUTTA. 


Appeal No. Cal.205/54. 


Messrs. Ispahani, Lid., Calcutta Appellant, 
versus 


Kartie Chaudra Mitra, represented by Ispahani Employees 
Union, Calcutte Respondent. 


In the matter of an appeal against the award of Shri M. N. Gan, Judge, 
Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, made on 5th July 1054, in respect of an 
industrial dispute between the above parties. 


Dated the Gth September 1054. 


PRRSENT : 


Mr. R. C. MITTER, Chatrman. 
Mr. L. K. JHA, Member. 


Appearances: 
For the appellant: Mr. P. R. Mukherjee, Advocate, with Mr. N. Roy, 
Advocate, for the Company. 
For the respondent: Mr. Jiten Banerjee, Secretary of the Union. 
State: West Bengal. 
industry: Jute. 


DECISION. 


This appeal was set down today for preliminary hearing under section 
9 of sub-section 2 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 
1960. The appeal is directed against the order hy which the lower 
Tribunal has refused permission to the Company to dismiss a workman of 
the name of Mr. Kartick Chandru Mitter. We have curefully followed the 
arguments of Mr. Mukherjee, who appears in support of the appeal but we 
regret to say that we could not find any substantial question of law. The 
appeal is, therefore, summarily dismissed as being incompetent. 


R. C. MITTER, Chatrman. 
.لا‎ K. JHA, Member.

The following shall be the syllabuses of studies in the subject mentioned

NEPALI (COMPULSORY). 
Class VI. 
Text-book.

Grammar. 


Varna Parichaya—Swar and Vyanjan, classification of Varma, Sandhi, Swar 
and Vyanjan, Natva and Shatva Vidhan. 


Nouns, Pronouns, Adjectives, Adverbs, Avyayas, Verbs, Gender, Number, 
Person, Case. 


Verb—transitive, and intransitive, complete and incomplete, present, past, 
future tenses, positive and negative, masculine and feminine, Voice. Grammar 
book should be rich in examples illustrating the rules. 

Rapid Reader. 

A book of about 100 pages of short stories, anecdotes, etc., of a slightly 
lower standard than the text book. 

Class VII. 
Text-book. 

A text book of about 120 pages containing 90 pages of prose and 30 pages of 

poetry. The book will be of a higher standard than the one for Class VI.’ 
Grammar. 
One text-book for Classes VII and VIII. 


Classification of letters, Sandhi, Conjunction of vowels and consonants (a 
detailed study). A detailed study of Nouns, Pronouns, Adjectives, Adverbs, 
Avyayas, Verbs, Samasa, different kinds of Samasa with examples of Sanskrit. . 

_ and Nepali Samasa of common use. 
Rapid Reader. 


A simple book of prose of about the size of the text book calculated to 
create a taste for literature in the students. ; 


Class VIII. 


Text-book. 
A text-book of about 150 pages containing about 110 pages of prose and 
AO pages of poetry. 
: Rapid Reading, 
A book of prose of about the size of the text-book and a smaller book of 
poetry. 


Grammar. 
As in Class VII.

General Remarks. 


The prose lessons of the text-books and rapid readers for Classes VI to VIII 
may be on the following topics. They may be articles or stories :— 


1. Patriotism. India’s fight for freedom. Indian culture and civilization. 
Geographical, historical, economic and scientific articles. 
Biographical articles. 
Descriptions of travels and voyages. 
Short stories. 
Stories about discoveries and expeditions. 
Classical stories from the Puranas, Jatakas, etc. 
Descriptive and reflective articles. 
. Articles On subjects relating to foreign countries. 
10. Selections from standard dramas. 
The lessons will be written in chaste, idiomatic and standard Nepali and 
should be graded in difficulty for different classes.

The following shall be the syllabuses of studies in the subjects mentioned 
below for the School Final Examination. The date of introduction of the 
syllabuses wil] be notified later on :— 


SCHOOL FINAL EXAMINATION.‏ ا 


NEPALI (Compulsory). 


School Final Examination. 


A text-book of prose and poetry selections to be published by the Board of 
Secondary Education, West Bengal. 


The first paper of three hours should be on the prescribed text. The alloca- 
tion of marks in Paper I should be as follows ہے‎ 


Prose—-60. 

Poetry—40. 
Paper II should have questions on Grammar, Composition and Essay. 
The marks will be divided as follows :— 

Grammar—15. 

Composition—15. 

Essay-—20. 

۰ Grammar. 

The grammar should include the following topics سے‎ 


Classification of letters, gender, number, case, elements, samasa in Sanskrit 
and Nepali compounds, the pronouns and their uses, the conjugation of 
verbs in all tenses, positive and negative, masculine and feminine, krit 
and taddhita affixes, Sanskrit and Nepali syntax and transformation of 
sentences. 


Questions on composition are to include homonyms, antonyms, expansion of 
ideas, substance writing, letter writing, punctuation, paragraph con- 
struction, phrases and idioms. 


ALTERNATIVE NEPALI. 
School Final Examination.

prescribed. এ

Prescribed text—50. 

Grammar—15 

Composition—20 ; : 

‘Translation in Nepali Of one of the two English Passages set—15 
Questions on the prescribed text should not be of a critical nature. 
The following topics should be included in Grammar :— 


Classification of letters (Varna), etc., gender, number and case with special 
reference to the gender ‘in the adjective and the verb, pronouns, conju- 
gation of verbs, simple affixes. 

Questions on composition should include phrases and idioms, letter writing, 
story building, substance writing and expansion of ideas.

UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION. 


Advertisement No. 41. 


APPLICATIONS invited from candidates belonging to 
acheduled castes, scheduled tribes and other backward 
classes only for award of 12 Government of India overseas 
scholarships of two years’ duration (four for each group) 
for post-graduate courses, or research work, preferably, in 
Medicine, Engineering, Agriculture, Science and Techno- 
logy in United Kingdom or other suitable countries. 
Candidates must be citizens of India or persons migrated 
from Pakistan with intention_of permanently settling in 
India or subjects of Sikkim or Jammu and Kashmir. Age:— 
Not more than 35 years on Ist October 1954, This will 
be strictly adhered to. Qualifications:—(I) For scheduled 
castes and other baokward classe8:—(i) First Class Master’a 
degree or equivalent qualifications. (ii) First Clase in 
Bachelor's degree examination for candidates with qualifi- 
cations in Kngineering. Where no class or division given 
in an examination, e.g., at the Bachelor’s degree examina- 
tion in medicine 60 per cent. marks will be considered as 
equivalent to Ist Class/Division. (II) For scheduled 
tribes:—(i) Second Class Master’s degree or equivalent 
qualifications. (ii) Second Class in Bachelor's degree oxa- 
mination for candidates with qualifications in Engineering. 
Whore no Class or Division is given in an examination 
e.g., at the Bachelor’s degree examination in medicine 50 
per cent. marks will be considered as equivalent to 2nd 
Class/Division. Present rate of scholarship is £420 per 
annum in Oxford and Cambridge and £382 in other insti-' 
tutions in United Kingdom and $1,500 per annum in 
U.S.A. excluding cost of books and study tour, equipment 
allowance and sea passaye and tuition and examination 
fees which will be paid to institutions direct hy Govern- 
ment. Particulars and application forms from Secretary, 
Union Public Service Commission, Post Box No. 186, New 
Delhi. Requests for forms should be accompanied by self- 
addressed unstamped envelope at least of size 9“ x4" 
superscribed ‘‘Application forms for overseas scholarship”’. 
Closing date for receipt of ডি 23rd October 1954 
(6th November 1954 for applicants abroad). If required, 
candidates must appear for interview.

Weekly Weather and Crop Report of West Bengal 
Subdivisional reports on the condition of Weather, Crops, etc., for the week ending the 15th Saptember 1954. 


Summary.——During the week under report there was rainfall in all subdivisions of the State. The weather conditions were un- 
favourable in two subdivisions. Aman transplantation completed in most subdivisions. Aua harvesting continued. The condition 
of the standing crops was on the whole fair. Fodder was reported to be insufficient in twelve subdivisions and cattle-disease was 
reported from one subdivision. The wages of the labourer varied from annas fourteen to rupees two and annas eight during the week.
